Instead I can get Daddy some shiny buttons that will sparkle on his boring grey shirts and some sticky glittery sprinkles, tons and tons! But the sprinkles will fade away and the shirts will turn grey again I need a gift for Daddy that will forever stay! Mumma says I should get him a book but that will make Daddy snore I have an idea, how about I teach Daddy how to cook! Aprons on, we chopped and mixed and stirred, all this while dancing on his favourite song. In my little kitchen, we cooked up a storm made a mess, sang a song, and savored our dish while it was still warm. No moon, no shiny buttons, not a crown even a delicious gift is what Daddy got to make and he said, this was best gift he was ever given!

title: My best friend, Mossie
text: Corey is missing Dadu, her little terrier dog. Dadu was her best friend. Corey had rescued Dadu from the ditch. He had silky brown fur and big floppy ears. He would go everywhere with Corey and waits patiently outside her school everyday. She felt lonely now that Dadu is no longer with her. Papa was thinking maybe it is time to get another dog to keep Corey company. He sometimes missed having a dog too. The next day Corey and her dad went to the animal shelter to look for a puppy. They looked at each cage hoping to find a small puppy. Corey looked and looked but none seems to be right. Disappointed, Corey said "Let's come back another day, maybe we will find one then." On the way home they pass by a fair. Corey saw a small crowd gathering outside the ticket booth. The crowd was laughing at a poor puppy. The puppy had no fur on him and looked dirty. Kids were throwing stones at him! Corey quickly stepped next to the puppy to protect it. "Stop! Stop! This poor puppy is helpless, you silly people!!"she said angrily. She bundled the poor shivering puppy and took him home. Corey and her dad gave the puppy a shower. They could see that the puppy had an old collar which said "My best friend, Mossie" The puppy looked tired and hungry. Corey grabbed Dadu's old bowl and filled it up with some biscuits. The puppy was hesitant at first but soon started to eat Soon Mossie's fur started to grow. Corey tried to teach him to do tricks like Dadu but he ignores Corey and kept running to the old mango tree. He is constantly digging around the tree. Even Papa was annoyed. Corey felt frustrated with Mossie as he would constantly sit by the old mango tree until its time for dinner. He would return home looking sad everyday. One day Corey decided to check the mango tree. She walked around and did not notice much. Just as she was about to leave, Corey caught something shining under the exposed roots. She reach down and pull the shining object. It looks like an old photo frame. She dust the frame and saw a picture of a puppy and a little girl. The puppy looked like Mossie. The photo was inscribed 'Our beloved daughter Sara and her best friend - Mossie' Tears started to stream down her face. While she missed Dadu so much. Corey realised that Mossie must be missing his best friend Sara too. She held the old photo and remembered many pictures of her and Dadu. Corey took the old photo home and cleaned it. She placed the photo next to Mossie. When he saw the photo, Mossie gave a small whine and put his head on Corey's lap for the first time. Corey hugged Mossie. "I know you miss your friend Sara, like I miss Dadu' she said tearfully. 'I think Sara and Dadu would want us to be best friends' Corey said. From that day onward, Mossie would follow Corey everywhere. He played with Corey and even learnt to dance with her. Papa takes picture of Corey and Missy to start a new photo album. Corey became Mossie's new best friend.

title: Share a Home
text: Underneath the bridge across the dry river bed On a tiny ledge, mama pigeon found the perfect spot For their nest. Papa pigeon laid his first twig. By evening, they had spread a dozen twigs. That night, a terrible hoot-toot-toot shattered their sleep. Two bright pairs of eyes glared at them from across the ledge. ‘Owls!’ mama whispered in fear. ‘Owls, papa!’ ‘They will eat our chicks!’ papa’s voice shook. Meanwhile, dark shadows were climbing up the pillar. Closer and closer to their ledge they crept. One owl hooted and flew straight at the pigeons. They fluttered their wings and hopped on the ledge. With a flurry of wings, the owl whooshed over them. Three angry miaows filled the night and the shadows fell off the pillar. The pigeons craned their necks and looked down. Three angry cats looked hungrily up at them. When the pigeons looked back up, papa owl sat in front. ‘Go away,’ he said with an angry frown. ‘With your gutter-gutter-goo, you have brought the cats here. Leave our home!’ ‘We made our nest and we shall stay here,’ said mama pigeon bravely. ‘We have lived here two years without a cat,’ said papa owl. ‘You have been here a day and the cats are already up on the ledge. You sleep away happily but the cats will get our chicks.’ ‘We can’t see in the dark,’ said mama pigeon. ‘We couldn’t see the cats.’ ‘Be gone in the morning,’ scowled papa owl. He fluffed his wings and flew to his nest on the ledge. Mama and papa pigeon couldn’t sleep that night. It was too late to find a new home. Mama would lay her eggs any day. At last it was morning. Papa flew out for food. ‘You stay here,’ he said to mama. ‘Or the owls may throw our nest out.’ But the owls were fast asleep and the day was hot. Shadows crept slowly towards the pillar. The cats were back! Mama pigeon sat up. The cats slipped around the pillar. She watched their shadows along the ground. The cats climbed soft and quick up the pillar. Mama looked across at the owl’s nest. Two chicks were out, squabbling on the ledge. Mama and papa owl were sound asleep inside. Should she shout? Will the owls wake up? The cats were half way up the ledge. Mama felt heavy, she hadn’t laid her eggs yet. She was scared of the owls. She was terrified of the cats. But, she fluffed her wings and shouted ‘Gutter-goo.’ Off the ledge she flew, right around the pillar And straight at the cats. The cats snarled from the thin ledge. Mama flew so close she saw their fierce green eyes. The cats swiped at her. She flapped her wings And flew past with another loud gutter-goo. ‘Hoot-toot-toot.’ The owls were wide awake. Papa owl shooed the chicks back inside. Mama owl couldn’t see well in daylight. But, she could hear well and she came hooting at the cats. The cats miaowed and tumbled down and they ran. ‘Our chicks are alive because of you,’ said papa owl to the pigeons. ‘You saved us and we saved yours,’ said mama pigeon. ‘We were wrong to ask you to leave,’ said papa owl. ‘We shall keep watch during night,’ said mama owl. ‘And we shall keep watch during day!’ smiled papa pigeon. The owls and the pigeons shared the ledge Beneath the bridge, guarding each other Until all the chicks flew away from home.
author: Madhuri Y

title: A Tiny Seed: The Story of Wangari Maathai
text: In a village on the slopes of Mount Kenya in East Africa, a little girl worked in the fields with her mother. Her name was Wangari. Wangari loved being outside. In her family’s food garden she broke up the soil with her machete. She pressed tiny seeds into the warm earth. Her favourite time of day was just after sunset. When it got too dark to see the plants, Wangari knew it was time to go home. She would follow the narrow paths through the fields, crossing rivers as she went. Wangari was a clever child and couldn’t wait to go to school. But her mother and father wanted her to stay and help them at home. When she was seven years old, her big brother persuaded her parents to let her go to school. She liked to learn! Wangari learnt more and more with every book she read. She did so well at school that she was invited to study in the United States of America. Wangari was excited! She wanted to know more about the world. At the American university Wangari learnt many new things. She studied plants and how they grow. And she remembered how she grew: playing games with her brothers in the shade of the trees in the beautiful Kenyan forests. The more she learnt, the more she realised that she loved the people of Kenya. She wanted them to be happy and free. The more she learnt, the more she remembered her African home. When she had finished her studies, she returned to Kenya. But her country had changed. Huge farms stretched across the land. Women had no wood to make cooking fires. The people were poor and the children were hungry. Wangari knew what to do. She taught the women how to plant trees from seeds. The women sold the trees and used the money to look after their families. The women were very happy. Wangari had helped them to feel powerful and strong. As time passed, the new trees grew into forests, and the rivers started flowing again. Wangari’s message spread across Africa. Today, millions of trees have grown from Wangari’s seeds. Wangari had worked hard. People all over the world took notice, and gave her a famous prize. It is called the Nobel Peace Prize, and she was the first African woman ever to receive it. Wangari died in 2011, but we can think of her every time we see a beautiful tree.
author: Nicola  Rijsdijk

Look at those tiny feet. It’s not like us. Do you think it’s dangerous? Do you think it wants to eat us? Achoo! Achoo! Aargh! Eek! Run! It’s chasing us! Be careful. Come back. What is it? It’s a baby just like me!

title: DeeSy short stories 3 : Connecting the Dots...
text: When we boarded the plane, my son took out his puzzle book and said to me, “Papa, let’s play ‘connecting the dots’.” “No beta”, I tried to explain, “You know Papa builds biiiiiig buildings....for that he has to work on his laptop even during vacation. But I have a surprise for you. Today, I’ll show you the tallest building I have built – my award winning project.” As the plane took off I exclaimed, ““Look son, that one is the city tower and just next to it is my dream project. I know we have boarded an early flight and so it is pretty dark outside but if you see carefully, you can locate it.” Disappointed, he said, “Oh that small dot....because of THAT you missed my school project exhibition....I won first prize Papa....I wanted you to be there...”. Shocked by this reaction, I kept staring at him, simultaneously trying hard to remember what the school project was. When I looked back out of the window, the dot...er...the building had vanished as the plane had soared high. Aghast, I kept looking out and thinking. I realized that for past many months, I had kept feeling that I was missing something but couldn’t pinpoint it. But now at 36000 feet above the ground, it dawned on me. I didn’t want to miss the ‘sun’rise. Suddenly, the sky seemed clear of any clouds. “Beta”, I called softly, ‘Let’s do the connecting dots puzzle.” His face lit up. Grinning, he asked, “but what about your dot I mean your work?” Holding his hand tightly I replied, “That can wait.....I have to connect some more important dots first....”

title: Little Sock and the Tiny Creatures
text: It’s wash day for the Socks. OH NO! Little Sock falls out! “I have to get home,” says Little Sock. “Do you know the way home?” asks Little Sock. “No, but take this,” says the Robot. “Do you know the way home?” asks Little Sock. “No, but take this,” says the Mouse. “Do you know the way home?” asks Little Sock. “No, but take… OOPS!!! ” “Maybe the marble knows the way home,” says Little Sock. “It does!” says Little Sock. Little Sock is happy. MAKE YOUR OWN LITTLE SOCK Different socks have different personalities, so pick your favourite. YOU WILL NEED: • a sock • two buttons • a needle and thread • a grown-up to help INSTRUCTIONS Ask your grown-up to sew the buttons onto the sock.
author: Jon Keevy

title: Londi: The Dreaming Girl
text: Londi was a dreaming girl. Up in the sky, she didn’t see clouds. Instead Londi saw flying geese, jumping fish, and fluffy sheep running home. One afternoon, Gogo came outside, looking tired. “Londi, stop dreaming!” she said. “It’s time to go and fetch the water.” Londi stood up and smiled at her feet. “Let’s go, feet! You know the way there!” Londi started walking to the tap. She hopped over the rocks. She crept past Mama Neli’s house. She dashed down the path. The line at the tap was long. “Oh no!” Londi said to her feet. “We’ll have to wait. Let’s stay in line. No dreaming away!” Ooh! Londi thought. But what’s that shining over there? I wonder who lost their shoe? Did it belong to a girl like me? Or something else… And what’s that under there? Cheep! Cheep! And what’s that big shadow? Uh oh, it’s Gogo! “Londi, your bucket nearly rolled away!” “Sorry, Gogo. I dreamed too far, again.” They filled up the bucket together. Londi watched the big sun sink into the hills. “Come let’s go, my dreaming girl,” said Gogo. “Look, Gogo! There’s a pink pig in the sky!” “Oh Londi… It’s just a cloud,” Gogo sighed. Londi took Gogo’s hand and they walked home together happily.
author: Nathalie  Koenig

title: A Biryani  Suprise

title: Corie :The New Girl
text: The conversation going on at Sandy's home; "Oh Sandy! you are getting late to go to school." "Yes mom, I'm leaving,"said Sandy. Sandy leaves for her school in haste and forgets her football at home, on top of it she has her football match. She reaches her school and goes to her classroom. She finds a new girl sitting on her benc. The teacher enters the class and introduces the new girl as Corie. She looked very sad and it seemed like she was missing her old school. Many days passed but Corie did not mix up with anyone, stayed alone. Sandy felt sorry for Corie and wanted to help her to adjust to the new school. Sandy went up to her and asked her politely, "Why don't you want to play with us? and stay away?" Corie answered, in a rude voice," Firstly, I would like to know your name? " " My name is Sandy ", said Sandy. Corie still angry, questioned Sandy," Why have you come here?" Sandy felt hurt, but she quietly replied to Corie, " I just wanted to help you." Corie smiled and said thank you. " Sandy my problem is that I miss my old friends, old school and old teachers." "I am not able to mix up with any one." " I understand your problem as even I was new to this school last year." Sandy continued to say," I too had to face many difficulties in making new friends, but now I have hundreds of friends and all the teachers like me too." " I would like to share with you my past experience of how I mingled with every one." " Sure," said Corie, "I would love to hear it." Sandy began," When I entered the school for the first time, I felt very different as it was a new atmosphere, new surroundings and a new life for me. The teacher introduced me to the class on the first day. A girl even took me around the School to show me where the Library and the laboratories were. Still in the lunch break no one shared their food with me or even spoke to me." " I did not loose hope.I behaved as if I was their friend and shared all my stuff and helped them when ever they needed. Slowly impressed with my helpful nature they all became my friends." "Thank you Sandy for your great help. I will never forget our talk," said Corie " All the best Corie, I am always around if you need me," said Sandy After a few months, Corie was enjoying her new school and had made many friends. She remained close to Sandy. Moral Everything is possible if you are determined not to give up.
author: Mehek Shobhavat

title: The Elephant in the Room
text: One morning, Lindi found an elephant in her room. “Look!” she called. “There’s an elephant in my room!” “No there isn’t,” her mother called back. “Elephants don’t live in houses. Everybody knows that.” The elephant yawned. At breakfast, Lindi’s dad asked her to pass the milk. “I can’t,” said Lindi. “The elephant drank it all.” “There isn’t an elephant,” said her dad. “Elephants don’t live in the city. Everybody knows that.” The elephant burped. At school, the teacher grumbled, “What’s wrong with this chalkboard? It’s all wrinkly!” “That’s not the chalkboard. That’s my elephant!” said Lindi. “There are no elephants at school,” said the teacher. “Everybody knows that.” The elephant ate the teacher’s sandwiches. At break-time, the elephant followed Lindi to the playground. He knocked over the swings by mistake. “Go away!” said Lindi. “You’re not real and you shouldn’t be here! Everybody knows that!” The elephant drooped. He walked away, wiping his eyes with his trunk. After school, Lindi couldn’t see the elephant anywhere. “Elephant!” she called. “Where are you?” Lindi went home without him. She felt lonely. So she went outside, and sat on the steps, and waited. And waited. And waited. And then … She saw a trunk. And tusks. And ears. The elephant was coming down the road! She ran up and hugged him. “I’m sorry,” she said. “I didn’t mean it! I know you’re real. You’re my elephant.” The elephant lifted her up and put her on his back, and she rode down the street. She waved to her neighbours. “Hello, Mr Green! Hello, Mrs Green!” “Look at Lindi!” said Mr Green. “How did she get up there? Maybe she grew!” “Don’t be silly,” said Mrs Green. “Little girls don’t grow that high. Everybody knows that.” The elephant took Lindi to the lake, and she slid down his trunk like it was a slide. “Wheeeee!” she shrieked. They played all afternoon, laughing and splashing and spraying each other with water. That night, the elephant tucked her into bed. “Good night, Elephant,” said Lindi. “Thank you for a lovely day.” He patted her head, and curled up to sleep outside her window. “Elephants are the best friends in the world,” Lindi said to herself. “Nobody knows that, except for me and my elephant.”
author: Sam Wilson

title: Zanele Situ: My Story
text: I was born in summer, in a town called Matatiele in the Eastern Cape. Matatiele is near Lesotho where there are many mountains. In the winter they are covered with snow. My father was a builder and he moved from place to place to find work. We moved to Lesotho and that's where I started school. I was very happy. But when I was eleven years old, I grew tired and weak, and then I couldn't walk. My parents took me to the hospital. "I don't know. We must do some special tests to find out." "What is wrong, doctor?" I had to stay in hospital for three years. I was very tired and I slept many hours every day. After three years the doctors told me I would not be able to walk again. I was very sad because I love sports. "We think Zanele has got TB in her spine. It has attacked her nerves. I am very sorry, but she will be in a wheelchair for the rest of her life." I went to a special school in Umtata, and my teachers encouraged me. It was a very busy school, with lots of activities like sport and sewing. On weekends we had tasks to do. We had to clean our rooms, polish our shoes and clean our wheelchairs. "Zanele, how far can you throw this javelin?" I decided to keep trying, and never give up. If you have a disability, you can still do something you love. I love to see how far I can go, so I entered a competition. I won a bronze medal for shot putt, a silver medal for discus and a gold medal for javelin. I wanted to get better and better at my sports, so I trained very hard. "Well done, Zanele – you are really improving!" When I rested, I loved to sew and listen to gospel music. I entered more competitions and I got many medals and prizes. I started to dream about maybe competing in the Paralympics one day. The Paralympics are just like the Olympics, where the best athletes in the world compete for gold, silver and bronze medals. But in the Paralympics, the athletes are disabled in different ways, so they have to try even harder to train and win! Then I heard that I was going to Sydney in Australia, to take part in the 2000 Paralympics. At last we were in the plane, flying over the Indian Ocean! ﻿ I am so excited! But when I got there, I suddenly felt very scared of all the people watching me. I just wanted to go home again. Then, when I threw my javelin it landed far in front of everyone's. I broke the world record and I got a gold medal! I was the first African woman to win a gold medal in the Paralympics. I was so happy and very proud. My motto is: Keep going, follow your dreams and never give up. Even if something happens to make you sad or scared. That is what I teach my little girl, Azamazi. She is eight years old and she also loves to do athletics and gymnastics. I am still training and going to competitions, and in 2016 I hope to go to the Paralympics in Rio de Janeiro.

text: A few years ago, There lived a small girl named Candy. She lived in a beautiful city of Mumbai. She lived with her mother in a big house. title: Fly By Bye!
text: Wondering what to do with wordless stories? Wordless stories are wonderful because they contain infinite possibilities. Here are a few ideas for engaging with children using visual stories: - Explore the story in a leisurely manner. Draw attention to the details - the expressions of the characters, setting, colours, etc. The idea is for each child to build her own story. If the story is being shown to a group of children, you could ask each of them to contribute a sentence or two for each illustration. Take joy in exploring each illustration and build the story as you go along. - Use themes explored in the story to start a discussion. For instance, in this story, you could talk to children about our vast solar system or about insects, or simply ask them to think of what the fly was thinking in this story. - Encourage children to create 2-3 different stories using the same set of visuals. This will help push their imagination.

title: Riddle-me-ree! Who do you think I might be?
text: Search if you wish, but you’ll only agree That there’s no one quite like me! Across light years and the galaxy, And as far as telescopes can see. Riddle-me-ree! Who do you think I could be? Now have I got you interested? Okay, here are some clues to figure out who I am… 1. I’ve developed bulges on my midriff and just can't slim down. I put on tons of weight every year! And it’s not my fault! 2. Some rude people may call me ‘empty-headed'. I can’t even protest, because, in a way, they’re right! 3. But maybe not having anything up there, keeps me from getting hot-headed and irritated the way ‘full-headed’ people do! Yes, I’d definitely swear I’m cool-headed! 4. Unfortunately, I’ve got fire in my belly. Not in the sense that I’m very ambitious. But, quite literally, my insides are always hot and bothered. You know, like when you’re eaten something with too much chilli? Sometimes the rumblings inside get so bad that I let out these really fiery, toxic burps and belches. 5. But the damage can be pretty bad! In fact all this ‘indigestion’ inside me has been changing the way I look. My nose no longer looks the same and my chin is not in the place it used to be. I bet that’s never happened to you! 6. Now would you think I was an alien from Mars, if I told you that my complexion varies from green to blue? 7. I can be pretty thick-skinned too, but there are spots where I’m sensitive. I’m almost scared to tell you about it, because you might just hurt me there. 8. I might be terribly, terribly old, but I’m iron-hearted. 9. True, over the years, in all my non-stop traveling, I’ve become a bit flat-footed and (this is more embarrassing!) flat-headed, too. Go ahead, laugh at me. 10. Like many ancient people, I too have a few weak joints, but not too many. 11. And the next time YOU grumble about getting head lice or tick-bites from the pet dog, think of my poor plight. My skin is permanently crawling with creatures. Some pesky ones pierce me deep in my skin, I wonder what they’re looking for? Oops! I think I’ve already given away too much! I’m sure my precious ‘identitee’ is no longer a mystery! Anyway, turn the page over to find out if your guess is right! So did you guess that I am the Earth? Let’s look at some of the clues carefully. 1.Yes, it is true that I put on tons of weight every year - about 25 tons a year! But honestly, it’s really NOT my fault! The 25 tons is all fine dust from space that lands on earth. 2. Unfortunately the 'empty-headed' clue is true. That’s if you consider the North Pole as my head and the South Pole as my feet. So the Antarctic ice cap (my feet) in the south, actually rests on a huge land mass. But beneath the ice cap in the Arctic North (my head), is nothing. If global warming melts the ice caps entirely, not only will the sea-levels rise over 55 metres, but there’ll also be NO North Pole left...that's what I meant by an empty head! 3. Since the sun’s rays strike the poles at an angle, the heat is more spread out and that’s why the poles are much cooler than the equator. 4. This is also true. Beneath my cool crust is molten rock. The temperature at my core is as high as 4000 degrees Centigrade which keeps the rock in a molten (liquid) state. Sometimes the heat and gases formed below my crust erupt through gaps like in violent volcanoes or hot water geysers. 5. The continental plates all over the earth are in constant motion, floating on the molten rock below. They move about 2.5 cms each year! When dinosaurs roamed all over me 146 million years ago, India wasn’t a part of Asia but was sandwiched between Africa and Australia. I the last 40 million years, India has inched its way towards Asia and collided with the continent to form the great Himalayas! 6. Yes, I am rds water and rd land! Hence blue and green – that was an easy clue, wasn’t it?! 7. Talking about my skin, in most places of land-mass, my crust is about 70 km thick. But under the ocean floor, it can get as ‘thin’ as just 6 kms! 8. Did you know that while my mantle is made up of molten rock, my heart or core, is molten metal –iron and nickel. 9. Because of my constant spinning on the North-South axis, my poles have got flattened out a bit and my midriff, the equator, bulges out. If you poked a giant needle through me, in the north-south direction, it would measure 42 kms less than a needle poked through me in the east-west direction, at the equator. 10. Like I said, I’m really, really ancient --about 4600 million years old! So naturally, I do have some faulty joints --with the continental plates colliding against each other or tugging away from each other. The San Andreas Fault, that runs down the West coast of North America is a classic example of old age. Here the plates are pulling away from each other, causing sudden movements of the earth and hence earthquakes hit California every century or so. My fault lines also run through countries like Japan, New Zealand and some parts of N. India. 11. And finally, the next time you do get bitten by a mosquito, think about poor me. Millions of creatures crawling over me; swimming in my waters, driving over me, even drilling holes deep into me for oil, gold or diamonds! 1. Can you think of other planets that you can invent riddles for? Saturn is a good one to start with. Then you can make your own riddle book! 2. Can you think of other correct yet confusing clues that you can add to my list about myself, the great Earth? A version of this article first appeared in the Deccan Herald's School Edition.
author: Kavitha Mandana
