title: How a Cow made Broccoli
text: Once upon a time, there lived a cow in a barn. The cow was very sad. The horse has a favorite vegetable to eat, an orange carrot. The pig has a favorite vegetable to eat, a red apple. Even chickens have their favorite, yellow corn. The cow was sad that she did not have a vegetable to eat in her favorite color, green. She cried. Soon, she made a small puddle of tears. Immediately, a fairy cow mother appeared before her. The cow expressed her desire to have a green vegetable. The fairy cow mother said it was possible for her to grant cow's wish. The cow stopped crying and patiently listened to her. The fairy cow mother said, "You have to cut, chew and spit the entire grass field by evening. At night, I will do my magic and you will get your favorite green vegetable to eat." The cow started cutting, chewing and spitting the grass. She finished the task before evening. In her excitement, she chewed and spat fast. The fairy cow mother was not satisfied and asked her to do a better job as the grass was not chewed enough. The next day, the cow patiently cut, chewed and spat the grass. But she could not complete the entire field by evening. The fairy cow mother said, "I cannot do my magic on a half chewed field. Try again tomorrow." The cow thought hard. The next day, the cow met with her friends and explained the task to them. They agreed to share her task. In exchange, the cow agreed to share her favorite vegetable with them. Soon they started cutting, chewing and spitting the grass. They finished the entire field by evening. The grass was well chewed as well. The fairy cow mother was satisfied with their work. That night, the fairy cow mother did her magic. The next day, the grass field turned in to a green vegetable field. The green vegetable is none other than - Broccoli. She was now a very happy cow. Hard work, Dedication and Teamwork gave her and others a green vegetable - Broccoli.
author: Gomathy S

title: We are all made of star stuff!
text: "Can you quite imagine this? You are made of star stuff, Aman!" exclaimed Suchi, raising her head from the book she was reading. "Star stuff! Come on Didi, I am too old to believe in such fairy tales," Aman cried out. "Why, I am in Grade 7!" Jango, never wishing to be left out of any conversation, started wagging his tail enthusiastically. "Of course, I know what I am made of," Aman continued, somewhat indignantly. "I am - we all are - made of cells. The cells are the building blocks of life." "And what do you think these cells are made of?" asked Suchi. "Don't I know! A cell has different parts like cell membrane, cytoplasm, mitochondion. These cell parts, in turn, are made of substances like water, proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates...." Aman's voice trailed off. "And what are they made of - the water, the proteins and the rest?" asked Suchi, a teasing twinkle in her eyes. "I know...these are all different molecules. So they must be made of atoms!" "There you are. If you think deeply, everything around us is made of atoms - you, Jango, I, this football, this table, the chairs, the walls of this room....everything." "Yes, but then why did you say that we are made of star stuff. Atoms are not the same as stars, are they?" Aman challenged his sister. "Well, not exactly. But most of the atoms have come from some star or the other." "Including the ones in my body?" Aman sounded incredulous. "I would think that the atoms in my body come from the food I eat, the water I drink and the air I breathe," he said. "Isn't that true?" "Of course, it's true," said Suchi, patting Jango's wet muzzle. "Then, why do you say that the atoms come from stars?" Aman never accepts anything without a proper reason. "Well, that's a long story," said Suchi grandly. "Let me start at the very beginning, always the best place to start..." Aman and Jango were all ears. "Well, at the very beginning, there was nothing. No earth or other planets, no stars or galaxies. No universe. Then, about 14 billion years ago, scientists believe, there was a.... BIG BANG!" "A big bang? You mean a deafening sound?" asked Aman. "Oh no. Big Bang means quite something else. It means that a huge amount of energy - no one knows where this energy came from - just burst forth in one grand explosion. And thus began time and our universe. This baby universe had no matter in it. It was only energy, was very hot. And this energy spread out in all directions making our universe grow larger and larger..." "...and then," continued Suchi, "some of the energy in this expanding baby universe started getting converted to matter." "Stop! I don't understand this. How can energy be converted to matter?" "To be honest, Aman, I don't understand it myself," admitted Suchi, somewhat sheepishly. "But the great scientist Einstein famously deduced that energy and matter, under special conditions, can convert into each other, and for now we just have to accept this to get along with our story." "So, getting back to our story, some of the energy got converted to matter," Suchi continued. "And, from this matter were born the the first atoms of the universe, the lightest atoms of all - the Hydrogen atoms. And also some atoms of the next two light elements, Helium and Lithium. All these happened in the first three minutes after the Big Bang, in the baby universe, which was then incredibly hot. And, these baby atoms too, just like the energy, started drifting away in all directions, and...." Suchi paused for effect. "And then?" " Then the creation of atoms suddenly stopped." "But why?" This seemed such o an anti-climax to Aman. "Well, the initial atoms had got created from the collision of matter. But for that you need a very hot and dense universe. As the universe spread out, its heat and matter spread out too. So, the universe got less dense and less hot and atoms could no longer get created." "Then?" "Then, a lucky thing happened for our universe. The atoms, which were spreading out, started clumping together under the gravitational force of attraction. So, in place of a smooth universe where matter was evenly spread out, there was a clumpy universe - an universe with clumps of atoms at different places." "Huh! What is so lucky about this?" "Well, you would know once I tell you what these clumps became. Guess what they became?" "What?" asked Aman, curiosity spreading uncontrollably in him. "Stars!" exclaimed Suchi. "Yes Aman, each clump of atoms pushed down at the centre and this made the inside of the clump very hot, giving birth to a star. The baby universe became dotted with billions of such stars." " Including our sun?" asked Aman. This was sounding more and more exciting. "No, the sun, our very own star, got born much later. We are talking here about the very early stars - the first generation of stars - of the universe." "OK, so what happened to these early stars?" "Well, with the weight of so many atoms pushing at their centres, the stars got really hot, so hot that the light hydrogen atoms inside the stars started joining up and formed heavier atoms of helium. This in turn produced more heat making the stars shine brightly." "And each star born would now shine for billions of years," continued Suchi, eager to share all she knew. "A small star would shine till all the hydrogen atoms in its center gets converted to helium. A large star, hotter because of more atoms pushing at its centre, would shine longer. A large star would be like a giant cauldron inside which the "cooking" of heavy atoms from lighter ones would go a l-o-n-g way - from hydrogen to helium, from helium to carbon, to nitrogen, to oxygen and so on...all the way till atoms as heavy as iron. But making atoms heavier than iron would need a HUGE amount of heat and even a large star would never get hot enough for that to happen. Inside a large star too, the cooking would stop one day - it would stop at the making of iron." "Then?" No stopping Aman now. "Then the star would die and the atoms inside would drift out into space. A small star would fade away slowly while a large star would die in one huge explosion and, guess what, more atoms would be formed in this explosion. These would be atoms heavier than iron - atoms like silver and gold. All these new atoms, along with the atoms from the exploding star, would rush out into space." "And finally, the most magical part", Suchi's voice trembled with ecstasy. "These atoms from the dead stars, the stardust that they are now, would spread out in space. With time, each drifting atom would find itself caught in some swirling cloud of gases and dust in space. The swirling cloud would, in its own time, become a new star, and there would be planets surrounding it, the planets too born out of the same swirling mass as the star. So just imagine this - an atom from an old star would eventually end up in a new home - a new star or maybe a planet or eve an asteroid!" "So are you trying to say that our solar system - the sun and all its planets - was born from the atoms that had rushed out from some older stars?" Aman needed his clarification here and now. "Exactly. The sun and all its planets, including our earth, were made from "recycled" atoms - atoms recycled from old stars." " "Recycling of atoms - why this seems like magic!" "Yes, and on earth something else happened that was even more magical - the blossoming of life. Over millions of years, many of these recycled atoms came together to form different complex molecules like proteins and nucleic acids. These molecules in turn teamed up to form the building block of life - the cell. And the first living organism, the simple single-celled organisms, were born. And over many more millions of years -" "Let me try to complete this," Aman was so excited. "Over many more millions of years, the single-celled organisms evolved into all the complex plants and animals that we see around us, right?" "Right. And everything happened from atoms that came from old stars. So now do you see why I said that we are all made of star stuff?" asked Suchi eagerly. "Yes!" Aman cried out, his eyes gleaming. "Well, this gives a rather curious feeling, doesn't it," he continued breathlessly "..to know that I am twelve years old but the atoms that make me up are billions of years old and come from the stars?" "Yes, it DOES give a curious feeling," Such agreed. "And humbleness too, to know that we are all living on borrowed atoms, to know that a carbon atom in my body wasn't always mine. I t came to the earth from some star and here on earth it belonged before me to some tree or animal, to some carbon-di-oxide molecule even earlier or maybe to a dinosaur once upon a time. The atoms will not belong to my body forever either..." "...I too will pass on my atoms to something else," Suchi concluded on a dreamy philosophical note, gazing out of the window as if connecting with the universe. Aman wondered why knowing all these should make one feel humble. All he knew was that it felt wonderful to be alive, to know that he was made of star stuff, to know that he was young yet ancient, to know that he was small yet connected to this vast universe, and above everything else, to know that he had such a wise and kind sister. Then Suchi read out in her dreamy voice: " Out of the cradle onto dry land here it is standing: atoms with consciousness; matter with curiosity. Stands at the sea, wonders at wondering: I a universe of atoms an atom in the universe." Aman, this is the great scientist Richard Feynman. You should read him some day, when you grow up." Aman knew that he would.
author: Tithiparna Sengupta

title: Dino my true friend!!
text: Once there was a very pretty butterfly. One day she was playing with all her friends in the garden. There lived a deadly spider nearby. The Spider trapped many insects like lady bugs, bees etc. by spinning web. One day spider planned to trap that butterfly. Other insects playing with her, warned her about spider coming. Butterfly flew away to her friend Dino, who lived near a river. Hearing about his friend butterfly and others in trouble. The Dino got ready immediately. The Dino followed the butterfly in his boat... The Dino roared and roared fast and reached the destination following the butterfly. Everyone was delighted to see the butterfly friend Dino. They all welcomed Dino by dancing and fluttering their wings. The honeybee flew away to warn spider about dinosaur coming. Hearing about butterfly friend Dino coming, all spiders got scared. All spiders started running away and left the place forever. Butterflies and other insects thanked Dino. Thank you Dino! You are our True friend! Then they all lived happily thereafter... Moral: A friend in need is a friend indeed.
author: Chaitanya Verma
illustrator: Bulbul Sharma; Herminder Ohri; Lavanya  Naidu; Sangeetha Kadur; Sou  Kimsan; Sweta  Roy Choudhury

title: Tara's Treetop Adventure
text: "Tara, it's nearly bedtime! Where were you?" Ma asked angrily. Tara replied, "You know that tall tree just outside our school? I climbed it. It’s sooooo high, it touches the sky! " "When I looked down, there were cushions of clouds. When I looked up, there were laughing leaves." "Leaves don’t laugh, I thought! Then I saw these giggling squirrels hiding among the leaves." "The big squirrels gave me lots of nuts to eat. The little squirrels played hide-and-seek in my hair!" "We played for hours and hours. Until I remembered that I had to come home. But I didn’t know how to climb down!" "So the squirrels started shouting for help. You should have heard them! Kee! KEE! KEEE! " "Luckily, there was a purple plane flying in the sky. Can you believe the pilot heard their squeaks?" "She swooped down, picked me up, and flew me back home." "And that is why I’m late, Ma." "Tara! Stop making things up," Ma said. “Kee! KEE! KEEE!”
author: Sangeeta Velegar

title: Fly in Space
text: Droso was a newborn fruit fly. He opened his wings for the first time, and flapped them up and down very fast. 220 times in one second, to be exact! “WOW I’m flying!” he shouted. Droso looked down at the rotten banana on which he was born. What a view! His sister Phila was finding her wings too. “How high can I fly?” Droso wondered, and flew a little higher. Phila liked going up too, but not as much as she liked to pose. One leg here, two legs there, and the other three over there. She posed in different ways. “I want to be a model,” she announced. The next day, Droso flew to the top of the fruit basket. The day after that, he made it to the top of the refrigerator. Higher and higher Droso flew, until... he hit the ceiling. He couldn't fly any higher! You see, Droso and Phila were inside Richa's house. Richa was an astronaut. In two weeks, Richa would sit in a rocket and shoot up into space. She had been so busy planning her trip, that she hadn’t noticed her bananas rotting. Richa the astronaut was not so different from Droso the fruit fly. Like Droso, Richa also wanted to go to higher places. Flying to space had always been Richa’s dream. And it was about to come true. How exciting! All Richa thought about was space! Space begins a hundred kilometres or so above the Earth. It has no air to breathe and no ground to stand on. There is no up and no down! So in space, nothing falls down. Astronauts like Richa just float around. What a strange place! Richa often wondered, “How would birds fly in a place like space where there is no up and no down?” There was only one way to find out. “I’ll take a bird with me to space!” she decided. B ut which one? A pigeon, perhaps? No, it has too many feathers. A crow? Too big. A sparrow? Too noisy. Also, it eats too much. Richa thought long and hard until she got very hungry. She reached for the fruit basket. “Yuck, rotten fruits!” And that’s when she saw Droso and Phila buzzing around. “Fruit flies!” cried out Richa. “They are perfect for space!” She put Droso and Phila in a jar. She also put some rotten banana goop in the jar for them to eat. Then, she threw out the rotting banana peel and made herself a sandwich. Today is the day that Richa flies into space. Look at what is in her hand! Phila is the first ever space model. Astronauts take many photos of her eating and resting in space. And Droso? Richa and her scientist friends closely watch how he uses his wings in space. Look! Droso the fruit fly is finally going high, high, high... higher than any other fly in the world. Animals in Space Drosophila is the scientific name of the fruit fly. The fruit fly was the first animal to travel to space. This happened in 1947. Did you know that fruit flies and humans have some things in common? They can remember things just like us, and they even fall sick like we do! Which is why scientists love to study fruit flies in space. After all, it's easier to send flies to space than humans! And this is why fruit flies are known as model organisms. Do you know who else has been to space? Albert the monkey, Laika the dog, Ham the chimpanzee, and Arabella the spider!
author: Aashima  Freidog

title: The Evil Forest
text: There were many snakes near Nyare village. The biggest was Lego. It swallowed whole goats and sheep. One day, Apiyo, Ajoh and Atieno went to fetch firewood. Grandmother said, “Be careful of Lego. Fetch firewood only.” Ajoh did not pay attention. The girls packed some food, ropes and a sharp machete. Apiyo said, “I am the oldest, so you must listen to me.” They talked and laughed as they walked. Suddenly, Apiyo said, “Be quiet. We are near where Lego lives.” Atieno said, “These are Lego's golden teeth. Let us take them.” Apiyo reminded them, “Remember what grandmother told us. We must fetch only firewood.” “Grandmother does not know anything. I will take the golden teeth,” said Ajoh. Apiyo and Atieno were not happy. Lego came looking for his golden teeth. They were not there. Lego thought, “The one who took my teeth will know who I am!” On their way home, the girls heard, “Hzzzzzzzz!” Lego was there with his mouth wide open, ready to swallow. Lego asked, “Who took my golden teeth?” No one answered. Lego said, “The innocent girl will sing well. The thief will not.” Apiyo sang: It's not me! It's not me who took the teeth! The one who took is near! Atieno also sang well. Ajoh sang badly and the words did not come out. Lego shouted, “Sing like the others.” Lego knew that Ajoh took his golden teeth. Lego swallowed Ajoh. Her sisters ran home to say what happened. The girls' grandmother said sadly, “I warned them, if only Ajoh had listened.”
author: Joseph Sanchez Nadimo

title: Going to the City
text: The bus stop in my town was full of people. The bus conductor shouted, “Going to the city! Leaving now!” People pushed to get on the bus. Women with children sat down. The journey was going to be long. I sat at the window, next to a man. I thought, “I am going to the big city! I will miss home.” There were many hawkers selling their goods. Some passengers bought things. I had no money to buy anything. Suddenly, the driver blew the horn. It was time to leave. The hawkers pushed each other to get out of the bus. “When will I return?” I asked myself. It was hot inside the bus. I closed my eyes. I thought about my mother and brother at home. Gradually, I fell fast asleep. Many hours later, I woke up. Almost everyone had left. It was time to find my uncle’s house.
author: Lesley  Koyi; Ursula Nafula

title: The Pottering Pig
text: Lalita is the pet pig of Mini Singh the potter. Mini loves his pig and lets her do whatever she wants to do! Now pigs do all sorts of pig-headed things. And that's what Lalita does as well. Harrumph! Harrumph! Lalita pushes stones all over the neat paths. Harrr harrr harrr! She snorts and digs up the garden. Grrrrr grrrrr grrrrr! Lalita tears up all the newspapers. Even the one Mini hasn’t read yet. Phurrrr phurrrr phurrrr! She blows bubbles into her water bowl and spills water all over! Chapaak! Jhapaak! Lalita chews up all the lilies and scares the fish in the pond. “Lock her up,” says Mini's Aai. “Tie her up,” says Mini's Tai. “Never ever!” says Mini. “She never ever messes with my pots and jugs.” One day, Mini comes to work bright and early. He whistles happily to Lalita. “ Harrumph, harrumph,” she grunts back. His happiness vanishes when he sees… Broken bowls, s hattered jugs Cracked cups, s mashed teapots Everywhere! Mini gets angrier and angrier and angrier! He ties Lalita up under the shady bougainvillea. Lalita doesn’t understand why she is tied up. She whines and whimpers. She cries and sighs. But Mini is too angry to listen. All day Mini works angrily and Lalita stays tied up. Then, Mini hears a noise. It isn’t a harrumph, it isn’t a harrr. It isn’t a grrr, i t isn’t a phurrr. And it isn’t a chapaak or a jhapaak! MEOOWWW! CRASH! MEOOOWWW! THUNK! It is a large, orange cat! It is the large, orange cat that knocked over the pots and jugs. Mini unties Lalita. “ Harrumph, harrumph,” she grunts. Lalita chases the cat. Round and round, and right out of the pottery! Then Lalita goes right back to doing pig-headed things. Because that’s what pigs do.
author: Rohit  Kulkarni

title: Rani's first day at school
text: Today is my first day at school. Mom is holding my hand and is walking with me "I have grown up now", I say. "Let's go" Mom is holding my hand tightly. There are a lot of children near school. Some come by bus. Some by car. Some come by rickshaw. Some by cycle, and some children walk like me. We reach the gate. Mom leaves my hand. There are a lot of unknown faces around me. I take a step. I take the second step. I turn back. As I go ahead, mom becomes smaller. I don't think I have grown up. I hold her hand and say, "Don't go." Everyone is already inside. Only I am outside. Teacher did comes outside. She looks at me and smiles. I also smile. Mom says,"Rani, when you come back, I'll meet you here." I leave her hand. She waves at me. I run and go inside. Mom will meet me here when school ends.
author: Paridhi Gupta

title: My house
text: This is my house. I live here with my family. We remove our shoes here. We wash our hands and face here. I hang my clothes on the hook. My grandfather keeps his stick in the corner. We keep our mats there as well. Father keeps motorcycle outside. But his helmet is kept on top of the almirah. My mother and grandmother keep their saarees in the box. Tasty food is cooked in the kitchen. When it is cold, we take out the blankets. When it is hot, we switch on a fan. When we have special guests coming, we take out the chairs. Please come to my home, and meet me. come quickly.
author: Paridhi Gupta

title: GOLU THE ELEPHANT
text: GOLU THE ELEPHANT Golu was a baby elephant. He loved to eat and sleep, and eat again. His mother often told him, ‘Golu, go and walk and play. Go to the river and bathe!’ But Golu was very lazy. One day, Golu tried to get up. He couldn’t move his legs! He couldn’t move his trunk! Suddenly he felt his mother’s gentle touch. Golu woke up. It was only a dream!
author: usha aswath iyer
illustrator: Ajit Narayan; Archana Sreenivasan; Greystroke; Herminder Ohri

title: The monk's new shawl
text: One day a monk came to see the great Budha. The monk wanted a new shawl. The Buddha asked him, "What happened to your old shawl?" "It had become very old and thin. I am using it as a bedsheet," replied the monk. The Budha asked again, "What happened to the old bedsheet?" "The bedsheet was torn, so I cut it up and made a pillow cover out of it," replied the monk. The Budha asked again, "What happened to the old pillow cover?" "The pillow cover had a big hole in it so I made a doormat out of it," replied the monk. The Budha was not satisfied. He asked again, "What happened to the old doormat?" " "The old doormat had broken down in to threads. I made a cotton wick out of them for my lamp," replied the monk. The Buddha smiled on hearing this and gave the monk a new shawl. Make your own cloth ball 1. Choose old clothes at home that you can reuse. You will need to cut out two pentagon shapes and five petal shapes like this. 2. Hand-stitch the pieces. Or get an adult to machine stitch them. Leave a small hole in one pentagon. 3. Turn it inside out. 4. Insert a strong balloon and blow it. 5. Twist the mouth of the balloon, tie a knot, and push it in through the button-hole. 6. Yippee! Your colourful cloth ball is ready. Fun with threads! Here is an easy way to have hours of fun with small bits of thread or wool. 1. Find an empty matchbox. 2. Thread a length of wool about 70cm long diagonally through the box. 3. Thread a length of wool in another colour through the other diagonal. Tie the ends together. 4. Ask a friend to hold both the ends of the wool. And you can slide the box gently across. Surprise, surprise! The wool seems to change colour as it comes out of the box! Recycle! Reuse! Reduce! We buy, use and throw away things without thinking much about them. We buy much more than we need and produce tonnes of junk that become mountains of garbage. But has it always been like this? Have we always been wasteful? No! Earlier people were more careful. Each object was used many times. This story is 2,500 years old, set in the times when the great sage and teacher Gautama Buddha lived. It shows how we can reduce waste by reusing things. It has many lessons for us.
author: Alok Kuchlous

title: Amogh's picnic
text: It was a warm sunny day, perfect for spending time outdoors! "Amma! I am bored at home", said Amogh. His mother said that they could go out for a picnic in the park nearby. They sat down and made a list of things to eat for the picnic. And they took an auto, went to the market to buy the groceries. At the vegetable shop, Amogh asked "Amma, can we buy some red juicy carrots? What are those yellow and orange vegetables called?" Amma smiled, " The yellow vegetables are capsicums and there are yellow red or green capsicums. A pumpkin is orange in color" Amogh's eyes became big like saucers seeing the bright, green watermelons; "Amma, can we buy some fruits for the picnic? " They bought a big watermelon and some ripe mangoes from the fruit seller. "Amma there are so many types of rice and dals. Should we buy some? ". Amma then bought some atta, rice, and dal. After coming back home, Amogh helped Amma to put away some of the vegetables and groceries. She then started mixing the atta with water to make the dough. "Amma can I help roll some dough for you? " Amma and Amogh rolled out the dough and made soft, puffy rotis. They then dabbed some ghee on the rotis and packed them in a round tiffin box. They made a mixed vegetable curry with pumpkin, carrots, capsicums, onions, and tomatoes. "Amma the curry smells yummy! Could I try some now please?", asked Amogh. Amma cooled down some of the hot curry and gave it to him. As they started cutting the watermelon, Amogh bit into a large juicy slice. The water from the melon dripped out of the corners of his mouth. The melon had lots of black seeds which he carefully removed from his mouth. Now that all of the food was ready and packed, both of them went to the park to play. Amogh had a great time on the swing, at the slide, and on the see-saw. After a while, they spread out the food that was packed and had a scrumptious meal together. "That tasted really great Amma!", said Amogh as he hugged his mother. He thanked her for the wonderful day! Dear Children, It is always better to eat fresh food which is colorful, healthy and tasty. Foods like idli-chutney, rajma rice, dosa, upma, poha, and biryani make great meals. This along with lots of fruits, nuts, dry fruits and water would make you healthy and strong. Love, momSAURUS
author: momSAURUS
illustrator: Jisha Unnikrishnan; Kavya Seshachar; Niloufer Wadia; Nina Sabnani; Priya Kuriyan; Rijuta Ghate; Santosh Pujari

title: Punishment
text: One day, mama bought different fruits. “When can we have some fruit?” we asked. “We will eat the fruit tonight,” said mama. My brother Rahim is greedy. He tasted all the fruit. He ate a lot of it. “Look at what Rahim did!” shouted my little brother. “Rahim is naughty and selfish,” I said. Mama was angry with Rahim. We were also angry with Rahim. But Rahim was not sorry. “Are you going to punish Rahim?” asked little brother. “Rahim, you will be sorry soon,” warned mama. Rahim started feeling unwell. “My stomach is painful,” whispered Rahim. Mama knew why Rahim was sick. “The fruit is punishing Rahim,” she thought. Later, Rahim said sorry to us. “I will never be so greedy again,” he promised. We believed him.
author: Adelheid Marie Bwire

title: Sheela wants to travel the world!
text: Sheela was a very curious sparrow. She wanted to explore the world. Her mother was scared because she thought that Sheela might get hurt while exploring the world. When Sheela asked, "Mamma, can I explore the world?" Mamma said, "No Sheela." Next day, Sheela went to school. There she met Sangam the snake. Sheela and Sangam were best friends. Sheela said, "Sangam, I want to explore the world, can you help me convince my mother?" Sangam the snake looked worried. He said, "Sheela, you should listen to your mother. If she says no, then you must not go." Sheela said, "But Sangam, I want to explore the world. I wat to travel to Africa and America and China and Australia." Sheela was very sad even in art class! Art was Sheela's favourite subject. Sangam also felt sad looking at her. Sheela drew a picture of the world and said, "See Sangam I want to go everywhere. I don't want to stay in Madandas Jungle and go to Madandas school everyday." ﻿That night, Sheela's mother saw Sheela very sad. She said, "Come, Sheela. I will tell you how to travel the world without getting hurt or going out of the safe jungle." Next day, Sheela and Sangam wrote a story about a sparrow and her best friend, snake who travelled the world. When Sheela was writing the story, she felt like she was that little sparrow and she was seeing Africa and America and China. She felt like she was travelling the world! ﻿ After Sheela wrote her story, she and Sangam hugged each other. "Yay!", said Sheela, "We finally travelled the world like mamma said."
author: Sanjana

title: SHAKTI AND SIMBA
text: SHAKTI AND SIMBA He jumped and licked Shakti’s nose at the very first meeting. His bright eyes, lolling tongue and soft golden coat made them name him Simba- the lion. Of course, right now he was only a lion cub- barely forty days old. Simba had his priorities right-right from the start. Shakti was his sibling, his friend, his playmate. Daddy was the disciplinarian, but with a soft heart underneath all that gruffness. Mummy was his walking talking kitchen- she supplied him with his food and clean water. She also slipped in a titbit when nobody was looking. Simba felt his friend and competitor was Shakti. He ran away with Shakti’s socks when he had to get ready for school. Did Simba feel lonely at being left alone for six hours? He would have loved to eat off Shakti’s plate but both Mummy and Daddy growled when he tried to sidle his way to the dining table from under Shakti’s chair. Poor Simba put his tail down and quietly subsided. At night he wanted to sleep with Shakti. He loved the cosy bed, the warm bed cover and Shakti’s presence. But parents were hard to convince and all Shakti’s entreaties and Simba’s mournful looks could not change their minds. The first few nights, all had sleepless slumber for Simba’s howls, barks, whimpers kept them awake. Both Mummy and Daddy knew that if they once allowed Simba into Shakti’s bedroom, there would be no separating them. About a week later, Mummy had a brilliant idea. She prepared a big box, placed one of her soft saris inside it and rolled up Shakti’s old T-shirt as a pillow. She coaxed Simba into the box. Simba sniffed suspiciously at first. What was this strange box and where had it come from? Was it a ploy to shift him somewhere else? But the warm, friendly, familiar smells soon lulled him to deep sleep. He had his beloved Shakti under his head and Mummy had wrapped all her warmth and affection in this old sari. Finally the family had a good night’s sleep!
author: usha aswath iyer

title: Little Hands
text: We can do many useful things with our hands. What are our hands for? Hands are for holding our elders when we go out. Drawing and painting with lots of colors, creating magic on paper all with our hands. While at home or at school, to hold a book, use a ruler and punch some papers all with our hands. Scrub and wash our hands carefully before and after a meal. Clean and tidy that is our home. P ut away toys and books in the right place. Save and protect the earth. Plant some seeds and water them every day. Warmth and love from our families.To give and get; hugs and cuddles. Folded palms with a smile on our face, to greet everyone. Dear Parents, Little children when unable to express themselves resort to using their hands. They have not yet developed complete control over their limbs; use their hands instead of words. But by continuously reminding them especially when they are calm, they would be able to restrain themselves. Do not forget to tell them with a smile - "Hands are not for hitting and pinching." Love, momSAURUS
author: momSAURUS
illustrator: Anupama Ajinkya Apte; Jagdish Joshi; Ouk  Ratha; P.G. Dinesh; Priyankar Gupta; Rohit Karandadi; Ruchi Shah; Sahitya Rani; Suvidha Mistry; Tanvi Bhat

title: The Thirsty Fox
text: One day a thirsty fox searching for water reached to the pond in the jungle. To it's dismay the pond was dry. The fox saw a crane by the pond. It had a vessel filled with water. The fox jumped in joy and ran toward the vessel. But on reaching near the vessel the fox was disappointed. The vessel had a long and tapering neck. It was imposibble for a fox to drink the water. The frustrated fox called for help. On hearing fox's cry the crane came to the fox's help. It asked the fox " what happened dear friend?" The fox replied " save me! I am thirsty." The crane flew to the nearest tree and tear a leaf from the tree. The crane dipped the leaf into the vessel. Then took the leaf to the fox. The water dripping from the leaf reached the fox mouth. The fox tasted the water and opened it's eye. Again, the craned dipped the leaf in the vessel and drew it to the fox's mouth. Gradually the fox came back to it's senses and stood on it's feet. It thanked the crane and walked into the jungle.
author: uma sharma
illustrator: Gracie; Gracie; Greystroke; Sugrib Kumar Juanga

title: Fati and the Soup Pot
text: Fati was a little girl who ran like the wind, who loved to laugh and who always tried hard to do as she was told. Today was Sports Day at school. Fati played football and ran in three races. After school, she walked home with her good friend Hawa. Hawa said, “Fati, you are a fast runner!” Fati arrived home and found her mother in the kitchen. She said, “Mother, good evening.” Fati’s mother replied, “Fine evening. How are you?” Fati said, “We had Sports Day at school, and I ran very fast. I am hot, tired and very hungry.” Mother laughed and said, “My dear little Fati, you were born with fast legs! I will make okro soup and dinner will be ready soon.” Mother put some palm oil in a big cooking pot and placed it on the fire. When the oil was hot, she added onions and garlic and stirred them until they were soft. She then put in pepper, tomatoes, added some water and six pieces of steamed cow meat. Mother said, “Fati, please help me to stir the soup.” Fati said,”Yes, Mother.” Fati stirred the soup once. She said, “This soup smells delicious.” Fati stirred the soup twice. She said, “This soup smells very delicious.” Fati stirred the soup three times. She said, “This soup smells very, very delicious.” Then, Fati looked at her mother. Mother was not looking her way. She was cutting green leaves for the soup. Fati took one piece of meat from the pot and ate it. Fati said, “Mmm...” Again, Fati looked at her mother. Her mother was not looking her way. She was cutting garden eggs for the soup. Fati quickly took a second piece of meat from the pot and ate it. Fati said, “Mmm... Mmm...” Once more, Fati looked at her mother. Her mother was not looking her way. She was cutting okro for the soup. Fati very quickly took a third piece of meat from the pot and ate that too! Fati said, “Mmm... Mmm... Mmm...” Soon, Mother came to the fire with the green leaves, garden eggs and okro. Fati was still holding the big wooden spoon. Mother smiled and said, “Thank you for helping to stir the soup Fati.” Fati did not know what to say. Mother put the green leaves, garden eggs and okro in the soup and took the spoon from Fati. She started to stir the soup. Mother looked into the pot. She could see the soup bubbling on the hot fire. Mother looked for the six pieces of meat in the pot. “One...two...three...,” said Mother. Mother saw three pieces of meat and no more. Mother said nothing. Fati said nothing. When Mother served the soup, Fati did not get any meat. Fati said, “Mother, I am sorry. I will not do that again.” And she never did. And that was the end of that.
author: Osu Library Fund

title: Mr. Bear's Camera
text: Mr. Bear left his lodge to go for sightseeing. He was joined by his friend the grasshopper. Mr. Bear took his camera with him. The grasshopper was astonished to see the camera. " what is this?" asked the grasshopper " It is a camera" replied Mr. Bear " What is a camera?" asked the grasshopper " Camera is device through which we can click still pictures. This process of clicking still pictures is called photography and still pictures are called photograph," said Mr. Bear " How do you click pictures from this camera," asked the grasshopper " The photos are clicked with this round button. To click a picture the camera needs photo reel. The camera reel is fitted at back of the camera. Every photo we click get imprinted on the reel," said Mr. Bear Mr. Bear and the grasshopper walked towards the river bank. On the way to the river Mr. Bear clicked few photos. He clicked the photo of the butterfly, trees and flowers. It was spring and path to the river bank was filled with flowers. Mr. Bear explained the process of photography to the grasshopper. The grasshopper was very excited to see the photography of Mr. Bear. He asked Mr. Bear if he could lend his camera and click few pictures. Mr. Bear was more than glad to see the grasshopper's excitement for photography. He explained the process and showed the button to click the photograph. The grasshopper took the camera and as directed by Mr. Bear focused on a flower. He stood with the camera for few seconds then pressed the button. A click sound followed after pressing of the button. The grasshopper was delighted to click the photograph. The river bank was full of tourists and boating expedition group. Mr. bear and the grasshopper reached the river bank and decided to go for a boating expedition. They choose a boat of Mr. Fox and immediately got on the boat. Mr. Bear clicked few photos of the river bank and the tourists. The expedition was to go to the other side of the river to sight the great tree. The expedition started and the Mr. Bear and the grasshopper could feel the calm of the water. The weather was bright and sunny and river water was still. The expedition was going very well. Mr. Bear and the grasshopper was very excited to be on the expedition. After few minutes the expedition could sight the great tree. " Grasshopper my friend can you sight the great tree," asked Mr. Bear " Oh dear! it is really a huge tree," said the grasshopper " The view is fantastic. I must click some photograph," said Mr. Bear and started clicking the photos The grasshopper laughed in delight and asked Mr. Beaver if he can click few pictures too. Mr. Bear gladly lend him his camera and they both clicked photographs in turns. Mr. Bear and the grasshopper returned from the expedition. At home Mr. Bear explained to the grasshopper the process to develop photographs from the reel which is called a negative. The grasshopper was glad that he learned a new thing and thanked Mr. Bear for such a wonderful day.
author: uma sharma

title: Sunena Devi - Story of a Madhubani Artist
text: India has its fair share of women achievers in various fields like banking, science and others. There is a different league of women achievers too. They may not have the privilege of education, but they still managed to make a mark in the world by sheer talent and determination. Meet Sunena Devi, an award winning Madhubani Artist from Bihar Sunena Devi was born on 28th July, 1951 in the Duhabi village on the Indo-Nepal border. It falls in the ancient Mithila region and the people across border are bound by marriage and blood. Young Sunena was married in 1966, at an early age to Shri Ganesh Jha of village Jitwarpur, located in Madhubani District of Bihar. Though, she did not get a chance to attend school, marriage gave her a chance to learn the art form of Madhubani. Initially she started to assist her mother-in-law in making the paintings, but when the young bride showed talent and understanding of the art form, her in-laws and husband encouraged her to learn it further. Sunena learnt about the different styles of Madhubani art like Bharni, Kachchi, Tantrik, Godna and Kohbar. ﻿ ﻿ When her children were barely 3 - 4 years of age, Sunena Devi lost her husband. But she did not lose hope and made paintings along with the rest of her family, to earn a living. In the initial days, she depended on traders who took the paintings to various places for selling but the income was not steady. The traders took the paintings and returned after months, sometimes with little or no payment. Soon she joined a center where other Madhubani Artists like herself gathered and created artwork for commercial purpose. This ensured her a monthly income, enough to run her household. Everyday she traveled from Jitwapur to Madhubani to paint. On seeing her talent, the managers of the center encouraged her to travel to various locations to display her work and earn better. They even taught her how to write her own name. ﻿ ﻿ She traveled to cities like Bangalore, Delhi, Mumbai with other artists where she made various paintings on large scale for hotels, offices or even celebrity bungalows. She mainly practiced the Kachchi and Bharni style of Madhubani. In a span of nearly 40 years, Sunena Devi has seen the recognition for Madhubani increase and her paintings find more takers in various crafts fairs organised across the country. Her hard work and talent got recognition and finally in the year 2013-14, Sunena Devi received the State Award for her painting by the then Chief Minister of Bihar - Shri Nitish Kumar. ﻿(﻿pictureof the award received on pg-9) ﻿ Sunena Devi currently lives in her village with her family. She is enjoying life as a grandmother and is also teaching her daughter-in-law and grand children this traditional art form, just the way her in-laws had taught her once. She now paints at leisure, in between her routine life. Her daughter Mira says that Sunena Devi usually works on the bharni style of art now, as Kachchi is a finer work and old age has affected her eyesight. Her son, Manish Jha and daughter Mira both have learnt Madhubani art from their mother. Manish currently works as a trader for these Madhubani paintings and participates in various exhibitions and handicrafts fair across the country. ﻿(﻿the award winning painting on ) Facts About Madhubani Art 1) Madhubani, also known as Mithila painting originates from the Mithila region which falls on both sides of the Indo-Nepal border. In India the region is located in the state of Bihar. 2)Its origin is traced back to the Ramayana, during the wedding of Shri Ram to Princess Sita of Mithila. 3) These paintings depict various occasions and were originally done by women of Madhubani region only. 4) The paintings are inspired by nature and mythology and use symbolic images like lotus, kalpavriksha, peacock, sun etc. 5) The colours used are traditional dyes and pigments and twigs, fingers, brushes or matchsticks are used to draw. 6) The Kohbar style of Madhubani is practiced across Bihar and is especially made in households during weddings in the family. ﻿(﻿ ﻿Picture of Kohbar Art made during weddings in Bihar)
author: Vibha Lohani

title: Kali Wants to Dance
text: In the fishing village of Kovalam, Kali Veerapathiran is a hero. Not because he is an actor. Not because he has fought off villains. He’s a hero because he learnt to dance. It's the year 2000 and Kali is eight years old. Like many boys, he goes to school, plays with his friends, watches TV. Unlike many boys, Kali also dances. Kali loves to watch Padmini dance on TV. She is a famous actor and a fantastic dancer. He pretends to wear a salangai (ankle bells) and dances Bharatanatyam, just like her. Thari thana jonnu thimi Thaka thari kita thaka Thathinginathom Thathinginathom Thathinginathom. Kali becomes such a good dancer that his teachers ask him to perform at school programmes. Soon, he is known in the little fishing village as a Bharatanatyam dancer. One day, Sarah Chanda, who manages a hospital in Chennai, sees him perform on stage. Ditheiyum tha thaa thei, Ditheiyum tha thaa thei She's astonished to see such a talented boy, and is moved that he’s gotten so far by himself. “Would you like to learn Bharatanatyam in Kalakshetra?” she asks him after the performance. Kali laughs at first. Dance? The Dalit community rarely had the opportunity to learn, let alone master, Bharatanatyam. In Kali’s family, there is never enough money to spare for dance classes. And who has heard of boys dancing for a living? But Sarah is serious. “You must learn Bharatanatyam in a proper school, Kali,” she says. “I will pay your fees.” Sarah arranges for Kali to visit Kalakshetra, one of the best dance schools in the country. It is a beautiful place in Chennai with lots of trees. Leela Samson, the head of Kalakshetra who is also a renowned Bharatanatyam dancer, tells Kali to perform for them. Kali ties a saree crookedly over his trousers and dances to a film song. The teachers think he has the makings of a classical dancer. But Kali can’t decide what he wants to be when he grows up. Should he be an actor, a Collector, a teacher, a biotechnologist, or a dancer? His friends and family don’t really help. “Who has ever learnt dance and made any money afterwards? It’s a waste of time!” growls Kali’s maama. “Only girls dance! You’ll become girlish,” his friends tease him. Amma asks Kali what his heart wants. “Do you love dancing? Does it make you feel good? Is that what you want to do always?” “Yes! Dance is all that and more for me, Amma,” he replies. “Then don’t listen to anyone. If it makes you happy, learn dancing.” As usual, Amma has all the answers. So after his final school exams, Kali begins to learn three kinds of folk dances at DakshinaChitra. Oyilaatam Dimtha nakadi naka dhina dhina Dimtha nakadi naka dhina dhina Thapattam Tha kukuku tha kukuku tha kukuku thaa tha Tha kukuku tha kukuku tha kukuku thaa tha Karagattam Datta daguna, daguna Datta daguna, daguna Next month, Kali begins learning Bharatanatyam at Kalakshetra. The first few days in school are scary and quiet. When the work gets too much, and his legs hurt, he cries to Amma. “Do you want to herd buffaloes?” Amma asks him sternly. “No!” “Then go back and do your best.” Kali begins to adjust to this new world. He makes friends. When language is a problem – not all his classmates know Tamil – Kali speaks using mudras. “Did you go home for the holidays?” “Have you eaten?” At Kalakshetra, he becomes a skilful dancer. He becomes lean and fit and full of energy. He can now dance for hours. He learns Carnatic music as well. He makes many friends among the students who have come from all over the country and the world. They share their hopes, dreams, and even the food they bring f rom their homes! Kali starts getting invitations to perform all across India and the world. He travels by bus, train and aeroplane to many places. His akkas tease him. “Do you remember you could not even sit in a bus without throwing up?” Kali laughs as well. It is true. As a child, he would carry a lemon and a plastic bag with him on bus rides. As the years pass, Kali wins awards for his performances. He starts a dance school called Koothambalam in Kovalam. Now, Kali is ready for another performance. He puts on his make-up carefully. He wears his costume with ease. The velvet curtain goes up. Kali begins to dance. Kali the dancer At the age of 25, Kali Veerapathiran is perhaps the only male dancer who has mastered the classical dance form Bharatanatyam, as well as three ancient Tamil folk dance forms, according to The People’s Archive of Rural India. Born in Kovalam, a struggling fishing village not far from Chennai in Tamil Nadu, Kali lost his father very young. It was his mother Ellamalli Veerapathiran, a construction labourer, who worked doubly hard to raise him and his many siblings. Sarah Chanda who is a member of the managing committee of Gremaltes Hospital in Chennai, sponsored his education at Kalakshetra, India’s premier dance school. He has also studied at DakshinaChitra under Kannan Kumar. Having completed his PG Diploma in dance, Kali has started Koothambalam, a dance school in Kovalam. Kali was featured in a documentary film by the People’s Archive of Rural India; many newspapers and TV channels have carried his interviews. He’s won awards for his dance, including the Music Academy’s ‘Spirit of Youth’ award. About The People’s Archive of Rural India (PARI) The People’s Archive of Rural India is a living journal on, and an archive of, the world’s most complex countryside. The Founder-Editor P. Sainath and his team, including an army of volunteers, hope to document the stories of 833 million people speaking well over 700 languages. PARI is also writing the textbooks of the future. That’s happening with the numerous stories, photos, videos and audio material going up on the site
author: Aparna Karthikeyan

title: We are all Tubelights!
text: Chiya spent the entire morning reading her new book. As she turned to the last page... SWOOSH! Neel yanked the book away with one swift swish. "Catch me if you can!" he challenged Chiya. "Arghhh! Give me my book back!" yelled Chiya. But Neel paid no heed. Mum and Dad heard the noise and came out to see what was going on. Neel was scribbling on the first page of Chiya's new book with an orange sketch pen - Chiya's favourite colour. (He writes 'This book belongs to Tubelight'.) Big drops of tears started rolling down Chiya's cheeks. She mumbled, "Everyone at school calls me tube light. I don't like it." "Neel, why did you write that?", Mum asked calmly. "It was only a joke, Ma," he replied. "But your sister didn't find it funny," explained Dad. "I quite like tube lights. I don't think we can do without them," laughed Dad. "Next time, someone calls you a tube light, think of it as a compliment. "For I know you better than them. And you are the brightest tube light in the entire world. You bring so much joy and light into our lives, " assured Dad. "I am a tube light too!" shouted Neel. Mum replied, "Yes! You took some time to figure that out." And they all had a hearty laugh.
author: Chandni  Shah
illustrator: Angie & Upesh; Fahad Faizal; Lavanya Karthik; Rajiv Eipe; Rijuta Ghate; Sonal Gupta Vaswani; Vinayak Varma; Vishnu  M Nair

title: Kasalina ali mu Igulu
text: mu mutwe gwe. Banagutoolamu batya? Gumukooyakooya. Gumudhiinadhiina. Gumuzitoogherera. Talya. Tanhwa. Tiyeyagala nga eira. Omusawo amulinga mu mutwe gwe. Aboineboine mwana waitu. Mukazi waitu omutwe gumuthuudha. Omusawo aboine ekitole mu mutwe gwe. Omusawo akoba,"kino ekitole kya musaayi." Tulina kukitoola mu mutwe gwo buti." Tulina ku kitoolamu butibuti. Omusawo bwakoba atyo. Baleeta ekitanda. Bategeka ebiso. Bamufumita empiso. Basala omutwe gwa Kasalina. Bamutoolamu obwongo. Basalamu ekitole ky' omusaayi. Kasalina alinga omwana omuto. Obwongo babumwizaamu. Omutwe baagutunga. Kasalina awulira byonaboyna bye bakola? Mbe naire! Kasalina ali mu igulu. Tawulira. Talya. Taloghooza. Okumala saawa kumpi 24. Olwonni yaira engulu! Buti ali bukalamu. Buti ayogera lwaatu. Nga akaana akato. Tweenatweena tusagamba Olwa mukwano gwaife Kasalina eyalega ku igulu.
author: Cornelius Wambi Gulere

title: Birds around Me
text: Crow why do you caw?Black as coal with beady eyes? You always sing caw caw and caw. Cuckoo is black but sings so sweetly of sunshine and spring. Kuhoo kuhoo kuhoo it sings in bushes and on trees.Even the grumpy Owl sings at night Tu-whit,Tu-who, a merry note. The Pigeons on the rooftop coos all day a soft and warm sleepy song. The Myna talks but never sings it loves to sit in the warm sun.Pecking for worms in the green grass it chatters kichir michir kich kich mich mich which means, "All the world is mine-I am the King!"It always quarrels with the small sparrows and chases them away. The poor small birds chirp "Weep,weep and weep we have no where to go!" The Weaver bird is too busy having no time to sing. It has to weave its nest for its little ones to save them from wind and rain.So it never rests but weaves weaves and weaves till it finishes weaving its nest. Then it sits on its nest and swings on it,a soft cozy and warm home,in which the chicks dream of the blue sky and green wood to which they will fly someday. The Bulbul likes to make a whistling sound loud and sharp at the peep of dawn. Sitting on the window sill it looks into the room crying "Get up getup it is morn!"The Parrot with its green coat and shiny red beaks sometimes sit on the tree outside the window shouting and crying " Teenha teenha teenha,I want some hot tea and bread with jam spread!" I love birds the warm feathered friends, bundles of colour and joy. They sing so sweetly sometimes in chorus,bringing messages of joy and love and warm sunshine from faraway deep green and lovely woods. ﻿
author: Joysree Das
illustrator: Holly; Joysree  Das; Kumudha Gomatam; Muniza Shariq; Natasha Sharma; Wiehan de  Jager

title: The Little Sparrow
text: Old Uncle Nair liked to sleep but the sparrow on the sill cheeped. He had left the window open because it was a very hot day. “ Cheep! Cheep!”the brown bird cried as Uncle Nair tried to sleep. He ran to catch the sparrow -- almost toppling the water jug near the bed -- but off it flew! Uncle Nair furrowed his brows and tightened his mouth. “Don’t come here again!”he shouted. The sparrow sat on a tamarind tree as he squinted to see. “ Cheep! Cheep!” Uncle Nair scowled. He looked up at the sky and spotted a round, orange sun. The air was sticky as gum. He straightened his pillow and lay on his bed. Uncle Nair dreamt about snow that day. He snored aloud, his lips fluttering like wings on a butterfly. His belly rose and fell. All of a sudden, his eyelids parted. He spied the sparrow land on his window sill. The bird folded its wings and cocked its head. Uncle Nair got up and sat erect. He tip-toed behind the window and peeked. “ Cheep! Cheep!” The sparrow tilted its head this way and that. It looked askance at the bed. Uncle Nair grinned and hoped the sparrow would come in. He wanted to teach the bird a lesson. The sparrow hopped across the sill, calling out to others of its kind. It wasn't sure if the time was right. Beads of sweat formed on Uncle’s Nair’s forehead. He was tired and thirsty. The little bird cheeped. “ Cheep! Cheep!” The sparrow flew to sit atop the water jug, its claws gripping the edge. Uncle Nair wiped the sweat off his face and watched. The bird dipped its beak in the cool water. It threw its head back and swallowed. Once, twice, thrice. Uncle Nair stared as it dipped lower, letting the water slide off its back. The sparrow ruffled its feathers and looked fresh as spring. Uncle Nair laughed and looked outside. The sun burned like a fireball. “It’s hot today, isn’t it?”he said, letting the sparrow flutter past him — through his window to the tamarind tree. “ Cheep! Cheep!”
author: Susheela Menon
illustrator: Deval Maniar; Greystroke; Jayesh Sivan; Lavanya Karthik; Nimret Handa; Parismita; Sangeetha Kadur; Shrujana Shridhar

title: Doong Doong, Dum Dum
text: One morning, during the rainy season, the sky was cloudy. A cool breeze was blowing. As the sky turned darker, it looked like it would soon start raining. Dambaru had left his home and was on the way to school. ﻿ ‘Doong Doong, Doong Doong!’ What was this sound? Dambaru stopped to listen. Who was telling him to go go, go go? (In the Juanga language, the word ‘doong’ means ‘go’) After a pause, there was another sound, ‘ Dum Dum, Dum Dum! ’ Dambaru stopped. (In the Juanga language, the word ‘dum’ means ‘stay’). He looked all around. There was nobody. Again he heard, ‘Doong Doong!’ and Dambaru started going forward. Then he heard ‘Dum Dum!’ and Dambaru stopped. He was foxed. Who could be telling him to go first, and then stay? He went to the grove of trees nearby. The sounds seemed to be coming from there. He saw two men beating two dhols. That explained the two sounds that he had heard! Dambaru started laughing. 'Doong Doong, Dum Dum! Ha Ha Ha! ’ he said to himself. He was still laughing when he reached the school. Didi asked him, “What is so funny Dambaru? Why are you laughing?” Dambaru told her he had heard very funny sounds on the way. ‘Doong Doong, Dum Dum!’ “When I would walk I would hear Dum Dum and when I would stop I would hear Doong Doong!” All the children began to laugh when he told them about the two dhol players. They made up a game called ‘Doong Doong, Dum Dum’ and had a lot of fun playing it. The Concept India’s diverse linguistic landscape has a rich seam of stories for children. Unfortunately, many tribal languages do not have literature for children in book form or books for reading pleasure. As increasing numbers of tribal children go to school, it is now more necessary than ever to create a body of children’s literature in their languages. Literature that reflects their own world and opens up the world beyond because books are magical, powerful things that inform, amuse, educate and entertain in the most interactive way. Books make every child an independent and life-long seeker of knowledge in her own unique way. For education to be truly meaningful to every child, she must get good books to read in her own language. The Project Pratham Books and IgnusERG, with the support of Bernard van Leer Foundation have created the first ten books for children’s reading pleasure in Munda, Kui, Saura and Juanga languages from Odisha. The stories were written and illustrated by authors and illustrators belonging to these tribes in a series of workshops. This series of books is called Adikahani. It is a significant first step towards giving a voice to cultures that do not find adequate representation in mainstream discourses. The Partners IgnusERG is a guild of resource persons working to support teachers and enhancing the quality of education, particularly in government schools. They focus their efforts on bringing equity in education and addressing the needs of marginalized children. Bernard van Leer Foundation is an international grant-making foundation based in The Hague. Its mission is to improve opportunities for young children growing up in socially and economically difficult circumstances. It has a particular interest in supporting mother-tongue based education. This story was written by the Juanga Writers’ Group consisting of Dambarudhar Juanga, Hitabandhu Juanga, Khetrabasi Juanga, Kodanda Juanga and Maheswar Juanga. With a background in ECCE, they all interact with children regularly. It has been illustrated by Sanatan Juanga using the Saura wall mural style as a base. The Juanga language is spoken by more than 1 lakh people in Keonjhar, Jajpur and Mayurbhanj districts of Odisha. It is part of the Munda language family. The spellings of the language in Odia script are not definitive as many new sounds are being rendered in print for the first time.
author: Paridhi Gupta
illustrator: Pradip Kumar Sahoo; Sanatan Juanga; Sugrib Kumar Juanga

title: The Tale of a Butterfly
text: Butterflies have a complete life cycle. That means there are separate stages in a butterfly's life. At each stage, the butterfly looks completely different and serves a different purpose in the life of the insect. The life begins when an adult female butterfly lays an egg on a leaf. The egg is tiny and oval in shape and it sticks to the leaf. Many females produce between one hundred and two hundred eggs. In several weeks, the egg hatches and out comes the larva, or caterpillar. The caterpillar is long and worm-like and often has interesting patterns and spine-like hairs on its body. Caterpillars feed on leaves and spend most of their time searching for and eating food. This is called the feeding and growth stage. As the caterpillar grows, it sheds its skin several times to enclose its rapidly growing body. Once it is fully grown, the caterpillar stops feeding and begins to look for a suitable place for pupation, often the underside of a leaf or other hidden location. Next, the caterpillar forms a pupa, within which its old body parts are broken down and new adult butterfly parts are formed. The pupa is usually brown or green and blends well into the background. In a couple of weeks, the adult butterfly breaks out from the pupa. The adult is usually a large and colorful butterfly. Often, the adult butterflies migrate to other regions to start a new home and continue its life cycle. The Life Cycle of a Butterfly KEY WORDS Egg - A butterfly starts its life as an egg. Larva - The larva (caterpillar) hatches from an egg and eats leaves or flowers almost constantly. The caterpillar molts (loses its old skin) many times as it grows. Pupa - It turns into a pupa (chrysalis); this is a resting stage. Adult - A beautiful, flying adult emerges. There is no growth during this stage. This adult will continue the cycle and reproduce. Migrate: Move in search of a new home
author: Sharmila Pal
illustrator: Brunda Anandarao; Herminder Ohri; Lavanya  Naidu; Muniza Shariq; Preeti Krishnamurthy; Sharmila Pal

title: To - do list
text: Sapna sat with her her to make her to do list like everyday. She has to do her homework. She has to go for her running practice. She has been preparing herself for school's annual sports day. She has to go to her friend Ramya's house for a group study She cut her hand yesterday so she will not go to the kitchen to help her mom. Instead she is planning to stay at Ramya's house till late and come back at dinner time. She looked at her diary for last time and decides to get up and start her homework. Make a habit to write your to do list everyday. A to do list consist of all the activities that you have to do that day. This will help you organise your thoughts and activities better.

illustrator: Ajit Narayan; Angie & Upesh; Greystroke; Jesse  Breytenbach; Rajiv Eipe; Rijuta Ghate; Rohit Karandadi

title: Tea with Mr. Beaver
text: Mr. Beaver’s lodge was a small but compact place with a little neat room for his guest. A warm fire place along the dining area and the rooms included a compact study room,where Mr. Beaver called his marvel session,twice a week along with the kitchen and guest room. The most astonishing feature in the house was the marvel chest at the study room. Mr. Beaver had two marvels and other unique pieces of artifacts in the chest that he collected during his travel. Both the marvels were neatly adorned in a glass case. A small space in the guest room had a bedding arrangement which could easily support a visitor for a night or two. “ We can discuss it better with some fresh sandwiches and tea,” said Mr. Beaver. The grasshopper laid down his boating gear and quickly joined Mr. Beaver at his lodge for tea. “ We can discuss it better with some fresh sandwiches and tea,” said Mr. Beaver. The grasshopper laid down his boating gear and quickly joined Mr. Beaver at his lodge for tea. The grasshopper politely passed the humble invitation of Mr. Beaver. He saw two marvels of Mr. Beaver, of which one took his fancy as he never heard of it. Mr. Beaver called it Panorama. The panorama actually was a camera. Mr. Beaver considered it a marvel of the future. “ I always include my pictures from the camera in my marvel sessions,”said Mr. Beaver. “ How does a camera works?” asked the grasshopper. “ A camera does not sight anything it actually captures a sight, ”said Mr. Beaver. The binocular was resting in its glass case. “Would you like try it again,” asked Mr.Beaver and took them out of the glass case and handed it to the grasshopper. The grasshopper took the binocular and put it on. “ It was beautiful what I saw,” said the grasshopper. He was still contemplating whether he really saw the tree or thought he saw the tree. “That was a jolly good spectacle,” said the grasshopper,when the tea was over. “I don’t know how to call it anything except the spectacle,” said the grasshopper. “Tell me, how many wonderful sights you have seen with a pair of spectacles like those?” ask the grasshopper still calling binoculars spectacles. “ I remember one that will amaze you, it was a turtle climbing the tree,” said Mr Beaver. “ It is impossible!” cried the grasshopper. “No turtle can climb the tree forget climbing they would not even try it,” said the Grasshopper. “Offcourse it couldn’t climb the tree but everybody does get offended just by the mention of this marvelous sight” said Mr. Beaver. “ I hope you are not offended my friend”, ask Mr. Beaver. “He tried but slipped after first step, it didn’t work for him. He went back to the lake sad and disheartened when I called him to have a chat. He told me how he felt but was taken aback by these binoculars,” said Mr. Beaver. “You saw me climbing the tree,” said the turtle “Tell me, my friend what do you call this amazing thing that you are looking from?”asked the turtle admiring the binoculars. “ Does it work with battery but I can’t see any button on them,” said the turtle while maneuvering them. “What does it need, it is really a fancy artwork,” ask the turtle. “It is a binocular,” I said “ You will need a pair of healthy eyes to look through the binoculars,” I said. “Oh my, they are not goggles not one of those fine ones I saw last year on the motor car driver,”said the turtle. “So, what do you plan to do next,” I asked “A few step made my morning,now nothing much to do but rest in the warm lake,” said the turtle. “ I think about the lake much these days,” said the turtle. “ I never thought through how to climb the tree,” replied the turtle slightly puzzled. “ I must confess,I am still stunned by your binoculars,it is indeed marvelous,” said the turtle. “What did stop you to climb the next step,”I asked. “ It didn’t stop,it just slipped,” said the turtle pointing at his toes. “Then maybe that’s all it can do when it comes to climbing a tree,”said the turtle with a smile. “I must tell you, this happened some twenty years ago and I have never again sighted a turtle on a tree,”said Mr. Beaver “ This sighting has been in my weekly series of counting marvels that I organize outside my lodge,once a month,” said Mr. Beaver. The grasshopper bade his goodbye to Mr. Beaver with much thanks from his heart. After the tea,Mr. Beaver decided to write his dairy till the supper. A fine evening is all about dining and singing where tomorrow will be an another day.He thought and opened his diary.
author: uma sharma
illustrator: Greystroke; Karthikeyan S.; Kathy   Arbuckle; Muniza Shariq; Neeta Gangopadhya; Vartika  Sharma; Vinayak Varma

title: Everything is Ups!de Down
text: Once there was a sun that rose below the hills. And a river that flowed right on top of the trees. All the kids swung by their feet. And their tiny noses were above their eyes. “Akash, why is your story upside down?” asks Teacher. “It’s TikTik’s world. It’s upside down.” “And who is this TikTik and what does he do?” asks Teacher. “TikTik runs across the ceiling. Like this.” “Akash,” says Teacher, “NO ONE runs across the ceiling. They will fall!” “TikTik does not fall. He runs up the wall. And up the glass window. And across the ceiling. Over my head, but never falls on it. "So tell me, Teacher, if TikTik can run upside down, why can’t I?” “Because, Akash, TikTik is a lizard and you are not!” “Because lizards have a forest on their feet. A forest you can’t see. A forest of millions of tiny hairs. "The hairs push into every tiny spot of every kind of surface – wet, dry, slippery. "And CLICK! They help the lizard stick,” says Teacher. Akash has an idea! “Teacher, when I grow up I can make shoes that are like TikTik’s feet, with a forest of tiny hair!" "Then I can walk on the ceiling too. And make my upside-down world come true.” DO YOU THINK people could look at TikTik’s feet and invent some things? Things that stick with a C-L-I-C-K? Some things with a forest of hair on them? Tape that doesn’t feel sticky Film posters that don’t leave marks on the wall Plaster that won’t hurt when you rip it off Shoes for Babu who brings coconuts down from the tree Now, tape, plasters and posters stick because of a gummy substance. But imagine if they had a forest of hair like a lizard’s foot. We could stick them on and peel them off at any time!
author: Jane De Suza

title: Lazy Raghu Mama
text: They gave him a big hug. Raghu Mama always told the best stories. He brought Amish and Soni fun presents. But there was one problem with Raghu Mama. Raghu Mama was lazy! He would sit in his chair for hours and hours and hours, reading or watching TV. Or just sleeping. He would not do any work around the house. He would not go to the market to buy food. Amma was fed up of his laziness. “So, Raghu,” said Amma. “Are you going to sit in your favourite chair all the time?” "Oh no!" said Raghu Mama. "I'm going to explore caves that are underwater. I'm going to climb tall mountains. I'm going to chase tigers in the jungle!" “Where, where?” said Amish and Soni. “We want to come too!” “Hah!” said Amma. “What a joke!” Raghu Mama smiled quietly. The next day Amish and Soni heard Raghu Mama talking to someone. “Wow!” he said. Then, “That’s AMAZING!” A little later, “OH NO!” The children ran into his room. “What happened, Raghu Mama?” Raghu Mama was in his favourite chair. He was wearing a pair of big black goggles. There was no one else in the room! Soni and Amish looked at each other. “Is everything okay, Mama?” Amish asked. Mama laughed. He took off the goggles. “Try this,” he said to Soni. “What is it?” asked Soni. The goggles were heavy. She had to hold them with both hands. Raghu Mama put the goggles on Soni’s face. The goggles were dark and she couldn’t see anything. Then Mama pressed a button. Suddenly Soni was in the ocean! There were colourful fish all around. There was a big turtle swimming beside her. "WOW!" said Soni. Then she turned her face to the other side... “Eek!” she cried as a big shark swam very close to her. “Let me see, let me see!” said Amish. “It is your turn now, Amish,” said Raghu Mama. Amish put the goggles on. Mama pressed a button. Amish was in a forest full of trees. He could hear different bird sounds. “Ooh!" he said, "I can see chital! I can see langurs!” “It feels so real,” said Soni. “When I wore the goggles I thought I was swimming underwater!” “Yes,” said Raghu Mama. “It is called ‘Virtual Reality’.” “But ‘virtual’ means ‘not real’.” Soni said. “You're right,” said Raghu Mama. “It is Virtual Reality. You thought you were in the ocean, right? It was almost real.” “It is like watching a movie,” said Soni. “Yes,” said Mama. “When we wear Virtual Reality goggles, it feels like the movie is all around us.” "Do you want to explore Virtual Reality with me?" asked Raghu Mama. Amish and Soni thought for a bit. “We like the REAL thing,” they said. “But why??” Raghu Mama asked. “I saw a juicy mango in the jungle,” said Amish. “And now I want to eat one. I can’t eat the mango in the jungle. I can eat the mango in the kitchen.” “I want one too!” said Soni. Both of them ran to the kitchen. “Wait for me!” said Raghu Mama. He jumped off his chair and ran after them.
author: Meenakshi  Khanna

title: Absent-minded Ajja
text: “Have you taken everything, Ajja?” Sujju asks. “Your cap? Your bag?” Ajja is ready for his evening walk. Ajja is about to step out of the house. He looks up at the clouds. Why is he hurrying back into the house? Ajja checks on the shelf above the window. He looks in the box below. What is Ajja searching for? No one knows! But everyone stays out of his way. Ajja hates being late. The bag seems more full than usual. Ajja empties it in a hurry. But whatever-it-is is not to be found. Ajja is getting more and more late. He shakes his head. He grinds his teeth. He grunts and tut-tuts. He hunts under the sofa. He scrabbles on the bookshelf over Chikkamma’s head. AIYO! Ajja’s toes are in front of Dinku akka’s nose. HABBA! Ajja disappears behind the door. He stops at the bottom of the stairs. He searches on top of the fridge. What could Ajja be looking for? He even looks near the dustbin! What is Ajja trying to find? Everyone runs far away from him. Sujju asks, “Ajja, what are you searching for?” And sends Ajja off on his walk. “His umbrella was with him all along,” everyone smiles in relief.
author: Arundhati Venkatesh

title: Clever Sona
text: One day Sona went to her Uncle's shop. Uncle was preparing variety of syrups with different fragrance. " Uncle I want to prepare the syrup with you," said Sona They were four types of syrup on the gas stove. " No Sona! just pay attention to what is being prepared," said Uncle while adding the color and fragrance in one bowl on the gas stove. After smelling the fragrance, Sona said" is it not the black sour syrup." " correct Sona," said Uncle while removing the syrup bowl from the stove " But there is another smell too," said Sona while crimping her nose " It is not a good smell," said Sona Uncle added spice mixture in the second bowl. It gave a light sweet fragrance. " It is pomegranate sweet syrup," said Sona delighted by the fragrance. " Good Sona! it is correct," said Uncle while removing the bowl from the stove " But there is a rotten smell too," said Sona crimping her nose " Now I am adding pink caramel spice mix," said Uncle while stirring the third bowl on the stove " It is a nice fagrance," said Uncle " Some thing is burning! Uncle!" said Sona with an urgency Uncle turned and peered in the milk syrup bowl. He quickly removed the bowl from the stove. " Excellent Sona!" said Uncle " You have saved my milk syrup from burning," said Uncle " Our clever Sona," said Uncle while offerring her the milk syrup flavored shaved ice dessert
author: uma sharma

title: Birthday Special
text: "My new school, my new class, my new friends, my new dress", Renuka cried in joy. Her Amma was also so happy. They are now in a new village. Renuka's father was a village administrative officer. Renuka was excited to make new friends. she was now in sixth grade and promoted to village high school It was her birthday too on the reopening day of the school. "I will make beautiful friends, smart friends, and true friends" she promised herself. Renuka was wearing her best birthday dress and proudly entered the class. "Good morning Dear", echoed the class teacher Mohana's voice. Renuka went bubbly, shy and suddenly calm. "Good morning teacher" she replied with humble voice. 'Please sit with your friends', guided Mrs. Mohana. Renuka's eyes dragged here and there finding her best clean spot to sit. Bell Rang and the prayer started. Everything was new for Renuka. Mrs. Mohana started taking attendance of the students while a thin looking girl entered the class wishing her. She panicked"sorry I am late". Mohana made her sit with other students. Renuka was laughing at the girl for the way she was dressed. "ok now, Being the first day of class I Wish you all to come out with flying colours and make your parents proud" said the teacher. Renuka was thinking inside "I will be the One". "I will become a pilot" said to herself. "Now we will wish the birthday queens and kings" giggled Mohana. "Here it comes",cheered Renuka. Children please wish Meena, said the teacher. Slowly the lean girl who came late stood with a light smile and heavy shyness. She was wearing a very rugged dress and with no chappals in her feet. "So how was your special day Meena?, asked the teacher. She rejoiced and said, "today was wonderful, my mother took me to temple in the mountain, my father gave me 2 rupees for mittai and aahhhh yes I need not take ganga the cow today to the fields", She finished as grand finale. Children clapped for her with thier wishes. The teacher said there is one more birth day too. "Renuka " called the teacher. Renuka stood in silent controlling her tears for Meena and her enjoymemt for birthdays. Now the teacher put the same question to Renuka. She replied, "today's special for me is I found a good friend already and her name is Meena".
author: Jamunarani Gopi
illustrator: Lavanya Karthik; Shailja Jain Chougule; Sonal Goyal; Sumit Sakhuja; Suvidha Mistry; Tasneem Amiruddin

title: My Dream Job
text: My dream has been for a very long time. I have had this dream for sixteen years now. Not that I don’t have other dreams. No. I have heard dreams like becoming the first Ugandan to win the Ballon trip to mars. And becoming the first Ugandan to play in the premier league. But this other dream is a much bigger dream. My dream is to become a lawyer. My father is a prominent city lawyer. This gives me inspiration and determination to look up to him. One day I might end up in his shoes and take up his law firm. I like the way my father conducts himself. He speaks with honor and pride as he resolves his clients’ cases. His writing and the paper work makes me wish I was him. I asked my father, "what does a lawyer do?" He replied, "a lawyer does different kinds of work." I was pleased to learn the different types of lawyers. I then asked my father to take me to one of his court sessions so I could listen to his cases. He agreed. The next day, I woke up very early in the morning and waited for my father to come and take me to court. On asking my dad what court session we were going to attend he told me it was a surprise. Indeed it was a surprise. Judge Precious entered the court room and everybody stood up. He was my father’s closest friend. They had started the law firm together. I can now see my dream coming true. The dream of working at the International Criminal Court in the Netherlands. I now walk to school with my sister determined to succeed. My sister wants to become a doctor. I tell her always, " we must work hard to become what we desire to be." My father tells me, "Lawyers read a lot of books. Without reading, one cannot succeed as a lawyer." I now read three story books everyday. My sister reads three storybooks too. But she also like to play. When she is out playing, i go in a nearby place to pray. "Look! That is one of the offences that lead to motor accidents on our roads." My sister observed. "When I become a lawyer, " I thought deeply, "I will not defend drivers who cause accidents."
author: Cornelius Wambi Gulere
illustrator: Paper Boat Drinks; Prashant Miranda; Rob Owen; Sugrib Kumar Juanga; Tracy Hanson

title: Panipuri inside a Spaceship
text: “Dinner time!” called Daddy. Chikki and Ninu, who were playing outside, came running in. Daddy was already at the table. “What are we having?” asked Ninu. “Mooli parathas,” said Mummy. “And raita.” Chikki wrinkled her nose. “Yuck!” she said.
