title: My City Rocks!
text: Devesh was very excited. He was going on a tour of his city - well no ordinary tour but a Rock Walk! Devesh and his family are new to Hyderabad. There was so much to explore.. so much to see! The next morning Devesh could barely hold his excitement. He was up early. His family had to be present at the Begumpet Public School, Hyderabad by sharp 9 AM. They would then meet fellow citizens and they would all embark on a walk to discover rocks around his city. Many families had arrived and were eager to begin the rock walk. The rock walk was organized by the Hyderabad Save the Rocks Society. There were a few do's and dont's that the project leader, explained to the people. The crowd could barely hold the excitement when they visited the first rock. Devesh squealed " Hey doesn't it look like a man's face, Look what a sharp nose he has! ", exclaimed Devesh. Devesh was delighted to see a rock shaped like a tortoise. "But how do rocks form?, asked Devesh. "I see rocks everywhere in Hyderabad ". "I didn't see them in any other city I visited ", he quipped. Uncle RamMohan was a geologist who was leading the rock walk. He began narrating about the formation of rocks. He smiled and began " Do you know that the rocks seen in this city are 2.5 billion years old?" Igneous rocks are formed by volcanoes. When a volcano erupts, it spews out hot molten rock called magma or lava. The magma will cool down and harden when it reaches the Earth's surface. This hardened magma or lava is called igneous rock. The present-day formations are a result of weathering and erosion that has occurred over millions of years. These rocks are home to many birds and smaller animals. Geckos and mongooses live among them, and Great Horned Owls, Spotted Owlets, vultures, mynas and swifts nest in their crevices and openings. What a wealth of wildlife! The rocks are very important components of the ecosystem. Most of them harbour micro flora and fauna and are known to support water conservation by generating waterfalls, springs and streams. They are also responsible for formation of lakes and other water bodies. But sigh! Uncontrolled quarrying and blasting happens in cities! in our quest to build high rise apartments. Out of the rocks that must have existed earlier, less than 40% must be existing today. These mute rocks are being done away with mercilessly. Devesh was overwhelmed with all that he heard from the geologist. "I wish all of us could do something to protect rocks!", he exclaimed. Do you know The Society to Save Rocks has been doing a lot of work to preserve rocks of the Deccan? They organize Rock walks which are nature treks to different rocky areas in and around Hyderabad. Hyderabad also boasts of rock gardens to preserve the rocks. The Government has included rock areas under the protection of Heritage Buildings and Precincts. Hyderabad is the only city in India where rocks are protected as a natural heritage. Under the UNESCO law, rocks come under physical heritage and they need protection. All the kids were delighted to know so many facts about their city. They decided to share their adventure with their teachers and classmates. They also decided to make colorful posters showcasing the beauty of rocks. "My CITY ROCKS! ROCKS ROCK!!!! ", yelled the kids. You can explore..... "Hillocks around Durgam Cheruvu", a lake situated between Jubilee Hills and Hitec City. "Rock Park" near Khajaguda, Nanakramguda Road. "Bear's Nose", now surrounded by Hotel "Trident", behind Cyber Tower, Hitec City. "Mushroom Rock", Formation in the campus of Central University of Hyderabad, Gachibowli. "Tortoise Rock", Formation in B.N.R.Hills, near Durgam Cheruvu. "Toadstool", Formation in Road No. 35, Jubilee Hills.
author: Vani B
illustrator: Aindri C; Ajit Narayan; Ashok Sharma; Deval Maniar; Greystroke; Maya  Ramaswamy; Ouk  Ratha; Pia Meenakshi; Srikrishna Kedilaya; Sunaina  Coelho; Vani B

title: Sir M. Visvesvaraya: The Builder of Dams, Bridges and a Nation
text: He autographed it for Muttajji, see?” Mangala sat next to her mother. “Did you know, your great grandmother went to college only because of him?” Amma asked. “But wasn’t Sir MV an engineer? What did he have to do with Muttajji’s education?” asked Mangala. “Oh yes, he was an engineer and built bridges and dams and buildings, but he also did so much more. You know what, tomorrow let’s go to Muddenahalli, the place where he was born.” The house in the hills In the small village of Muddenahalli, near present-day Bengaluru, is a house surrounded by rocky hills. Here a baby boy was born on September 15, 1860. Next to his house is a small office that he built when he became an engineer. The office is now a museum. Each exhibit tells a story about this engineer – Sir Mokshagundam Visvesvaraya. Now that’s a really long name! So people started referring to him as Sir MV. His friends called him Vishwa. Off to the city As a young boy, Vishwa had to walk a long way to school. Looking at his precariously frail build, a teacher is supposed to have remarked that he would not live long. But this did not worry young Vishwa or his family. All they wanted was for him to have a good education. When he was 15, Vishwa’s father passed away. He continued his schooling in Chikkaballapura and Bengaluru, and then studied Arts in Central College. He barely had money. Luckily, a couple took him in. In return for board, lodging and a small sum of money, he tutored their two children. Vishwa graduated in 1881 and got a scholarship to study civil engineering at the College of Science in Pune. He topped the course. When Visvesvaraya graduated from Central College, Bengaluru, Principal Charles Waters presented him with a dictionary. Visvesvaraya used it for the next 80 years! A very thrifty person, he once said in a speech: “If you buy what you do not need, you will need what you cannot buy.” Riding to work As the university topper, Visvesvaraya was appointed assistant engineer in the Public Works Department of the Government of Bombay. Within months, he built a structure called a syphon to bring water from the Panjra river to a village called Datari. While there, he came to work from the camp office across Panjra river. How did he travel to work? On horseback of course, since this was in 1884! One evening it rained so hard that the river was flooded and Visvesvaraya could not ride back to the travellers’ bungalow. For two days, the villagers of Nandwan and Datari offered him food and accommodation. But on the third morning, he had to return to the camp office. What did he do? He just swam back with the help of his Bhil workers. Can you imagine how strong he had become contrary to that early prediction? Visvesvaraya’s public works, which started then, went on for over seven decades! Team clearing sand from the bed of the stream Visvesvaraya was passionate about water conservation. He designed many water supply, drainage and irrigation systems across the country. Visvesvaraya also designed or advised on water supply systems in Aden (now in Yemen), Kolhapur, Indore, Gwalior, Bhopal, Nagpur, Goa, Rajkot, Bhavnagar, Baroda, Sangli and across Bihar and Odisha. 1894 Service in Sind: Designed a water filtration system on the riverbed to supply clean water to Sukkur, in Sindh, now in Pakistan. 1889 New Irrigation System: Designed a system of irrigation for the Bombay Presidency that could distribute water to large blocks of land and increase the output of crops. It was called the Block System of Irrigation. 1908 Drainage for Hyderabad: Cyclonic rains caused the Musi river to flood. Thousands of people were killed. The Nizam of Hyderabad invited Visvesvaraya to design a drainage and water supply system to prevent such losses. Automatic Sluice Gates: The Khadakvasla reservoir, Pune’s water source, would overflow every monsoon. But the water that it could hold wasn’t enough for the summer. Visvesvaraya designed a system of automatic gates that increased the capacity of the reservoir, which he patented* as the Automatic Sluice Gates. Similar systems were installed in Tigra dam, near Gwalior, and Krishna Raja Sagar dam, near Mysuru. *Patent: A government authority or licencse conferring a right or title for a set period, especially the sole right to exclude others from making, using, or selling an invention. The Mysore years In 1909, after he finished his work as a consulting engineer in Hyderabad, Visvesvaraya received a telegram from the Dewan of Mysore offering him the post of Chief Engineer. But Visvesvaraya was no longer interested in routine work. So he asked if he could work on developing industries and technical education in the state. The government agreed. Sri Krishna Raja Wadiyar IV, the Maharaja of Mysore, asked him to design a dam across the river Cauvery. Previously, Visvesvaraya had visited large irrigation projects like the Aswan Dam in Egypt. He had observed how engineers there worked and came up with a design for the Krishna Raja Sagara Dam. Built over many years, it is a spectacular construction and thousands of people still visit it every day. In 1912, when KRS Dam was built, * it supplied power to the Kolar Gold Fields * it had a tunnel that was nearly 3 km long, bored through a hill range * it led to the cultivation of sugarcane, giving rise to large sugar mills in the region * it was the largest dam in India Education for all In 1912, the Maharaja offered the post of Dewan to Visvesvaraya. But he was anxious to have opportunities to develop technical education and industries in the State and he did not want any high office. However, the Maharaja insisted, and Visvesvaraya became the Dewan. As someone who knew the worth of a good education, Visvesvaraya wanted to set up schools and colleges. During his period as Dewan, between 1912 and 1918, the number of educational institutions in the state went up from just 4,568 to 11,294. The Maharani’s College in Mysuru became the first in the state to include degree courses for women. Visvesvaraya was also responsible for starting technical education colleges, engineering colleges and agriculture education. He introduced compulsory education, which is now a fundamental right in the Indian Constitution. On a visit to his old school in Muddenahalli, he gave a packet of chocolates to the students. When he was asked to give a speech, Sir MV spoke only for five minutes because he wasn’t prepared. Unhappy with that, he came back a few days later with a well-prepared speech! When he resigned as chairman of the Mysore Iron Works, which he founded, a large sum of money was due to him. Visvesvaraya wanted it to be used to start a college where boys could learn a profession. So the Sri Jayachamarajendra Occupational Institute was set up in Bengaluru. It is now called Sri Jayachamarajendra Polytechnic. The first Ganesha made at the Mysore Iron Works, later renamed Visvesvaraya Iron and Steel Plant. Institutions that Sir MV helped to set up Government Engineering College (Renamed University Visvesvaraya College of Engineering), Bengaluru. Hebbal Agricultural School, that led to the formation of University of Agricultural Sciences. Sri Jayachamarajendra Polytechnic College, Bengaluru Mysore University An honour for the genius By now, Visvesvaraya was recognised for his work as an engineer and a leader in many parts of the country. In 1915, while he was the Dewan of Mysore, the British government made him a Knight Commander of the Order of the Indian Empire (KCIE). From then on, he was called Sir M.Visvesvaraya. The visionary that he was, Visvesvaraya visited factories and big construction projects in many countries, not only to provide them with his services, but also to see how he could bring development to India. He felt India’s poverty could only be reduced if education and employment were available to everyone. He often boldly declared, “Industrialise, or perish!” But, during the same time, Gandhiji used to say, “Industrialise and perish!” Even though the two great men did not have the same views about industrialisation, they respected each other. Strong beliefs Visvesvaraya was a very simple man. He focussed almost all his energy and thoughts on nation-building. He believed that all people should be respected for the work they did. During the Mysuru Dasara celebrations, British officers sat on chairs while Indian officers had to sit on the floor or remain standing at the back. Visvesvaraya stopped going to these durbars because of the discrimination. The government noticed this and got chairs for the Indian officers too. A special car ride Once, when Visvesvaraya was quite old, he wanted to go to his village. Chief Minister Kengal Hanumanthaiah said he could take a government car. But as he wasn’t going on official business, Visvesvaraya refused. So the CM drove him in his personal car! Team leader Big buildings and structures cannot be built by a single person. Dreamers, researchers, funders, masons, labourers and many others have to work together to build them. Sir MV worked hard and efficiently, inspiring everyone around him to give their best too. Once when he was on a study tour in America, Visvesvaraya’s host said the group had to climb a four-floor-high ladder to see how a particular machine worked. Everyone was scared. Not Sir MV! He climbed nimbly all the way to the top. He was 85 years old. In his 90s, he was called upon by Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru to examine several proposals for bridges to be built over the Ganga. He first did an aerial survey of the region. No one expected him to come to inspect the rocky and dangerous terrain. Since Sir MV never did anything without thorough study and preparation, of course he travelled to the region to make notes. Based on the location selected by him, a road-cum-railway bridge was built near Mokama, Bihar. Love for reading Sir MV was always eager to learn. When he was more than a hundred years old, a relative asked him what he wanted from Chennai. “Get me a good, modern dictionary,” he replied. The dictionary is now in the Muddenahalli museum. Sir MV helped to set up the Mysore Agricultural Residential School. It later became the University of Agricultural Sciences. The rock on which he liked to sit has been named after him. Among the books in his personal library were Poems of Kabir, Arabian Nights, Mark Twain’s Tom Sawyer Abroad, Charles Dickens’ The Pickwick Papers, Dr. Peter Schmidt’s Don’t Be Tired, Macmillan’s Promotion of Happiness and Rabindranath Tagore’s Stray Birds. Also in the library were books that he wrote: Memoirs of My Working Life, Constructing India, Nation Building: A Five-Year Plan for the Provinces and Prosperity Through Industry. As an engineer, and a person who valued education and discipline, Sir MV was an inspiration to millions of people. Among them was a boy called Ramu who used to read out to him from the newspapers when Visvesvaraya’s eyesight became weak. He wanted Ramu to come on time, read to him and leave for school on time. For this, Sir MV paid him 10 paise every day. Ramu’s reading improved and he grew up to become a teacher. After he retired, he became a Scoutmaster in Tumakuru and taught physical exercise, memory games, first-aid and sports to children for free. Mangala and Amma had been learning about Visvesvaraya for a week. “Amma, so Muttajji could get a degree because Sir MV introduced graduate studies in Mysuru?” Mangala asked. Amma nodded. “Ajji had an account in Mysore Bank founded by Sir MV?” Amma nodded. “You worked at the Kannada Sahitya Parishat?” Amma nodded again. “And now, I want to visit Visvesvaraya Industrial and Technological Museum which was set up in his memory,” said Mangala. “Yes, let’s go there next week, on his birthday!” said Amma. Visvesvaraya Industrial and Technological Museum September 15 is celebrated as National Engineers’ Day in honour of Sir Mokshagundam Visvesvaraya, an outstanding engineer and visionary. Visvesvaraya helped set up the Karnataka Sahitya Parishat (later renamed Kannada Sahitya Parishat) in Bengaluru to bring together people who spoke different dialects of the language. --- Sir MV’s office turned into a museum. Timeline of life events September 15, 1860 Born to Venkatalakshmamma and Srinivasa Shastry in Muddenahalli 1875 Went to Bengaluru to pursue BA 1883 Graduated with a degree in civil engineering at the College of Science, Pune 1884 Started working at PWD, Government of Bombay 1909 Appointed Chief Engineer, Mysuru 1912 Appointed the Dewan of Mysore 1915 Became Sir MV when King George V of Britain made him a Knight Commander of the Order of the Indian Empire for his contributions to public good 1955 Honoured with the Bharat Ratna for his contribution to engineering, education and nation building April 14, 1962 He passed away five months short of his 102nd birthday Khadakvasla, Maharashtra Dhule, Maharashtra Kannada Sahitya Parishat Mysore Sandal Oil Factory State Bank of Mysore Always an inspiration Sir MV’s room, at the Muddenahalli Museum A farmer’s tribute: Art on a bullock cart
author: Mala Kumar
illustrator: Krupa Thakur-Patil; Sachin Pandit; Sheshadri Mokshagundam; Visvesvaraya National Memorial Trust

title: Neelumbera on a Full Moon Night
text: A long time ago, in the village of Pakshipur, situated at the edge of a forest, lived a young boy called Baku. He loved counting things. After school, he helped his mother weigh vegetables and count money. One evening, Baku saw a pair of colourful birds. They laughed and took off. Baku followed them. They flew through a cave and into the forest. Everything here was so different, just like the birds. Were those blue monkeys whistling? And the pink elephants? They seemed to be humming! Baku didn’t see the sun go down. Soon, it got dark, and he was lost. A short distance away, he saw a roaring fire. A woman was pacing up and down. Her name was Midu. Baku went up to her and asked softly, “Wha...what is the matter?” “My ten-year-old daughter Koya came down with a rare illness six months ago. She hasn’t been able to sit up since then!” “Is there no cure?” asked Baku. “Only one—the nectar of the Neelumbera flower,” she said. “It blooms every seven days. But only the nectar collected on a full moon night can cure her. In the past six months, the flower hasn’t bloomed even once on a full moon night. Koya is getting weaker every day!” Baku’s mind raced. “Please don’t cry! The flower will bloom on a full moon night...hmmm...in nine days,” he said confidently. “How can you be sure?” asked Midu. Baku had worked it out. The full moon shone every thirty days and the flower bloomed every seven days. This meant it would bloom on a full moon night once every 210 days - roughly seven months. Six months had gone by. The Neelumbera would bloom on the next full moon night. That was only nine days away. Midu thanked Baku and led him back to his village. Three weeks later, when Baku was picking jamuns, he saw Midu again. She came running and hugged him. “Baku! Look, that’s my Koya!” she said. “The flower bloomed on the night you said it would. The nectar worked its magic!” Koya was cured. Baku was very pleased. All was well in Midu’s world. How did Baku work it out? Baku knew the Neelumbera flower bloomed once every 7 days and that the full moon appeared every 30 days*. How did he know that the blooming of the flower would coincide with the full moon? Mathematics! Actually, something called Lowest Common Multiple (LCM). What is LCM? The LCM of two numbers—let’s call them a and b — is the smallest number which is a common multiple of both a and b. *The lunar cycle—that is one full moon to the next—can last anywhere between 28 and 31 days. The average full moon cycle is 29.53 days, which is rounded off to 30 days. How do you find the LCM? To find the LCM of 3 and 5: Write the multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30, 33... Write the multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35... The common multiples are 15, 30… The least or smallest common multiple is 15! LCM of 3 and 5 is 15. Prime factorization method We usually use this method to find the LCM of larger numbers. This means that we list out each number as a product of prime factors. Let’s find the LCM of 20 and 30. First, we write each of the numbers as a product of its prime factors. 20 = 2 x 2 x 5 30 = 2 x 3 x 5 Now we multiply all the factors**. 2 x 2 x 3 x 5 = 60 How often does the Neelumbera bloom on a full moon night? The answer to this is the LCM of 7 and 30. 7 = 7 30 = 2 x 3 x 5 LCM = 2 x 3 x 5 x 7 = 210 So, the Neelumbera blooms on a full moon night once in 210 days. **If a factor is common to both lists, we need to take it only once for each pair, unless it occurs more than once in the same list. Here, 2 is common to one pair, but it occurs twice in the list for 20. Imagine you have planned to serve spicy vada-pav from the neighbourhood snack shop. You go to the shop and realise that vadas come in packets of 3 each and pavs come in packets of 4 each. What is the minimum number of packets you have to buy of each so that you can pair vadas and pavs without either remaining extra? (Hint: LCM will help you here.) Have a great party!
author: Aparna Athreya

title: Riddler Fiddler - The boy who loved riddles
text: Juggler was clever.He sent Riddler Fiddler a letter - but no ordinary letter but a letter that was filled with riddles! Riddler Fiddler set off to visit his uncle with the letter in his pocket. Fiddler simply could not contain his excitement and sang along. Watch me sing, hop and run.. under the sun.. I am visiting my uncle. Oh What fun! Oh What fun! When Riddler Fiddler reached his uncle's village, he opened the letter that held the clues. The first clue read.. All houses here are yellow... But you are a smart fellow.. hmmm. The first clue was confusing. So Riddler read Clue two. That had lines a few.. My house is not round.. Did it make you frown? Riddler Fiddler frowned and he exclaimed! But all I see are houses round.. Firmly on the ground! Riddler Fiddler turned the page to find the final clue. My house is not thatched. I hope now you found the catch! Yes! indeed! uncle's house did not have a thatch! That was a clever catch.. and Riddler Fiddler sang his way to his uncle's house.. Your house is all concrete. Very different from the others on this street. Your house has levels three! Do I get to climb the coconut tree? Out came uncle with his children three Hey! it's summer and we are all free! As an add - on, you can probe children To distinguish a pakka house from a Kutcha house in the story. Where do they see Pakka houses and where do they see Kutcha houses? Have they seen Kutcha houses in real? Have they visited villages? What do they see in a village that they don't see in a city? What do they see in cities that they don't see in a village? If they were to live in a Kutcha house, how different would it be? People in the story are seen chit chatting with neighbours. What would children do if there was a power cut? The houses in the story have loads of greenery around. Ask children if they have a garden. If so what do they grow in it. Have they read other riddles. Ask them to share!
author: Vani B
illustrator: Sanatan Juanga; stavroula l; Sugrib Kumar Juanga

title: The Best Birthday Present
text: Meenu was spending her summer vacations with her ajja in Channapatna. "Ajja, I miss my classmate Ranga". He is moving to a new school. "How I wish I could contact him!", sighed Meenu. But ajja had no internet connection at his ancestral home. **ajja - grand father in Kannada "Ajja! it is Ranga's birthday in a few days. How I wish I could send him something", said Meenu. Ajja was busy reading his newspaper. He looked up and said "Why don't you send him a handwritten letter?. I am sure he would get a lot of gifts. But a letter would be very special ". Meenu went to her desk and started writing a letter.She wished her friend a wonderful birthday. She wrote about all the fun she was having in the town. She wrote about the milkman and his buffaloes, the vegetable vendor that went "Tarakaari Tarakaari". She also wrote about her colorful Channapatna wooden toys and all the fun she had playing with them. She decorated the letter with colorful drawings and a bold "Happy Birthday" message. *Tarakaari - vegetable in Kannada ﻿She took the letter to ajja and said " I think we are ready to post the letter. Can we buy some colorful stickers and paste here?? It says "Stamp here ". Ajja chuckled and said " No putta, we need to buy stamps and fix them there. We will have to visit a post office for that". **putta - little one in Kannada Ajja and Meenu walked to the town post office. Ajja exchanged pleasantries with the post master. Meenu was amazed to know how well ajja knew the postmaster at the counter! "I am sending this birthday wish to my friend ", said Meenu, excitedly. "That is so nice of you, said the postmaster". Meenu watched as he scribbled something on it. Meenu affixed a stamp and took the envelope to the post box. She could barely reach the red letterbox and stood on tiptoes to drop the letter. This was the first time she was posting a letter. Meanwhile, after a few days, the postman in Bengaluru was sorting the letters. He saw Meenu's letter that was to be delivered to a special birthday boy in JP Nagar. He too scribbled something on the letter. Ranga could barely contain his excitement when he received a letter in his name! He kept showing it to all his friends in the neighborhood and his family. " 1 2 3 4 5..... ", five birthday wishes each signed by a different person!", squealed Ranga. Ranga's joy knew no bounds because he had not received just Meenu's wish in the letter - but the postmaster in Channapatna, ajja and the postman in Bengaluru had added their wishes to him! Ranga exclaimed, " This is the best birthday gift ever!" Do you know.... Channapatna is famous for wooden toys. Channapatna is known as Gombegala Ooru (toy-town) of Karnataka. The "toy town of Karnataka," Channapatna, is 60 km from Bangalore on Mysore Road. The origin of these toys can be traced back to the reign of Tipu Sultan. Vegetable dyes are used in the coloring process to ensure that the toys and dolls are safe for use by children.
author: Vani B
illustrator: Henu; Kaveri Gopalakrishnan; Megha Vishwanath; Ouk  Ratha; Smitha Shivaswamy

title: Sitara Grows Up
text: Sitara has a hobby. Playing, helping her parents, dreaming of flying cows or upside-down owls, she always sucks her thumb. One hot summer day, she is reading her favourite book about a child who set up home in an ice bucket. Usually, when Sitara wants to know the meaning of a big word in a story, she asks her father. But today Papa asks her, “What is the meaning of adventure?” “Doing something exciting,” says Sitara. “What is the meaning of magnificent?” asks Papa. “Very beautiful,” says Sitara. “What is the meaning of monument?” “A grand thing.” “Good,” says Papa. “Now listen to me. We are going on an adventure. Next week, we’ll take a train to see a magnificent monument. The Taj Mahal.” Sitara is so happy she forgets to suck her thumb. She can draw a train but she has never been on one! “But,” says Papa, “children who suck their thumbs are not allowed on trains.” How can that be! Sitara decides to talk to her mother about it. “Ma, we are going to see the Taj Mahal,” she says. “Yes,” says Ma. “Do you know what it is?’ “Something mag-ni-fi-cient that you go to see in a train,” says Sitara. “Four hundred years ago a king brought together twenty thousand people to make it,” says Ma. “But children who suck their thumbs are not allowed on trains.” Sitara is miserable. Twenty thousand people! Four hundred years! She wants to see the Taj Mahal. Sitara goes to bed and dreams she is all alone. Everyone else has gone on the holiday. But look, what is Chotu doing? Sitara wakes up and shouts, “You fooled me!” She runs to her parents. “Chotu also sucks his thumb,” she yells at them. “How can he go on the train?” “Dinner is ready,” says Ma. Papa says, “You will be grown up soon, Sitara.” Ma says, “Grown-ups need both their hands.” Sitara asks, “What do grown-ups need both their hands for?” “You need both your hands to tie your shoelaces with,” says Ma. “You need both your hands to shell peas with or peel potatoes,” says Papa. “I am grown up! I can do those things,” says Sitara. “Then show us you are grown up,” says Papa. Ma says, “Please take your thumb out of your mouth, Sitara.” Papa says, “You need both your hands to…” “I know,” says Sitara. “I need both my hands to bat. I need both my hands to plait Ma’s hair. I need both my hands to hold a skipping rope.” “I need both my hands to make a string butterfly. I need both my hands to pretend I am an aeroplane. I need both my hands to stand on my head. I also need both my hands to...”
author: Anjum Hasan

title: Belly Monsters
text: Dhruvi was a very fussy eater. All he wanted to do all day was PLAY, PLAY and more PLAY!!! Every time his maayi called him to eat he would turn his face away and let out a LOUD NOOOOOO... **maayi - grand mother On Monday, Dhruvi was busy playing with his imaginary friend Gittu. Maayi had made some tasty Pesarattus for breakfast. As usual, he refused to taste any! **Pesarattu - special dosas cooked in Andhra using Moong Dal But by 11 AM, Dhruvi's belly began to rumble. He imagined angry rakshasas creating a ruckus in his belly. What if the rakshasas got very angry and tore open his belly. Reluctantly he took a small bite of the pesarattu dipped in coconut chutney. hmmm! not bad! he gobbled one - and then one more and soon Dhruvi had gobbled three!!! to satisfy the rakshasas. It was past 3 PM. Dhruvi had still not eaten his lunch. Maayi had made Vadiyaalus. She had dried them in the hot summer sun. And then had fried a few in oil. But Yuck! pooo! who tastes something new!..so Dhruvi let out a loud NOOOOOO! **Vadiyaalu - crispy fryums that are sun-dried and then fried in oil But by 3:30 PM, Dhruvi could barely sit silently. The rakshasa in the belly was shouting and pounding louder, so much so Dhruvi feared the rakshasa would appear in front of him any moment. Oh! how terrifying the rakshasa looked - with red fiery eyes and a mouth WIDE open that could gobble up a child! So Dhruvi ate not just rice and dal but also tasted some of the vadiyalus... yumm!!so tasty! "Why didn't you tell me it tastes so nice?", he chided his grandmother. And at 5 PM, for the first time, Dhruvi tasted jackfruits. The rakshasas didn't growl this time around. Dhruvi gobbled more of the tasty fruit dipped in honey because it was simply irresistible. His mouth started to water. With each passing day, Dhruvi was tasting something new that Maayi prepared. One day he even mixed some red Mamidikaya pickle with steamed rice and a dollop of ghee for lunch! and he didn't scream SPICY!!!! **Mamidikaya - Mango And with each passing day, Dhruvi realized the rakshasas growled and shouted lesser and lesser when he ate on time and on a full belly! and Dhruvi had to no longer worry about the rakshasas attacking him! And soon Dhruvi was plucking guavas from maayi's garden and gobbling them up too! yum! mouthwatering, juicy, crunchy green guavas! - mixed with salt and red chilly powder! hand-picked from the garden And you know what Dhruvi has been gobbling this summer - tasty, juicy, sweet Totapuri mangoes - THE KING OF FRUITS! from the markets in Vijayawada. And as for the rakshasas...they just FLED from his belly!
author: Vani B
illustrator: Ajit Narayan; Archana Sreenivasan; Diana James; Greystroke; Priya Kuriyan; Rae  Zachariah; Rijuta Ghate; Shailja Jain Chougule

title: Beautiful butterflies
text: Joey and Savy loved colourful things. And the best place to see different colours was small little garden in their schools left wing. They would go there hopping along, Holding hands and singing a song! What an amazing sight lay ahead, There were butterflies in yellow, green, blue and red! From one flower to another they do hop, Fluttering their wings non stop! The scent of the flowers, was oh so sweet! Many butterflies Savy and Joey did meet. Butterflies were such a beauty, Spreading pollen was one of their duty. Beautiful designs their wings had, In their company no one could be sad! They created such positive vibes There were butterflies of different breeds and tribe! A yellow butterfly came and sat on Joeys face, Oh, with excitement it made her heart race. ‘If I can hold it once.’ She thought. For she loved the butterflies a lot! The butterfly flew and went over a puddle. Joey ran after it, As she wanted to hold it and cuddle! But to her surprise she saw, Mumma and baby butterflies with an awe! As she went a little further to catch them, She saw an egg, a larva and a pupa under a stem. A little caterpilla r crawled by.. Eating leaves without any sigh! O what a beautiful day it had been! Beautiful butterflies Joey and Savy had seen! Being with nature is always a delight... It makes one feel so happy and bright!
author: Shristee Chandel Singh

title: Miss Laya's fantastic motorbike at the Railway Station
text: Summer vacations had begun. Minku and Tinku have been counting days to the vacation! They are off to meet their grandparents at Mysore. The bags are packed and the day has finally arrived! Rinku and Minku are very excited. Their mom has booked a cab that will take them to the station. It is 5:30 PM and the cab hasn't arrived. Amma is frantic and tries to reach the cab driver. The cab driver is stuck in a major traffic jam at Silk Board junction. "Oh no! what are we supposed to do? What if we miss the train? ", wail the kids. Amma is worried too. But looks like smart Minku knows what to do! She dials her teacher Ms.Laya, the games teacher at Big Tree School. Ms.Laya stays close by and agrees to drop them at the station. The kids and their mom let out a huge sigh of relief because Ms.Laya is a very helpful person. Ms.Laya arrives. The kids load their luggage on her motorbike. But the motorbike doesn't seem happy. There is a huge suitcase, two children and two adults to be seated on the bike! But looks like Ms.Laya always has a solution to any problem. Tinku is seated at the front. Minku and her mom are seated at the back!, while her mom holds on to the suitcase! Minku does a clap-clap, clap-clap, clap-clap, 6 times! Tinku does a dhup, dhup, dhup, jumping up and down three times and their mother counts backward - 9 - 8- 7 - 6-, 5- 4 3- 2- 1 - start! drrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrr... starts the motorbike......................drrrrrrrrrrrrrrrr...unmindful of the load it is carrying. Racing past speeding cars, BMTC buses and scooters, Ms.Laya and her passengers arrive at the station. There is no time to waste! They race past crowded platforms, stream past hawkers selling chai and porters carrying luggage to arrive at Platform 2. Minku and her family hop on to the train in the nick of time. The station master waves the green flag. The train starts to pull out of the station chug - chug - chug. Minku and Tinku wave to Ms.Laya and scream " Happy vacations Ma'am and THANK YOU!" Ms.Laya waves back. Ms.Laya and the motorbike go back home. They are tired at the end of the day but immensely happy to have helped the kids!
author: Vani B
illustrator: Abhishek Choudhury; Bhramara  Nayak; Louwrisa Blaauw; Rijuta Ghate; Santosh Pujari; Zainab Tambawalla

title: Buzzinga!! Lets learn about some bugs!
text: Our Earth is big and beautiful There's place for every animal! Short and tall, Big and small. Dragonfies and ants, Rhinos and elephants, Snakes and frogs, Wolves and dogs. Birds and bats, Lions and cats, Crabs and starfish, Sharks and jellyfish. Ants love anything sweet, Sugar is their favourite treat! Some ants bite, some don't bite, Red or black, but not white! Their head is round, They make no sound! They walk in a line, To reach home in time! All grasshoppers lea p, hop hop hop, They eat plant leaf, chomp chomp chomp, Their colour may be brown or leafy green, In a garden or field they can be seen. Earthworms are friends of plants, They have no legs or even hands! Earthworms are long and thin, Soft and wet, is their skin! Spiders weave lacy webs, And they have eight legs! The webs are pretty but sticky, So insects get trapped quickly! Crabs have two claws, that snap snap snap, Near a pond or sea, they nap nap nap! Tiny crab, huge crab, But never try to grab!
author: Swathi Bhat
illustrator: Debasmita Dasgupta; Deepa Balsavar; Greystroke; Herminder Ohri; Megha Vishwanath; Sanjay Sarkar; Vishnu  M Nair

title: Talkative Teja
text: Teja was a talkative boy. He loved talking about his school, his friends, vehicles, animals and almost everything under the sun. Teja asked many questions too. Thaatha* listened patiently to everything Teja had to say. *Thaatha- Grandfather in Telugu One day on his way back from school, Teja kept talking endlessly. But, Thaatha was not in a mood to listen to him that day. Suddenly, Teja stopped at a toy shop. He gazed at a toy he had been eyeing for a long time. He asked "Can you please buy me this red and black bike, Thaatha?" Thaatha thought of a plan to escape from Teja's chatter. He said, "Sure, but on one condition." Teja jumped eagerly and said, "What is it?" Thaatha said, "If you keep quiet and not talk to anyone till I come back from my evening walk, I will buy you the bike." Teja said, “Done. I accept your challenge, Thaatha.” All set to stay quiet, a determined Teja entered the house. Thaatha left for his evening walk. “Will you have milk, Teja?” asked *Baamma. Teja nodded his head without saying a word. Baamma was surprised as she had never seen him so silent. *Baamma – Paternal grandmother in Telugu. Sometime later, Teja's Akka* walked in. “Hey Teja! What did Vanaja miss teach at school today? I saw you having fun with a rope in the playground”, she said. Teja just nodded his head again and didn’t utter a word. Teja’s Akka was puzzled. She thought he would jump with joy to answer such a question and share what had happened. *Akka - Elder sister in Telugu After a little while, Teja’s parents came home from office. “Teja, what happened to your craft project? Did the teacher like your greeting card?”, asked Amma* eagerly. “Teja, you will be thrilled to hear what happened near the market today”,said Nanna*. Though he was excited about all that his parents wanted to share and know, he tried hard not to speak. Teja focused on playing with his toy car. *Amma- Mother in Telugu *Nanna - Father in Telugu “Don’t you want to know what happened?” asked Nanna. “Is everything alright, Teja?” asked Amma. Teja’s Akka and Baamma walked into the hall to tell his parents that he hadn’t spoken a word that evening. “Teja, say something!” said Amma. “You are such a chatterbox. What happened to you today?” asked Baamma. “Let’s take him to the doctor!” said Nanna. “We must consult the doctor. Poor boy! Hope nothing is wrong with him” prayed Baamma. Even after hearing about the consultation with the doctor, Teja didn’t open his mouth. He was as tight-lipped as he could get, all-determined to win his bet with Thaatha. All the worried members of Teja’s family were on their way to the hospital. They met Teja’s Thaatha on their way. “Where are you all going without me?” asked Thaatha. “Looks like Teja has lost his voice. He hasn’t said anything ever since he came from school. We are taking him to the doctor”, explained Baamma. Thaatha figured out that Teja had won in the challenge and burst into laughter. “Oh no! Did you all think he lost his voice?” he exclaimed. Thaatha told them all about the deal between him and Teja. “You win, Teja! Say something now and show them that you are alright.” said Thaatha. “Before you forget about the promise you made, can we go to the toy store T haatha?” smiled Teja. The relieved family members returned home. Teja and Thaatha headed out to bring home his hard-earned reward.
author: Pavithra V S

title: Where do bubbles go?
text: Where do bubbles go? I blew a bubble And it flew away. I blew another bubble And it popped right away. A question floats into my mind. Where do bubbles go? So off I venture to learn and find. I ask my Papa and he says “ Hmm, won’t bubble stop after they pop ”. I see my Momma with a wet mop and a raised eyebrow. Before I pop my question, she demands “ Did you spill the bubble juice on the kitchen floo r? ” Without answering her, I sneak into my room upstairs to escape the cleaning chore. I find my sister studying for her science test. I ask her “ Do you know where bubbles go?” She shoos me away like an annoying pest, And after I plead her again, she opens her mouth and blurts out a jar full of jargons. “ Bubbles pop due to evaporation of water content, air turbulence, contact to dry objects and many times due to dryness and one more, the Surface Tension ”. Impressed with her answer and she goes back to her pile of books. I think maybe she is right as she reads a lot of books and has a nerdy look! But aren’t bubbles full of fun? So to the garden, I make a run. I see my grand-mom sitting in her favorite long white-cane chair, Knitting a baby blue sock, without a care. I ask her “ Do you know where bubbles go? ” She says with a smile “As a matter of fact, I know.” She puts her hand into her knitting basket, And pulls out a sheet of a bubble wrap. (almost the size of a baby blanket!!!) While popping the bubbles one by one and putting the bubble wrap on her lap, She tells “ The bubbles which escape turn into bubble wrap ”. I hug her tightly and look over her shoulders And see a chalk-white arrow mark pointing to a place "Where the sidewalk ends And before the street begins" I blow her a kiss and walk that slow measured walk to that place. Left first, Right next, A roundabout at the end. A quick hop over the mulberry hedge, A brave step beyond the white picket fence. Trotting down on a loopy slope, Galloping up on a stretchy uphill route. Under the cold-old creaky water bridge, Over the age-old, wind-blown, sturdy brown-boulders, And through the silver-white snowcapped tall wise mountains, I finally see a giant wooden purple door bolted with an ornate delicate silver lock, of which only I hold the magical golden key. I put the key into the lock and turn it. I hear the click of the opening lock. I push the heavy door wide open, And I see A giant bubble tree upon which Bubbles of all sizes, from all over the world, Have come to their nest After the children who played with them have gone to rest.
author: Gowri Nagarajan

title: Reya's Big Surprise
text: Say Hi to Reya! She's 8 years old. She loves reading, drawing and watching cartoons. She adores animals.Of all the animals, she loves Elephants the most! Today, Reya and her class have gone on a school excursion to the city zoo. She was thrilled to see so many animals, but the best was yet to come... The Elephant compound came into view. Reya squealed in delight as she saw Elephants for the first time in real life. They were bigger than she had thought. She spotted a mother Elephant and its cute baby Elephant. When Reya got back home, she told her parents and her brother Rohan all about her lovely zoo trip. Rohan didn't look pleased and said "You know Reya, the zoo is a cruel place. It keeps animals in a jail without any freedom." Her father said "Yes, that's true but the zoo also shelters injured animals from the wild and rescued animals from the circus." Reya went to bed feeling sad for the animals, especially the Elephants in the zoo. In all the shows she watched and books she read, the Elephants were always free and happy in the wild. She was so sad, she forgot that tomorrow was her birthday. "HAPPY BIRTHDAY!" yelled Rohan to wake her up next morning... "Here sleepyhead ", he said as he handed Reya a surprise gift. Reya woke up all excited and tore apart the wrapping. Inside was a plush toy, you guessed it, a cute & cuddly elephant! "YIPPEE!" yelled Reya as she jumped for joy! "Thank you, Rohan! I shall call him ' Zolu '." In her mind, she and Zolu had already begun exciting adventures in the jungle. A bigger surprise awaited Reya. Her dad had booked vacation tickets to visit the Masinagudi forest reserve in Tamil Nadu, which is famous for its Elephant safaris. Reya was overjoyed and eagerly awaited her trip to see Elephants in their natural habitat. Do you love Elephants too? Come join Reya on her next adventure!
author: Arun Ramkumar

title: The Number Game
text: Mom says " Wake up, Anu… wake up… It’s 10 o'clock " Anu says " Please Ma... it's Sunday... Can I sleep for 5 minutes more? " Mom says " If you get up now, we can play number game all day, if not no games today " Anu says " Yahoo! " and wakes up. Mom asks " So, tell me how many toothbrushes do you have? " Anu says " I have 1 blue brush ". " That’s correct! " says Mom Mom asks " How many idlis do you want for breakfast? " Anu says " 2 Idlis! " Mom asks " Do you want 1 more? " Anu says " Yes " Mom asks " So, how many idlis did you eat? " Anu says " First I had 2 then 1... so 2+1 equals 3 " Mom says " Correct! That’s like my girl! " Mom says " Come, let’s go to the market and buy some vegetables " Mom asks " See there! How many coconut trees do you see on the street? " Anu says " 1, 2, 3 and 4... it’s 4 Ma " " Correct! " says Mom And that’s how it went... They kept playing all day...
author: Sushmita Viswanathan

title: Joey
text: Opening Page Dedication Page Not a very long time ago, there was a dog named Joey. His family was rather large, and everyone loved him. He loved everyone too. Anyone and Everyone Anyone who rang the door bell, or anyone who gave him food. Anyone who played with him, or anyone who crossed him during his walks. But even after all the love he gave, he was still left with more. He sat by the window and looked at the endless sky, and wondered if it could hold all his love. So he tied himself to love, and flew to the sky. On reaching the sky he pulled down a star, and every other from near and far. Like this he made space for his love in the sky, Which continues to shine on everyone, even though he has said good-bye. The End.
author: Sonal Choudhury

title: Vegetable soup for Amma
text: This is the house of Somu, a boy who was a very fussy eater. He made faces whenever he found vegetables in his food. He did not believe that vegetables make people strong and healthy. Somu tried his best to convince his Amma, not to add vegetables to his favourite food. But Amma was Amma. She knew what was best for her children. The mere sight of a vegetable would make Somu frown. He hated capsicums, broccoli, carrots, peas and radish too! One fine day, he came home after school, only to find the kitchen empty! His tummy was making weird noises. He was hungry. And so was his little sister, Soni. They found Amma in her room, weak and shivering! Soni was worried. Somu had to act fast. He immediately called his grandma for help. Ajji suggested that Amma be given a bowl of hot vegetable soup. Ajji told them the recipe and Soni wrote it down. They thanked Ajji for the help. Somu opened the refrigerator and looked at all the vegetables inside. They then made a list of what all they wanted to make a soup. Somu and Soni took out the vegetables they wanted and washed them clean. They later chopped the vegetables carefully, without getting hurt. Soni felt sad because Amma was unwell. Somu felt bad because he always made faces when she served him vegetables. When Ajji told them how to make soup, Somu and Soni thought it would be easy. But it wasn't easy after all! Somu now realised how difficult it was for Amma to cook for everyone, every day and take care of the family! Somu and Soni patiently waited for the vegetables to cook and finally when the soup was ready, they poured it into a serving bowl. They made soup on their own without the help of any elders in the house! Somu and Soni were thrilled. Now Amma can have the soup and get well soon... After having the soup, Amma did get well and hugged her children for all the efforts they put in. Even the neighbours were surprised. Now Somu does not make faces; he relishes vegetables instead. He now believes that vegetables make people strong and healthy. Amma, Somu and Soni ate their vegetables. Did you?
author: Adithimanasa T S

title: The Journey
text: "How long will it take for us to reach our village in Himachal?", Vihaan asked his mother as she tucked his shirt on the pants. "Oh, it will take more than 12 hours from here to reach the village. It's a long way to there," his mother replied back. As Vihaan's mother tied the laces of his shoes, his thoughts wandered to the village where they were travelling to. Many of his aunts, uncles and cousins lived there. Though he had met most of his cousins from village before, but that had happened when they came to the city where he lived in. He had never gone to meet them in their village in Himachal. He was very excited about meeting them and showing them his toys that he was carrying along. But there was one thing that he was even more excited about - The journey! He couldn't wait for the long travel to start and get on the various transports they had to take to reach there. As his mother packed the travel bag and readied the lunch box for the journey, he went to stand in the balcony to look at the passing vehicles. Looking at the vehicles was his favourite past-time. He had counted about 10 scooters, 2 bikes, 15 cycles, 5 cars when his mother called out that it was time for them to leave. Vihaan's mother carried a big bag for their journey while he carried his small backpack that had his lunch and water bottle. As they got down to the road, his mother called out for an auto rickshaw. They stacked their bags and sat inside the rickshaw. "Maa, are we about to reach the village?", Vihaan asked his mother as the rickshaw took a turn towards the metro station. "No my dear, it's still a long journey ahead", his mother replied. They got down at the metro station and boarded the train to the bus stand. As they settled inside the metro. Vihaan looked wide-eyed at the tall buildings and the city from the windows of the metro train. "Maa, are we about to reach village", he asked his mother again as the train went inside a long tunnel. "No my child, not so soon. Village is still far away," his mother told him. Soon the metro reached the bus stand where they had to take the bus to their village in Himachal. The went inside the bus stand, located their bus and took the seats. As the bus started, night had fallen and Vihaan soon slept cosily on the seat with his mother. Next morning as the day cracked, Vihaan woke up to a sun beaming down the tallest mo untains he had ever seen. He rubbed his eyes and excitedly asked his mother, "Is this a village?". His mother smiled at him and replied, "Yes it is a village but it is not our village." A few hours passed before the bus stopped at its destination. Everyone picked up their bags and got down, and so did Vihaan and his mother. "Is this our village, Maa?", Vihaan asked. "Yes, it's our village. We've reached. Look there who has come to receive us," his mother smiled at him. Even from far Vihaan could make out his cousins. He was very happy to see them. As he was about to run towards them, he took a look back at the long journey he had made to the village from the city. And now he couldn't wait for them to make the return journey back to their city.
author: ritika puri
illustrator: Ajanta Guhathakurta; Kaveri Gopalakrishnan; Kruttika Susarla; Lauren   Nel; Sonali Zohra; Suvidha Mistry; Upamanyu  Bhattacharyya; Vishnu  M Nair; Zainab Tambawalla

title: Planet SafeYou's Messenger
text: Dia and Jon were best friends. They loved going to school and they loved their teacher Miss Nitya very much. Miss Nitya had a big collection of books and told them many stories and read them many books. One day while Miss Nitya was reading them a story about aliens and the entire class was absorbed in it. Suddenly they heard a loud crash. Everybody was shocked. They all ran outside the class to see where the noise came from. A big spaceship had landed in the school playground. The spaceship was beeping loudly. The children crowded around the spaceship, they all were slightly scared. Just then they heard a beeping sound and some muffled voices. Since the children were very scared, Miss Nitya asked them to step aside so she could investigate. She cautiously stepped inside the spaceship. There was smoke everywhere. After five minutes, Miss Nitya came out holding a cute looking creature in her arms. The creature looked like a teddy bear. She brought him outside. The creature was an alien. He was wearing a badge that had a strange symbol on it. There was a Hash # inside a circle. Perhaps that was his name for the creature wouldn’t utter a word. They all decided to call him Hash bear. Hash bear was taken inside the classroom. The children gave him food and water and pretty soon he warmed up to everyone. The creature however hadn’t uttered a word so far. Soon it was play time so everyone rushed out to the playground. At the playground... Dia saw a beautiful butterfly. She ran behind it and tried to catch it but the butterfly fluttered off. Jon saw a bird hopping about. He quietly tiptoed so he could catch it but the birdie saw Jon and flew away. A few children were troubling a puppy. They were pulling its tail and poking it with sticks. Though tiny, the puppy began to bark…woof woof woof… Just then Hash Bear began speaking. He was speaking a funny language that no one could understand. Then he took out a strange looking gadget from his backpack. The gadget looked like a remote. Hash bear switched it on. It was a translator. Hash bear spoke in his language and the translator translated his words into the language the children understood. ‘You are a genius Hash bear.’, the children shouted. ‘What if someone tried to catch you - what will you do?’, asked Hash Bear The children looked confused. Soon they all gathered around Hash Bear. ‘You will run away from there, won’t you? Just like the butterfly and the bird did. What if someone tried to hurt you? Wouldn’t you do something to protect yourselves? Just like the puppy did even though it was a tiny puppy. It barked at the naughty children.’ ‘Do you children like swimming?’, Hash Bear went on ‘Yes I love swimming. I have a lovely swimsuit which is blue in colour.’, Said Dia excitedly ‘What about you Jon? How does your costume look?’, asked Hash Bear ‘I have two swimming trunks. One is red and the other is green.’, Said Jon proudly. ‘So a girl’s swimming costume looks different from a boy’s swimming costume? Doesn’t it?’, Asked Hash Bear The children nodded in agreement. Then Hash Bear showed them a picture. It was the picture of a swimming costume. ‘Children, on my planet we have a very important rule. It is called the swimming costume rule. Do you want to know what that rule is?’ The children wanted to know. ‘No one can touch you in the parts that your swimming costume covers - Chest - Bottom The part between the legs or your private organs And add one more thing to this list - Your mouth.’ ‘When someone hugs you with love, like mamma’s cuddles and papa’s kiss on the forehead. Grandpa and granny’s tickles and you like them for they make you feel loved. It is called Good touch. But if someone hurts you, slaps you or breaks the swimming costume rule - you feel uncomfortable and yucky- it is called bad touch. Whenever anyone tries to touch you or asks you to touch them in the parts that the swimming costume covers and your mouth you have to shout STOP! really loudly. Can you do that?’ Asked Hash Bear ‘STOOOOOOOOP!’, shouted all the children really really loudly ‘Sometimes people might say let’s play a game. Tickle me on my lips, tickle me on my chest, tickle me on my bottom, tickle me on the part between my legs - What will you say or do?’, Asked Hash Bear ‘NOOOOOOO!’, shouted all the children really really loudly ‘Well done little friends. Shout STOP and run away for HELP to someone in your circle of TRUST and never ever keep a secret. It is never your fault.’, added Hash Bear ‘What is the circle of trust?’ asked Jon ‘The circle of trust has people who love and care about you in it.’, Said Hash Bear ‘Ah! my circle of trust has Mom, dad, Miss Nitya and you Jon.’, Said Dia. Just then they all heard someone clapping. It was Miss Nitya. ‘Very well done Hash bear. Where did you learn about all this from?’, she asked him ‘I learnt about good touch and bad touch and about staying safe from my family back home. I come from a planet called SafeYou and we are on a mission to make this world a safe place for children. Wherever my space ship crash lands, I choose two messengers who then help me spread the message far and wide’, He said In Planet SafeYou we sing a song ‘My Body belongs to me me me My mouth, my chest, my bottom, and even my knee knee knee A good touch makes me feel warm and fuzzy...ee...ee and a bad touch makes me feel bad and sort of Yucky…ee...ee When you feel Yucky…ee...ee Shout STOP, Shout No and flee flee flee Stay Safe, have fun and be happyy…ee…ee…ee.' The children loved the song and they all sang along. Just then the wind started blowing ‘woooooo’ and a storm began coming. The children ran inside the classroom to be safe. Another rocket ship landed in the playground. It was time for Hash bear to leave. Just before leaving he said, ‘Dia and Jon I have chosen you as SafeYou messengers. You have to spread this message now. Go and teach this song and all the rules to all your friends.’ Dia and Jon felt mighty proud. Then Hash bear took out two badge and pinned them on their jackets. The badges had a Hash symbol inside a circle. ‘Hash stands for You and the circle stands for your circle of trust. The symbol means a Safe You within your circle of Trust.’ The children cheered aloud. Dia, Jon, Miss Nitya and the children gave Hash Bear a nice and tight hug. One that made them feel nice and not yucky! Hash bear sat in his rocket ship and went Whoosh! up in the sky Dia and Jon shared this story with me and I am sharing it with you. Now I nominate you as a SafeYou messenger. So dear friend, go and share this story, the song and the rules with every child you know. And hey! Don’t forget to make yourselves a SafeYou badge. Stay Safe, have fun and be happy!
author: Rohini  Vij
illustrator: 211 Studio; Abhilasha Sukrut Khatri; Angie & Upesh; Catherine Groenewald; Helga Parekh; Jithin Jacob; Kalyani  Ganapathy; Lavanya  Naidu; Lavanya Karthik; Priya Kuriyan; Rijuta Ghate; Samidha Gunjal; Santosh Pujari; Sarah Bouwer; Shailja Jain Chougule; Shambhavi Singh; Sheetal Thapa; Suvidha Mistry; Taposhi Ghoshal

title: Going to Japan
text: Anam's mother's brother was visiting them at their home. He lived in Japan and had brought many gifts for Anam and her mother. He got Anam a traditional Japanese Hina doll, a kimono dress, a hand fan and a bird shaped kite. She loved all the gifts that her uncle got her. Her uncle spent most of his time during his visit playing with Anam and telling her stories from Japan. He spent some days with Anam's family before flying back to Japan. The day her uncle left, Anam felt very sad. She missed her uncle and wanted to go with him to Japan. She wanted to see all the things he talked about - volcano mountain, shrines, flying lanterns, noodles in a museum. She wanted to live in a world that was more interesting than her own hometown. So she set out on foot, following her uncle to Japan. As she walked on the road her uncle's car had taken, she got confused whether it had turned left from or right from the signal. Just when she thought it must have been a right, she saw her favourite sweets shop on the left. Now taking the left turn made more sense to her. As she approached the sweets shop, Saleem uncle, the shopkeeper, recognised his favourite customer. "So where are you going Anam beti?", Saleem uncle asked her. "I am going to Japan, Saleem uncle," Anam replied. "That's wonderful. Here have some jalebi for your journey. Maybe you won't get them in Japan," Saleem uncle said offering her a jalebi. Anam walked along, nibbling at the jalebi and wondering about her new life in Japan. She had walked only a block when she saw Preeti, Asif and Suman climbing a Jamun tree. "Hey Anam, where are you walking to?," asked Suman holding on to the jamuns she had collected. "I am going to Japan," said Anam boastfully. "Oh that will be fun. But before you go, come up and have some jamuns with us. Maybe you won't get them in Japan," Preeti said. Anam climbed the tree, collected handful of jamuns and walked on. She kept the jamuns safe in her pockets for her journey ahead. As Anam reached the crossroad and contemplated in her mind her next course, she saw Meenu, Habiba and Kiran playing hopscotch in the park. "Hey, Anam! What's up?" called out Habiba. "I am going to Japan," replied Anam. "Do you want to play with us for a while before leaving? What if no one plays hopscotch in Japan?" asked Kiran. Anam thought maybe she could spare some time to play with her friends. Also, it'll be a long time before she may meet them again, once she leaves for Japan. Anam, Meenu, Habiba and Kiran played hopscotch for a long time and then played with rope and later with marbles. The four friends also gobbled up all the jamuns which Anam had collected. Anam didn't realise that the sun had set by the time they finished playing. "We all are going home now, Anam. Good luck with your journey to Japan," shouted Meenu as she ran along with Habiba and Kiran back to her home. By now Anam was very tired and hungry and the thought of going to Japan did not seem appealing anymore. Japan will not have any of her friends, nor her favourite sweets shop, neither the jamun trees. And most importantly, Japan will not have her mother. The thought of her mother made Anam rush back to her house. As she ran back she thought, "What if the city I lived is not as interesting as Japan, but it is my home nonetheless."
author: ritika puri
illustrator: Angie & Upesh; Jemma Jose; Priya Kuriyan; Rohit Kelkar; Samidha Gunjal; Soumya Menon; Vinayak Varma

title: SANUs NEW CYCLE
text: Sanus Father: Such a wonderful day, Sanu – can you hear the chirping of the birds? Or smell the wonderful fragrance from the wet garden soil? Sanu: Yes Papa, I too like the smell of wet soil like you. Sanu: Papa, see there – Khrisha is riding her new green cycle. I too want a cycle, just like Khrishas. Sanus Father: OK. When we visit the market, I will get you a new cycle, just like Khrishas. Sanu: Papa, I know where we can get cycles. Come, let me show you the shops. Sanu – Papa, lets go this shop (Sanu and her father walk into a bank) Sanu – Uncle, do you have a cycle? I want a green colored cycle. Banker: Beta, this is a bank; you can get money here to buy a cycle, but we do not have cycles here. Sanu – Uncle, I want to buy a cycle. Do you have a cycle? Chemist – This is a medical store, you will get all kinds of medicines, creams, and antiseptics here; but no cycles! And incase you ever happen to fall off a cycle, we have bandages as well. Sanu – Uncle, I want to buy a cycle. Please give me a green colored cycle. Dairy Owner- Oh, this is a Dairy – you can have fresh milk, curd, and lassi over here. It will make your bones strong, and give you energy to go cycling, but we do not have a cycle. Sanu – Uncle, please can you give me a cycle? Bakery Owner- I can give you fresh bread, cakes and pastries, which you can enjoy after a good round of cycling. But, we do not have cycles over here. Sanu – Thank you Papa for bringing me to a cycle shop. I like the green cycle, kept at that corner. Sanu - Thank you Papa for the cycle. I am enjoying the ride.
author: Manish Gajjaria
illustrator: Aindri C; Henu; Kabini  Amin; Ketan Raut; Khushbu Vala; Preeti Krishnamurthy; Rahul Kulkarni; Rijuta Ghate; Santosh Pujari

title: KHRISHA GOES TO THE MOON
text: Khrishas Friend Navya, pointing to the moon which is just about emerging from behind the clouds, to Khrishas father – Uncle, look, there is such a white big colored ball there coming out from behind the clouds. Papa – Navya, that is the moon which is emerging from behind the clouds. The moon is an astronomical body which is thousands of kilometres away from the earth, and rotates around the earth. It reflects the light from the Sun, and thus appears like a white colored round shaped ball. Navya – Uncle, Khrisha has thrown the ball, and now we cant find it. Khrisha – where have you thrown the ball?? Khrisha – I have thrown the ball very far away; its now on the Moon. Navya – Go to the moon, and get the ball now. Khrisha – Dont worry, I will go to the moon on my rocket, and get the ball back for you. Papa – Do you know girls, that our countrys premier space agency, ISRO is working on sending humans to the moon. And probably, if you are lucky, you might be the fortunate ones to go to the moon on one of ISROs rockets! Papa - If you girls decide to become scientists, you can design your own rockets as well!
author: Manish Gajjaria
illustrator: Angie & Upesh; Avishek Sen; David Knight; Fahad Faizal; P Tamizh muhil; Rijuta Ghate; Suvidha Mistry

title: Mission Dosa
text: Grrrrrrr Grrrrrr Grrrrr, went the desert cooler at Daadi's house. Every summer Deepa and her Didi stayed with their strict Daadi. Both of them loved watching TV and playing carrom. But their favorite timepass was finishing Daadi's chiwda and ladoos. They got scolded by Daadi every now and then. Daadi stayed alone on the third floor of a building. The building was at Aath Rasta Chowk - a square which had eight lanes instead of four. This colony was like a flower with eight petals. Zzzzzzoooomm. Deepa was learning to skate and Didi used a wheelchair. So they would often race in the corridor outside. Until Daadi came yelling after them. They didn't mind Daadi because they had each other. Tantantantantan ….. One Friday evening, Deepa and Didi were in the balcony. They saw a man pushing a cart full of giant steel dabbas. He also had a huge tawa which looked like a blackboard to Deepa. "Wow! I think he has Dosas, Deepa", said Didi. Deepa asked "Dhosaas? What is that?" Didi explained: "Dosa is a moon shaped roti made out of rice" "It is soft… ….as well as crispy" "It is served with hot sambhar… …as well as cool chutneys" "It is rolled into a tunnel… …with some tasty potato bhaji tucked inside" "YUMMM…" both of them roared at once, looking at each other. They really, really, really wanted it. But they saw the man moving fast towards the end of the lane. "I can run down and get it", said Deepa. "But we don't have money", Didi reminded. "Wait!" she said. The man reached the end of the lane and turned, and Didi also turned her wheelchair into the hall. She started going to Daadi's room. "Daadi, you look so tired today" Daadi raised her grey eyebrows. "You do so much work. Making chiwda, laddoo, filling the cooler tank, preparing lunch, preparing dinner….." Didi went on and on. Daadi was surprised. "How about this, you relax today and let us take care of dinner?" said Didi. Deepu peeped into the room and giggled. Tantantantan… the sound grew louder, as the man was coming closer again. Daadi understood at once, that this is nothing but teamwork for Mission Dosa. She took out a 50 rupee note from her pink batua and gave it to Didi. She even smiled a little. Perhaps even her mouth was watering, Didi thought. Didi rushed back with her excited hands on the wheels. Deepa was already holding her skates in one hand and a giant steel plate in another. As soon as she got the money, Zzzzoooommm. Deepu ran down and put on her skates. But the man had disappeared. She looked up at the balcony, and Didi looked as worried as her. Tantantan …the sound grew faint. "If he is not in this lane", Didi told her, "he must be in one of the other seven lanes." Deepa took off. She skated into the second lane, but he wasn't there. She checked the third lane and the fourth and the fifth. The man was nowhere to be seen and the sound was nowhere to be heard. Uhh Phh Uhh Phh Tired, Deepa started panting and taking big and heavy breaths in the sixth lane. Through her rising and falling nose traveled a sweet and salty smell. Mmmmm … She started following the fragrance. It grew stronger and stronger as she skated into the seventh lane and Tantantantan … the sound was loud and clear once again. The man was right there, making Dosas for two ladies. Deepa skated and reached the cart and Bam! She slammed the plate onto the steel dabba. The ladies were surprised and started staring at Deepa. She cleared her throat. "Hello. Are both of you sisters? I also want Dhosaas for me and my sister" she told them as they smiled. The man grinned too. "Oh oh and one more for my Daadi okay?," she giggled. Deepa skated back very slowly and reached home to Didi and Daadi. Nom Nom Nom Nom... Mission Dosa was successful. Have you ever been on a mission with someone? Isn't it interesting how two people, however similar or different they are, can play equal roles in teamwork? All of us have strengths and weaknesses. While some are visible, some, not so much. Just like Deepu and her Didi who had different skills and qualities, people with different abilities can not only eat yummy food together, but also be friends or love each other.
author: Rajashree Gandhi
illustrator: Aindri C; Antra Khurana; Ashok Sharma; Diana James; Jayesh Sivan; Jesse  Breytenbach; Jit  Chowdhury; Lavanya Karthik; Paneendra  Suresh; Rae  Zachariah; Renuka Rajiv; Sandhya Prabhat; Shreya  Sen; Shrujana Shridhar; Shyami Sathiaseelan; Sonal Gupta Vaswani; Sonali Zohra; Soumya Menon; Sunaina  Coelho

title: WE ARE A FAMILY
text: I hate them! I hate! I…” She begins to put the torn paper together like pieces of a puzzle. “What did they tell you?” she asks. “They always talk about their father. When they ask me, I make up stories and they start teasing me…” he mutters. “Aai, why don’t we stay with our Baba? Why are we not like all other families?” he asks. "It’s true, our family is different. Every family is unique, both in human and animal world.” “You see, the elephant herd is always led by Aaji, the Grandmother elephant. A family of women and children, the father elephant never lives with his family.” Bhiku imitates, “I’m a baby elephant stuck in mud, help me!” “Right away to your rescue, my little calf!” Aai giggles. “We are the Elephant family!” they trumpet. “You know, our neighbours are like the Orcas, the killer whales from the Dolphin family,” says Aai. “How, Aai?” “From five to forty members, the Orcas live in pods. A joint family, where all live together.” “During Ganesh festival, I wonder how many ladoos their Aaji would have to make?” asks Bhiku. “Ha..Ha.. Maybe, forty ladoos or more!” laughs Aai. “Sometimes I wonder what happens to those children who don’t have both mother and father?” questions Bhiku. “A lot of times, such children are adopted by families. These parents are godly people. They are like the Northern Elephant Seals.” “How, Aai?” “Due to a crowded beach, some of the pups get separated from their family. An adult seal adopts a lost pup and becomes its parent.” “Aai, Mitu stays with her Papa. She says her Papa is her Mumma too!” “They are like a family of Seahorses. The father seahorse takes care of the eggs in his pouch until they are ready to hatch.” “She comes out of her dad’s tummy! What a hue and cry! Peek-a-boo! I am a little fry.” “That’s a good try!” Aai hugs Bhiku. “Good news! A baby girl is born to your aunt and uncle!” “Let me guess, what kind of family they are?” wonders Aai. Pat comes Bhiku's reply, “Just like the Clownfishes make a special room before the arrival of their baby, aunt and uncle have been working together to prepare a nursery for their new born.” “Can you please make your bed?” Aai asks. “Aai, but the Orangutan babies take four years to learn to make their own beds in tree tops. Yawwnn… Can you make my bed?” says Bhiku coyly. “Remember, we are not the Orangutan family," smiles Aai. Did you know? Elephants 1) Elephant families have a matriarchal head, meaning that an older, experienced lady elephant leads the herd. 2) Elephants are known to develop strong, intimate bonds between friends and family. They form lifelong friendships with each other, and they even mourn the death of their loved ones. 3) Elephants actually do walk in single file when they go in search of food and water. The calves will sometimes hold on to their mother’s tails with their trunks to keep up. Did you know? Orcas 1) Orcas make family bonds that last for a lifetime, they will travel together for the rest of their lives and are protective over young & old orcas. 2) Social structure of Orcas is as complex and evolved as elephants and humans. Also known as "the wolves of the sea" because they occasionally hunt in packs. 3) The use of dialects for communication and certain social behaviors are passed down through each Orcas species and this has been dubbed as animal culture. Did you know? Seahorse 1) The courtship between two seahorses involves a "dance" where they entwine their tails​ and may change colors. 2) Unlike any other species, male seahorses become pregnant. They have a brood pouch to carry the eggs. 3) The father seahorse monitors the salt levels inside his pouch to ensure they match the surrounding environment to keep his baby healthy. Did you know? Northern Elephant Seal 1)The seals may be solitary at sea, but become very social on the beach. Even during nonbreeding times of the year, they will lie close together on the sand. 2) Once a year, hundreds of Northern elephant seals are born on the Ano Nuevo islands. Sadly, due to rough surf, crowded beach, some of the pups each year get separated from their family. An adult seal adopts the young pup. 3) Right after birth, the mother will nudge and cry out to her newborn pup until it responds by moving and crying back. Did you know? Clownfish 1) Clownfish create very close bonds with those that they will mate with. 2) Even though very large amounts of eggs can be deposited most of them won’t survive long enough for a Clownfish to develop. The males will guard the eggs for several days to help them have a chance of being able to survive. 3) Before arrival of their young one, the clownfish meticulously cleans the anemone to transform it into a perfect nursery. Did you know? Orangutan 1) In the rainforests of Sumatra, the mother Orangutan looks after her young ones for eight years, longer than any other animal single parent. 2) The babies take three to four years to learn to make their own mattress for sleeping in tree tops. She helps them find edible fruit and when these treats are ripe and good to eat. 3) Mothers and their children have a very close bond. They stick together for the baby’s first six or seven years of life.
