Then she went 'Miaoooww', even louder than usual. “I will take her back tomorrow!” roared Sringeri Srinivas. “Silly cow!” Then, Shiva, the eldest son, had an idea. “Amma, just for now, let us keep Laxmi and Manuli on the other side of the house,” he said. “Then our other cows will not hear her even if she miaows.” So they moved Laxmi to her new home. Manuli got a new basket near Laxmi. Once Laxmi was gone, the other cows began to give milk again. Manuli wandered around the farm, making friends with all the cows. Many people came from everywhere to see the cow that went 'Miaow'. They paid extra to taste her sweet milk. They also bought a lot of Sringeri's famous banana halwa. Sringeri stopped frowning. He was happy with Laxmi, the special cow. Then all the cows wanted to be friends with her too. Suddenly, Manuli said, “Moo!” One evening, the family sat down to watch TV. It was not a 'Miaow'. It was a small, cat-sized 'Moo'. Moo? Everyone looked at the cat, who was swishing her tail like a cow. “Moo?” asked Sringeri, getting angry again. “Why is this cat mooing?” Aha! Now that is another story.
author: Rohini Nilekani

title: Shh! What's That?
text: “Good night Dia. Good night Tara!” Dada turns off the light. Fliff! Swish! What was that? Tara looks at Dia. Dia looks at Tara. “Monster!” Dia and Tara hide under their blanket. “What are we going to do?” says Dia. Clunk! Uff! “Let’s scare it away,” Tara says. “With a monster of our own,” says Dia. “The scarf-inator!” “Who has a football head.” “I think we scared it,” Tara says. “Oh no, it’s getting up!” Dia hides. Yaa! Aiyo! “Quick, get your sheet,” Dia says. “We’ll make a sheet-osaur!” “Where is the torch?” Tara asks. Dia points at the street light. Flump Flump! “And I’ll use the torch to make a chair-acabra with my raincoat,” Dia says. “Two monsters should scare it away,” Tara says. “Move the torch close. We’ll make chair-acabra bigger!” Shump Boof! Tara waves her hands under her sheet. Clish! Creaaak! “What are you both doing?” Dada says. “ You are the monster?” Tara and Dia yell. “What monster?” Click! Blink! Ha ha! Hoo hoo! They all laugh and make shadow monsters.
author: Sanjana  Kapur

title: Pride Leads To Danger
text: Once upon a time, in a lake, lived a gang of crows and other of sparrows. The leader of the crows was calm and peaceful but the leader of the sparrows was very proud and confident. he was proud of his flight. he knew many ways of flying. one day, the leaders of the sparrows challenged the leader of crows to a flying race. The leader of crows accepted the challenge. In a few minutes, the race begun. The crow and the sparrow raced off in full speed. after a while, the leader of the crows slowed down his speed for he should save energy for some more time. The leader of sparrows continued with his swift speed. When he came across a sea, he begun to swell up. He was about to drown but at the correct time the leader of crows saved him. he said, "Because of your pride you were going to drown.But I saved you. The leader of the sparrows said, "Thanks. I will not show pride to anyone from today".
author: Krishna and Priya Rai
illustrator: Madhuri Purandare; Padmanabh; Sonal Goyal; Sumit Sakhuja

title: Stories Are So Much Fun
text: Story Description Paul and Pam are neighbours. One day, when Paul wants to play, Pam just wants to read. Paul tries to understand Pam by reading her story books, and suddenly he is transported into a world of creativity. Pre-Reading Vocabulary and Phonics Discrete ﻿dis-cr-eat ﻿ ﻿Pam read very privately and discrete ly. Satisfied ﻿sat-iss-f-eye-d ﻿Paul was not satisfied with his toys and he wanted to play more. Venomous ﻿ven-um-uss ﻿The snake was very dangerous and venomous. Enthralled ﻿in-thr-all-d ﻿Paul was enthralled by the exciting stories he had read. Paul saw Pam relaxing on the swing under the tree. "What do you think, Hopper?" said Paul to his little friend. "She looks busy. I should scare her now." "You should be careful," said Hopper. "You remember what happened the last time you tried scaring her." "Oh, yeah," said Paul. "She suddenly turned around and fired a water pistol in my face. I'll be more discrete this time." Paul's attempt at throwing a paper plane at Pam failed. Besides, Pam was too absorbed in her reading. She was enjoying fantasy and mythical stories in the books she'd borrowed from the library. "So the prince used the girl's long hair to climb up the tower?" said Pam to herself. "That sounds silly. Surely he would pull her hair out." "What are you doing?" said Paul, sneaking up on Pam. "I'm reading some library books," said Pam. "They look boring. Let's go and play down by the river. It's much more exciting." "I'd rather read these stories," said Pam, trying to send Paul away. Pam read some cat stories with witches and goblins. She laughed to herself and Paul heard her. "How can she be so taken in by stories?" he said. "What could be more fun than throwing huge boulders in the pond and catching fish?" Paul paced around to find someone to play with, while Pam sat satisfied reading her books. "I bet you can't beat me to the river," said Paul. "Let's have a race. The winner gets that lollipop." "No, thanks," said Pam. "I'm busy." Pam had read up to her last library book. She had been reading all afternoon. "Not fair," said Paul. "We go back to school tomorrow. Can't we have fun today?" "Go and play something with Hopper," said Pam. "Like hide and seek." Paul knew Hopper always won at that game. "It's no good," said Paul to Mr. Caterpillar, his favourite cuddly toy. "I'll have to wait for Pam to get bored of her books. Then she'll play again." Paul decided he would learn to play on his own. Paul played his snare drum, floated his boat on the river, pretended to fight with a sword, and jumped over some hills on his trike. Nothing seemed to be enjoyable, so he rolled some marbles. "It's more exciting to share fun with a friend," he said. The next day, Paul found Pamela after school. She was reading a new tale about a venomous snake in a forest. "Wow," said Paul, discovering the book. "These stories have characters like us!" He was so enthralled, he ran straight to the library to get his own books before it closed. When Paul got to the library, it had already closed. Feeling upset, Pam noticed how much he wanted to read, and she gave him the books she had borrowed from the library. Paul was so excited to get home and start reading. He stayed up past his bed time reading. Paul and Pam sat reading in a tree. Pam was reading a book about a sneaky, swindling man and his dog taking part in races. They cheated by setting up traps for the other drivers so they would win. But their traps always backfired. "That sounds really funny," said Paul. "I imagined that we were in the snake book." "You did?" said Pam. Paul talked about how they rode on a bull, facing off the furious red cobra by firing arrows, while also trying to rescue a princess called Ping. Pam attacked the cobra with her sword as Ping hid behind a rock. The cobra tried to snatch them in its mouth. Finally, Pam slayed the cobra after Paul shot it with arrows. The cobra collapsed and they both rescued Ping, taking her back to the palace to be safe with her family. Paul and Pam borrowed more library books, reading about stories such as the brave sailors surviving a rocky storm, the mermaid, the genie in the lamp and the flying partners. Sometimes friends got involved and played other parts in the stories, such as Peter Pun. The children entered into an entirely new world - a world where anything was possible. A world created in stories that pulled their attention in. "A flying rocking horse?" said Paul. "That's not very realistic." "The trick is to say yes to anything," said Pam. "Allow yourself to go there in your mind. See where your imagination takes you." Pam went to bed after reading her new stories. In the morning she woke up with a great energy, and a want to go outside and bring the stories into the world. The other neighbourhood kids joined in. Paul and Pam worked together to take the adventure stories out of the books and put them into real life. The stories just grew out of the page, and now their world was much more colourful and interesting, all thanks to an interest in reading. "Who would have known that reading could lead to this?" said Paul. Post-Reading Questions What triggered Paul's want to read books? What did Paul and Pam discover they could do with the stories? Re-read. Ask: What did Paul discover about playing? Re-read pages 13-15. Ask: What did Paul and Pam do with the snake story? Re-read. Ask: ﻿According to Pam, what is the secret to having a good imagination? ﻿ What is your favourite book? What character would you like to play?
author: Hello English

title: Friends Under the Summer Sun
text: Nimmi peered out of the window and yowled like a cat. Down in the park, her friends were busy playing. She turned to Ma, big saucer-like eyes misting over with tears, and moaned miserably. But Ma wasn’t having any of that. “Go see if Momo’s clothes have finished drying, Nimmi,” she said, cradling Momo to sleep. “No!” Nimmi crossed her arms. But Ma smiled and said “Please!” the way she always did, making Nimmi’s heart melt. It had only been a month since her brother Momo had come into this world. Poor Ma was working all the time – looking after the household, feeding everyone, and tending to Momo. Nimmi had to help her out. After all, she was the big girl of the house now. But still, here she was, trapped in her house while her friends were having fun. “But summer is already ending!” Nimmi shouted desperately. This made Ma laugh, and even as Nimmi stormed away to check on the washing, Ma called out, “And when you come back, I have another job for you!” Nimmi sulked. But as she folded up Momo’s clothes, she smiled. Momo was so very tiny and beautiful. Later, Ma carefully placed twelve shiny white eggs into a big bowl and handed it over to Nimmi. They were to be delivered to a neighbour. Why eggs? To whom? Could she go play afterwards? Ma brushed aside Nimmi’s questions with a smile and gently nudged her out of the door. Nimmi made her way up, balancing her fragile load. A hand-carved sign on the door read – Welcome to Akka’s Cakes and Bakes. A cake! Nimmi’s heart leapfrogged with joy as she rang the bell. But who for? All birthdays were past or too far away, and it wasn’t Ma and Pa’s anniversary either. Maybe she would ask Akka herself. But the door wasn’t opened by a white-haired grandma Akka, as Nimmi had expected. Instead, there stood a slender tall boy, about as old as her mom. His rich black hair fell down to his shoulders, framing a friendly face. “Hello, I am Shri! You have the twelve eggs?” “Twelve and heavy!” said Nimmi, as she stepped in. “Quick then, bring them in, my cake is burning!” With that, Shri spun on his heel and ran into the kitchen. Nimmi placed her heavy bowl onto a table and took her shoes off. She placed her slippers carefully next to a big collection of shoes. Some shoes were mens’, made of fine leather, while others were colorful sandals with heels on them. The kitchen was in chaos. Stacks of pans and pots littered the counter. Breadcrumbs, pieces of cake and gooey batter everywhere, and the smell of burnt cake filled the air. “Oh what a terrible day! Won’t you stay back and help me with the cakes?” asked Shri, holding out a baking tray with a black-brown thing that used to be a cake. “Me?” said Nimmi. “But I don’t know how to bake.” “Oh it’s easy. You take something you love, and give it a shape.” “But I love summer, and it’s going away!” Nimmi pointed to the window. “How can that become a cake?” At that, Shri’s eyes twinkled. “The things you love, never go away,” he explained. “Just close your eyes and remember the smell, the touch, the colors and the taste. That way, summer will forever stay!” “The summer smells of mangoes and peaches, lemons and grass. It’s blue and green and golden. Look, like the colours on your nails.” Nimmi pointed to Shri’s hands, his carefully shaped fingernails were painted playful shades of sky blue and lemon green. Then she led Shri to the big window in the living room, and opened it. The soft curtains embossed with branches and leaves billowed with the wind, and caressed them as they danced in circles. “What a delightful summer!” said Shri. And that is what they made. A heart-shaped cake, covered with golden-green icing. Little blades of green grass were lined evenly along the sides. On top, a bunch of bright lilies and petunias nestled amongst golden-brown leaves. Later, as she watched Shri pack the cake into a box, Nimmi couldn’t help but ask, “Shri, who is Akka, the name on your door?” “Me!” smiled Shri. “So are you a girl or a boy?” asked Nimmi. “Does it matter?” said Shri. Nimmi thought about it and replied, “No, not at all.” and held out her hand, “ It’s all the same, as long as I get more cake. Anyway, we are all friends under the summer sun.’’ Shri shook her hand and grinned. As Shri helped carry the big cake back to her house, Nimmi kept wondering who the cake was for. She rang the bell, and the door opened. “SURPRISE! It’s your Un-Birthday!” All her friends crowded around and cooed with delight as Nimmi opened up the box of her Summer Cake. Nimmi looked back and saw the love in her mother’s eyes, and a smile that was brighter than summer itself. A letter from the real Akka ​ As a child, I always felt like a girl, even though I had the body of a boy. My feminine behaviour attracted unwanted attention and I realised very early, that the world was not an easy place for me. Thankfully, I felt safe at home because my parents never really harassed me for my feminineness – be it wearing makeup or women’s clothes. At school too, my teachers were loving and this is where I found other amazing friends who also identified themselves as girls. Such an inclusive atmosphere, free of discrimination and bullying gave me confidence to grow up freely, without any guilt or shame. When I was growing up, it was almost impossible to come across a children's book that had a trans character in it. Times are changing. As an artist and filmmaker, I have always tried to bring the world of queer folks into the mainstream, through my work. And I'm thrilled to find that this book tries to do the same. The author has sensitively portrayed 'Akka', the trans character. And her interactions with Nimmi, the little girl, are both playful as well as informative for young readers. Pradipta Ray Mumbai, 2018
author: Ashutosh  Pathak

title: Blast Off!
text: Story Description Some children know what they might want to be when they grow up. But Sandy is more certain. She is a very intelligent girl with a specific dream - she wants to fly rockets and a chest of drawers into space. Pre-Reading Vocabulary and Phonics Spacesuit sp-ay-ss-sue-t Sandy had to wear a protective spacesuit in space. Lightweight lai-t-way-t ﻿She designed a lightweight rocket with not much weight. Astronomical ast-row-nom-ik-ul ﻿The space mission was an astronomical attempt. Countdown cow-n-t-down ﻿She gave the countdown to lift-off. There are some children who know what they might want to be when they are older. Some want to make art and draw pictures. Some want to be police officers or go into the military. Some want to be doctors or surgeons. But Sandy is different. She is a very intelligent girl who is certain of what she wants to be. Sandy loves science, and she dreams of firing rockets into space. She also dreams of being the first person to somehow put a chest of drawers into space too, complete with a goldfish. Sandy used to dream of being on top of the moon. That was before she realised the moon was gigantic, being roughly one quarter of the size of the earth. That was before she realised she could not survive in space wearing only a goldfish bowl, and that she would have to wear a protective spacesuit. Still, the flaws in her logic led her to learn more, and over time, Sandy understood the science behind space travel. She designed a rocket to go in to space. Doing the calculations, she knew that the force of acceleration had to be greater than the force of gravity, for her rocket to make it into space. Very soon, Sandy had built her own rocket. As she explained to the dog, the rocket was a shell made out of a basket base, spoilers for fins from a car, and a metal trash can for a body. She painted a yellow star on the blue background. "It's lightweight so it will travel fast!" Sandy said to the dog. "Or it will blow up." Sandy did her calculations. She discovered a serious problem. The rocket she had built - it was far too small to even get off the ground. "Let's test it anyway," Sandy thought, and one day, she invited her friends to witness her rocket test. Sandy dragged the rocket on a trailer. The rocket was so light that it bounced all of the way to the launchpad. "Wow, it's so impressive!" Sandy's friends said. They cheered at the rocket. Sandy performed the countdown: "Tea minus sugar to lift off. Three...two...one..." Poof! A little bit of air escaped from the rocket and it fell over. "A successful test!" Sandy declared. Her friends gave her a round of applause. "It needs to be bigger..." she thought. "...bigger than my house." Sandy realised she had torn off the roof when building the new rocket. It stuck out of her house like a giant metal lipstick. "I guess this will have to be the launchpad," she said to herself, seeing the living room carpet. The day of the launch finally arrived. Blast off! Everyone cheered as Sandy's rocket lifted off and soared through the clouds on its way to space. Sandy was inside the rocket and she couldn't believe her eyes, so she listened to her ears instead. She heard the sound of a gigantic rocket screaming into the sky, until she arrived in space, where there was only silence, and she floated around inside the rocket. During the next launch, Sandy's friends cheered again as another little rocket blasted off into space. There was not one, not two, but three rockets that Sandy had designed, and they all met each other in space, forming a trio of rockets known as 'Cheese', 'Man', and 'Cow'. Sandy made a broadcast back to earth. She said, "Following the success of my launch, I shall return to earth. But before, I will be the first human to try and breathe in space." She took off her goldfish bowl helmet and a few seconds later she put it back on. "I cannot hold my breath anymore," she said. From the three rockets, Sandy removed the contents they were carrying and she assembled them together. "I present to you the first goldfish and chest of drawers complete with socks, ever put into space," she said. "Next, I plan to build the most expensive house in space. Its value will be astronomical." Post-Reading Questions ﻿What was Sandy's ambition, and what else did she want to do? What happened to Sandy's house when she built the bigger rocket? Re-read. Ask: ﻿Sandy's rocket was so light, what was it doing? ﻿Re-read. Ask: ﻿What are the three rockets named after? ﻿Re-read. Ask: ﻿Was Sandy able to breathe in space? ﻿What would you like to be when you are older? ﻿
author: Hello English

title: Priya in Lever Land
text: Priya was a little girl who lived in Vidyanagar. She was very excited. You see, her tenth birthday was fast approaching. This time she was expecting her cousins from the city to join her. Mona, Aden and Seon had all said that they would surely come to her birthday party. “Maa, please bake a walnut cake. And for dinner, I would love some aloo parathas!” When Priya’s birthday arrived, she could barely wait for it to be 6 p.m ---party time. Aunt Tina had said that they would be there by 5 p.m. Priya’s mother insisted that she sleep for a while in the afternoon. But hardly had Priya shut her eyes when she heard a din. It seemed to come from the kitchen. Slowly she tiptoed to the kitchen and true enough the din did come from there. “You must all agree that I am the greatest! After all I let the walnut cake in to be baked” shouted Darwazelal, the door of the oven. “Oye Darwazelal, if I had not to assist, Priya’s mother would never have cracked the walnuts for the cake. Imagine a walnut cake without walnuts!” retorted Nutkhat the nutcracker. “Well Nutkhat, all you do is something mischievous like cracking some one. I am important here because I helped to cut open the packets of flour” screamed Katribai, the kitchen scissors. “Katribai, you are known to cut others with your sharp arms. But I don’t do destructive work like that you know. I mould shapeless dough into the most perfect circles. If not for me, Priya would not have had her favourite aloo parathas today” answered Chotti the roti maker. Immediately Toaster the Boaster bellowed “Chotti, I think Priya will prefer the crispy toasts that I have generated….” Without giving him a chance to complete, Pehelwan Pakkad flexed his muscles and said “Sit quiet Chotti and Pehelwan. Remember that the hot parathas and the toasts need me to handle them. Priya’s mother would have burnt her fingers if I didn’t exist.” Next all of them heard a giggle. It was Chammach Chachi the spoon. “Listen, if it hadn’t been for me, Priya’s mother could not have opened any of the storage tins.” Listen, if it hadn’t been for me, Priya’s mother could not have opened any of the storage tins. The next moment all were quiet. They noticed that while they were all fighting over whose contribution was the most important; Tarazu Tauji sat most serenely in one corner. Chammach Chachi broke the silence “Tauji, why are you so quiet? Who do you think is the greatest? Give us your opinion, Oh Sir. After all, there is no one with a balanced mind like yours” “Yes, besides, you are an epitome of justice. Your verdict shall be final. Speak out your thoughts, dear Tarazu Tauji” quipped in Pakkad Pehlwan. “Well thanks for all your compliments. But I really do not know what to say to all of you. Don’t you realize that you are all from one family and fighting like this is unbecoming of you all?” “One family? We are all brothers and sisters. Impossible! How can some one as boastful as Toaster be my brother? Or how can that sharp tongued scissors be even distantly related to some one as cultured as myself?” asked Chotti, the roti maker. “Well, all of you, sorry all of us, come from the family of levers. Look closely.We all have a fulcrum. It gives us our balance” “Hey I found my fulcrum. Here is it, the spot where my blades meet”. That Eureka moment exclamation was from Katribai. (She was sharp when it came to understanding how things work.) Very soon, Darwazelal discovered that his hinges were his fulcrum. Pakkad Pehelwan, Chotti the roti maker, Nutkhat the nut cracker--- all found their fulcrum. This is my fulcrum! “I realize this is where our balance lies. This is the steady point that helps us work.” All this while, Chammach Chachi was quiet. “Don’t worry Chachi, you too are from our family. Very soon I will help you find your fulcrum” assured Tarazu Tauji. Help me find my balance!!! Tauji solemnly continued “…and then we all have two more important aspects- a load and an effort. The work you do depends on where the load is. The effort is something that a person applies to get the work done.” “Yes my load is in the centre. The dough is shaped into a ball and placed at my centre and then Priya’s mother presses this handle, so I suppose that is the effort” attempted Chotti. “That’s right!” confirmed Tauji. “Well the same goes for me too. Without an effort applied to me, I could not possibly be shut” said Darwazelal. “Absolutely right!” said Tauji “But then our load, effort and fulcrum are at different places. In my case, or in the case of Katribai and Pakkad Pehelwan, the fulcrum is at the centre and the load and effort are on either side. We are called first order levers. In case of Chotti, the roti maker, the load is between the effort and the fulcrum. And so is it with Darwazelal. They are called second order levers. So you see I don’t think it is right to be fighting over who is the greatest. In our own way, we are all great as we can make difficult work easy.” “Do I belong to your family?” whined Chammach Chachi. “Of course you do. Let me explain” said Tauji. “When Priya’s mother uses you to open a tightly fixed lid, the end in her hand is where she applies an effort. You exert pressure on the lid. That is the load.” “I get it” screamed Chachi “One part of my body takes support on the lid. That is my fulcrum, right?” “Now you get it. So you too are related to us. With her fulcrum between her load and effort, Chachi is …” Without waiting for Tauji to complete, the rest shouted in unison “….. a first order lever.” “Oh Ain’t I glad to be related to a level headed and just person like you, Tarazu Tauji?” said Chachi. Tauji smiled and said “In fact, we have some more relatives, where the effort is in between the fulcrum and the load. They are called third order levers. For example, the fishing rod that Priya’s father uses has the load at one end, where the fish is caught. The fulcrum is his elbow where the balance is maintained and the effort is exerted by his forearm. We levers are extremely useful and help humans do their work easily. We are also classified as simple machines” “I wonder, if I am in alien land!” That was Khulja Tim Tim, the bottle opener. One would think he was permanently yawning. “Oh no, you are no alien, you are a second order lever with your load between your effort and fulcrum.” “Who is a second order lever, Priya? I think you are dreaming. Wake up, it is nearly four o’clock. Your friends Brainy and Brawny are already here. In a short while your cousins will be here. And then we will have a lovely party.” Priya woke up with a smile. What a strange yet informative dream! She went to the kitchen. Khulja Tim Tim gave her a wide mouthed smile. Katribai too had her blades apart. Pehelwan Pakkad had stretched his muscular arms. Tarazu Tauji was swaying a bit. Chammach Chachi stirred slightly. She listened carefully. They were all humming “Happy Birthday dear Priya.” “Thank you folks for the wishes and thanks for assisting mother in the kitchen! Thanks for teaching me never to underestimate anyone. I realize that all of us with our virtues can make this world a better place. You have made my day.” They continued to sing “Happy Birthday” and Priya could assure you that she wasn’t dreaming now!
author: Agnes Dcosta
illustrator: Ajanta Guhathakurta; Arkapriya Koley; Avishek Sen; Chaaya Prabhat; Ellen Heydenrych; Kabini  Amin; Kruttika Susarla; Lê Thị  Anh Thư; Proiti  Roy; Rajeev Verma 'Banjara'; Rajiv Eipe; Ramkumar Iyer; Sandhya Prabhat; Sonal Goyal; Sorit Gupto; Soumya Menon; Sumit Sakhuja

title: I Shouldn't Have Done That
text: Story Description Billy wants to see how high he can climb and feel safe. He thinks he can get down from the table and the stairs, but when he realises it's too high and he needs rescuing, he thinks to himself, "I shouldn't have done that." Pre-Reading Vocabulary and Phonics Particularly ﻿pur-tic-you-lur-lee ﻿The table was particularly high to reach. Attempt ﻿a-temp-t ﻿ ﻿Billy made an attempt to climb on the table. Wobbling ﻿wobbling ﻿He felt himself wobbling at the top of the slide. Spluttering ﻿spl-uh-tur-ing ﻿He was wheezing and spluttering, trying to get on to the table. Billy wanted to see how high he could climb and feel safe. He knew the dining room table was particularly high, so he fetched a chair, stretched his legs and climbed up. It was tough to get up, so he pulled himself upwards with his arms and elbows. Billy climbed on to the table, looking down to see how high up he was, and getting scared. It was too late for him to get down. He had already lifted his foot off the chair. Now he was alone and there was nobody to help him. Billy cried out. Billy's mother arrived as he collected his car. She found him standing on the table. "You must not climb on to high places," she said. "You could fall and hurt yourself badly. Be more careful." "Sorry," said Billy, and his mother picked him up and put him on the ground. Billy climbed on to the table again. He was disappointed about getting upset and scared, so he made another attempt. He watched the chair carefully, worried that it would move or fall over if he put a foot on it. He felt like calling for help again, but then he sat on the edge of the table, then fell into the chair. "That was lucky," he said. "The chair could have tipped over." The slide didn't really worry Billy. He climbed up the steps, got a wobbly feeling at the top, and feeling safe by gripping the railing, he wasn't scared. The ride was fun, and he slid all the way down. "The steps are trickier," Billy thought, climbing up his outside porch steps. He scaled them one by one until he made it to the top. "These are not like the slide steps at all!" The world seemed smaller at the top, and Billy felt the wind. It was strong. He could slip over and tumble down the steps at any moment. "I don't think I can get back down," he said. "I'll have to play indoors now." Billy was too frightened to go down each step. "I know," said Billy "It's safer to play on the ground. That way, I can't fall. I can only trip up." He played with his car on the kitchen floor and ignored the table and the chair. "I did it!" Billy said, celebrating. "I can climb on my own bed. If I can do this, then I can surely climb up and down the kitchen table without feeling scared." Billy climbed on the chair again, looking over the back rest at the floor. "It's not that far down from here," he said. Billy then coughed and spluttered and wheezed as he tried to climb on the kitchen table. "I can't do it," he said. "The table is too high up and I don't have enough strength." Billy suddenly felt dizzy. "What's worse," he said. "Now I can't get down off the chair! The world is spinning! I shouldn't have done that!" Billy cried out for help again. Post-Reading Questions Why did Billy keep trying to climb on the table and get down? What did Billy realise at the top of the outside steps? Re-read. Ask: Why wasn't Billy afraid of heights on the slide? Re-read. Ask: Why did Billy only play on the floor? Re-read. Ask: ﻿Why couldn't Billy climb on to the table? ﻿What do you think of Billy's behaviour? What did he learn?
author: Hello English

title: Who's the Best?
text: Story Description A man calls a dance and performance competition for animals, and lots of wildlife turn up to take part. The winner gets to donate a prize to the charity of their choice, so the competition for first place is fierce. Pre-Reading Vocabulary and Phonics Organiser or-ga-n-igh-zur The organiser created a dancing and performing competition for the animals. Routine roo-tee-n Each animal performed their routine to try and win. Suspicions sus-p-ish-uns The animals' suspicions were roused when they saw the stage and microphone. Bravado br-u-var-do The elephant danced with such bravado and flair to win. Bunny and Deer were walking up the hill to the village hall, when Bunny mentioned something that caught Deer's attention. "There's a competition for charity," said Bunny. "Both group and individual." "That sounds interesting," said Deer. "The first event is dancing. The second is performing solo. The best dancer and the best performer both get to choose a charity to give their prizes to." Deer imagined herself performing a funny stand-up comedy routine, even though she had not stood up properly in years. She imagined herself making everyone laugh and winning the competition. Bunny thought that Parrot would win, because he often heard her singing from the high branches, telling him to look out for nearby birds, and to not go hunting in the open fields. Bunny and Deer saw some of the other animals by the pond. There was the elephant, the chimp, the peacock the squirrel, the duck and more. They all felt something was in the air, but they were not sure what was happening. Bunny told them about the competition, and it confirmed their suspicions. They had seen a man building a stage with a microphone. "Let's all go over there now," said Elephant, and all of the animals rushed in a big group towards the stage. They felt so excited about trying to win the competition. The organiser explained the rules of the competition, and immediately the animals started dancing. Elephant was very lively, raising his hoofs and walking with his head high. The squirrels used the trees to perform their dance moves. The organiser judged the competition as the animals danced for a long time, well into the afternoon. The organiser had never seen so many animals with so much energy before. The toad climbed on to the tortoise's back to do a double flip into the pond. The deer waved its front legs around, and the dragonfly showed off its colours. "Well, that's a difficult choice," said the organiser. "Because you are all terrible dancers, it's hard to pick a winner." Everyone laughed. "But for the bravado and the eccentricity, I'm going to choose Elephant as the winner." Elephant cheered and raised his trunk. He donated his cash prize to the local elephant zoo. After everyone had performed their individual talents, such as singing, comedy, body movement and magic tricks, the bird judge gave the microphone to a dove. The dove swept away all the competition with its powerful chirping voice. The dove continued its act through performing poetry and telling jokes. Everyone was captivated by the dove. The bird judge declared the dove as the winner, and gave it a cheque. The dove chose to donate its winnings to the local nature reserve, which looked after local birds. At the end of the competition, both judges shook hands to say thank you. At the very end of the event, the organiser received a text. He read it to the crowd of animals. There would be another competition the following week. The first prize would be a week's holiday on the island of Bali. The animals quickly went away to practice their moves and talents to try and win that holiday! Post-Reading Questions What two things did that animals have to do for the competition? Who won the contest with their comedy and poetry? Re-read. Ask: What trick did the toad do? Re-read. Ask: ﻿Who won the prize for being the best dancer? ﻿Re-read. Ask: ﻿What did the organiser announce? ﻿What competition would you enter?
author: Hello English

title: Simple Machines : Inclined Planes
text: Priya’s father had purchased a new motorcycle. He had promised Priya a trip to Funland during the vacation. The road to Funland was just the right kind of road to try the new bike. “Sunday will be the right day to go there” said Priya’s dad. “Could cousins Allwyn and Mona come too?” asked Priya. “No problem, if their dad agrees to get them. I can just take one person as a pillion rider, you know! I think if Uncle Ronnie agrees to get the car along, we can take Brainy and Brawny too.” “Wow, that’s wonderful. The more the merrier” exclaimed Priya. The following Sunday, Priya and her father took their bike along. Uncle Ronnie drove behind with Mona, Allwyn, Brainy and Brawny. The road to Funland was uphill. Priya looked at the road closely. “Daddy, why is this road all curved?” “Well, this is a slope that we are ascending. It is easier to go up a slope, if the road is winding. That way the power exerted by the engine of the vehicle is low and even low powered vehicles as bicycles can go up. It may take slightly longer, but it is less labourious. This is the principle of an inclined plane” explained Dad. “An inclined plane?” thought Priya. Almost immediately, she heard a little voice “If you have the inclination, I have the time. I will teach you all about inclined planes once we get to Funland.” That was the road talking! “Don’t be surprised, Priya. I am the road. Yes, I will follow you right up to Funland and show you many interesting things on the way.” Very soon Priya and her father reached Funland. Uncle Ronnie and the rest were already there. They bought their tickets and headed to the play area. Allwyn ran towards the slides. “Priya, this slide is an inclined plane. Watch how your cousins slide down without much effort. Had this slide been flat that would be impossible. A plane is a flat surface. For example, a smooth board is a plane. Now, if the plane is lying flat on the ground, it isn't likely to help you do work. However, when that plane is inclined, or slanted, it can help you move objects across distances. And, that's work!” explained the road. Next Priya joined her cousins and enjoyed a few rides down the slide. Her little cousin Mona preferred jumping on and off the steps. “Hey Mona, come here. These slides are fun.” “The steps are fun, too.They too are an example of an inclined plane” said the road to Priya. “How can that be? They don’t seem plane to me at all.” countered Priya. “Well, if you had to climb from one level to another up a wall, like Spiderman, would that be easy?” “Easy for Spiderman, not for me” said Priya. “Exactly, to help you climb walls easily, you have these steps. Watch carefully. The flight of steps is actually a flat surface set at an angle against a horizontal surface. Only thing it is at different levels so as to make climbing easy. The steps help you move from a lower level to a higher level by cutting a little space into the incline to make it easier for you to use.” explained the road. “Oh Yes I get your point. But dear Mr. Road, I need to say bye to you for now because I see my cousins are having fun on the roller coaster. Bye.” “Bye Priya. Enjoy yourself on the roller coaster. But I am sure you will think of me even there.” Priya joined her cousins on the roller coaster. It was a huge, monstrous coaster, so her father decided to sit along with the children. Priya screamed aloud as the coaster slid, twisted and turned. As she did so, she thought “I wonder if this is an inclined plane too! It surely is at an angle with the horizontal.” “Yeah, now you are thinking like a true scientist by applying what you have learnt. Good! Well, the roller coaster is indeed an inclined plane!” True to his word, Mr. Road was there, helping Priya understand more about inclined planes. “In the simplest form, the coaster is just an inclined plane, in which a force is applied to push a block up the plane and then released and allowed to slide back down the plane” continued Mr. Road. By now the sun had come nearly overhead and Uncle Ronnie suggested that they should have some thing cool. “Yippee, I will have some ice-cream” said Mona. “We will have some lassi ” shouted Brainy and Brawny. And off marched the giggling gang to the cafeteria. At the entrance of the cafeteria, they saw a little girl on a wheelchair. “How will she get to the cafeteria?” asked Priya. Before anyone could say anything, Brawny marched up to her and offered to lift her up the stairs. (He was always confident of his strength.) “Wait, Brawny, there is no need to do that.” said Brainy. “What do you mean? It is our duty to help the physically challenged.” retorted Brawny. “Yes of course. But you need not use your muscles for that. Do you see that ramp over there? The wheelchair will easily go up the ramp." So all of them accompanied the girl in the chair to the ramp and she easily rolled up the ramp with the twins holding the back of the chair. “Oh thank you” said the girl. “You are welcome” replied Brainy. “We would be pleased if you joined us for some refreshments”. All this while Priya was thinking “Now wasn’t that an inclined plane too?” ‘Yes my dear. You are thinking right” Mr. Road reinforced her thoughts. The children found a new friend. The girl in the wheelchair---her name was Trupti. She loved drawing and painting. Soon Trupti’s parents joined them. Over their glasses of cool drinks and some snacks, they introduced themselves and exchanged their contact numbers, promising to keep in touch. When Priya went to wash her hands, she realized that the wash basin was an inclined plane as well. It allowed the water to go into the drain pipe easily. After refreshments, Uncle Ronnie suggested that they should now enjoy themselves at the indoor theme park as the outdoor park was getting hot. So off marched the group to the indoor park and the first thing that met their sight was a giant snow world. Excitedly, they got into a set of warm clothes and entered a room that resembled the Tundra region. There was an igloo, a sledge, a snowman, some reindeer statues and yes.. it was snowing. Brrrr! It was cold too. Priya and Mona got into a sledge. It has no wheels and could slide on the snow. All of a sudden they found themselves on a slope and whoop came the sledge sliding down. Another inclined plane! Wow, this is fun, thought Priya. The children thoroughly enjoyed themselves and returned home at five that evening. Priya’s father had to put his motorcycle up on the verandah. To do this, he placed a strong plank over the steps and carefully slid the motor cycle up to the verandah. “Uncle, that’s easy work. I was just wondering how you would take that heavy bike up!” remarked Brawny. Priya’s father answered “Brawny, that’s smart work. The ramp that I just used is …” “… a simple machine called as an inclined plane” completed Priya. “Exactly. Do you know Priya, these inclined planes were used extensively during the construction of pyramids?” added her father. “Oh Uncle, do tell us how” said Brainy. Priya’s father continued “The pyramids in Egypt are made of huge stone blocks. For years people have been wondering how they moved all those heavy blocks around. The best guess is the Egyptians pushed the blocks up inclined planes in order to build the pyramids. Earthen ramps were used at least in the initial stages of construction. Ramps have been found at the pyramids of Amenemhat I and Senwosret I at Lisht as well as at several other sites. Traces of disassembled ramps at pyramid sites are even more common. The ramps were made of brick or earth and rubble dressed with brick for strength. They were built up as the pyramid progressed upward, and removed as the pyramid was finished downward.” Priya realized that simple machines were used effectively in ancient times as well. The visit to Funland was enjoyable. She had a great time with her cousins, found a new friend in Trupti, learned so much about inclined planes. Truly, science is all around us. If only we can see and perceive, it is all so meaningful. Priya slept soundly that night. Before she went off to sleep, a crazy thought came to her mind… what if the bed was an inclined plane! Just imagine…. That would be fun, wouldn’t it?
author: Agnes Dcosta
illustrator: Adrien Folly Notsron; Alankrita Amaya; Amrita Dasgupta; Diana James; Kalyani  Ganapathy; Keo  Phunphalla; Madhuvanti Anantharajan; Mary Anne Hampton; Meenal Singh; Ntibile Zonke  o hweditše; Nyambura Kariuki; Rajeev Verma 'Banjara'; Reyansh  Sudhir
