illustrator: 211 Studio; Ajit Narayan; Alicia Souza; Angie & Upesh; Delwyn Remedios; Greystroke; Nina Sabnani; Rijuta Ghate; Soumya Menon; Suvidha Mistry

title: Patience
text: Story Description Justine loves playing football with her friends, but one day, she must go home to help her mother cook dinner instead. Justine learns the value of patience as she cooks, and that it is sometimes better to wait for something than to demand it straight away. Pre-Reading Vocabulary and Phonics Peeling p-eal-ing Justine's mother was peeling the vegetables. Stirring st-urr-ing Justine kept on stirring the pot. Repetitive re-pet-it-iv The stirring was a repetitive action. Patience pay-shun-ss Justine needed lots of patience to cook well. "Are you joining us for football practice today?" said Meena. "I can't come," said Justine. "I have to help my mother cook. She wants to teach me how to make meals, but I'd rather be playing football. Cooking sounds tiring and boring." "Why don't you give it a try?" said Meena. "Your mother will appreciate your help." Justine went home and found her mother in the kitchen peeling vegetables. Justine's mother asked her to prepare the big cooking pot. It was very heavy and it had to balance on the stove. "I knew this work would be tiring," complained Justine as she thought about playing football. Justine's mother added some oil and spices to the cooking pot and settled it back on the three mounds raised from the ground, inside of which a small fire was burning. Suddenly Justine began to walk away. "Hey, come back," said Justine's mother. "We're nowhere near finished yet. You have to keep stirring the pot as I add the vegetables and the meat. I need your help, Justine. I can't do this alone." "But I'm missing my football practice, and this isn't fun," said Justine. "Then you have to find a way to make this fun," said her mother. "This isn't as boring as it seems," said her mother. "I'll add the vegetables and the meat and you keep stirring. Keep watching so that it doesn't over boil." "Well, all right," said Justine. "I suppose cooking can't be that bad." Justine found the stirring very tiring and repetitive, but after a while, she got into a rhythm. Something in her, the voice that wanted her to be somewhere else playing football, was suddenly silenced. She felt peaceful and quiet. She began to enjoy the rhythm of stirring. It was like an art form, and a body movement. She stopped thinking of the cooking as work, and instead, she treated the task as play. When her mother wasn't looking, Justine took a small handful of food and put it in her mouth. She coughed it out. It was too hot and it didn't taste right. "You have to wait for the rest of the ingredients to go in before it's ready," said her mother. Justine's mother kept giving her ingredients to add to the pot, and Justine enjoyed watching the food slowly develop into a meal. She realised patience was a good thing to have, and she enjoyed the process of cooking. "You can taste it now," said Justine's mother, and Justine dipped her fingers in the food. It was delicious. She poured out a portion for herself and her mother, and they ate together. "Do you see?" said her mother. "Good things come to those who wait. If you rush something, you ruin it." The next day, Justine played football with patience and attention. She had more focus and determination, and she scored three goals for her team. The food had also given her extra energy and stamina. She thanked her mother for the advice. "You really are the best mum in the world," said Justine. "I hope I am like you when I grow up." "Thank you, dear," said her mother. "Are you going out to enjoy your football?" "Later," said Justine. "First, I'm going to help you cook again!" Post-Reading Questions How does Justine's friend persuade her to cook? Why does Justine try to leave after preparing the pot? What does Justine's mother tell her to do as she adds the vegetables? What does Justine discover over time? How does Justine treat cooking to make it fun? What is something that you don't like to do?
author: Hello English

title: What Does The King Want?
text: Story Description The king is feeling restless and nervous. He wants something, but he's not sure what he wants. His guards and advisors do their best to help him, but only the king knows what the problem is. Pre-Reading Vocabulary and Phonics Acrobatics ﻿ac-row-bat-ik-s ﻿The circus performers did acrobatics and balanced on ropes. Puzzled ﻿puzz-ul-d ﻿The king was still puzzled. He didn't know what the problem was. Enthusiastic ﻿in-th-ew-zee-as-tic ﻿Everyone was enthusiastic about seeing the circus. Peacefully ﻿pea-ss-full-ee ﻿The king slept peacefully through the night. The king stayed up all night because he couldn't sleep. He was in deep thought. He felt there was something wrong, but he didn't know what it was. The king walked around his castle, trying to discover what was wrong. But no matter how hard he tried, he couldn't shake the problem off his mind. Finally, the king sent for his best guard and explained the problem. "Your majesty, what you need is some entertainment," suggested the guard. "I'll get my men on the case at once." The guard called his assistants to practice some singing and dancing moves for the king. "Sing better than that when you see the king!" the guard snapped at them. The entire group of guards gathered together, and they stood in a line holding arrows behind their backs. "I want to see you come up with acrobatics, spins, dances and dangerous stuff to do with those arrows, so the king is impressed," said the best guard. The guards performed magic tricks but they went horribly wrong. One of the guards tried crossing his eyes, and they remained stuck together. He had to go to the hospital. The best guard was very disappointed in his assistants. "No," said the king to himself. "It's not entertainment that I crave. It is something else, but I don't know what it is. What is the problem? Am I bored?" None of the castle's staff could figure out what the king really wanted. The best guard gave up and went back to doing his work. "I know what his majesty wants," said a local townsman. "He wants to be surprised. I think he is utterly bored in that castle, stuck inside and all alone. I have an idea! If the king eats these magical worms, they will make him feel better and he will go outside." Just then, the man had an even better idea. "Your majesty," said the townsman, presenting a gift. "I have brought you this unique bird. Not only can it speak, but it is also a doctor. You can tell the bird all of your problems, and it can find you a cure." The townsman bowed and waited with clasped hands, ready for his reward of gold. But the king was puzzled. "No, I don't want a bird," said the king. "Something else is bothering me." The king released the bird from its cage, and it immediately went to the bowl of magical worms, gobbling them all. The bird sat on the ground with a big stomach, unable to fly with the heavy food inside him. "The townsman failed to cure the king," said the land keeper. "But I won't. I have a masterful idea that will cure the king once and for all." The land keeper went to see the king. The land keeper organised a fantastic and funny circus for everyone including the king to see. The king was enthusiastic through the performance, and he smiled at the juggler and the performers balancing on the ropes, but still he had a problem, and the land keeper was annoyed that he had failed. Finally, the king understood his problem. "It's all been in my head!" he said happily. He immediately took off his crown and placed it on a table. "Ah, that's much better," he said. "What a relief. That hat has been messing with my head. It was so tight! I don't have a headache anymore. Now I can think properly!" The king rested peacefully that night, for the first night in a long time. He had no more problems, his head got better, and he decided to order a bigger crown. He sank into a deep sleep, dreaming about the bird eating the entire bowl of worms. Post-Reading Questions How was the king feeling? What did the guard get his men to practice for the king? How did the townsman think he could help the king? What happened after the king set the bird free? What did the land keeper prepare for the king? What do you think is the message of the story?
author: Hello English

title: Ratty Rat And The Magic Fruit
text: Story Description Ratty Rat leaves her home and goes on a mission to the beach, to find the magic fruit and keep it safe in the jungle. She encounters trouble and danger along the way, along with some strange characters. Pre-Reading Vocabulary and Phonics Investigation ﻿in-vest-ee-gey-shun ﻿Ratty prepared to go on an investigation to find the magic fruit. Sunglasses ﻿sun-glass-is ﻿Ratty wore sunglasses to both protect her eyes from the sun, and to look cool. Flattened ﻿flat-un-d ﻿Ratty was almost flattened by the huge wave. Exploring ﻿ex-pl-or-ing ﻿ ﻿A boy walked past while exploring, and he offered to help Ratty find the woods. Once again, Ratty Rat had been called up for an adventure. She was the best explorer both in her field, and in her hideout, and she had been waiting a while to go on her next investigation. She had been chosen to find a magic fruit. She packed everything she needed into a bag, including binoculars, diary, a first aid kit and blocks of hard cheese for her journey. "I'm ready to go," she said, putting on her trendy sunglasses and heading outside. As she was heading out, she saw the portrait of the rat family hanging on the door. She looked at it and saw herself wearing those same sunglasses pulling a pose. She saw her brother Randolph landing in a red hat. She saw Mama with her black spotted head scarf, and Rick, her eccentric cousin wearing a blue bow tie, and her sister Ruby sticking her mouth into the picture. She felt proud of her family, even if they were a little strange. Ratty went on her way, burrowing through the maze of tunnels underground, finding little pieces of food, litter and small creatures, and she didn't stop tunnelling and scurrying until sunset. She slept through the night, and in the morning she carried on with her journey. The end was getting closer. Ratty popped her head out of the ground. She had made it all the way to the beach. When she surfaced, she found three nasty little crabs all laughing at her. "Wow, a rodent out here!" they said. "This place is not fit for a mouse." "I'm a rat," said Ratty. "Same thing!" said the crabs. "You'll be devoured by scorpions, or fish, or those monkeys in the woods." "I'm not listening to those no good crabs," said Ratty. "I can look after myself out here." Suddenly, as Ratty was walking along the beach, a massive wave came to the shore and struck her. The wall of water hit Ratty hard, and she was almost flattened against the sand. She got up quickly as the next wave arrived, and she ran away. "I have to find the magic fruit and give it to a jungle animal," she said, reminding herself of her important mission. Ratty looked down at her tail. Being flattened by the wave had caused her tail to twist and almost break. She stretched her tail back out, which caused her a lot of pain, and she continued on her way to finding the magic fruit. Ratty was hiding behind some rocks when she heard somebody walking close by. She popped her head up to see a boy. He explained that he was exploring and had been through the woods. Ratty told him about the magic fruit. "I know where you need to go," he said. "I'll take you there." Ratty followed the boy towards the woods. They walked down a steep hill, and neither of them saw a big bundle of rocks at the bottom. They both tripped on the rocks and fell. Getting up, they were all right. The boy had cut his arm, and Ratty applied a plaster to the cut. The boy took Ratty all the way to the edge of the woods, where she thanked him and continued her journey alone. She kept following the path, taking her deeper inside. She saw something shining from the grass with a yellow light. It was a partially eaten fruit. "This is it," she said, holding up the fruit. A mysterious white monkey saw Ratty and she gave him the fruit for safekeeping. "I will guard this with my life," said the monkey. "Thank you for coming all the way here and finding it. You have saved our woods and our land." Ratty was so happy that she jumped for joy. She saw a huge pile of soft berries gathered by the path, and she leaped high into the air, crushing the berries when she landed. Ratty made her way back to the beach. It was still sunny, and there was a discarded spade left on the beach. She picked it up and started building a sandcastle. When it was finished, Ratty put a stick in the top and attached a sock to it. "I have to go home," she said. "But right now I feel so tired. I have to rest before my journey." Ratty curled into a little ball, slept through until sunset, and when evening came, she went into the underground tunnels, scurrying and hurrying all night long, until the very next morning, she arrived back at her house. Post-Reading Questions ﻿What object had Ratty been asked to find? What did Ratty look at just before she left the house, and who did she see? What caused Ratty to be knocked down by the beach? What did the boy agree to help Ratty find? Who did Ratty give the magical fruit to? What kind of adventure would you go on?
author: Hello English

title: Life's Journey
text: Story Description A short reading about life, the things that happen to us, our journey and destination, and where we are heading. Pre-Reading Vocabulary and Phonics Universe you-nih-vur-ss The universe is contained in a single breath. Wobble mob-bull Try to stay steady, and don't wobble. Cherish cheh-rish Cherish the good moments. Admire ad-my-ur Admire the sunset and the countryside. Life is a special journey, from failure to success, from misery to happiness, from chaos to stability. Life has a strange way of pointing you in the right way. You may be the king of a country, or the commander of a small village. You may have all the money in the world. You may be desperately poor. What is gained can be lost. What is lost can be regained. Treasure those joyful moments. Get out as much as you can. Remember to breathe. The whole universe is contained in a single breath. You didn't come into this world. You came out of this world. Discover what makes your heart pound, what makes you tick. Discover your calling. What gets you up in the morning? Find a craft and practice it all of your life. Someday you will be a master. When you enjoy something so much, you make little effort. Life seems to flow through you. You don't control life, the flow of life controls you. Try hard enough. If you try too hard, you will fail. Too little effort and you miss out. Life's journey has no destination and no beginning. It is like a turning wheel. Wherever you go, there you are. If you want to get ahead, stay in one place. Cherish the sunset. Look at the rays. Admire the fields and colours. Your being is like this world, immense in variety and unlimited in potential. Pay attention to the simple things and dismiss the complex. Take a road and see where you go. Keep to the narrow path. Don't veer either side of it, and above all else, don't wobble. On life's journey, why stop when you can go anywhere? The universe is your classroom. The world is your teacher. Life is the lesson you learn.
author: Hello English

title: My Brother's Wheeeeelchair
text: Wheeeeeeeeeeee! Here’s me and my brother on his wheelchair. Everyone who sees us, Says we make a crazy pair. He has painted both the wheels, In blues, yellows and maroons. And sometimes, just for fun, He also ties balloons. My brother’s very smart, He’s got plenty of brains. He helps me across puddles, When it rains. When we go to the park, In the evening to play, He uses a horn, So people make way. Going to the market with him, Is such a treat. He has a rear-view mirror, For when we’re on the street. Sometimes he takes his chair Into a shallow stream. I give it a good splash. Oh, how he does scream! When baba and aai take us To the hills for a hike, He puts on special wheels -- Like a mountain bike! All our friends wait, For their turn to ride, It feels so good, With the arms out wide. He goes so fast, He is called the wheelchair champ. And now all our friends know... Their house must have a ramp!
author: Salil  Chaturvedi

title: Did Tiger Take the Rain?
text: For many generations, people called the Tharus have lived here on s mall farms surrounded by jungles. At the base of the Himalayan mountains, where fields touch the village edge, is a flat land known as the Terai. Anjali lived in a Terai village with her parents, her grandmother and grandfather, one brother, and two sisters. That summer it was drier and hotter than the villagers could remember. There was very little water in the river. One day a tiger left the forest. She crossed the riverbed and walked through a field near the village. Afraid, the people ran to their houses. The tiger looked at the sky. She returned to the forest. “You see? The tiger comes. There is no rain,” said a woman. “The tiger is angry. She took the rain,” said a man. “Why is the tiger angry?” Anjali said to her best friend Usha: “Let’s go to the forest and ask Tiger why she took the rain.” They ran across the field and over the riverbed to the other bank. They pushed their way through the tall, hot grass, lifted up a branch, and entered the forest. Sunlight played through the trees and made patterns on their clothes. They heard the voices of birds and monkeys. Insects buzzed and creatures moved in the leaves at their feet. The air was heavy with the smell of dry leaves and grass. Suddenly, there stood a curious jackal. “Girl children, why are you here?” he asked. “We came to ask Tiger why she took the rain,” said Usha. “We came to ask Tiger why she is angry,” said Anjali. “It’s so quiet here,” said Usha. “The air in the forest makes me happy,” said Anjali. “There was a time when the trees touched the river’s edge as far as you could see,” said Jackal. “There were many tigers then.” “My grandfather told me that back then Tiger never crossed the river,” said Usha. “Yes, the forest was and is her home. Many animals live in the forest. They live in the trees and on the ground, protected by the trees,” said Jackal. “We need the forest, too. We find herbs and medicines in the forest,” said Anjali. “And wood for our homes,” said Usha. “There was a time when forests covered most of the Terai. Much of it has been cut,” said Jackal. Suddenly, the birds stopped singing. “Tiger is near,” said Monkey. “Come with us.” “I will show you where the rain is,” said Monkey. “Every leaf gives off water. The sun pulls that water to the sky and makes a cloud,” said Monkey. “It takes a cloud to rain.” “When there is no forest, there will be less rain,” said Monkey. “And less rain would mean no new forest. New forests need water,” said Usha. “No forest, no cloud,” said Anjali. “No cloud, no rain,” said Usha. “No rain, no forest,” said Anjali. “No forest, no cloud,” said Usha. “Take these seeds to your village,” said Monkey. “Plant them, and they will grow into new trees.” “And new trees will grow into a forest!” said Usha. “And new forest will bring back the rain,” said Anjali. “ We all live under the same sky, “ said Anjali. “When the sun shines, it shines down on humans and tigers together. When it rains, we share the same rain.” “We feel the same wind. We breathe the same air,” said Usha. “When we harm the forest we harm Tiger. What harms Tiger harms us, too,” said Usha. “We have taken too much.” “Let’s put it back,” said Anjali. “Let’s plant a new forest.” It began to rain. The tiger looked at the sky. She returned to the forest.
author: Charles  Norris-Brown

title: The trip to Italy
text: There was a family that came from India to Italy. The family had 5 people and 1 dog. There was Mrs Sharma, Mr Sharma, Aditi, van, don and s.a.d. the dog. Mr Sharma got a job in Italy and decided to move there with his family. They did not know Italien. So that was a problem. The kids went to a international school, there they learnt Italien and English they knew English. They loved how pizza tasted. And they also learnt a bit Italien. One day they went to a italien restaurant. “Arre you a foreign that has come to Italia if yes where do you come from. Ai am zo interested”. Said the waiter.” We are from India.” Said Mr Sharma. “ India? Nice country.? I have been to India Ai visited Dheli there ai visited Taj Mahal. Red Fort it was nice and I loved the food. What would you like to order?.”said the waiter. “Uhh maybe a 5 pizzas. “ said Mrs Sharma. “Amma why did that waiter ask us that? I thought waiters always just take orders “. Asked van. title: Gudugu Thadugu
text: Muni was a mason. He had built all the buildings in his village, big and small. One morning, Doctor Sheila asked him to build a clinic for her. “Muni, please break down my old shed,” said Doctor Sheila. “That’s where I want the new clinic to be built.” “I can do that, Doctor Amma,” said Muni, “But first, I need my helpers, Anju and Sanju. They live up on the hill.” Muni set off to fetch his helpers. On the way, he met Bahadur the plumber. “I will help remove the taps and pipes in the shed,” said Bahadur. “Wait here, Bahadur, while I fetch Anju and Sanju.” Further up the hill, Muni met Babu the milkman and his buffalo, Rani. “Will you help me break down Doctor Amma’s shed, Babu and Rani?” asked Muni. “No, no,” said Babu. “She’s a good doctor. I won’t break her shed down!” Muni met Mastan, the carpenter. “I will help remove all the wood in the building,” said Mastan. Finally, Muni met Anju and Sanju atop the hill. “We need your big and heavy hammer,” said Muni. The hammer was so big and heavy that Muni tripped over. “AAAAIEEEE! Careful,” said Anju. Muni caught hold of Sanju. Sanju caught hold of Anju. GUDUGU-GUDUGU-GUDUGU! Muni, Sanju and Anju came sliding down the hill and fell on Mastan. Muni, Sanju, Anju and Mastan rolled down the hill. “Hey!” said Babu. “Bey!” said Rani. THADUGU-THADUGU-THADUGU! “I am coming too!” said Bahadur and joined the helpers. Muni, Sanju, Anju, Mastan, Babu, Rani and Bahadur came rolling down the hill and… BADAGADA-THAGUDUGU, BADAGADA-THAGUDUGU! …hit the doctor’s shed with a loud THADABUDAAAL! The shed broke into a hundred pieces. Doctor Sheila was very happy. She paid them and gave everyone sweets to eat. “Thank you, Muni and helpers,” she said, “You broke down my shed very fast. Now please help me build my clinic quickly, too!”
author: Ashok Rajagopalan

title: A song of personal space
text: She tips her head and greets the snail, With an enthusiastic swing of her tail. “Sluggy sloggy, sluggy sloggy! Won’t you stop for a while? And grace me with a radiant smile?” The snail does not spare a glance. But the canine takes an eager chance. Bends her head and sniffs real close, Nudges the snail with her wet nose. “Sluggy sloggy, sluggy sloggy! Doesn’t that feel nice? My precious friendship is your prize.” The snail gives a mighty start. Then just drags ahead it’s domed cart. The canine is not ready to give up, For she is one persistent pup. “Sluggy sloggy, sluggy sloggy! Where do you think you are you going? Stop being so rude and boring.” The canine now extends a muddy paw, And the snail invokes the jungle law. The startled canine is swept back. She cries, “Why? What do I lack?” “Sluggy sloggy, sluggy sloggy! What did you just do? You are such a mean shrew!” The snail explains without slowing it’s pace, “You got to respect another’s personal space.” “I have clear boundaries of my own.” “Without assent you shall not trespass into my private zone!” “Nudgy nosy, busybody grossy! That is just the way it goes. How the essence of freedom flows.” The canine frowns then nods. As awareness dawns she applauds. Then in silent understanding she leaves. And lets the snail pass in peace. “Sluggy sloggy, sluggy sloggy! Now that was one fine lesson. I shall not step close without permission.” The snail moves on with a serene smile, Having conveyed the message in her own style. To her favourite place the canine retreats, While the observant bird on the tree merrily tweets, “It applies to all, applies to all! You shall not stick your nose where it does not belong. You shall remember this like a catchy song.”
author: A.R.  Sara
illustrator: A.R.  Sara; Chandana Bandara  Samarakoon; Preeti Krishnamurthy; Priya Kuriyan; Rohan Chakravarty; ROSH; Vishnu  M Nair
