title: Anuradha Dances the Bihu
text: Anuradha can hardly wait! She is in a hurry, just like the weather. Anuradha begins gathering wild white orchids, the Kapau phul. “I will put these in my hair.” She colours her lips red using the buds of the Barhamthuri plant. She borrows a pair of silken mekhela-chador from her neighbour Rima aunty. Suman, her elder sister, lends her a pair of Gamkharus (thick golden armlet) and a Galpata (a golden choker). But what is this? There is no dhol, only thunder. The wind is blowing and rain is pouring down. Anuradha is very sad. Girgir girgir khit, Girgir girgir khit Anuradha hears the sound of the dhol, and runs out. Her Koka asks her, "My darling Anuradha, what makes you so sad?" Anu said, "See Koka, this rain shows no sign of stopping." "This is quite natural, my dearest Maina. This is the season of howling winds and rains." "You mean I will have to sit indoors during Bihu? No, no, I can't let that happen Koka! Please do something." Koka whispers to her, "The gusty wind is called 'Bordoisila' (Bordoixila). If you want her to go away, you should place a comb and a mirror on a peera (a low wooden stool) outside." Anu asks everybody at home if Koka is right. "Yes, yes it is true," her Ayita says. "But you should pierce a ripened red chili with a bamboo stick and plant it in the open. Then the sun will come out quickly after the rains are gone." Deota laughs and says, "God alone can help you in this situation, Anuradha." Ma quickly adds, "By pleasing Varuna the rain god by offering him pan and betel nut to make the rains stop." Anuradha is not convinced. Anuradha covers her head with a big Kochu (colocasia) leaf. She goes out to meet her friends Bitoo, Kankan, Mani, Himani and Runjun. Anuradha tells them everything she’s found out. "Rain and wind belong to nature, and so does the Bihu,” her friends say. “Even if none of these ideas work, we will dance Bihu in the rain." And they start getting ready. They keep a comb and a mirror on a peera. It keeps raining. They plant a bamboo stick pierced through a red chilli. It keeps raining. They keep paan and a beetel nut to please Varuna. It keeps raining. Anuradha keeps staring at a big puddle of rainwater. Slowly, the clouds begin to move. The wind drops. Finally, the rain stops and the sun peeps out in the sky. A smile peeps out on Anuradha’s face. She quickly dresses in her Bihu clothes. Anuradha dances Bihu merrily with her friends, dhol and pepa (a hornpipe) accompanying them for music.
author: Rajesh Khar

title: The Grass Seeker
text: Photographer: Ruhani Kaur ​Every year, when the snow starts to melt, 67-year-old Gaddi shepherd Room Singh packs a few of his essentials. Food to last him for three to four months, 40 kgs of salt for his animals, pots and pans, a worn-out radio, medicines, a torch and solar lantern, and an old rifle to scare bears away. Rounding up his flock of about 300 goats and sheep, he bids farewell to his wife Hitmani Devi, his family and his village Shiah in the Garsa valley of Himachal Pradesh—and sets off. ​Grass. Juicy blades of grass high up on the hill slopes, fed by meltwater streams and clean mountain air that his flock loves to graze on. That is what Room Singh goes looking for, when summer reaches the valley. For hundreds of years, nomadic Gaddis have responded to the changing seasons, heading up in summer and turning back from the high grasslands before the freezing winter. For the last 40 years, Room Singh has followed in their footsteps, wrapped in his woollen chola (knee-length coat) and tapping his trusty stick. ​Finding pastures isn’t always easy. Some years ago, when he reached his final camping ground at Donspaan, it snowed for two days without stopping. His animals went without food because the grass was buried deep. He couldn’t bear to eat, either. “If they go hungry, I do too,” he says. ​He begins his long uphill trek from a village called Kalga. After crossing Kheerganga, Room Singh enters a wild and unspoilt landscape, where settlements have musical-sounding names. Tundabhuj, Thakur Kuan, Patra Ghat, Pandu Pul, and finally Donspaan. KALGA KHEERGANGA TUNDABHUJ THAKUR KUAN PATRA GHAT PANDU PUL PARVATI RIVER DONSPAAN PIN PARVATI VALLEY Map not to scale. ​The 60-kilometre journey takes him along​ ​the raging Parvati. The bridge across is broken, and there’s only one trail ahead. He crosses icy torrents and melting snow bridges; he climbs across steep rock faces and navigates chilly waterfalls. The tinkling of the flock’s bells​ ​keeps him company in the silence. Here, 13,000 feet up in the Pin Parvati valley, Room Singh likes to walk in the wide open spaces, collecting firewood and letting his flock graze at its own pace. There is no rush to get anywhere. The air is pure. The water is clear and sweet. Wildflowers are abloom and herbs grow waiting to be picked. Room Singh has seen these high places change over the years. There was a time when no rock could be seen on the mountains nearby because they were always covered by snow. Now, with temperatures rising because of climate change, the glaciers are melting and grassy pastures have become rare. ​​​He worries that if it stops snowing,​ ​the rivers will run dry and the world​ ​will come to an end. ​To the Gaddi, each stone, each spring, each slope is precious. Room Singh loves the mountains like he does his family, and never feels lonely. The shepherd sleeps under the open sky, his flock gathered around him. He wastes little and barely pollutes, taking only what he needs from nature and leaving no trace of his stay. ​​​Room Singh knows that the days of his past​ ​are drawing to a close. Finding pastures is getting harder, and his animals aren’t as​ ​healthy as before. With their wool no longer​ ​being what it used to be, selling the Gardu​ ​blankets and shawls isn’t easy. ​A Gaddi shepherd migrates to grasslands that are high up, unfit for agriculture. Over the years, the climb has become more difficult, with old routes closing down and trees being planted on pastoral grounds. ​The nomadic way of life of these generations of pastoral wanderers is fast disappearing. Now, the young men in his village see the city as their future. One of his sons is a driver, and his eldest grandchild studies at a local college. But Room Singh continues to walk to the place he feels most at home.
author: Uddalak Gupta

title: Hauz Khas: A School by the Lake
text: Would you like to go on a secret trail? You will find a lake, a mosque, some tombs, a garden, and a very old school. Where will you find all this? At Hauz Khas, in the capital city of India, Delhi. Scattered around the modern megacity of Delhi are the cities of its past. Some of these are Qila Rai Pithora, Mehrauli, Siri, Tughlaqabad, Firozabad, Dinpanah and Shahjahanabad. If you look carefully, many neighbourhoods stand on the ruins of a fort, a palace or a tomb. Siri was Delhi’s second fort-city, built by a king called Alauddin Khilji. Hauz Khas was close to Siri. Why is Hauz Khas special? ‘Hauz’ means man-made lake. ‘Khas’ means it was special. Hauz Khas was built in 1295 by Alauddin Khilji to store rainwater for the residents of Siri. After Khalji, the tank lay neglected. Till, in 1352, another king took over Delhi—Firoz Shah Tughlaq. Around Hauz Khas you can spot peafowl, barbets, hornbills, sunbirds, babblers, parakeets, hoopoes, kingfishers, spot-billed ducks and herons. The air is filled with the calls of birds. Firoz Shah Tughlaq loved to build new things and restore old structures. He built hospitals, inns, canals, bridges and palaces. He had Hauz Khas cleaned and filled with water again. Firoz Shah also built schools. These schools were called madrasas. He built one at Hauz Khas. What do you think schools looked like 700 years ago? Did they look like the schools you study in? Firoz Shah was called the architect king. He ruled from the fort-city of Firozabad. ​Let’s walk towards the madrasa that Firoz Shah built.​ ​This is a two-storey building, where students read the Quran, the holy book of Muslims. They also learnt subjects such as astronomy, history, mathematics, medicine and calligraphy. Students from near and far came to study here. Maulana Jalaluddin Rumi, the famous Sufi poet, taught here. There are small rooms on the ground floor of the building. Students lived here. You can still see the shelves where they kept their books and other belongings. There is a hall with three domes, the Majlis Khana or assembly hall. Classes were held here. ​The Hauz Khas madrasa is a symbol of Tughlaqi architecture. The doorways, which are stone columns topped by an arch, are an example of this. There are covered balconies called jharokhas. Rain or shine, the jharokhas always offer shelter. Wouldn’t you like to study in a place surrounded by nature, hear bird calls and maybe even go swimming in the lake between lessons? ​Jharokhas and chhajjas are elements of architecture from the ancient period in India. Chhajjas are also structures that provide shade. Besides the school, Hauz Khas is special because of the tombs it houses. Let’s head to the tomb of Firoz Shah Tughlaq. It’s the large chamber with a dome. He had it built before he died. The walls of the tomb are made of limestone plaster. There are black patches on the walls. This is fungus that has formed with damp and neglect. Firoz Shah paid a lot of attention to older styles of art and architecture, and used them in his own buildings. ​The ceiling is like an upturned bowl. The design has a star with eight points. There are lines written in a fine script within the star pattern. They are taken from the Quran. Similar lines are written on the arches over the doors. This ornate design, it is believed, was added during a later period. Under the dome, are four unmarked graves and the central one is said to be Firoz Shah Tughlaq’s. Can you spot the hidden passageways? Yes, the tomb has two doorways to passages that lead into the classrooms next door. The passages are at right angles and anyone entering from the classroom cannot see who is on the other side. Hauz Khas has a mosque which faces the lake. There are symmetrical stairs on both sides that lead to a mihrab. ​A mihrab is a prayer niche in the western wall (facing Mecca), found in most tombs and mosques. This is the direction that people face to say their prayers. Mihrabs are usually ornately designed. In this mosque, the central mihrab is a decorative window. There are more tombs in the garden. It is believed that they belong to the scholars who taught at the madrasa. Are you wondering what happened to Hauz Khas after Firoz Shah Tughlaq? In 1398, Timur, a Central-Asian conqueror, attacked Delhi. He set up camp at Hauz Khas. From a peaceful madrasa, and beautiful garden and lake, it became a camping site for soldiers. Timur wrote: “The tank is filled by the rains in the rainy season and it supplies the people of the city with water throughout the year.” Today, Hauz Khas is a busy area. People come here to shop, eat and walk in the Deer Park adjoining the lake. They are transported to the past and hear students memorising their lessons and wise old teachers reading from books. They feel a gentle breeze blowing from the lake and over a sultan’s resting place. At Hauz Khas, ancient tales are all around. Hauz Khas Timeline 1295 - A reservoir was built by Alauddin Khilji for the city of Siri. For almost 50 years, the reservoir was not in use. 1320 - The first Tughlaq king, Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, fought a battle with Khusrau Khan somewhere around Hauz Khas. Ghiyas-ud-din won. 1352 - Firoz Shah Tughlaq, the third Tughlaq king, built a madrasa and restored the reservoir. 1398 - Timur invaded Delhi and set up camp at the Hauz Khas madrasa. The madrasa was abandoned after that. References Cunningham, A 1871, Four Reports made during the Years 1862-63-64-65, Archaeological Survey of India. Elliott, HM & Dowson, J 1871, The History of India as told by its Historians: The Muhammadan Period, Teubner and Co., London. Safvi, Rana 2018, The Forgotten Cities of Delhi, HarperCollins Publishers, India.
author: Sudeshna  Shome Ghosh; Tilottama Shome

title: Friendly Meena
text: Everyday Meena use to play with her friends. Akram baba, local grocery seller, used to come every evening with heavy bags of all goods for society people. He rang bell of each house. Most of the people refused to buy things. He never stopped coming, everyday he came and knocked at each door, with a hope people might buy something. Meena saw Akram baba, and felt sad. She asked her father " Dadda! why are people not buying anything from Akram Baba?". " He is tired old man! at least to support him, they can give some cash?" Meena's father was touched by her concern. He told her, " Meena, you are right, he needs some support, however instead of giving cash without any purchase, will not make him happy. Let us think for some other way to support him." Meena thought whole time, how can she help Akram baba. She came up with an idea. Next day she called her friends and shared with them story of Akram Baba. All children decided to help Akram baba. They knocked one by one at each household to collect orders on behalf of Akram Baba. He then did not have carry heavy bag to each house. Children collected the orders and distributed to houses. They collected the cash and gave to him. Akram baba was very thankful to Meena and friends for such a big help and support. This was also a learning for society people, to help each other and needy people.

title: The Cat and the Fiddle
text: Hey, diddle, diddle, The cat and the fiddle, The cow jumped over the moon! The little dog laughed To see such sport, And the dish ran off with the spoon! PERHAPS you think this verse is all nonsense, and that the things it mentions could never have happened; but they did happen, as you will understand when I have explained them all to you clearly. Little Bobby was the only son of a small farmer who lived out of town upon a country road. Bobby's mother looked after the house and Bobby's father took care of the farm, and Bobby himself, who was not very big, helped them both as much as he was able to. It was lonely upon the farm, especially when his father and mother were both busy at work, but the boy had one way to amuse himself that served to pass many an hour when he would not otherwise have known what to do. He was very fond of music, and his father one day brought him from the town a small fiddle, or violin, which he soon learned to play upon. I don't suppose he was a very fine musician, but the tunes he played pleased himself, as well as his father and mother, and Bobby's fiddle soon became his constant companion. One day in the warm summer, the farmer and his wife determined to drive to the town to sell their butter and eggs and bring back some groceries in exchange for them, and while they were gone Bobby was to be left alone. "We shall not be back till late in the evening," said his mother, "for the weather is too warm to drive very fast. But I have left you a dish of bread and milk for your supper, and you must be a good boy and amuse yourself with your fiddle until we return." Bobby promised to be good and look after the house, and then his father and mother climbed into the wagon and drove away to the town. The boy was not entirely alone, for there was the big black tabby-cat lying upon the floor in the kitchen, and the little yellow dog barking at the wagon as it drove away, and the big moolie-cow lowing in the pasture down by the brook. Animals are often very good company, and Bobby did not feel nearly as lonely as he would have, had there been no living thing around about the house. Besides he had some work to do in the garden, pulling up the weeds that grew thick in the carrot-bed, and when the last faint sounds of the wheels had died away he went into the garden and began his task. The little dog went too, for dogs love to be with people and to watch what is going on; and he sat down near Bobby and cocked up his ears and wagged his tail and seemed to take a great interest in the weeding. Once in a while he would rush away to chase a butterfly or bark at a beetle that crawled through the garden, but he always came back to the boy and kept near his side. By and by the cat, which found it lonely in the big, empty kitchen, now that Bobby's mother was gone, came walking into the garden also, and lay down upon a path in the sunshine and lazily watched the boy at his work. The dog and the cat were good friends, having lived together so long that they did not care to fight each other. To be sure Towser, as the little dog was called, sometimes tried to tease pussy, being himself very mischievous; but when the cat put out her sharp claws and showed her teeth, Towser, like a wise little dog, quickly ran away, and so they managed to get along in a friendly manner. By the time the carrot-bed was all weeded, the sun was sinking behind the edge of the forest and the new moon rising in the east, and now Bobby began to feel hungry and went into the house for his dish of bread and milk. "I think I'll take my supper down to the brook," he said to himself, "and sit upon the grassy bank while I eat it. And I'll take my fiddle, too, and play upon it to pass the time until father and mother come home." It was a good idea, for down by the brook it was cool and pleasant; so Bobby took his fiddle under his arm and carried his dish of bread and milk down to the bank that sloped to the edge of the brook. It was rather a steep bank, but Bobby sat upon the edge, and placing his fiddle beside him, leaned against a tree and began to eat his supper. The little dog had followed at his heels, and the cat also came slowly walking after him, and as Bobby ate, they sat one on either side of him and looked earnestly into his face as if they too were hungry. So he threw some of the bread to Towser, who grabbed it eagerly and swallowed it in the twinkling of an eye. And Bobby left some of the milk in the dish for the cat, also, and she came lazily up and drank it in a dainty, sober fashion, and licked both the dish and spoon until no drop of the milk was left. Then Bobby picked up his fiddle and tuned it and began to play some of the pretty tunes he knew. And while he played he watched the moon rise higher and higher until it was reflected in the smooth, still water of the brook. Indeed, Bobby could not tell which was the plainest to see, the moon in the sky or the moon in the water. The little dog lay quietly on one side of him, and the cat softly purred upon the other, and even the moolie-cow was attracted by the music and wandered near until she was browsing the grass at the edge of the brook. After a time, when Bobby had played all the tunes he knew, he laid the fiddle down beside him, near to where the cat slept, and then he lay down upon the bank and began to think. It is very hard to think long upon a dreamy summer night without falling asleep, and very soon Bobby's eyes closed and he forgot all about the dog and the cat and the cow and the fiddle, and dreamed he was Jack the Giant Killer and was just about to slay the biggest giant in the world. And while he dreamed, the cat sat up and yawned and stretched herself, and then began wagging her long tail from side to side and watching the moon that was reflected in the water. But the fiddle lay just behind her, and as she moved her tail, she drew it between the strings of the fiddle, where it caught fast. Then she gave her tail a jerk and pulled the fiddle against the tree, which made a loud noise. This frightened the cat greatly, and not knowing what was the matter with her tail, she started to run as fast as she could. But still the fiddle clung to her tail, and at every step it bounded along and made such a noise that she screamed with terror. And in her fright she ran straight towards the cow, which, seeing a black streak coming at her, and hearing the racket made by the fiddle, became also frightened and made such a jump to get out of the way that she jumped right across the brook, leaping over the very spot where the moon shone in the water! Bobby had been awakened by the noise, and opened his eyes in time to see the cow jump; and at first it seemed to him that she had actually jumped over the moon in the sky, instead of the one in the brook. The dog was delighted at the sudden excitement caused by the cat, and ran barking and dancing along the bank, so that he presently knocked against the dish, and behold! it slid down the bank, carrying the spoon with it, and fell with a splash into the water of the brook. As soon as Bobby recovered from his surprise he ran after the cat, which had raced to the house, and soon came to where the fiddle lay upon the ground, it having at last dropped from the cat's tail. He examined it carefully, and was glad to find it was not hurt, in spite of its rough usage. And then he had to go across the brook and drive the cow back over the little bridge, and also to roll up his sleeve and reach into the water to recover the dish and the spoon. Then he went back to the house and lighted a lamp, and sat down to compose a new tune before his father and mother returned. The cat had recovered from her fright and lay quietly under the stove, and Towser sat upon the floor panting, with his mouth wide open, and looking so comical that Bobby thought he was actually laughing at the whole occurrence. And these were the words to the tune that Bobby composed that night: Hey, diddle, diddle, The cat and the fiddle, The cow jumped over the moon! The little dog laughed To see such sport, And the dish ran away with the spoon! Classics on: about the project At we understand the need for children to read good literature as it nurtures growth and development of personality and social skills, it helps develop emotional intelligence, it provides opportunity to learn about and appreciate your culture and that of others and it transmits important literature and themes from one generation to the next. Keeping this in mind, we were looking for ways of bringing some of these classics back to children who have perhaps not been introduced to them. title: A Smiling Donkey
text: Photographer: Hashim Badani There was a village near the bank of a river. Everyone in the village lived happily and peacefully. One day a strange situation took place. There was a huge crowd on road. The people were distress and confused. They were discussing something to one other. A donkey was sitting on the middle of the road since the morning and was teasing everyone who passed by the road. He would not get up and was lazily staring at everyone. One man said" This donkey has some special powers. Whenever a person looks into his eyes, he hypnotizes with his smile. And then for the rest of the day that man has to follow the donkey's command. And from the morning he has jammed the road and is refusing to move." The rowdy donkey who was listening to all this, stared at the man and gave an enchanting smile. A fat Hawaldar came with his stick. He showed his stick and frightened him. But of no use, the donkey smiled coyly at Hawaldar and did not get up. The Hawaldar warned him that he will lock him in the jail.But the donkey was lost in his own exotic world. Lastly,the Hawaldar gave up. Then the villagers called a sophisticated strange looking Tantrik or the magician. The magician sat on the road with garland in his hand made up of marigold. He closed his eyes and called loudly" jhum bhum whon bhummmm this donkey sitting in front of me, You are the animal of God.If you get up now the God will be happy and gift you this beautiful garland. To his horror and terror when he opened his eyes the garland was already half eaten by the enchanter. The donkey with all his broad square teeth smiled again at the magician. After sometime, a little boy came by. He told that it was very easy for him to make the donkey get up. He brought some fruits, grass and hay in the basket. He kept the basket in front of the donkey. The donkey who did not eat anything since the morning ate up the basket too. He was full and his teeth shone even brighter. He got up and smiled gleefully at the boy and moved to the other side of the road. Everyone in the village was proud of the boy. He became their hero and savior.
author: SUMAN SINHA
illustrator: Deepa Balsavar; Hashim Badani; Jess  Jardim-Wedepohl; Rob Owen; Sayan Mukherjee; Sumedha Sah; Wiehan de Jager

title: Nema, the little girl
text: Nema is a little girl. She doesn't have any siblings to play with. So, she plays outside home and often plays in the sand. She loves planting trees, collects different kinds of seeds and sows them in her garden. One day when Nema was collecting seeds from the near by field, she saw a white cat with black spots. She was really scared of the cat because she heard a story from her cousin that cats are cunning and attack the strangers. At first she got scared and her legs got frozen; but after a while she found courage to run away. Nema is also scared of bees. But her grandmother told her that bees are important insects and build beehive to store delicious honey for us. Although she fears them, she wants to follow the bees where they are going and how they build beehive for keeping sweet honey. She likes watering the plants and taking care of them. She collects the seeds and sorts them out properly. Then she sows them in the soil. She enjoys the sight of a little sapling growing into a plant. Nema loves reading story books. She sits under her favourite tree and reads fairy tales for hours. While reading, she enjoys the fragrance of the beautiful white flowers around her and over the trees. She enjoys looking at the worms and wonders how tiny they are and twist their body to move from place to place. While watching these small creatures, she thinks that they may hurt their chest when they move. Nema believes that if she ties a red ribbon around the little branch of the yellow tree, it will bring good luck to her and her family. Every Wednesday she goes to the field and ties ribbon around the little branch and she prays for her family and friends. Everyone loves Nema a lot because she cares for others and helps others in need. She wants everyone happy and smiling around her.
author: Chayanika Sarkar

title: Hotel Cat part 1
text: Oliver the cat was an indoor cat, but he had always dreamed about going outside, he always dreamed about all of the fun stuff he would do like...... stare at other cats and judge them, get a tan and spots and stripes on his fur not get blown up by evil S-I-L-V-E-A-W-A-R-E, but most of all, he wanted friends but, it was nothing but a dream TO BE CONTINUE

title: That Night
text: ​The voices woke Chaitu up. They sounded angry. Loud and angry. She clutched Noonu, her blanket, closer. It smelled of sleep, milk, and dreams. ​Chaitu went out to the passage. She could see Mummy standing in their balcony. The voices had become louder and angrier. They rose higher and higher until they became an ugly giant. “Mummy?” she whispered. Mummy didn’t hear her. She was listening to the voices, telling a story with her hands. ​There was no moon that night. The sky was hazy with fog and smoke. It stung her eyes. Far across the rooftops, Chaitu could see fire leaping like the furious dragon in her storybook. Wasn’t that where her friend Kabir lived? Chaitu’s tummy squirmed. ​Mummy came in from the balcony. She picked up Chaitu and turned to Papa, who looked anxious. “They want you to go out,” she said quietly. “They won’t leave until then. They want to make sure that you aren’t—” Her voice trailed off. ​No, no, no—Chaitu wanted to scream. But her voice wasn’t working. She didn’t want Papa to go out. What if the shouting voices and the furious fire swallowed him up? She had heard stories from her friends at school. People were called out in the night and they never returned. Chaitu clung on to Papa’s hand. Gently, he shook it free. And he was gone. ﻿ ​“What do the angry people want, Mummy?” Chaitu whispered. “They want to know where we are from,” she said sadly. “But we are from here, aren’t we?” “Yes, we are from here. We all belong here. But not everyone thinks that way. Anyone who isn’t the same as them, they want to send away.” “But where would they go? Why should they go? This is their home too. I don’t understand.” “I also don’t,” Mummy said, with a sigh. ​Where was Papa? He still hadn’t returned. It felt like forever since he’d walked out of the door. Mummy was clutching her too hard, but Chaitu didn’t mind. She was clutching Noonu just as tight. It felt like someone was clutching her heart. ​At last they heard footsteps on the stairs and the key turning in the lock. Was that Papa? The door opened and Papa walked into the room. He looked tired and sad. Chaitu felt her heart go fumppp. Papa was back. ​She looked outside the window. It was almost morning. The shouting voices had gone. There was an eerie silence in Chaitu’s neighbourhood. She shut her eyes and leaned into Papa. The sun was coming up, hazy behind the smoke.
author: Bijal Vachharajani

title: The crane and The boy
text: Once upon a time, there lived a boy named "Chand" in the city of Chinigar. He belonged to a family of farmers who worked very hard but were not able to earn enough to meet their needs, This is why, he was not send to school. One day, Chand sat on the river bank and started to cry. A crane flew past him. Suddenly, Chand heard a animal whining. He saw a crane held captured in a bear trap. Chand helped the crane to escape. Suddenly the swan started talking. It said "Thank U for saving my life, little boy, I will try and repay you the same kindness you showed me." Chand said " I don't need any reward, I am happy that you are free." After talking, the crane flew away. The next day the crane returned, Chand and the crane started to become best friends. One day while coming with his toy car, he saw the crane weeping on the bank. He was shock to see his best friend cry. He approached towards him and asked "What happened? " The crane replied " My friends left me because I am your friend." Chand said "So what, at-least, you have a best friend who understands you. " The crane was deeply touched. He rushed to hug his friend and said " Chand you are the friend I needed the most, here, take some money, go educate yourself and your family. " Chand was so deeply touched that he hugged his friend. Chand did everywhere with his friend, the crane. They eat together, slept together, bath together. They became best friends together.
author: Rishita Dev

title: The girl
text: Once upon a time, there lived a girl named Joey who lived with her mother, father and her little sister. One day she was scolded because she accidentally hurt her sister. So, she sat by the window watching the rain, feeling sad. When the rain finished, she saw a beautiful mango tree at a distance. It was full of ripe mangoes. The mangoes looked very delicious. She went outside to eat some of the fruits. Outside there was a beautiful smell of rain. When she went closer to the mango tree, she could see water dripping from the mangoes and leaves. Joey took a mango to satisfy herself. She washed it properly than ate it. After eating the mango, she felt like she was alive again. The mango had given her so much energy, that she finished her home - work in 20 minutes! She was so happy. Everyday she gave the tree a lot of water and hugged it. She drew a picture of herself and tree standing together. She plucked one fruit everyday and the next day, a new fruit would have grown at the same spot. She loved the tree a lot!
author: Rishita Dev
illustrator: Debbie  Faber-Human; Marleen  Visser; Tapas Guha

title: Zakib: The Great Singer
text: Zakib was a really good singer. He had won several medals in school for her good voice. He was regarded as the best singer in the whole school. One day as Zakib was practicing for the annual function, her Music teacher came with a brilliant idea in her mind. She told Zakib," Zakib, why don't you go for an audition in a reality singing show. I think your voice is perfect and you have the capability to get selected. Zakib first refused to go as his parents wouldn't permit him to go. But after he confirmed from his parents that he could go, he called his Music teacher and asked him what time to set out for the auditions. He was surprised when he heard that he was going for auditions of 'Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Little Champs'. Next day, they reached the set at 9:00 a.m. Zakib went to the counter were contestant nameplates were being sold. He was very happy when he saw that his number was 18. He saw many contestants there.Out of the 16 who have already given their performance, only 5 were selected. The next contestant was a lucky one. He got selected on the basis of his beatboxing. His overall performance was rubbish. Now it was Zakib, contestant no. 18's performance. His nervousness was on its top height. He went on the stage. There were three most popular judges. Zakib's performance started. Mrs. Lata Mangeshkar wasn't satisfied. When it came to Mrs. Asha Bhonsle, she was also not agreed. But, Mr. Mohammad Rafi was very much convinced by him. But the final result was that Zakib was not satisfied. When the auditions were over, Mohammad Rafi came to him and said,"don't worry my child, I will make you a good singer." He took Zakib to his house and taught him everyday the best he could. Zakib went on to win 5 reality shows. He also sang songs in many films. one day, his assistant informed him that he has been invited on 'Sa Re Ga Ma Pa' as a celebrity guest of honor. Zakib thought of his days when he got rejected from the 'Sa Re Ga Ma Pa' auditions. It was because of Sir Mohammad Rafi that he became an outstanding singer.
author: Krishna and Priya Rai
illustrator: Diya Ullas; Hin Kimyean; Juhi  Agarwal; Kalyani Naravane; Nivong  Sengsakoun; Priyankar Gupta; Tapas Guha

title: Zayd's counting my BLESSINGS series.
text: Zayd is happy as he can be, spending his holiday with his grandparents in Nigeria for the first time is so much FUN and he loves it. He enjoys singing his favorite song as he plays in the garden with his grandpa. But it is now time for bed and Zayd is not ready! "Zayd, can I have the butterfly jar, so you can get ready for bed.?" Grandpa says. "No, I want to get more" Zayd says pleading. Grandpa smiles warmly and says "when your grandma calls, you have to go in to take a bath." "Got it" Zayd says as he flee away thinking about getting some ladybugs. "How fun will itnbe to get some ladybugs in the jar...Oh!! Maa shaa Allah!" And he ran back to the field. "AlhamduliLaah I have my hands" "AlhamduliLaah I have my grandpa" "AlhamduliLaah am having fun" "AlhamduliLaah I got some ladybugs!" Zayd sings with excitement as he tries to catch some ladybugs. "Zayd!!" Grandma calls out. "What are you doing out there, it is late." Grandma added. "I am counting my BLESSINGS" Zayd shouted back happily. 'AlhamduliLaah I have you Grandma" he says shouting behind the garden. "I am just not ready for bed" Zayd says to himself. "Thank you Zayd, AlhamduliLaah!, I am grateful for having you too. But it is time for bed" Grandma calls out. "I wonder why the insects come out only in the evening?" Zayd asks. "It is not so late Zayd, but you need to sleep early because you have a long flight tomorrow InShaa Allah" Grandpa tells him. "Oh, I do not want to go BACK" Zayd cries,"It is beautiful here" "AlhamduliLaah I have my eyes" "AlhamduliLaah I can see" "AlhamduliLaah I have my legs" "AlhamduliLaah I can walk" "But I am not ready to go back" Zayd sings quietly, as he is trying to hide from his grandparents. "Come here Zayd, you need to get a bath NOW. " Grandpa says But, Zayd is not ready to go into the house or back to New York where he comes from. Zayd just wants to have FUN and count his blessings. "In Shaa Allah, you and your cousins would come to Nigeria for Eid. Now you need to go back for school" Grandpa tells Zayd after he found him from where he was hiding. "really!!!" his eyes light up and he jumps for joy. "ALHAMDULILAAH I have you Grandpa, you are the best!" Zayd is now happy and ready for bed.
author: Ummuh  Aiman

title: How to Catch the Wind
text: Air is always around us. Moving air is called wind. When wind blows, it carries energy. The wind’s energy can lift kites into the sky. When something resists the wind’s movement, its energy can build up... before releasing in a violent burst. But we can also capture the wind’s energy and change it into energy that we can use. Turbines help us transform wind energy into electrical energy. The energy of moving air makes the blades of a wind turbine spin. And the spinning blades change wind energy into electricity. We can use this electricity long after the wind stops blowing.
author: Anjali Vaidya

title: Pranav the Pattern Detective
text: “You climb the tree. It’s your turn!” says Arjun. Pranav looks up at the tree, and says, “Okay. I will go.” “Can you see the ball?” Maansa shouts from below. But something else catches Pranav’s eye. “Look! It’s a beehive!” Pranav cries. Maansa looks worried. “What about all the bees?” “Don’t worry, it’s empty,” says Pranav, peering at it. “There are so many holes! And they’re all the same shape…” “Why did the bees choose this shape? Why not a circle?” Pranav wonders. He imagines the hive in circles. “That would not work.” “Bees are very clever,” Pranav tells his friends the next day. He has been reading all about them. “They have discovered the best shape for their home. Hexagons come together with no holes or gaps, just like a jigsaw puzzle.” Their maths teacher, Mr Das, overhears them. “The six sides of the hexagon provide more room for the bees,” he adds. “Where did they learn how to do that?” asks Pranav. Mr Das says, with a smile, “Patterns are everywhere!” At the market the next day, Pranav looks carefully at the fruits and vegetables. He looks at the pineapples, ridge gourds and the insides of oranges. So many sizes, colours, shapes... but Pranav can see the patterns! “Are patterns really everywhere?” he wonders. Pranav becomes a pattern detective! “There are so many things in nature that are created using repeating patterns,” Pranav tells his class the next day. “We use repeating patterns in our man-made world as well,” says Mr Das. “Why don’t you try to create something using a pattern? That can be your homework.” “What shapes shall we use to make the pattern?” Pranav asks. Mr Das writes the answer on the blackboard. Use any shape you want. At home, Pranav thinks about his homework. He imagines making his own hive, perhaps with squares. Or triangles. He thinks about what Mr Das said. “Patterns are everywhere.” Then, he starts seeing the patterns. Carpet. Bookshelf. Windows. Patterns everywhere! Wherever he looks, he sees shapes coming together. “Bees are not the only clever ones,” Pranav thinks. “We use shapes and patterns for so many things!” And so Pranav gets busy drawing his dream house. Red rectangular bricks. Black and white square tiles at the entrance, like in his grandmother’s house. Who knew simple shapes could make a home—for bees, for me and for you! Spot the Patterns Nature has clever ways of taking shapes and putting them together. Pranav sees this in the world around him: the outside of a pineapple, the inside of an orange, the hexagons of a beehive. Some shapes, like hexagons and squares, fit together perfectly, leaving no gaps. But others, like circles, don’t. When shapes in nature fit together in repeating patterns, leaving no gaps or holes, it is called tessellation. Pranav sees that humans also use tessellation. We repeat shapes to form patterns, and use these patterns to design bookshelves, build castles and create works of art. A simpler word for tessellation is tiling.
author: Aditya Swaminathan

title: The Waiting .....
text: Not once upon a time but this story is from the prevailing times….. In the city of Mumbai, in a cosy little apartment lived little Ria with her Dadi, elder brother Raj, Daddy and Mummy. It had been more than a few days now; Ria was cooped up at her home. Ria realized that things were not like before. Whenever she peeped out through her balcony at anytime of the day, she could clearly hear Koel’s kuu..kuu, Parrot’s kee….kee, Crow’s caw….caw, Squirrel’s chee…chee, Sparrow’s chew.. chew…., pressure cookers whistling shewww…shewww from the many kitchens around. Unlike before when she could hear the bird songs only in the early mornings and then these sounds would be muffled under the sounds of the car honks, zooming bikes, moving buses and yes people talking and bustling around. From her balcony Ria could see the once busy streets. She could see the park where she and her friends played everyday. But now the streets were deserted, the park swings and slides were empty, the playground looked abandoned. Oh! How she longed to go there and swing on her favourite swing, the one with the little orange flowers. Oh! How Ria longed to play catch and cook and hide-n-seek with her friends. Earlier Surekha Aunty who used to help Mummy with the house work used to take her to the park. But now she doesn’t come home at all. She ran inside the house to tell her Dadi to take her to the park, but then she remembered now even Daddy, Mummy & Raj Bhaiya were at home. Yesss!!! Ria’s engineer daddy had transformed the dining table in the living room into his office table. The family ate sitting on the couch now. These days Daddy cooked breakfast. But soon after he finishes cooking and eating breakfast he works from his new office desk with his laptop and earphones. Ria found it amusing that in the day time Daddy wore his track pants along with his office shirt and a tie. As Ria came running into the living room to talk to Daddy, he said, “Shhh!” He was busy talking to some man from his office on the laptop. Ria ran towards the bedroom to tell Mummy, she saw her teacher mummy talking to her entire class, all of them who were in her laptop now. Ria then ran calling out “Raj Bhaiya…Bhaiya...!” Mummy said, “Shhh!!!” Ria then went to the other balcony where Raj Bhaiya was drying the day’s washing and was listening to his class lecture audios. Raj Bhaiya said “Shh!!!” Ria ran to her Dadi’s room. Dadi was watching the news and she said, “Shh!!!” Ria ran back to the balcony with tears swelling up in her eyes. “I want to run in the grass with Anu and Alia, I want to swing in the park with Neel and Kyra, I want to play with my friends. I want to shout loudly “ Aaaaahhh!!! ” “What happened Ria?”, said Daddy, Mummy, Dadi and Raj Bhaiya. They all came rushing by her side. Ria said I want to go to play outside… I want to go to my school…I want to play with my friends. Daddi said, “But Ria beti we cannot go outside now. We are safe inside the house.” Ria asked, ”But why? Dadi, I cannot see anything dangerous outside.” Daddy Said, “My dear Ria, outside there is a dangerous monster Covid-19. He is so tiny that we cannot see him at all however he runs very very very fast. He is roaming everywhere now, all over our world. He is playing catch and cook with whomever he sees, and once he touches a person, that person gets really sick. Ria said, “Oh! But daddy, why don’t you grownups go quietly behind him and catch him and then put him in jail. “Good thinking Ria”, said Daddy, “Ria the doctors and the scientists are thinking and working on ways in which they could catch the Covid-19 monster to put him in jail. Trust me Ria very soon they will catch the terrible Covid-19 monster and get rid of him. And then we will all go out freely just like before.” Dadi said, “ Ria beti, but until then we have to stay in our home so that the horrid monster cannot catch us.” Ria said, “Ok Dadi now I understand why we cannot go out. But Dadi I'm getting bored sitting in the house.” Mummy smiled at Ria and said, “Ria this is the time when we get to spend more time with our family. We can think of fun things to do together or alone. We can learn so many new things. Come with me.” Mummy took Ria to the balcony where she had kept many potted plants. Mummy lifted a few tiny leaves from the Money Plant creeper pot and showed Ria. Ria squealed with delight, “Caterpillar!” Seeing Ria happy all of them smiled too. Then Mummy pointed to the big pot in which the Palm tree grew, there in one of it's leaf a small cottony light sack like thing was hanging. Ria asked, “What is this Mummy?” Mummy replied, “Ria this is a cocoon. After eating well for many days together, the caterpillar one day builds itself this cocoon around himself. This becomes his cosy house for many days. He does not come out from his cocoon. Because he knows he is safe here. It will be best for him to be inside the cocoon now. Inside his house the caterpillar sleeps, learns many things in his way and he grows beautifully here. When the time is right he comes out of his cocoon as a strong and a beautiful butterfly. He then flies freely under the sky and goes to all his happy and safe places and makes use of all that he learnt inside his cocoon once. We are just like this caterpillar inside the cocoon now. We have to stay inside our house." Ria stood on her tippy toes and asked, “Mummy but how are we growing inside our house now?” Mummy replied, “We are growing by learning new things every day.” Dadi said, “Ria, I learnt how to use the Youtube on our smart TV, now I can watch my favourite movies anytime, Raj taught me.” Daddy Said, “I am learning to cook breakfast for the whole family.” Ria said, “Daddy you even learnt to tie my chotti (Plaits) he…hee….” Raj Bhaiya Said, “I’m learning that I can survive without eating junk food.” Mummy smiled and said, “Ria I’m also learning as to how to teach my whole class through my computer." Ria said, “I’m learning everyday something new too. Yesterday, Dadi taught me to sew a button and she also taught me to meditate, Mummy taught me how to write and send letters through the computer to Lata aunty, Raj bhaiya taught me to draw my favourite cartoon pictures, Daddy taught me how to wipe the washed dishes and keep them in their homes neatly." “My goodness Ria, you are growing as you are learning so many new things. Trust me very soon you will get to go to your happy places too”, said Mummy. Ria smiled at everyone around and said, “Inside my cosy cocoon I will wait. Learning and growing. Very soon I can go out freely like the butterfly.” Ria then looked at her Mother and said, “Mummy, from now on I will water the plants. Please tell me more about caterpillars, butterflies plants and...…….” The Learning….
author: Sarita Shetty

title: Shruthi Floats an Idea
text: “It’s Grow a Plant Month, everyone!” Sukanya Miss said. Everyone in the class was excited. Everyone but Shruthi. Shruthi hated the soil. She did not like touching it. She did not like the earthworms that wriggled in it. And she hated how the soil made her hands feel icky. “How was your day, Shruthi?” Appa asked. Shruthi dropped to the floor. “We have to grow a plant, Pa, and I hate touching soil!” “You don’t need soil to grow plants,” Appa replied. “But plants need air, water, soil and sunlight to grow!” said Shruthi. “Sukanya Miss told us that they get all their nutrients from the soil.” “You’re right,” Appa replied. “But plants can also get their nutrients from water, like a lotus in a pond.” “Can I really grow a plant in water?” Shruthi asked. “Yes,” Appa replied. “All you need is a sapling, some coconut husk, a big plastic bottle and some plant nutrients to help it grow.” money plant sapling plant nutrients coconut husk plastic bottle Appa cut a bottle in two halves. Shruthi filled the bottom half with water and mixed in some nutrients. She flipped the top half of the bottle and put the coconut husk in it. Finally, she placed the sapling in the top half. Shruthi took care of her plant every day. Three weeks later, she took her plant to class. Everyone was surprised. “Shruthi, how is your plant so big?” Sukanya Miss asked. “It’s because I grew it in water, Miss!” Shruthi replied. No one in her class had seen a plant grown in water before. No one even knew it was possible. “Your plant is so beautiful, Shruthi!” her classmate said. Shruthi was prouder than ever. How did Shruthi grow her plant in water? Shruthi grew her plant using hydroponics. Hydroponics is the method of growing plants in water. Plants need air, water, sunlight and nutrients (salts and minerals) to grow. When they are planted in the ground, they gather their nutrients from the soil. But when plants are grown in water, nutrients have to be fed to them. Shruthi gave her plant all the nutrients it needed, and made sure that it had enough water, sunlight, air and space to grow. Would you like to grow a plant in water, just like Shruthi? How to Grow a Plant in a Bottle You will need: A 2 litre soda bottle | A pair of scissors (make sure you ask an adult to help you with the scissors) | Money plant sapling Coconut husk | Water-soluble plant nutrients (you can use sugar as a substitute) Drinking water You will have to: Cut the bottle into two halves (ask an adult to do this for you). Pour water into the bottom half of the bottle and mix in some nutrients. Flip the top half of the bottle and place it on the bottom half. Fit the coconut husk into the top half of the bottle. Place the money plant sapling in the bottle. Make sure the roots touch the water. Make sure to keep the bottle somewhere it gets plenty of sunlight. How to Grow a Plant in a Bottle You will need: A 2 litre soda bottle A pair of scissors (make sure you ask an adult to help you with the scissors) Money plant sapling Coconut husk Water-soluble plant nutrients (you can use sugar as a substitute) Drinking water You will have to: Cut the bottle into two halves (ask an adult to do this for you). Pour water into the bottom half of the bottle and mix in some nutrients. Flip the top half of the bottle and place it on the bottom half. Fit the coconut husk into the top half of the bottle. Place the money plant sapling in the bottle. Make sure the roots touch the water. Make sure to keep the bottle somewhere it gets plenty of sunlight.
author: Navin Dorairaju

title: Why Do Sunbirds Eat All Day?
text: Meet Loten. He is a long-billed sunbird. His feathers are purple and maroon. The yellow and grey bird is his sister, Lily. Sunbirds like Loten and Lily live in parts of India and Sri Lanka. They are as long as a 100-rupee note and weigh as much as a ten-rupee coin. 15cm 14cm Loten and Lily have curved beaks and tube-shaped tongues to gather nectar from flowers. When Loten and Lily were babies, they had short, wide beaks so that their parents could feed them easily. Their parents digested the food a little in their stomachs before feeding it to them. When they grew strong enough, Loten and Lily learnt to fly. They also had to learn to find their own food. Loten and Lily get energy from what they eat and drink. This energy allows them to use their muscles to fly. Unlike us humans, Loten and Lily cannot store much energy in their bodies as fat. They have to stay very light. Otherwise, they will not be able to fly. This is why sunbirds have to eat many times a day. In fact, they spend most of their days flying around, looking for food. Loten and Lily drink nectar from flowers. They also like to eat insects and spiders. Sometimes, they eat small, juicy fruit. If you spot a bird like Loten or Lily in a garden or a park, take a peek at what they are eating! Where Does Energy Come From? Energy comes from food. Animals, including humans and birds, need energy to stay alive. It allows our bodies to work and our brains to think. Some birds have to eat every two hours, otherwise they wouldn’t have enough energy to stay alive. Bigger animals, like adult humans, can survive about two months without any food, if they really have to. But to live well, we need to eat many times a day!
author: Anusha Shankar

title: Why Do Sunflowers Love the Sun?
text: Viveka wants to paint the sunflower field near her house. She looks at the sunflowers carefully one afternoon. “I wonder why they are called sunflowers,” she says to Montu and Bontu. “Maybe it is because they look like the sun?” In the evening, Viveka takes Montu and Bontu outside to eat. She watches the sunflowers in the distance swaying in the breeze. “Look!” she says to Billi, the cat, “The sunflowers look like they’re going to fall asleep, just like you!” Finally, Viveka sits down to paint. First she paints the sun high in the sky, just like it was in the afternoon. Then she paints the sunflowers with their heads looking down sleepily, like she saw them in the evening. In the morning, Viveka goes to the sunflower field to check if her painting is correct. “Oh no,” she says, “I’ve painted them all wrong! I will have to do it again today.” “The sunflowers look like they are waking up, but the flowers in my painting look like they are falling asleep.” “This time, I will get it right!” Viveka tells Montu and Bontu. She goes out to the field at noon and makes a drawing of how the flowers look. The next morning, Viveka runs to the field to check her new painting. “How can this be?” she cries. “Are these sunflowers full of mischief? Or is this magic?” Curious, Viveka climbs the tallest tree in her garden. “I’m going to watch their every move!” Over the next few days, Viveka observes the sunflowers carefully. She paints them every day for a week. Then, on Sunday, she looks at all her paintings together. Suddenly, she understands what the sunflowers have been doing. “It isn’t magic or a trick,” she says, smiling. “The sunflowers just love to follow the sun!” Why Do Sunflowers Follow the Sun? The Earth revolves around the Sun while also rotating on its axis. As it rotates, half of the planet faces the Sun, and we call this “daytime”. At the same time, the other half is in the dark, and we call this “night”. We see the Sun rising in the east in the morning and setting in the west in the evening. Throughout the day, plants use the Sun’s light to prepare their food. But not all plants follow the Sun. The stems of young sunflowers contain cells that make them turn towards the Sun’s light. This property is called heliotropism. This is why sunflowers follow the Sun’s journey across the sky.
author: Siddharth Mehta

title: Cover Your Sneeze!
text: Achoo! went the monkey. Achoo! went the bird. Achoo! went the porcupine. Achoo! went the boar. Why did all the animals sneeze? Which sneeze was the biggest? Achoo! went the deer. ACHOO! went the buffalo. Which sneeze was the biggest? Can you make a bigger one? AAACHOO! went the tiger. Was that the biggest? Can anyone make a bigger one? Maybe... an elephant can? AAAAA... CHOO! Cover your sneeze, please! The end.
author: Lea Shaver

title: The Dog Who Knew Sadness
text: It was the first day of summer vacation. Feroz should have been happy. He had all the time in the world to play. But instead, he felt sad. Feroz didn’t feel like eating. He found it hard to fall asleep. He didn’t want to play with his friends. He didn’t want to read his favourite comics. He didn’t even want to play hide and seek with Noah, his best friend. Feroz and Noah shared a special bond. Feroz had rescued Noah from a shelter. And these days, Noah lived with Feroz and they did everything together. They went on walks together, Played silly games, Shared yummy meals And slept next to each other every night. Feroz loved spending time with Noah. No matter how sad he felt, Noah could always make him smile. Maybe that was because Noah understood sadness. Before Noah became a part of Feroz’s family, he had been sad too. When sadness kept Feroz in bed even on sunny days, Noah would curl up beside him. Sometimes, sadness felt like Feroz’s shadow. It followed him everywhere. But even on bad days, taking a walk with Noah always raised his spirits. The sadness didn’t seem so overwhelming when Feroz was out with Noah. The more time he spent with him, the better he began to feel. Though he still felt sad sometimes and some days were worse than others, Feroz knew that he would always have Noah. Slowly, he found things to look forward to again. Comics to read, Football to play, Games of hide and seek... With Noah by his side. Ready to follow him anywhere.
author: Nisarg Prakash

title: Two friends
text: Raju were two friends living in a forest. Because of the good friendship of the two, they used to walk in the desert, eat, play, and get together. One day Raju wanted to eat coconut in a tree outside the forest. He told it to Gaju too. Gaju became happy. But the problem was that neither of the two could reach the coconut. Then Raju said, I collect coconut, you need to push the tree. ﻿ Gaju shook the tree loudly. The coconut began to fall down the same instant. And all the coconuts fell like stones on Gaju ﻿ Gaju started to run from there. And one of the coconuts fell on Raju's head. Both of them fled towards the dense forest.
author: Dr.Abhay Karandikar

title: Ira Investigates the Invisible
text: Where did I put that petri dish? Oh, hello! Have you seen a small glass dish with a lid? It’s for an important experiment I’m doing. I’ve put about a billion cells inside it. I know what you’re thinking: How can you fit one billion of anything inside a small dish? My name is Dr. Ira and I’m a microbiologist. I’m not the kind of doctor you see when you have a fever or an earache. I’m a doctor that studies invisible things. I know that sounds ridiculous but let me explain. What if I told you that all around us in the air, soil, water, and even inside us—in our stomachs, noses and ears— are thousands, no, millions, no... TRILLIONS of tiny living creatures called microbes? Ewww! YUCK! Cheee? There are around one trillion kinds of microbes on our planet. While each of these microbes looks different and lives in a different habitat, most microbes can broadly be divided into Bacteria Algae Fungi Protozoa Viruses As a microbiologist, I spend my time studying bacteria. Would you like to see where I work? Welcome to my lab! Yuck! What’s that smell? Ugh! This orange has been sitting on my friend Tashi’s desk for a week now. See how it’s covered in green fuzz? That’s fungus. Shall we take a closer look? Let’s use a microscope. It helps us see things that our eyes aren’t powerful enough to see on their own. I know they look scary but some microbes can be very helpful. For instance, this fungus tells us that the orange is spoiled and that we shouldn’t eat it. Did you know that there are microbes that can eat plastic? They could help solve plastic pollution! Not all microbes are friendly though. Some types of the bacteria E.coli can cause tummy aches. But if we get to know them better and understand why they make us sick, we can try to prevent illnesses. That’s why I study how E.coli cells react to changes in their environment. I use some very cool tools to do this. Microscope: an instrument which makes really small objects look bigger by magnifying them. Petri Dish: a circular, transparent dish with a flat lid used to maintain microbes in certain conditions. Pipette: a slender tube with a bulb at one end used for transferring or measuring small quantities of liquid. Autoclave: a strong heated container that uses high pressure and temperature for chemical reactions and other processes. Let’s ask Tashi if he’s seen my petri dish. And tell him to throw away that orange! Hi Tashi! Tashi was my first friend at university. When I first came here to study, I felt lost. I didn’t speak much English and all my classes were hard. Plus, everyone else seemed so smart and I just couldn’t keep up. I wanted to give up so many times and just go home, but how could I? I'm the first woman in my family to go to college and they supported me every step of the way. I didn’t want to let them or myself down. Besides, I loved exploring this invisible world around me. So I kept trying. Learning to not give up is important, especially when you’re a microbiologist. Because a lot of the experiments I do fail. What keeps me going is when things work. It’s so exciting when you’ve learned something that no one else knows yet! But even when things don’t work out, it’s alright. It helps me ask the next question. Like, ‘Where is my petri dish?’ Tashi hasn’t seen it either. I need to do the experiment again. Will you keep me company? I’m going to take some E.coli, grow it in a conical flask and see what happens when I don’t give it enough to eat. I’ll take another E.coli sample in a second flask and give it food. Then I’ll wait and see what happens to the number of E.coli in both these flasks. This is called making an observation. After the experiment is completed, I’ll compare the E.coli growth in both the flasks and write down my observations. These are the results of my experiment. It will help me answer the question: Does the amount of food affect the growth of E.coli? What I learn from the results is called an inference. A typical E.coli growth experiment takes 10 to 12 hours to complete. Since I don’t need to sit here and watch the cells the entire time, I read about new discoveries, attend meetings and talk to other scientists about their work. This is important because I learn exciting new things from them and often get ideas for my own work. Sometimes, we also just sit around, have tea and chat! Scientists may seem very serious, but really, we’re just like you and your friends. We like to play hockey, sing in the shower and read scary stories! We are also curious about the world around us. We like to ask questions constantly: We’re like detectives who look for clues that help answer all these fascinating questions. Even if they’re inside your stomach. Speaking of which, I’m hungry. Let’s eat! Why? Why not? How? What if? Tashi! Grow your own mould! The fungus that grows on old food is called mould. To grow your own mould, take a piece of leftover roti or a slice of stale bread, sprinkle it with water, place it on a plate and cover it with a clear glass bowl. Keep at room temperature and out of direct sunlight for two days. Check the food and see if white, blue, green or gray fuzz has appeared on it. Leave it alone for 2 more days and then check on it. How does the mould look now? Make a note. Repeat this every 2 days until day 10. What do you think will happen? The water and room temperature create the perfect conditions for growing mould! The mould will look different on different items of food. That is because different kinds of mould spores like some foods better than others. At the end of 10 days, carefully dispose of the mouldy food with the help of your teacher. Maybe you could add it to a compost pit!
author: Menaka Raman

title: JUMP AWAY LILY!
text: Lily loves to jump! Do you like to jump? Lily jumps all over the house every day. Today lily was having a tea party so she was baking a cake. But she wanted to jump so badly that she was baking the cake so fast that when her friends ate it, the cake tasted like spicy curry! Today lily and evan were jumping up and down to there favorite song. While they were jumping, lily twisted her ankle because even before going to evan's house she was jumping on this same song now, lily gave up her jumping career!
author: Aathira Karthik

title: WHERE TO HIDE?
text: Rhino has no choice but to be "it". All animals split up in every direction. "Where is a good spot to hide so that Rhino won't find us?", they ask each other. Rhino closes her eyes while counting: "five, ten, fifteen..." She opens her eyes after counting to one hundred. "Where are you guys? How do I find you guys now?", she asks. Monkey bounces right on the top of a branch on the left. "You have a long tail. I can see you, Monkey!" Rhino says, excitedly. Squirrel rushes to a tree's hole on the right. Rhino smiles as she spots Squirrel: "Hey Squirrel, I can see you with your fluffy tail too!" Rabbit panics, crawls right under a nearby cave. Outside, Porcupine is too busy using flowers to disguise herself as a shrub. Unfortunately, they, too, are spotted by Rhino's sharp eyes. "A-ha, Porcupine and Rabbit! You guys are hiding in such obvious spots!" Snail slowly hides under a tiny leaf. Red Parrot is confident about her hiding spot on top of a tree. Yet, Rhino is still able to find her. Silly deer tries to be like one of the small trees, while Giant Bear hides behind a pile of rocks. "We can all see you guys" Rhino laughs as she points them out. Turtle hides in his own shell, pretending to be a stone. Frog finds cover within a bush across from Turtle. Both are also spotted by Rhino. There is only clever Chameleon left. He is nowhere to be found. "That's it for Rhino." say the animals. After looking everywhere for Chameleon, Rhino's feet are now sore. She is exhausted and decides to return to the pond. Rhino sits back down by the pond. "I don't need any help." she cries "Chameleon may have a good hiding spot, but I will find him." Feeling bad, Rhino bends down to look at the pond. Suddenly, "I have found Chameleon!" Rhino screams. "Yeah," Chameleon chuckles "I have been on your horn the whole time. Not a bad idea at all!" "It is now my turn to hide, and you guys have to find me. I already know where I am going to hide" Rhino chuckles.
author: Scott Luu

title: What should Soma sow?
text: He ate the fruits of the trees in the jungle. One day, while roaming in the jungle, he came across a stream. The stream asked him, "Why don't you start farming?" Old Soma then cleared all the bushes from both the banks of the stream. He cleared the land and sowed oats. When the crop was ready, a squirrel came there and started eating the grains. Soma asked her, "Dear squirrel, why do you eat my crop? The squirrel replied, "I wouldn't have eaten if you would have sown kulith (it is also called horse gram). So, old Soma sowed kulith in his farm. When the kulith was ready, a deer came there. The deer started eating the crop. Soma said, "Oh deer, why do you eat my kulith? The deer said, "If you would have sown maize, I wouldn't have eaten your crop." So then, old Soma sowed some maize in his field. One day, a parrot came to eat the maize. Soma asked, "Hey parrot, why do you eat my maize? The parrot replied, "I wouldn't have eaten your grain if you would have sown groundnuts." Then, old soma sowed some groundnuts in his field. After some days, a fox came and started eating the groundnuts. Soma asked the fox, "Why do you eat my groundnuts?' The fox replied, " If you would have sown yam, I wouldn't have eaten them." Then old Soma sowed some yams. A pig came there to eat the yams. Soma asked the pig, "Why do you eat my yams?' The pig replied, "If you would have sown sesame seeds then I wouldn't have eaten." Then old Soma sowed some sesame seeds. In this way Soma harvested many different crops. He and his animal friends lived happily ever after. Do you like to eat such foods? Concep t India's rich linguistic diversity means a veritable treasure trove of children's stories. Unfortunately, there is a lack of published children's literature in many tribal languages or even colourful, enjoyable, storybooks. The need to create children's literature in tribal languages has become evident as the number of tribal children joining schools has increased. Literature that opens up the world to them while staying grounded in their culture. Books have the magic to communicate with children in affective ways to inform, engage and entertain them. Books help children think independently and seek answers in unique ways. It is important that each child has access to good books in her own language for education to be truly meaningful. Project Pratham books and IgnusERG, with support of Bernard van Lear Foundation have created the first ten children's books in Munda, Koi, Saura and Juang languages from Odisha.
