title: My Train Journey
text: During my summer holidays we planned to go to Lucknow we booked our train tickets and headed for our journey. Me and my sister were very excited for the journey.We had planned a lot of fun activities for our entertainment. During the journey we ate lot of chips and muffins and soon I felt very thirsty I asked for water but it seems that all the water bottles were finished. My father asked me to wait till the next station Kanpur. But i was impatient and started crying. The next station was a small village and my father had to fill up the bottles from the water cooler. Soon after drinking water I started having stomach ache, fever,vomiting and diarrhea. I was sick due to the impure water I just drank. I was sick and completed my journey with great difficulty. As soon as we reached our place, my father took me to the hospital where I was diagnosed with diarrhea and was given O.R.S (Oral re-hydration solution) and other medicines for treatment. It took me a few days to recover and I learnt that we should always drink clean and pure water.
author: Akshat Gupta
illustrator: Niloufer Wadia; Rai; Sadhna Prasad; Sahitya Rani

title: Hide and Seek
text: Author Rabindranath Tagore was born on 7 May, 1861 to Maharshi Debendranath Tagore, one of the leaders of the Brahmo Samaj, and Sarada Devi. He was a distinguished Bengali poet, writer, painter, playwright and composer of songs. He was homeschooled by a variety of teachers in a variety of subjects. He composed ‘Sishu’, ‘Dakghor’, ‘Birpurush’, ‘Proshno’, ‘Sahaj Path’ and others for children. He was the recipient of the Nobel Prize for Literature in the year 1913. In 1915, the prestigious ‘knighthood’ was awarded to him by the British Raj but he soon renounced it as a protest to the Jallianwalah Bagh massacre of 1919. A highly renowned artist, he was known for introducing the Indian culture to the West which led to his establishment of the ‘Vishwabharati’ University in Santiniketan which is a mosaic of the East and the West. Two of his song compositions, “Jana Gana Mana” and “Amar Shonar Bangla” were chosen by India and Bangladesh respectively as their national anthems. Rabindranath Tagore passed away on August 7, 1941. About the poem Published as a part of the collection Sishu by Tagore in the early 20th century, the poem harps on the beautiful relationship between the mother and her child, where a leisurely picture of a household is painted, as seen revolving around the mother, by the child from afar.The poem is endearing in its portrayal of the child who plays hide-and-seek with his mother while observing her. If I turn very naughty one day If I bloom on a frangipani tree When the sun puts out its first ray On tender leaves I roll around so free. That is when you lose to me dear mother, For would you know me then, from any other? “Where’s my boy?” you call out all the while I sit quietly – silently I smile! As you go about your daily chores, I’ll watch you ma with eager open eyes Freshly bathed, beneath the tree you pass Your tumbling hair free of binding ties Into the prayer room ma then you go A scent from flowers surround you so. There’s something that you simply do not know From your baby does this fragrance flow! Once the feeding of the lot is done In the afternoon with book in hand, You sit near the window in the light There the shadow of my tree will land. My little shadow then, on you I spread Swaying on the page that you just read But you will not know, O Mother wise Whose shadow that is on your eyes! The evening lamp – when you light its flame, And to the cowshed outside gently walk Suddenly, playing nature’s game, On the ground I’ll fall–a flower stalk. Once again I’ll be your little one Say, “Ma, tell a story when you’re done”. You will scold and ask, “Where’d you go?” And I will say, “Ah, that you’ll never know.”
author: Swagata Sen Pillai

title: The Winter Night
text: Premchand went on to become one of the most prolific writers in the Indian subcontinent. He was bestowed with the honorary title of ‘Munshi’ due to his mastery over words. He is considered to be the pioneer of the modernist Hindustani literature. He authored (roughly) 300 short stories and several dozen novels in his lifetime. Premchand was also a popular dramatist and a translator. His famous works include novels like Karmabhoomi, Seva Sadan, Godaan, Nirmala.... and short stories like Eidgah, Lottery, Bade Bhai Sahab, Do Bailon ki Katha and Poos Ki Raat amongst many other notable titles.. He was given the title of ‘“Upanyas Samrat’” (Emperor among Novelists) by the other writers of his times.Majority of his writings present a slice of life of the pre-independence era. His writing is steeped in realism and he is known for his Hindi-Urdu literature. His style of writing is more direct and he is considered to be the first Hindi writer to showcase the concept of realism in his writings. Subjects like colonialism, corruption, poverty, child widowhood and exploitation of the poor etc. feature prominently in his works. He wrote extensively about the life of common people of his times. Munshi Premchand died on October 8, 1936 but his work continues to be commemorated even today. About the Story With great difficulty farmer Halku and his wife had saved three rupees to buy a blanket but were compelled to give the money to Sehna to repay their loan. On a chilly winter night, keeping a watch at the field Halku shivered in the freezing cold. He lighted a fire to stay warm. While he slept wrapped in his sheet, a herd of nilgai grazed his crop but he failed to muster the will to come out of the cocoon of warmth and chase away the animals. When his wife Munni asked him about the ruined crop in the morning, he lied about having had a terrible stomachache. Munni was worried about how they would pay the taxes now that the crop has been ruined but Halku found relief in the fact that he won’t have to sleep in the field on cold winter nights anymore. **nilgai: blue bull, a large antelope. Halku asked his wife- “Sehna is here. Bring me the money you have, let me pay him and get him off my back.” Munni was sweeping the floor. She turned around and retorted- “It’s only three rupees, how will we buy the blanket if you give him the money? How will you survive the deep winter nights of Maagh and Poos in the field? Tell him, we will pay him at harvest time. Not now.” For a moment Halku stood indecisively. Winter was around the corner. He wouldn’t be able to keep watch over the fields without a blanket. But Sehna wouldn’t agree, he’d rebuke and curse them. Thinking ‘we might die in winter, but far better to have this trouble off my back’ he ambled to his wife and pleaded with her. “Come on now, give me the money. Let’s get rid of this loan once and for all. I’ll think of some way to get the blanket.” **Maagh and Poos: Months of the Indian traditional calendar corresponding to January and February. Munni moved away and glared at him, - “You will never be able to find a way. Will someone donate us a blanket? What a loan! There seems no end to it. I say, why don’t you give up farming altogether? We break our backs over it and come harvest, we pay the loan and that’s it. It’s as if we were born only to pay the loan. We have to labour for others in order to feed ourselves. Enough with farming! I won’t give the money, I just won’t give it.” A saddened Halku said- “So, should I just get abused?” Distressed, Munni retorted- “Why would he abuse you, does he rule over us?” As she uttered these words, her raised brow relaxed. The harsh truth inherent in Halku’s question was glaring at her like a fearsome animal. She brought the money from the alcove and placed it in Halku’s palm. She then pleaded - “Quit farming now. Better to be a labourer and be happy eating less. At least we won’t be bullied. What good is farming? We shovel our earnings from hard labour into farming and then get bullied on top of that.” Halku took the money from her and went out as if he carried his very heart to give away. He had painstakingly saved each paisa from his labour work wages to save these three rupees for a blanket. And now they were going away. With each step, weighed down with the burden of poverty his head bent lower. The dark night of Poos *! Even the stars in the sky seemed to quiver. With just an old rough sheet to keep him warm, at the edge of his field Halku lay shivering on a bamboo cot under a shackthatch of dried sugarcane leaves. Under the cot his dog, Jabra lay curled into a ball, shivering and whimpering in the cold. Neither of the two could fall asleep. Hugging his neck with his knees, Halku spoke- “So Jabra, feeling cold, eh? I told you to sleep on the haystack at home, why did you have to come with me? Now enjoy the cold, what am I to do? You knew (thought) that I was coming here to eat a feast, so you rushed ahead of me. Now regret it all you can.” Jabra wagged his tail, yawned, whined, then fell silent. Perhaps his canine wisdom sensed that the whining is not allowing the master to sleep. Halku stroked Jabra’s cold back - “Don’t come with me or you’ll freeze. This witch of a westerly wind is carrying ice from who knows where. Let me get up and fill my chillum and somehow pass the night. I have already smoked eight chillums. This is the thrill of farming! And there are the lucky ones whom cold would never dare to touch. Thick and soft mattresses, quilts, blankets, the works! Winter just would not survive! It’s sheer destiny, we are the ones who slog, while the fruits are enjoyed by others!” **chillum: Small country Indian clay pipe to smoke tobacco in. Halku rose, took a tiny coal from the pit and filled his chillum. Jabra sat up too. Puffing at the chillum Halku said- “Want to smoke some? It doesn’t shoo away the cold, just lightens the mood.” Jabra gazed at his face with its eyes brimming with affection. Halku- “Today’s your last day of enjoying the cold. I’ll lay some hay here tomorrow. Snuggle into it. Then you won’t be cold.” Jabra rested his paws on Halku’s knees and rested his face next to Halku’s. Halku felt the dog’s warm breath on his face. Having smoked the chillum, Halku lay down with a firm resolve to sleep come what may but within a moment his heart began to palpitate. He turned and tossed, but like a demon the cold was stubbornly pressing down his chest. When it became unbearable, he gently picked up Jabra, patted his head and lay him in his lap. A strong stench emanated from the dog, yet Halku felt a pleasure he hadn’t felt in months. Jabra perhaps thought that heaven was here and in Halku’s pious soul there wasn’t a trace of hatred towards the dog. He would have embraced a close friend or cousin with the same warmth. He was not distressed by his poverty which had brought him to this state. No, this unique friendship had thrown open the doors of his soul and every speck of it was illuminated. Suddenly Jabra sensed some animal. This special warmth had filled him with a new vigour which considered the chill gusts of wind insignificant. He leaped out of the shack and began to bark. Halku lovingly called him several times but Jabra ran in the field barking. Even if he came to Halku for a second, he would immediately run away. Duty bounced in his heart like desire. Another hour passed. The night began stoking the cold with the wind. Halku sat up and hugged his knees to his chest, he hid his head in them and yet the cold didn’t abate. He felt as if his blood had frozen, as if ice flowed in his veins. He craned his neck to see the sky to/and gauge how far the daybreak was. The Ursa Major hadn’t even crawled up halfway in the sky. It was just a little after midnight. There was a mango orchard a stone’s throw away from Halku’s field. Autumn had arrived. The orchard was strewn with fallen leaves. Halku thought, “I will gather leaves from the orchard, make a fire and warm myself. Anyone who sees me gathering leaves at night, will think it’s a ghost. Who knows if there’s some animal hiding in there, but I can’t bear the cold any longer.” He pulled out several pigeon pea stalks from a nearby field and made a broom out of them. Holding a smoldering cow dung cake in his other hand he walked towards the orchard. Seeing Halku, Jabra lumbered towards him and began wagging his tail. Halku burst out, “I can’t bear it any longer Jabra. Let us gather leaves from the orchard and make a fire. Once we’re warm, we’ll come back and sleep. The night is still young.” Jabra yapped in agreement and walked towards the orchard. It was completely dark in there and the harsh wind crushed the leaves. Condensation dripped from the trees. Suddenly, a gust of wind brought in the scent of henna blossom. Halku remarked- “What lovely fragrance Jabra! You can smell it as well, can’t you?” Jabra had found a bone somewhere and he was busy gnawing it. Halku placed the smouldering cow dung cake on the ground and began to gather dried leaves. Within no time he had gathered a large heap of leaves. His hands trembled, his bare feet were numb with cold. But he continued to pile up a mountain of leaves. He was set on reducing the cold to ashes with this fire. Soon, the fire was blazing. Its flames rose high to fleetingly touch the leaves of the trees. In that fluttering light, huge trees of the orchard seemed to be balancing the bottomless darkness on their heads. In that infinite ocean of darkness, the fire seemed like a frail boat, bobbing up and down. Halku sat facing the fire, warming himself. Soon, he removed the sheet and tucked it under his arms. He then spread out his legs, as if challenging the cold to do what it could. Having triumphed over the boundless might of the cold, he couldn’t help but flaunt his pride in the victory. He asked Jabra - “So Jabbar, not cold now, are you?” Jabra yipped as if to say, “Why will I feel cold? Halku went on, “If I had this idea sooner, we wouldn’t have been so cold all these days!” Jabra wagged his tail. “Ok, come, let’s jump over this fire. Let’s see who can. And boy, if you get burned, I will not buy medicines for you.” Jabra looked at the big fire with scared eyes. “Don’t tell Munni tomorrow or else she’ll bicker with me.” Halku leaped over the fire and landed on the other side. The flames licked his feet slightly, but he did not mind it. Jabra went around the fire and stood near Halku. Halku said- “Come on, that doesn’t count! You have to jump over it.” Halku jumped again and landed at the other end in a jiffy. The leaves had burnt away. The orchard was dark once again. There was still a hint of fire underneath the ash which would stir when a gust of wind swept by, but it would close its eyes in a moment. Halku wrapped the sheet around his body again and began to hum. His body had warmed but as the cold grew stronger lethargy overpowered him. Jabra barked loudly and ran towards the field. Halku felt that a herd of animals had entered the field. Perhaps it was a herd of nilgai. The sound of their gamboling and running amok could be heard. Then the sound of grazing was loud and clear. Halku convinced himself - “With Jabra there, no animal can enter the field. He’ll claw it away. I am hallucinating. Why, I can’t hear anything now. What an illusion I had!” He called out loudly- “Jabra, Jabra!” Jabra continued to bark. The sound of grazing was heard again. Halku couldn’t deceive himself any longer. To move away from the warmth felt like a curse. The very idea of chasing the animals in such bitter cold was unbearable to Halku. He did not budge. He shouted aloud- “Liho-Liho! Liho!” Jabra barked again. The animals were grazing the field away. The crop was ready for harvest. It was such a fine crop but these evil animals were destroying it all. Halku rose with firm resolve and walked a few steps when suddenly a chilling, biting gust of wind struck him like a scorpion sting. He returned to the dying fire and began to poke at the ashes to warm his cold body. Jabra was barking his lungs out, the nilgais were grazing the field clean. Halku sat calmly next to the fire. Indolence wrapped itself around him. He pulled the sheet over and slept on the warm ground next to the ashes. When he woke up next morning, the sun was shining and he heard Munni - “Are you going to sleep all day? You are relaxing here, and the whole field has been ruined.” Halku got up and asked, “Are you coming from the fields?” Munni replied, “Yes, the entire field is ruined. For God’s sake, who sleeps like this? What was the point in having a shack here then?” Halku lied, “I nearly died and all you are worried about is your precious field. You have no idea how terrible a stomach ache I had last night.” They returned to the edge of the field. They stared at the field. It had been trampled and Jabra was lying motionless under the shack. Munni’s face was clouded with sadness but Halku was happy. Munni was worried, “We will have to work as labourers to pay the taxes.” Halku smiled, “At least I won’t have to sleep in the cold anymore.”

"I definitely do not know, but Rita should not know that I don't know. Let me trick her" Appa thought " Oh Appa, you silly fellow" said Amma. " You should explain nicely to Rita, she is just a kid," Scolded Amma "But you see," Appa said going red, " Even I don't know what an astronomer is!" Their daily routine was to steal Tender Coconut from the nearby vendor at the end of the street and bring it back to their home and enjoy it. They loved their life until…………………. A new family moved into the empty house. Poor squirrels did not know they will have a fierce competitor for their Coconuts! The new family had a little dog named Rusty.Rusty was a very naughty dog, he loved chasing small animals it was his sport...He felt like a champion when he played it.One afternoon Nutty and Kutty came back from stealing Coconuts. They sat on their favorite branch and were just about to eat it, sad for them Rusty spotted them. Rusty gave them a big growl. Rusty started barking nonstop, Nutty and Kutty panicked and dropped the Coconut and it fell down the tree. Rusty picked up the Coconut and ran away. Days passed and this became Rusty’s routine and he started liking Coconuts too. Poor Nutty and Kutty had lost their freedom, they were being chased every day. One final day Nutty and Kutty could not take it anymore. It had been more than a week since they had a yummy Coconut or happily roamed around in the yard. They planned to put an end to this and went into Rusty’s house. They made sure he was sleeping. Nutty and Kutty tip toed into the kitchen. They dropped all the food on the floor, poured the flour down and made a mess of the kitchen. Then they arranged a trail to lead Rusty to the kitchen, they knew Rusty could not resist his favorite treat trail. When Rusty came to the kitchen they started dropping vessels to wake the owners up and then they ran away. Rusty now realized it was a trap. He was caught. That day Nutty Kutty enjoyed their lovely Coconut meal …when they saw Rusty come out with his leash to get tied up in the backyard.He glared at Nutty Kutty …Kutty said “what a yummy Coconut “to Nutty! … and winked at Rusty 😊 Rusty said I will get my revenge you horrid squirrels! title: Moonlight in the Sea
text: Nihla meets Fatima Nihla smiled at Fatima, the baby, just moments after she was born. Full and bright, Nihla smiled radiantly at the baby girl. Her cool gaze washed over the little island, off the tops of coconut-laden trees, and bounced off the green waters of the lagoon. The island was so little that it was only a speck in the middle of the big blue ocean, a smudge with nothing around it for hundreds of miles. So teeny that the tiny tots of the island could run around it in a half a day. So tiny that a teeny turtle could swim around it in an hour. Too minute for a map. Too small for the world. And Fatima grew up there, smelling the salt air all around her, the white sand of the beaches below her cradle, the open ocean to her left, the lazy lagoon to her right. Fatima meets Nihla Fatima smiled at Nihla much later. Her first memory was the sand and the water, and the light in it. She imagined that someone had gathered up light from the streets, the houses, the shops, and thrown it helter-skelter into the water. And then one day she thought to look up and there was Nihla wearing her broad grin, almost saying, ‘Well now, you’ve finally found me, haven’t you?’ And she looked up at the moon and down at the water and marveled that Nihla could swim so easily. Fatima loved the swimming Nihla, loved watching the light splash and flow through the water. She imagined she could chase Nihla in the water, cup her in her palm, and bring her home. She dug her toes into the sand and let the gentle waves of the lagoon lap and drown her feet. And the little twinkling algae lit up like sparklers in the water. And later, when she walked home, her feet were covered with bits of the minute living sparklers, green and glowing, lighting up every footprint she left in the sand. Fatima Falls In Fatima spent much of her day on the beach by the boats. Fatima loved boats. The little one that her father used to fish in the lagoon, the lapping sounds of the paddle in the still of the night. The big one that he used to fish at sea, the growl of the motor against the whitecaps in the noon sun. One day, her father decided he would take her with him to fish in the lagoon, just a short trip. Fatima could not believe her luck. Her father lifted her onto the boat and his boys jumped in and paddled the boat out. Slowly they put their nets out to catch bait for their tuna. One of the nets snagged, and as they pulled, the boat tilted to a side and Fatima saw the world tilt over, until suddenly she was in the water. Later, she remembered the sound of her father yelling at the boys, but she remembered the light in the water more. The light in the water that was swimming around her and reflecting off these strange and wonderful sights. It seemed like the longest time, but within seconds, a hand grabbed her and brought her on to the boat. And she knew then that she would have to go back, to join Nihla in exploring this world that she did not know about. Still life in coral Her mother said she should learn how to swim. Her father wasn’t sure, but her mother insisted. After she learned to paddle about, her father bought her a mask and snorkel and fashioned fins for her pint-sized feet. She swam near the shore among the fronds of seagrass that waved to and fro with the gentlest of tides. One day, her father rowed to the middle of the lagoon and lowered her into the water. As she adjusted her mask and looked below, the world exploded into colour - purple, red, blue, green. She saw fingers of branching coral, the huge boulder like massive coral, the table coral, the brain coral. Fatima realized suddenly that in the flurry of colour, the shock of shapes, she had forgotten to breathe. With the smidgeon of air left in her little lungs, she blew water out of her snorkel and took a deep gulp of air. She paddled around, with her head under water, absorbed with the world below, oblivious to the one above. Every chance Fatima got, she would get her father or one of the boys to row her out into the lagoon. She would spend hours in the water watching the coral, trailing the turtles, following the fish. And there were so many different kinds. Giant and midget, fat and thin, long and short, and every colour of the rainbow, sometimes on the same fish! The colorful little damsels, the threadfin butterfly fish, the regal angels, the sturdy surgeons, the slow-looking snappers, the roguish rabbitfish, the painted parrotfish, the stuffy puffers, and the groupers that waited stealthily to ambush their prey. Grumpy and pompous Fatima loved to compare the fish to the people she knew. Grumpy grouper was her uncle who came home to eat tea and biscuits. Pompous puffer was her father’s friend who owned the big shop down the road. Of course, beautiful butterflyfish was her mother, and exquisite angelfish was her little sister. And needless to say, she was a baby sweetlips, brightly coloured, yellow and black, swimming wildly and dashing about in fits and bursts of energy, but trying to stay far from big fish with bigger teeth. And one night, swimming near the reef, she saw something she would never forget. Her father was fishing nearby and she jumped into the water with a torch. Suddenly, she was surrounded by a snowstorm, a powder cloud, of pink and white little coral spawn. Fatima goes fishing Much as she liked fish, she liked fishing even better. First, she learned to fish from the jetty, throwing lines in the water and pulling up small silvery fish. Sometimes, she went fishing with her father. They would go out with live baitfish in a big box on the boat and search for tuna shoals. Once they found one, her father would guide the boat through the shoal, spraying water and scattering baitfish into the sea. In the feeding frenzy that followed, the tuna would snap at anything silvery and shiny, including the hooks that dangled from the lines that hung from the poles. Her father and his boys would swing the tuna up and about and flick it off the hook into the boat. Fatima liked to catch rainbow runners on the lines that trailed behind the boat. She loved feeling the line jerk against her hand, and the weight of the fish as she pulled it in. Already, she would be thinking of the spices her mother would use to make the curry. And sometimes, the boys would cut and clean the fish on the boat itself, add some salt, chop it into little pieces and throw them into the boiling rice along with other spices. Fish biryani. It was heaven! One day, while Fatima was snorkeling, she saw a big green turtle, a male with its long tail protruding behind it. She had seen it in the lagoon many times. This time, she decided to follow it as it lazily swam on. It was an old turtle, with crud on its carapace, and half a flipper missing. What shark had chewed on this grizzled giant, she wondered. There had once been hundreds of green turtles in this lagoon but now there were just a few. Her father said that the turtles had eaten all the seagrass here and then gone to other islands to feed there. They are pests, he said, eating all the grass in the lagoon and leaving the fish with nowhere to rest, breed or hide. He said that was why there was so little of the baitfish they used to catch the tuna. But watching the old male drift languidly through the green waters of the lagoon, Fatima could not bring herself to dislike him. And where had he traveled – thousands of miles across the open ocean? Fatima imagined herself swimming across open seas and meeting wondrous sea creatures along the way. The sudden storm When Fatima was nine, she often took her father’s boat and paddled into the lagoon to snorkel on her own and sometimes, to fish. The storm came without any warning. Big dark clouds, drum rolls of thunder, lightning streaking across the sky and wet sheets of rain. Fatima was not afraid, for she was in the lagoon, but she could not even see the island any more. She huddled in the boat and waited for the storm to pass, bailing water out of the boat. An hour later, the storm had not passed. Two hours later, it was still raining buckets. Three hours later, it was clear that the heavens had sprung a major leak. And the waves were getting bigger. And bigger. The sea looked like it was boiling. Big bubbling swells rose up as if from the very depths of the ocean, lifted the boat high up towards the sky and brought it hurtling down. For hours and hours and hours, the little boat was rocked by gigantic waves. And Fatima realized she had been swept far out to sea. Fatima clung to a plank, as she was tossed about like a little rag doll. When the boat filled with water, she waited for a moment of calm and bailed furiously. For a while, she believed that the storm would pass and her father would come out in his big tuna boat and rescue her. But then she realized that she was too far away, being swept south towards the vast expanse of ocean. Where the turtle swam on his long distance travels. Where the tuna came from. Where whales and dolphins cavorted. But she knew she was no turtle or whale or dolphin – and she was ready to give up hope. At that moment, sitting in a boat filled with water, with not a whit of energy left, Fatima felt a gaze upon her. Looking up, she saw her old friend, Nihla, holding the curtain of clouds apart, straining to send her a message. Fatima looked at Nihla and her heart filled with hope. Nihla’s smile was warm. Then Nihla danced in the water, kissed the tips of the whitecaps, ran her soothing gaze over the heads of the truculent waves and calmed the angry sea. Till its fury was reduced to an unhappy but harmless grumble. Fatima looked around, and in that moment of silence saw, in a little cone of moonlight, an itsy-bitsy island, a little blip in the ocean. Bailing and paddling furiously, Fatima made her way into the lagoon and towards the haven. Smaller even than the one she had come from. She landed on the beach and dragged her boat ashore. Dancing with Dolphins Fatima had found Suheli, a little island in a large lagoon that fishermen visited during fair weather. Now, there was no one here. She found a few sheds where they had left food supplies. Fortunately, Fatima knew how to fish. Each morning, she set out into the lagoon and put out some lines. With supplies from the shed, she made herself tea and later roasted the fish with salt and chilly powder. The menu never changed, but at least the fish were different every day. At the edge of the lagoon, she watched the dolphins play and sometimes she swam with them. The dolphins liked Fatima and adopted her as a somewhat strange cousin. She did not see them every day but when they did come, there would be much frolicking around her. A young calf was particularly fond of Fatima and would playfully poke her in the side. Fatima had heard stories about how dolphins helped people and wondered if they might take her home if she rode on them, like in some pictures she had seen in a book. But the adult dolphins never let her get close enough for that. And as friendly as they were, Fatima was still just that little bit afraid of them. Moonlight and Manta One day, she paddled out to the reef and found a little opening into the ocean. The sea was calm like a sheet of glass and Fatima could not resist paddling a little further. The blue water was so clear, she could see the coral twenty metres below. From the little compartment below the planks, she pulled out her little mask and snorkel, and jumped into the water. Holding her breath, Fatima could now dive several metres underwater. She saw the familiar shapes of the blue tangs, the butterfly fish, a Moorish idol, a regal angelfish. And the larger shapes of a Napoleon wrasse, a school of bump-headed parrotfish swimming near a coral mound some distance away, jacks and trevallies circling. And suddenly from a distance, she saw a manta ray swim towards her, gliding through the water like a sci-fi stealth jet, wing tips upturned ever so slightly. It swooped towards the reef and passed below her, its grace and elegance so complete that once again, Fatima realized she had forgotten to breathe. At that moment, Fatima realized that she wanted to spend the rest of her life in the water. To watch and learn and understand this beautiful world. Queen of the island Suheli was serene, but Fatima knew she had to leave soon. To go back to school, to college, to university, to go around the world. To come back to Suheli. Fortunately, this was the end of the rainy season and a few days later, the first fishing crew arrived. As they approached, they saw a gigantic lagoon with two idyllic islands in the middle. As they came closer, they saw that the turquoise blue waters cradled two palm-covered mounds of sand, blissfully unaware of the buzz of life elsewhere. As the boat hummed across the lagoon, they saw a white sliver of beach, stark against the trees. As they slid towards the beach, they saw a little girl who resembled the moon, a hand on her hip, queen of the island, content to be there, but ready to go home. Dakshin Foundation’s mission is to inform and advocate conservation and natural resource management, while promoting and supporting sustainable livelihoods, social development and environmental justice. We adopt interdisciplinary approaches in our research and conservation interventions to promote ecologically and socially appropriate approaches to conservation and management in coastal, marine and mountain ecosystems in India. title: Healthy Life
text: I live in Gurugram. Due to corona pandemic my parents have shifted to my grand parents house. My grandparents lives in a small town and I am in my hometown from last 2 months. I am very happy as this is the first time I am living a village life for such a long duration. In my home town I have observed a very different lifestyle compare to cities. People here lives a healthy life and follows a daily routine like - everyone wakes up early in the morning, most of my family eats food before sunset, everyone goes to bed early. Life here involves lot of physical activities and people here use less vehicles, they mostly walk. In cities most of the times we eat ice cream, pizza, burgers, and candy. I don’t remember eating anything like this here from last 2 months. In my home town we eat a very varied diet that mostly have fruits, fresh vegetables and milk. My grandpa helped me understand value of eating healthy food. I am feeling fit and healthy here, both adults and children are full of joy and good moods.
author: Divit  jain

title: The good fox
text: Fox awoke and she was very hungry. She wanted some food for her dinner. She walked through the forest to go to the town. Many stores in the town had food. She needed to find a store with food. She met her friend, Crow. He was very hungry, also. She walked by the toy store. She saw balls and boats. She saw planes and trains. But, she saw no food. The fox was still hungry and now she was sad. She walked by the clothing store. She saw shoes and shorts. She saw skirts and shirts. But, she saw no food. The fox was still hungry and now she was sadder. She walked by the book store. She saw books about bats and birds. She saw books about monkeys and donkeys. But, she did not see any food. The fox was still hungry and now she was even sadder. The fox walked by the meat market. She saw the butcher chopping meat into thick slices. The fox wished she could have some meat. Meat costs money and the fox had no money. She was still very hungry and very sad. She walked by the bread and cheese store. She saw a woman making cheese. The baker was making delicious bread. The fox wished she could have some bread and cheese. But, bread and cheese cost money and the fox had no money. What could she do? She saw a farmer planting apple trees. He looked very tired. She had an idea. The fox ran to the field. She dug holes for the apple trees. She dug the holes very fast and in a very straight line. The farmer was very happy. He paid her three coins. She put the coins her mouth and ran back to the town. At the bread and cheese store, she bought bread and cheese. She paid the baker two coins. At the meat market, she bought a thick slice of meat. She paid the butcher one coin. She ran by the bookstore. The books about donkeys, monkeys, birds, and bats were still there. She ran by the clothing store. The shirt, skirt, shorts, and shoes were still there. She ran by the toy store. The train, plane, boat, and ball were still there. She ran into the forest. She was still very hungry but now she was happy. The fox ran to her den and saw her friend, Crow. He was sad and still very hungry She gave her friend the bread. She barked to call her kits. They came out and ate the cheese. She ate the meat. Crow ate the bread. Now, everyone is happy and not hungry, anymore. She is a very good fox.
author: Harley Hamilton

title: It's not my Fault!
text: Little Savi lost her Tubby, “ It’s not my Fault ”, she cried. “ I can’t find him, I just cannot find him", "even though hard I’ve tried!" Little Savi Slipped on a Banana Peel! And just how did she feel? She blamed her big brother, her big sister of course, Or maybe it was baby’s rocking horse! Who ate little Savi’s homework? Of course, it was the dog… Or was it that large green frog? She’d seen while doing homework, sitting on the log… Little Savi broke Robbie’s plane! What did Savi have to say? “Robbie, please don’t complain,” “You got other toys, it’s all the same…” She played and pranced in the rain, Sniffles and Aches she did gain. “Miss Rain, Mr. Thunder ALL YOUR FAULT,” She cried in vain! Never her fault! Nor was it her mom’s fault, when she served Savi food with no Salt! Always someone else to blame, “Savi your favorite doll just flew out of the window,” “It’s such a shame, you’ve got others, it’s all the same!!!” Take-Aways: 1. Is it never Savi's fault? 2. Do you say sorry when you are wrong? 3. Do you do your homework on time? 5. Do you fight with your friends, sometimes? 6. Is it okay to be wrong at times? 7. Would you like to say anything to Savi? "The dog ate my homework": is an English expression. It is a bad excuse made by schoolchildren for not doing homework on time.
author: Rutuja Joshi

text: This is month of July and rain is common these days. It rains day and night and sun is very rare. I see greenery all around and cool breeze. I started liking this rainy season. title: The Things Some Can Do
text: THE GOOSE: SEASONAL SKY-ROUTE TRAVELLER THE AVIAN TRAVELLER Though a goose is a waterfowl, it spends most of its time out of water. A gosling (baby goose) follows the first moving object or living creature it sees when it comes out of its eggshell. The ‘moving’ he/she/it becomes gosling’s ‘mama’! A goose will sleep on land, water and even when while flying in the sky. It keeps one eye open to keep a look out for DANGEROUS nearby predators! A pet goose will honk loudly and chase away strangers at your gate. It will also EAT unwanted grass and weeds in your garden! Geese migrate (fly) to warmer places during the cold winter months. THE BEAVER: AQUATIC CONSTRUCTION ENGINEER THE AQUATIC CONSTRUCTION ENGINEER A beaver is a large rodent with thick, water-proof fur. It uses its thick, flat, scaly tail like a rudder while swimming It has closable nostrils and ears to help it to swim under the water, and transparent eye membranes that serve as underwater ‘goggles’! Beavers use their BIG, SHARP front teeth to fell trees and to cut its woody parts. The beavers use the woody parts of trees, stones, and mud to build strong dams in the waters of narrow parts of streams, creeks, or lakes. A beaver dam creates a still-water pond which becomes home for beavers, semi-aquatic animals, birds, insects, fish, frogs, and plants. THE DUNG BEETLE: INSECT DUNG COLLECTOR THE DUNG HUNTER Dung beetles love fresh, moist dung (animal poop). These beetles fly several miles to find dung. The beetles locate the dung by using their antennae to 'sniff' out the smell of dung in the air! The collected dung is buried underground. The female beetle lays eggs inside the dung. The larvae and adults feed on the rich nutrients in the moist animal poop! Dung beetles are rollers, tunnelers, or dwellers. Roller beetle uses the spurs on its back legs to roll a dung ball which is much heavier and bigger than it! Tunneler beetle pastes the insides of its tunnel with animal poop. Dweller beetle makes its home inside the dung! THE NUMBAT: MARSUPIAL ANT EXTERMINATOR THE MARSUPIAL ANT EXTERMINATOR The Australian numbat is a marsupial anteater. However, the female has no baby pouch. The numbat has a small, pointed head; a long, sticky tongue; a long, pointed snout; and eyes on the opposite sides of the head. It has 50-52 small, blunt teeth as it does not chew its food. This animal puts it long snout into holes of logs, tops of termite hills and other crevices to sniff for the presence of termites. The long, sticky tongue yanks the termites out! Baby numbats start feeding on termites only when they are nine-months old. Until then, they feed on their mother’s milk. Predators of numbats are red foxes and feral cats. THE FOSSORIAL INDIAN DANCING FROG TADPOLES THE ENERGETIC BURROWER TADPOLE A few years ago, biologists found tadpoles of the Indian Dancing frogs living inside the sand and gravel beds of forest streams in the Western Ghats (India). These tadpoles are fossorial as they burrow inside the river’s sand and gravel bed to find food. This tadpole has an eel-like body. The long, muscular tail helps it to burrow inside the grainy stream bed. Ribs help to protect the internal organs of this tadpole when it wriggles inside the sand in search of food. These burrowing tadpoles have no teeth. Instead, serrated jaw sheaths help the tadpole to ﻿ prevent big sand grains and gravel from entering into its mouth.
author: Hema Rao

title: The Magic Letter
text: Vikram were best friends. They lived far away from each other. They loved playing cricket, solving riddles, and eating biryani. They celebrated all festivals and birthdays together. Ijas was sad because his best friend was not with him. Vikram wrote many letters for Ijas. Ijas loved reading them. The letter had many puzzles that Ijas loved to solve! On the day of Eid, a letter came for Ijas. It was from Vikram! Eid Mubark, Ijas! A surpirse is waiting for you. Read the letter. Ijas opened the letter. He was guessing what Vikram had sent him. The last time, it was a number puzzle. But it was a blank letter! Ijas tried to fold it. Nothing happened. Ijals holds the paper to the light. He tried to touch and feel it. But nothing happened. He rolls it. Ijas looked at the card again. That's when he noticed the orange and yellow flame on the top. Ijas went into the kitchen. He said to his Ammi, "I need something hot to heat this letter!" Ammi helped him light a candle with the flame on the stove. Ijas took the paper close to the candle. "If you hold the paper too close to the flame, it will burn," Ammi warned him. Ijas kept the paper above the candle flame. What will happen? After sometime, brown lines appeared on the paper! It was like magic. "WOW! Look at these words, Ammi!" said Ijas. Ammi read the letter to Ijas. "Go to the place where we play with marbles" Ijas started running! He went down the stairs. He ran past the car. He reached a bench under the tree. He turned around and was shocked. "VIKRAM! What are you doing here?" Ijas could not believe his eyes. This is the best surprise ever! "I came to celebrate Eid with you," said Vikram. Vikram and Ijas hugged each other. "BIRYANI IS READY!" said Ammi. Vikram and Ijas went running to the house. Top Secret To create your own secret letter, you will need the following: Lemon A bowl A blank paper A paintbrush Water Method: 1. Squeeze the juice of half a lemon into a bowl. 2. Add a few drops of water. Stir well. 3. Dip the paintbrush into the lemon juice mix and write your message on the sheet of paper. 4. Allow the invisible ink to dry. 5. Share your secret message with a friend! The message will be revealed only when the paper is heated with a candle, gas, or a warm light bulb. Have fun!

title: Mitthu and Golu wants to be free
text: Golu was sad. He had not gone out to play for months now. Neither has he gone to the markets or parks. He meets his friends and teachers only through his laptop during his online classes. "There's Corona outside. Golu, you should be at home"... says Ma. Golu plays inside the house with his Dadu and talks to his only friend, Mitthu. Mitthu was a clever parrot. It could talk to Golu. Mitthu would wake up earlier than Golu every morning and call his name "Golu, Golu, Golu!!!" to wake him up. Mitthu would munch on his food while watching Golu and Dadu play cricket. But he would get excited if he saw other parrots pecking on the guavas in the garden. He would try flapping his wings and call out at the parrots with all his might. "Dadu, what's is wrong with Mitthu?" asked Golu. "Mitthu misses his frineds just like you. He wants to fly and go enjoying with his friends" explained Dadu. "Is he sad inside the cage? But we love him so much. We give him so many things to eat. He is safe inside the cage"... Golu said. "Everyone wants to be free. Free to go to places places they like and choose what to eat. Like the way you like to go to the market to buy ice creams"... Dadu said. Golu understood. "So should I set him free, Dadu?" he asked. "Yes, Golu. Let's set Mitthu free. If he loves us he would comes back to meet us"... Dadu said. Golu took Mitthu's cage to the garden and opened the door. Mitthu came out of the cage and spread his wings. It flew past Golu in a flash and joined his friends on the guava tree. Mitthu was happy. He could fly and go anywhere and eat anything the way he wanted. Golu was happy too. He wished the pandemic would end soon and he too could be free. Free to go out, play, go to school and go to the market to get his favourite ice cream.
author: Aditi Das
illustrator: Alicia Souza; Nivong  Sengsakoun; Phan Thành  Đạt; Tanvi Bhat

title: I love Butterflies!!!
text: There was a girl named Ananya, and she loved nature. One of her favorite things was to watch butterflies. One day, she was sitting in her backyard enjoying her flowers. Suddenly, she saw some birds flying. At first, she thought they were butterflies because butterflies can fly just like birds. Then, she saw some butterflies fly in too! They just came and sat on her beautiful flowers. The butterflies had different patterns and colors. Some were blue, green, red, and yellow. Some had spots, stripes, and dots, and some were plain. She loved watching them as they flew from one flower to another drinking nectar. Then the butterflies were all gone except for one. This last butterfly was golden and golden was Ananya's favorite color. She watched the golden butterfly until it was gone too. Ananya was really, really, happy 😊❤️!!! THE END!!!

title: Aadi Wants to Play
text: Aadi was a spunky little 3 year- old who loved his playtime like all of us. One day he was a fish swimming in a pond, on another a frog hopping around or a tiger roaring in the jungle. But his favourite creatures of all were dinosaurs! He was fascinated with anything and everything about dinosaurs. He loved the T-Rex the most! One day, he was roaring like a T-Rex and stomping about the house when he started coughing badly. He couldn't control coughing when he ran or jumped and had to sit down. He had a tough time breathing, his chest hurt and he called his Mama. Mama rushed to him and hugged him. She said that he was going to be ok. "Just relax and I will bring out your nebulizer," she said. Once he was fitted with his nebulizer, Aadi asked, "Mama, why do I feel sick, why does this happen to me all the time? Will I be able to play my games again?" Mama said that he had Asthma; remember they had been to Doctor Lata aunty last week? "It will get better soon, don't worry dear. But first, let's play a new game. Can you wear this mask and sit here? Let me tell you a story. Let's pretend that you are a scuba diver with his mask diving underwater. Can you imagine all the fishes under the sea?" Mama told him the story of a scuba diver who dives into the deep sea and spots an octopus, some clownfish, a squid, loads of jellyfish, a pufferfish and even an angler fish. "Ok, time's up! Let's get back to land now," said Mama. Aadi removed his mask and was feeling much better. He could breathe better and his coughing had ceased. "Thanks, Mama! I feel much better. You know what, tomorrow could you tell me the story of a pilot? Or a race car driver?" said Aadi, thrilled with his new ideas. "Anything for you, my dear," said Mama. "Can I get back to my play now?" asked Aadi. "Sure, my little dino!" said Mama, kissing him on his forehead. And Aadi got back to being a T-Rex again, the loudest one ever! "ROAR!!ROAAAR!!ROAAAAAAR!!" ABOUT THIS BOOK This book talks about a 3 year old boy who is confused about what is happening to him. Asthma is a condition in which your airways narrow and swell and may produce extra mucus. This can make breathing difficult and trigger coughing, a whistling sound (wheezing) when you breathe out and shortness of breath. Asthma is getting quite common among children nowadays and as a parent of a child with asthma, I found my child worrying about what would happen to him and why this was happening to him. I find that books and stories help him calm down and understand better. This book is an attempt to provide an insight and awareness about this condition from the point of view of a child and parent. Please check with your doctor regarding medication for asthma. For more information:

title: The Town of Sajjalagunddam
text: Sajjalagunddam was on top of a mountain, near a spring. At the height of the spring, grew millet. It grew so high and robust that it was seen from far away. Sajjalagunddam in Telugu, the language of the town, means “town of millet.” Every citizen of the town had their profession. The Mangalis were the barbers, the Chacalis washed clothes, the Vadranguis built tools to work in the fields and the Kuruvas bred sheep. There were also a large number of people who worked as day labourers in the fields. The men and women of Sajjalagunddam covered food with a wet fabric so that it would not get ruined. They ate dishes like Ragisangati, Korrasangati and Jonnasangati. Also, rice and a bread called chapati. They therefore grew strong and healthy. The houses were built with clay walls and straw roofs. In every house, lived a family made up of 7 to 10 people. The women wore a sari and the men wore a dhoti (sarong) and a jubba (a long shirt.) When it was hot, the teacher and her students sat in the shade under the trees near a temple called Ramalingeswaram. Not all children could go to school. Some parents believed that it was better for them to stay and help at home and to get married early. There wasn’t a hospital in the town. To cure ill people, they used charms or medicinal plants. For boys and girls with a fever, they practise a ritual called chitiquelu. In the fields, they grew millet, korra, sajja, raji, rice and peanuts. There were black, red and sandy soils. Tractors didn’t exist and the fields were ploughed with carts pulled by oxen. There wasn’t a bus and the closest train station was in the neighbouring town of Irongal. To get to the station, the citizens of the town followed the train tracks until they reached Irongal. The men and women of Sajjalagunddam believed in different religions. Each religion had its temple and its festivals. Muslims went to the mosque and celebrated Ramadan. Hindus had lots of gods and celebrated Ugadhi. Christians went to church and celebrated Christmas.

title: Our Little River
text: Author Rabindranath Tagore was born on 7 May, 1861 to Maharshi Debendranath Tagore, one of the leaders of the Brahmo Samaj, and Sarada Devi. He was a distinguished Bengali poet, writer, painter, playwright and composer of songs. He was homeschooled by a variety of teachers in a variety of subjects. He composed ‘ Sishu,’ ‘Dakghor,’ ‘Birpurush,’ ‘Proshno,’ ‘Sahaj Path’ and others for children. He was the recipient of the Nobel Prize for Literature in the year 1913. In 1915, the prestigious ‘knighthood’ was awarded to him by the British Raj but he soon renounced it as a protest to the Jallianwalah Bagh massacre of 1919. A highly renowned artist, he was known for introducing the Indian culture to the West which led to his establishment of the ‘Vishwabharati’ University in Santiniketan which is a mosaic of the East and the West. Two of his song compositions, “Jana Gana Mana” and “Amar Shonar Bangla” were chosen by India and Bangladesh respectively as their national anthems. Rabindranath Tagore passed away on August 7, 1941. About the poem Published as a part of Sahaj Path, in 1937, this beautiful poem describes a little river that the poet calls their own. Widely attributed to the Kopai river that flows past the Birbhum district in West Bengal, this poem portrays the typical river-side happenings, from children bathing to women using the water for household chores and so on. It also beautifully sketches the changes the river goes through over seasons. Our dear little river, twists and turns Knee-deep water, in the month of summer The cows cross, the cow carts cross and run Sides are steep and down it slopes. The sand shines, not a spec of mud One side is lined with white Kash Group of mynahs chirp and chirp Sometimes, foxes bark in the dark. Mango and palm trees run on the other side Brahmin villages harboured under their shade, Children bathe at the riverbanks In fun, collect water in towels and pour. In mornings and evenings they catch fish After bath sometimes using their cloth piece. With sand, women clean their dishes and pots And go back home after washing clothes. The monsoon months make the river swell And it runs fast in madness and in speed. Its roars make loud noise in a great whizz Swirling muddy water makes, moves and runs. Forests are awake on both sides All are awake in the festivities of monsoon.
author: Sanghamitra Ghosh

title: Sara's Canoe
text: Sara has a canoe. Her canoe is big. It is by the riverside. Some women come to the river. One woman has a basin of fruit. Another woman has a chicken. Another woman has a goat. Another woman has two goats. They ask Sara, "How can we get to the other side of the river?" Sara says, "Get in my canoe!" Then, some men arrive. One man has a fish. Another man has a bicycle. Another man has a sack of maize. Another man has two sacks of maize. They ask Sara, "How can we get to the other side of the river?" Sara replies, "Get in my canoe!" Some animals come to the river. They ask Sara, "How can we get across the river?" Sara says, "Get in my canoe!" The animals get in the canoe. The dog gets in the canoe. The cat gets in the canoe. The monkey gets in the canoe. The rabbit gets in the canoe. The turtle gets in the canoe. The gazelle gets in the canoe. The elephant arrives at the river. He asks, "How can I get to the other side of the river?" Sara says, "Get in my canoe!" The elephant gets in the canoe. The canoe fills up with water. The canoe is too small. There isn't enough room. Sara says, "Hold on! First I'll take the women." Sara says, "Second, I'll take the men." Sara says, "Finally, I'll take the animals." The elephant says, "I'm just going to walk!"

title: Sentence Street
text: We are punctuation marks. We are the superheroes found on Sentence Street! We will show you how and where to use punctuation in sentences. Let us guide you in reading and writing. We will help you to write clear and meaningful sentences, and to read punctuation with understanding. We are nine punctuation marks who will introduce ourselves today. There are more of us, but you can meet them later. We hope you will ask us for help when making sentences. You will find me at the start of: a list, or a title, or an explanation, or to introduce something. Call me: Colon. My name is Comma. I help you to pause between thoughts, and I also separate items in a list. I love exercising, reading and playing. Would you tell me about the things you love doing? Curiosity is my super power! My mission is to ask questions and find answers! Please call me Question Mark, would you? I am Semicolon; I am a guard on Sentence Street. I'm a longer pause than a comma, but I'm not a full stop. I sometimes play Cupid by helping lonely clauses connect and become friends instead of strangers. I can also separate items in a long list to avoid confusion. When a letter or two is missing from a word, I'll stand in for the letters. I also show possession or that something belongs to someone. Call me Apostrophe. "I am Quotation Mark and my super power is direct speech!" When you see me wrapped around the words someone says, it means those are the exact words that the person spoke (or thought). I open and close quotations. Sometimes I show sarcasm. Hey there! I am Exclamation Mark, the emotion mark! I express strong emotions. I express surprise and excitement! I shout, scream, laugh hysterically and wail! I am always willing to help you express your strong feelings. We are three.... 3 dots that represent missing or unsaid words. This happens when people are unsure of what to say next and don't complete their sentence. We are called ellipsis. I end sentences. I am the stop indicator. Without me, everyone on Sentence Street will run out of breath and need to visit a doctor often. My name is Period, or Full Stop. People like to say that Ellipsis and Period are cousins. Others say Question Mark, Exclamation Mark and Quotation Mark are siblings. There are those who say Comma and Apostrophe are twins. What do you think?
author: Mimi  Werna

title: P.S. What's up with the climate?
text: Dear Reader, We have a problem. A huge problem. A problem so huge, it’s impacting all of planet Earth! The problem is climate change. Our climate is changing because we’re adding too many greenhouse gases and other pollutants into the atmosphere. The impacts — floods, droughts, heat waves, cyclones, etc. — are felt by all (including you and us) everywhere. But we can help! By saving trees, following the 4Rs (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle and Refuse), respecting all forms of life, and taking many more green actions. Archana (Part-time illustrator, full-time animal person, has been saved by tree-therapy multiple times.) For the Earth, Bijal (Grouchy author trying to write but distracted by the climate crisis.) P.S. Let’s do this together! Dear Penguin, How’s the weather there? Here, it’s moody every day. Grmph, Grmph! Even the seals are hiding. But it’s lunch time. How to find them? Grmph, Grmph! Warmly, Polar Opposite Bear P.S. Have you heard from Mosaic-tailed Rat recently? Dear Polar Opposite Bear, It’s hot. It’s very hot. It’s very, very, very hot. I can’t bear it. I just can’t bear it. I just can’t bear it at all. We’re in a flap. Flap, flap. Flap, flap, flap. The fish have swum far, far, far, far, far, far away. Off, off, off to look for them. Too warmly, Penguin P.S. Rats! Not in a while. Let me find out. Hullo, Ummm… Here it’s not hot. At all. Would you like to come visit us? Brrrr… it’s too cold to fly. (You won’t mind, as you can’t fly, Penguin. You don’t, right?) Flying kisses, Flying (not right now) Squirrel P.S. Sorry, not a squeak from Mosaic-tailed Rat. Hi, It’s raining. Cats and dogs! We’re hanging on. Just about. Ant P.S. That’s strange. Not just Rat, my sugar’s missing too. Call the police. OYE! Stop complaining. Your sugar must have dissolved in all that water. Send us some rain clouds, HAAN? All the acidity in the sea is giving me acidity. BRRRRP! There’s too much carbon in the sea. PHHHHRP! I need to find a suitable shell before it gets hotter. Or my shell dissolves like your sugar. HSSSSS! Getting crabbier by the minute, Hermit Crab P.S. Even Golden Toad has disappeared. Maybe they went on a holiday together? Somewhere where it’s raining. BAH! KHROAAAA, KHROAAAA! My life is very confusing. Here, there are fewer trees and little water, so there are very few seeds. But, hooray, we found some seeds because Mama Bear (Grizzly, not Polar) is so good at finding them. I ate so much, my belly became round as a ball. Then it snowed! Usually, when it snows, my family and I are fast asleep in our den. But we weren’t because it snowed so early in the season. We ran to our den to sleep. But we hadn’t eaten enough. So, we ran back out to eat some more. Now I have an upset tummy and am still confused. To hibernate or not to hibernate? Hungry and upset, Bear (Grizzly, not Polar) P.S: I will help look for Toad and Rat when we wake up. Good night! Oh, lucky Bear (Grizzly, not Polar), We didn’t get much snow all winter. So I had to climb up, up, and up to get to the snow. But my food went down, down, and down to get to their food. So then I went down, then back up. Then back down and up. AAAAAAAH! Try running around with so much fur when it’s hot. Also, mud rolls are not the same as rolling in the snow. Sulking, Snow Leopard P.S. Not seen either Toad or Rat. But will check after I get some rest. Let me ask Olive Ridley Turtle. A forest fire⁠— Scared we run, wrapped up in smoke. Pouncing, hungry beast Pow-wow-dish-dhoosh-ouch I boxed the crackling fire. Burnt paw, cannot write O Sulking Snow Leopard Sorry, too hot to haiku Poetroo Joey P.S. Oh, Koala says the Olive Dear Busy Bee, Where do we go? The lake water’s salty here. The lake water’s salty there. The lake water’s salty everywhere! Off to find a less salty lake. On a wing and a prayer, Northern Pintail Duck P.S. Is Olive Ridley Turtle visiting a new beach now? She’s stopped answering my letters. Sorry, not friends with Toad or Rat. Bzzzzzzz, Bzzzzzzzzz Zzzzz Zzz Stressed and sleepy, Bee P.S. Bzzzzz To Golden Toad To Mosaic-tailed Rat To Mosaic-tailed Rat Return to sender Return to sender Return to sender To Olive Ridley Turtle Return to sender No longer visits the beach as the waters are too warm. No forwarding address available. To humans Be a climate champion: Write a letter to our home, planet Earth. World Wide Fund For Nature India (WWF-India) endorses Pratham Books’ P. S. What’s up with the climate?, a picture book that raises awareness about complex environmental issues like climate change among young audiences. In today’s time and era, it is critical to nurture appreciation and respect in young children for the environment and its biodiversity. It’s only when they understand, they will act to create a better and brighter future for all.
author: Bijal Vachharajani
