title: How Will Amma Live!
text: She loved eating sweets. One day she really felt like eating a laddoo. So, she sat down in the courtyard of her house and started making laddoos. In the courtyard was a big tree. On top of the tree sat a crow named Kag. When Kag saw the laddoos his mouth started watering. He swooped down, grabbed a laddoo in his beak, and flew to a tree branch. Amma ran after him, but couldn't catch him. She called out, "Kag, oh Kag, give me back my laddoo!" But Kag shook his head. Kag won't return the laddoo, How will Amma live! Amma told the tree, "Shake, shake tree! Make Kag fall." The tree said "Amma, I can't do that!". Arrree! Tree won't drop Kag, Kag won't return the laddoo, How will Amma live! Amma went to the carpenter and said, "Carpenter, Carpenter, cut that tree. It won't shake and drop Kag." The carpenter said "Amma, I can't cut a tree for no reason." Arrree! Carpenter won't cut the tree, Tree won't drop Kag, Kag won't return the laddoo, How will Amma live! So Amma went to the King, "King, King, punish that carpenter. He won't cut the tree." The King didn't understand anything Amma was saying and refused to listen to her. Uffff! King won't punish the carpenter, Carpenter won't cut the tree, Tree won't drop Kag, Kag won't return the laddo, How will Amma live! Annoyed, Amma went to the Queen, "Queen, Queen, get upset with the King. He is not listening to me." The Queen said, "Why should I get upset with the King? He still listens to me."Uffff! Queen won't get upset with the King, King won't punish the carpenter, Carpenter won't cut the tree, Tree won't drop Kag, Kag won't return the laddoo, How will Amma live! Now Amma was starting to get angry. She went to the snake. "Snake, Snake, go bite the queen." "Why should I bite the Queen? She has not harmed me," replied the snake. "I'm not going to do this." Oh! Snake won't bite the Queen, Queen won't get upset with the King, King won't punish the carpenter, Carpenter won't cut the tree, Tree won't drop Kag, Kag won't return the laddoo, How will Amma live! Then Amma went to the stick and said "Stick, Stick, you must beat the snake." But the stick replied "Amma, I'm very busy right now. I don't have any time at all." Arrree! Stick won't beat the snake, Snake won't bite the Queen, Queen won't get upset with the King, King won't punish the carpenter, Carpenter won't cut the tree, Tree won't drop Kag, Kag won't return the laddoo, How will Amma live! Then Amma went to the rope and said, "Rope, Rope, you must tie up that stick." The rope coiled up even tighter and replied, "Amma, I'm resting right now. I don't feel like doing anything at all. Maybe later." Oh! Rope won't tie the stick, Stick won't beat the snake, Snake won't bite the Queen, Queen won't get upset with the King, King won't punish the carpenter, Carpenter won't cut the tree, Tree won't drop Kag, Kag won't return the laddoo, How will Amma live! Then Amma went to the mouse to asked him to chew the rope, but the mouse was fast asleep. Amma shook him, and shook him, but the mouse would not wake up. Mouse won't chew the rope, Rope won't tie the stick, Stick won't beat the snake, Snake won't bite the Queen, Queen won't get upset with the King, King won't punish the carpenter, Carpenter won't cut the tree, Tree won't drop Kag, Kag won't return the laddoo, How will Amma live! By now Amma was very tired, angry, and upset, but she would not give up. She went to the cat and asked, "Cat, Cat, do you want to eat a mouse?" The cat jumped up happily, "Yes, Yes, I would love to eat a mouse! Where is it?" All of a sudden, everyone started hurrying and scurrying! The mouse heard the cat coming and ran to chew the rope. The rope saw the mouse coming and said "No matter how busy I am, Amma I will do your work first." As soon as the stick heard this, she ran to beat the snake. The snake saw the stick and said, "Why are you coming to beat me? See I'm going right now to bite the queen." The Queen was so scared of the snake that she got upset with the King right away. The King saw the upset Queen and sent his soldiers to punish the carpenter. The carpenter saw the King's soldiers and ran to cut the tree. The tree saw the carpenter coming and started shaking with fear. Kag realized what was happening. He opened his mouth and cried "Oh No!" The laddoo fell from his beak and landed straight in the pallu of Amma's sari. Amma finally got her laddoo back. And Kag thought... Amma won't give the laddoo, How will Kag live...
author: Smiti Gandhi

title: The Abandon Dog
text: Isabella had a lively, playful dog named Max. She adopted Max when he was 3months old. Max was a very cute puppy and Isabella would impatiently wait to reach home after school to play with Max. She loved Max and took care of him as her own sibling. She would playfully call Max her brother. He was very fierce and protective about Isabella and her family would not allow anyone around them. Isabella felt very safe when Max was around. Everything went well until one day Max started biting. One fateful day, Max bit Isabella for no reason at all. He bit her so bad that blood was dripping from her finger. Isabella felt traumatized. She was shattered and all of a sudden, fear grew within her. Although she loved Max, she was scared to be with him. She went weeping to her parents and told them what happened. Her parents felt depressed after what they saw and heard. Her mother decided to give away Max after what he had done to her lovely daughter. With the fear that grew within them, they decided to abandon Max. They thought he was meant to be in the wild and not at home. The home became an empty place for Isabella who loved Max’s company. Isabella was very upset because she had taken all the responsibility to take care on Max from a very young age. All night she kept wailing for Max and the entire family was in grief with thoughts of now having Max at home. On second thoughts, Isabella’s mother asked Isabella “honey, would you like to search for Max tomorrow?” Isabella said, “Yes, I do want to search for him” The next day Isabella and her mother went to look for Max but they did not find him. They continued their search for several days but in vain, Max was nowhere. They were now sure Max had found either a new home or a family to live with. Everything returned to normalcy until one day Isabella’s father found Max while he was out on his regular morning walks. He shrieked out saying “Max, Max!” Max came running to him but was wounded and in a pathetic condition. Max!1 Max!! He looked starved and bitten by other stray dogs. He was weak and could not carry himself around. Isabella’s father was terrified to see him in such a condition and immediately decided to bring him home and take care of him. Everyone was overjoyed to see Max home, but knew it will take a long time for him to recover. Max was sick and needed a lot of attention and medication to get back to normal. Isabella worked very hard to see that Max slowly but steadily recovered and got back to normal. Max got back him loving and caring family once again.
author: Reyna Ameen
illustrator: Nicolene  Louw; Candice  Botha; Jayesh Sivan; Lê Thị  Mai Phương; Siddhi   Vartak

title: Jennifer - The Lazy Log !
text: Jennifer she woke up late again! She slept late yesterday night as she was playing video games on her mother's mobile. Jennifer was searching for her brother James, he slept usually on time & had a good sleeping habit. Jennifer was brushing her teeth in silence. She was so sleepy that she din't have energy to hold her toothbrush properly. Jennifer kept her toothbrush, but she did not bother to clean her teeth or have a bath properly. She really wished she could sleep for another hour or so! Jennifer quickly came upstairs to eat her breakfast. She was a little bit fresh from that bath but didn't wash herself properly. She found her brother was having breakfast and seemed full with energy as he had washed and cleaned himself properly. While Jennifer was getting ready and feeling lazy, James was talking and enjoying his meal with his mom and dad happily. J ennifer came running with a messy ponytail and her unorganized backpack. Her brother was not happy with her bad & lazy habits; however invited her to eat with the family. Jennifer quickly rushed to the door took her backpack and came out the door but realised that the school bus was not there. Her family was so confused especially her brother considering she had eaten her breakfast so fast! Her mom asked " Whats the rush Jenny ". Jennifer said in a rushed tone " Mom! i am late for school! Where have you kept my school bag! " Her brother came up to her and said "Jenny; there is no school today. Come; lets do some reading together! Jennifer then realised that it was a Saturday & that's why there was no school today. She went upstairs with a gloomy face downstairs and went to sleep. She was feeling angry that her brother James was asking her to do reading & did not want her to go to sleep. He wanted her to stay awake even though knowing that it was a Saturday. He tried to convince her but Jennifer was adamant that she did not want to do any reading as she felt tired and sleepy. Jennifer went to sleep while her brother ate breakfast and took a morning walk. Jennifer felt lazy, her brother tried to convince her to eat healthy, mindful of her personal hygiene and regularly exercise by taking a walk in the park. Jennifer listened to her brother carefully and realized the importance of his advice. She promised James that she would follow a healthy routine and lead a disciplined lifestyle.
author: chaitali sharma
illustrator: Ajit Narayan; Canato Jimo; Ira S.B; Mbongeni Fongoqa; Minu Nandakumar; Rai; Shreeya Wagh; Shriya Nulkar

title: My Good Healthy Charter
text: Hi! I am Jahnavi Rai and I am going to tell you about My Healthy Charter.. I will follow 5210 rule, where 5 means eating healthy food. We should not hesitate to try different fruits and vegetable, we should take three bites of every fruit and vegetable; 2 means fixing time for our entertainment. If we will spend much time on eletronic gadgets and television, we will have poor eye site and it may damage our eyes. So, we should fix time for watching television and computer etc; 1 means doing physical activites such as - exercise, dancing, playing etc to have a good health; 0 means drinking enough water and avoid sugary drinks, soda, coldrinks. All these drinks are not good for your body.
author: Jahnavi Rai
illustrator: Abin  Shrestha; Caroline Faysse; Niloufer Wadia; Poorva Harihar Shingre; Rijuta Ghate

title: Mani and the tooth fairy
text: Mani was a little girl who liked brushing her teeth. One day she called her mom and said, "Mom, look I am brushing my teeth". "Good Girl!", said the mother. Mani brushed her teeth and came running to her mother and started crying. Worried mother asked Mani "What happened? Why are you crying?" The worried Mani said, "My tooth just fell". "Don't worry Mani. You will grow a new stronger tooth." "But I brush my teeth everyday. Why is this happening to me?!", cried Mani. Mother tried to calm her daughter, "Kids loose their weak milk teeth to grow stronger teeth. You will be a strong girl, my child.", she said. "I don't want my teeth to fall off", said Mani. "Don't cry dear. A fairy will come visit you tonight", said Mother. Mani stopped crying and listened to her mother. "Keep the teeth below your pillow at night. There will come a tooth fairy, wave her magical wand turn your tooth into a shining coin." Excited Mani kept the tooth under her pillow and slept. The tooth fairy came and waved her magic wand "Abracadabra", she said and turned Mani's tooth into a shining coin. And left it under her pillow. Mani woke up and found the coin under her pillow. She was happy and thanked the tooth fairy for the coin. Mani never cried over a fallen tooth again.
author: Aishwarya Sathe
illustrator: Meera Satheesh Kumar; Shailja Jain Chougule; Shreya Shruti; Sushmita Viswanathan; Zainab Tambawalla

title: Short stories about Animals
text: Jackie the camel was shaking her butt happily, in the deserts of Arabia. A sudden sand dune came whooshing, and many creatures were blown away. But not Jackie. Jacki's body was so strong, so powerful, that it could not be blown away. After that sand dune, Jackie met another Survivor Camel and they were joking around. "What do you call a camel with no humps?" "Humphery, that's a popular one!!" "Fine then you win" Billy the Buffalo Billy was attracting many flies to his body. He hadn't listened to his sister to wash his body, but he had no hands! Can cows talk to their brother's? He only wished to get these annoying flies and poop off his body. Billy's Sister married a human and they had a daughter, trying to concentrate doing school without all the 'Mooooo'ing from the shed. Can cows marry humans? Billy figured out the hard math and saw that his sister's daughter and husband had hands. Can Buffalos do math? Her husband was busy earning money for the family, so only her daughter was free, she wasn't even interested. Billy was able to get her to make her wash all the disgusting poop off. After that cleaning of poop, she chose to study rather than wash Billy's filthy body. "Run faster, run faster", Hilly Hare told herself. She was going to be late for school. She was running away from the fox who was coming to eat her. When the fox caught her, she was screaming loudly. The fox told her "I'm gonna eat you, delicious hare" "Oh, really," The bunny told him "Yes really, say your last wish," The fox said. "My last wish is to rule the fox world because after you kill me, I am going to go to my immortal life and in my immortal life I am a royal fox with no heirs," The smart hare told the cunning Fox. The fox got scared and never captured any bunnies from her school ever again. But in the end, the hare got captured by the fox's sister, and maybe just maybe she knew what Hilly Hare had told the fox. A salt seller used to carry the salt bag on his donkey to the market every day. On the way, they had to cross a stream. One day the donkey suddenly tumbled down the stream and the salt bag also fell into the water. The salt dissolved in the water and hence the bag became very light to carry. The donkey was happy. Then the donkey started to play the same trick every day. The salt seller came to understand the trick and decided to teach a lesson to it. The next day he loaded a cotton bag on the donkey. Again it played the same trick hoping that the cotton bag would still become lighter. But the dampened cotton became very heavy to carry and it suffered much. It learnt a lesson. Afterwards, it did not play the trick and the seller was happy. Layla, the pig was very dirty. She kept dipping her head in the mud, and kept playing in it. But even if she was very dirty, she also had dreams. Her owner, Mrs. Templton had a very bad case of Malaria, and to keep the flies away, she got Layla. Mrs. Templton never let Layla go out because then Mrs. Templton would die without her Licky Layla. Layla desperately wanted to leave. She was treated like a prisoner at Mrs. Templton's house. Layla planned her escape with one frog who was also treated like a prisoner at the Templton house. One stormy night, when Mrs. Templton was not looking, Layla and the frog escaped. After escaping, the frog and Layla knew what freedom is like, but then Mrs. Templton found them on the street, swooped them up and put them in the Animal Jail. A wolf was walking in the countryside. He found a sheep-skin spread on the ground. He thought, "If I wear this skin and get mixed up in the flock, the shepherd will not suspect me. At night, I will kill a sheep and then take him away with me". The wolf covered himself with the sheep-skin and got mixed up with a flock of sheep. As he had expected, the shepherd took him like a sheep and shut him also in the pen. The wolf was waiting for the night. The shepherd had a feast that night. He sent a servant to fetch a fat sheep. The servant saw the sheep-skin covered wolf by chance. That night, the guests had the wolf for supper. Once, a man had a pet dog. The faithful and strong dog used to guard the master's factory at night. The master loved him, fed him well, and took him out for walks. One unlucky day, he was hit by a car. He got hurt very badly. One day, the dog smelt some ginger in the air. He sniffed around and saw a ginger plant growing in the factory's ground. The master saw the dog sniffing the ginger plant. He checked and found out that the soil near the plant was excellent for growing ginger plants. He then planted plenty of ginger plants and made a huge profit. Then the master realized that a physical injury does not make anyone useless. He started loving and caring for his dog once again. There lived two silly goats in a village. There was a narrow bridge over a river in the village. One day, the goats wanted to cross the bridge. One silly goat was on one side. The other one was on the other side. One of them said, “I shall go first. Allow me to pass." The other goat said, “No. I must cross first. You move aside." Neither of them yielded. At last, they came to the middle of the bridge. They began to fight terribly. As they were fighting, both of them fell into the river and were drowned.
author: Aathira Karthik

title: Jugnu
text: Jugnu is a firefly. Jugnu glows in the dark. Jugnu is loved by all her friends. All the insects can play in the dark because of Jugnu. One evening all the insects call Jugnu to play. Jugnu rushes out from her house as fast as she can. After all the insects gather, they ask Jugnu to light up. Sadly, Jugnu is not able to. All her friends tease her and make her feel sad. Payal, the ladybug feels bad for Jugnu. Payal tells all her friends that it is not Jugnu’s fault. She tells them friends should never make each other cry. All the insects feel bad about what they did. They say sorry to Jugnu and ask her to play.
author: Swati Ramtilak

title: Cloud Ice-cream
text: It always tried to please Sarla. It even changed colour! When Sarla laughed, it turned pink. If Sarla was angry, it grew red. When Sarla was sad, the kite would turn blue. Sometimes it even turned yellow. When Sarla chattered happily, it grew green. One day, the kite soared high in the sky. Sarla giggled as she held the string and said, “Fly! Fly higher, kite!” The kite flew higher and went past the clouds. It met a little fairy there. The fairy was happy to meet the kite too. They whispered to each other. They even flew together. Sarla pulled at the string as it was getting late. The kite said, “I must go now. My friend is calling me.” The fairy gave her a parting gift of Cloud Ice-cream. It was fluffy and soft! The kite said, “We will meet again.” “I’ll come and see you,” said the fairy. The kite gave the fairy’s gift to Sarla. Cloud Ice-cream! “You are my lovely kite!” said Sarla.
author: Manisha Chaudhry

title: Inseparable
text: Somewhere over the slope of the mountain, there was a ruddy, magical and quite countryside, where animals could live and speak... Ben the Rat and Perry the Goat were known for being Super-Friends! They respected and cared about Miss Nature very much, she gave them a place to live! Ben the Rat was very early-rising, he loved to admire the beautiful sunrise and lying in the fresh lawn... the right opposite was Perry the Goat, sleepyhead was still in his warm bed, he didn't even notice the squeak of Ben once he arrived at his wooden house... So Ben decided to knock at the door. He knew that Perry the Goat was still sleeping, but he had to woke him up! That day, was a very important day for his friend, he had to participate at the Miracolus River's Competition. It was his desire since he was a little goat...HE'D HAVE WIN!!! Perry the Goat was deeply absorbed in his wonderful dream... He finally won the Miraculos River's Competition! This magical waterway was a gift of Miss Nature, indeed in the depths of this, lived an extraordinary golden fish... ancient times' legends said that he could express one desire of happiness for the one who'd have catch him. Bothered by the energetic knocked, after a long time he opened his big eyes... he perfectly knew who was the thunder in front of his house's door, but he was too lazy to lift himself up! Energetically, Ben walked inside of the room and found out his friend...still laid in bed, gurgling something about the magical gold fish. He did not realize what day it was, but he had to! Completely disinterested about what Ben was trying to say, Perry turned around in his blanket... Come on, stand up my friend! It's time to go Nothing could discouraged Ben by his intent... with all his willpower, he grabbed Perry's paw and screamed out loud that he had to move fast because the competition was about to start. Finally Perry jumped out of his bed and started to prepare!!! Once they were outdoor, suddenly Perry the Goat got very nauseous...he was anxious about the competition now, he highly cared about this! However, Ben the Rat tried to comfort his worried friend, he knew how much time he spent practising his techniques of fishing, it was a big opportunity for him... Perry the Goat was comfortably sitting on a rock, the competition started hours before and many of his relatives got really tired and left, he was getting sad. There wasn't trace of the Gold Fish and this thing made him even more glum. He was about to give up, naturally dejected. Once he stood up, he saw his Super-Friend Ben the Rat, who was lying on a leaf, dreaming about something... In the middle of the competition, while he was waiting for his friend, Ben the Rat fell asleep and had a dream, a fantastic one! He dreamt about Perry the Goat and him playing hopscotch... it was their favourite game to play together. Perry the Goat wasn't good at sports, but none could try to beat him on hopscotch, it was impossible. Perry the Goat and Ben the Rat were coming back home and obviously Perry was very unhappy and disappointed, Ben didn't know what to do when, all of sudden, he thought about his dream and proposed a match to Perry. After a bit of time, they were finally playing their favourite game, together... blissful in each other company, Perry was really great and joyful now. This friendship was very special, they were inseparable!
author: Giulia  Brambilla

title: The Hare and the Tortoise (Again!)
text: We all know that the rabbit was defeated because he was lazy and overconfident. We know that the tortoise won the race because he was slow and steady. The forest animals knew this too, and continued to respect both creatures equally. Even the two competitors remained friends. The tortoise did not assume airs because he had won, and the hare, realizing he had been defeated fair and square, bore the tortoise no grudge. Many months passed. The king of the jungle where the hare and the tortoise lived had some important matters to discuss with the king of the neighbouring jungle. But the first king could not leave his jungle just then. He decided, instead, to send the hare and the tortoise to the neighbouring king, as his representatives. “At least one of you must go to the neighbouring kingdom,” ordered the king, when the hare and the tortoise had presented themselves. “I want you to discuss certain important matters with the king there, and come back to me with his thoughts on those matters.” “Now go!” he said, as he dismissed them. “And mind, you only have a day to complete the task.” The road to the neighbouring kingdom was not smooth or easy. It was rocky and full of thorns. There were also two rivers to cross on the way. After some thought, both the hare and the tortoise realized that neither of them could complete the task alone. They had to travel together. The plan was for the hare to carry the tortoise over the thorny parts of the route, and for the tortoise to carry the hare across the two rivers. The next day, they collected the various messages from their king and were ready to go. The hare made short work of the thorny parts of the route with his giant loping strides, while the tortoise held on for dear life. When they came to a river, they switched places, and the hare clambered on to the tortoise’s back. The tortoise swam across the river swiftly and gracefully. Once both the rivers had been crossed, it did not take them long to arrive at the neighbouring kingdom. After extensive discussions with the neighbouring king on all the matters raised by their own king, the hare and the tortoise were ready to leave. The return journey was even smoother than the onward journey, since both the hare and the tortoise now knew exactly what to do. The two old rivals had worked together so well that they reached their king a few hours before the deadline! Use your imagination and colour this picture anyway YOU like. Use your imagination and colour this picture anyway YOU like.
author: Divaspathy Hegde

title: Smart Sona
text: I shall make one too,” said Sona. Papa began to saw the wood. “I shall cut some wood too,” said Sona, stretching out her hand. “Yes, of course, but first you must watch carefully,” said Papa. Next, Papa began to fix the wheels. “I want to hammer the nails too,” said Sona and picked up the hammer. “Yes, of course, but first watch carefully,” said Papa. Soon the cart was ready. Papa was about to tie a string to it. “But where have I kept the pencil and thread?” Papa started looking for them. Papa was worried now. Sona began to laugh, “Shall I find them for you?” And, from behind Papa’s ear, Sona drew out a pencil. From behind the other ear, the roll of thread. “I was watching you very carefully,” Sona said to her father. “True! You have been a big help, Sona,” said Papa, lovingly patting her on the head.
author: Ritu Singh

title: Ginni
text: Author Rabindranath Tagore was born on 7 May, 1861 to Maharshi Debendranath Tagore, one of the leaders of the Brahmo Samaj, and Sarada Devi. He was a distinguished Bengali poet, writer, painter, playwright and composer of songs. He was homeschooled by a variety of teachers in a variety of subjects. He composed ‘Sishu’, ‘Dakghor’, ‘Birpurush’, ‘Proshno’, ‘Sahaj Path’ and others for children. He was the recipient of the Nobel Prize for Literature in the year 1913. In 1915, the prestigious ‘knighthood’ was awarded to him by the British Raj but he soon renounced it as a protest to the Jallianwalah Bagh massacre of 1919. A highly renowned artist, he was known for introducing the Indian culture to the West which led to his establishment of the ‘Vishwabharati’ University in Santiniketan which is a mosaic of the East and the West. Two of his song compositions, “Jana Gana Mana” and “Amar Shonar Bangla” were chosen by India and Bangladesh respectively as their national anthems. Rabindranath Tagore passed away on August 7, 1941. About the Story Published in 1891, this is the story of a shy boy who wants to blend in with the crowd. His expectations are mercilessly ripped apart when his teacher, who spots him playing with dolls, starts calling him Ginni in class. Ginni, loosely translated, can mean a housewife, a matriarch or a matronly woman in charge of the household. A brilliant, ahead-of-its-time tale by Tagore, Ginni explores the nuanced emotions of Ashu as it takes a hit at society’s tendency to put labels on people, their demeanour, physical attributes and so on.This hits hard, especially because it comes from a teacher, who is, by profession, expected to impart knowledge, empathy and wisdom and lead us to light, instead of darkness. Shibnath pondit was our Sanskrit teacher, two or three classes below the scholarship class. He was clean-shaven, had close-cropped hair, and an abbreviated ritual tuft at the back of his head. The mere sight of him petrified the boys. Among living beings it has been observed that those who possess venomous tongues lack sharp teeth. Ponditmoshai had both. He would not only mete out slaps and blows like hailstorms on a flower nursery, but also squeeze the life out of us with his poisonous barbs. He was given to expressing his regret over the discontinuance of the traditional relationship between teachers and pupils—students are no longer devoted to their gurus as to the gods; stating this, he would hurl his overlooked divine glory at the heads of the boys, and roar at regular intervals. But these roars consisted of such profanities that no one could possibly mistake them for a manifestation of the wrath of the gods. If invectives that extend to the forefathers of the target put on the garb of divine eruption, their petty Bengali character is certain to come out in the open. Be that as it may, no one confused this deity of the second section of the third class for Indra, Chandra, Varun or Kartik; there was only one god with whom a certain similarity could be perceived, his name was Yama. After all these years, there is neither shame nor fear in acknowledging that all of us fervently prayed for him to tarry no further in departing for the abode of the abovementioned god. It was evident, however, that there was no greater nuisance than a human deity. The gods in their heaven have no demands, a flower plucked from a tree will satisfy them, but its absence will not bring forth reminders. Our human gods want much more, and the slightest transgression on our part makes them pursue us with inflamed eyes, their appearance not remotely godly at the time. Our Shibnath pondit had a particular weapon with which to torment boys. It may sound insignificant, but in truth it was mercilessly cruel. He would rename his students. Notwithstanding the fact that a name is nothing but a sound, humans usually care more for their names than for themselves; they will undergo great suffering in order to broadcast their name, they do not even hesitate to die so as to protect its honour. To distort the name of a name-adoring human, therefore, is to strike a blow at what is dearer to them than their very life. Why, even a Bhootnath finds it intolerable to be addressed as Nalinikanta, no matter that a lord of the ghosts is turned into a someone as beautiful as a lotus. This yields to us the learning that humans consider the abstract more valuable than the material, maxims more than gold, reputation more than life, and one's name more than one's life. By virtue of these innate, deep-rooted principles, Shashishekhar was stricken with despair when Pondit moshal named him Bhetki, for the fish. His agony increased manifold with the knowledge that the name in question had paid particular attention to his physical appearance, and yet he had no choice but to swallow the insult quietly. Ashu was named Ginni, but there was some history attached to the application of this word referring to a housewife. Ashu was a harmless and innocent student, who never spoke to anyone, for he was painfully shy. Possibly the youngest boy in the class, he only smiled. He was rather good at his studies, and many of the other boys were eager to make friends with him, but he didn't play with anyone, rushing home as soon as classes gave over. A maid from Ashu's house would appear at one every afternoon with a plate of sweets and water in a brass tumbler. He seemed embarrassed by her presence, looking as though he would be relieved if only she went back home. Ashu was extremely reluctant to be known as someone who was more than just another student, it was as though he fervently desired to keep it a secret, as though his schoolmates should never come to know that he had a family, that he was a son, a brother. There were no shortcomings in his academic performance, other than the fact that he was sometimes late in coming to class, and unable to provide a suitable reason when asked. Ponditmoshai would make him stand near the stairs leading to the terrace, bent over with his hands on his knees, where the boys from other classes could see the unfortunate Ashu, who was overcome with shame. Once, we had a holiday because of an eclipse. Back in school the next day, Ponditmoshai took his customary seat and looked out the door to find Ashu entering the classroom with his slate and ink-stained bag filled with books, appearing more diffident than usual. With a wry smile Shibnath pondit said, 'Here comes Ginni.' When the lessons were done, and before the class was to end, he said to all the students, 'Let me tell you a story.' The entire gravitational force of the earth attempted to draw the boy into the folds of the planet, but little Ashu remained sitting on his bench, his feet and the end of his dhoti dangling, the focus of all eyes. Ashu must be much older today, and is certain to have faced greater happiness and mortification, but none of these can be compared to what his young heart had to withstand that day. And yet, it was a most trivial matter, worth little more than a few words. Ashu had a little sister. Having no friend of her own age, she only had Ashu to play with. The porch of the house where Ashu’s family lived lay beyond an iron gate. It was raining torrentially, and the handful of pedestrians who passed by with umbrellas, carrying their footwear in their hands, had no opportunity to look around. Under a dark sky on that day-long holiday, accompanied by the sound of rainfall, Ashu was playing with his sister on the steps of the porch. Their dolls were getting married. Deeply preoccupied with the ceremony, Ashu was dispensing grave advice to his sister on the details. There was an argument over who should preside over the wedding. The little girl ran up to someone standing nearby, asking, 'Will you be our priest?' Turning in that direction, Ashu found Shibnath pondit standing in their porch, nearly soaked to the skin, his umbrella folded. He had taken shelter from the rain here, and it was to him that Ashu's sister had made the proposal of acting as the priest. At the sight of his teacher Ashu fled from the scene and his sister at once, disappearing inside the house, his holiday ruined. The next day, when Shibnath pondit gave an account of these events with his acid humour to explain why he had chosen the name 'Ginni', Ashu smiled at first as he was wont to, making an attempt to join in the amused laughter around him. The bell rang, all the classes gave over, and the maid from Ashu's house appeared at the door with two sweets on a plate and a gleaming brass tumbler of water. As he laughed, Ashu's face grew red, the veins stood out on his humiliated brow, and his tears knew no restraint anymore. Shibnath pondit ate his elevenses in the room designated for teachers and smoked peacefully, while rapturous students surrounded Ashu, calling out to him repeatedly with his newly-given name, Ginni. As for Ashu, he began to consider playing with his little sister a grievously shameful error, convinced that the citizens of the world would never forget it.
author: Arunava Sinha

title: The Postmaster
text: Author Rabindranath Tagore was born on 7 May, 1861 to Maharshi Debendranath Tagore, one of the leaders of the Brahmo Samaj, and Sarada Devi. He was a distinguished Bengali poet, writer, painter, playwright and composer of songs. He was homeschooled by a variety of teachers in a variety of subjects. He composed ‘Sishu’, ‘Dakghor’, ‘Birpurush’, ‘Proshno’, ‘Sahaj Path’ and others for children. He was the recipient of the Nobel Prize for Literature in the year 1913. In 1915, the prestigious ‘knighthood’ was awarded to him by the British Raj but he soon renounced it as a protest to the Jallianwalah Bagh massacre of 1919. A highly renowned artist, he was known for introducing the Indian culture to the West which led to his establishment of the ‘Vishwabharati’ University in Santiniketan which is a mosaic of the East and the West. Two of his song compositions, “Jana Gana Mana” and “Amar Shonar Bangla” were chosen by India and Bangladesh respectively as their national anthems. Rabindranath Tagore passed away on August 7, 1941. About the story Published in 1912, this story revolves around Ratan and her Dadababu, the postmaster. Having recently shifted from the city to a village, the Postmaster finds home in little Ratan. However, the fear of society, the expected but unnecessary possibility of explanation wrought in social hierarchy hinder him from extending the warmth and recognition that Ratan deserves. The bard’s brilliant creation is quite different from any other stories written for children. Even though the entire story is wrought with humane emotions, the last paragraph brilliantly portrays the philosopher in Tagore. The postmaster had to go to the village of Ulapur on his first posting. An indigo factory was situated nearby; its manager had gone to great lengths to have a post-office established here. Our postmaster was a young man from Calcutta. His condition on being set adrift in this remote hinterland was not unlike that of a fish hauled out of the water on to dry land. His office was located in a dark hut; there was a moss-covered pond close by, and around it, a dense wood. The cashier and other employees at the factory had no leisure to speak of, and not worthy of the company of a gentleman, besides. Those who are from Calcutta do not know how to mingle with people in a new place, where they either turn arrogant or diffident. As a result, they do not succeed in making friends and acquaintances locally. But the postmaster did not have a heavy workload. He tried his hand at poetry now and then, expressing thoughts to the effect that life is blissful when it is spent watching the leaves on the trees sway gently and the clouds drifting across the sky—but the almighty knew only too well that were a djinn from the Arabian Nights to appear and replace the trees and their branches with paved roads, and to erect rows of mansions to obscure the view of the clouds, this half-dead young man from a genteel family would be given a new lease of life. The postmaster earned a paltry salary. He had to cook for himself, and a young orphan girl from the village did all his other chores, getting her meals in return. Her name was Ratan. Aged about twelve or thirteen, she did not appear to have bright prospects for marriage. In the evening, when smoke spiralled up from cowsheds, when crickets began to call from the bushes, when the drunken bauls in a distant village started singing loudly, accompanied by their dhol and kortal, when even the poet’s heart quivered on watching the trees sway as he sat all alone outside his front door, the postmaster would light a faint lamp in the corner of the room and call out, ‘Ratan.’ She would be waiting for this very call, but she wouldn’t enter at once, saying instead, ‘What is it Babu, what do you need me for?’ Postmaster: ‘What are you doing?’ Ratan: ‘I have to light the oven... the kitchen…’ Postmaster: ‘You can do your kitchen work later. I want to smoke.’ In no time Ratan would go in, blowing for all she was worth on the bowl of the hookah. Taking it from her, the postmaster would suddenly ask, ‘Tell me Ratan, do you remember your mother?’ That was a long story; Ratan remembered some of it, and had forgotten the rest. Her father loved her more, she did remember him a little better. He would come home tired every day after work; memories of an evening or two with him were imprinted in her mind as clearly as a picture. As the conversation progressed, Ratan would sit down on the floor near the postmaster’s feet. She remembered a younger brother... how, on a rainy day long ago, they had played at fishing from a pond with a broken branch from a tree... it was this incident, rather than many other momentous ones, that would spring to her mind. It would get late as they talked, after which the postmaster would feel too lazy to cook. There would be leftovers from the morning, and Ratan would quickly light the oven and make a few rutis—that would suffice as dinner for both of them. On some evenings the postmaster would sit on the wooden cot that was part of the office and talk about his own family—his younger brother, elder sister and mother, those for whom his heart would ache here in this distant village. Many things came to mind, but could in no circumstances be mentioned to the clerks at the indigo factory; however, he found it easy to tell the young girl all of these, it did not seem in the least bit unwarranted. Eventually it came to pass that she began to refer to his family as Ma, Didi, or Dada, as though she had known them for years. Ratan had even imagined their appearances in her tiny heart. One cloudless monsoon afternoon, a slightly warm but pleasant breeze was blowing; a scent emanated from the moist grass and trees drizzled by sunlight, it was like the warm breath of an exhausted planet on the skin. Somewhere an indefatigable bird kept up an uninterrupted, mournful litany of melodious protest at the court of nature. The postmaster had no work—the swaying of the silken rain-washed boughs and the sunshine-white clouds, remnants of a temporarily vanquished monsoon, were truly a sight to behold. Gazing at them, the postmaster wished he had someone with him who was close to his heart, a human being, a source of affection. Soon he began to believe that was precisely what the bird was saying repeatedly, and that the murmuring of the leaves in this desolate land full of trees indicated the same thing too. No one would have believed it, no one even came to know, but this was the notion that arose in the mind of a lowly postmaster with a meagre salary during the long afternoon hours on that quiet day. With a sigh, the postmaster called out, ‘Ratan.’ She was seated beneath the guava tree, busy eating an unripe fruit. At the sound of her master’s voice she ran up, short of breath, saying, ‘You called, Dadababu?’ The postmaster said, ‘I’m going to teach you to read.’ He spent the entire afternoon taking Ratan though the vowels, and in this manner soon crossed the barrier of conjoint letters. The rain in the month of Srabon was relentless, filling the creeks and ponds and canals with water. Frogs croaked all day and night, accompanied by the sound of rainfall. Negotiating the roads became impossible, even the market had to be reached in a boat. One day, when it had been raining incessantly since the morning, the postmaster’s student waited at the door for a long time. But when the regular invitation was not issued, she entered the room tentatively with her books, to discover the postmaster lying in his bed. Assuming he was resting, she was about to tiptoe out when she suddenly heard his voice.‘Ratan.’ Going back up to him, she asked, ‘Were you asleep, Dadababu?’ The postmaster said faintly, ‘I’m not feeling too well... can you see if I’ve got a fever?’ There in that godforsaken exile that morning, his sick body sought a spell of loving care, recalling the tender touch of a mother’s hand on the brow. Caught in the throes of his illness, the postmaster wished for his mother and sister to be by his side, figures of feminine love. In this case his desire did not go unmet, for Ratan remained a young girl no more, stepping into the mother’s shoes at once and sending for the doctor. She administered medicines at the right time, maintained a vigil near the patient’s head all night, cooked nutritious food for him, and asked a hundred times, ‘Feeling a little better now, Dadababu?’ Several days went by before the postmaster managed to get out of bed, still frail after his illness. He wouldn’t stay here any longer, he decided, he had to get himself transferred somehow. At once he sent off an application to the authorities in Calcutta, citing the unhealthy conditions hereabouts. Released from her duties as a nurse, Ratan reclaimed her position by the door. But she was no longer called inside as before; sometimes she peeped in to find the postmaster sitting on the cot or lying down in his bed, lost in thought. While Ratan awaited a call from him, he waited impatiently for a response to his application. The girl sat by the door, revising her old lessons a thousand times, for she was worried lest she forget the conjoint letters when the call finally came. Finally, it did come, one evening a week or so later. Her heart overflowing, Ratan entered and said, ‘You called for me, Dadababu?’ ‘I’m going tomorrow, Ratan,’ said the postmaster. Ratan: ‘Going where, Dadababu?’ Postmaster: ‘I’m going home.’ Ratan: ‘When will you be back?’ Postmaster: ‘I won’t be back.’ Ratan didn’t ask any more questions. The postmaster volunteered the information that he had applied for a transfer, but his application had been rejected; so he had resigned and was going home. Neither of them spoke for a long time after that. The lamp flickered in a corner, and rainwater dripped from a worn-out spot in the roof into an earthen pot. After a while Ratan left the room on slow footsteps, going to the kitchen to make rutis. She wasn’t as quick as she usually was; perhaps her mind was assailed by questions. After the postmaster had eaten, she asked him, ‘Will you take me home with you, Dadabu?’ The postmaster laughed. ‘How can I do that?’ He did not feel it necessary to explain the reasons it was impossible. All through the night his words rang in Ratan’s ears, in sleep and in wakefulness, ‘How can I do that?’ Rising early in the morning, the postmaster saw a bucket of water placed for him as usual. As in Calcutta, he was used to bathing in water stored overnight, and not in the river. For some reason Ratan had not been able to bring herself to ask what time he was leaving; in case he had to bathe early in the morning, she had fetched the water from the river last night. After his bath the postmaster called out for her. Ratan entered in silence and gazed at her master’s face without a word in anticipation of his instructions. The master said, ‘Ratan, I’ll tell the new postmaster to look after you as well as I did. You don’t have to worry.’ There was no doubt that he was saying this with much affection and compassion, but who can fathom a woman’s heart? Ratan had often endured her master’s harsh admonitions without protest, but today she could not bear his gentleness and burst into tears, saying, ‘No, you don’t have to tell him anything, I don’t want to work here anymore.’ Not used to seeing Ratan behave this way, the postmaster looked at her in astonishment. The new postmaster arrived. Handing over charge to him, the old postmaster prepared to depart. Before leaving, he called Ratan and told her, ‘I’ve never given you any money, Ratan, I’m giving you some now before I go, you can live on it for some time.’ Keeping a little for his expenses during the journey, the postmaster took out all the money he had earned in this time. Flinging herself to the ground, Ratan wrapped her hands around his feet. ‘I beg of you Dadababu, I beg of you, you don’t have to give me anything. I beg of you, no one has to worry for me...’ She ran away. With a sigh the former postmaster picked up his travel bag, shouldered his umbrella, instructed the porter to gather his blue and white patterned trunk, and began to walk towards the river where the boat was waiting for him. When he boarded the boat and it began to move, the river, swollen with rain, lapped around him like tears flowing from the earth. He felt an ache in his heart—the wistful face of a nondescript village girl began to convey to him the unexpressed pain of the entire world. Once or twice he felt an urge, ‘Let me go back and take the orphan girl forsaken by everyone with me.’ But the wind was in the sails of the boat by then, the monsoon currents were flowing swiftly, and they had gone past the village to draw abreast of the crematorium on the river bank—the detached traveller drifting on the tide realized in his heart the essence of life: it was replete with separation and death, so why go back? No one could lay claim to someone else. But no such awakening came to Ratan. She kept wandering about outside the post office, flooding the ground with her tears. Perhaps a faint hope had arisen in her heart, that Dadabu might come back... it tethered her to the spot, preventing her from going away. Oh this foolish human heart–it never stops believing in illusion, the principles of reason penetrate its borders far too late, making it possible to disregard irrefutable evidence and cling to false hope with all one’s might, until one day this lie cuts through each and every vein, sucks all the blood out, and makes good its escape. That is when realization dawns, and the heart longs to fall into the trap of yet another illusion.

title: What a sweet smell!
text: Where are you coming from? Not coming from here! It is a floral fragrance. Not even coming from here! It smells of cow dung. Shit! It stinks of my dirty socks. Ahh, let's just say I've seen better. Oh! Understood now. That sweet smell is coming from this new candy store. The sweet smell comes from these fresh rose jamuns. Friends, did you know that there are millions of cells in the inner layers of our nose? They are useful for us to see the smell. Because of them, we can tell if it smells good or bad. If you look at the smell, you can imagine what it tastes like. The smell also indicates how far away the object is. Animals smell better than humans, Insects can still smell well. Have you ever noticed that mosquitoes can sniff us wherever we are? Who tells ants about the food that falls under when we eat? Their olfactory (olfactory) power! Now do you understand why we breathe air full of hearts as we walk through the beautiful garden? Why do we close our noses when we go to the side of the trash can? Something is telling us to do so. The same power that can smell amazing without us!

title: What Dashu Did
text: Author Sukumar Ray was born on the 30th of October in 1887 and went on to contribute a great deal of creativity and freshness to the genre of children’s literature. He was a celebrated writer and poet from Calcutta who was born to Upendrakishore Ray, a famous painter, illustrator, musician and a Bengali writer himself, and Bidhumukhi Devi. Sukumar Ray studied the art of photography, lithography and printing technology at the School of Photo-Engraving and Lithography in London and became the pioneer of the same in India. His illustrations, writing and unique sketches often found their way in Sandesh, a children’s magazine which was launched by his father in 1913. He opened up a refreshing genre of nonsense literature that combined a great sense of humour, absorbing wit and a sharp ability of observation that fascinated both children and adults alike. Some of the famous and quirky fictional characters he invented include Kumropotash, Huko Mukho Hangla, Pagla Dashu, Hijibijbij and so on. Abol Tabol is a popular collection of his rhymes and poems for children which first appeared in Sandesh but was later published as a book. Sukumar Ray passed away on the 10th of September in 1923, leaving behind his son, Satyajit Ray. About the Series Pagla Dashu, a fictional character

title: Chipi's Acorn Crime
text: Once upon a time, there was a small, soft brown chipmunk. Her name was Chipi. Chipi lived in a high Oak tree where she got the view of the forest. It was Autumn and the days were getting shorter and the nights were getting longer. The leaves were falling off and you could see the leaves on the ground were in all shades of red,yellow, orange and brown. Chipi ran down the trunk of the big oak tree and started collecting a lot of acorns for winter. After a while, she had collected plenty of acorns and she said to herself " That's a lot of Acorns. I am going to take a nap". She took a nap and after she woke up she went outside to take a stroll. As she was walking she bumped into her friend Minki. Minki invited Chipi to her house so both girls set off to Minki's house. They talked about how beautiful the leaves were, how many acorns they had collected so far and how long it was since they saw each other. Minki offered Chipi a ride home in her brand new bright red car and Chipi agreed. After Chipi went up to her home as Minki was ready to leave, she heard a crying noise coming from Chipi's house. She immediately rushed up the tree trunk and found Chipi crying. "Chipi, what's wrong, why are you crying?" asked Minki." Somebody stole all my acorns!" replied Chipi. "I had so many acorns that I had collected and now they are all gone!"." That's awful" replied Minki. "I will help you find the acorn thief." Both Chipi and Minki looked around for clues when at last Minki found some footprints. They did not know what animal's footprint it was. Then Chipi took out a poster from her cupboard. It was a poster of footprints. The poster of footprints was a class project given by her teacher. All the students had to dip their feet into their favourite colour paint and then press their foot onto a piece of poster paper. Right beside their footprint, they would sign their name. Each student got a copy of the poster paper. Chipi then realized that Penny the hen was the thief. The footprints both matched. Chipi and Minki headed over to the police station and reported Penny as the thief. The police then decided instead of a fine he would give Penny a punishment. The punishment was that instead of Chipi collecting the acorns, Penny would have to collect the acorns and give them to Chipi every year. Chipi got all her acorns back and everyone lived happily ever after {except Penny}.
author: Sachitha Pappireddy

title: The Changemaker Trio Help Cut Paani
text: In a nearby forest live three friends named Hali, Kenn, and Maya. Hali, an elephant, is extremely friendly, curious and loves to hang out with her friends. Kenn, a turtle, is a bit shy and cautious when met with new things. Maya, a bird, is funny, bold, and never afraid to try something new. Together, they make up “The Changemaker Trio”. One day, these three friends decided to go to lunch at a restaurant close to their home in the forest. “Let’s go out to get some food,” Maya exclaimed, “I’m so hungry!” “Sounds good with me,” Hali replied, “What do we want to eat?” “How about we go to the Ashoka Cafe,” Kenn suggested, “It’s not too far from here.” “Sounds good,” agreed Hali and Maya, “Let’s go!” When The Changemaker Trio arrived, they were promptly sat down. They chatted and giggled while waiting for their waiter to come. A few minutes later, their waiter, a small brown monkey, swung from the branches above them and came to halt above their table. The monkey hopped down and waved. “Hi! My name is Kai and I will be your waiter today. Can I get you anything to drink?” “I’ll have water,” said Hali. “Me too,” Maya answered. “Can I have some as well?” Kenn asked.“Of course. Would you like to help cut Paani?” Kai asked. “What does that mean?” Maya questioned. “It means you would like half of a glass instead of a full glass,” Kai kindly replied, “Cutting Paani by only taking half of a glass at a time reduces the amount of water wasted. It is better to fill your glass halfway five times instead of filling it full three times.” “I guess that makes sense,” Hali stated, “but why do we need to reduce the amount of water wasted?” “Did you know that 14 million litres of water left in our glasses is wasted every year? That’s enough water to fill more than five and a half Olympic Swimming Pools,” Kai explained. “Wow. That’s a lot of water,” Kenn observed, “and you’re saying we can help this by Cutting Paani and only filling our glass up halfway?” “Yes, if everyone were to Cut Paani, there would be a lot less water wasted,” Kai described, “People would become more mindful of how much water they are leaving in their glass and more willing to try to reduce the amount of water wasted.” “That’s a really cool idea to try to reduce water waste,” Maya declared, “I only want my glass half filled.” “Me too,” Hali added, “I never realized how big of an issue water waste is.” “I want to Cut Paani as well,” Kenn stated, “I don’t want to be part of the problem, I want to be part of the solution.” “That’s really great!” Kai exclaimed, “It’s so important that people better understand the issue of water waste so that they can make more knowledgeable decisions about their water use.” “I really want to help reduce water waste,” Maya said, “Is there any way we can make others aware even though we are kids?” “Of course!” Kai remarked, “The simplest way for you to help is by pledging to do your best to Cut Paani and by asking everyone you know to Cut Paani as well. You can also help by speaking to other places like restaurants where there is a lot of water waste.” “That sounds like a fun adventure,” Maya said. “And a helpful one as well,” Hali added, “We should definitely go talk to some restaurants that are nearby.” “Great!” Kai exclaimed, “Thank you for your help!” The next morning The Changemaker Trio met at their favorite meeting spot underneath the tallest tree in the forest. They had each prepared flyers to give to the restaurants to describe the goal of Cutting Paani. They decided to head to the Rio Eatery first to make the people there more aware of water waste. When they arrived, they were greeted by Rio, the tiger who owned the restaurant. “How can I help you?” Rio asked. “We came to ask you to take the pledge to Cut Paani by only filling your customer’s glasses up halfway,” Hali explained. “Water waste is a big issue that not enough people are aware of,” Maya added. “Did you know that 14 million litres of water left in our glasses is wasted each year?” Kenn asked. The three friends continued to explain the issue further in order to make sure that Rio understood the problem as a whole. “We’d love to take the pledge to Cut Paani here at the Rio Eatery,” Rio exclaimed, “I’m so impressed that young animals like yourselves are taking it upon yourselves to make a difference in the world.” “Thank you!” Maya, Hali, and Kenn responded, “We have learned so much about how we can make a difference despite our age. We hope that all youth are able to see their potential to make a change.” Maya, Hali, and Kenn felt really happy that they were able to help. They were hopeful that they’d find more ways to help change the world in the future. They hope that you take the opportunity to help the world as well.

title: Where is my ring
text: "Where is my ring?", wailed Adi. "Is it under the table?" asked Adi "Is it inside the cupboard?" asked Adi "Has my little brother hidden it in his box of blocks?"asked Adi. No. Adi covered his face with his hands and sat in some steps. "I cannot find my ring anywhere. I have lost it." muttered Adi. When he looked up he saw two angry parents and an angry, little brother shouting his name. "Adi!, what a mess you have made!" they said. "Hey, what's the matter? You look sad.". "I have lost my ring." Adi said. "And I cannot find it anywhere.". "Ring? It's in your finger!" shouted everyone. Adi looked at the ring in his finger and grinned.

text: Its back to school time, and i really waited to go back and tell my friends this memory! We were telling each other what we did on our vacation! i had also brought some minature mangos from my vacation! Meena: haha! you ate that mango like an animal! saisha: Hey! it was extra sweet! everybody laughed* Meena: hey Vidhatri, what did you do during summer vacations? Me: oh! Me and my family went to visit the village to show me how the village life is like! Saisha: Wow! what was it like? Meena: Yeah! it sounds intresting! tell us tell us! Vidhatri: haha ok ok! When we headed there, it was so different from the city! Some of our family members live there. They told me about so many things village have and cities don't like the bright clear sky! and i was introduced to "daatoon" it is neem twigs, they use it to brush their teeth! it is natural and an antiseptic which cures all teeth ailments naturally! it also is toothache reliever! So you see they dont need a dentist:-). They have a very good habit of using it often and keeping their teeth clean and germfree. Washing hands often and gargling mouth every time eat keeps their teeth shiny and healthy Meena: that sounds so interesting! Vidhatri: And when it hit night time, the electricity went out! so we slept on the roof and such a beautiful sky full of stars and used our imagination to make things out of the stars! My sister said at those star form a butter chicken! and i m getting already hungry thinking about it! everybody laughed*. I was unknowingly learning so many good habits, using natural products, live in fresh open air, close to environment They have such good healthy habits as they walk for miles! Doing so many physical activities in their day to day life. they are not potato couch like most of us. They wake up early sleep early and have all their food on time. All home cooked food, no junk good. I also taught yoga to some of the villagers which i learned from school and had fun! Then all the villagers said goodbye and we came back home with such sweet memories and so many good habbits which will definitely keep me healthy. Saisha: wow! next vacation i will also ask my parents if we can also go to the village! Healthy habits is a book about village life and healthy habits they have. And also telling what Indian village life is like. I have taken inspiration from my mothers stories when she was little!

title: Healthy Hilda and Her Friends !
text: One lovely sunny morning Hilda sat beneath her favourite oak tree enjoying a delicious sweet apple. Her friend Fifi the Bunny came and sat beside her. Fifi looked very hungry. Hilda offered her apple to Fifi. Fifi looked at the apple for a brief moment and was disgusted, she refused to eat something healthy. "Why are you eating that? Come let's go to the shop and buy some chips, those are yummy, " Fifi called out to Hilda. Just then, Randy the bear came out of the bushes. Randy was their good friend. " Hilda! Randy! Come on! Let's go get lots of chips and cold drinks for us to eat, the shop won't close until 7:00. We have time, " Fifi insisted. Just then some more friends were walking by. "Hey guys!", called Tammy the tortoise and Louise the Lion. Louise and Tammy came into the park. " Come on! Why don't we go to the shop and get some chips! Why don't we! why don't we!" Said Fifi getting very frustrated. Louise looked at Hilda. "Aren't you going to tell her? ", she said. "Listen, Fifi", Hilda, Randy, Louise and Tammy said, " These 'chips' and 'cold drinks' that you are always eating, they are not healthy.", they explained. "What do you mean 'not healthy'?!" Fifi asked, puzzled and irritated. The sun started to set. " They are yummy, sure. But they have no nutritional value. All these chips, cakes etc., they are not good for your body and makes it sad, upset and unwell. You wouldn't want your body to be sad, upset and unwell, right?" "Oh, now I understand. But, does that mean I won't eat chips, cold drinks and all these ever again?" Fifi asked. "Of course you'll get to eat them,but you should eat less of them and exercise,that means doing anything at your own pace as long as you get moving." The friends told Fifi. "Now I understood, I'm going to do these things and get healthy!" Fifi said,motivated. "That'll be great! " everyone smiled and had fun playing in the park until it was time to sleep. They looked at the night sky and wished each other a good night.

title: STORY OF A PENCIL
text: One day there a boy was sitting along with his grandmother. Grandmother was writing a letter. The boy looked at the grandmother and asked,is it about me that you are writing? Grandmother stopped writing and looked at the boy and said"I am writing about you, but more than that it is the pencil I am using is important " "I hope you will also be like this Pencil when you grow up" The boy was thinking "It looks like any other pencil which i have ever seen!! " "That depends on how you look at things" Said Grandma. "This pencil has got 5 qualities which if you adopt it, you will be a better person when you grow up" The First quality: You are capable of doing great things and are guided by an invisible hand and we call it God. "Second quality is that we have to sharpen the Pencil while writing. It causes sufferings for the Pencil but it gets sharpened. So you must be ready to take pain and sacrifices it will make you a better person" ﻿ "Third quality of a pencil is that it allows us to erase the mistake done by it means correcting the mistakes we have done is not a bad thing,and instead it lead us to justice" "Fourth quality of the pencil is that even though it has a beautiful wooden exterior, the graphite inside it, that matters. So try to look into the inside of you and see what happens inside" " And finally the fifth quality of the Pencil is that whatever it writes it always leaves a mark. So you also remember that you will leave a mark in everything you do, be conscious about what you do"

title: THE BALD EAGLE
text: You must have heard the saying "birds of a feather flock together". This proverb will definitely apply to the eagle, as it does not mix with other birds species but enjoy flying solo at a very high altitude. The bald eagle is a bird species unique to north america. This majestic bird has distinctive snowy feathered head and tail, and brown body. A national symbol of the united states, it is an authoritative bird that never surrenders to the size or strength of its prey the bald eagle can sore over 10,000 feet high and has great eyesight that lets it see fish and other prey upto 1.6 kilometers away. When it attacks, it drops down at about 161 kilometers an hour to swoop up and grab prey with its powerful talons! A bald eagle's white head may make it look bald. But actually the name comes from an old english word,"balde," meaning white. These graceful birds have been national symbol of the united stated since 1782. Bald eagles were on the brink of extinction because of hunting and pollution. This magnificent bird nurtures its young and both male and female work together to build nest at the very op of tall trees so the eggs will be safe. Some parents comeback year after year to the same nest, adding more sticks, twigs, and graa each time.

title: Daisy and Goldie
text: Once upon a time there was a small town. The people in that town were living happily and peacefully. There was a river near the town. In that river there were many water animals living. In the river lived a school of fish and the leader was Goldie fish. Goldie was kind and helpful fish. She always helps other and protected her school of fish from other big creatures. One day when Goldie was swimming near the bank of the river she heard someone crying. She went to check that who was that. She found a little girl was standing near the river and crying. When Goldie asked her,the little girl said, "My name is Daisy. I am crying because I have no friends. There is no one with whom I can play. " Goldie said, "You can come here to play with me and my other fish friends, we all will be your friends.. This made Daisy very happy. She has found friends and she can play with them. She went back home happily. After that day Daisy came to the river everyday and wait until Goldie and her fish friends will come to play with her. Daisy got a red balloon one day. She was very happy to get the balloon. She wanted to show it to her fish friends. Daisy was very excited and she ran with her balloon, with the strong wind her balloon flew away. She ran behind it and tried to catch it. The balloon got stuck in the bushes in the river. She wanted her balloon back but could not swim. Daisy became sad and started waiting for Goldie. When Goldie came, Daisy told Goldie about her balloon. Goldie told Daisy to sit on her back and they both swam across the river where the balloon was. With the help of Goldie fish Daisy got her balloon back. She thanked Goldie and said I am lucky to have a friend like you. Daisy happily went back home with her red balloon.

title: Crackers in a Pot
text: Author Sukumar Ray was born on the 30th of October in 1887 and went on to contribute a great deal of creativity and freshness to the genre of children’s literature. He was a celebrated writer and poet from Calcutta who was born to Upendrakishore Ray, a famous painter, illustrator, musician and a Bengali writer himself, and Bidhumukhi Devi. Sukumar Ray studied the art of photography, lithography and printing technology at the School of Photo-Engraving and Lithography in London and became the pioneer of the same in India. His illustrations, writing and unique sketches often found their way in Sandesh, a children’s magazine which was launched by his father in 1913. He opened up a refreshing genre of nonsense literature that combined a great sense of humour, absorbing wit and a sharp ability of observation that fascinated both children and adults alike. Some of the famous and quirky fictional characters he invented include Kumropotash, Huko Mukho Hangla, Pagla Dashu, Hijibijbij and so on. Abol Tabol is a popular collection of his rhymes and poems for children which first appeared in Sandesh but was later published as a book. Sukumar Ray passed away on the 10th of September in 1923, leaving behind his son, Satyajit Ray. About the Series Pagla Dashu, a fictional character

title: The rude girl
text: Once upon a time, there lived a girl called Amelia. She was super mean. She always used to be super rude and never talked to her friends nicely. Even while she was so impolite, her friends were always so well- mannered and polite with her. One sunny day, Amelia's friends came over to her house to call her to play. Amelia, Amelia called her friends. Come out and play with us please said one of her friend's Sophia. The moment Amelia came out, she looked super grumpy and annoyed. Amelia said all of you stop calling me! I don't care about you guys. Get out. You all are so annoying! Her friends were now sick of her behavior. Amelia super mad at her friends, just because they were calling her. Amelia's friends were super tired to go to Amelia's house, and always getting yelled at, and if they didn't go to Amelia's house, then Amelia would find them and be super angry. She would always say, you all are not my real friends! Sophia said, guys, I came up with an idea. Others wondered. What idea? Do you want to know what idea did Sophia came up with? You gotta wait. The next day none of her friends went to Amelia's house. As mentioned before, Amelia came marching towards her friends. Although she couldn't find them anywhere. She went to all the places, she thought where her friends could be. At last she came to Sophia's house. She knocked and rung the bell. Although, no one came out. She started to get mad. She started screaming. Sophia, Emma, Everyone come out. Amelia called out all of her friends names. Then all of sudden all her friends came out. They said, stop screaming Amelia! We don't like you. You are the worst! We don't care about you. So just leave my house and get out! Amelia was shocked. She was speechless. She said Ummm Ummm.......... guys why are you being so rude? Just stop. Amelia started to cry. On the other hand, her Friends started laughing. Amelia was confused. She asked, why are you laughing? Her friends said, because it was a joke. Now I think you should know how we feel when you act so rude. Amelia thought about it. She felt so sorry. Amelia said I am so sorry guys. I didn't know how bad you felt. I have learned my lesson. I now never going to be rude to anyone ever again. And was Amelia ever rude to anyone again?... No! she wasn't. All of her friends never complained. Amelia was now a polite girl. She learnt her mistake and never made it ever again. The girls were so kind and polite. This is where our story ends. Hopefully, Amelia stays the way she is.

title: Ms. Meow, Super Kitty
text: N ani is our lovely neighbor, she lives downstairs. She always wears lipstick, pretty dresses, tinkling bangles on her wrists, and her glasses are perched in her gray hair or on the bridge of her nose. Her home is warm and welcoming to everyone. It is filled with beautiful things she has brought back from her travels all over the world. My favorite is the musical cuckoo clock with a dancing couple, that pops out every hour to do a little jig. Also the colorful, hand painted wooden clogs that I secretly slip my feet into sometimes; and the African mask with feathers and beads that used to scare me when I was small- now it does not. I stay with Nani after school, till Ma returns from work. We have a snack together, Nani sips her hot tea, and I have milk. After I finish my homework, Nani teaches me to play the piano, and I help Nani in the garden and the kitchen. We play board games, we paint, sometimes we just get lazy and watch a movie. T here is a cat that used to linger outside the house. Meow! Meow! Meow! We would hear it at lunch and dinner time. Anytime there was a delicious smell wafting out the windows, the cat would appear. Meow! Meow Meow! Smart cat, she often got a small share of leftovers. S he sneaked in through the front door one day when Nani was picking up the newspaper. Since then, she has been Nani’s home companion. Nani asked me what to call her. Since we heard so much “Meow… Meow… Meow”, guess what I suggested? We named her Ms. Meow. Ms. Meow has a shiny black coat, sharp pointed ears and striking golden eyes. She struts around like a panther, tall, lean and proud. S ince then, she has been Nani’s home companion. Nani asked me to name her. As we heard so much “ Meow… Meow… Meow ”, guess what? We call her Ms. Meow. M s. Meow has a shiny black coat, sharp pointed ears and striking golden eyes. She struts around like a panther, tall, lean and proud. N ani made her a special bed with a small padded mattress and a soft fleece blanket. She even got her some toys to play with. If Ms. Meow wants some chicken kebabs or fish cakes, she rolls out her tongue and circles around the kitchen rubbing against Nani’s legs. Meow! Meow! W hen Nani watches her evening shows, Ms. Meow cuddles up in her lap and softly purrs, arching her neck up to gaze at Nani for some attention. Mew! Mew! Nani dotes on Ms. Meow. Oh! but for being a newcomer, that cat puts on such airs. "Is she a cat or some kind of royalty?" I have yet to see Ms. Meow chase after a mouse. At dawn, in the light of the golden sun, she skitters across the garden with her tail up high. As the birds peck on the grass, she chatters loudly, and terrorizes them with her light footed stealth action. Errr! Errr! S he quietly stalks visitors up to the door, and then startles them by sniffing their feet. I n the stifling heat of the afternoon, Ms. Meow parks herself at the gate in the shadow of the mango tree. She sprawls out on the soft grass, between yawns she catches a quick slumber. As the kids walk back from school, she springs up! She sticks out her paws and hisses at them, swatting her tail if they mistake her for an affectionate pet. Sfffshhhh! Sffffshhhh! W hen I return from school, she rushes ahead of me as Nani opens the door. S he climbs up on the table, to cover up my homework. When I sit at the piano, she glides down, then pounces on the keys. Tadadada! Clang! Boom! "What a cacophony! Practice. Don't goof around!" I hear Nani from the kitchen. I can almost see the smirk on Ms. Meow's face. W hen I sit on the sofa to read a book, she snuggles in at the back, and rolls down nudging me out of the seat. Then she splays lazily! The sofa all to herself, she licks her fur, and gives a squeaky little trill of victory. Rrrwwww! "Ms. Meow!!!" I chide, I stomp my foot. Not a care in the world. "Is this cat naughty or what?" O ne night the moon is full, up high in the sky. It is a bit chilly, so everyone has huddled under their blankets and fallen asleep. Except for the hum of the refrigerator, the tick tock of the clock, and the occasional gurgling snore, all is quiet. In the pitch black, a slow creaking of the door is heard, followed by soft shuffling of feet scampering around. Ms. Meow who sleeps in Nani’s room perks up her ears, sniffs the air and rises up tall from her soft bed. Nimble on her paws, she advances out to the living room. T here is a burglar prowling around, he reaches for something from the cupboard and stashes it in his sack. Ms. Meow climbs up onto the piano, and then... Tadadada! Clang! Boom! Jolted out of the silence, the burglar drops one of his sacks. Crash! Clatter! Objects are scattered all over the floor. Ms. Meow then leaps from the piano onto the top of the cupboard. She growls a deep, scary snarl. Gggrrrraw! In the darkness, the burglar searches for the sound. He sees the edges of sharp white teeth, and glowing golden eyes hunting down on him. Shivering he stammers "D...de...devil". Ms. Meow dives down on the head of the burglar. It's an ambush! She scratches with her claws and hisses in his face. Shrrrrrr! Terrified, the burglar screams in panic. "Leave me!!" He stumbles over the objects on the floor, falling to the ground. Nani wakes up to all the commotion, and calls the police. B y the next morning, everyone hears the story of Ms. Meow catching the thief. The town newspaper comes by to take her picture. Meow! Meow! Meow! M s. Meow has become our local hero. The brave cat who saved the day...or rather the night!! Ms. Meow, Super Kitty!
author: Yogita Soman

title: Flower blind
text: She knew their faces by touch. One day, Chat was strolling in the garden. She liked the sweet scent of flowers. She loved to touch their soft petals. Chat wished she could see flowers, just once. "They are lovely," she said to herself. Every day, Chat walked in the garden. She knew her way around. Today, she raised her head to the skies. Suddenly, she heard thunder and lightning. "I need to hurry back to the house," Chat thought. Rain began to fall. Chat slipped, lost her balance and fell. She hit her head on a stone. When Chat woke up, there were people around her. "What happened?" she asked. "You fell and bumped your head," her father said. "Thank God you are fine," said her mother. "Daddy, mummy?" asked Chat. She also called the names of her brothers and sisters. "Please, get me a flower." Everyone was surprised. Her sister returned with a flower. Chat held it gently. "It is so lovely," she said. Her family looked at one another. "Chat, can you see the flower?" her mother asked. Chat played with the flower in her hand. "You are all so beautiful, just like this flower," she smiled.
author: Nathaniel Bivan
