title: Tell it in one breath!
text: one breath, Chirped the insect under the grass. Flap-Flap-Flap, Flap-Flap-Flap Tell it in one breath, Flapped the bird in the sky. Chug-Chug-Chug,Chug-Chug-Chug.... Tell it in one breath, Chugged the train at the station. Slither-Slither-Slither,Slither-Slither-Slither Tell in one breath, Slithered the snake through the bamboo. Bloom-Bloom-Bloom,Bloom-Bloom-Bloom-Bloom Tell it in one breath, Bloomed the tree. Buzz-Buzz-Buzz,Buzz-Buzz-Buzz.... Tell it in one breath, Buzzed mosquitoes in the ear Glitter-Glitter-Glitter, Glitter-Glitter-Glitter... Tell it in one breath, Glittered the fireflies in search. Clang-Clang-Clang,Clang-Clang-Clang.... Tell it in one breath, Clanged the coins falling into the glass. Someone jumped into the cotton, then what should be told in one breath?
author: Gayatri Devulapalli

title: Who will cook food for the plant?
text: "I am so hungry", told the hungry stem to the green leaf and the root. "I am hungry too", told the hungry root to the green leaf and the stem. I am so hungry. I am hungry too! "I have an idea! I will cook food for all of us!", told the leaf to the root and the stem. "Haha, cook? How will you cook?", asked the stem and the root to the green leaf. I have an idea! I will cook food for all of us! Haha, cook? How will you cook? Haha, cook? How will you cook? "Yes, I will cook. But I need your help", told the green leaf. "We will help you. What do you need from us?", asked the stem and the root. Yes, I will cook. But I need your help We will help you. What do you need from us? "Dear root, can you please draw up water from the soil and give to the stem?" requested the green leaf to the root. "Yes, Yes I can do that" told the root happily. Dear root, can you please draw up water from the soil and give to the stem? Yes, Yes I can do that The root drew the water from the soil and gave it to the stem! "Dear stem, now can you transport it through your body and give it to me?", asked the green leaf to the root "Yes, Yes I can do that" told the stem happily. Dear stem, now can you transport it through your body and give it to me? Yes,Yes I can do that "Thank you dear friends. I have water from you. Now I need help from dear Sun friend" told the root. "Sun friend? What do you need him for?", asked the stem and the root. Thank you dear friends. I have water from you. Now I need help from dear Sun friend Sun friend? What do you need him for? "I need his bright light and heat to cook", told the root. I need his bright light and heat to cook. "Dear Sun, will you share your light and heat with me? I need to cook food.", asked the green leaf to the bright sun in the sky. "Sure dear green leaf, you can have my light and sun as long as it is day", told the Sun to the green leaf. "Dear Sun, will you share your light and heat with me? I need to cook food. Sure dear green leaf, you can have my light and heat as long as it is day. "Thank you, dear Sun. Now I need to breathe in air through my tiny pores to start cooking", told the green leaf. "Oh Yes! There is plenty of fresh air around us. You can breathe in as much as you want." told the stem. Thank you, dear Sun.Now I need to breathe in air through my tine pores to start cooking Oh Yes! There is plenty of fresh air around us. You can breathe in as much as you want. "Yes! Now I have everything I need to make a yummy meal for all of us. I have water, sunlight and air. But wait I forgot something!", told the green leaf? "Oh no, what is it? tell us if we can get it for you.", asked the stem and the root. Yes! Now I have everything I need to make a yummy meal for all of us. I have water, sunlight and air. But wait I forgot something! Oh no, what is it? tell us if we can get it for you. "Oh it is something I need to have in my cupboard. A green paint!", told the green leaf. "You are so green in colour, you must definitely have it!", told the stem. "Can you cook a meal for us please?",asked the stem and the root. Oh it is something I need to have in my cupboard. A green paint! You are so green in colour, you must definitely have it! Can you cook a meal for us please? "Oh yes, I can cook now. Let me start", told the green leaf. The stem, the root waited patiently for the green leaf to finish his cooking. And FINALLY.......... Oh yes, I can cook now. Let me start The food was ready! The leaf, the stem and the root had a delicious meal and they even stored food for the dinner at night!
author: Gayatri Devulapalli

title: The red ribbon
text: Once upon a time there lived two twins, Anya and Tanya. They both were 8 years old. They lived on a farm with their parents and their 3 year old sister, Maya. The two twins went to I.P.S - India Public School. In those days, schools didn’t have any buses, so they used cycles or walked. The twins took turns riding on one cycle that they had. When Anya was riding the cycle, Tanya would run after Anya and when Tanya was riding the cycle, Anya would run after Tanya. Maya only stayed home and played with her doll. Even if she was 8 years old like the twins, she said she would rather play with her doll that she got from Cousin Naina for her birthday. She did not know that going to school was a privilege and that not many people had the money to go to a school. Anya and Tanya were very grateful to have a school to go to. Everyday, before school mother would tie the twins hair in two ponytails and pack thier tiffin boxes. Anya’s tiffin box and hair ribbons were orange and Tanya’s tiffin box and hair ribbons were red. Father had got it for them on thier first day of school. They tried hard not to lose the tiffin boxes and hair ribbons. One day when the twins were cycling to school, Tanya’s red hair ribbon got hooked onto one of the branches of a tree while she was cycling. But she didn’t even realise it! On the way back from school, Tanya saw one of her hair ribbons hanging from the branch. She thought it wasn’t hers but when she looked at her hair, she saw it was open. The ribbon was dirty. Tanya took it home and told mother about it. Mother took the ribbon, washed it and put it on the clothesline outside to dry. The next morning father went to town. He bought two sets of ribbons, since the others were very old. Anya and Tanya liked and took care of their new ribbons. Every day after school they washed thier hair ribbons and put it out to dry. They didn't lose the ribbons ever again.
author: Anushka Nair

title: Tara, get up!
text: "Tara, get up! The sun is already above our heads. Get up!" said Mrs. Brown, entering the room. "Ohh mom, just a sec, I am very sleepy," said Tara while rolling in her bed. And she again slept. Mrs. Brown said in anger, "If you don't get up now you won't get your lunch today." Tara got up from her bed and said, "Okay! i am awake now." What else does she expect from me? She whispered. Mrs brown slowly came near Tara's ear and whispered, "Hammmh, what?" Tara haggling said nodded her head in disagreement. Mrs brown took her to the bathroom to brush her teeth. Tara did some chores, took a shower and went to the kitchen to help her mummy in making the breakfast. There she saw her mother angrily making the breakfast because she took time to bath. She told her mother a joke to improve her mood. Mrs. Brown smiled at her. She replied, "Oh dear, my hand is paining, would you like to help me in making the idli?" Tara had no option than to say yes. She helped her and after sometime idli is ready. And then they both enjoyed their breakfast. Tara went back to her room. She was very sad because of her mother's behaviour. Tara said in a nervous voice, "Whenever I listen to her she behaves nice with me and whenever I don't, hmmh." She cried for a while and slept. Mrs. Brown heard all this and felt really bad about how she treated Tara. She sat next to Tara looking her sleep calmly and smiled at her. She decided to take her outdoors. As Tara woke up her Mrs. Brown told her to get ready. Tara did as her mother said and got ready. And then Mrs. Brown took Tara to a park. They both enjoyed their trip and Mrs. Brown was very happy that she was able to make her daughter happy. That day she decided to treat her daughter well.
author: Princi Vijay Rajratna

title: The Lost Doll
text: Once upon a time there lived a little girl called Antara. She was five years old. She was a happy and cheerful girl. She danced and sang and prayed everyday. She had a lot of toys, and she loved them all, but do know which one she loved best? She had a doll called Nina, who she loved best. Nina had long black hair, and she had blue eyes which would open and close. Wherever Antara went, she took Nina with her. One day she took Nina to bed. Soon Antara was fast asleep. When she woke up in the morning, Antara brushed her teeth, drank her milk, and got ready for school. She went looking for Nina, but Nina was nowhere to be seen. Oh! Where is she? There was no time to search, so Antara went off to school. When she came back from school, Antara searched everywhere. She could not find find her. She asked her brother Aarav, ‘ Could Nina have gone out by herself?’ Aarav said, ‘ No, silly, dolls cannot do that.’ They searched everywhere, but could not find her. Antara was sad. Aarav did not like to see her sad. To cheer her, he said, ‘Come let’s play catch, with a ball’. They went to Antara’s bedroom to play catch. Soon both children were having a nice time throwing the ball at each other, and trying to catch, and Antara was again smiling. Oh, oh! Aarav threw the ball, Antara could not catch it, and it rolled between the cot and the wall. Both children lay on the floor and tried to get the ball out. to catch, and Antara was again smiling. Oh, oh! Aarav threw the ball, Antara could not catch it, and it rolled between the cot and the wall. Both children lay on the floor and tried to get the ball out. SURPRISE! There was Nina, well and truly stuck between the cot and wall. Antara gave a whoop of joy, and pulled Nina out. The children ran down to share their good news!
author: Vimala Vaidyanathan

title: 9 Types of Intelligence
text: Howard Gardner, an American psychologist, claimed that people had multiple intelligences. He described nine types of intelligence. They are as follows. Logical or Mathematical Intelligence: A person with mathematical intelligence is good with number calculations, solves mathematical problems, and has good logic. Examples of people with mathematical intelligence are math teachers, engineers, and chartered accountants. Linguistic Intelligence: A person with linguistic intelligence knows how to use words effectively while writing and speaking. They have a good vocabulary and easily win word games. Examples of people with linguistic intelligence are poets, journalists, and public speakers. Interpersonal intelligence: A person with good interpersonal intelligence knows the moods of different people and accepts differences among people. They have good emotional intelligence and understand other points of view. They communicate well. Examples of people with good interpersonal intelligence are human resource specialists, public relation officers, and social workers. Musical Intelligence: A person with musical intelligence can understand rhythms, pitch, and tone of the music, learn the tune of a song quickly, and also create music. Examples of people with good musical intelligence are music composers, singers, music instrument players, and sensitive listeners. Intrapersonal Intelligence: A person with intrapersonal intelligence is aware of their own feelings and needs. They are self-aware and can plan and make decisions that benefit their life. They know their strengths and weaknesses. Examples of people with good intrapersonal intelligence are psychologists and counsellors. Bodily or Kinesthetic Intelligence: A person with kinesthetic intelligence can move around easily. They have a good sense of timing for physical movements. They can handle objects with ease. Their mind and body are well coordinated. Examples of people with good kinesthetic intelligence are dancers, athletes, and surgeons. Visual or Spatial Intelligence: A person with spatial Intelligence can think in three dimensions. They are good at visualizing objects in 3 D form when you mention any shape. They can visualize how an image will look even before drawing. They can create art. Examples of people with good spatial intelligence are architects, photographers, and pilots. Naturalist Intelligence: A person with naturalist intelligence loves nature. They are good at growing plants. And love pet animals. They can also differentiate well between different plants and different animals. They are also in tune with natural clocks and cycles. Examples of people with good naturalist intelligence are gardeners, botanists, and astronomers. Existential Intelligence: A person with existential intelligence is good at finding answers to questions such as what is the meaning of life. Why do people die? Examples of people with good existential intelligence are philosophers, authors, and inspirational speakers. One person can have a combination of four or five intelligence. For example, one person may sing well, be good at math, and write well. Another person may be a good athlete, draws well, has good relations with people, and ponders a lot about life. It is possible to strengthen a type of intelligence through practice. Now, when you look at people, can you identify the different intelligence they have?
author: Anitha Selvanathan
illustrator: 211 Studio; Abin  Shrestha; Angie & Upesh; Catherine Groenewald; Gail Spencer; Lara Berge; Meghna Pant; Partho Sengupta; Priya Kuriyan; Rajiv Eipe; Rashmi Gopal; Suvidha Mistry

title: Everyday Superheroes
text: ​The world looked different. Many grown-ups had stopped going to work. Children had stopped going to school. They could no longer play in the park or meet their friends. ​There was a virus in the air. The virus was called the novel coronavirus. It made many, many people very sick. ​Superheroes stood up to save the world then. Some tried to find a cure. Some cared for the sick. And some tried to stop its spread. These superheroes did not wear capes. They did not fly. They did not carry swords or lassos. They wore masks and protective suits. They carried stethoscopes and thermometers. They looked through microscopes and examined lab reports. ​They could be found in people’s homes, in neighbourhoods, in laboratories, in hospitals. Everywhere. ​The community health workers started their day early. They went from house to house in villages and cities. They asked people to wash their hands, stay home, wear a mask when they stepped outside, and keep a distance of at least 2 metres from others. ​When people fell ill, the laboratory technicians and molecular biologists collected samples of body fluids and ran tests. They used laboratory equipment and computer programs to conduct tests and analyse results. They recorded the findings and shared them with doctors. ​The nurses looked after patients and treated them — sometimes at home, sometimes at the hospital. They gave patients medicines, and checked their pulse, temperature and oxygen levels. They helped patients recover. ​If the virus attacked the lungs, the pulmonologists took care of it. They treated patients with lung disease​ ​or respiratory problems. They looked at the medical reports and decided the course of treatment. ​Virologists and doctors conducted research. They studied the virus. They developed new medicines to treat the sickness, and vaccines to prevent people from falling sick. ​When the virus first appeared, the epidemiologists conducted investigations. Like detectives, they asked questions. Where did it start? How did it spread? Why does it work so fast? Who is at risk? They tried to figure out how to stop the disease from spreading. Their work can be used to prevent similar outbreaks in the future. ​When people were scared, worried, confused, angry or exhausted, the psychologists listened and guided them. The psychiatrists gave them medicine for anxiety or sadness. ​Ambulance drivers took patients to the hospital in their ambulances. ​ ​Delivery persons carried essential supplies, like food and medicines, to people’s home. ​Reporters brought information and news from all over the world. Garbage collectors collected the waste in the community. ​All these superheroes worked long hours. They put their lives at risk to protect people. They always showed up when they were needed. They were everyday superheroes.
author: Minakshi  Dewan

title: Game of Colours
text: Kannan and Meera were playing games outside their house. Then Kannan said, “Let us play a colour game. I will tell a colour and you have to tell me two objects in that colour.” Meera said, “Ok. Shoot your questions.” Kannan said, “Yellow.” Meera said, “Lemons, Corn.” Kannan said, “Brown.” Meera said, “Jaggery, Tree trunk.” Kannan said, “Blue.” Meera said, “Sea, Blue Sapphire Stone.” Kannan said, ”Pink.” Meera said, “Lotus, Tongue.” Meera said, “Now I will tell a colour. You can tell the objects in that colour.” Kannan said, “Ok. Ask.” Meera said, ”Red.” Kannan said, “Strawberry, Tomato.” Meera said, “White.” Kannan said, “Cotton, Milk.” Meera said, “Black.” Kannan said, “Crow, Hair.” Meera said, “Green.” Kannan said, “Parrot, Bitter Gourd” Meera asked, ”Who is the winner of this game?” Kanna said, “Both of us gave answers for all the four colours we got. So both of us are winners.” They showed a thumbs up and continued playing other games.
author: Anitha Selvanathan

title: Dadi, Dadi, What Colour Do You See?
text: ​“Come, buy chashmas, colourful and bright. See the world in a whole new light.” ​“Come on, Dadi, let’s play a guessing game. We’ll point at a colour, you tell us its name.” ​“Hurry up, Dadi, let’s start soon!” “What’s the colour of this balloon?” ​“This is easy. It’s green, I see.” “No, Dadi, that’s not true! This balloon is bright blue.” “What colour is your gola, Dadi?” “This is easy, it’s orange, I see.” ​“No, Dadi, that’s not true. It’s flaming red all the way through.” ​“Guddu and Golu, Now you give it a try. What colour is that kite, Up there, flying so high?” ​“That’s easy, Dadi, it’s purple, see?” ​“No, children that’s not true. Can't you see, it's bright blue?” ​How did Dadi, Guddu and Golu see so many colours? ​Try out these combinations Red + blue = purple Blue + yellow = green Red + yellow = orange
author: Ekta Bharti

title: THE GOLDEN CROWN
text: Archimedes lived in the 3rd century BC, in the city of Syracuse (Sicily) which was part of the old Greek empire and ruled by King Heiro II. Archimedes was a great mathematician, scientist, astronomer, and inventor. King Heiro ordered a special golden crown by supplying pure gold to the royal goldsmith. The goldsmith brought the crown to the king with the same weight of the pure gold which was supplied to him. The king suspected that the crown not made of pure gold and he mixed some amount of silver. The King asked his ministers "can someone find out whether the goldsmith had cheated, without damaging the crown". No one had the answer. The King called Archimedes to the royal palace. He ordered Archimedes "Archimedes you have three days, to prove whether the goldsmith cheated me or not". Archimedes thought " Normal way is to melt the crown to a regularly shaped body to find its volume". "Then divide the mass by volume to find the density. How will I do without damaging the crown?". The next day, neighbors of Archimedes saw, a funny incident Archimedes was running in the streets naked exclaiming "Eureka, Eureka" (I found it, I found it)". People thought he became mad, as he could not find the solution for the King’s problem. But the reason was different…. ONE HOUR BACK Archimedes was in deep thought while taking bath. He noticed the water overflowed from the bathtub as he got in. He thought "I can use this effect to determine the volume of the crown". The submerged crown would displace an amount of water equal to its own volume. Thus density of the crown could be obtained. This density would be lower if the crown is contaminated with silver. Archimedes went to the King and requested "Can you provide two containers with the same level of water?". In one container, he put the pure gold bar with the same weight as the crown, and in another container, he put the crown The King noticed the volume of water displaced was more in the container with the crown. Thus Archimedes proved the density of the crown was less than the density of pure gold This proved, the goldsmith was dishonest and punishment was given to him for stealing the gold Archimedes principle explains the behavior of objects placed in any liquid or gas which is called the Principle of Buoyancy. The buoyant or lifting force of an object submerged in a fluid is equal to the weight of the fluid it has displaced. It explains how ship Floats, how hot air balloons fly, how submarines dive. The volume of the ship is so great that, weight of the water displaces much higher to weight of the ship, so it floats.
author: Srikrishna Chandrasekaran

title: How cool I stayed this summer
text: How cool I stayed this summer Though summers are very hot but still we can refresh ourselves and make it cool. Summer is the only season in which we can learn and explore. I started my summer journey by refreshing my body by drinking different kinds of drinks like coconut water, mango shake and buttermilk. I also joined a summer camp in which they made us do jogging, warm ups,drills and some fun games. In sports I played badminton and did swimming for good growth of my body. I enjoyed eating ice creams, popsicles and juicy sweet mangoes. So, similarly you can stay cool like me.
author: Reya Jain

title: Animal Kingdom
text: It was 22 nd January. The next day was Myra’s birthday! Myra was watching her favorite movie “MIRACULOUS ANIMALS” on television. It was 11:55 PM when Myra glanced at the clock. She wished she could go and meet those animals and perform miracles like them. She yawned and did not even realize when she slipped into deep slumber. Suddenly, a FAIRY GOD MOTHER appeared. The reason behind her presence was Myra’s good deeds from the previous year. She thought of fulfilling Myra’s dream and taking her to the animal world. Myra did not feel the movement of the fairy and when she opened her eyes, she found herself in the Animal Kingdom. Her face lit up and she was amazed. The sun was shining bright and smiling with glee. The birds were chirping and the sheep was jumping with laughter. There was a happy and vibrant vibe in the air. She realized her birthday had begun when she heard the animals singing the birthday song for her. She giggled and danced in jubilation. The animals gifted her the charm of the Animal Kingdom. At the end of the celebration, they dropped her to her HAPPY BIRTHDAY MYRA!! house in their swaying chair. THE END!
author: Reya Jain
illustrator: Candace di Talamo; Mamun Hossain; Patrick Latimer; Raju Babu Shakya; Vartika  Sharma

title: Kavitha Eats Rotis
text: It was a weekend and Kavitha did not have school that day. So, she decided to spend time with her mom. First, she carried grass for the cow and helped her mom to feed the cow. Then, Kavitha watched her mom milking the cow. She drank a little of the fresh milk. After they came home, her mom heated the milk in vessels. Kavitha helped to carry the vessels with boiled milk and place them on the table to cool. Then, her mom mixed water with curd and churned the curd with a wooden hand churner or mathu. Kavitha tasted the butter that came at the top of the buttermilk while churning. It was yummy. Her mom would later make ghee from the collected butter. Then her mom made roti with wheat flour. Kavitha loved the fluffy rotis her mom made with ghee and was eager to eat them. Kavitha ate the roti. Meanwhile, her mom was preparing greens to cook for lunch. Kavitha could not wait to taste the greens her mom would make for lunch. It was a happy weekend for Kavitha.
author: Anitha Selvanathan

title: My Little  Brother
text: Abeer is my little, cute,loving brother.He only is sixteen months old. But did you know how my brother was born? One day I was in my school,I got a wish. My wish was to have a cute brother. Soon on /19 I got a brother, just the way I wanted. Now I will take him all around the world. Ex Tajmahal.
author: Anaya Yadav

title: Baby Brother Karthi
text: Savitha aunty has come to see my baby brother Karthi. My mom came with my baby brother from the hospital yesterday. My baby brother Karthi was born in the hospital near our house. Mom and Savitha aunty played with Karthi. Savitha aunty waved a toy over Karthi’s tummy. The toy made sounds ting, ting, ting. Mom adjusted Karthi's nappy. Everyone was giving a lot of attention to my baby brother now. I was feeling a bit jealous. Will they also pamper me if I lie in the cradle? Haha. Sounds funny. I ran to my mom and told her, “You are now only taking care of Karthi. You have forgotten me.” Savitha aunty laughed when she heard this. Savitha aunty said, “Do you forget your old friends when you get new friends.” I said, “No, not at all.” Aunty said, “The same way, your mom will not forget you because of your baby brother. She loves you both equally.” I was very happy to hear this. From then on, I also took care of my baby brother whenever possible and played with him happily. Sometimes, he was troublesome. That is ok. I love my brother.
author: Anitha Selvanathan

title: Gappu's favourite food
text: It was a holiday and Gappu was in his room reading a book. The smell of food distracted him. He quickly got up and went into the kitchen. He asked his mother, "Are you making anything special? It's smelling delicious!" His mother laughed and said, "I made your favourite Paneer sabji." Gappu's mouth started watering by listening to this. His mother understood this. She said, "I will knead the dough and make hot Poori. It's not yet time to eat, go and study." Gappu came back to his room but he was not able to concentrate on studying. He was thinking about having Poori with Paneer sabji. As soon as the food got ready his mother called him. Gappu ran from his room and started eating. He ate till his stomach was full!
author: Deepika Dinesh
illustrator: Ajit Narayan; Partho Sengupta; Priya Kuriyan; Rob Owen; Sonal Gupta Vaswani

title: Where is my bat?
text: I am not able to find it anywhere. I looked for it behind the door. But it was not there. I climbed up and searched for it. I did not find it anywhere! I looked for it under my bed. It was not even there! I hunted for it in the boxes. But I did not find it there. I searched up, I searched down. Looked for it here and there. It's not here. It's not there! It's nowhere!
author: Deepika Dinesh

title: The River
text: River is the home to so many! All our thirst is quenched by the river. Fishes breathe in the river. The river is the moving clock of crocodiles. Is it a river or a cloud? The river is illuminating the faces of the fields. Farmers stare at the clouds. The river changes the color of the soil. The river moves from tree to tree. Look she is standing upright on the bank. Is it a river or a cloud? The sun fisherman traps the birds in the river. The river will be completely new whenever you see it again. The hand of the river is the magic wand. Is it a river or a cloud?
author: Deepika Dinesh

title: My Baby
text: She said, "See, the cute face, the small fingers. This is my baby." Grandma and Grandpa came. They saw the baby. They picked up the baby and called it 'Cutie pie'. They totally forgot about me. My aunt came. She brought small clothes. She said 'Don't touch the baby, don't pick the baby up!" She made me cry! Is this not my baby too? Does it not want me? Then I heard a sound. "Wa...Wa...Wa..." cried the baby. I ran and hugged the baby. I sang a lullaby, "La...La...La..." Even I closed my eyes with the baby. Shhh.....!!!
author: Deepika Dinesh
illustrator: Angie & Upesh; Huynh Thi  Kim Lien; Lavanya Karthik; Madhuri Purandare; Rajeev Verma 'Banjara'; Saurabh Pandey; Thea   Nicole de Klerk

title: Appapa is with the Dinosaurs
text: One November morning, Adu's parents tell him that they are going to visit Appapa. 'But we aren't meant to go till Christmas!' wonders Adu. When Adu, Ma and Da reach Appapa’s town, they don’t go home like they always do. Instead, they take a taxi to the hospital. Ma tells him, “Appapa is sick.” “Sick? But I just spoke to Appapa yesterday, and told him all about my sports day!” Ma says, “Appapa’s lungs have become very weak. So the doctor has put him on a ventilator. It’s a machine that will help Appapa breathe.” This makes Adu sad. The next evening, Adu sees Ammama, Ma, Da, and his Aunt crying. He has never seen big people cry before. He thought only kids cried! Da comes to Adu, holds his hands and asks, “Adu, remember that book on dinosaurs you love? How it said that the dinosaurs are EXTINCT?" "Do you remember what ‘extinct’ means?” “Yes,” nods Adu. “It means that the dinosaurs were on the Earth for a long, long time - but then something happened, and now they are gone forever.” “That’s right,” says Da. “Just like the dinosaurs, Appapa was also with us for a long, long time - but now he is extinct. He is gone forever.” Adu doesn’t like this at all! Appapa was very special. There was no one else like him. His Appapa was a superhero who wore a cape to work. He sang funny songs that made Adu laugh out loud. And just like Adu, he too was scared of loud sounds. Adu doesn’t want his Appapa to be extinct. Who will he call every evening and tell stories from school? Who will he go to the kutti stream with? Who will protect him from Ma’s shouting when he plays cricket inside the house? Adu goes to bed crying. That night, Appapa visits him in his sleep. Adu wakes up the next morning and goes looking for him all over the house. When he tells Da about it, he says, “Adu, that was a dream. It was Appapa’s special goodbye just for you.” Now, when Adu visits his Ammama, Appapa is not there in the house. His clothes are still in his cupboard, his glasses are on his study table - but Appapa is not there. Everytime Adu thinks of Appapa, he remembers what Da told him - Appapa is extinct. So now when Adu misses Appapa, he just closes his eyes and imagines him singing funny songs with the dinosaurs.
author: Sahana Jose

title: The Big Beach Clean-Up
text: Arzu loved the beach more than any other place in the world. There, she could watch her favourite animal, play her favourite game and have her favourite drink, coconut water. She would go as often as she could with her best friend, Umeed. One afternoon, they found Thatha decorating his coconut stall. “Thatha, which beach is this?” asked Arzu, pointing at a photograph. “It’s so clean and beautiful!” said Umeed. Thatha told them how he grew up on this very beach. He would play barefoot and take naps on the sand without having to worry about pieces of glass or garbage. “It was heaven! It pains me that you will never see it like that.” The next day in school, Arzu told her entire class about Thatha’s old photos and stories. She described how beautiful the beach once was. “We have to do something! And I have a plan.” Everyone wanted to help! Arzu showed them the map she had made. She had drawn the whole beach and divided it into four equal parts or quarters. The plan was to divide themselves into four equal teams. Since there were 16 children in the class, this meant that each team would have four children. Each team would collect and separate garbage from one quarter of the beach. “Arzu, maybe each team can also be divided into two equal parts? One half of the team can collect garbage and the other half can separate it,” said Dia. “That’s a great idea!” Arzu replied. “Half of four is two. So, two of us will collect and two will separate.” “Wow, I never thought we’d use all this maths class stuff to solve real problems,” said Umeed. “Why do you think we’re learning maths?” asked Arzu, giggling. On Saturday, which was also Thatha’s day off, all the children got together at the beach. They divided their tools into four equal parts. Tools Total Quantity One Quarter for Each Team Chapati tongs for picking 8 2 sharp or dirty things Sacks for collecting garbage 16 4 Paper for labelling the sacks 16 4 Pens for writing on the labels 4 1 Hour 1 Hour 2 Hour 3 Hour 4 At sunset, Abu arrived as promised with the garbage truck. He weighed all the sacks before loading them. The children had collected 120kg of garbage! “There are 30kg of glass and paper, which can be recycled, ” he said. “30kg out of 120kg, that’s one quarter!” said Arzu. “That leaves 90kg, which means that three quarters of the garbage is plastic,” said Umeed. “Yes,” said Abu. “We will take it and separate it further to see what can be recycled or reused. The rest will go to the landfill.” On Sunday morning, everyone arrived early and waited for Thatha. Thatha’s eyes teared up. This time with happiness. “I did not think it was possible!” he said. Arzu smiled her biggest smile. “Anything is possible, Thatha! All it took was some muscle power...” “And some maths!” Umeed said, laughing. SURPRISE! What are fractions? A fraction represents part of a whole. If we divide the whole into two equal parts, each part is 1⁄2 or half. If we divide the whole into four equal parts, each part is 1⁄4 or a quarter. Find some fractions with Arzu and Umeed Arzu and Umeed have been monitoring plastic waste in the bins. One week, this is what they found. 1. What fraction of the waste is water bottles? 2. What fraction of the waste could be reduced if all the stalls kept paper straws? 3. What fraction of the waste could be reduced if everyone carried their own reusable bottles and bags? Item Quantity Plastic straws 10kg Plastic water bottles 20kg Plastic bags 10kg ANSWERS

title: You Won't Believe Me
text: You won’t believe me, but I actually like my school very much. It has lots of places to run and play. And when it’s too hot outside, it has a big library, where I go and hide. But most times, my school doesn’t like me very much. You won’t believe me, but my school has a big pond with lots of fish in it. When my friends are not talking to me and the others are tired of hurting me, I like to stand next to it and count the fish. I’m so bad at things, I keep forgetting how many fish are in it. But you know what, I know them all: The tiny blue ones, they keep together. The orange ones with black spots spend all their time nibbling at the stones. The goldfish can be terribly moody. The silver ones are always in a rush. But there’s just one red fish with white fins… who I feel is the loneliest of them all. You won’t believe me, but I feel she is also the most special. She moves like a shadow. Only I know where she lives in the pond and when she likes to come out. Sometimes I wait hours for her and I end up missing class. The thing is, I am not good at anything. My eyes are weak, my nose is always runny and when I speak, it sounds like a squeak. My teachers are always shouting at me, and no one wants to sit next to me. In fact, I’m so bad at things, sometimes I can’t even cry. You won’t believe me, but all this is 100 per cent true. When no one is looking, they punch and kick me. They make little pebbles out of spit and sand to throw at me. And when I shut my eyes to cry, my scream gets trapped inside me, and I can’t even breathe. I’m so bad at things that I’m not even good at breathing it seems. And the words, they just don’t come out of me right. In fact, what I think is often not what I want to say. And whatever I do or say, they all just laugh at me. You won’t believe me, but I too have many friends. They’re always around me, telling me stories of distant lands to which I can escape with them. They just aren’t real, I know. I’ve made them up from the books I’ve read. The boys say I’m like a girl and the girls say I’m not strong and brave enough to be like them. And maybe they’re right. I can’t even tell where it hurts when I fall on the ground and gasp for air. The teachers, even the nice ones, feel sad when they look at me. They say I’m a good boy and I can be smart, too, but I don’t try hard enough. And when I do try, I forget things. Even the happy stuff. You won’t believe me, but I like making people laugh. I do funny things in class when the teacher is not looking at me. Like sticking pencils in my ears, or trying to touch my nose with my tongue. And sometimes, just sometimes, someone will notice and smile back at me — and I’ll feel happy. But the thing is, I am not really good at anything. In fact, I’m so hotchpotch at things that I can’t even think straight. When I stare at the blackboard, it looks like the sea does in the dark, and the chalk scribbles look like waves. And when I open my books to study, I see ants crawling about. My eyes, they hurt a lot. I’m so bad that whenever I see someone angry I think it’s because of me. You won’t believe me, but something terrible happened the other day. I was by the pond, trying to count the fish all over again, when I saw them pushing a boy into the water. He was just like me. When the principal called us, it was just him and me. The thing is I’m not good at anything, and I was afraid. When she asked who pushed him, while she glowered at me, he didn’t say a word. I felt bad for him, I really did. Even I would have said it was me. And then he pointed his finger at me. I closed my eyes, I couldn’t breathe… You won’t believe me, even the principal didn’t, when he softly said that it wasn’t me. “The thing is,” he said slowly, “I am not good at anything..the boys and girls, they pick on me. And the teachers, they’re always shouting at me…” I looked at him and realized: it wasn’t just me.
author: Jairaj Singh

title: E C George Sudarshan: The Man Who Loved Physics
text: ​Ennackal Chandy George Sudarshan made one of the greatest scientific discoveries in the 20th century. It wasn’t a machine or a device. It didn’t help make our everyday lives easier. What is this universe? Where did it come from? George’s discovery helped answer some of these very important questions. ​​When George was a boy, he loved​ ​mathematics. Every day, he would walk miles to get to school, from his village in Kerala. His mother, Achamma, taught him how to add and subtract very large numbers. As he grew older, George discovered physics. He realized he loved it as much as maths. Maybe even a little bit more. As a young student at Madras Christian College, George met people studying zoology or botany and told them how physics was the science​ ​of everything. ​The love for physics grew and grew and grew. George wanted to know what the tiniest particles are. Our world is made up of tiny particles called atoms. Atoms are made of even smaller particles, neutrons, protons and electrons. George wanted to know everything about the atom and its nucleus. ​​​As a research student at the​ ​Tata Institute of Fundamental Research,​ ​George met the quantum physicist​ ​Paul A M Dirac. George assisted Dirac in making his lecture notes and greatly impressed him. ​It was also at TIFR that George met the physicist Robert Marshak, who asked George to join him at Rochester University in the United States of America, as his student. There, young George solved one of the biggest mysteries of the atom and its nucleus. ​George worked through the day. He worked through the night. It was lonely and George​ ​was far from home. He researched the work of many scientists. He studied many, many experiments. Until he was confident of his findings. ​Robert reported George’s findings at a small conference in Padua, Italy,in 1957. But very few in the science community got to know about this work. Before they could publish their work in a scientific journal, scientists Richard Feynman and Murray Gell-Mann also came up with the same result by a different method. They published a paper and the whole world came to know of their work. George and Robert’s findings were published only two years later. ​For years, people did not recognize that it was George who had made the first breakthrough. However, later Feynman himself described the theory as “invented by Marshak and Sudarshan and published by Feynman and Gell-Mann.” Everyone realized George’s theory was right. They named his findings ‘vector minus axial vector’ or ‘V-A’ theory, an important step to the complete understanding of the atom and its nucleus. George Sudarshan made many more pathbreaking contributions to various fields of advanced physics like quantum optics and elementary particle physics. He was also first to put forward the idea of particles called Tachyons which can travel faster than light. ​Although George spent a large part of his life in the United States, he never gave up his strong ties with the world of Indian science. He set up the Centre for Theoretical Studies at the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru. He was the Director at the Institute of Mathematical Sciences in Chennai. In 1974, George was honoured with the Padma Bhushan and in 2007, with the Padma Vibhushan. Three years later, he was awarded the Dirac Medal.George was recommended for the Nobel Prize nine times. He died in 2018 at the age of 86. What are atoms made of? At the centre of an atom lies the nucleus. It is made up of protons and neutrons. Surrounding the nucleus is a cloud of electrons. This makes the atom not unlike a tiny solar system, with the nucleus as the sun and the electrons as planets orbiting it. What is the ‘V-A’ theory? The nucleus of the atom sometimes breaks down into smaller nuclei and other particles. This is called decay. This happens according to a rule called the ‘vector minus axial vector’ or ‘V-A’ theory. What is physics? Physics is the study of how everything in the universe behaves. People who study physics are called physicists. Some famous physicists are Isaac Newton, Albert Einstein, Stephen Hawking, C V Raman, Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, Homi Bhabha and George Sudarshan. What can physics tell us about the universe? Physics can tell us everything about the universe. It can tell us how the universe began and how it will end, why planets orbit the sun, how water flows in rivers, how snow is formed and why tsunamis happen.

title: Daddy Makes Masala Omelette
text: On the menu for breakfast today is Daddy’s masala omelette. Packed with protein and bursting with flavour, it's the best way to start the day, I bet! I fetch all the right veggies and spices. After all, I am daddy’s little helper! He waits for the pan to get hot enough and in it adds a dollop of butter. I watch as the chilli and coriander go under the knife’s sharp blade. Sliced, diced and ready to be fried, onion and tomato join the parade. Into a bowl go all the prepped veggies, they’ll soon meet the star of the dish. CRACK, CRACK, OPEN, POUR - 3 fresh eggs I add with a mighty flourish. A teaspoonful of milk goes in next along with freshly ground pepper. Also mixed in is the all-important salt in just the right measure. A hint of turmeric I sprinkle on top with a dash of red chilli powder. WHISK, BEAT, STIR, everything is blended, the bowl’s a stormy sea of colour! Into the hot pan goes the swirling, frothy mixture. HISS! HISS! It squiggles like jelly. With a great big toss, Daddy flips the omelette revealing its golden belly. The aroma in the kitchen tickles my nose, my tummy goes RUMBLE RUMBLE. “Give me my omelette quickly, please!” The hunger makes me mumble and grumble. Bright, sizzling, dazzling and glowing, the omelette looks like sunshine on my plate. Each fluffy bite is a party in my mouth, the dish has turned out really great. “How is the Masala Omelette, kiddo?” asks Daddy, proudly watching me chew. “It’s super-duper tasty, Daddy,” I say. “Let’s now make another one for you!”
author: Niveditha Reddy

title: At Home
text: Coor, coor, cooor... Ammini rubs the sleep out of her eyes as she wakes up to the call of the chembothu nesting in the mango tree. “I didn’t keep my school uniform ready last night,” grumbles Ammini. “Oh, I forgot, I don’t have to go to school.” Achan is making coffee and idlis in the kitchen. Ammini runs downstairs and gives him a good-morning hug. She hopes that the family can go out for a walk today. “The idlis are so good, Achan!” says Ammini. Her four-year-old brother Unni walks into the kitchen. “Kamala cheriyamma?” he calls out, sleepily. Ammini and Unni’s aunt is his favourite playmate. “She is still at the hospital, Unni. She said that she would come home as soon as the sick people get better,” says Achan. Unni’s face crumples. Kamala cheriyamma is a nurse, and has not come home for weeks now. “Come, Unni. Let’s see the flowers that have bloomed in the garden,” says Ammini. “Look, there is the arali. See the yellow in the middle? The honeybees will come to carry that away. And look at the techi, see the big bunches? My teacher says it is called jungle flame in English.” “Hello!” “Abu uncle, I like your mask,” Ammini says. Abu uncle salutes, and asks, “What are both of you doing?” “Looking at the flowers. Where is the police car?” Ammini asks. “Still asleep after screaming with her siren all night long. Stay at home, otherwise she will wake up and say, weeeewoooweeeewooo,” says Abu uncle. Abu uncle waves and walks towards his mother Zeenat aunty’s house. It is almost time for Eid. Every year, Zeenat aunty makes delicious biryani and sheer korma. Will they be able to go for the feast this year, Ammini wonders. “Ammini, time for school,” Amma says. “Good morning, Maya teacher!” Ammini’s classmates are waving at each other from the tiny squares on the laptop. School is so different now. Ammini’s best friend Nina is absent today. She shares the computer with her big brother, so she attends school twice a week. Ammini misses Nina, but she misses school even more. She misses the bumpy rides to school in Gigi chettan’s rickshaw. She misses splashing in the puddles on the playground with Nina. She misses whispering and exchanging tiffin boxes at lunchtime. And her favourite set of colour pencils is still in school. When will she ever get it back? School ends at lunchtime. “Chechi, can we go to the playground?” Unni asks Ammini. Ammini looks at Amma, who shakes her head. “Not today, Unni. But we can play the volcano lava game Amma showed us!” Ammini says. Ammini and Unni race through the house gathering up cushions, pillows and blankets. They take their toy animals and arrange them around the room. “Come on, Unni, we have to rescue the animals. And remember, the floor is lava!” “That was so much fun!” Ammini says as she and Unni lie on the blanket with their toys. “Yes, but I miss the slides and swings and grass, chechi.” “Me too,” Ammini says. “I also miss the beach and the cotton candy and the balloons and going to Ammumma and Appoopan.” They imagine going for walks, running in the playground, hugging their grandparents tight. The sun is an orange marble now. “Time for a walk, maybe,” Ammini thinks. It has been a while since she last put on her shoes. Amma and Achan are sitting on the sofa, listening to music. Ammini takes Unni’s hand and they run to squeeze in between Amma and Achan. “I hope we can go for a walk soon or to the beach. But until then, I’m glad that I can spend so much time with Unni, Achan and Amma,” Ammini thinks.
author: Shweta Ganesh Kumar

title: Our Beautiful World
text: We live in a beautiful world. A world filled with wonders. A world of soaring mountains, of deep oceans. A world teeming with life and joy. It is a world we call home. Here, we reign supreme. We design new technological miracles, we shoot for the stars, we build amazing things. We study the world, the universe. We try to make our lives easier, and easier and easier with new gadgets, that aim to make everything better. Easier, yes. But is it better? Our home is paying a terrible price. We’re changing the Earth, killing birds and animals with whom we share this planet, endangering our fellow humans. The world is becoming a desert. Oceans are rising, glaciers are melting, crops are failing. The heat is rising. There is a monster that haunts Earth. It is called… climate change. Humans are its creator. This is the story of how we made it. It is a story of how we betrayed our home, Earth. About 12,000 years ago, the Earth entered a new geological epoch called the Holocene. It was paradise. This is when the gigantic sheets of ice that covered much of the northern hemisphere and large parts of the southern hemisphere retreated towards the north and south poles, and the world entered a new era of plenty. New forests grew, and life flourished. The world’s climate became warmer and then stabilised. Ever since then, for about 11,000 years, the Earth’s climate has been stable and calm. Humans have been around for about 2,00,000 years. But before the Holocene, we never had it this good. In the past 11,000 years, we have thrived. We discovered agriculture, we settled down in villages and towns, we created art, built grand civilizations. The pyramids of Giza, the cities of the Indus Valley Civilization, the Mauryan Empire and the Roman Empire - all happened during the Holocene. This was all possible because of widespread agriculture and trade. We grew crops, we made things, we exchanged them with each other. We grew prosperous. Our ancestors started clearing forests to grow more crops and, slowly, their footprint expanded. Even then, much of Europe, North America and South Asia were covered in thick forests. It all happened very slowly, over thousands of years. The effect of human beings on the environment was still very small. The Earth still had enough resources to replenish what was depleted. But as the centuries went by, we started using up the Earth’s resources faster and faster. By around 500 years ago, Europe’s ancient forests were mostly gone, and even in other parts of the world, forests were in retreat. Humans have always used the Earth’s resources, be it trees, minerals like iron, or animals for domestication and food. We have always wanted the planet to give us more. Then, about 250 years ago, something happened. The Industrial Age, the age of machines, began. Until then, we had mostly used handheld tools for work. As a result, there was only so much damage we could do. But with machines, we could do anything. For the first time, we started using machines, like the power loom and the steam engine, to mass produce goods for trade. We burned fossil fuels like coal and oil to power machines to do our work for us. Every aspect of our lives today comes from the Industrial Revolution. Cars, planes, mobile phones, space flight, computers, it all began 250 years ago. But while this lit the fire of human progress, it also unleashed its dark shadow: climate change. The Earth is very old. Over four billion years old. Life on Earth began more than three billion years ago. How do we know? Because that is when the oldest fossils are from. What are fossils? The planet has been home to a dizzying variety of plants and animals. All trees and creatures, including humans, are primarily made of carbon. As they die, and as continents shift, their remains go back into the earth, where they lie. Over thousands of years they return to forms of carbon: coal, gas, oil. This is how the Earth’s fossil deposits are created. When we started digging up the coal and oil to burn them and power our machines, we gave rise to fossil fuels. That has been the basis of our modern prosperity. For nearly everything we do, we burn coal and oil. We dig into the bowels of the earth, we mine the coal, we extract the petroleum, we burn it. We live our lives. But we have dug so much and burnt so much, that we have upset the balance of the Holocene. The more coal and oil we burn, the more carbon dioxide we release. This gets stored in the atmosphere. The carbon dioxide traps the sun’s heat. And the world grows hotter. The world is becoming an oven, and the heat is changing the climate. The Earth is slowly becoming unlivable. It is now 1.2 degrees celsius hotter than two hundred years ago. If we continue like this, by 2050, the world will be 2.4 degrees celsius hotter. If that happens then the sea level will rise. Cities like Mumbai and Kolkata might be deserted. Himalayan glaciers will start vanishing, rivers like the Ganga and Brahmaputra will be flooding all the time. And when the glaciers vanish, the rivers will dry up. Heatwaves will make it impossible to go out during the day. Even indoors, people will suffer. Supercyclones will rise out of the sea and hit India every year. Drinking water will be harder and harder to get. The Arctic Circle and Greenland will lose all their ice. Forests will burn every year. From the deepest jungles to the highest mountains, animals will starve. Epidemics and pandemics like COVID-19 might become more common. It is a scary future for the whole world. Yet, there is hope. We don’t need to keep burning coal and oil. In fact, the whole world can stop burning fossil fuels by 2050. No fossil fuels. No extra carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. No more heat. Humans are smart, and we have already built technologies which can draw energy from the sun, wind and water. If every country around the world says NO to fossil fuels, we can defeat the climate change monster. We live in a beautiful world. We can preserve this beautiful Earth, filled with wonders. A world of soaring mountains, of deep oceans. A world teeming with life and joy. It is a world we call home.
author: Bibek Bhattacharya

title: Aarna and Iris' Big Task
text: ​Aarna and Iris had been given a big task! The task of showing Norgay, the new student, around. “Make him feel welcome,” Rai Guruama, their class teacher, said in her stern voice. ​As soon as the morning bell rang, they went up to Norgay, and invited him to the next class. ​In Dharma class, Lopen La brought out a big singing bowl. “Let’s get ready for meditation,” he said. Lopen La tapped the bowl with a wooden mallet. There was a loud CLANG. He moved the stick along the rim of the bowl. A humming sound filled the room — like many bees buzzing. Aarna felt the vibration on her skin. She peered at Norgay and saw him smiling at the singing bowl. C L A N N N N G G ​Soon it was time for lunch. Aarna and Iris took Norgay to the canteen. “What do you think we have for lunch?” Norgay asked. Aarna stopped and sniffed. It was a familiar aroma of ginger and garlic and all kinds of spices she didn’t know the names of. “It smells like my Mam’s kitchen when she makes chicken curry!” she said excitedly. ​Indeed, there was fluffy white rice and soft and juicy chicken curry. They gobbled up the food, smacking their lips and licking their fingers. Even Norgay! ​After lunch, Aarna and Iris went out to play. Norgay quietly followed them. They picked up big globs of mud and squished them between their fingers. They let the soft and slimy mud slide down their hands and run inside their sleeves. It made Norgay laugh. “I can teach you how to make a castle,” he said softly. So they made castles, laddoos and mud pies together. ​Just then, it started to drizzle! “Let’s taste the rain,” Norgay suggested, feeling the droplets hitting his skin. He opened his mouth, stuck his tongue out and let the raindrops fall. His friends did the same. “It tastes like tap water,” said Iris. “It tastes like nothing!” said Norgay. Aarna thought it tasted sweet, just like the water from the stream that came down the mountains. The bell rang for science class. But as they ran back to their classroom… ​A thick fog was rolling up the hill. A blanket of white soon covered everything, even the mighty Kanchenjunga. It was hard to sense anything around them. Aarna, Iris and Norgay huddled closer together and slowly made their way back through the dense fog, laughing and talking. Their new friend was so much fun and they couldn’t wait for another day of adventures with him. OUR SENSES What do you think allows us to experience a spicy chicken curry, squishy mud, and everything else around us? Humans have sense organs that help us see, smell, hear, taste and touch. Not everyone experiences the world in the same way. Nevertheless, we all use our senses to learn about and navigate the world around us. Imagine you are playing with your friends just like Aarna, Norgay and Iris. Describe your experience with your friends using sensory words. Sensory words describe how we smell, see, hear, taste or feel something. Can you spot the sensory words in this story?

title: Mona Goes on a Train
text: I'm Mona. I was waiting at the railway station with my parents to board a train. Many travelers or passengers were walking around with their luggage in their hands. The porters carried the big luggage of the passengers like suitcases on their heads. The passengers will later pay the porters for carrying their things inside the train. We got inside the second class compartment on the train. I sat near the window and opened a book to read. My mom said, “While travelling by train, you should not miss the moving scenery you can see through the window.” So, I peeped outside the window. I saw trees, mountains, paddy fields, and cows moving fastly. The train also ran over a bridge over a river. The train also ran into a tunnel inside a mountain. It became dark inside the train at that time. Then, I sat down. My father started telling stories of how they once pulled the emergency chain inside the train when a passenger missed boarding the train at a stop. The passenger had gone to buy biscuits and water bottles and missed the train when it started. Luckily, no such incident happened this time. Then, my mom shared stories of how she shared food items with fellow passengers during her travels. Now, our stop was going to come and we carried our bags and waited near the footboard. We will get down on the platform once the train stops. It was a fun-filled journey.

text: Asha told her mom, “Mummy. My teacher has asked us to write an essay about mothers. I was wondering what to write.” Her mom told, “Watch me today when I do all the work at home. title: A Tree's Heart
text: To those who stop to look, trees tell stories. Touch the trunk, listen to the rustling leaves, and lie down under the tree to watch the branches sway. There are stories hidden everywhere — In the fold of a leaf. In the soft petal on which a beetle slips. In the fruit that a bird bites into. In the bark where a mantis hides in plain sight. But leaves fall. Flowers turn into fruit. Fruit is eaten. Bark peels away. What lives on, is the trunk of the tree. And in the centre of the trunk, near the heartwood, is where trees store their memories. Memories of — A cold winter 36 years ago A harsh summer 62 years ago A thunderstorm 108 years ago A drought 116 years ago A forest fire 246 years ago Trees are the original historians. By storing memories around their heartwood, they give us a glimpse of events of the past, to a time before there were human historians. To understand these stories, it is essential to know the language of trees — a language that scientists have been working to understand. Like all living beings, trees are made up of cells. Plant cells have a short life and grow constantly. This is why leaves grow and fall and new ones grow in turn. This way, trees continue to grow in height or girth as long as they are alive. Trees live longer than most other living beings! A Bristlecone Pine tree in the White Mountains, USA, has been growing for about 4,850 years. An Alerce tree in the Andes Mountains, Chile, is over 3,600 years old. A Giant Sequoia tree in Sequoia National Park, USA, is 2,700 years old. A Sacred Fig tree in Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka, is the oldest known human-planted tree, at 2,300 years. The only way to tell the age of a tree is to peek into the trunk. Heartwood: Inactive cells that provide structural support to the tree Sapwood: Soft wood with tissues that transport nutrients and water Cambium: The active growing layer of the tree Bark: The hard outer layer that protects the tree Every year, new wood cells grow in the cambium layer. In regions where there are distinct seasons — spring, summer and winter — the cells are light during spring, and darker during summer. In winter, the cells don’t grow at all. The cells grow in circles, creating a pattern of contrasting rings. The oldest rings are in the centre, and the newest rings are outside, close to the bark. Each ring could mark the passage of a year. In tropical regions, like most of India, where there is rain almost all through the year, tree rings don’t have distinct patterns, making it difficult to calculate age. With the right temperature and enough rainfall, the tree stays healthy and grows fast, creating a wide ring. When the summer is too hot, or if there is a drought, tree growth slows down, creating narrow rings. By drilling an increment borer to the heartwood, and extracting a thin long piece of wood, scientists are able to determine the age of a tree. They count the annual rings and read the patterns to understand how old the tree is and how many summers it has lived. Dendrochronology is the study of tree rings to determine the age of a tree. All the trees in a forest will have similar tree ring patterns. So, studying tree rings across a forest helps to understand what an entire landscape has experienced. A mass outbreak of insects that ate up all the leaves or bored into trunks of all trees will cause identical scars in tree rings. Tree rings tell the story of weather conditions and climate change. Climate change is a change in the weather conditions of a particular region, such as temperature and rainfall, over a long period of time. Studying changes in tree ring patterns of old trees over a long time gives an insight into how climate change is affecting the ecosystem. This is called dendroclimatology. When trees in dry, cold climates face a very warm summer, or when trees in warmer climates face a very cold winter, the patterns of tree rings become irregular. Bristlecone Pines have had wider growth rings in the last 60 years than they did in the previous 3,500 years. In Sikkim, India, trees are losing more water through their leaves in summers, affecting their growth. Alpine trees could now be growing higher up than usual in the Tibetan plateau, in search of colder weather. Trees are hardy and many survive forest fires. However, fires cause stress to a tree and this is seen in damaged barks, and scars in the tree rings. Giant Sequoia trees witnessed frequent forest fires before the 19th century, but the fires did not destroy the forest. Now, the fires occur less often, but are more intense and destroy entire forests. Most recorded weather data exists only from the early 19th century. Building a record of past climates helps scientists predict what will happen in the future — like how often forest fires will arise in a region, at what temperature ranges droughts occur, and how heavy rainfall will be. Sadly, humans have interfered a lot with the natural world. Weather calamities are occurring more often, and more fiercely. Historical climate records cannot be relied upon for accurate predictions anymore. But the solutions to all these problems continue to lie with trees — they give us a way to learn from the past and a path ahead to look into the future. Trees are keepers of memories of the planet’s ecology and help trace human activity. They store an entire era in a few wood cells. Every layer of the tree’s trunk unravels a chapter in the history of the Earth.
author: Radha Rangarajan

title: Three Paper Children
text: Once upon a time there were three paper children. They were 2 boys and a girl. They were called Antonio, Jose and Carmen. They were four years old. They lived in Spain, in a city called Valencia. They were born from a single piece of paper so they did not have parents. But very often, a boy (called Manuel), who lived in their house, played with them. They always wore brightly coloured clothes, made of paper. The three children were very close and loved each other very much. They were always together as they didn't have any friends, because the children their age at school teased them. But they had fun anyway. They had tiny little brains, so they weren't very good at studying, so their classmates teased them about this as well. The first child was Jose. He wore a black and white jumper. His hair was black and white too. He always played with Manuel and they had so much fun together. That is how he became his favourite toy. While Manuel slept, he always took his boat to the bathroom sink. But after a while he got bored as he couldn't talk to other paper children, like him. He couldn't play with other children, like him. He wanted to have someone that he could share his adventures with. He felt very lonely and he didn't know what to do. He spent the days crying inconsolably in his bed. He didn't want to do anything. He just wanted to cry. But one day he had an idea. He could make another paper child, with the paper that the boy kept in his desk. So he took Manuel's paper and scissors. He began cutting the paper to make his new friend. After a few attempts, he managed it! He had made a girl. She was a redhead and she had long, smooth hair. Her T-shirt was red too. Jose called her Carmen. Finally he had someone to play with, and he felt so happy. The girl was very nice. Carmen liked horses and she wanted one of her own. So they made a horse. They could ride it all over the house and outside. They dreamed of moving to Madrid and making a band. But they needed three people, and there were only two of them. So they decided to make another paper child. They were happy and excited, and they went to get the scissors and everything else they needed... but there was no paper. They looked all over the house but they couldn't find any. The children were so upset and they cried, because their dream was out of reach. But one day, when they were riding their horse in the park, they saw a paper ball on the ground. They could not believe their eyes... they could make their new friend! They picked it up. It was quite wet. They waited a few days, and after a few days the paper had dried. Finally, they could make their new friend. When they had made him, they called him Antonio. He had brown, curly, very long hair and wore a red T-shirt. So they decided to move to Madrid together. The following week, they left the house, climbed on their horse and arrived in Madrid a month later. The three paper children formed a band in Madrid and called it "Paper Children". They were very successful and got very rich, singing for the rest of their childhood. They've had their fun, this tale is done.
author: Catherine Davis

title: Noisy!
text: Lucas were very excited to have a new baby brother. But since Mum got home with the baby, Lucia and Lucas were not very happy. They were not allowed to make any noise while the baby was sleeping. If they want to run, play or shout, they have to go outside. Playing outside can be fun. But sometimes you can not play outside. Playing inside, without making a noise was VERY hard. One day the story that they were reading was so funny, that they burst out laughing. Oh no! The baby was sleeping! When they realised, it was already too late. The baby woke up, crying. Mum told them to play outside. The baby needed silence. Lucia was unhappy. Lucas tried to cheer her up. He told her that they could have fun outside, as they could make as much noise as they liked. After playing outside with a ball for a while, Lucia and Lucas were happy again. Lucas kicked the ball.... GOAL! The ball went from one end of the garden to the other.... CRASH! Oh no! The baby woke up! The baby started to cry so loudly, that it almost lifted the roof off the house! As the baby was still crying so loudly, Lucia and Lucas ran into the house. Where is Mum? Lucia sang to the baby, but the baby kept crying. Lucas pulled funny faces and did crazy dances, but the baby kept crying. Why are babies so noisy? How can we make the baby be quiet? Lucas and Lucia started to cry as well. Then Mum came back. Mum took the baby and calmed him. Mum sang a song. The baby, Lucia and Lucas stopped crying. The whole house was calm and quiet. Lucia and Lucas understood that the baby can also be noisy. They learned that noise is not always fun, and that you can be happy and quiet at the same time. Especially when the baby is sleeping.
author: Catherine Davis

title: Facts about animals
text: Facts about elephant 1. Elephants are the largest living land animal. 2. Elephants are afraid of bees. 3. Elephants spend 16 hours per day eating. 4. There are two types of elephants found in the world. 5. Elephants can communicate with each other over far distances. Facts about Giraffes 1. Giraffes are the tallest mammals on Earth. 2. Giraffes only need to drink once every few days. 3. They can run as fast as 35 miles an hour over short distances. 4. Both male and female giraffes have two distinct, hair-covered horns called ossicones. 5. A giraffe’s spots are much like human fingerprints. Facts about lion 1. LIONS DON'T NEED TO DRINK EVERYDAY, BUT THEY DO NEED TO EAT. 2. FEMALE LIONS (LIONESSES) DO MOST OF THE HUNTING. 3. LIONS ARE SUPERB HUNTERS. 4. LIONS COMMUNICATE IN MANY WAYS. 5. LIONS ARE THE SECOND LARGEST CAT ON EARTH. Facts about tiger 1. Tigers are the largest amongst other wild cats. 2. Tigers are nocturnal animals. 3. Tigers love to swim and play in the water. 4. Tigers live for about 25 years. 5. A group of Tigers are called an ambush or streak. Facts about cheetah 1. Cheetahs Are the World's Fastest Land Mammal. 2. The name ‘cheetah’ comes from Sanskrit word ‘variegated’. 3. A normal chase speed for a cheetah is 60-65 miles per hour. 4. During a chase, they can run up to 1,600 feet in short bursts. 5. The Latin name for the cheetah is Acinonyx jubatus. Facts about monkeys 1. There are currently 264 known monkey species. 2. Monkeys can be divided into two groups, Old World monkeys that live in Africa and Asia, and New World monkeys that live in South America. 3. Different monkey species eat a variety of foods, such as fruit, insects, flowers, leaves and reptiles. 4. Spider monkeys get their name because of their long arms, legs and tail. 5. some monkeys live on the ground, while others live in trees. Facts about pig 1. Pigs are smart!. 2. Pigs have excellent memories. 3. In their natural state, pigs are very clean animals. 4. Pigs like to get massages, enjoy scratching themselves on trees, relaxing while listening to music, and playing with enrichment toys. 5. Newborn piglets learn to respond to their mothers’ voices, and mother pigs communicate with their babies through grunts while nursing. Facts about cow 1. Cows Originated in Turkey.. 2. Female Cattle Are Called Cows, and Male Cattle Are Called Bulls. 3. They Are Highly Social Animals. 4. Cows Are Good Swimmers 5. Cows Don't Sleep Very Much. Facts about Yak 1. Yaks are friendly to people they know. 2. There Are 2 Different Yak Species. 3. Wild Yaks Were Domesticated Around 5,000 Years Ago. 4. Yak Milk May Be a Superfood. 5. Yaks Can Handle Temperatures as Low as Minus 40 Degrees. Facts about Zebra 1. THERE ARE THREE SPECIES OF ZEBRA. 2. ZEBRAS ARE WILD ANIMALS THAT CANNOT BE DOMESTICATED. 3. A GROUP OF ZEBRAS IS CALLED A ‘DAZZLE’. 4. ZEBRAS CAN TRAVEL LONG DISTANCES 5. ZEBRAS ARE BLACK ANIMALS WITH WHITE STRIPES. Facts about snake 1. In the world of snakes, female King Cobra (Ophiophagus hannah) is the only snake that builds nest. 2. Snakes don't have eyelids. 3. Snakes have internal ears but not external ones. 4. Snakes can't bite food so have to swallow it whole.
author: yazhini pradeep
illustrator: Adrija Ghosh; Ethan Thomas  Bishu; Horn Samon; Isaac  Okwir; Marleen  Visser; Nitya Mishra; Preyanka Tikku; Rob Owen; Wambi Cornelius; Wiehan de Jager; Yihenew  Worku
