title: Amyra Turns 10
text: Amyra sat cross-legged on her bed, staring out of the window. The late afternoon sun cast a warm, golden glow over the streets, but her thoughts were far from bright. She had been counting down the days to her 10th birthday for months, imagining the laughter, the music, and the joy of having all her friends over for a grand celebration. But now, just a week away from the big day, her excitement had dwindled. "It's not fair, Amma," she sighed, her voice heavy with disappointment. "Why do exams always have to happen during my birthday?" Her mother closed the book and set it aside. "You know, sweetie, birthdays aren't just about the party or the noise. Sometimes, they’re about something more special." Amyra looked puzzled. "More special than cake and friends?" Her mother smiled gently. "Yes, much more special. Why don't you try thinking about it differently this year?" Amyra frowned, clearly not convinced, but she knew better than to argue further. Instead, she grabbed her schoolbooks, flipping through the pages half-heartedly. Her mind wasn’t on the math problems in front of her; it was on her birthday - her double-digit birthday - and how it would be ruined. The next day at school, during the lunch break, Amyra and her eternal partner in celebration and crime, Saanvi, sat under their favourite tree in the playground, picking at their food. “I can’t believe your birthday’s during exams,” Saanvi said, her voice full of sympathy. “It’s so unlucky.” “I know,” Amyra grumbled, stabbing her sandwich with unnecessary force. “I was going to have the best party. You, me, everyone from class… now all I get is a bunch of textbooks.” Saanvi thought for a moment before her face brightened. “Hey, what if you do something small? Like just you and me after exams? We could still celebrate.” Amyra looked at her friend and smiled. Saanvi always had a way of making her feel better. “Yeah, maybe that could work.” As the bell rang, signalling the end of lunch, the two girls packed up their things and walked back to class. But as they passed the school gate, Amyra noticed a girl about her age standing just outside. Her clothes were faded, the blue of her kurta washed out to a pale hue, and the edges of her dupatta frayed from use. In her hand, she held a small basket of wilting marigolds and jasmine buds, their petals slightly browned from the heat. The girl’s eyes met Amyra’s for a fleeting moment before she shyly looked away. Amyra slowed her pace, curiosity piqued. “Who’s that?” she asked Saanvi. “Oh, that’s Maya. I’ve seen her around. I think she sells flowers.” Amyra nodded but didn’t say anything more. Something about the girl’s presence lingered in her mind. The week passed by slowly, and as her birthday approached, Amyra’s mood was still blue. On the morning of her birthday, she sat at the breakfast table, poking at her dosa. “Happy birthday, Amyra!” her father said cheerfully as he handed her a small gift. “Double digits now!” “Thanks, Papa,” Amyra mumbled, unwrapping the present to find a beautiful journal. Its cover was a vibrant blue with gold stars scattered across it. “I thought you could write down all your thoughts and dreams in here,” her father said, smiling. Amyra managed a small smile. “It’s lovely. Thank you.” But as much as she appreciated the gift, she couldn’t shake off the disappointment inside. After breakfast, she spent the rest of the morning studying for her exams, her mind wandering to what could have been. Later that afternoon, when her parents surprised her with a small cake, Amyra’s spirits lifted a little. They sang the quintessential birthday song, and she blew out the candles, but there was no crowd of friends, no party games, and no loud laughter filling the house. “I wish Saanvi were here,” Amyra said softly as she cut a slice of cake. “Why don’t we take a walk outside?” her mother suggested. “It’s a lovely day, and it might make you feel better.” Reluctantly, Amyra agreed, and soon they were walking through the narrow lanes of their neighbourhood. The air was warm, carrying the tempting aroma of biryani from the nearby Paradise outlet. As they passed a street vendor frying mirchi bhajjis, the cacophony of its sizzling sound and the usual honking of autos filled Amyra with comforting energy. Ambling along, they had almost reached the main gate of her school, when Amyra saw Maya again, standing in her usual spot with the basket of flowers. Amyra walked over to her instinctively, holding out a piece of cake. “Hi, I’m Amyra. It’s my birthday today. Would you like some cake?” Maya looked surprised, but her face broke into a shy smile. “Thank you,” she said in a tender voice, taking the slice. “Happy birthday.” As Maya ate the cake, Amyra noticed the small notebook tucked under her arm. It was old and worn, but there were neat handwriting marks on the visible pages. “Do you go to school?” Amyra asked, curious. Maya shook her head. “I used to, but we don’t have enough money for it anymore. I help my mother sell flowers now.” Amyra’s heart sank. She couldn’t imagine not being able to go to school. “But you like to study?” Maya nodded. “I love it. My favourite subject is English.” Amyra’s eyes lit up. “Really? Mine too! Can you speak English?” “A little,” Maya replied, looking embarrassed. “I’ve learned from my old school books.” “That’s amazing!” Amyra exclaimed, impressed. “But why don’t you go to school now?” Maya shrugged. “We don’t have the money for it. My father passed away last year, and it’s just mom and me now. We barely make enough to eat.” Amyra felt a lump in her throat. She had never thought about what it would be like not to have all the things she took for granted - school, food, birthday parties. She looked at Maya, who seemed so calm despite everything, and a thought struck her. “I have an idea,” Amyra said excitedly. “Wait here!” She ran back to her parents, who had been watching the interaction from a distance. “Mumma, Papa, I know what I want for my birthday!” Her parents exchanged amused glances. “And what’s that, dear?” her father asked. “I want to help Maya go back to school,” Amyra declared, her voice filled with determination and delight. “Can we sponsor her education? It would be the best birthday gift ever.” Her mother’s eyes narrowed, trying to gauge the seriousness of her request. Her father placed a hand on her shoulder. “Are you sure, Amyra?” Amyra nodded vigorously. “This is what I want, I am sure Papa. Please, can we help her?” There was a pause as she took in the moment, and then she noticed her parents beaming with pride. “Of course,” her mother said. “It’s a beautiful idea.” Amyra’s heart swelled with joy. She ran back to Maya, her face glowing with excitement. “Maya, we’re going to help you go back to school!” Maya’s eyes widened in disbelief. “Really? But... but how?” “My parents will sponsor your education,” Amyra explained, unable to contain her happiness. “You’ll be able to study again, just like you wanted!” Maya hesitated, her forehead creasing slightly as she took a step back. She clutched her dupatta, unsure if she could trust this sudden offer from a stranger. The idea of someone stepping in to help seemed almost too good to be true. But then, as she looked into Amyra's eyes, filled with genuine excitement and kindness, the doubt slowly melted away. Tears welled up in Maya’s eyes, and she hugged Amyra tightly. “Thank you. Thank you so much.” As they walked home that evening, Amyra felt a sense of peace and fulfilment, the kind she had never experienced before. Her special milestone birthday hadn’t been filled with parties or loud celebrations, but it had turned out to be the most meaningful one yet. She realized that sometimes, the best celebrations weren’t about the noise or the fun. Sometimes, they were about making a difference in someone else’s life. Her parents had always spoken to her about her privileges, and she was glad she had used them for the right cause when it mattered. She opened her new journal later that night, and she wrote her first entry. "The best birthday ever wasn’t the one with the biggest party, but the one where I made a new friend and gave her the chance to dream again."
author: Anupama Dalmia

title: Sam's Christmas Present
text: She smiled and said, “It is hidden in a secret place, Sam.” Sam stuck his tongue out and went in search of his father. “Daddy, where is my Christmas present?” asked Sam. “It is hidden in a secret place, Sam,” his father replied smiling. “I know what to do!” Sam said. “I will go gift hunting!” He looked behind his father’s desk. And he found... a gift box wrapped in red paper. “But this is for aunt Juju,” said Sam reading the tag. So, he slipped into his parents' room. And he found... a gift box wrapped in gold paper. “For uncle Alfie,” Sam read aloud from the tag. Then he opened his mother’s cupboard. And he found... a gift box wrapped in purple paper. ‘For our daughter Sophie’ was written on the tag. ﻿ Sam went back to his room and sat on the floor feeling very sad. He had badly wanted to find his present! And then he saw a gift box wrapped in silver paper under his bed! “This is for me!” he shouted, reading the tag. Sam shook the box. He turned it around in his hands. What was inside? Oh, what could it be? Did he open it or leave it in the secret place? Are you curious to know what curious Sam did with his gift? He put it back under the bed and decided to wait for Christmas.
author: Devika Mathur

title: The Adventures of Wiggly The Worm
text: In a lush green garden, lived a little worm named Wiggly. Now, Wiggly wasn’t like the other worms. While most worms liked to stay underground, minding their own business and wriggling around in the soil, Wiggly was curious. He wanted to see the world above the ground. One sunny morning, Wiggly poked his head out of the dirt and looked around. The world was HUGE! There were colorful flowers swaying in the breeze, buzzing bees darting around, and even a butterfly fluttering by. Wiggly had never seen anything like it! He was so excited, he wiggled with joy and wobbled over to a nearby flower. Hello, flower!” Wiggly said, with a little wriggle of his tail. The flower, of course, didn’t reply. But that didn’t stop Wiggly. He was determined to make some new friends. He wriggled over to the bees. “Hello, buzzing bee!” he said. The bee paused for a second, buzzing a little slower. “Hey, Wiggly! You sure are brave to be up here. We bees love the flowers, but it’s nice to see someone new. Wiggly felt proud. He was making friends! But then, a big shadow passed over him. Wiggly looked up, and there above him, was a large bird! The bird looked down and said, “Ooooh, a tasty little worm. Maybe I’ll have you for lunch.” Wiggly’s heart raced. But instead of running away, he took a deep breath and said, “I’m too wiggly to catch! You’ll never catch me!” With that, Wiggly wriggled faster than he ever had before, zipping around and darting through the grass. The bird was so surprised by how quickly Wiggly moved, it gave up and flew away. Wiggly let out a sigh of relief. "Phew! That was close!" After that adventure, Wiggly decided that maybe he wasn’t quite ready to explore the whole world above the ground just yet. He wriggled back into the soil, where it was safe and cozy. After that adventure, Wiggly decided that maybe he wasn’t quite ready to explore the whole world above the ground just yet. He wriggled back into the soil, where it was safe and cozy. Moral of the story: Even when you're small, you can do big things. Believe in yourself and be brave enough to try something new!
author: POORVI NARAYAN

title: Bheema & Golu by Swati Kakodkar
text: Once upon a time in a beautiful forest there lived an elephant named Bheema. Bheema, and all the animals lived peacefully. One day a giant came into the forest. As he was huge, all the animals were afraid of him. Bheema said – “I know he is a giant. Just because he is huge, we need not worry. Let us try to talk to him.” Bheema walked to the place in the forest where the giant lived. “Hello!” said Bheema in a friendly voice. “Hello,” greeted the giant, but not in a friendly manner. Still, Bheema continued – “My name is Bheema. I live here with my many friends. May I know your name?” Now, the giant smiled a little and replied – “I am Golu. As you can see, I am a giant. Why have you come here? No one likes to be with a giant." “You are new to the forest. I just came to make sure you are comfortable here,” replied Bheema. Hearing this, Golu smiled a little more. “That is very kind of you. Most animals fear me. That is why I do not have any friends,” said Golu. “From tomorrow, I shall take you along with me. I am sure my friends will be happy to meet you,” said Bheema. The next day Golu went with Bheema and met his friends. In the next few days, the animals realized that Golu was kind-hearted. He was also fun to be with. From then on, Golu was no longer feared. He became everyone’s friend. They all called him – Golu, the gentle giant!

title: The Ant and the Dove Inspiring Kids Story About Good Deeds
text: The Story Begins: A Thirsty Ant in Trouble Once upon a time, a very thirsty ant went to a river for a drink. While quenching his thirst, he lost his balance and fell into the rushing water. Frightened and helpless, the ant cried out, “Help!” but no one could hear him. A Dove Comes to the Rescue 🕊️🌿 Nearby, a dove perched on a tree saw the ant struggling in the water. Recognizing the ant’s distress, the dove quickly plucked a leaf from the tree and dropped it into the river. The ant climbed onto the leaf, saving himself from the strong current. Filled with gratitude, he thanked the dove for her kindness. The Ant Saves the Dove 🐜🕊️🎯 A few days later, the roles reversed. The dove sat peacefully on a tree branch, unaware of an approaching danger. A hunter, aiming his arrow at the dove, prepared to shoot. The ant, noticing the threat, acted quickly. He bit the hunter’s leg, causing him to cry out in pain. Distracted, the hunter missed his target, and the dove flew away to safety. A Friendship Forever 🤝❤️ The dove, realizing what had happened, thanked the ant for saving her life. From that moment, the ant and the dove became lifelong friends. Moral of the Story 🌟✨ One good deed deserves another. This beautiful story teaches children the importance of helping others and how kindness often comes full circle.

title: Nilu and Zubeida
text: It is their last meeting of the season. Has Nilu left without meeting her Zubi? How could she do that! Zubi pulls out the red ribbon from her braid and waves it in the air, again and again. Her neck hurts from looking up at the sky. But the sky is empty. Oh it’s blue, but without the brilliant blue of her Nilu. With heavy steps, Zubi walks towards the mela. Yellow jalebis, crisp imarti, new golgappa flavours, mouth-watering rabdi and kulfi, and Nilu’s absolute favourite—corn, and, of course, popcorn for Zubi! They had planned to gobble it all. Then they would play the new, melodious flute and hum together tons of tunes. But now what? The silly-billy has left her alone! Zubi’s tears are bitter with rage and she’s lost all taste for sweets. The mela is bursting with colours—ruby red, oh-so-bright orange, blackest black, shimmering golden yellow. What’s missing is a brilliant blue to tease all the other colours. The Giant Wheel is turning. Zubi’s stomach is churning, with worry. Nilu is her best friend, so why hasn’t she come? Is she anxious about going away? Did Nilu’s uncle stop her from making friends with humans? Or did a hunter… oh no! Zubi gets off the Giant Wheel and runs. She wraps corn in a leaf and buys two red lac bangles. A bangle for her and a bangle for Nilu. The semal tree is just ahead, quiet and lonely. The frogs are croaking merrily in the stream, “Finally, the blue-winged nuisances have scooted!” Under the semal, she digs a small hole and buries one bangle. The other bangle she leaves by the river. “Two friends never love each other equally. One loves more, the other less. I love more, Nilu loves less. I don’t want such a selfish friend!” Zubi curses them. She stuffs all the corn into her mouth and then spits out half. At home, Dadi asks, “Did you eat something at the mela, Zubeida?” Zubi wipes her tears, rubs her nose and darts straight into her room. She flies, like Nilu, and falls on her bed, so no one can see her tears and her swollen face. The pillow turns into a lake of Zubi’s tears. She lifts her nose. Nilu is sitting at the window! She is holding something red in her beak. She has come for Zubi. Zubi leaps, Nilu flies! The red ribbon in her mouth, Nilu chases Zubi for one last game. In the pale blue sky, a brilliant blue, a long dangling line of such a red hue, and on the ground, laughing, Zubi yoo-hoo. Zubi jumps and flies and bounces! She doesn’t let go of the ribbon. They fly over villages, eat wild berries, bop dogs on their heads, scatter the hay from haystacks, chase grasshoppers, and stitch some clouds together. Zubi freezes. The blue kite becomes small. She pulls in the string and rolls it up, but the kite has its own mind… Who knows, maybe Nilu will come again next year to celebrate the summer holidays with Zubi?
author: Salil  Chaturvedi

title: Kadogoo Changed His Life
text: Last year, I came last in my class. It felt terrible, and I could see my classmates whispering and laughing at me. Some of them even said, “ Kadogoo will always stay behind.” Their words hurt but they also made me think. Why was I doing so poorly? One day, our teacher said, “ Kadogoo, why don’t you reflect on why you came last in the class?” Her words stayed in my mind. I decided to observe my classmates. What were they doing differently? I noticed something important – they read books, took notes and studied with focus. When I went home, I told my mother, “Mom, I want to do better in class.” My mother smiled and said, “Of course, you can, Kadogoo. All you need is to manage your time wisely. There should be time for study, play and helping out at home. I realised that if I wanted to improve, I had to change my habits. That evening, I opened my books and started studying. My sister saw me and offered to help with my homework. My mother also gave me tips, saying, “Read books every day, finish your homework on time, and don’t hesitate to ask your teachers when you have doubts.” At first, it was hard. I wasn’t used to studying regularly. But slowly, things started changing. The more I read, the better my reading became. I started paying attention in class and taking notes like my classmates. M y friends, Matata and Jeni, encouraged me and even studied with me sometimes. I even gathered enough courage to approach my teachers when I had a question. To my surprise, they were happy to help and praised me for asking. “Well done, Kadogoo! Keep it up,” they said. Their words motivated me to keep trying. Then came our class test. I worked hard to prepare. When the results were announced, I was no longer last! I was so happy. "Hurrrayyyy!" “I can do it!” I told myself. From that moment, I decided to work even harder. At the end of the term, our teacher announced the final rankings. “The third place goes to Matata. The second place goes to Jeni. Guess who was first? And the first place goes to… Kadogooooo!” Everyone clapped and I couldn’t stop smiling. The teacher handed me a prize – a new bag and some books. “Kadogoo, do you have anything to tell your friends?” she asked. “Yes,” I said confidently. “I want to tell everyone that you can achieve anything if you work hard. I was last, and now I’m first because I didn’t give up. I had help from my friends and family, and I kept trying.” When I got home, my mother saw my cheerful face and asked, “ Kadogoo, why are you so happy today?” “Mom, I came first in my class!” I exclaimed, showing her my prize. “Look at my new bag and books! From now on, I will always work hard.”
author: Gyanita

title: Champi and the Fig Tree
text: I like them all. But it is figs that I love best of all! Cheev... cheev “Anna, Anna, come fast. Look, the baby squirrel is eating figs,” shouts Champi. “Coming, Champi!” says Anna. “Oh look at those birds, Anna,” says Champi. “What big beaks they have!” “They are Malabar grey hornbills,” says Anna. “They love figs very much.” “See this, Champi,” says Anna. “Who could it be, Anna? Could it be a porcupine?” asks Champi. “Porcupines cannot climb trees, Champi,” says Anna. “This must be a civet cat’s droppings. Both eat figs. But they are both very shy animals, and come out only at night.” “Could that be a porcupine? Or is it a civet cat?” wonders Champi. Champi wakes her brother up and points to the tree outside the window. “Oh… There, look, Anna. It’s a porcupine!” Anna wakes up. “Yes! It must be dinner time.” Squirrels, hornbills, civet cats, porcupines and I, we all love figs the most!
author: Deepa Bhasthi

title: Kamakshi and her Sock
text: Once upon a time, there was a girl named Kamakshi. One day, she was getting ready for school when she found out that her sock was missing. She started to search for it. They both started to look for the sock but they couldn't find her sock. Finally, they saw a basket with the sock in it. Kamakshi picked it up. It seemed to be a little heavy than usual. title: What is the purpose of learning in life?
text: Einstein's wonderful quote: Did you know that Einstein once said "If I were not a physicist, I would probably be a musician. I often think in music. I live my daydreams in music. I see my life in music." He was of the opinion that all that a physicist needed was a physics book and a violin! It often confuses a common man as to why would he praise a violin and in what way was it related with he becoming a physicist and proposing his "Theory of relativity." I assure you that you would receive the answer for this question at the end of the book. What does the term 'Interdisciplinarity' mean? The word 'inter' means in between and 'discipline' in this sense means 'liking' or 'expertise'. Thus, the term interdisciplinarity is defined as capability of a human's to have expertise in different domains of knowledge. A person who has imbibed interdisciplinarity is called an interdisciplined person or in common language a multi - talented person. Why is interdisciplinarity important? 1.Interdisciplinary people are liked by all Inter - disciplinary people are highly liked in the society. The simple reason is that they are of great use at the time of need. They do not find much difficulty in gaining recognition for what they achieve. 2. Interdisciplinarity is a friend in need, who is a friend indeed. When troubles haunt a person in his life, it wouldn't always be feasible to stretch your hand and beg others. The society aims at exploiting any person who begs for help from head to toe. Hence, it is a primary duty of you to cultivate an open mind and be inter - disciplined, be thirsty to learn new lessons by the technique of association and relate them with your past experiences. 3. Interdisciplinarity prevents an idle mind from becoming a devil's workshop. An eminent English proverb says: "An idle mind is a devil's workshop." The inner meaning of the proverb is that a person who doesn't engage his mind in productivity becomes a criminal (devil's workshop). Human mind is a dynamic mind, a baby and must be allowed to explore. Lack of tuning, channelling and engaging a human mind can force you to confront detrimental conditions on a long run. Hence, interdisciplinarity goes hand - in - hand with engaging a human mind. "A good learner becomes undoubtedly, a multi - talented man but not the reverse." 4. Interdisciplinarity fetches you respect, knowledge and money without much worry or agony Every individual has a deep desire to be treated with respect, acquire a lot of knowledge and be rich. It would remain only a dream if one did not work on becoming an interdisciplinary personality. By becoming interdisciplinary, you grow, you achieve and most importantly, you are content and happy. How does one become interdisciplinary? 1. Always be ready to learn Learning is a life long process. Therefore, it is essential to accept or acknowledge about what we do not know intelligently and be keen to seek guidance from a person who knows what you do not know. To learn, you need the HIPP: Humility, Inquisitiveness, Patience and Practice. 2. Like what you learn, learn what you like Try to like what you learn by understanding its benefits and admit its usefulness. Try to learn what you like as it is your passion. Learning to balance liking what you learn and learning what you like is an art. 3. Learn any new concept completely (from A to Z), make yourself a filled vessel and do not be an empty vessel We encounter many people who do not know about a particular topic deeply but just keep boasting. When demanded for a logical reason, they shout aloud. Such people are neither knowledgeable nor happy. Always question before accepting. Always have self-motivation to self-learn any concept deeply without depending on external resources. This helps you in comprehension, retention of memory and proper execution. 4. Cultivate the habit of reading biographies or autobiographies written by great authors, leaders and achievers. Listen to the lectures of their life history. Cultivating the habit of reading books can create ideas and thoughts and feelings that you have never felt before. It helps you get inspired and helps you to get motivation, gives you suggestions and real time life lesson, if implemented can leverage you to become a successful person. It helps you improve your imagination and reading skills which can improve a child's brain. Reading books can engage, create curiosity and things which help you. Listening to biographies can help you analyse the mistakes and ideas and solutions that you can use in your life. 5.History repeats if you don't learn lessons from it. Learn from your mistakes and improve. You must be doubly sure not to repeat the same mistake which made you suffer. Learning may take time and differs from person to person, but always be truthful to yourself. Transform for your sake and not to please the society. ﻿ and might differ from person to person. But, you need not worry about it. Focus on achieving for your sake and not to impress the society. 6. Always maintain self confidence, be positive and have a vibrant personality. It is vital for a person to maintain self - confidence, esteem, train oneself to see good in everything and should be open to receive as well as give. This is called ﻿vibrant personality. ﻿ ﻿Hence, following these tips, I hope you can also become a multi - talented person with no hurdles whatsoever. "﻿ ﻿ ﻿Just because something doesn't do what you planned it to do doesn't mean its useless." -A quote of Thomas Alva Edison A road - side stone has no value in a market, but is a diamond in a Museum. ﻿

title: Where is My Momma?
text: I just woke up. ''Mom....Mom!'' Where is momma? I am looking for momma. I looked for momma in her bedroom, but she was not there. I looked for Momma in living room, but she was not there too. I looked for Momma in the kitchen, but she was not there too. I looked for Momma in terrace, but still Momma was not there. Where did Momma go? I looked up Momma in the backyard garden, Momma was not there. Maybe Momma is in the bathroom. ''Momma...Momma?'' There is no sound of Momma. I feel sad. Knock, Knock, Knock! I heard someone knocking on the door. I was surprised. Who could it be? I heard Momma's voice. ''Dear, please open the door. I have a lot of groceries!'' I quickly ran to the front door. I opened the door for my Momma. It turns out Momma went to the market. She bought lots of vegetables, fruits, fish, and meat. Wow...that's a lot of groceries! I'm happy, because my momma finally home. I am hungry, and my Momma made my favorite vegetable soup.

text: In our life, we see many strange incidents and weird stories which are very true. In our life, we have many emotions, and therefore, we have to control our emotions and we have to be balanced. title: Growing from Scars
text: Anneliese was a young girl known as a diligent and intelligent student at school. Even at her age, she was widely recognized for her seriousness in learning. Since she was little, Anneliese had always prioritized books and studying above everything else. While her friends played games or ran around outside, Anneliese would sit quietly in the library, absorbed in her textbooks. Her school, located in the heart of the city, was filled with talented and ambitious students. Yet, despite her undeniable intelligence, Anneliese never felt comfortable among her peers. They all seemed too caught up in their own worlds. Unlike them, who spent their time socializing or having fun, Anneliese chose to stay in class, focusing on what her teachers taught. Her dedication to studying made her stand out, but it also made her seem odd to her classmates. In class, Anneliese often became the target of teasing. One of her biggest tormentors was Malucia, an older student known for her arrogant and selfish behavior. Malucia loved being the center of attention and had plenty of friends who followed her lead. Unfortunately, she also enjoyed bullying younger students especially Anneliese. “Anneliese, don’t act like you’re so much better than everyone just because you’re smart,” Malucia sneered one day, catching Anneliese in the school library, deep in a math book. Anneliese simply gave a faint smile, choosing to ignore Malucia’s words. But the more Malucia observed Anneliese’s unwavering focus on studying, the more irritated she became. Malucia felt as if Anneliese was trying to make her look stupid, even though that wasn’t the case at all. Day after day, Malucia mocked Anneliese, humiliating her in front of others and making her feel even more isolated. One afternoon in the cafeteria, Malucia and her friends began their usual teasing. “Anneliese, you’re way too serious! Don’t you know life isn’t just about studying?” Malucia jeered, her voice dripping with sarcasm. “Try having some fun for once! Or are you afraid your big brain will shrink?” Her friends burst into laughter, while Anneliese stayed silent. The words stung, but she chose not to respond. She knew fighting back would only make things worse. Days turned into months, and months into years. Despite the constant bullying, Anneliese never gave up on her studies. She believed that education was her path to a better future. She was determined to prove that, even though she was often overlooked, she could achieve great things. When the time came to graduate, Anneliese earned a spot at a prestigious university with a full scholarship. There, she continued to shine as a hardworking and brilliant student. Over the years, Anneliese excelled academically, earning her degree with honors. Even as she moved forward, the memories of her school days lingered. She often recalled the harsh treatment she’d endured at the hands of Malucia and her friends. Though she had grown stronger and more successful, the scars of her past still haunted her. After graduating, Anneliese landed a job at a renowned company, working in the human resources department a highly respected position. She took pride in her achievements, knowing they were the result of years of hard work and perseverance. Several years into her career, the company held a recruitment drive. As part of her role in HR, Anneliese was tasked with interviewing potential candidates. One day, as she sat in her office preparing for the next interview, she noticed something unusual. When the next candidate walked in, Anneliese felt a strange sense of familiarity. The woman standing before her was neatly dressed and carried herself with confidence. Her face sparked a memory, and Anneliese stared, trying to place it. Then it hit her—it was Malucia, her old classmate and former bully. Anneliese was stunned, but she maintained her composure. Deep inside, old feelings of hurt and resentment began to surface. How could it be that Malucia, who had once belittled her, was now sitting in front of her, seeking a job? With a professional smile, Anneliese began the interview. “Welcome, Malucia. Thank you for coming in today. Could you tell me a bit about your work experience?” she asked, keeping her tone steady despite the storm of emotions inside her. Malucia gave a faint smile and began explaining her previous jobs. “I’ve worked at several companies and feel that now is the perfect time for me to join yours,” she said confidently. But Anneliese wasn’t particularly interested in Malucia’s answers. She was more focused on the whirlwind of emotions swirling within her. As the interview progressed, Anneliese asked increasingly challenging questions, causing Malucia’s confidence to falter. A small part of Anneliese felt satisfied watching her old bully struggle. “How do you handle conflict within a team?” Anneliese asked sharply, the question echoing memories of their school days. Malucia hesitated before answering, her composed demeanor starting to crack. “I always try to listen to all sides and find the best solution for everyone,” she replied, her voice trembling slightly. Anneliese nodded, but inside, she couldn’t deny the bittersweet sense of justice she felt. By the end of the interview, Malucia looked visibly shaken. Just before closing the session, Anneliese took a deep breath and said, “Before we finish, there’s something I’d like to share, Malucia. I’m Anneliese, the classmate you used to bully back in school.” Malucia froze, her eyes widening in shock. A mixture of guilt and regret washed over her face. “You… you’re Anneliese?” she stammered, her voice barely audible. Anneliese nodded slowly. “Yes, I am. I’m the girl you mocked and belittled. But as you can see, I’ve come a long way since then.” Malucia’s face fell, and she bowed her head. “Anneliese… I’m so sorry. I… I regret everything I did to you.” To Anneliese’s surprise, tears began streaming down Malucia’s face. Watching her former bully break down, Anneliese felt an unexpected shift in her heart. The thirst for revenge she’d once held onto so tightly began to fade. Finally, she spoke gently, “I don’t need revenge, Malucia. I’ve already overcome the pain you caused me. You can move on, too. But remember, the people you hurt may one day rise above you in ways you never imagined.” Malucia nodded, her sobs subsiding. Slowly, she stood and left the room. As Anneliese sat alone in her office, she felt a sense of relief. Perhaps, in life, the greatest victory isn’t revenge but the ability to forgive and let go.

title: Sweet Celebrations: A Birthday Filled with Love
text: I am a little girl everyone calls me Calla. I am a beautiful girl, with brown hair, hooded eyes, and a beautiful smile. My beauty comes from my mother, whom I call "Mama." She is my guardian angel; she gives me everything that I want and has a pure heart. On December 25th, I had my 7th birthday, and my Mama and Papa made a birthday cake for me, and I felt 'HAPPY!!' This is my father, whom I call "Papa." He is the first love of my life and my hero in this world. Papa loves me and Mama very much. On this sunny morning, Papa and I went to the cake shop to buy ingredients for the cake that Mama and Papa was going to make. I'm so happy to have parents like them. Papa, I'm proud of you so much!! Thank you Calla, papa is proud of you too. I love you so much! After arriving at the store. Papa chose the ingredients to make a cake, papa explained one by one the ingredients to me. Papa said that the main ingredients for making cakes are eggs and flour. And, w hen I listened, Papa looked very enthusiastic. Calla, this item that I am holding is Flour, we need flour and eggs as the main ingredients to make cakes. After arriving home, we gave the ingredients we had bought to Mama. Mama also explained that to make cakes we need flour, eggs, sugar, milk, butter, chocolate and a little of water. After that, mix all the ingredients until they become one, mom said that was the baking process. Falvour Eggs Sugar Water Butter Milk Chocolate I wanted to try to help Mama and Papa. With great enthusiasm, I opened the cake ingredients one by one, read the ingredients listed on the packaging carefully, and felt the texture to feel the uniqueness of each one. The fine flour, sweet sugar, and soft butter all gave a different sensation in my hands. But when I opened the flour, my nose suddenly itched! And.... HATCHIMMM!!! I sneezed. "HATCHIMM!!!" " HATCHIMM!!" While imagining the aroma of cake that would fill the kitchen, I began to mix the ingredients carefully, following the recipe that mama had taught me. But suddenly by accident I broke an egg, “When the egg was tapped on the edge of the bowl, there was a ‘tock... crunch!’ sound. The shell broke, and the golden-yellow contents slid down to the floor”. All was solved, mama taught me and helped me clean up the broken egg. Every step was fun, and I felt proud to be able to contribute to the process of making a cake that my family would enjoy together. Broken Egg After that, I resumed the activity of mixing the ingredients and kneading the cake. Carefully, I poured the flour into a large bowl, followed by the glistening granulated sugar and melted butter. Using a spatula, I began to stir the mixture, feeling the texture getting smoother and softer with each movement. A sweet scent began to waft out, making me even more excited. Once all the ingredients were well mixed, I added the eggs one by one, making sure each one was fully incorporated before adding the next. Then, I stirred in the milk and chocolate, which gave the batter its distinctive aroma. Attentively, I kept stirring until the batter became thick and bright in color, ready to transfer into the pan. After that, I poured the batter into the buttered and floured baking pan, making sure the batter was evenly distributed. Gently, I tapped the pan on the counter to release any trapped air bubbles. Now, it was time to put the pan into the preheated oven. I waited patiently, imagining how this birthday cake would look and taste when it was done. Every minute that passes makes me more excited, imagining the special moment when this cake will be served, decorated with beautiful creams and decorations, and the happy smiles on mama and papa's faces as they celebrate this special day. On the other hand, I saw papa helping mom and me make the cake. Papa was stirring the dough vigorously, his face looking serious yet cheerful. “Come on Calla, let's make this the best cake ever!” He moved the mold in a regular rhythm, as if he was playing a musical instrument. Occasionally, he glanced at me and Mama, giving a big smile that made the atmosphere even warmer. I was happy to see papa involved in this process. He always has a unique way of making things more fun. While stirring, papa also told me about his childhood memories of helping his grandmother in the kitchen. The stories made me laugh and feel closer to my family. I could feel how important this moment was for the three of us, not just to make cookies, but also to create beautiful memories together. “How about we add some three candle on top?”. Once the batter was well mixed, I turned my attention to the prepared garnish ingredients. Papa and mama agreed with my idea, and we all started preparing the decorations for the cake that would make it even more special. This moment of togetherness made me feel grateful, and I knew that this cake would be more than just food; it was a symbol of our love and hard work as a family. This is the first birthday cake that mama, papa, and I have made. This tantalizing chocolate-colored cake not only looks beautiful, but is also full of the love and hard work we put into the process. With its soft cake layers and abundant chocolate cream on top, this cake looks so appetizing. On the other hand, Papa made a new batch of dough for the second cake. Eagerly, he mixed the ingredients in a large bowl, and as he worked. I was very happy to hear that, because it meant that we would be celebrating not only with my family, but also with my friends who had always supported and accompanied me, Calla said. Hearing that plan made me even more excited. This second cake would be a nice surprise for my friends when they came to celebrate my birthday. I imagined their cheerful faces when they saw the cake that papa had lovingly made. “The first cake is for mama, papa, and you. The second cake is for your friends.” Thank you, Papa. I'm very happy to hear that. You are the best Papa. My second birthday cake After making the birthday cake for the second time, I smelled a strong chocolate smell that pierced my nose. It seemed that the cake was done! The sweet, rich aroma of perfectly baked chocolate filled the entire kitchen, making me eager to see the result. Carefully, I opened the oven door and took out the pan containing the tantalizing chocolate cake. The cake looked perfect, with a shiny surface and a slight rise, indicating that the batter had risen well. I could see that the cake had a deep and seductive chocolate color, as if it was inviting an immediate taste. After the cake was finished, mom handed me the birthday cake with a warm smile on her face. She held up the chocolate cake lovingly, as if it were her most precious treasure. “Happy birthday, Calla, my dearest child. May in this new year, all your dreams come true and you are always surrounded by love and happiness.” “Thank you, Mama! This cake looks amazing!” Papa also gave me a second birthday cake with a big smile on his face, his eyes full of hope and affection. I felt warm inside at the words, and gratefully. "Happy birthday, my little daughter Calla! May you always be happy, healthy, and continue to shine like a star." “Thank you, Papa! This cake looks amazing!” And, this is for you my best friend. Thank you, Calla! May you always be surrounded by happines. On that day, I was very happy, because my parents celebrated my special day in a very special way. They not only made a delicious cake, but also invited my friends to celebrate my happiness together. The atmosphere at home was so cheerful and full of joy. The laughter and cheerful voices of my friends filled the room, creating an unforgettable moment. At the end, every second was precious, and I couldn't stop smiling. Seeing my friends' happy faces and hearing their laughter made me feel so loved. The day was not just about cake and presents, but about togetherness, love, and beautiful memories that I will always cherish.
author: Wiwin Eko

title: The Coloring Conflict
text: It was a sunny Sunday morning, and little Rose, a cheerful 5 years girl, sat cross legged in the living room. Her face lit up as she opened her favorite coloring book, filled with pictures of animals, flowers, vegetable and transportation. Beside her lay a set of colored pencils neatly arranged in a tin box. She loved coloring, and today, her two older brothers, Maja (8 years old) and Elang (11 years old), had decided to join her. "Look, Maja! Look, Elang! I’m going to color this teddy bear! See, how good it is!" (She held up a picture of a teddy bear, waiting to be filled with colors.) "That’s nice, Rose. I’m going to color this car. It’s going to be yellow. Yellow car is like bumble bee that I like!" (Maja grabbed a sheet from his own coloring book and smiled proudly.) (chuckling)"You always pick yellow, Maja. I’ll color this sky. It needs a lot of blue. coloring Nature is the best!” The three of them sat together, giggling and chatting as they colored, Rose was happily using her pink pencil for the teddy bears when suddenly, Maja reached over and grabbed the pencil without asking. I got it!! "Hey! That’s my pencil, Maja! I need it for teddy bear!" "But I need green for my car! I’m drawing a stripe on it. I’ll give it back when I’m done." "No! You have to ask first! It’s mine!" (She reached over to grab the pencil back, but Maja held it tightly.) Maja: "Rose, don’t be such a baby. It’s just a pencil!" (Maja pulled the pencil away, causing Rose to fall back slightly on the floor.) "I want my pencil back! You’re mean!" (She started crying loudly, her face scrunched up in frustration.) (singing) "Oh no, not again. You two fight over everything. Maja, just give her the pencil." "But I only need it for a minute! She has so many pencils, Elang. Why can’t she share?" (sobbing) "It’s mine! He didn’t ask!" Hearing the commotion, their mother, Mrs. Jasmine, walked quickly into the living room. She had been folding laundry in the next room and immediately recognized the sound of Rose’s upset cries. (calmly but firmly) "What’s going on here? Why is Rose crying?" (pointing at Maja) "Maja took Rose’s pink pencil without asking, and now they’re fighting over it." (defensive) "I only needed it for a minute! She has so many pencils, Mom. It’s not a big deal." (sniffling and screaming)"But he didn’t ask, Mommy. He just took it!" (gently but firmly) "Maja, it doesn’t matter if it’s just a pencil. When something belongs to someone else, you need to ask for permission before taking it. How would you feel if someone took your favorite toy without asking?" (thinking for a moment)"I guess… I wouldn’t like it. "Exactly. It’s not about the pencil, it’s about respecting Rose’s things. Even if she has a lot of pencils, that doesn’t mean you can take them without asking. Do you understand?" "Yes, Mom. I’m sorry." (Turning to Rose) "Rose, Maja has something he’d like to say to you." (looking at Rose) "I’m sorry, Rose. I should have asked before taking your pencil." "It’s okay. But next time, you have to ask, okay?" (smiling) "Okay, I promise." "Good. Now, Rose, can you let Maja borrow your green pencil for just a little while? Sharing is important too, and it’s nice to help each other." "Okay, but just for a little bit. I need it for my Teddy bear" Thanks, Rose! I’ll give it back as soon as I finish the stripe." (grinning) "See? That wasn’t so hard. Now can we all get back to coloring without any more drama?" The three children returned to their coloring books, this time in harmony. Maja used the pencil to finish the stripe on his car, then handed it back to Rose with a smile. "Here you go, Rose. Thanks for letting me borrow it." (smiling)"You’re welcome. Look, my Teddy bear is almost done!" (She proudly held up her coloring book to show the bright pink butterfly she was working on.) "That looks awesome, Rose. And look at my picture of cloude! I think it’s coming along pretty well." (He held up his page, which was filled with shades of blue and white.) Mrs. Jasmine: (peeking from the doorway) "Well, that's better." -------------------------------------------------------------THE END----------------------------------------------------------------
author: Alien Lenda

title: The History Life of Lembayung
text: Story of Lembayung Life can be cruel, and for Lembayung, it unravelled far too early. At just 12 years old, Lembayung experienced a loss that would forever change the course of her life. Her mother, her anchor and source of unconditional love, died in a tragic car accident one rainy autumn evening. Lembayung had been waiting for her mother to come home from work, her small hands clutching a book her mother had promised to read with her before bed. But instead of her mother’s warm embrace, Lembayung received the unbreakable news from her father, Mr. Blue, who could barely hold himself together. That night, Lembayung’s world shattered. The house that had once been filled with laughter and warmth became a cold and silent place, and her childhood innocence was replaced with grief and loneliness. Lembayung’s father, devastated by the loss of his wife, was not the kind of man who knew how to express emotions, let alone deal with his own. Mr. Blue had always been strict, but after the accident, his temper grew worse. His grief turned into anger, and he often lashed out at Lembayung, not physically but with harsh words and cold indifference. He blamed the world for taking his wife and, in moments of frustration, even Lembayung for reminding him too much of her. Lembayung, too young to fully understand the depth of her father’s pain, internalized his anger. She began to believe that she was a burden, a child who had to fend for herself in a household where love was now a distant memory. Despite the emotional turmoil at home, Lembayung found refuge in school. She was a bright and curious girl, and books became her escape. Her teachers often praised her intelligence, though they also noted her stubbornness. Lembayung had a fiery spirit, one that had only grown stronger in the face of her father’s temper. She refused to let anyone pity her, and she refused to let her struggles show. But her strong will often got her into trouble. She clashed with classmates who teased her for being “too serious” and argued with teachers who misunderstood her defiance. Lembayung wasn't trying to be difficult, she was simply trying to protect herself. Her stubbornness was her armor, shielding her from the vulnerability she couldn’t afford to show. At home, Lembayung’s relationship with her father deteriorated further. Mr. Blue, unable to cope with his grief, buried himself in work and often came home late, exhausted and irritable. Lembayung learned to cook her own meals, do her own laundry, and take care of herself. She grew up faster than most kids her age, but the emotional void in her life left a scar. She longed for her mother’s gentle presence, for someone to tell her that everything would be okay. But instead, Lembayung endured her father’s harsh words and cold silence. She wanted to hate him for his temper, but deep down, she knew he was broken too. Still, the absence of affection made her harden her heart, and she vowed to never rely on anyone again. Through her teenage years, Lembayung’s independence became both her strength and her weakness. She excelled academically, driven by a fierce determination to escape the life she had grown to resent. She wanted more than the small, suffocating town she lived in and the angry man who barely spoke to her. But her stubbornness often alienated others. She pushed people away, afraid of being hurt again. Even when well meaning teachers or friends tried to reach out, Lembayung kept her walls high. She didn’t want anyone’s pity, and she didn’t want anyone to see the cracks in her tough exterior. After graduating high school, Lembayung worked several part time jobs to save money for college. Her father offered no financial support, though she suspected he felt guilty about it. He would mumble things like, "You’re strong, Lembayung. You’ll figure it out," as if his approval could replace the help she needed. Lembayung didn’t argue with him, she had stopped expecting anything from him a long time ago. Instead, she threw herself into her work, determined to build a future that didn’t depend on anyone but herself. It was during this time that she discovered her passion for teaching. She took a job as a tutor for younger kids and found joy in helping them learn. For the first time in years, Lembayung felt a spark of purpose. College wasn’t easy for Lembayung, but it was a turning point. She majored in education, driven by her dream of becoming a teacher. The stubbornness that had once been a source of conflict became her greatest asset. Lembayung refused to give up, even when the workload felt overwhelming or when she doubted herself. She worked late nights, balancing her studies with part-time jobs, and graduated with honors. Her professors often remarked on her tenacity, though some noted that she had a tendency to be overly critical of herself and others. Lembayung’s high standards were a reflection of the life she had lived. She believed that success required nothing less than relentless effort. As a teacher, Lembayung brought the same determination to her classroom. She was firm but fair, a no nonsense educator who demanded the best from her students. Some found her intimidating, but most admired her. Lembayung saw herself in the children who struggled. The ones who felt unseen or unheard and she made it her mission to help them succeed. She wasn’t afraid to fight for her students, whether it was advocating for better resources or standing up to parents who underestimated their children’s potential. Her passion and dedication earned her respect among her colleagues, though her stubbornness occasionally led to clashes. Lembayung didn’t mind she was there for the kids, not to win popularity contests. Despite her success, Lembayung couldn’t entirely escape the shadows of her past. Her relationship with her father remained strained, though as he grew older, his temper softened. He would occasionally call her, awkwardly asking about her work and remarking on how proud he was of her. Lembayung appreciated the effort, but the wounds of her childhood were not so easily healed. She forgave him, but their relationship would never be the same. Still, Lembayung knew that her father’s struggles had shaped her into the person she had become. His anger had taught her resilience, and his absence had taught her independence. In a way, she was grateful for the lessons, even if they had come at a cost. Looking back on her journey, Lembayung saw a life defined by both pain and perseverance. She had survived the loss of her mother, endured her father’s temper, and fought her way to a career that gave her purpose. But more than that, she had transformed her struggles into strength. Lembayung’s story wasn’t just about overcoming hardship it was about using that hardship to build a life of meaning. As a teacher, she gave her students the support and encouragement she had once longed for, ensuring that they would never feel as alone as she had. And in doing so, Lembayung proved to herself and to the world that even the most difficult beginnings could lead to extraordinary endings.
author: Alien Lenda

title: The Star
text: Once upon a time, in a small, peaceful village nestled between rolling hills and dense forests, there lived a young girl named Azalea. She was a beautiful child, with bright, curly hair that bounced and swayed like the petals of a wildflower in the breeze. Her skin was a rich, warm brown, the color of the earth after a summer rain, and her big, sparkling eyes seemed to hold the mysteries of the world. But despite her many wonderful qualities, Azalea often felt out of place. In her village, the other children all had fair skin with straight, smooth hair, and their features were all alike, almost as if they had been shaped by the same mold. They looked like they belonged together, and Azalea couldn't help but feel like she was different. Her hair was wild and untamed, and her skin stood out in a way that made her feel isolated. The children would sometimes whisper behind her back, pointing at her curly hair or her dark skin. It made Azalea feel like she didn’t fit in. She longed to blend in, to look like the others, to be the same. One quiet afternoon, while the other children played in the village square, Azalea wandered off to a peaceful spot by herself. It was a place she often went when she wanted to be alone—a large, ancient tree that stood on the edge of a meadow. Its gnarled branches stretched high into the sky, and its roots were deep, twisting into the earth like the veins of the land itself. Azalea would sit under the tree, resting her back against its rough bark, and gaze up at the clouds, wondering why she didn’t look like everyone else. As Azalea sat there, feeling lonely and lost in her thoughts, she didn’t notice the soft footsteps approaching until a warm voice called her name. "Azalea, my dear, what’s troubling you?" It was her grandmother, who had come to sit beside her. Azalea looked up, surprised to see her grandmother, a kind-hearted woman with silver hair and a gentle smile. Her grandmother had always been her rock—someone Azalea could turn to when she felt sad or confused. "I don’t know, Grandma," Azalea said quietly, her eyes downcast. "I just feel... different. I don’t look like the other children. I don’t fit in. My hair is all messy, and my skin is so dark. I just don’t belong." Her grandmother nodded, understanding the pain in Azalea’s voice. "I see," she said softly. "But let me tell you something, my dear. Let me share a story with you, one that might help you see things differently." Azalea looked up at her grandmother, her curiosity piqued. Her grandmother smiled warmly and pointed up at the sky, where the stars were beginning to twinkle as the sun dipped below the horizon. "You see those stars up there?" she asked. "Each one shines brightly, lighting up the dark sky. But do you know something else about the stars? They are all different." Azalea squinted up at the sky, her gaze drawn to the shining stars. Some were small, twinkling faintly, while others were large and bold, casting a strong light. Some were blue, while others were red, yellow, or white. "I never thought about that," Azalea murmured. "Exactly," her grandmother said with a gentle nod. "It’s the differences that make the stars special. The variety is what makes the night sky so beautiful. If every star were the same, it would lose its magic. And, my dear Azalea, you are like those stars." "You are different, yes," her grandmother said, her voice filled with warmth and love. "But that’s exactly what makes you special. You don’t need to look like everyone else. You don’t need to have straight hair or light skin to be beautiful. You are unique, and your differences are what make you shine. Just like the stars in the sky, you are meant to stand out and make the world a more colorful and wonderful place." From that day forward, Azalea began to look at herself differently. She no longer felt the need to blend in or hide her unique features. She began to embrace her curly hair, letting it grow wild and free, just like the forest that surrounded her village. She wore her dark skin with pride, knowing it was a part of her that made her who she was. She no longer tried to change herself to fit in with the other children; instead, she focused on what made her unique and beautiful. "Look at the stars," she would say, pointing up at the night sky. "They may all be different, but that’s what makes them beautiful. And you, just like the stars, are special just the way you are." And so, Azalea grew, a shining light in her village, just as unique and beautiful as the stars above.

title: Family Ties: Cherished Moments at Grandma and Grandpa's
text: Hello everyone! My name is Una, and I am currently 6 years old. I am a jolly, cheerful, and beautiful girl. Every day, I am always excited to play and learn new things. I love drawing, singing, and playing with my friends in the park. I also enjoy helping others and making them smile. With high spirits, I'm ready for an exciting adventure in this world! This is my mom and dad, they are great parents. Mom is a loving person and m y father, is a passionate and inspiring person. He worked hard for our family and always taught us the values of discipline and responsibility. Every weekend, we often spend time together, playing in the park or cycling. They complement each other, and I feel very lucky to have them. This is my little brother, Uno, who is 5 years old. He is very playful and always full of energy. Every day, Uno never runs out of ideas to play, whether it's playing with his friends, or drawing with colorful crayons. His playfulness makes the atmosphere at home lively, and he always makes people around him smile. We are a happy family! I also have a very special pet, a dog named Guguk. Guguk is my loyal friend who is always beside me, both in happy times and when I feel sad. With his soft fur and cheerful eyes, Guguk can always make me smile. Every morning, he would wake up early and wait by my bedside, ready to start the day with enthusiasm. Besides school, my daily activity was helping my mom cook. Although I mostly just watched and watched her cook, I really enjoyed every moment we spent in the kitchen together. Mom was a great cook, and whenever she cooked, the appetizing aroma of cooking always filled our house. Besides that, I also often help my mom clean the house. This activity has become one of my favorite routines. One of my favorite tasks is folding clothes. Mom always taught me how to fold neatly, and I also swept the floor. Although I sometimes felt a little tired, I was always satisfied to see a clean and shiny floor after I swept. Every afternoon, my father would take me, my mother, and my sister to visit my grandmother's house on his blue motorcycle. Dad's beloved blue motorcycle was not just a means of transportation, but also a symbol of our togetherness as a family. The thunderous sound of the motorcycle engine and the wind blowing as we drove made me feel excited every time the trip began. Arriving at my grandparents' house, they always welcomed us happily. The big smiles on their faces and the warm hugs they gave me made me feel very welcome. Grandpa, with his bushy white beard and sparkling eyes, was always ready with interesting stories from his youth. Hi, Grandpa and Grandma! How are you? My grandparents' house was always crowded every day as their children and grandchildren visited regularly. Every time I stepped into the house, a warm and laughter-filled atmosphere greeted me. Grandparents have five children, and each of their children has their own family, so their house is a gathering center for the whole family. We are a happy family, every moment we spend together is a priceless treasure. From the joyful laughter of children playing in the courtyard, to the stories full of wisdom shared by grandparents, every second is precious. We support and encourage each other, share our joys and sorrows, and create memories that we will always cherish.

title: The story of Sadi Carnot, the father of modern engines
text: We all use engines today: no matter how many times but we always use it. From the tiniest of the activities of grinding the chutney for the kitchen to the highest work of flying an aeroplane, engines are used everywhere. But have you ever wondered what an engine is? In this book, we shall study what is an engine, how it works and appreciate the amazing scientist (s) behind this principle and its application in every walk of life. What is an engine? An engine is defined as an object that produces internal mobility in an immobile object. In other words, it generates internal movement in a rigid body. Some of the good examples that illustrate an engine are turbine of a washing machine, a bicycle when peddled and also a motor cycle. In all these cases, we see that there is a force supplied that creates both rotational and translational movement. It is derived from the old word 'Ingenious' which means 'internal movement or vibration'. In olden days, engines were manufactured only for industrial purposes for humans to perform repetitive tasks. Later on, their technology was kept as a secret since the countries were keenly thirsty to wage wars or battles on other countries. But, later on, they were used to manufacture locomotives like trains, buses, cars, scooters, aeroplanes, etc. It is interesting that engines have become an inseparable part of our lives. Come on! Lets befriend the engines. What are the characteristics of an engine? 1) An engine in ideal terms, is a consumer of fuel. Engines work only with the help of fuel supply from external sources. Fuels can be fossil fuels, renewable energy, mechanical, chemical, electrical etc. 2) An engine gives high or maximum output with minimum fuel Since there is an internal movement as a result of work done by the engine due to fuel supply, this movement must help in generating maximum output for machines to work. Thus, if there is less output, machines cease to work and such engines are practically unaffordable. 3) Ideally, it should cause least pollution or loss of energy Every engine that we use causes some amount of pollution to the environment. But, a best engine is the one that contributes least amount of energy loss and contamination of natural resources. 4) They should be highly economical and durable. All the thermodynamic processes taking place in it should be reversible to a large extent i.e. highly efficient. Engines are used or employed based on their economic as well as mechanical advantage. Economic advantage is a property that defines less cost and more durability whereas whereas mechanical advantage advocates higher efficiency. Every engine has numerous internal thermodynamic process occurring in it. Here, thermodynamic process refers to the transfer of heat in different forms. It should be done with highest efficiency and maximum energy must be utilised. It is these engines that run our vehicles, simplify our day - to - day tasks to a large extent. Don't you think it is prudent to always know a scientific principle behind any scientific discovery? Let us first begin with the underlying history behind the fabulous 'engine'. In this piston, we see that the lid is connected to the axle to the wheel with a rod called shaft. When an external force is applied on the lid, the shaft that is connected to the axle pushes the axle and thus the wheels rotate. The interesting part is that the shaft, if closely observed is screwed with the axle of the wheels to make it rotate. In Physics, this phenomenon is called torque. Mathematically, it is defined as the vector (any physical quantity with direction) product of force applied and the perpendicular displacement of the object. i.e. Torque = Force * displacement * sin(theta) where 'theta' is the angle between the force applied and the displacement. Here, since the angle is 90 degree and sin (90) = 1, it generates a high torque. So, we can say that more the torque, more mechanical efficiency is developed in the engine. But, have you ever wondered how is the torque generated in the shaft in spite of the fact it is not operated by our external force i.e. human intervention? Here, we need to know about Carnot engines. The history of the Carnot engine During the 17th century, there was a famous French emperor called Napoleon Bonaparte whom you have all heard off. Right? He had an army general named Carnot, who had a son named Sadi. Sadly, he lost his father at a very young age in a fierce battle. His mom stayed with his uncle at Yugoslavia. So, unable to protect himself from the French society unrest and upheaval, he migrated to Yugoslavia, where his uncle was a great scientist who was then working on the engines! He observed his Nephew closely and understood that Sadi was a pioneer in intelligence and science. Sadi worked with his uncle for many years and came with this wonderful 'Carnot Engine'. How does the Carnot Engine work? The Carnot Engine is an engine that works on the principle of completely reversible thermodynamic process. For this, we first need to understand the 2 types of work an engine does: Reversible and irreversible. What is reversible work? Any work done by an object by completely utilization of a supplied energy is called reversible work. It is itinerary or repetitive, cyclic in nature and energy consumed is equal to the energy supplied. There is no wastage or storage of energy. Practically, there is no reversible work in universe. Irreversible work On the other hand, work done by utilization only some part of the energy supplied is called irreversible work. It is a one - time process, non - cyclic in nature and not repetitive. There is either storage or wastage of energy or both. The best example of irreversible work where energy is lost is the cooking of food. We supply heat from the gas stove and in that some heat is used for cooking whereas some of it gets dissipated into the atmosphere. In the case of solar cell, all the energy of sunlight supplied is not completely used to generate electrical energy. Some of the generated electrical energy is stored in electrolytes of batteries as ions. Hence, here the energy is saved. In the similar case of Carnot Engine, pure reversible work takes place. There is no dissipation of energy and the supplied heat is completely utilised to do work. The above GIF (Graphics interchange format) shows you the working of the Carnot Engine. In the next page, we have illustrated it using a graph for better understanding. From the graph, we observe that the processes of heat transfer in the Carnot Engine is of 2 types: Adiabatic and Isothermal. This engine works only for gases. Adiabatic work takes place when no heat is transferred to the surroundings and none of the physical parameters of the object change: pressure, temperature and volume of the gas. On the other hand, isothermal work takes place when there is a change in volume and pressure at constant temperature. In the above graph, the coordinates of Pressure, volume and temperature are represented by (P,V,T) respectively. There are 2 isothermal processes and 2 adiabatic processes in this whole cycle. One is the expansion of gas from (P 1,V 1, T 1) and (P 2,V 2,T 2) and the other from (P 3,V 3,T 3) to (P 4,V 4,T 4). Similarly, the expansion of gas from isothermal processes is from (P 2,V 2,T 2) to (P 3,V 3,T 3) and (P 4,V 4,T 4) to (P 1,V 1,T 1). So, the calculation of total work done by the engine is: So, even in the case of a piston, it is enclosed in a gas chamber. When the mechanical external force is supplied to the shaft of via the axle of the wheel, it pushes the piston ad the gas expands. This expansion is what causes an engine to further combust the supplied fuel and move the vehicle i.e. either locomotion or internal movement. This is how our vehicle's engine works. Second application of the Carnot Engine: The second application of the Carnot Engine is seen in the flywheel. Here, instead of mechanical force heat is supplied and then withdrawn suddenly. The supplied makes the gas expand and the wheel moves!! Did you know that this simple method was used in locomotive steam engines during the British period? Explanation in detail: In the first case, we see that when the temperature was increased exponentially huge below the flywheel and stopped, the gas expanded at a constant temperature and the flywheel moves up and rotates, thus generating a movement. Now, suddenly, if the temperature is condensed immediately and stopped, then the gas begins to contract again at a constant temperature. These 2 processes are isothermal. But since none of heat used by the gas is transferred to the surroundings, it is also adiabatic. In this way, the Carnot engine is maintained with 100 % efficiency. The engine contains 3 parts that make these processes happen. Source - The object that generates heat for the piston to move Sink - the object that absorbs the high temperature from the gas This is the most ideal type of engine. Even though it forms the basis of other engines, as such there is no engine in practicality. 2. Internal combustion engine This type of engine is found in vehicles that run on petrol or diesel. Even though it runs on the principle of Carnot Cycle, it is perfectly not. The major difference is in the efficiency. These engines have an efficiency of 90 % and above. The below figure shows you the working of an internal combustion engine. ﻿An electrical spark is produced using a component called spark plug. That spark helps the petrol fuel to get combusted at a constant temperature. In the case of diesel, there is no need of a spark plug. Hence, in both the cases, the process is isothermal (constant temperature). The total work done by such engines is given below. In an internal combustion engine, the combustion of fuel takes place within the engine's components. It is much easier to repair in case of a damage at a lesser cost compared to an external combustion engine. What is an external combustion engine? In the case of an external combustion engine, combustion of fuel takes place at a constant temperature and pressure outside the engine's components. Unlike an internal combustion engine, it produces lesser output and has lesser efficiency due to higher loss of energy into environment. A blast furnace is a best example of external combustion engine. In these types of engines, the combustion is also at a constant temperature and pressure i.e. it is both isothermal and isobaric but there is change in volume. The work done by this engine is also similar to that of an internal combustion engine. Steam engines are the best examples for external combustion engine where the fuel is combusted, and the steam is liberated outside the engine's chamber. You need not worry about the mathematical derivation because it might seem a little difficult. But, with this knowledge, you can understand that this calculation is done by any engineer before manufacturing any engine. This science of an engine is called 'engineering'. I hope you enjoyed this book on engines and let us meet in the other book with a new topic. Till then, be tinkering and learning. Let us end this book with a wonderful quote. "A mathematician knows how to solve a problem; he cannot solve it." - Milne

title: The Garden of Wishes
text: On a bright day, a sparrow flying through the sky Gazed down and saw a swarm of bees sipping nectar nearby. It whispered aloud, in a soft, longing tone, "How I wish I could gather nectar too, on my own!" The bee, busy and bright, ready to move to the next flower, Spotted a grasshopper, unhurried, resting on a bower. With a hum, it sighed, in a voice full of distress, "I wish for a life so carefree, without all this stress!" The grasshopper, hopping with joy on the leaves, Saw a frog by the pond, among reeds and fleas. It felt a sudden gloom and grumbled aloud, "Oh, I wish I could stick out my tongue and feast so proud!" The frog, with its belly so full and content, Watched a turtle in the water, so slow and bent. It croaked with a longing that echoed through night, "How I wish I had a shell that held me tight!" The turtle, gliding down the stream, Eyed the bird, soaring above like a dream. Bitter with envy, it frowned at the sky, "Oh, how I wish I could soar, and learn to fly!" While each creature longed for another’s life, An owl watching from above, wise beyond strife, Smiled with no worry and wished to be nobody, It said, "To be without envy is the secret to be happy. Gratitude is the key to living joyfully."

title: Piku and His Magical Pishi
text: At noon, as the final bell rang, Piku and his friends marched up to the school gate, single file. Mothers and fathers waited outside to pick up their children. The cotton-candy man rang his tinny bell. The snack-seller with a Santa-beard fried savoury pakoras. Taxis honked and buses hooted. And Piku looked around for his Baba. On some days, Piku spotted his Pishi instead—and his face broke into a big smile. Those days were special! Pishi meant stopping for a tutti frutti, while Baba led Piku straight back home. Pishi meant waiting for the red double-decker bus, while Baba flagged the first cab that came their way. Pishi meant new comic books and scary masks, while Baba meant maths homework and handwriting practice. Other children lived with their Baba and Ma. Piku lived with his Baba and Pishi. Baba, the quiet and serious elder brother, and Pishi, his loud and fun-loving sister. On weekdays, Baba went to office and Pishi went to college. On Saturdays and Sundays, Baba took Piku to the park, where Piku fed the doggies and booped their cute, wet noses. Back home, Pishi read him all the books that Ma once did, and taught him to fly kites. But one Sunday evening, Pishi took Piku and Baba to a place he had never been before. It was a mysterious building called The Theatre. There were rows and rows of chairs inside, facing The Stage. Piku sat with his Baba and waited. In The Theatre, the grown-ups sat quietly or spoke in whispers. Even when they coughed, they did it softly—khuk… khuk. And then… Shhh... Then a light came on. It shone on... Pishi. She was on The Stage! Piku gasped. He wanted to call out to Pishi. But she was no longer Piku’s Pishi… That day, she was a princess, wearing fine clothes and a lot of gold! The next time she was an old woman, her hair all white, her eyes wild. Pishi could speak like a queen. She could sing like a village girl. Sometimes she wore a sari, not her usual T-shirt and jeans. Other times, she left her hair open, not in her usual ponytail. No one had a Pishi like Piku’s. Other children had one Ma and one Baba. Piku had one Baba and one Pishi—who could magically turn into different people! “How do you become so many people?” Piku asked his Pishi one night. “How do you know how an old woman feels, when you aren’t old?” So Pishi told him her big secret. “To know how another person feels, all you need is to pay attention! To the way they move, the way they speak, the way they think. Ask them questions if you can, make friends, lots and lots of friends, and then let your mind fly, fly, fly…” So Piku did just that. One day he followed the vegetable-seller, who pushed his cart in the midday sun, with his shaggy old dog. Another day he sat with a boy at the park and made friends with him. When his Dadu came to visit, Piku wanted to know if he liked to do homework when he was a little boy. To know how it felt to be someone he was not, all Piku had to do was let his mind fly. The whole world was a stage for Piku.
author: Somak Ghoshal

title: WHO WERE THOSE LADIES LAST NIGHT?
text: This story takes place in a haunted village of HARYANA. This story starts with a night which drastically changed Rohan`s life. Rohan woke up in the middle of the night cause he had a very dry throat. He looked up and turned to the clock. It was exactly 3:33 am. Rohan tried to wake his mother up but no such luck.Usually his mother used to wake up to the slightest of noise. He sighed and decided to get off his bunk bed to get himself some water. His kitchen was near the balcony and it was a very cold night. Just as he got down he heard a creek sound and realized it was from his old bunk bed which he thinks is a piece of crap.
