Or cats, lions, goats, roosters or frogs,” said Bir, Aaliya, Jehan, Kul, Aatish, Meer and Mia. “OK then, I am not Adar,” said Adar. “I am a dog!” “We know how a dog barks,” the children shouted. “BOW WOW BOW.” And eight dogs went down the road barking, bow wow bow. “But why should we all be just one animal?” asked Adar. Bow Bow Bow Bow ﻿Bow Meoww Meowww Haaooon Haaooon Mainnhh Mainnhh Trrr Trrr Kukarukarooooo Kukarukarooo Cheee Cheee Bow Bow “I’m a butterfly,” said Mia. But what sound does a butterfly make? No one knew. “Maybe she does make a sound but we can’t hear her?” said Mia. Which animal would you be? And what sound does that animal make?
author: Paro Anand

title: Lola's Bahay Kubo
text: I dedicated this book to Sam & Abi, who love adventures and stories.... Abi was a little girl with wide curious eyes and a heart full of wonder. This Easter holiday, she wasn’t going to the beach or a theme park. Instead, she was going somewhere special— Owakan, a quiet village in Jimalalud, Negros Oriental, the hometown of her beloved yaya. She traveled with her Mommy, her Kuya, and her yaya's whole family: Tita, Tito, and her three daughters— Ate Jena, Ate Jeje, and si Joe. They travelled around four hours using Ceres bus, then climbing the hill using habal-habal. Habal-habal is motorcycle taxi commonly used in the Philippines, especially in rural or mountainous areas where roads can be narrow, steep, or unpaved. When they arrived, Abi saw a bahay kubo —a small, cozy house made of bamboo and nipa palm. “Welcome to Lola and Lolo’s home!” Tita smiled. The next morning, Abi woke to the sound of roosters. She watched as Tito gently caught a native chicken. “This will be for lunch,” he said. Abi was amazed—they didn’t buy food from a store. They raised it! Later, she followed Tita to the garden. “This is sayote, and here is malunggay,” Tita explained. “Very healthy. Good for the body.” Sayote is chayote and malunggay is moringa. “Do they grow by themselves?” Abi asked. “We help them grow, but yes—they love our soil and sun,” Tita said, handing her a basket. Abi helped pick vegetables, feeling like a little farmer. That afternoon, they ate lunch under the shade of the trees. The rice was from their own harvest. The food tasted fresh and full of love. After lunch, everyone walked to the river. “Let’s ligo here!” shouted Ate Jeje. Ligo is taking a bath in Bisaya language. Abi hesitated. She’d never taken a bath in a river. But the water looked so clear and cool. Splash! Soon, they were all laughing and playing. “Look there!” Kuya Sam pointed. A karabao stood by the water, and on its back sat a bird. “They help each other,” he explained. “The bird eats the bugs on the karabao’s back.” “That’s mutualism!” Abi remembered from science class. “Like teamwork in nature!” She looked around. Everything here was working together—people, animals, and plants. It felt peaceful. Each night, they gathered outside the bahay kubo. Lolo told stories about the old days. Lola taught them Bisaya words. “Say ‘Maayong buntag,’” Lola smiled. “Maayong buntag!” Abi shouted, proud of herself. They also prayed together, thanking God for family and food. Abi learned that religion here was part of daily life—simple, sincere, and filled with kindness. As the holiday ended, Abi hugged everyone tightly. “I don’t want to leave,” she whispered. “You’ll always have a home here, Abi,” Lola said. “Family is not just by blood—but by love.” In her heart, Abi knew she had found something special. She may be a foreigner, but in Owakan, she discovered a second home—a place where science lived in nature, where culture was shared with joy, and where hospitality made everyone belong.
author: WIDA SARI
illustrator: Alina  Aphayvanh; Amalendu Kaushik; Isaac Sikhakhane; Maithili  Joshi; Promina Shreshtha; WIDA SARI

title: Kindness
text: Once upon a time, in a small town, a young man lived. The name of the young man is Dev. Every day after waking up, he came out of his house with food for cats and dogs around 7 am. He always had a special affection for cats. He often patted cats and dogs whenever he saw them. Dev was new in this town, he didn’t know many things about this place, but he quickly made friends with dogs and cats of the neighborhood. As time passed, people around neighborhood who used to go for jogging, yoga etc. in the morning started noticing him. Gradually Dev became popular around the locality and people knew him and admired him for his good and kind behavior. Some of the neighbors even became his friends. Children grew fond of him and they started playing with dogs and cats.. One day around midnight, two thieves were trying to enter the building where the Dev also lived. The localities' dogs and cats noticed these two thieves. They found their movement suspicious by the way they were dressed up and their sneaky behavior. Before these thieves steal something or harm someone, dogs started barking and even cats started meowing. Hearing the loud cries from the animals, Dev woke up to check what is going on. He found the thieves being afraid of dogs, he quickly called the police helpline and woke up his neighbors. Soon the police arrived and arrested the thieves. One of the police personnel appreciated Dev for immediately alerting police as these thieves were habitual offender and were on run. Dev beaming with pride, told everyone around him that real heroes are the these dogs and cats. Their alertness at night helped us caught the burglars. This act made Dev's friends and neighbors recognize the role of animals in the society. Though they cannot talk, but they show their feelings through their act. Moral of the story, we should always be kind to animals and people.
author: Nikita Sharma

title: The Scary Night in the Forest.
text: Once upon a time, in a small village called Zambezi, there lived three sisters—Lila, Maya, and Tara. They were all aged Fourteen, thirteen and ten years old. The girls were very curious, playful and naughty. One bright summer morning, the girls decided to go on a picnic by the Whispering Woods, a forest known for its tall trees, huge animals, beauty and a GHOST. They played by the river, splashing water and skipping stones. They chased each other through the tall grass and laughed as butterflies danced around them. As the sun began to lower, they noticed a strange, glowing path leading deeper into the forest. The girls, puzzled but excited, followed it ignoring the advice of parents of not going into the forest. Soon, they realized they were lost. The trees looked unfamiliar. They stopped and looked around, their faces filled with confusion. “Which way did we come from?” Tara asked. None of them knew. After walking for a while, they saw fireflies in the middle of grasses. forgetting about the problem that they are lost, three sisters started playing with the fireflies. Suddenly, they heard branches snapping behind them. “What was that?” Maya whispered. A ghostly figure appeared in the mist—a tall shadow, barely visible, but moving. Looking at the figure, he girls screamed and ran for their life. Back in village, their parents had grown worried. When the girls didn’t return by nightfall, a search party was quickly formed. Trying to hide from the Ghost, they entered a cave But in the cave, they saw a huge Mother bear and her baby cub. The girls again started running an exited the cave because they were scared seeing a huge bare. They darted through the forest, not knowing where to go. The sun had set, and the darkness wrapped around them. Desperate to hide, they climbed up a strong tree and hid in its branches. Villagers with torches, dogs, and lanterns entered the forest, calling out the girls' names. The rescue team was finally able to spot the children sleeping on the tree. The girls finally reunited with their parents and apologized for not listening to them and entering the forest.
author: Charmi mehta
illustrator: Barkha Lohia; Isaac Sikhakhane; Suvidha Mistry; Tara Shivakumar

title: The Knock on the Kitchen Door
text: The May vacation had finally arrived, and Agatha's heart fluttered with anticipation. Visiting her village, Alappuzha, a charming little town nestled in Kerala, was always the highlight of her holidays. It meant reuniting with her beloved cousin brother, Christy, who eagerly awaited her arrival. Alappuzha was a town of vibrant days, filled with the chatter of people and the bustle of daily life. However, as dusk descended, a profound quiet would settle, cloaking the streets in an impenetrable darkness. Whispers of lurking thieves deterred people from venturing out after nightfall. Despite these tales, Agatha's excitement remained undimmed. Her village held a special allure, a place where she could freely play with her brothers. Being the only girl cousin who visited during vacations, she was the center of attention, showered with affection. Stories would be shared, laughter would echo, and adventures to nearby places would unfold. The day Agatha finally reached Alappuzha was filled with joyous reunions. The familiar warmth of her family enveloped her, and soon, she was immersed in games and animated conversations, including the inevitable spooky stories. It was during one such session that she truly understood the reason behind the village's nocturnal stillness – the fear of thieves and the chilling tales of ghosts. These narratives, unfortunately, began to cast a shadow on Agatha's nights, filling her with a creeping unease. The darkness outside, coupled with the eerie stories, confined her indoors, stealing the joy of evening playtime. Her days, however, remained bright. Waking up, sharing meals, and engaging in lively games of cricket and cards with her brothers, Christy among them, filled her time. Despite Christy being nine years her elder, they shared a remarkable bond. One particular night, as everyone prepared for sleep, a familiar predicament arose. In Kerala, many houses had their toilets situated outside. The thought of venturing into the pitch-black night to use the restroom filled Agatha with dread. Before heading to bed, she found herself lingering near the kitchen, which had a back door leading outside. The darkness that greeted her gaze was absolute, and standing there alone, the horror stories Christy had recounted flashed vividly through her mind. Mustering all her courage, Agatha edged closer to the door. Before her fears could overwhelm her, she swiftly locked the bolt and flicked off the outside lights. She stood there in the silent kitchen, waiting for her mother to finish her bath, her own need to use the restroom growing. The silence was so profound that the rhythmic ticking of the clock – tick-tick-tick – seemed amplified. Suddenly, a distinct knock echoed from the back door – knock-knock. For a fleeting moment, Agatha dismissed it as her imagination. But then, it came again, more insistent this time. A jolt of fear shot through her. It was undeniably real; someone was outside, knocking persistently. In a trembling voice, Agatha called out, "Whoooo is itt?" No response. The silence that followed was more unnerving than the knock itself. "Who is it?" she asked again, her voice barely a whisper. Still, only the relentless knocking answered her plea. Panic began to set in. Christy's warnings about thieves lurking in the village at night echoed in her ears. What if it was one of them? Her mother was still in the washroom, and Agatha felt utterly alone and vulnerable. Should she open the door? The terrifying possibilities swirled in her mind – a thief, danger, even death. As these thoughts raced through her head, the knocking continued unabated. Finally, summoning every ounce of courage she possessed, Agatha decided to open the door. A silent prayer escaped her lips, "Oh god, please save me!" With her eyes tightly shut, she reached for the latch. A loud screech pierced the silence as the door swung wide open. Expecting the worst, Agatha braced herself. But then, a familiar voice, laced with tension, broke through her fear. "Whooo switched off all the lights?" Agatha cautiously opened her eyes. Standing before her was Christy, his face etched with worry and a hint of fear. A wave of relief washed over her. It was just Christy. "It was me," Agatha replied with a nervous smile. Christy's tension didn't ease. "At least see if someone is outside or not! You scared me to the core!" he exclaimed, a forced smile now playing on his lips. It was then that the realization dawned on Agatha. The brave brother who had regaled her with tales of his courage was just as scared of the dark and the unknown as she was. A giggle escaped her lips, which soon turned into full-fledged laughter. Christy, the self-proclaimed brave heart, had been terrified by a locked door and a switched-off light. His heroic stories suddenly seemed less convincing. That night became a turning point for Agatha. She learned a valuable lesson: true courage lies in facing one's fears, and often, the things we fear the most are not as daunting as they seem. It was with courage that one could confront any situation and emerge stronger. A few days later, the vacation drew to a close. Agatha bid farewell to her beloved village and her family. As the train pulled away, she waved back to Christy and her other brothers, carrying with her not just fond memories, but also the newfound courage she had discovered in the quiet darkness of Alappuzha. She knew she would see them all again in her next vacation, ready to share new stories and perhaps even a laugh about the night the lights went out.
author: Aishwarya Nambiar
illustrator: Aditi Mahapatra; Biplob Chakroborty; Henu; Kalyani  Ganapathy; Krishna Bala Shenoi; Partho Sengupta; Siddhi   Vartak; Sushant Ahire; Tapas Guha; Tarique Aziz; Zainab Tambawalla

title: Kavya: Queen of Oops!
text: Kavya was known far and wide—not for her genius,not for her charm, but for her clumsiness. Her life was basically a blooper reel in HD One fine day, Kavya finished her studies and wanted to hear some music, She was very fond of music,she plugged her earphones in her ear and and was walking toward her bed she bumped into the bed.. 'ouchhh that hurts' she expressed. After few seconds she talks to herself 'where are my earphones?, not again where did I keep it...' she started searching for her earphones in the drawer and created a mess in the room but couldn't find her earphones. She then thought to herself "that bunty must have taken my earphones, BUNTYYYYYY...." She yells. She bashed into his room and asked, "it's you, right who took my earphones right,can't you buy your own earphones why you are using my earphones?" Bunty was in shock and disbelief with wide eyes opened he said, "Kavya kindly go and look yourself in mirror" She looked herself in mirror with complete shock and in her mind she thought, was it there all this time?? and bunty replies as if he understood her facial expressions "indeed yes, they're in your ears all this time...hahahah...." So this was clumsy and forgetful Kavya... The girl who searched every corner of the house—under the sofa, inside the fridge, even behind the curtains— all while her earphones were already in her ears. The next morning, Kavya woke up in her messy room and got freshed had breakfast and as usual she wore spectacles and was on her phone watching movies Kavya gets a call from her friend and slides her specs up. "Hello, yes sara?" Her friend says, "Kavya, we got an important college mail you haven’t checked or replied. Sir asked me to remind you!" Kavya gasps,"Oh no, I totally forgot! Thanks, Sara!" She hangs up, rushes to check her mail but couldn't see clearly. Confused, she starts searching for her specs not realizing they’re still on her head. Kavya was looking around "Arghhh... where did I keep my spectacles?!, I have to reply to that mail and i can't read a thing without them! she created a mess while searching " Ugh! Where did I put them? I just had them!, I can't see anything properly... this is so annoying!" “chiku!” she called, picking up her very unimpressed cat. “Did you see my specs? Did you hide them again?Don’t play innocent with me!" Chiku blinked. Slowly. Judgingl y. As she didn't receive any reply from cat frustrated kavya started pacing in her room and then suddenly she saw her face in the mirror and she realised it was above her head,she gave a relief sigh" Thank goodness I found it" she was laughing to herself. After all the searching, the confusion,even accusing her poor cat, the silly moments, and her brother's endless teasing.Kavya was still a happy girl. She laughed at herself, hugged her cat, and carried on with her day,r eady for the next disaster. Because that’s just who she is, Clumsy. Funny. Full of chaos. But always cheerful. Always Kavya.
author: Carmeline  Dsouza
illustrator: Carmeline  Dsouza; Jayesh Sivan; Joe Werna; Karen  Vermeulen; Moses  Dhladhla; Rijuta Ghate; Samidha Gunjal

title: THE MISSING MARBLES
text: In the peaceful little town of Willow Creek, time moved a bit more slowly. Neat rows of houses lined the cobbled streets, and tall willow trees swayed gently by the river that curled around the town like a silver ribbon. Children played hopscotch on sidewalks, neighbors greeted each other with warm smiles, and the town square, with its old clock tower, chimed every hour like a heartbeat. Among the many children of Willow Creek was a boy named Samir, who lived with his parents and younger sister in a cozy yellow house with blue shutters. Samir was eleven years old, with curious brown eyes, messy black hair that always looked windblown, and a habit of daydreaming during class. He was known for two things: his big imagination and his even bigger collection of marbles. Samir’s marbles weren’t just toys to him—they were treasures. He kept them polished, counted, and sorted in a soft cloth pouch. There were shiny ones like glass raindrops, others with colorful swirls trapped inside like frozen fireworks, and his most prized possession: a rare glow-in-the-dark marble he called “The Moonstone.” At night, he would hold it up to the light, then watch it glow softly on his windowsill as he drifted to sleep. Everyone at school had heard about the Moonstone, and some kids even came over during recess just to look at it. One sunny morning, Samir brought his pouch of marbles to school to show his best friend Nila. At lunch, he eagerly opened the pouch on their table—and gasped. The Moonstone was missing. “It was right here this morning,” he said, panicked. His heart thudded in his chest. He searched his bag, under the desk, and even retraced his steps to the playground. But the marble was nowhere to be found. “Maybe someone took it,” Nila said gently, not wanting to upset him more. Samir looked around. Only a few classmates had seen the marbles today. Could it have been Jay, the quiet new kid who always stared at his collection? Or Mira, who once asked if she could borrow a marble for “just one day”? But instead of accusing anyone, Samir sat quietly. After a few minutes, he sighed and said, “I’ll give it a day. Maybe someone will return it.” The next morning, something surprising happened. When Samir entered the classroom, he noticed something on his desk—a small envelope. Inside was the Moonstone, glowing faintly in the light, along with a folded piece of paper. “I’m sorry. I was jealous and took your marble without asking. I felt bad all night. I hope you can forgive me.” (There was no name.) Samir stared at the note, then at the Moonstone resting in his palm. He could have shown it to the teacher. He could have tried to guess who wrote it. But instead, he smiled slightly, placed the Moonstone gently back in his pouch. He picked up his pen and wrote, “Thank you for being honest. I forgive you.” He left the note on the desk where the envelope had been. From that day on, no one ever stole from Samir again. He never found out who had taken the marble—but deep down, he didn’t need to. He knew he had done the right thing. And sometimes, that was enough. MORAL: Sometimes, forgiveness helps people become better. Giving others a chance to make things right is a sign of true strength.
author: Sebastina  Durairaj

title: Snow Ice Cream
text: Snow ice cream, Snow ice- cream, Dolma’s awaited winter’s dream. She hops around, under the blue sky, Chasing butterflies around the marigold fields, In her mind all she could think was snow ice cream. The fire crackles, warm and bright, The kitchen is engulfed in its golden light. Dolma sits on a murah, with her chin on her hand. Watching Ama shaping the yeri with care, As Apa sips Sol-Chya, brown and bland. She glances at the rack, where the steel cup lays, A cup of snow ice cream for the winter days. “Snow ice- cream, snow ice- cream! Much better than the broth, at least for me, Snow ice cream, that's the dream.” Dolma and her chizo cleared the kateyra, Collecting the firewood, creating a space to gather for warmth. From a distance, continuous moos and the barks echo. Lhamu aize screams, “ Lu hai chito garum hai! hiw parnu atyo.” The villagers quickly moved to collect hay and straw, Signalling the coming of the snow. With her tummy full and facing the wall, Dolma counts the days until snowfall “Ama, it is going to snow tomorrow, right?” “Maybe, Nani,” Ama replies. “Dolma! Dolma! Come out quickly!” Brush-Wash-Dress, Wearing layers upon layers she takes flight. Outside the door, it’s her favourite sight! Everything is covered up, all in white! “Yangchen, Lakpa!” Dolma runs towards them. Chi- Nhi- Sum, Chi- Nhi- Sum. Rolling balls of snow and throwing them around, They all jumped, making the crunch crunch sound. Dolma scooped up the snow into her steel cup. Her cheeks flushed red as she gobbled it up. “Aiya! My teeth hurt, my teeth hurt,” Dolma screams. “Mine too,” her friends laugh, gulping down their own snow ice-cream. One scoop, two scoop, three scoop – four, Until Ama stopped them from eating more. Now, with their tummy full of ice, Holding up the cup, they all smiled.
author: Tashi Chong Sherpa

title: Yapom
text: The grass used to be green; the trees were spread all over. There was a forest here, once. There was much din and chatter. I move from here to there. I am a homeless wanderer. I stare all around me and still wonder when all this changed. Round and round his bicycle goes, I see his ane and abo leave each morning in their big, big cars. Does he not miss his parents? Does he not feel my presence? Oh, he is looking around. I wonder… Does he see me? He sure reminds me of someone. My son. Oh, how my heart aches for my little one. I wonder if he is playing somewhere too. I should not have left him alone. I should not have let him go. Is it me he is talking to? He can see me? Oh, how wonderful is that! “Who… who are you?” “Come here,” I gently swoop up this child. “Where am I? Where am I?” he frantically cries. Why is he crying? What have I done? I only wanted to have some fun. But the boy keeps shouting, “Let me go!” Ah! He is afraid. “You are free to go,” I calmly say. I only wanted to talk, not harm him. “Who are you?” he asks again. “I am a yapom. I’ve known you long. Your house is where we once lived by.” “Really? How? That’s my HOUSE?” he gushes. “I was here long before any of your ancestors,” I reply. “Friends and family moved away, but I could not leave it all behind.” “Don’t you miss them?” leaves his lips, as he leans closer to me and offers his little hand. For so long, high up and lonely, I had been on the hirek tree. Has he guessed my need for company? “I do miss them, but I can’t leave for the unknown,” is my quiet response. “My son, oh, he left with them, too. Thinking of him, I kept looking at you. That’s why, perched upon my tree’s branch, I have watched your daily dance.” “Oh, I never knew that you were watching me, as I spent my days playing around.” “You should have come to me. We could have played many games. I wouldn’t have been so lonely then.” “You say that now, but wouldn’t have so, when people around would have riled and raged.” “Do you hear the car’s honk?” “Oh, I do. Sadly, I do.” He seems to want to linger, but he has to go. “You should go home, now. I’ll watch from afar.” *HONK!* This day will be a blur to him. But I will keep this memory. And watch from afar, again. Waiting at my lonely tree.
author: Moge Basar

title: Summer Adventures
text: Summer Adventures By Dr. Cerena D'Cunha It was the first day of summer break, and the sun blazed like a golden spotlight over the small town of Willowbend. Four best friends—Liam, Arjun, Mateo, and Zeke—were out on their bikes, riding aimlessly along the dusty river path, looking for something epic to do. That’s when they saw it. A boat. Old, wooden, but still floating. Tied loosely to a crooked post on the riverside. “Guys,” Liam said, hopping off his bike. “Adventure awaits.” Moments later, the boys were pushing off from the shore, paddling down the gentle current with wide grins and zero plans. As the boat floated lazily down the river, Mateo pointed. “Look! Over there!” On the far bank, a group of animals stood stranded—two goats, a scruffy dog, and a baby deer, all looking confused and unsure how to cross back to safety. “Rescue mission time!” shouted Zeke. They steered the boat to the riverbank and, one by one, helped the animals into the boat. It was a bit of a squeeze, but somehow they all fit—four boys, four animals, and a boat creaking under the weight of spontaneous heroism. Then came the elephant. A massive one, half-submerged in the river, flapping its ears and blowing bubbles through its trunk. It looked at the boat, clearly amused, and before anyone could stop it, lifted one big, soggy foot… SPLASH! The boat flipped like a pancake. Boys, goats, dog, deer—all tumbled into the warm, shallow water. For a second, there was chaos—splashing, shouting, barking. And then, laughter. The boys laughed till their sides hurt. The deer pranced in the shallows. The dog shook water all over everyone. Even the elephant let out a joyful trumpet, clearly proud of the surprise splash party. By the time they got back to shore—soaked, muddy, and grinning—the sun was setting, painting the river gold. “Best. Day. Ever,” Arjun said, flopping down on the grass. And no one argued.
author: Cerena D'Cunha
illustrator: Iddi  Marumba; Olivia Villet; Rachel Greer

title: The Heroes of Tarifa
text: Stormy waves crashed against the rocky beach of Tarifa as Marco sat on the sand lost in thought thinking about the misfortune his family had been going through for the past few decades. He thought about how his family had helped their town and protected those who needed them, even after all of this nobody respected them always judging them by their economical status. He suddenly remembered that Emma, Alexa and Leonardo were paying him a visit. He scrambled up and made his way back to his boat house. He cleaned things up a bit and set the table for supper. He couldn’t even sit down before he heard a knock on the door and opened it to realise it was his ever punctual cousins. All of them were going through a lot but they managed to keep a bright face and Marco really admired them for that. He kept a bright face and greeted them in. Leonardo at once started cracking jokes to lighten the mood. He felt at ease when he was with his family but the things they were going to talk about brought a frown to his face. All of them had decided that they couldn’t live the way they were and wanted to do something about it. Alexa had come up with an idea of finding their Great-Grandfather long lost treasure, it felt like a far fetched idea but it was all they had got. Everyone tried brainstorming ways of finding it until Emma hit the bull’s eye. She explained how she had been trying to figure out about the piece of parchment that they had inherited from their great grandfather Silverbeard and asked if everybody had their piece. Suprisingly, all of them had it with them. They each drew their parchment piece out of a velvet lined pouch and placed it on the table. Everyone looked at their own piece. Emma’s had an island in the shape of a skeleton, Leonardo had the Silvershore island marked, Alexa had the Alboran sea marked and finally Marco had a X marked between two points supposedly the Silvershore island and Skeleton island in the strait of Gibraltar. Everyone woke up to the first rays of sun and packed the basic essentials rope, torches, blankets, tins of soup, loaves of bread, canned pineapple, oxygen masks and spades. They settled in the Schooner and Marco took the rudder while Emma navigated. The cousins were joking and laughing aboard the boat unaware that their unknown “arch-nemesis” had spotted them. One-eyed Bill was a descendent of Black beard who played a vital role in the sinking of Silverbeard’s ship. One eyed Bill had been waiting to get his hands on Silverbeard’s treasure since birth and now the cousins were leading him right to it. After a tiring 3 hours of journey the cousins arrived at the shore of Silvershore island. They took a break there for breakfast and relaxed for about an hour until they took the Schooner and tried to locate the sunken ship. Approximately in between the Silvershore island and Skeleton island, Leonardo, Alexa and Marco already in diving gear leaped in to the sea to uncover the sunken ship while Emma kept Almanda the Schooner aloft. After just 30 minutes the cousins came up to the shore holding a golden doubloon, they had found the treasure! They hadn’t brought all of it up as it was a lot of load and Leonardo was starting to feel uncomfortable under water. They made their way back to Silvershore island with joyful faces and set up camp for the night. After a night of peaceful sleep the cousins woke up in the morning to realise Almanda was gone. Panic struck them like lightning and they rushed to the shore hoping it had just drifted away. But the truth stood anchored in the distance, the Almanda their Schooner was tied to a massive black ship with a pirate skull floating eerily near Skeleton Island. They stared in shock as none of them had expected something like this. The ship was unlike anything they had ever seen. Marco’s eyes narrowed as he said they needed to get to their Schooner somehow and the only way to do it quietly was to build a raft. The cousins worked together using logs, ropes and palm branches and after hours of hard work the raft was finally ready. It was decided that only Marco and Alexa would go, while Emma and Leonardo would stay back and keep watch. As the raft built by the cousins approached the huge ship, a tall man stepped onto the deck. He had a deep scar running down one side of his face and wore a dark Eyepatch over his right eye. He introduced himself in a rough voice as One-Eyed Bill, the great-grandson of Blackbeard who had once been Silverbeard’s greatest enemy. He said he had been waiting his whole life to find Silverbeard’s treasure and that the cousins had led him right to it. Marco wanting to uphold his family honour, stepped forward and challenged Bill to a duel. He said that if he lost, he would hand over the treasure map, but if he won, One-Eyed Bill would give up his ship and the Almanda. The pirate agreed with a crooked grin and pulled out his sword. The deck turned silent as the two faced off. The duel was fierce. Marco moved quickly, dodging and blocking Bill’s heavy swings. Alexa watched from the side, barely able to breathe. At last, with one fast move, Marco knocked Bill’s sword out of his hand and held his own sword to Bill’s chest. Everyone froze! Without saying a word, One-Eyed Bill slowly walked to the edge of the ship. He stood on the plank, ready to jump into the sea. But just before he could take the step, Marco stopped him. He said he wasn’t going to throw anyone into the ocean, even if they were enemies. Bill looked surprised, but said nothing. He climbed into a lifeboat and rowed away into the sea without another word. Once he was gone, Marco and Alexa signalled to Emma and Leonardo. The cousins climbed aboard the ship and started planning their next move. They decided to go back into the sea one last time to get the rest of the treasure. Using the ropes, sacks and pulleys from Bill’s ship, they dove into the deep blue waters and brought up chest after chest filled with gold coins, silver bars, and sparkling jewels. That night, they sat on the deck, tired but happy. They divided half the treasure equally among the four of them. The other half, they agreed, would be given to the poor people of Tarifa, who had worked hard all their lives but had always been looked down on. As the sun rose the next morning, the cousins set sail two ships now under their command, their hearts full of pride. They had faced danger and uncovered their family’s treasure and still chosen to share it. They all knew that their family’s brave and noble acts would now be recognised. Their family’s beacon would showcase courage, kindness and perseverance.
author: Bhanvi Naveen

title: Max and the Lost Kitten
text: Max was a small brown dog. He lived in a big park with many trees and flowers. Max was friendly, but he had no close friends. Every day, he walked around the park alone. One sunny morning, Max heard a soft sound. "Meow… meow…" He looked around and saw a tiny kitten under a bench. The kitten was white and gray. She looked scared and cold. “Hello, little kitten,” Max said kindly. “Are you lost?” “Yes,” said the kitten. “I can’t find my home.” “Don’t worry,” said Max. “I will help you.” Max and the kitten walked together. They asked the birds, the squirrels, and even the old owl, “Have you seen the kitten’s home?” “No,” they all said, “but keep looking!” Max gave the kitten some water and shared his biscuit. They sat under a tree and talked. The kitten’s name was Luna. She liked butterflies and soft pillows. “I like you, Max,” said Luna. “You are kind.” “I like you too, Luna,” said Max. “You are funny and sweet.” Suddenly, Luna jumped up. “That house! I remember it!” They ran to the small yellow house near the park. A girl opened the door. “Luna!” she shouted. “You’re home!” The girl hugged Luna and thanked Max. “You are a good friend.” Max smiled. He felt happy. He walked home, but now he was not alone. Every day, Luna came to play in the park. Max and Luna were best friends forever.
author: Ali İhsan

title: Aksara's Loose Tooth
text: There was a girl named Aksara.One day she has a loose tooth. She went to her mother and asked for help! Her mother said " Don't worry let me help you! Her mother tied a string in her loose tooth and pulled up. But it didn't come out as expected. Her mother tried everything to take out the loose tooth. Then the nightdrew she went to sleep. The next day her tooth came out,She shouted "MOMMYYYYY MY TOOTH CAME OUT",Her mother ran to her with cheerful and said "Good! finally your tooth came out". After that she was happy and enjoyed playing with her friends. Aksara was free happily ever after!!!
author: Lepaacshi Sathyarajan

title: Runaways These Days
text: It was a windy, freezing evening in NY. The clumsy, foolish dorks who mustered up enough courage to walk on the pavement in T-shirts and Nikes looked like ice creams from the freezer, the petunias in the neighbor’s garden resembled icicles from the North Pole, and trees sagged like hunchbacks in their eighties. However, Daisy Drive No. 9’s residents, Patrick, the daddy, Rebecca, the mom, and Grace, the daughter, were as cool as cucumbers, as their walls were quite thick. They were enjoying a lavish dinner of broiled spiced veal, warm white macaroni and cheese, hot fried potatoes, tender grilled chicken and blueberry pie for dessert. Then they happily tidied up, not aware of a danger that would befall Grace. The next morning, Patrick and Rebecca woke up. Patrick walked into Grace’s room to wake her up, but she wasn’t there. He told Rebecca and they both searched every nook and cranny of their house and they found a pair of footprints near the door, but they weren’t Grace’s size. After an hour of searching, they took the matter to the police. “Choo’ bunch doin’ ‘ere, eh?’’ questioned Sergeant Thomas, chewing on a Boston Cream and twirling his keys as if they were toy ballerinas. “Murder? Runaway? Rob-’’ "Yeah, I think runaway is it. Don’t ramble on, Tom,’’ Patrick replied, clearly irritated and a bit sad. “Oh, the pity! Why, oh why did it have to be her? Why couldn’t it have been you?” sobbed Rebecca. “Rebecca,’’ said Patrick in a menacing tone. “Just start, Tom, my dear,’’ said Rebecca, a bit more comfortable. “Righto, on it,’’ replied Thomas, cheeks as red as tomatoes. He told his fellow police employees to file a report for Grace. Some police officers thought it had something to do with a few disappearances going on with the kids who go to bed but disappear, but Tom ignored them. After a day, they started the search. Krrrrrrrrrk went Grace’s claws. She was captured by the MSUM, a place where little kids who go to bed are captured at midnight and genetically modified to become coldhearted monsters who are merciless. She roared a horrifying, beastly roar, one that pierced the monsters’ eardrums. In a ghastly voice, she growled, “Food!’’ and a bunch of miniscule monsters the size of cookie crumbs carried a piece of what looked like sausages from a dog’s restroom break. Grace wolfed it down in an instant, but her nose suddenly started burning. In exactly one minute, the Fire-o-Meter went to ten, her eyes turned bright red, and a bit of Monsta-Gasoline was right next to her hand. Her mouth started smoking, and suddenly, the MSUM was a pile of ashes, but Grace somehow survived. She jumped out the window and flew all the way to her house in NYC. At this point, the whole of New York could see this bone-chilling creature. Patrick stepped out of his house and gaped at Grace. He could see it was her; the big eyes, soft face, pursed lips. Even through Grace’s buffalo skin, Patrick could see what her real personality was. Without a hint of fear, hesitation or embarrassment, he walked to the spot where Grace was and embraced her then and there. Grace turned into a human the very second and walked back home with a wide smile. They lived happily ever after……..or did they now?
author: Sowmya Rajan
illustrator: Abhishikta Dutta; Johan Jubin; Sonia Dearling; Sunaina  Coelho

title: Meena's Market Math
text: One sunny afternoon, Meena and her mother set out for the bustling local market. The air smelled of fresh vegetables, and the sounds of bargaining echoed from every corner. First they stopped at the cloth shop. Her mother wanted to buy lining cloth to stitch a blouse and a dress. " I need 80 centimetres of lining cloth, "her mother told to the shopkeeper. The shopkeeper smiled, "1 metre is ₹30, madam. You can calculate the cost." Meena's eyes sparkled, She loved numbers, but sometimes they danced too fast in her head. She quickly tried to divide and multiply but got confused. Seeing her struggle, her mother gently placed a hand on her shoulder and said,"Slow down, dear. Think step by step." So Meena took a deep breath and tried again. Okay... 80 centimetre is 80 divided by 100, which is 0.8 metres," she whispered to herself. "Now, 0.8 times ₹ 30 is...... ₹ 24, right?" The shopkeeper nodded, "Exactly!" Meena felt a little taller just then. Later, they stopped by the fish shop. Her mother pointed at a large shiny fish. 'Let's get one," she said. The shopkeeper weighed it. "This one is 770 grams. 1 kilogram is ₹ 300." She paused and calculated slowly. "0.77 times 300 is.... ₹231!" Her mother smiled proudly." Correct again!" As they walked home with their shopping bags full, Meena felt proud. thought math was something that belonged in classrooms and notebooks. But today, she saw it comes alive- in cloths, in fish, in money. It wasn't just numbers; it was a part of her world. Have you ever used math while shopping or cooking? How did it help you? Why is it important to understand simple calculations in our daily life?
author: Sowjanya Sundar
illustrator: 48 Arti; Deepa Balsavar; Henu; Rijuta Ghate; Santosh Pujari

title: Fraction fun in Pizza Party
text: It was a sunny Saturday afternoon, and Rohan's family had decided to throw a pizza party for his birthday. Rohan's mom had ordered a large pizza that was cut into 16 equal slices. Rohan's friends, Aisha and Karan, were thrilled to see the pizza and couldn't wait to dig in. Rohan's mom asked him to serve the pizza to his friends. Rohan gave Aisha half of the pizza, which was 8 slices. Karan was given one-quarter of the pizza, which was 4 slices. Rohan decided to keep 2 slices for himself. The Fraction Fun Begins: Aisha was thrilled with her half - pizza and exclaimed, " Wow, I got 8 slices! That's half of the total pizza!" Rohan Smiled and said, " That's right, Aisha! you got of the pizza." Karan, who got one- quarter of the pizza, asked,"Rohan, how much of the pizza did I get?" Rohan replied, " you got 4 slices, Karan! that's or of the pizza." Rohan's mom was impressed with the kids' understanding of fractions and said, "you all are doing a great job with fractions! keep it up!" As Karan reviewed what he had learnt about fractions on the way back home..... Aisha got of the pizza which is also, myself got of the pizza which is equal to and Rohan got of pizza which is equal to. Finally he was very happy hat he learnt the concept well.
author: Vidya Arunkumar
illustrator: Abhishikta Dutta; Brian Wambi; Hylton Warburton; Kishor Joshi; Pranaya  Chaudhry; Sowndarya Velmurugan

title: THE GREEDY PERSON
text: There was a man who was so greedy in a town. While he was walking in a street he saw a gold bar. He took it to his home and dug a hole near his house and kept his gold bar in that hole. He always went to see it and one day a Business man followed him and saw that he was hiding a gold bar in that small hole. one day when the greedy person went to see the gold bar suddenly it was missing because the Business man stole it. He screamed a lot that some people wanted to know what happened. The greedy man said every thing what happened. One man came forward and said '' keep a rock instead of that gold bar in the hole. '' he said. The greedy man agreed and said '' yes''. From that day onwards he did the same as what the person told and he was never greedy from that day onwards.
author: Ramachandra pola

title: Charcoal

title: Lost in Ultapani
text: “Shoooo!!! Go Away!” “Ahhhhhh!!!!” “Ouch!” “Mama!!!!!!!!?” “Wahhhh, Mama!!!!!!!” “Ah dear, here you go.” “Now, is that better?” “Thank…thank you. Who are you?” “My name is Jwngthi. What happened to you?” “A fire came and we ran away. I lost Mama in the chaos and now I cannot find her.” “Oh you must be hungry! Follow me, I will get you something to eat.” “Oh no!” “What is that?” * GROWL * “Thank you!” “Do not go there! That’s a swamp!” “Ahhh” “Come on, follow me.” “Here, eat this!” “Nommm..…nommm…Yummy!” “Hehehe I think I am messy.” “Come along.” “Hahahahaha.” *Splash* *Splash!* “Hahahahaha.” “Huh!” “When will I find my mama?” “Soon, my friend” “What about your family? Where are they?” “A huge fire came and took them away…..” “But do not worry about your family. They will come look for you.” “Get some rest now.” “Wow” “Mama?” *Rustle rustle* “Mama!!! I am so happy to see you!” “The fireflies led us to you!” “Huh? Where did Jwngthi go?” About the story Ultapani Forest Block Village is a biodiversity area situated under Holtugaon Forest Division of Manas Biosphere reserve situated in Kokrajhar district, Assam, India. The name literally translates as ‘The Reverse Water’ that flows through the forest from west to east, although other rivers most likely flow from east to west. It is close to the Indo-Bhutan border; settlements of Bodo and Nepali communities can be found in the area. Ultapani is known as the “Haven of Butterfly” and is the native habitat of several rare, threatened, and endangered (RET) species, including the Golden Langur and the well-known Great Pied Hornbill. Another asset of Ultapani Reserve Forest is its orchids. Unfortunately, the overuse of forest resources have put this forest's important asset under jeopardy. It negatively impacts the ecological balance and causes numerous issues for wild creatures. Ultapani is also a abode of spirits and deities, there are frequent occurrences of paranormal activities happening inside the forest and village areas. Jwngthi is based on a mythical dwarf spirit that resides in the jungle of Ultapani Village. Many people residing in the village are said to have encountered this spirit. The spirit is said to have not been harmful in anyway, but rather mischievous. It is believed that he has been living there for ages.

title: Little Big Things
text: Once upon a time, in a sunny jungle, there lived a tiny baby elephant named Mira. Mira had the biggest, fluffiest ears and the tiniest, wiggliest trunk. She was absolutely enchanted by everything that was small and cute. Lucky for Mira, the jungle was full of delightful little wonders! A nd so, Mira always had a smile on her face and a dance in her steps! When the clouds rolled in and the wind whooshed through the trees, little Mira would swing with the breeze, her floppy ears flapping and a friendly honeybee buzzing by her side. She would splash in puddles with a croaky frog on a shiny rock, both of them giggling in their own funny ways. Rainy days, like all days, were full of tiny wonders—and Mira never missed a chance to play! In the daytime, Mira would find a little sunflower to play hide-and-seek with, its golden petals tickling her ears as a fluttery butterfly danced by—her tiny, twirly friend. And at night, when the sky turned deep and the stars blinked awake, she would curl up beside a softly purring cat, their dreams tangled together in the hush of moonlight. Whether it was bright and sunny or calm and quiet, Mira always found a little magic to hold close. On one such happy day, Mira snuggled close to her mama beneath the wide, leafy arms of a big mango tree. The air smelled sweet and a cheeky monkey swung lazily from a low branch, watching them with curious eyes. Mama smiled, brushing a leaf from Mira’s head. “Tell me, my little one,” she asked softly, “how are you such a warm bundle of joy?” Mira looked around, her voice bright and certain, like she was telling a secret she’d always known. "My dearest Mama, my curious eyes seek small, silly wonders that make my big heart beat with joy!” A honeybee caught her attention as she continued in that thoughtful-little-elephant way of hers- “The world is full of these little treasures…I just have to keep looking!"
author: Mansi Sharma

title: The Fishing Trip
text: Thoni had a plan. “I will catch so many fish today.” “Nu, I want to eat fish curry! Take me fishing.” “Not today, Thoni,” Nu replied. But Thoni wanted to eat fish curry today. “I will go by myself!” “Thoni, where are you going?” asked Niffu. “I am going fishing for fish curry!” “Fishing? Do you even know how to fish?” “You will see!” “Bubu, Come with us!”, Thoni and Niffu called out. “But fishing will be fun! Do you not want to eat a delicious fish curry?” “No, no, I cannot” said Bubu. “If I am late, my Nu will scold me.” “Delicious fish…” “Lots of delicious fish!” “Let’s Go!” “Fishing is not as easy as it looks.” “Do not worry, you will catch some fish, Thoni.” “This isn’t fair!” *Rustle Rustle* Who? What? Oh! Oh No! Huh! “OH. It is just foolish Jamdai!” “Huh! I have seen my mother fishing many times. I know exactly how to catch fish!” Thoni retorted. “Trying to catch some fish, I see. But you are not doing it right.” “Really? Then show me the fish you have caught?” “Haha, why don't I show you a better way to catch fish? With a little magic of mine. Now, calm your tempers and watch carefully” “Oh, and give me a snack, please” “Hmmmm... nom... nom... nom... fish, appear, fish, appear.” “Get ready to catch some fish!” “Whoa! Look at them, let us catch them all!” “So many fish!” “STOP! Take only what you need. Leave the rest” “But why?” “If we take everything today, there will be none left for tomorrow” “But why?” “It is really not magic, you see. I only used some roots to make the fish a little drowsy. This makes them float on the surface so we may catch them easily.” “Jamdai, what is the secret behind your magic trick?” “But would it not be easier to use an electric machine than some leaf or root?” “My uncle uses a battery made electric machine to catch a lot of fish, as it shocks them” “It is true, you can catch a lot of fish and catch them quickly with the machine…” “But the machine kills the fishes, their eggs, and harms them before they even have a chance to grow” “It is important to think about the future as well” “Hmmmmm” “That’s so sad.” “You are right.” “Bye Bye Jamdai. Thank you!” “Go on, now. It is getting late” “How did you catch so many fishes?” “Nu we are back!” “Come along! I will make some fish curry.” “We had some help,” Thoni replied. And they all enjoyed the delicious fish curry! “ Thank you Jamdai! ” the three children silently whispered
author: Thomas Malsom

title: Piku and the Light Within
text: If there was any adventure to be had, Piku was always the first to jump in. She loved climbing trees, leading treasure hunts up the hill, swimming in the stream nearby, cycling along winding roads and just being outside - wild and free. And if being outside meant playing with her friends, that was even better. Every evening, Piku, her friends Maya, Priya and Deepu and several other children from the neighbourhood would gather to play games, fly kites or race each other across the hilly slopes near their homes. Everyone admired Piku's adventurous spirit. She always made every game feel like an exciting quest. When summer vacation began, the children could play all day long. One evening when they were in the middle of a game, Maya's mother called her in for dinner. Maya didn't want the fun to end. She suddenly had an idea, "Why don't we plan a camping trip? That way we can play together at night too." The other children lit up with excitement and agreed right away. They shared their plans with their parents the next day. It was soon decided that Maya's older brother and Deepu's older sister, both in college, would join them as supervisors. Everyone was thrilled. They began packing for the one-night adventure - snacks, sleeping bags and loads of games to play through the day and into the night. Well everyone, except one. Piku wasn't so sure about the plan. It wasn't the day she was worried about - it was the night. A night out in the open, in the dark wilderness, with no lights around!! How will I manage? What if I get scared? What do I tell my friends? What if they laugh at me? Piku wrestled with her fear but couldn't bring herself to tell her friends. So she ended up agreeing to go on the trip. The night before, she lay in bed, tangled in worry, staring at the soft shadows on her wall, bathed in the warm glow of her not-so-small night lamp. On the day of the camping trip, the kids jumped out of bed bright and early, buzzing with excitement. Backpacks on and water bottles clinking, they set off together, chatting and laughing as they followed the forest path. They crossed a wooden bridge over a bubbling stream, listened to the rustling leaves and bird song and finally arrived at a sunny meadow, surrounded by tall trees - their campsite for the night! The two young adults guided the children as they pitched their tents. It wasn't easy. The poles wobbled and the ropes tangled, but everyone was eager to try and do it on their own. There were a lot of giggles, a few "Oops!" and finally loud cheers as the tents stood tall. They kept their bags inside and stepped out to have fun. The children spent the day joyfully tossing balls, skipping ropes and running around in endless games of tag. Laughter echoed through the meadow as the sun slowly made its way across the sky. As the evening drew closer the children decided to play hide and seek near the trees, giggling as they darted behind trunks and bushes. Slowly, the light began to fade and long shadows crept across the meadow. The elder siblings called out, urging everyone to leave their hiding spots and gather in the open space near the tents where they had lit a small bonfire. The soft glow of the flame flickered across their faces as they sat in a circle, unwrapping their dinner and sharing stories under the darkening sky. After dinner the children headed into their tents and lit up torches. The tents glowed softly in the darkness, like little lanterns in the meadow. They snuggled into their cozy sleeping bags and played board games, their laughter and cheerful chatter echoing into the night. As yawns grew louder than the giggles, the children slowly drifted off to sleep under the starry sky. Well everyone, except one. All the torch lights were off. Her friends were fast asleep, but Piku couldn’t close her eyes. She just didn’t like sleeping in the dark. Every creak, every shadow, seemed like a monster lurking. Quietly, she unzipped the tent and stepped out. She sat near the bonfire, its gentle glow keeping her company in the quiet night. Sitting there, fidgeting restlessly, Piku remembered something her grandmother once told her- "Fear is like a balloon, the more you blow into it, the bigger it gets. But if you face it, even a little at a time, it slowly begins to shrink." She held on to those words, staring into the flickering firelight, wondering if maybe, just maybe, she could try. Piku took a deep breath. She began paying attention to the sounds she had found scary before, the owl’s hoot, the rustling leaves, the gurgle of the stream and realized they were just the forest whispering its own bedtime story. Then she looked around at the shadows. “Crickity-Crack,” she whispered to the one near the tent pole. “Shadow Noodles” danced near the trees. And that one by the log? Definitely a “Giggly-Wiggly.” Soon, the dark didn’t seem that scary at all. Slowly, her breathing settled. She smiled as the clouds drifted by, forming silly shapes in the sky. The stars sparkled gently, and the crescent moon hung like a glowing brushstroke in a peaceful painting. Feeling lighter, Piku tiptoed back into her tent, snuggled into her sleeping bag and drifted into a sound sleep. Waking up to the soft sunlight and fresh morning breeze was a magical experience for all the children. They packed up their games, rolled up their sleeping bags, folded the tents and got ready to leave. As they walked back home through the forest and across the stream, their laughter echoed through the trees. They sang songs, already dreaming of their next adventure. The experience at the campsite made Piku realize that the dark wasn't scary after all - it was her own imagination playing tricks. From that night on, Piku carried with her a quiet confidence. She called it her light within. She had learned that when we take time to u nderstand what we’re afraid of, the fear starts to shrink, just like her grandma had said. Courage doesn’t mean you’re never scared. I t means you try your best even when you are!
author: Garima Sinha

title: WATER BIRDS
text: How lovely are the water birds. Colorful and beautiful, water birds. How cute does the quacking duck look. We learn to work hard and stay focused from the heron, it waits patiently to catch fish. The cranes teach us to stay together. See how proud the big-beaked pelican looks in the water. Only our friendship can protect the beautiful world of birds. We must work together to make sure no one hurts them.

title: ON HIS WAY TO THE MOON
text: Krish was a little boy who loved the moon more than anything in the world. He got his love for moon from his mother who said fascinating stories about the moon. He dreamed of flying to the moon using helium balloons sold by the street vendor Somu who sold a variety of random things in his bicycle(from grocery to stationery) AFTER A FEW YEARS, Now krish is in grade 7. He discovers at school that he can only go to the moon by travelling in a rocket and not using helium balloons. He sets his eyes on becoming a astronaut(People who travel to space in rockets). YEARS later, after completing his degree in IIT (Indian Institute Of Technology). He got his job in ISRO (Astronauts typically need a master's degree in a STEM field (Science, Technology, Engineering, or Mathematics) and experience in their field). The Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO) After 3 years, Finally he got selected as an astronaut in the GAGANYAAN MISSION(ISRO is launching this mission in the 2027). Krish was subjected to rigorous training and severe health checkup to get ready for the mission. After years of hard work and dedication Krish succeeded in reaching his dream of becoming a astronaut who went to moon. " dream is not that you see in sleep, dream is something that does not let you sleep." - A.P.J. ABDUL KALAM (INDIA'S MISSILE MAN) SOME FAMOUS ASTRONAUTS OF INDIA KALPANA CHAWALA Kalpana Chawla was the first woman of Asian origin to go to space. She was an Indian-American astronaut and aerospace engineer. She achieved this milestone by flying on Space Shuttle Columbia (STS-87) in 1997.
