title: THE TIME MACHINE OF FAMOUS FIVE
text: THE TIME MACHINE OF FAMOUS FIVE BY ADVIT MEHRA Once there were 5 friends, Fatty, Larry, Daisy, Pip and Bets. they live in Peterswood which is far away from school. On going towards the school they found a huge machine. Fatty said to his friends, "lets go there and have a look". On checking the machine they found out that it's a Time Machine. Bets suggested, "Friends we are already late for the school. So let's try this machine, if it can help us reach school in time". Pip added " and save us from scolding of Miss Meenu". Everyone laughed and they started exploring the machine. Soon they fed the time as 7am instead of 7:30am but forgot to change the year and switched on the machine. Within fraction of seconds they reached to a hilly place where there were no humans. Daisy said " let's go towards that tree as I can see some leaves moving there". As soon as they reached near the tree, they were all shocked and couldn't believe their eyes. Behind the trees their was a huge valley where many Dinosaurs were sleeping. They started running towards the machine but by now it was fully surrounded by Dinosaurs. They move back towards the tree and waited. By late evening all the Dinosaurs moved towards the valley. All the kids couldn't believe their luck. They reached towards the machine, fed all the correct details and reached near the school in time. Fatty shouted " Look there, we got a baby dinosaur in our time machine". They thought of entering the machine again to drop it back home in Dinosaur era, but Mr Goon was coming near them. So they have to hide the machine with leaves. Mr Goon, the policeman thought that there is something fishy. So started looking for it but couldn't find anything. He knew that kids will definitely come back and then he will get to know the conspiracy. When 5 of them arrived, Mr Goon hid behind the bushes. Unaware of Mr Goon's presence kids opened the machine, fed the details and machine suddenly disappeared. Mr Goon couldn't believe his eyes and fainted. Everyone hugged and said good bye to Dino-kid and came back to their Era. They saw Mr Goon lying on the ground and understood the situation. They threw the machine in a deep valley and left from that place. Next Day Mr Goon contacted each one separately to know what happened last night, but everyone made him believe that it must be his dream.
author: Advit Mehra
illustrator: Abeer Jaiswal; Aindri C; Ajay Hembron; Akshaan Jain; Kabini  Amin; Ketan Raut; Prabha  Mallya; Shrijeet Somani

title: A Friendship That Changed Everything
text: About the Author Shah Zeeshan is a young author, speaker, and changemaker from Kashmir, India. Known for his powerful storytelling and deep emotional insight, Zeeshan captures the voices often unheard—especially those of women, dreamers, and rebels in silence. He has been recognized for his eloquence as the Best Speaker at IIMUN and awarded Best Essay Writer by the TATA group. Some friendships are like roaring rivers—loud, fast, and ever-changing. Others are like deep-rooted trees—silent, steadfast, and unshaken by time. The story of Saima and Fareeda was the latter. It was not built on grand moments but on quiet sacrifices, invisible gestures, and a love so deep that it never needed to be spoken aloud. I first heard their story in the old town of Sopore, Kashmir, where the chinar trees whispered secrets of the past and where women like Saima and Fareeda carved spaces for each other in a world that often tried to erase them. Their friendship was not a fleeting phase but a legacy—one that lived on in the lives they touched. The Girl Who Refused to Let Dreams Die:- In the late 1970s, when the world still saw education as a luxury for women, two young girls sat under the shade of an ancient chinar tree, whispering dreams too big for their small town. Saima, the daughter of a bookseller, was born into the comfort of stories and education. Fareeda, the daughter of a struggling farmer, was born into the expectation of sacrifice. From the moment they met, Saima and Fareeda became inseparable. Saima would smuggle books into Fareeda’s home, pushing her to read beyond what their school taught. “If they don’t teach us everything, we will teach ourselves,” she would say. Fareeda, eager but hesitant, feared what her family might say. “One day,” Saima promised, “no one will decide for us.” But fate had other plans:- When Fareeda turned 14, her father fell ill, and her family decided she must leave school to help at home. The night she cried herself to sleep, believing her dreams had ended, Saima had other ideas. Every evening, under the cover of darkness, she would slip into Fareeda’s home, hiding books under her shawl. By candlelight, she became both teacher and friend, making sure Fareeda never fell behind. And when exam results were announced, Fareeda—who had studied in secret—stood among the top scorers. Her father, once certain that education had no place in a girl’s life, wept when he saw her name in the newspaper. “I didn’t know my daughter was this brilliant,” he whispered. Saima had not just taught Fareeda—she had taught a father to believe in his daughter’s worth. But life would not allow them to stay in that moment for long. Separation: Testing a Bond over Distances:- Traditionally, family and society married you at 18, and with great pomp, Saima was married off to a wealthy family in Srinagar, and Fareeda stayed back to be a teacher like them in the same school where they once dreamt. In the course of time, letter writing took the place of their long walks together, and their friendship became a quiet echo of the past. True bonds do not fade; they simply deepen with distance. Home lost, drowning under the weight of expectations, Saima was saved from going insane by the letters Fareeda wrote, reminding her of who she was. And when even the people of Fareeda’s town resisted her for having the nerve to remain unmarried, Saima’s emotional support could always be relied upon. There were no grand declarations, no flowery words, only presence: unwavering and constant. Years went by. Fareeda became a mentor to young girls who, like her, once thought education was a dream too far. Saima was buried in family commitments, but she clung to the one truth that she had always known: when women lift each other up, nothing can tear them down. And then, how it does change at times such as these in life. The Return: A Hand That Never Let Go:- One of those winters in Srinagar, when snow fell heavier than usual, was when loss crashed down on Saima’s world. Again, as had been the case for decades, her husband-the man she’d spent those years building a life with- visited the next world, leaving her in a household that now did not recognize her as belonging to it as family. ﻿ Widow. Burden. Afterthought:- Suddenly, the walls that had been her home for years became a prison. But just when despair was about to settle in, someone knocked at the door. It was Fareeda. No hesitation, no questions. Just presence. “Come home,” she said with a voice that was commanding, as if those two words alone were enough for the reconstruction of all that had been lost by Saima. And so she did. Back in their old town, under the same chinar tree where their story started, Saima had begun anew. She took the job of teacher in Fareeda’s school, guiding young girls who reminded them of themselves at this age: girls who had big dreams but still made them shy in the eyes of the world. And as they sat side by side watching yet another generation of women rise, they knew one thing beyond all doubt: They had won, not for themselves but for all women who had been told they could not. For sisterhood is not just standing shoulder to shoulder; it’s making sure that no one is left behind. For in the quiet, unseen ways that only women understand, Saima and Fareeda have built.
author: shah zeeshan

title: The Boy Who Cried Wolf
text: A Shepherd Boy tended his master’s Sheep near a dark forest not far from the village. Soon he found life in the pasture very dull. All he could do to amuse himself was to talk to his dog or play on his shepherd’s pipe. One day as he sat watching the Sheep and the quiet forest, and thinking what he would do should he see a Wolf, he thought of a plan to amuse himself. His Master had told him to call for help should a Wolf attack the flock, and the Villagers would drive it away. So now, though he had not seen anything that even looked like a Wolf, he ran toward the village shouting at the top of his voice, “Wolf! Wolf!” As he expected, the Villagers who heard the cry dropped their work and ran in great excitement to the pasture. But when they got there they found the Boy doubled up with laughter at the trick he had played on them. A few days later the Shepherd Boy again shouted, “Wolf! Wolf!” Again the Villagers ran to help him, only to be laughed at again. Then one evening as the sun was setting behind the forest and the shadows were creeping out over the pasture, a Wolf really did spring from the underbrush and fall upon the Sheep. In terror the Boy ran toward the village shouting “Wolf! Wolf!” But though the Villagers heard the cry, they did not run to help him as they had before. “He cannot fool us again,” they said. The Wolf killed a great many of the Boy’s sheep and then slipped away into the forest. The End Moral: Liars are not believed even when they speak the truth. Thanks for reading

title: Grandma's New Tale -The Mango and the Clever Sparrow
text: The Mango Tree and the Clever Sparrow One summer afternoon, as the sun painted golden rays across the fields, Meera tugged at Grandma's sari and said, "Grandma, tell us a new story! One we haven't heard before!" Grandma smiled, adjusted her spectacles, and began, "Alright, let me tell you the story of a mango tree and a clever sparrow..." In a quiet village, there stood a tall, old mango tree. It had seen generations grow, seasons change, and had given its sweet fruit to all- birds, children, even the cows! High on its branches lived Chikki, a little sparrow with shiny eyes and a sharp mind. Chikki loved the tree and always made sure to keep the other animals in check, especially the naughty monkey named Gunda. Gunda had a bad habit. Whenever the mangoes ripened, he would pluck all of them- not just for himself, but to hoard and waste. One day, the tree whispered to Chikki, "My fruits are ready. But I fear Gunda will take them all again." Chikki chirped, "Don't worry, dear tree. I have a plan!" The next morning, as Gunda leaped onto the branches, ready to pluck every mango he could see, Chikki flew down and said, "Wait, Gunda! These mangoes are cursed. The first one who eats them will forget how to climb trees!" Gunda froze. "Forget how to climb? But I'm a monkey! Climbing is all i do!" Chikki nodded, "Yes, and imagine- if you can't climb, you'll have to walk on the ground like a goat!" Scared and confused, Gunda scampered away, scratching his head. Later that day, Chikki invited all the children of the village. "The mangoes are ready and safe now." They laughed, played, and shared the mangoes under the warm shade of the tree. Even Grandma came by, smiling at Chikki. From that day on, Gunda never took more than one mango, and the mango tree stood proudly, full of joy and shade. Moral of the Story Wisdom is more powerful than strength
author: Pandeep Sethi

title: Mikki and the Banana Trick
text: Once upon a time, Ajji began, her voice soft and warm like a blanket, “in a jungle not far from here, lived a clever monkey named Miki. Miki loved bananas more than anything! One day, he found a huge bunch of the ripest, yellowest bananas he had ever seen, right at the top of the tallest tree.” “Wow!” whispered Anand. “But just as Miki reached for the bananas,” Ajji continued, “a tiny, grumpy scorpion, named Pinchy, scuttled out from under a leaf. Pinchy was very proud of his sting, even though he was so small. ‘These are my bananas!’ he squeaked, raising his tail.” Krishna frowned. “But monkeys eat bananas!” “Indeed,” Ajji nodded. “Miki was kind. ‘Excuse me, little friend,’ he said politely. ‘I just want one or two. There are so many for both of us.’ But Pinchy was stubborn. ‘No! All mine!’ he insisted.” Seenu whispered to Sumathi, “He’s like me when I don’t want to share my toys!” Sumathi quietly giggled. “Miki thought for a moment,” Ajji went on. “He knew he could just grab the bananas and run, but he didn’t want to hurt Pinchy. So, Miki had an idea! He saw a small, juicy berry bush nearby. ‘Pinchy,’ he said, ‘I have a game. If you can count all the berries on that bush before I climb down this tree, you can have all the bananas!’ “ Priya clapped her hands. “Pinchy, who wasn’t very clever but loved challenges, puffed out his chest. ‘Easy!’ he chirped and began counting. ‘One… two… three…’ He was so slow!” Ajji chuckled. “While Pinchy was busy counting berries, Miki quickly grabbed a few bananas from the bunch, enough for a good meal. He ate them happily, leaving plenty for Pinchy and any other jungle creature. When Pinchy finally finished counting and looked up, Miki was gone, and the bananas were still there, just a few less.” “So Miki was smart!” exclaimed Raghu. “Yes, Raghu,” Ajji confirmed. “Miki showed that you can be clever without being mean. He got his bananas, and Pinchy learned a lesson about being stubborn and maybe a little selfish.” The children smiled. “That was a good story, Ajji!” said Meenu. Ajji patted her bag. “And there are many more where that came from, my dears. Always remember, a kind heart and a clever mind can solve many problems.” And as the sun began to dip, painting the sky with orange and pink, the children knew that tomorrow, Ajji would open her magical bag of stories again, filled with new adventures and gentle lessons.
author: Tuvish Sadana

title: Wise and Kind
text: Grandma's Story "Come, children," Grandma said, "gather around, and I'll tell you a story about the importance of wise investments and education." Siblings In a small village, there lived two brothers and a sister: Priya, Arun, and Arjun. Their father, a kind woodcutter, worked hard to provide for them and ensured they received a good education. A Wise Decision Their father divided his savings equally among the siblings. Priya and Arun spent their share on party and games. Arjun invested his money wisely and continued his education in business and finance. Arjun's Business Arjun started a small shop and sold goods to the villagers. His business flourished, and he became known for his kindness and generosity. Learning a Lesson Priya and Arun's money ran out. They realized their mistakes and asked Arjun for help. Arjun welcomed them with open arms and offered Arun a job in his shop. Working Together Arjun's business continued to grow, and Priya started a small school for the village children, using her education degree. Arun learned new skills and helped Arjun expand his business. The siblings worked together and thrived. Grandma's Wisdom "Children, remember that wise investments, hard work, and education can lead to great success. Always think carefully about your decisions and pursue your passions." Moral Wise planning, hard work, and education lead to success, while recklessness and lack of planning lead to failure.
author: Rakshith Sai Saravanan

title: The Magic Seeds of Knowledge
text: One day, while exploring the forest, Aarav met an old man planting tiny seeds in the ground. The man looked wise, with a long beard and twinkling eyes. “Why are you planting seeds here?” Aarav asked. “These are magic seeds,” said the old man, smiling. “They grow into trees that give you fruits of wisdom, skills, and success. But they only grow if you water them every day with learning.” Aarav was amazed. “Can I plant one too?” “Of course,” said the man, handing him a shiny blue seed. “But remember, skipping a day of learning is like forgetting to water your seed. It won’t grow strong.” Excited, Aarav took the seed home. Every day, he read books, asked questions, solved puzzles, and learned something new. Slowly, a tiny plant began to grow in his backyard. As Aarav grew older, so did his tree. It became tall and strong, and its fruits were magical. Whenever he ate one, he gained a new ability—like fixing things, solving problems, or helping others with smart ideas. Years passed, and Aarav became a wise man in the village. People came from far away to ask for his help. He always told them, “It all started with a small seed—and watering it every day by learning.” And in the corner of his garden, the old tree still stood, full of glowing fruits. Moral: Education is like a magic seed. If you take care of it every day, it will help you grow and succeed your whole life.
author: KIAAN BANSAL

title: Villagers vs Monster
text: Once upon a time, in the heart of a mock desert, there was a small village named Rampur. Life there was extremely tough. The scorching heat often soared up to 47 0 C, and the land was so dry that nothing grew. The villagers had no choice but to walk 120 miles each day just to fetch water from the only source available—an Oasis that was guarded by Drako, a fearsome dragon who considered the water his own treasure. Drako was ruthless. To fetch even a single drop of water, the villagers had to risk their lives. Yet, they had no other choice. One morning, as the villagers marched toward the Oasis, something unusual caught their eyes—a fresh pumpkin, growing in the middle of the barren desert. Everyone stopped in disbelief. “If this pumpkin is growing here, there must be water nearby!” one of them thought. Excited and hungry, they all tried to pull the pumpkin from the ground. But the moment they did, a terrifying monster burst out of it. Towering and furious, the Pumpkin Monster warned them, “Touch this pumpkin again, and I’ll kill you all!” Before anyone could react, the monster grabbed a few villagers and dragged them underground, declaring them his eternal slaves. All villagers were filled with fear. But one smart young man named Ravi stepped forward with a bold idea: “Let’s ask Drako for help. If he defeats the monster, we might be able to save our people and find a better water source.” Desperately, the villagers approached the dragon. At first, Drako denied. But when he heard of the powerful monster hidden beneath the pumpkin, his eyes gleamed with jealousy. He had always believed himself to be the most powerful creature in the desert. “I’ll destroy the monster,” he growled, “but in return, you must bring me food every day—forever.” The villagers, with no other hope, agreed. Drako flew with them to the pumpkin. The monster roared as he emerged again, and an epic battle began. Drako finally killed the monster, burning him into ashes with his blazing fire and razor-sharp claws. When the villagers pulled the pumpkin again, something magical happened—a hidden underground river burst forth, flowing with cool, clear water. The monster’s underground lair had been hiding it all along. The enslaved villagers were freed, and Rampur was never thirsty again. True to their word, the villagers thanked Drako and brought him food daily—not just out of fear, but out of respect and gratitude. 🌱 Moral of the Story: Even in the harshest conditions, unity, wisdom, and courage can uncover unexpected blessings—and sometimes, even the fiercest enemies can become allies when goals align.
author: Yug sharma

title: The Magic Ingredient!!
text: The Missing Recipe for the Monsoon Feast Seated on her well-worn armchair, the afternoon sun warming her spectacles, Ajji (Grandma), with her silvery bun and a smile that crinkled the corners of her eyes, was in a pickle. Not the tangy, spicy kind she usually made, but a genuine predicament. The annual monsoon feast, a tradition older than her youngest grandchild, was just days away, and the cornerstone of the meal – her famous Ambode, crispy lentil fritters – felt… incomplete. It wasn’t that she’d forgotten the recipe. Ajji’s memory, like her brass coffee filter, was sturdy and dependable. No, the problem was the magic ingredient. Just yesterday, while recounting the tale of the clever jackal to her wide-eyed grandchildren, Raghu and Meena, she’d paused, a frown creasing her forehead. “Children,” she’d said, “the Ambode needs something special. Something… from the heart of the earth.” Raghu, ever the pragmatist, suggested, “Is it a special kind of lentil, Ajji? Or a new spice?” Meena, the dreamer, piped up, “Maybe it’s a secret chant you whisper while frying them!” Ajji chuckled, but her eyes held a hint of worry. She knew it wasn’t an ingredient in the usual sense. It was something she’d learned from her own grandmother, a tiny, almost imperceptible addition that made her Ambode legendary, a flavour that sang of rain-soaked earth and warm family gatherings. That evening, as the first fat drops of the monsoon began to tap against the windowpanes, Ajji rummaged through her old recipe books, not for the Ambode, but for clues. Tucked between the yellowed pages of a recipe for mango pickle, she found a faded sketch. It was a crude drawing of a banyan tree with a small, almost invisible symbol etched into its trunk – a spiral. “The old banyan in the village!” she whispered, a spark igniting in her eyes. It was the same tree under which her grandmother had always shared her stories, her wisdom, and yes, her cooking secrets. The next morning, despite Raghu’s protests about the impending rain and Meena’s insistence that she could just “imagine” the ingredient, Ajji set out. The air was thick with the scent of wet earth, and the parched fields were greedily drinking in the rain. When she reached the ancient banyan, its sprawling branches offered a natural umbrella. She traced the spiral on its gnarled trunk, a feeling of deep connection washing over her. As she stood there, a young boy from the village, Anand, known for his quiet nature and love for the outdoors, approached her. He had a small, woven basket in his hand. “Good morning, Ajji,” he said softly. “My grandmother asked me to bring you these. She said they bloom best after the first monsoon rains.” He opened the basket. Inside, nestled on a bed of fresh leaves, were several small, delicate wild turmeric rhizomes, their skin a vibrant orange, emitting a subtle, earthy fragrance. Ajji’s eyes widened. Wild turmeric! Not the common spice, but this specific, freshly dug kind, brimming with the essence of the rain-fed earth. This was it! This was the magic ingredient her grandmother had taught her about, a secret that transcended mere flavour and infused the Ambode with the very spirit of the monsoon. She smiled at Anand, a warm, genuine smile that reached her eyes. “Thank you, Anand,” she said, her voice filled with quiet joy. “You’ve brought more than just turmeric. You’ve brought back a memory, a story, and the heart of our feast.” That evening, the aroma of the Ambode filled Ajji’s home, mingling with the drumming of the rain. Raghu declared them “extra crispy,” and Meena swore she could “taste the rain” in them. Ajji, watching her family feast, knew the secret wasn't just in the wild turmeric. It was in the journey, the memory, and the enduring power of stories that connected generations, one delicious bite at a time. The monsoon feast was not just a meal; it was a celebration of continuity, a testament to the magic found in the simplest of traditions, and a reminder that some of the best ingredients are found not in a pantry, but in the stories we share and the earth beneath our feet.
author: YATHARTH SALDI

title: THE KINGDOM OF BUZZWOOD
text: THE KINGDOM OF BUZZWOOD Once upon a time, in a peaceful village, lived two grandkids named Aarav and Ria. Every summer, they visited their Nana and Nani’s big, old house, which was full of stories, laughter, and secret corners. This year, something special happened. One afternoon, while playing near Nani’s garden, Ria followed a golden honeybee that buzzed in a strange circle and then flew into the hollow trunk of a tree. Curious, the kids crawled through—and in a flash of golden light, they found themselves in a magical world called Buzzwood. Buzzwood was ruled by a kind King Bumble and his three wise Queens: Queen Nectar, Queen Blossom, and Queen Pollen. The land was filled with giant sunflowers, candy-flavored rivers, and tiny talking animals. “Welcome, brave children,” said Queen Nectar. “Buzzwood needs your help!” “What happened?” Aarav asked, surprised. “Our royal honeycomb has been stolen by the Sour Spider Gang,” said the King. “Without it, the bees can’t make honey, and Buzzwood will lose its magic.” Just then, Uncle Raj and Aunt Meena, who had followed the kids through the tree trunk, arrived too! “I knew this tree looked magical,” said Uncle Raj, always ready for an adventure. Together, the kids, their uncle and aunt, and the honeybee army went on a mission through Sugarcane Forest and across the Jelly Hills. With clever ideas from Ria, strength from Aarav, and some sweet honey traps, they finally tricked the Sour Spiders and brought the honeycomb back! The King and Queens held a grand feast with glowing cupcakes and dancing bees. “You have saved Buzzwood,” said Queen Blossom. “And shown the courage and love that lives in every family.” Suddenly, with another flash, the kids were back in Nani’s garden—with sticky fingers and giggles. Nana came out with a smile. “You’ve been gone just ten minutes!” But Aarav and Ria looked at each other. They knew a whole adventure had passed. And from that day on, whenever a honeybee buzzed around, they smiled—because they remembered the magical land of Buzzwood, where they had once been heroes.
author: Aanya Chawla

title: The Lost Ring and the Lesson of the Well
text: It was a sunny afternoon in Shiggaon. After a game of lagori, Meena suddenly shouted, “My silver ring is gone!” Everyone searched—the mat, the porch, the mango tree—but it was nowhere. Ajji, ever calm, said, “Let’s take a break. And listen to a little story.” Ajji's Story Once, a girl named Bhavani lost her shiny bead. She got angry and accused everyone. Her grandfather took her to a well and dropped a pebble. ‘See the ripples? That’s anger,’ he said. Then he dropped a flower. ‘This is kindness. It spreads gently.’ Bhavani calmed down—and later found her bead under a mat. No one had taken it.” The children were quiet. Then Krishna said, “Let’s check again, slowly.” Sure enough, Raghu found the ring near the tulsi pot, under a stone. Meena grinned. “Ajji, your story saved the day!” Ajji smiled. “Sometimes, calm eyes find what rushing feet miss.” Moral: Patience and kindness often solve what panic cannot.

title: The Starlit Promise
text: Lina lived in a sleepy village nestled at the foot of the Whispering Hills, where every night the stars seemed to whisper dreams across the sky. Her grandfather, Old Arun, always told her the stars answered heartfelt wishes—if one had enough courage. One crisp evening, Lina tiptoed out to the hill above her cottage. Filled with hope, she whispered, “Please, help my sister find joy again.” That night, a single shimmering star blinked. Lina smiled and raced home. Days passed. Her sister Mina, who had lost her smile after a fall, began humming softly while painting little sunflowers. She laughed at Lina’s silly dances and even helped Grandpa collect wild berries. Lina felt the stars had heard her plea. Then, during the village’s midsummer night festival, a sudden storm swept in, drenching the lanterns and silencing laughter. The villagers panicked, but Mina stood tall. She stepped forward, lifted a soggy lantern, and braided wildflowers into every villager’s hair. One by one, they calmed, joining in humming songs. Sunshine broke through the clouds at dawn—and joy filled every heart. That night, as Lina and Mina sat on the Whispering Hill, they looked up to see the same star winking brightly above. Mina squeezed Lina’s hand and whispered, “Thank you.” Lina whispered back, “It was a promise under the stars.

title: Chilo the Chicken
text: Chilo the chicken always gets into trouble but thinks he's a superhero. One evening, he went for a walk without his friends. Chilo tried to open the door but failed. Then he asked the books the way to go out of the library. They said, "Only if you dance Bharatanatyam, I will let you out." Chilo did not know any dance. Then Chilo tried dancing. And finally, the door opened! After he came out, he showed everybody his dance. And did not enter the library again.

title: Where Does My Anger Go?
text: It finds my grey and lavender teddy bear. And, hides its face in it, giving a tight hug. Cries out loudly - "waaaah waaah... huu - huu - huu..." Gets tired. Breathes. My anger sleeps - " Zzzz…mmmm…zzzz...” And, when it sleeps, Anger dreams.. In the dream, Anger becomes a sparrow - Small. Fragile. Fluttering. This Sparrow takes a flight And sits into a boat, Singing: “ Zi-zi- zi-ra-ra-ra-mi.. Mi - mi - ra-ra ra- ho - ho” On its way to the edge of a silent sea. There, its song wakes the Fairy of Falling Lights - She is the fairy of the garden of dawn and dusk. The fairy listens to sparrow’s song and smiles, And lets her sleep in her garden. In the morning, The anger finally turns into single tear, Leaving a soft, wet mark On my mother’s blouse, just by her bosom... Do you get angry? What does your anger become? A roaring lion? A stomping elephant? Or a gentle breeze? What is its journey - from its start to the end - from its eruption to its melting? Can you write or draw about it - Where does your anger go?

title: The Fabrics of Our Identity
text: “The motifs of Assamese attire are nature's whispers—reminding us to observe, to belong to this land, and to preserve it with care.” Biswajit Thakuria Assamese, Assam “They travelled with me Off we went to Cultural Sundays Off we went to NSF programmes Off we went to our Festivals Now they sleep in my closet until one of those days come.” Niboli K Chophimi Sumi-Naga Tribe, Nagaland “Traditional garments carry stories through generations, passed down with memories. After my grandma passed away, my aunt gave us some of Atsa’s favorite pieces—a piece of her woven into our lives.” Chorovelu Ringa Chakhesang Tribe and Angami Tribe, Nagaland “Watching my Ane weave Gale all day while sitting/sleeping beside her is one of the best feelings I still cherish.” Marba Kamki Galo Tribe, Arunachal Pradesh “‘Puanchei’ and ‘Kawrchei’, traditional Mizo attire, tell stories of our heritage. More than just a dress, it's a symbol of unity that weaves together the hearts of the Mizo people.” Joan lalramngaihsangi Lusei Mizo, Mizoram “I simply love to wear the red and white luirim shawl. It invariably gives me a sense of pride as a native Tangkhul and a motivation to go on in life.” H.A Sothing Shimray Tangkhul Tribe, Manipur “These traditional shawls for me represent love, warmth and home.” Kemya Yanlem Konyak Tribe & Tangkhul Tribe, Nagaland “Tucked away and only worn for occasions makes the garments feel extra special when worn.” Keneisenuo Solo Angami Tribe & Tangkhul Tribe, Nagaland “To me, my Indigenous cultural attire and wearing it, is more than just normal outfits – It carries epistemic living, knowing and being– it is a living identity and a covert resistance, with its each thread, lines and designs carries the pride, distinctness, and beauty of my community.” Thomas Malsom Hwrangkhawl Tribe & Malsom Tribe, Tripura “I truly cherish how our traditional attire feels during special occasions. No matter the weather, the soft silk shawl always provides warmth, even when paired with just a simple top. The lower garment, the phanek, is more than just clothing; it carries a sense of empowerment. Growing up, we were told stories of legendary women like Queen Linthoingambi, who went to war wearing a phanek, and Princess Thoibi, who rode a horse in one. As a writer, I’ve always enjoyed attending events dressed in the vibrant hues of phanek, whether in a simple design or the more elegant Mayek Naibi—each shade and style tells its own story.” Potsangbam Linthoingambi Chanu Meitei Tribe, Manipur “As a child, my sister and I would practice draping the mekhela sador weeks before Bihu and yet would fumble for Maa's help on the day of the occasion simply because we felt more confident when maa made the pleats. Alot of my love for the attire comes from the tenderness with which maa treated the cloth. Maa's tenderness for the cloth eventually translated to her carefully embroidering little flowers all throughout the edge of my first very own Sador, which I have now outgrown but continues to warm me.” Kasturi Dev Choudhury Assamese, Assam “This is the traditional attire of the Galo tribe worn during their main festival, Mopin.” Moge Basar Galo Tribe, Arunachal Pradesh “This bakhu is very special as my Sano Gaga (Grandmother) bought it for me last Losar. It has my favourite colour pink.” Tashi Chong Sherpa Sherpa Tribe, Sikkim “Every time I wear my dokhona it feels like a challenge that I have accomplished because of the way it is worn and that nothing can beat the feel of that panache.” Chalini Basumatary Bodo Tribe, Aassam “Wearing my traditional attire is one of the ways to show my love and pride for my identity and culture.” Longang Luklem Konyak Tribe, Nagaland

title: Ajji and the Great Boredom Buster
text: It was a hot summer afternoon. A young boy named Ravi sat outside the house, feeling very bored. “There’s nothing fun to do,” he sighed. Just then, his grandmother, Ajji, came out with a smile and a glass of mango juice. “Bored again?” she asked. “Let’s go on a treasure hunt!” Ajji opened a small old box filled with buttons, coins, and feathers. She handed Ravi a tiny note. “Clue 1: Where the cat takes naps, a secret map perhaps…” Ravi laughed and ran to the windowsill. One by one, he followed Ajji’s clever clues around the house and garden. He dug near the tree roots, peeked behind pots, and even searched under the swing. Finally, he looked up and asked, “Ajji, where’s the treasure?” Ajji smiled and said, “You already found it—fun, adventure, and time with me!” Ravi grinned. Boredom was gone, and a beautiful memory was made. Moral: Even simple moments become special with love, imagination, and an awesome Ajji.
author: Anunay Garg

title: Just the Beginning
text: All my friends knew exactly what they wanted to be when they grew up. One wanted to be a magician. Another, a doctor. One even dreamed of becoming a tuition teacher. Magical, right? One of them had known since he was 2- he'd watch piano shows and just knew. All my friends knew exactly what they wanted to be when they grew up. One wanted to be a magician. Another, a doctor. One even dreamed of becoming a tuition teacher. Magical, right? One of them had known since he was 2- he'd watch piano shows and just knew. But me? I'm 15 now... and I still don't know. Everyone teased me. "Maybe he'll end up jobless", someone joked. I laughed it out. But it stung. So, I tried everything- baking, skating, journalism, crocheting. I even knitted a sweater once. Nothing clicked. Then one day, at school summer camp, I tried to climb a hill that everyone else had climbed. I failed. Tired and muddy, when we had a lunch break everyone was enjoying pastry, I sat in a clearing. The twilight filtered through the trees like hope and peace. But at that time, I was thinking something completely the opposite all the embarrassing things I have said and done. Giving it a thought can I, do it? The summer camp was about to finish in 2 long boring days without friends, even I don't know how I passed time. When I reached home, I took a breath of relief and rushed to my room because I had a crazy idea. After all the sadness, hope and depression at the camp, I decided to write short stories about my misadventures and embarrassing moments to feel lightened. And when I decided to publish one of the best stories I have written "When gravity hated me", BOOM! People loved it and smiled their hearts out while reading it. That's when it hit me. I didn't want to dance or model like others. I wanted to write heartfelt stories expressing my feelings that actually made people happy. I even decided to give tis multiple genres- motivation, inspiration, horror. And mysterious? My cuppa tea. I'm highly mysterious. Except... I spill every secret. So apparently now no one tells me theirs. Stil.... I've found my thing. And guess what? It's just the beginning.

title: Adventure of Yuven
text: There lived a boy named Yuven, he was going to Ladakh. He went by plane that took one hour and thirty minutes. He heard that its a paradise for the people who love to eat. After some mins they heard voices of someone crying. They followed the voice and entered a room and felt that someone is there. Yuhaan took two stones and started rubbing them to make fire. When the fire was ready they saw a girl crying. Yuven asked her " what happened? ". She said "I was searching for a magical pen and now I am lost ". Yuhaan asked "what is your name?". They crossed the water and found the Magical Pen, but the problem was that the pen was one and they were three. Suddenly a fairy appeared and said ''you worked hard together, so you all will get a magical pen ". The fairy gave all of them a magical pen and disappeared. The next day it was time for Yuven to leave but, he was happy knowing that he will come again.

title: Hospital Management System
text: A Visit to the Hospital Arjun held his mother’s hand tightly as they walked into the big hospital. It was his first time there. His grandmother was sick and needed a check-up. The hospital looked busy. People were talking, walking, and waiting. “Why is everyone sitting in lines?” Arjun asked. His mother smiled. “We’ll get a number soon. It’s all managed through the hospital’s computer system.” At the reception, a friendly nurse typed something into a computer. “This is your token,” she said. “The doctor will call you soon.” Arjun peeked at the screen. “What is that software?” he asked. “That’s the Hospital Management System,” she replied. “It helps us keep everything organized.” The nurse leaned down and explained, “A Hospital Management System—or HMS—is like a super brain for the hospital. It stores patient records, schedules appointments, and keeps track of beds, medicines, and even bills!” “Wow!” said Arjun. “It’s like a robot manager!” Later, the doctor opened her computer. With a few clicks, she had grandma’s full medical history on the screen. “See this?” the doctor told Arjun. “I know what medicine she took last time, and what tests she needs now. All thanks to the HMS.” “It’s faster than searching through papers!” Arjun laughed. At the end of the visit, Arjun watched the bill being generated. “Grandma’s tests, medicines, and consultation—all calculated automatically,” the billing clerk explained. “And now,” the pharmacist added, “her prescription is already in my system.” Arjun’s eyes widened. “This hospital is like one big computer!” On the way home, Arjun asked, “Can every hospital have this system?” “Many already do,” said his mother. “But some small clinics are still learning.” “I hope they get it soon,” Arjun said. “Hospitals should be smart and fast—for everyone!” That night, Arjun drew a picture of a hospital with computers, tablets, and happy patients. “I want to make smart hospital software when I grow up,” he told his mom. She smiled and said, “Then you’ll help care for many people—even without being a doctor.” ﻿ At the end of the visit, Arjun watched the bill being generated. “Grandma’s tests, medicines, and consultation—all calculated automatically,” the billing clerk explained. “And now,” the pharmacist added, “her prescription is already in my system.” Arjun’s eyes widened. “This hospital is like one big computer!”

title: Echoes of Childhood
text: “Ane, I am going out to play!” Marba called out. “Alright, be back by five and be careful.” “Ke, ane.” “These look nice and ripe.” “Don’t squash them!” “Coming, coming!” “Oi Bommar, come out fast!” Splat! Splat! Splat! Splat! “They have started already!” Marba yelled. Splat! Splat! “Wait! Let us get ready,” Bommar cried. “Hahahahah, not a chance!” Yapi giggled. “Oh yeah! Then take this!” Splat! Splat! Splat! Splat! “Ouch!” “Catch me if you can!” “You can’t get me, haha!” “Yay! We win!” Yapi and Yanga cheer. “Hahahahahaha.” “Of course, it was three against two. We were at a disadvantage,” Marba said. “Anyway, I need a new pipe,” Bommar remarked. “Let’s go down to the river,” Marba said, “we can make a new pipe for you.” “And also wash up,” Bommar added, “I am all sticky.” “Wowwww” “Let’s go! Let’s go! The others could be there.” “Let’s jump in,” Marba said, excited. “We are washing our clothes first,” Yapi called out. “We can’t go back like this.” “Okay, okay,” the boys responded. “Let’s do that.” “And done!” The boys look proudly at the washed clothes. “Marba, Bommar, are you coming?” Tago called out. “Yes!” They both jumped into the water. “I am hungry,” Yapi said, drying her hair. “Me too. Let's stop by Abo Tanya’s shop!” said Bommar. “Yes!” everyone cried in unison, “We can get some mithai!” “Abooooooo!” “Ah, you urchins! Your box of stuff is here with me.” “Ohhhh! We had forgotten about this! Why don’t we play gotti then?” Marba asked. “That’s a great idea! The loser buys us sweets!” Yanga chimed in. “Yay!” “Ey, that will not be counted!” “I got three!” “Oi Bommar, don’t cheat, okay?” “I am not cheating! It’s not my fault that you suck at this.” “One more left!” “Wohoooo! I win!” Bommar happily cries. “Hahahaha, here you go, children!” Abo Tanya gives everyone toffees. As they chew on them, they see Takar coming with his gaari. “Oi Takar, where are you going?” Marba yelled. “I am going to play with this!” Takar said. “All alone, huh? Why didn’t you call us?” Bommar exclaimed. “C’mon, let’s go by the slope then. Who’s stopping you?” Takar quips. “Okay!” “Ta-ta, Abo!” “Be careful, kids.” “My turn, my turn!” “Let us go together! “Hahahaha.” “Wohooooooooooo... Ahhhhhh” Crash! “Marba! Bommar! Your Anes are looking for you!” A nyiji passing by said. “Oh no! It’s already getting dark,” Marba exclaimed. “Let’s go!” “We’ll continue this tomorrow!” “Ah, we forgot about your pipe!” Marba said. “It’s alright, we’ll make one tomorrow!” Bommar replied. “Okay, and tomorrow we will not leave those three!” The two went back home, laughing all the way.

title: The Magical Dog
text: Once upon a time there was a kid who always wanted a dog from the minute she saw a dog. Her name was Lucy. Her parents wanted to make Lucy's birthday special so when Lucy turned 8, her parents gave her a dog as a present. Lucy was soo surprised and overjoyed that she was almost about to cry because of happiness. Lucy named her dog Zoey. But little did Lucy know that Zoey had special powers. title: The Fiery Pencils
text: “Rani, eat your lunch—I have to deliver this material to a customer later.” I was at my father’s store, eating rice and sambar from a steel tiffin box, still in my school uniform. His lab supply shop fascinated me. The shelves were lined with glass tubes, beakers, test tube stands, plastic tubing, metre scales, and mysterious glass jars filled with preserved snakes and worms. To me, it wasn’t a shop. It was a lab of wonders. After school, it became my secret world. “Daddy, what’s this gooey blue stuff?” I asked, poking into a plastic box in his storeroom. “That’s gum paste,” he said. “I use it to stick paper.” “Can I touch it?” “You can—but don’t put it in your mouth.” “Why?” “It has a chemical called copper sulphate. It’s poisonous.” I quickly pulled my hand back. He smiled. “We’ll talk more later. Let’s finish this delivery first.” My father tied a cardboard box to the front of his scooter. I climbed on behind him, wrapping my arms around his back. As we rode, he said, “I have something fun for us this Diwali—we’ll make our own firecrackers.” My eyes lit up. We reached a nearby college, where he went in to deliver the supplies. I sat in the reception, swinging my legs and counting to 100. “Count to a hundred. I’ll be back by then,” he had said. He wasn’t. But I didn’t mind. I loved sitting there, imagining myself in college one day, in a lab of my own. We picked up Amma from her office and my little sister from day care on the way home. After dinner, Daddy got busy in the kitchen. He boiled water, mixed in some flour and cold water, and added the same blue powder. “Are you making that gum paste again?” I asked. “Yes,” he said. “The copper sulphate keeps it from spoiling. The flour will make it sticky once it cools.” “But why do we need it?” “You’ll see tomorrow.” The Next Evening After dinner, Daddy brought out old newspapers. He began rolling them into small cylinders and sealing the edges with the blue paste. “Can I help?” I asked eagerly. He handed me a pencil. “Place the pencil on the edge of the paper, roll it tightly, and pass it to me.” I rolled. He sealed. One after another. Fifty cylinders in all. My little sister lay on Amma’s lap, half-asleep but watching us with curious eyes. “What are these for?” “They’re the base for our Diwali firecrackers.” “Ooh! Show me how!” “Tomorrow, kanna. Good things need patience.” Fire and Wonder The next night, he spread some sand on a newspaper and dipped the bottom of each paper tube in it. I frowned. “This isn’t firecrackers, Daddy. It’s just sand.” He smiled. “Have patience, Rani. We’re making mathaabalu.” Once the sand settled in the tubes, he carefully spooned in a black powder. “What is that?” “Fireworks powder. No touching—this is not safe for kids.” “What’s in it?” “Potassium nitrate, magnesium, sulphur, and charcoal.” He sealed the tops and took one outside. Lighting the edge carefully, he stepped back. A brilliant shower of sparks burst from the tube, dancing in the air. “Wow! We made that?” He laughed. “Yes. The chemicals make it burn bright, and magnesium gives those sparkling stars.” “Can we make different colours?” “Yes, Rani. Different metals give different colours. Red, green, gold…” I listened wide-eyed until I drifted off to sleep. Diwali Day “Rani, put the crackers out in the sun.” “Why?” “To dry them. If there’s moisture, they won’t burst well.” That night, after Lakshmi Puja, Amma lit dozens of clay lamps in front of our house. My sister sat bundled in her lap, eyes wide. I carried the “fiery pencils” we made with Daddy. We lit one together. It sparked just like yesterday—bright and beautiful. “Why does it stop halfway?” “Remember we filled sand at the bottom?” Daddy said. “That’s so the fire doesn’t reach your fingers. It’s for safety.” I smiled. “I love our fiery pencils.” “They’re called mathaabalu, nanna.” “No, Daddy. We rolled them with pencils—so they’re fiery pencils!” My little sister giggled. “I want to light one too!”

title: Lungdai and the Hornbill
text: It had many tall trees with hollow trunks and branches filled with golden mangoes and ripe papayas. The rustling leaves and a shallow gentle stream made it a nice place to relax on a hot summer day. *Pipi: a Hrangkhawl word for grandmother. Pipi’s* garden was Lungdai’s favourite place in the whole world. Lungdai ran towards the papaya trees, a skip in his steps. “So many juicy papayas! I will…. gasp Pipi, look!” Lungdai cried. “That bird is eating my papaya! Oh no, they are taking all the fruit! Shoo! Shoo! Go away, bad bird!” “Do you think the papayas are fully ripe, Pipi?” “Yes, they are,” Pipi said, smiling. “How would you like to eat them? Small pieces or cut lengthwise?” “I want them sliced lengthwise,” Lungdai replied. “Alright! As you wish.” “Yay, I can’t wait!” “Ah, let it be. It’s a hornbill bird,” Pipi explained. “But it’s taking and destroying all the fruits. Chase it away! Shoo!” “Now, now, let it be,” Pipi said, gently pulling him back. “We have plenty, so let them have some. Also, look up there.” “What? Not just the papaya, but all the fruits?” Lungdai was annoyed. “They will finish everything. This is your tree Pipi, why don’t they go somewhere else?” Lungdai followed Pipi’s hand as she pointed to the hornbill bird which landed on the mango tree. “That’s a dada hornbill going to feed his family. It uses the fruit to feed the mama and the baby inside their nest,” Pipi said. “Oh? But I didn’t plant this tree,” Pipi replied, “who knows, maybe this hornbill did it.” Lungdai was shocked. “The bird did it?” “Hornbills do more than eat fruit, my dear. They help the forest grow. When they eat, they scatter seeds, planting new trees. Without them, many trees would not be there in the forest, and certainly not in this garden” Pipi explained. Pipi let out a sigh, “While the forest is their home, they are disappearing. You must have learned this in school, right?” “So, the forest is their home?” Lungdai asked, a lot less annoyed now. Lungdai recalled how his teacher had told them about trees being cut down, the river drying up and the smoke filling the air. “When their homes disappear, they have to look for a new place to live, which is very difficult,” Pipi continued. “And sometimes, there are some wicked people who even kill them. Now tell me, dear, should we not protect them?” Lungdai thought about the hornbill bird flying over the dried-up river, choking on the smoky air. Will the air clear? Will the river flow again? Will we find a home? “How sad,” Lungdai quietly whispered. “Hornbills do more than eat fruit, my dear. They help the forest grow. When they eat, they scatter seeds, planting new trees. Without them, many trees would not be there in the forest, and certainly not in this garden” Pipi explained. “So, the forest is their home?” Lungdai asked, a lot less annoyed now. Lungdai quietly watched the hornbill gently pick up the ripe fruit and fly near the hollow bark of the tree. It brought the fruit close to the hole in the trunk, and another beak stretched out, taking the fruit. Lungdai’s face lit up, and he said, “Pipi! Pipi! Did you see that? Dada hornbill just put the fruit inside the hole!” “I did. That's the mama bird, who stays inside with the baby bird. They wait for the food that the dada brings them,” Pipi explained. “Pipi, what if there are no fruits?” Lungdai watched the hornbill family, the dada passing the fruit through the small hole. “Well, the dada bird flies and flies till it can bring back food. After all, the mama and the baby are waiting for it. The mama protects the baby inside the nest while the dada brings them food. That’s how the baby stays safe, Lungdai,” Pipi said. “Sometimes only fruit is not enough. Mama hornbill needs nutritious insects, which they don’t usually get nowadays. Therefore, they have to fly far away to get food,” Pipi added. “What if…what if the dada doesn’t come back?” Lungdai asked. Pipi sighed. “Then the poor birds would have nothing to eat, and they would die.” Lungdai couldn’t hold back tears at the thought of that happening. “It’s alright, my dear.” Pipi gently patted his shoulder. “These birds are safe.” “I am sorry I chased you away earlier. Here, you can feed your family.” He laid the papaya on the ground and slowly backed away. “I understand now, Pipi,” Lungdai said, “this papaya is not just mine, but it is for all of us to share.” He turned to the hornbill bird sitting up at the branch. Then, he made his way to the papaya tree and grabbed a juicy papaya. A few minutes later, the bird swooped in and took a piece of the fruit. “Pipi, look, it took it!” Lungdai cried. “That’s the spirit, my child,” Pipi said with a chuckle. “You have learnt how to share. Now come along; let me cut up some of the papaya for you as well.” Pipi’s garden was still Lungdai’s favourite place in the world. However, now, along with the tall trees and juicy fruits, he also looked forward to meeting the little bird family that had made this garden their home. About the story Human-Hornbill Relations in Tripura In Tripura, the oriental pied hornbill (Anthracoceros albirostris) shares a long-standing relationship with the state’s indigenous communities, such as the Molsom and Hrangkhawl communities. This is echoed in their beliefs, folktales, oral traditions, and everyday practices that are aimed at protecting these birds. These communities consider the hornbill bird sacred and strictly forbid their killing or for any of their body parts to be used for any decoration (like as part of a costume). One of the key reasons for the traditional prohibition against hunting hornbills is rooted in the belief that anyone who kills a hornbill will be cursed, leading to the death of a family member in a future generation. While this may be seen as superstition, this very belief system shows an understanding of the bird’s monogamous nature and their vital role in the ecosystem and hence is a way to protect the hornbills. Especially during the nesting period, the female hornbill remains sealed inside the nest until the eggs hatch and the chicks are ready to fly. During this time, which lasts around 6-8 months, the male hornbill is solely responsible for feeding the female hornbill. Killing the male hornbill is thus seen as the killing of an entire family. This belief system reinforces the perspective that protecting hornbills is not just an act of biodiversity conservation but also an expression of traditional ecological knowledge and a deep-rooted sense of coexistence between humans and nature/animals. Beyond the hornbill’s cultural and spiritual significance, these birds play a vital role in forest regeneration by dispersing seeds and contributing to biodiversity – an aspect that is well understood by the indigenous (Molsom and Hrangkhawl) communities of Tripura. Acknowledgement The TFFP Fellowship team is grateful to Pu. Chaitra Kumar Hrangkhawl for sharing extensive information about the importance of hornbills in the Hrangkhawl and Molsom communities, without which this book would not be possible.

title: Hair Cut
text: I are very big friends. We really like to do everything together. Mother takes us to get a haircut when we need one. Meena likes long hair. So she doesn’t need much to be cut. But I only like short hair. I always get it like that. One day Meena and I were very bored. Meena said, “I don’t want to draw pictures today”. Suddenly I got an idea. I said very excitedly, “Meena, let’s play hair cutting saloon!” “Will it be okay, Dhani? Later, I don’t want trouble with mother.” “Everything will be okay! Stay here.” Taking a scissors from the kitchen, I cut Meena’s hair “snip, snip.” I definitely know how to cut hair very well. Oh, no! I forgot that Meena only likes long hair. Then I heard someone walking into the kitchen. Mother was home. Mother came inside. She saw Meena screaming at all the hair that was on the floor. “What is going on here?”, she said. Meena was crying. “Dhani cut my hair. Now it has become very short.” I realized that all this was my idea from the beginning. I was only paying attention to what I wanted. I should have thought about what Meena wanted. Mother was not happy and I was very sorry for what I did.

title: Bhattu
text: Bhattu is a 6-year-old boy. He is studying in Class 1 and lives in a city with his parents and elder brother, Tuttu. He is very talkative and naughty. One day, his teacher scolded him in front of the whole class, which made him very sad. That evening, he shared his experience with his mother. After hearing what had happened in the class, his mother felt sorry for him. She told him to forget about the incident. But her words didn't heal his sadness, so he went to his father. Before saying anything, he hugged his father with tears in his eyes. After some time, he explained everything that had happened in class. Hearing his words, the father also felt sad. He hugged his child again and again, very affectionately. Seeing Bhattu's dull face, Tuttu guessed that something had happened. So he asked, "What happened? "Hearing his brother’s words, Bhattu started crying and said, "Madam scolded me today without any big reason." “Cool, dear… be cool…” said Tuttu. Tuttu hugged his brother. What's up dear? That night, the whole family sat together after dinner. Bhattu was still feeling low, but his family knew how to lift his spirits. Tuttu brought his favorite storybook and sat beside him. "You remember the lion who was brave even when others didn't believe in him? You're just like that lion, Bhattu. One scolding doesn't decide how good or smart you are." Bhattu looked up with teary eyes, slowly nodding. Mother smiled warmly and brought him a small bowl of his favorite ice cream. “Sometimes, even teachers have a bad day,” she said gently. “It doesn’t mean you’re bad. You’re our bright, sweet boy, and we love you no matter what.” His father added, “You know what helps when I’m upset? I take a deep breath and think about something that makes me happy. Like when we go to the park and race. Want to race with me tomorrow?” Bhattu’s face lit up a little. “Really, Papa?” “Of course!” his father said, tickling him gently. That night, Bhattu slept cuddled between his parents, with Tuttu reading softly nearby. The sadness hadn't completely gone, but in the warmth of his family's love, it began to fade — little by little, like clouds parting after rain.

title: Malin Kundang
text: Once upon ﻿ a time, in a coastal village in Sumatra Lived a poor mother and a boy, named Malin Kundang. As time passed, Malin grew into a mature young man. He left his mother to seek fortune. Years later, he became rich and married a beautiful woman. Returning to his village, Malin’s ship docked, and his mother came to greet him. Ashamed of her poverty, Malin denied knowing her, calling her a beggar. Furious, his mother cursed him. As Malin sailed away, a storm struck, turning himself into a stone. The stone still stands on the beach, reminding people to respect their parents.

title: The Fox and The Crow
text: Early one morning, a fox is walking through the woods. He is hungry and he is looking for something to eat. He sees a crow sitting on the highest branch of a tree. The crow has a piece of cheese in her beak. Fox says "I think i have found my breakfast". He wanting the cheese. He thinks and he thinks then he has a clever idea. The fox flattered the crow, saying her voice was beautiful and asking her to sing. The crow, flattered, opened her beak to sing, and the cheese fell. Then the fox grabbed it and ran away, leaving the crow to regret her vanity.

title: The Turtle and The Rabbit
text: One day, Turtle is walking in the town then he meet Rabbit and friends. Rabbit says "I am faster than everybody, no one can win a race against me" and the Rabbit boasted about Turtle speed, mocking a Turtle for being slow. The turtle angry with the rabbit. So he challenged the rabbit to a race. During the race, the rabbit ran far ahead but stopped to nap, thinking he would win easily. Meanwhile, the turtle kept walking steadily. When the rabbit woke up, the turtle was near the finish line. He tried to chase the turtle but he could not cacth it. The turtle won, proving that perseverance beats arrogance.
author: Putri  Siti Aisyah

title: My Pastry House
text: I dream of a tall house.....my TALL HOUSE. I want it to look like a Pastry!!!! Why a Pastry, you ask???............. Why Not!!! I love pastries....colourful, delicious, vibrant and dense. Yes, I want my house to be dense. The ground floor will be Radiant Red....like Red Velvet, soft and tender, like my mother. I will devote this floor to my mother. She would love it....she loves red too. The first floor belongs to my father and his favourite colour is Green. He loves gardening a lot. Why I did not give him the ground floor then? Well, the kitchen is on the ground floor and mummy loves cooking. Daddy can have a Pot Garden. My sister should get the second floor.... Vibrant Yellow for sure. Yellow Yellow, dirty fellow suits her well too. Mine is the Top Floor. As Bright and Blue as the sky. I will be the happiest there. It will be a beautiful sight. My tall and colourful house.....that looks like a Delicious and dense Pastry!!!

title: Taco's adventure
text: Taco is a black cat with soft hair, and the eyes are green like the grass. He is one years old. He lives in a nice house with a big garden with his human family. Two weeks ago he heard some noises coming from the new neighbor's house. He went to see who was there. They were painters working on a scaffolding. The painters didn't realise they dropped a bucket of white paint, which fell on Taco's body. Taco was very scared and run to his family but they didn't recognize him because he was full of white paint. So they pushed him away. But when he started "meowing" his family recognized his voice. MEOW, MEOW MEOW And they took him in the house to take a bath. So now Taco is happy again with his family and he's more careful.
author: matilde spreafico

title: Becoming Saturday
text: I want to be a Saturday, loved by all. A near to perfect one. Not a Sunday....but Saturday, without rush.... and bringing along a long morning to sleep in. I will be like a Sundae....not Sunday, but Sundae!!! Like a burst of flavours, all delicious and sweet. That would be fun....A Saturday that tastes like a Sundae!! I want to be like an Americano....a huge cup of Americano. I will comfort the tired and fill them up with energy. Imagine that....a Saturday....that energizes like an Americano!! Or.....Tea, for say!!! Why not a cup of tea then.....I want to be like a refreshing cup of tea. I will be warm and cozy. A Saturday that is warm and cozy....WHAT FUN!! I want to be like a delicious bowl of Udon Noodles. Soft and Chewy....tender and vibrant. I want to be a Saturday that tastes like the comforting Udon Noodles....a bowl full of it!! I want to be colourful like the Raspberries....sweet and earthy. Oh!!!!.....what aroma would I spread. Imagine....a Saturday that is sweet and earthy....and can be used in various ways!! I want to be like a Dandelion....one that brings the wishes come true. I will move with the wind and still stand tall. I want to be a Saturday that grants wishes and make people look at me with a hopeful smile!! I want to be a Yellow Mango too....a Saturday that tasteful would be a dream come true! I want to fill the hearts with love and laughter. I want to bring the picnic- flavours out. Yes...Yellow Mango suits me well!! That said....I will pick up all those letters out of - Sundae, Americano, Tea, Udon noodles, Raspberries, Dandelion and Yellow mango.....and curate a Perfect Saturday. Yes....I want to be a Saturday....loved by all....in all shape and forms. That's my dream!!!

title: SOME DAYS WITH OUR ROOTS
text: "The summer holidays have started! maa and bapa let's go to our village". shouted Krisha, Riya and Trisha they are excited to go to their village which is in Odisha. They will meet their Aai and Aja. " Yes kids you are right but this time our holidays have shortened and we can only go for 4 days." said maa and bapa sadly. Then the phone rang it was sanju aai 's call while maa spoke with aai the kids were thinking what will happen they were really sad. Then all of a sudden maa told "you kids will go to Odisha with your Alekh mamu who is coming here for his work he will pick you up tommorow. " They danced. Krisha asked " what about you maa and bapa "? Maa replied " beta we will not go this time you go and enjoy your trip". "Okay" said the sisters. "Now sit for dinner it is already 9 pm" said maa. They ate and went to sleep. The next day they were going at 6:30 am. They were ready early in the morning their mamu came. They all ate breakfast together maa,bapa,the siblings and Alekh mamu.Maa who was worried said" Alekh bhai please take care of the kids and yourself". "Yes didi I will take care do not worry". And they were off. The next day they reached at Dhenkanal railway station early in the morning. As soon as they reached their mamu made a call to Sukanta bhai, their driver. He said" Sukanta bhai please come to pick us". "Yes Alekh I am coming to pick you up" said uncle Sukanta. After they reached their aais,ajas,masis,mamus and all welcomed Riya,Trisha and Krisha. They were happy to have them. They did many things in 1month like playing,cooking and more. They were also enjoying as they played with Ved their baby brother. They visited their Babuli aja's farm full of dragon fruit plants. They daily liked running and looking how one cared for the other. Their holidays were soon over. While they were going every one offered them money some said buy toys and some said buy toffees. After they went back home they told everything to their parents. And do you know, they only took little bit of the money everyone gave. THE END

title: Ammachi's Surprise Gift
text: Mr. Satish lived with his wife, Sarala, a six year daughter, Sundari and his Amma, Satyabhama, in a small village called Thiruchery. They were lovingly called the 'S' family by the villagers. They were a wonderful family of four. Sundari was a kind girl. She loved her family a lot. In the mornings, she helped her mother with cooking. She also helped her father with gardening. She was very fond of her Ammachi. Every evening after school, Sundari and Ammachi went for a walk around the village. Sundari wanted a puppy for a long time, but Appa did not get her one as she was very small. It was her seventh birthday in a few days. Sundari went to Appa and said, "Appa, I will be turning seven tomorrow, so why don't you get me a puppy?" Appa was silent. Sundari was sad. She kissed him and went to bed. She wished she had a puppy to play with. It was her birthday. Appa brought a big cake. Amma decorated the house with balloons. Ammachi made her special samosa with khatta meeta chutney. Sundari invited her friends for the party. They enjoyed the party. That evening, like every other day, Sundari went for a walk with Ammachi. While crossing a bush, she heard a rustling sound. Sundari was scared. She held her Ammachi's hand tightly. Ammachi said, "Sundari, don't get scared. Let's go and see what is there in the bush." Slowly, Sundari and Ammachi moved forward. Sundari peeped and looked into the bush. She gave a loud cry and jumped with joy. There was a little puppy in a basket. She took the puppy in her hands. The puppy started licking her face. Sundari loved the puppy. Then Ammachi said, "Happy birthday, my dear Sundari." Sundari was very happy. It was her best birthday. She hugged her Ammachi. The trio went home happily. Now it was a wonderful family of five. The fifth member was the puppy, Shambu.
author: DEEPIKA Y

title: Alphabet - Z
text: The English alphabets are from A to Z. Let us look at a few words that start with the alphabet Z. Z for Zebra Z for Zoo Z for Zodiac Zodiac means sunsigns like Cancer, Taurus, and Leo. Z for Zip Z for Zone Z for ZigZag Z for Zesty Zesty means spicy flavour. Z for Zombie Zombie means a person who seems only partly alive. Z for Zing Zing means energy or enthusiasm. ﻿ Z for Zephyr Zephyr means breeze. Assessment 1. Write 5 words that begin with the alphabet Z. 2. What is the name of the animal that starts with Z? 3. What is the word that starts with Z that means breeze? Answers 1. Zen, Zodiac, Zing, Zesty, Zigzag. (You can write your own answers here). 2. Zebra 3. Zephyr
author: Anitha Selvanathan

title: Luca and the Magical Breadstick
text: Luca loved food especially pasta, soup, and breadsticks. One rainy day, he found a shiny breadstick on his plate. It sparkled! Hello!” said the breadstick. “I’m Benny. Let’s go on a food adventure! Luca blinked. “Did you just... talk?” Benny giggled. “Hop on!” WHOOSH! The table spun like a tornado. Luca landed in a world made of food. Spaghetti trees swirled in the wind. Meatball mountains rolled. Soup rivers flowed. Try the creamy Alfredo slide! said Benny. It’s slippery and cheesy! Luca slid, giggling, covered in sauce. He ate his way down. Then, he saw a sad Pizza Prince. “No one likes my crust. Luca smiled. “I do!” He took a bite. “Crispy and perfect! The Pizza Prince cheered. “Let’s have a feast! Everyone came: Salad Fairies, Breadstick Knights, and Pasta Pirates!
author: Tristan Thomas
illustrator: Arpita Bhattacharjee; Dharmesh Singh; Eric Nii  Addy; Lê Hoàng  Long; Lê Nam  Đã; Magriet Brink; Nguyễn  Minh Hải; P Tamizh muhil; Pankaj Saikia; Raymond Diby; Saloni Chopra; Studio Babakiki; UK Nhal

title: The Little Acorn
text: Once upon a time, in a big oak tree in the middle of a sunny forest, lived a tiny acorn named Ollie.Ollie was round, shiny, and full of potential—but he didn’t know that.Every day, the wind would blow gently, and the leaves would whisper,“Ollie, it’s almost time to fall to the ground and grow into a big oak tree!"But Ollie didn’t want to go.“Why would I want to fall?” Ollie pouted. “Up here I have the best view, the birds sing to me, and I’m safe and warm!” “But you’re meant for more!” said a wise old leaf. “You can grow roots, branches, and shelter animals someday!”“I’m too small,” Ollie argued. “What if I fall and nothing happens? What if I just disappear into the dirt?”The other acorns around him nodded nervously. Falling sounded scary.But one breezy morning, a strong gust of wind shook the tree, and POP!—Ollie tumbled down, down, down… plop! right into the soft earth.It was dark, cold, and quiet. Ollie was afraid. “I’m growing!” Ollie gasped.Seasons changed, and Ollie grew taller and stronger. Years later, he had become a mighty oak tree, just like the one he came from. Birds nested in his branches, squirrels played in his limbs, and children rested in his shadeOne day, a little acorn fell near his roots and said, “I’m scared to grow.”Ollie rustled his leaves and whispered kindly,“I was scared once too. But you were made to grow. And the world needs what you can become.” 🌟 Moral of the Story: Sometimes change feels scary, but it helps us grow into who we’re meant to be.
author: Sharanya Bhatnagar
illustrator: Jemma Jose; Jesse  Breytenbach; Nimret Handa; Roshni Vyam

title: The Kind Girl - Part 1
text: Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Tina. She was very kind and helpful. Tina lived with her mother near a forest, far away from the town. They were poor, so her mother collected wood from the forest and sold it in the nearby town every day to earn money. Tina always helped her mother. One day, her mother fell sick and couldn't go to the town to sell the wood. Days passed, and they ran out of money and food. So Tina decided to help her mother by going to the town alone and selling the wood. She put some small pieces of wood in her toy trolley and started her journey. She walked with a mix of joy and a little fear. On the way, she suddenly heard a voice saying, "Help me! Help me!" Tina stopped and looked around but couldn’t find anyone. She continued walking, but the voice came again. This time, she listened carefully and found the source — a little butterfly was stuck in a spider’s web! The butterfly cried, “Please help me! The spider will come and eat me!” Tina, being kind-hearted, gently removed the webs and set the butterfly free. Suddenly, a bright light flashed! The butterfly transformed into a beautiful angel. The angel smiled and thanked Tina. “You may ask for a wish,” the angel said. But Tina politely said, “No, thank you. I just wanted to help.” It was getting dark, so Tina decided to return home without selling the wood. The angel followed her quietly, without Tina knowing. When they reached home, the angel appeared in front of Tina’s mother and told her everything. The angel was so touched by Tina’s kindness that she granted them wishes without being asked. She cured Tina’s mother, gave them food, clothes, and enough money to live a better life. Tina and her mother were very happy and thanked the angel. The angel smiled and disappeared. From that day on, Tina and her mom lived happily ever after.
author: Manju Priya

title: The Ant and The Grasshopper
text: In a hot summer, a grasshopper rests on the tree to sing and dance all day. While under the tree, the ant was sweating because the ant worked hard collecting the food for winter. "Hi Ant, life is too short to work so hard" Grasshopper said to Ant. Because ants were working all summer long. "Listen grasshopper, if you don't prepare for winter now, you're going to starve". But the grasshopper didn't listen to the ant, he thought there was still plenty of time, so no need to worry. The grasshopper back to singing and dancing all day. And the winter is coming, the wind howled and buckets of snow fell from the winter sky. The grasshopper was starving, cold, and looking for food. But instead of finding food, he got lost in snow. Luckily, grasshopper found ant's house. He knocks the door. The ant opens the door and lets in the grasshopper to eat some food. Finally, the grasshopper understood why the ant worked so hard in the summer. And he was thankful because he had such a good friend.
author: Putri  Siti Aisyah

title: Lakshya's first day at school
text: It was the first day of school, for Lakshya, as they recently had shifted their house to that village. She was slightly excited but more nervous than usual, and scared, her face said it all... She waved her mom bye and entered the school. Everything was new teachers, friends, playground, classes and the entire atmosphere. Let's find out what happens next! The classroom was a complete chaos when Lakshya had a look. The teacher seemed calm. Some students were talking, some were crying, some were running, playing. This made Lakshya feel more terrible, everybody knew each other, and she was just the new one. As soon as she entered the class, an awkward silence was experienced. Her teacher called her inside and introduced her to others. The others were least bothered and kept on doing their work ﻿ ﻿ The school was over. Lakshya went and hugged her mom as she was sad. Her mom asked, " Why dear, what happened? Did anyone bully you? Or did they not talk to you? Say what happened. " Tears started rolling from Lakshya's eyes. She said, " Maa, no one wanted to talk to me, I have no friends, everybody aldready has their own and didn't want to be my friend... I don't want this school... Please take me away from here! ". Then her mother said, " I exactly know how you felt but that's normal. What if not today, you have tomorrow and day-after-tomorrow to make friends... Believe in me you're going to like this school and soon you are going to make friends... If you want, I will talk to your teachers regarding this, maybe they can help you out. " The next day, her mother talked to her teacher regarding this. Her teacher, Nayana said her mother not to worry at all, and she will make sure that Lakshya is having the best time at school. Lakshya felt a bit better, and something sparked inside her head, her mother was very good at cooking and her friends from previous school liked her mother's dishes. So, she thought of calling all of her classmates for lunch at her house the next Sunday. Her teacher said that it was a fabulous idea, and she was sure it would make her some friends... As soon the bell rang, and it was recess time, Lakshya stood up bravely and said everyone regarding it. Everyone agreed and now she felt a bit better. Sunday had come and everyone had come a bit early before the lunch. That's when Lakshya thought was the best time to introduce herself and ask others for their introduction. After some chit-chat her mother called everyone for lunch. All of them sat in living room and tried dishes prepared by her mother. All of them liked them a lot and became close with Lakshya. They even took some food with them in boxes before going home. Lakshya was very happy and was waiting for Monday, as she knew everyone now and all of them were her friends from that day on. All of them were rushing to school and so was Lakshya. She felt so happy. She had made many friends and knew the teachers. From that day on she went happily to school. She got adjusted and made best friends and started liking school and was very excited for school. From those days, school was a place of great solace to her. She liked the life there and lived happily with her mother.
author: Likita V

title: The Lion and The Mouse
text: Once upon a time in a magnificent forest there live the lion who was known as the king of all the animals. The lion was very proud of his strength and power. And all the animal in the forest respected and feared him. One hot summer day the lion was sleeping under the tree. While the lion sleeping, suddenly a small mouse was running through the forest for search some foods. Accidentally, the mouse ran over the lion's body and waking him. The lion caught the mouse but decided to let him go. One day, while the lion wandering through the forest, he was trapped in a hunter’s net. The lion struggle to free himself. The mouse heard his roars and chewed the net to free him. The lion thanked to the mouse, and they became friends. This proving that small acts of kindness can make a big difference.
author: Putri  Siti Aisyah

title: Milo Finds the Colors
text: Milo was a small squirrel. He loved his bright forest. One day, the colors were gone! The trees were grey. The flowers were grey. Even the sky was grey. Milo met the Wind. “You have the colors,” Milo said. “Yes,” said the Wind. “But why should I give them back?” “Because the forest needs them to be happy,” said Milo. The Wind smiled. He let the colors fly. The forest was bright again! Milo was happy. MORAL: Caring brings back joy.
author: Vartika Malik

title: Bawang Putih and Bawang Merah
text: In a village in Java, Bawang Putih lived with her cruel stepmother and stepsister, Bawang Merah. They treated her like a servant, forcing her to do all the household chores. The next day, Bawang Putih was asked to wash clothes in the river. But accidentally, Bawang Putih lost her stepmother’s scarf in the river. While searching for the scarf, Bawang Putih met an old woman who had found her mother’s scarf. The old woman set a condition for Bawang Putih, if she wanted the scarf returned, she had to help with the old woman’s household tasks. Bawang Putih did the household tasks with happily. After finishing, the old woman offered her a pumpkin to take home, and Bawang Putih chose the smallest one. Bawang Putih back to house, she split open the pumpkin, which turned out to be a magical pumpkin revealing gold and jewels. Jealous, Bawang Merah tried to get a pumpkin by pretending to lose a scarf But Bawang Merah was rude to the old woman, and she choose the bigger pumpkin. Because of her greed, the pumpkin contained snakes instead. Bawang Putih’s kindness earned her a happy life, while Bawang Merah faced the consequences of her greed.
author: Putri  Siti Aisyah

title: The Proud Chest
text: Once apon a time there was a proud and beautiful box. Inside it there was a lot of gold. One day he was sitting on a high shelf. Then he started to move here and there because he wanted to show the world how much gold he has inside it. The toys told him that he will fall but he did not listen to them. Then because he did not listen to them while moving he fell down. He broke into many pieces. Moral-We should not be very proud of our self. Thank you
author: Kanika Gupta
