title: The Adventures of Carbon: The Shape-Shifting Friend
text: Long, long ago, in the magical Kingdom of Elements, lived a tiny but powerful element named Carbon. Carbon wasn’t the biggest or the strongest, but he had a secret gift—he could change form and become many different things! One morning, Carbon woke up in the Royal Garden. He looked at himself and giggled, “Today, I am shiny and strong! I am Diamond, the hardest thing in the kingdom. I sparkle like the stars and protect the Queen’s crown.” In the evening, just as the sun set, Carbon stretched and yawned. “Hmm, I feel different now,” he said. He transformed into Graphite, smooth and black. “Ha! Now I can help children write stories and draw pictures inside pencils!” The other elements were amazed. “How can one little element do so many things?” asked Oxygen. Carbon smiled. “That’s my power. I can join hands with myself in many ways—straight lines, sheets, or even cages. Each time, I become something new!” The next day, Carbon skipped into the village. He turned into Charcoal to keep the people warm with fire. Then he became Coal, giving trains the energy to move. He even joined hands with Hydrogen and oxygen to become Sugar, giving children the energy to play! One child asked, “Carbon, you’re everywhere! Why do you help us so much?” Carbon knelt down and said kindly, “Because I am part of all living things. Your body, the trees, the animals—all carry me inside. I am the building block of life. Without me, there would be no stories, no laughter, no you!” The children hugged Carbon. “Thank you for being our invisible friend!” That night, Carbon twinkled like a diamond under the stars and whispered, “Big or small, shiny or simple, I’ll always be with you.” Moral: Even the smallest things can be magical and powerful. Just like Carbon, we too can take many shapes in life—helping, creating, and shining in our own way.
author: Ira Periyavallur (aka Indira VMD)
illustrator: Wesley van Eeden; Aditi Kakade; Ira Periyavallur (aka Indira VMD); Nan Hom Noon; Preeti Krishnamurthy; Sachin Bapat; Studio Babakiki

title: The curious case of the missing socks
text: Little Miss. K is late for the school..............late again!!!! And she couldn't find her socks..............again!!!!!!!!! She made a braid and decided to go to school without her socks!!! "Strange!!!".....she thought. "That's the third pair that I have lost...............Why do I keep losing them!!!!" They were not under the table.... Not in the almirah.... Neither in the kitchen.....nor in the bathroom!!! Neither on the clothing line.....nor in the laundry!!! Little Miss. K was anxious. She tried to hide herself......and her socksless feet....but... She was caught by the English teacher. "Little Miss. K, how can you be this careless." Her mouth was zipped, but she explained her adventure of searching the socks to the teacher. "Little Miss. K, you might be pretty bad at dressing up in the uniform....but you're quite good with telling a story." Little Miss. K blushed. "Well, I might write a story about your missing socks one day..............and I would give you the credit too, and I would name it - THE CURIOUS CASE OF THE MISSING SOCKS", the teacher said. Everyone laughed....so did Miss. K. "Did you look into your bag though?"....the teacher asked and left. Little Miss. K decided to search the bag finally!!! Sometimes they are right under our noses....for Miss. K it was right in her bag!!! Got'em!!!!
author: BHARTI PANWAR

title: VEERU AND HIS MOM
text: Veeru loves his mom. Do you love your mom? What is your mom's name? It was bedtime for veeru! Veeru is waiting for his mom to come. Where is mom? Here mom is! Can you find out from the picture, what mom is doing? Yes! She is washing the vessels! Veeru follows her. Veeru is waiting! After mom finishes washing the vessels she is writing the grocery list on a paper and is sticking it on the fridge!! Does your mom do that? Then mom goes to take a bath! Mom says taking bath helps us to stay clean and healthy. Veeru is waiting! Now, what is mom doing? Yes, she is brushing her teeth! She also tells veeru and all of you to brush two times a day, because it keeps your teeth and gums healthy! Veeru brushes his teeth. Then veeru's mom told him, "come on darling, let's go to sleep" so,finally veeru and his mom slept peacefully! Do you love your mom? What is your mom's favourite food? What is your name? Do you love yourself? Say one thing you love about yourself. Thank you friends for reading this book! This is adhvika.p.r signing off and shall be back with even more engaging stories!
author: Adhvika  Prefulla Rajiv

title: MONDAY BLUES
text: It was Monday again! "How boring it is to wake up early in the morning, to our routine in a hurry, gobbling all the food in the worry of being late for the school bus, forgetting half the books at home while packing the bags in the morning, Mummy shouting and Papa scowling! Oh, my Gods! Just thinking about it makes my head ache. Why can’t Mummy let me take leave for one day. Just one day! What's the harm in that?” thought Parvathi as she lay lazily on the bed thinking about the day ahead of her. "Parvathi! Parvathi! It's time for school dear! Come on, wake up!” yelled Ma. "5 minutes Ma," said Parvathi as she curled up comfortably in her bed. Soon, the 5 minutes became 7, 10,15… The school bus came outside but Parvathi was still sleeping even though her mother had told her to get up. The school bus started honking hoping that Parvathi would come and board it. But no! Parvathi would still be sleeping! At last, it was time for Papa to go to office and Ma to go to school as she was a teacher. Parvathi’s little brother Ashwin also went with their mother to school. Ma went grumbling to Parvathi about how this laziness would develop into a habit and how it will affect her future. But to Parvathi all that scolding was nothing as she was in her own heaven- Ma had finally allowed her to take one day off at school! “Oh, what fun I am about to have,” she thought while she was laying down in her bed. At 9:45 am, she woke up yawning and stretching as she went to brush her teeth. She was dancing in joy while she ate her breakfast, unable to sit down in one place. After breakfast she made a list of stuff, she was to do that day: # 1: EAT SNACKS # 2: WATCH TELEVISION # 3: MAKE MY OWN DANCE PARTY # 4: KARAOKE TIME # 5: OPEN MA’S ALMIRAH AND DO A MAKEOVER!! Parvathi went to a tall cupboard were Pa kept all the snacks. Parvathi and Ashwin were always forbidden to eat any of those snacks as those were not good for their health, especially the gut. Pa never encouraged those snacks in their home but people who came to visit them brought all of those. She was tempted to eat those Kinder Eggs, M&Ms, Peanut butter cups and that divine looking Toblerone. She switched on the television and started munching on the chocolates. Soon it was 10:40 am and Parvathi was bored that she had watched television for a long time and ate many chocolates that her teeth were aching. She went to her room and took the Amazon Alexa to the living room, there she played songs and started to dance. But one can’t dance all day. Parvathi was soon laying on the floor, panting as she looked up at the time hoping it would be noon. Alas, it was only 11:20 am! She still had many more hours until her Ma and Pa came home. “Aaaahh… My stomach is aching!! Ouch!” cried Parvathi, suddenly. “It must be all those snacks! Why did I have to eat all of them? I should have listened to Pa!” She moaned in agony. She tried to sleep, but as she had already woken up late, she couldn’t drift back to sleep. Then she decided to keep a hot pack on her stomach, like her Ma did when she used to have stomach aches. Even after she kept the hot pack, she didn’t feel any different so she decided to eat some homemade, healthy Idly. After some time, she felt better. “Looks like eating healthy actually helps our body,” thought Parvathi. Later she went to Ma’s almirah and took out a long T-shirt which was like a gown for Parvathi. Then, she put on makeup and viewed herself at the mirror. “Not bad. Maybe some more lipstick.” said Parvathi. But Parvathi’s sensitive skin was not at all used to this heavy makeup and started erupting rashes all over her face! Parvathi got scared. She started to cry. “Oh God! help me! Please! I shall hereafter go to school like a good girl and will not think it is blissful to sit at home. I shall not take mother for granted and will not complain about studying. Please help me to get rid of these ugly rashes!” begged Parvathi. Then suddenly Parvathi spotted a bottle which read “USED FOR MAKEUP REMOVAL.” “Aha! If I remove my makeup with this, I may be able to find a solution for my skin problem,” saying this Parvathi uncorked that bottle, took a piece of cotton in her hands and began to remove the makeup. When she was done, Parvathi looked at the mirror. “My beautiful face! All ruined because I wanted to apply makeup. Only if I had listened to Ma when she said that makeup was only for adults,” moaned Parvathi. Then she saw another bottle that read “FOR PIMPLES AND SCARS REMOVAL.” Parvathi jumped with joy. God had heard her at last! She applied it. Then later stood the same Parvathi who stood before the mirror in the morning while brushing her teeth. Only a little bit wiser. All of a sudden, she knew what to do! Later, the doorbell rang. “DING DONG DING DONG.” Parvathi was overjoyed! She ran and opened the door. AND LO BEHOLD THERE STOOD MA AND ASHWIN!! Ma couldn’t recognize her daughter and the house! Parvathi for a change had taken bath, combed her hair and wore neat dress instead of her usual jeans and shabby top. AND THE HOUSE! OH, MY GODS! MA WAS LOST FOR WORDS AND SHE COULD ONLY STARE AT THE SPARKLING TILES AND THE GLEAMING WALLS. Then, as even more of a surprise, Ma saw that Parvathi had been doing her homework and had even tidied her room! “My Parvathi! What made you see sense? How did you do all this?” asked the astounded Ma hugging her beloved daughter. “Well Ma, as a proverb once said “EARLY TO BED AND EARLY TO RISE MAKES A MAN HEALTHY AND WISE,” said Parvathi, wisely. Ma never had to wake Parvathi again as she woke up on her own every morning and was always prompt to board the school bus, whether it was Monday or not. Parvathi had learnt her lesson. She now knew that even if it was Monday again, she would still have two days of holidays after five working days, ahead of her. LET’S ALL BE LIKE THE NEW PARVATHI AND MAKE SURE THAT WE DO ALL WORK WITH DEDICATION AND DEVOTION.
author: Adhvika  Prefulla Rajiv
illustrator: Alina  Aphayvanh; Alison de Villiers; Angie & Upesh; Bulbul Sharma; Canato Jimo; El Huyno; Fahad Faizal; Heather  Jenkins; Helga Parekh; Kalyani  Ganapathy; Kavya  Bagga; Manobendro Golder; Melany  Pietersen; Priyankar Gupta; Raghu  Ramachandran; Shreeya Wagh; Sujan  Chitrakar; Suman  Maharjan; Tanvi Bhat; Taposhi Ghoshal; VERUSHKA DHOUNDIYAL; Yashasvi Chhabra; Yuvaka  Srestha; Zainab Tambawalla

title: Bebo's First Day on Planet Earth
text: Hi, I’m Bebo! When I opened my eyes, I found myself on a soft green leaf. Mom told me I had just come out of my pupa. Inside it, I changed from a crawling larva into a ladybug - a cute little red beetle with black dots. I agree with her. I am very cute, aren’t I? Come with me as I explore this big, beautiful world. But first… I need to eat. I’m so hungry! Mom said aphids are yummy. They are tiny, green bugs, which suck plant juice. I don’t know where they are, but I hope I find some soon! Oh! What is this warm, crumbly stuff? It feels so different from the smooth green leaf I was on earlier. Oh! What is this warm, crumbly stuff? It feels so different from the smooth green leaf I was on earlier. This is soil! Plants grow in it. It’s like a big brown bed for their roots. Just as I was getting tired of walking, I felt something tickle my back. I turned and noticed… I have wings!! Wings? That means… I can FLY??? I stretched them out. My shiny wings were hidden under my red-spotted shell. Whoosh! The wind lifted me up. I’m flyiiiiiing! Look at those tall plants with bright yellow flowers. They shine like little suns in the garden. I’m going to land on one. Hey, look - aphids! Loads of them! They are sitting in rows on the stem, slurping plant juice. Aha! Snack time! Mmm… Mom was right. Aphids are delicious! And guess what? By eating them, I also saved the plants. Suddenly, I hear giggles behind a leaf. Yes. I'm Bebo! Who are you? Hi! I’m Click. That’s Jewel. You are new here, aren't you? We’re all insects. We have six legs. We may be different in colour, shape, or size, but we can all be friends. Yay! I love making friends. What a wonderful first day! I’m so sleepy now. This curled-up leaf looks just right for resting. Today I flew, made friends, ate yummy aphids, and learned many new things. Tomorrow, I’ll explore even more. Goodnight, Planet Earth.
author: Garima Sinha

title: Amitav Mohapatra: A Life Rooted in Service, Legacy, and Family Values
text: Remembering My Grandfather: Late Amitav Mohapatra Born: 19th November 1924 | Died: 3rd September 1985. Parents: Late Sarala Devi and Late Bhagirathi Mohapatra. Spouse: Late Bishnupriya Mohapatra | Children: Six (Three sons and three daughters). My grandfather, Late Amitav Mohapatra, was the only son of the remarkable Sarala Devi and Bhagirathi Mohapatra. Born on 19th November 1924, he inherited not just the legacy of our family but the spirit of service, integrity, and social responsibility that defined my grandmother’s life. Early Life and Education Grandfather grew up surrounded by ideals of justice, compassion, and activism. From a young age, he participated in the freedom struggle, including the Banara Sena movement, and actively engaged in Indian National Congress activities. He pursued his studies at Ravenshaw Collegiate School, completed his B.A. at Ravenshaw College, and earned an LL.B. from Madhusudan Law College, preparing him for a life of service through law and civic engagement. Legal Career and Public Service As a lawyer in Cuttack, he earned a reputation for honesty, fairness, and dedication. He worked with eminent leaders and lawyers like Pandit Nilakantha Das, Pandit Gopabandhu Das, Ashok Das, and Bipin Bihari Rath, yet he never sought personal glory. During 1942–1945, he was imprisoned for three years for his involvement in the freedom movement, emerging as one of the youngest recognized Congress leaders of his era. Leadership and Social Contributions Grandfather’s contributions went beyond politics and law. He served as President of the Cuttack City Congress Committee and General Secretary of the Ravenshaw College Managing Committee, guided student movements, organized the National Lawyers’ Conference in Bombay in 1981, and led flood relief efforts in 1982. His intellect, kindness, and cultural grounding inspired everyone around him. Family Life and Legacy Despite his public commitments, he always remained the pillar of our family. He shared a devoted life with my Grandmother Late Bishnupriya Mohapatra and together they raised six children: Nivedita Mohapatra, Late Mihir Prakash Mohapatra, Late Bharati Mohapatra, Laxmi Prakash Mohapatra, Sasmita Mohapatra & Bhavani Prakash Mohapatra (My Father). His grandchildren including me, Shannaya Mohapatra, along with Debangshu Mohapatra, Bignesh Das, and Ashvika A Mohapatra as we continue to cherish and uphold the values he lived by: honesty, service, education, and integrity. A Life Inspired by Sarala Devi’s Ideals My Grandfather Amitav Mohapatra’s life reflects my great Grandparent’s (Bhagirathi Mohapatra & Sarala Devi) quiet continuity &legacy. While Sarala Devi & Bhagirathi Mohapatra lived in the public eye, my Grandfather Amitav Mohapatra represented their ideals through private service, family nurturing, and social responsibility. His gentle nature, sense of duty, and respect for cultural and moral principles allowed him to maintain a strong ethical compass while guiding his family and community. Even after his untimely passing on 3rd September 1985, at the age of 58, Grandfather Amitav’s life continues to resonate through the values he instilled in his children and grandchildren. He remains a symbol of honesty, selfless service, and family devotion, embodying the enduring legacy of Sarala Devi in the modern era. My Grandfather Late Amitav Mohapatra was not just the son of a legendary freedom fighter; he was a leader, social reformer, lawyer, motivator, and devoted family man. His contributions to law, society, and his family reflect a life of purpose, integrity and quiet heroism. To me, he was more than my grandfather; he was a mentor, a moral compass, and a living testament to the values of courage, dedication, and social responsibility. Through his life and the family he nurtured, the legacy of Bhagirathi Mohapatra and of Sarala Devi continues to inspire generations in Odisha and beyond.
author: Shannaya Mohapatra

title: DANCING WITH GRANDMA
text: Paru danced everywhere—on the sidewalk, in the car, in the middle of a shop, even while waiting for the school van! “Paru, stop that! Dancing is for the stage!” people scolded. But Paru couldn’t help it. Dance lived in her heart. Only Grandma understood and cheered her on. “Dance, my beautiful. The world needs to see your grace!” At home, Paru begged, ‘Grandma, please play the dance video on TV!’. She would watch, eyes wide, then ta-da!- copy every move. Grandma joined in too. Together, they twirled and danced. Even her shy brother, Unni, tried a step or two. One day, Paru’s teacher noticed her twirling gracefully, “You’ll dance at the school annual day!” Paru, bursting with excitement, ran to Grandma and hugged her. “Grandma, I’ve been selected for the dance program! The teacher says I have to practice and stay healthy. So, no more crying for junk foods.” Grandma hugged her tight. “Oh, my beautiful, I always knew you would shine!” They practiced daily- laughing, spinning, stumbling, trying again. The big day arrived. Paru was beaming with excitement. She loved every bit of it—the makeup, the costumes, the lights, and the music! On stage, she looked out to the crowd. There they were—Grandma and Unni, waving and cheering. Paru smiled, and her eyes started shining. Under the spotlight, she danced her heart out. She was again selected for the second dance performance in school, and her excitement continued. But not every day was a happy one. One afternoon, Paru came home disappointed. Grandma asks, ‘What happened, beautiful?’. ‘The teacher did not call me for annual day dance practice,’ she said. Grandma hugged her. ‘Oh, my beautiful,’ she said, holding her face. ‘Remember, Paru, a little cloud doesn’t stop the sun from shining. Your moment will come.’ Unni gave a hug and said, ‘Let’s dance here instead.’ And Paru was smiling again and dancing to her own music. After a few days, Paru rushed home, beaming. ‘I told you, my beautiful, the stage was waiting for you!’ Grandma said. On the big day, Paru danced with all her heart. She saw Grandma and her brother clapping in the audience. Grandma whispers to herself, “That’s my Beautiful,” as Paru twirled and shinned like a star. The next day in school, she was looked upon by kids, and Paru was feeling very excited. The teacher came inside the class. “This is Gitanjali by Rabindranath Tagore,” the teacher said, holding up a book. ‘This book won the Nobel Prize for being musical and graceful. Do you know what Gitanjali means? It’s a song offering.’ The teacher looked at Paru and smiled. ‘Like Tagore’s Gitanjali, we have our own graceful ‘Gitanjali’ here—Geethu, who dances from the heart!’ Paru’s face just brimmed with pride and joy. She couldn’t wait to tell this to Grandma. At home, she ran straight to her. Grandma, did you know Tagore’s Gitanjali won a Nobel Prize? My teacher said I am like Gitanjali—graceful!’ Grandma’s eyes twinkled. ‘Oh, my beautiful,’ she said and hugged Paru. ‘You are graceful, musical, and full of talent. Just be yourself and believe in yourself.’ That evening, music filled the room, and Paru danced with happiness, swaying and moving like a perfect music note. Grandma and Unni, as always, clapped and cheered her on: ‘Oh, beautiful Gitanjali, live your dreams.’
author: Anjali A

title: The crow at the window
text: It was a bright, sunny morning in Tiruchi, a small town in Tamil Nadu. In a small house in a quiet colony, the day began as usual with bustling household chores. The lady of the house placed a morsel of rice, dal, and ghee at the backyard and called out, “Ka, ka, ka… Sundaresa, vaa, vaa!” Her little daughter, Radha, a fourth grader, curious as ever, asked, “Amma, who is Sundaresa? You call him every day and give him food.” Her mother smiled gently. “He’s the crow that comes here. But we believe our ancestors come in this form to partake of the food we offer. That’s why we call him Sundaresa—your great-great-grandfather.” The thought sank quietly into the back of Radha’s young mind, never forgotten. Radha grew into a compassionate, nature-loving woman of fifty-four, one who found joy in the smallest rituals of daily life. She saved rice water to nourish her plants and never ate breakfast before watering them. She also made sure to give her maid a share of food and coffee each morning, remembering her mother’s words: “Vaai vaazhthaatalum vayaru vaazhthum” — “Even if the mouths don’t wish you well, the stomachs will.” For the last one and a half years, a crow had appeared at her kitchen window every morning at exactly eight o’clock, cawing insistently. Radha, almost instinctively, offered it a morsel of food—rice, dal, and ghee—just as her mother once did. The crow would eat in silence and fly away. Though she had always fed crows on festival days, she had never done it with such regularity. This routine had begun only because the crow itself kept arriving, as though demanding the ritual. Slowly, the memory of her mother’s words resurfaced. Radha began to wonder—was this her father, who had passed away one and a half years ago, now visiting her every day? She remembered the morning when it all began, one and half year back. Still grieving her father’s loss, she had been busy cooking when loud cawing startled her. She placed some food on the window ledge. The crow ate, but lingered even after finishing. Amused, she offered more, saying softly, “Eat this—and call your friends too.” The crow cawed in reply, ate every grain, and finally left. The visits continued day after day until one morning, as Radha watched through the kitchen window, disaster struck. She had just placed the food when, by accident, she dropped the water jug in her hand. Splaaaash! Water spilled everywhere as she cried out, “Oh no!” The sudden commotion startled the crow, sending it flapping away in fright. Radha froze. Her heart sank. “Maybe he won’t come back,” she thought, her chest tightening with guilt. “Crows are clever—they remember everything.” She was so possessed with this thought that she googled about crow’s remarkable long term memory and cognitive abilities. Everyday, she kept longing for the return of the little creature. From that day, her mornings were filled with restless waiting. The window stayed empty. The silence weighed heavily on her. Her daughter dismissed her worries, her son laughed at her beliefs, but Radha could not shake the ache of losing the visitor she had begun to see as her appa. On a festival day, her appa’s favourite snack came to mind—vada. With a strong conviction, she placed one on the window ledge and waited, her eyes fixed on the empty space. Minutes dragged on. Then, at last, the crow appeared, cautious and alert, looking here and there. Radha held her breath, afraid even the sound of it might drive him away. The crow pecked at the vada. Relief flooded her. Tears welled in her eyes. She knew then—this was no coincidence. This was her father’s presence. Since that day, the ritual continued daily. Once the crow cawed, Radha would immediately place a small morsel on the window ledge, careful not to make the slightest noise. Sometimes she even spoke softly to it: “Wait, I’m coming.” The crow seemed to pause, tilting its head as if listening. At times, it even met her gaze through the window mesh, its dark eyes locking with hers in a quiet moment of recognition. Once, when her husband carelessly moved near the window, she stopped him, whispering not to disturb the crow. Skeptical at first, he peered through the mesh and saw it eating. Surprised, he too began to respect the routine, even asking her daily whether “their guest” had eaten. Radha often reflected on how Hindu traditions quietly weave compassion into everyday life. Simple ritual like feeding a crow isn’t just about belief—it is about care, gratitude, and remembrance. Whether or not it was tru ly her father, Radha felt grateful. Yes, such small things shape our everyday lives. Some of us do them mindfully, while others follow them without realizing. But traditions like these must be understood at their core, through logical reasoning, rather than brushed aside as blind belief.
author: Anuradha

title: Meet Me Where The Shadows Echo: Chapter One
text: Meet Me Where The Shadows Echo Chapter One: Stranger In The Hallways Loneliness had teeth. Syphen felt its bite every morning when he dragged himself out of bed, every night when he lay staring at the ceiling while the rest of the world seemed busy living. At thirteen, he wasn’t invisible in the literal sense—no cool superpower, no comic-book glitch. But it still felt like people’s eyes just slid past him, like he was some smudge in the corner of their lives. Teachers praised his grades, classmates whispered about his brain, but no one ever sat with him at lunch. He was the smart kid. The quiet one. The… nobody. Teachers praised his grades, classmates whispered about his brain, but no one ever sat with him at lunch. He was the smart kid. The quiet one. The… nobody. And maybe, just maybe, the emptiness ran deeper because somewhere, out there, he had a twin sister. He only knew the story in fragments—words overheard late at night when his parents thought he was asleep. They’d been young, broke, and scared when he and his sister were born. Raising one child had felt impossible. Raising two? Out of the question. So his sister had been given away, a “better chance at life” wrapped in someone else’s arms. Syphen couldn’t remember her face. Couldn’t remember her voice. But sometimes—when he was scribbling lyrics in his notebook or humming half-formed songs—he felt her absence like a missing note in a melody. An ache shaped like a person. Then life threw his family a plot twist. One evening, his father came home with wide eyes and shaking hands. “I got the job,” he whispered, as though saying it too loudly might make it vanish. It wasn’t just a job—it was the job. More money, more security, a real chance to breathe. Within weeks, their crumbling apartment was emptied into cardboard boxes, and they moved into a house with sunlight and space and curtains that didn’t smell like mold. Syphen finally had his own room. A window that opened to the city skyline. A desk where he could spread out his notebooks. His mom hummed while cooking, his dad actually smiled. For the first time, the future didn’t feel like some collapsing roof waiting to crush them. But none of that changed the way Syphen felt about people. When his parents enrolled him in the city’s most prestigious school, his stomach twisted into knots. “You’ll do great, sweetheart,” his mom said, brushing his hair back. “This is where you’ll shine.” Shine. Right. That was hilarious. The morning of his first day, the school loomed in front of him like some modern-day castle. Marble steps gleamed in the sun, glass windows reflected clouds, banners fluttered high with gold lettering about Excellence and Innovation. Groups of kids laughed at the gate, already belonging. Syphen gripped his backpack tighter. “Ufff,” he muttered under his breath, “this is gonna be a whole disaster.” Inside, the hallways stretched like endless rivers of polished tiles. Lockers clanged, footsteps echoed, chatter swelled like waves. The air smelled faintly of citrus cleaning spray and new books. He felt… small. Like a ghost drifting through a palace built for everyone except him. He stopped at the reception desk, cleared his throat, and muttered, “Uh, I’m Syphen. New student.” The receptionist gave him a polite smile, handed him a schedule, and said, “Class 8B. Second floor, down the left wing.” He nodded, thanked her, and tried to look like he knew where he was going. Spoiler: he didn’t. At his locker, he fumbled with the lock combination. His palms were sweaty, his heartbeat annoyingly loud. Finally, with a satisfying click, the door swung open. He stuffed his books inside, organizing them by size like the nerd he secretly was. Just as he reached to shut the locker— “You new here?” Syphen jumped so hard he almost slammed the locker on his own fingers. Spinning around, he froze. A girl stood leaning against the locker next to his, arms crossed, watching him with eyes, that glittered like they already knew his secrets. She was his age, maybe a year older. Her hair fell in messy waves that somehow looked intentional, and her grin? Chaotic. “I—uh—sure—I mean yes, I’m new,” Syphen stammered. Smooth. Real smooth. The girl laughed, not in a cruel way but like she found him genuinely entertaining. And then, without warning, she grabbed his hand. “Come on,” she said. “Wait—what—hey!” Syphen yelped as she tugged him down the hallway. Students turned their heads as they sprinted past, but the girl didn’t care. Her laughter spilled into the air, reckless and loud. Syphen stumbled, half running, half dragged, his brain short-circuiting. Wth is happening?! Is this kidnapping?? Am I about to die on my first day??? But… weirdly, he was laughing too. His heart wasn’t pounding from fear this time. No—this was something else. Something electric. Something terrifying in a good way. Hope. They stopped abruptly in front of a door with golden letters: Music Room. Both bent over, gasping for breath. “What—was—that—about?” Syphen panted, hands on his knees. The girl didn’t answer. Instead, she slipped into the room like it was hers. Syphen groaned. “Ufff, are you serious right now? Stranger girl just drags me into the void, and I follow? Yep. Totally logical. Great choices, Syphen.” Still, he went in. The room was dim, curtains drawn tight. Dust floated lazily in the air, catching faint streaks of light. Instruments waited in silence—rows of guitars leaning like soldiers at rest, a piano glimmering faintly as if breathing, drums with skins stretched tight. It almost felt alive, like the room itself had been waiting for them. The girl stood in the middle, shadowed and still. “Uhmm… ayo, stranger girl?” Syphen said cautiously. “Geez, you’re creeping me out!” A laugh rang out, low and mischievous. “Oh my, do you think I’m some kind of witch who’s gonna devour you?” she teased, stepping forward. “Well, I’m not. Disappointing, huh?” “Uh—no, I mean—” Syphen stuttered. His brain screamed WHAT THE HELL BRO SAY SOMETHING COOL. His mouth betrayed him. The girl tilted her head. “Relax, stranger boy. I don’t bite. Name’s Stellar.” Stellar. It fit her too perfectly—like the universe had named her for chaos and light. Her gleaming ocean blue eyes, mid length and curly hairs with the darkest shade of brown with highlights of golden that shined in the dim sunlight, A scar on her neck, surprisingly the features that Syphen had too. Before he could respond, his eyes flicked to the clock. Panic. “Oh crap, I’m late!” he yelped. And just like that, he bolted. His sneakers squeaked against the polished floor, his backpack smacking against his side as he ran toward class. By the time he stumbled into 8B, his lungs burned. Students turned to look. He ducked his head and slid into the first empty desk he found, trying to look invisible again. As he unpacked his notebook, a voice floated through the room. A familiar voice. “Hmm… left me in the dark with so many things, huh? God listens.” Syphen’s head snapped up. Stellar. She strode into the classroom like she owned it, the sass in her walk practically glowing. Conversations hushed, eyes followed her. But she didn’t care. Her gaze locked onto his, and she smirked. Syphen’s stomach did a wild somersault. She slid into the seat beside him, plopping her bag on the desk. “Well… what’s your name, stranger boy?” she asked, eyebrow raised. Syphen swallowed. “Oh, uhh… I’m Syphen. Nice to meet you… again.” Her grin widened. And just like that, something shifted. The world didn’t feel so empty anymore. title: My Role
text: One girl lives in a village with their parent. Her mother and father always take care of her, but she dreams about what my role is. She always thinks about her role. She wanted to help her parents, but due to her young age, she was unable to help her parents. She decided to do her own work without their support. The next morning, she brushed, washed, and combed her hair. Mom was happy, but her Father said You are our child, you don't need to do any work. We will do your regular work. But the girl said Papa, tell me what my role is in this house. I am not a doll. Papa said you are my doll, you don't need to do any work. The girl said I want to do my work, like keep my shoes in place, arrange all my books on the bookshelf. Finally, parents said, whatever work you want to do as per your wish, do it; we are always supportive of you. The girl is happy about her role. You all are thinking about your role. You are all young; think about how you can give happiness to your parents. You all study well, it is your best help to parents, and right now your role is a student.
author: Rita Kumari

title: Ramayan
text: Ayodhya was a magnificent city on the banks of the river Sarayu in Kosala Country. It had wide roads, huge buildings, beautiful parks and glittering shops. The people of the city lived a happy and contented life as they were ruled by a wonderful king called Dasharatha. He cared for his people very deeply. King Dasahratha had three wives, Kaushalya, Sumitra and Kaikeyi. Kaushalya was the eldest queen. Though the king loved all his wives deeply, it was Kaikeyi, his youngest queen who was his favourite.But in spite of leading such a good life. Dasahratha was still an unhappy man.This was because he had no children. He was getting old and had no son to ascend to the throne. Unable to see the king being sad, the sages advised him to undertake a yagna and pray for children. Heeding to their advice, he performed the yagna and pleased with him, Agni, the fire God, emerged out of the fire pit, handed over a cup containing sweetened milk to the king and told him "O king! This kheer is the nectar of life. It was prepared by the gods in heaven. Distribute it among your wives. You will be blessed with sons." Dasahratha was delighted. He thanked Agni for this boon and in the royal chamber, gave Kaushalya half of the kheer. He divided the remaining kheer into two portions and gave one portion to Sumitra and the other one to Kaikeyi. Subsequently all the three queens gave birth to sons, Kaushalya gave birth to Rama, after which Bharata was born to Kaikeyi and later on Sumitra gave birth to Lakshmana and Shatrugna.King Dasahratha was very happy and so were the people of Ayodhya.With great rejoice, they celebrated the birth of the four princes. Dasharatha loved all his sons but Rama was his dearest. He was very proud of his handsome eldest son and could not bear to be away from him even for a moment.
author: Rita Kumari
illustrator: ANAND KASHYAP; Angie & Upesh; hemanth__ shashi; Rishika R

title: I like to play and learn
text: Titu and Mitu Titu and Mitu are best friends. Today, Titu says, “I don’t want to study.” Mitu smiles and brings some play money—fake rupees! They play shop-shop. Titu buys fruits, Mitu sells toys. Both laugh and learn numbers while playing. 1....2......3......4.....and 5. ﻿ At the end, Titu says, “Wow! Learning can be fun!”

title: The Humble Weaver and the Boastful Tailor
text: In a bustling town on the edge of a wide river lived two men known by nearly everyone: Devan the Weaver and Prakash the Tailor. Devan lived in a small house near the riverbanks. His hands were rough, his clothes simple, and his days long. He spent hours at his wooden loom, weaving cloth thread by thread, rhythmically and patiently. His cloth was soft, strong, and lasted for years. Though his earnings were modest, Devan lived a peaceful life. Just a few streets away, in a grand house with tall gates and a golden nameplate, lived Prakash. He was the town’s most fashionable tailor. With his sharp scissors, expensive fabrics, and clever tongue, he stitched coats for the mayor, vests for the merchants, and dresses for the wives of noblemen. Prakash had grown wealthy and proud, and never missed a chance to boast about it. One day, as fate would have it, Prakash passed by Devan’s stall in the market. "You still selling plain cloth, Devan?" Prakash asked with a smirk. "People want style now, not rags!" Devan smiled. "Plain cloth is like honest work—it never goes out of fashion." Prakash laughed. "Perhaps. But it never makes anyone rich either." He strutted off, his shoes clicking loudly against the stone path. That evening, Devan returned home and continued weaving by lamplight. A traveler from a distant village had ordered several rolls of cloth for an upcoming festival. Though the payment was small, Devan treated the work with his usual care. Meanwhile, Prakash was preparing for the Grand Fashion Fair, an event held every year in the nearby city. Designers and tailors from all around came to show off their best work, and wealthy clients came to place big orders. Prakash saw this as his opportunity to become famous beyond the town—perhaps even open a shop in the city itself. But there was one problem. He had spent so much money on advertising and decorating his booth that he couldn’t afford the expensive imported fabric he usually used. His suppliers were late, and time was running out. Frustrated, he came up with an idea. The next morning, he went to Devan’s home with a fake smile and an offer. “Friend, I’ve realized the beauty of your cloth. It’s... timeless. I’d like to buy all of it for a spec- -cal project,” Prakash said. Devan hesitated. “It’s already promised to a traveler.” “I’ll pay you double,” Prakash added quickly. Devan thought for a moment. He needed the money—his roof had been leaking for weeks—but he also believed in keeping his word. “I’m sorry, Prakash,” he said. “It’s not just cloth. It’s a promise.” Prakash’s smile faded. “Foolish,” he muttered, and walked away. Angry and desperate, Prakash sent his apprentice to the market to buy any cloth available, even if the quality was poor. He stayed up all night stitching elaborate designs and adding glittering buttons to distract from the fabric’s roughness. t the Grand Fashion Fair, his stall glittered with color and shine. People stopped to look, impressed by the fancy designs. “City people want sparkle,” Prakash told himself. “They won’t notice the fabric.” He was right—for a while. A few city nobles placed large orders. One merchant even promised to fund a new shop for him. Prakash returned to the town boasting louder than ever. “A new era begins!” he shouted from his balcony. “From tailor to tycoon!” But the celebration didn’t last. Within a few weeks, complaints began to arrive. The coats lost shape after one wash. The thread came undone. The buttons fell off. The garments made for nobles itched their skin and tore at the seams. Word spread fast in the city—and not the kind Prakash had hoped for. Soon, the orders were canceled. His sponsor withdrew funding. Even his own townspeople stopped coming to his shop. His reputation, once dazzling, faded like sunlight on old fabric. Humiliated, Prakash shut down his shop and disappeared from public view. One evening, as the sun dipped behind the hills, he found himself walking by the river. There, sitting on a low stool under a mango tree, was Devan—his loom softly clicking, a cup of tea steaming beside him. For a moment, Prakash wanted to turn away. But his pride, once tall, had been humbled. He approached slowly. “I made a mess of things,” he admitted. “I wanted to rise fast... but I fell faster.” it Devan looked up, his hands still weaving. “Cloth teaches us, Prakash. Pull too hard, and tears. Weave too fast, and it’s weak.” There was a long silence. “I’ve come to ask,” Prakash said finally, “if you’ll teach me.” Devan nodded. “Then sit. The first lesson is to listen.” From that day on, Prakash returned each morning to Devan’s home. He learned to spin thread, to prepare dyes, to feel the rhythm of the loom. The work was slow, and at first his fingers ached. But slowly, he grew patient. As the months passed, a quiet friendship bloomed between the two men. They began selling their cloth together—one weaving, one tailoring. Word spread again, but this time for different reasons. “Honest hands,” people said, “and humble hearts.” Their shop became known for durable, beautiful garments—simple in appearance, but rich in care and meaning. Years later, a young boy in the market asked Prakash, “Didn’t you used to be the tailor with the golden sign?” Prakash smiled. “I used to chase gold,” he said. “Now I weave it into every stitch—only, you can’t see it. You feel it.” Moral: True success is woven with patience, honesty, and humility. Pride may shine quickly, but only character endures.

title: I am the first born
text: I am the first born of the family!! I was the first grandchild of both sides of my family - Paternal and Maternal. I was born first!!!!!!! I was the first grandchild of my Grandparents - Nana, Nani, Dada and Dadi. They must have cherished me like a flower...that's such an amazing thing to think. I was the favourite of all my uncles and aunts. A perfect little jingling toy for them. I must have made them laugh a lot....I think!!! I have no Didi and Bhaiya though..... to save me from falling and tripping. I miss being consoled and counselled. I have plenty of cousins....all younger to me. They have taught me to be patient and accepting. They make me smile and sometimes get annoyed!!! I love being the Forever Didi for all. I love being called up for consoling and counsel. I love being loved by both the generations....my uncles and aunts....and their numerous kids. It's fun being at the threshold....balancing the dynamics. I feel blessed!! I feel happy...too happy to be born as the first child of the clans.

title: Are you comfortable?
text: Sami was seven years old when she got a little brother. She was very happy to play with him. Together, they played happily. She was very happy to play with him. Together, they used to play happily. When she was in class six, one of her relatives came to her home. He used to give toys, chocolates and kissed her when she was alone. She felt awkward. One Friday evening, when Sami was going upstair to have dinner, he was on the way. He grabbed her body and hugged her forcefully trying to kiss her cheeks. Luckily, she escaped. He never did it when she was with her family. She did not enjoyed the hug, the kiss and the touch. It was not a good touch. It was not warm, safe and comfortable like her mother's hug. Sami was a quiet person at home as well as in her classroom. She had very few friends. Her parents were poor and not well educated. She began to worried. She was afraid because she thought something was wrong with her. Otherwise, he would not always touch her body in that way. But no one said "Oh! My sweet Sami! Nothing is wrong with you." The man was happy to see Sami struggling with her confusion. He took advantage of her silence. He suppressed her words with his giant body. He pretended to be a gentleman in front of her parents. They used to trust him a lot. So, Sami became more lonely and helpless. Sami became more lonely and helpless. Neither she could explain it to her friends nor her teachers. Suddenly, one day her father told her,"Sami, you need to take a tuition class with your uncle from tomorrow. Your marks is getting lower." "Oh no! That night she could not sleep properly. Sami was very frightened to study with him. But there was no choice. She could not focus on her study, but still tried to stay calm and attentive. Everyday, she had to be cautious and escape from his touch. Poor Sami! One day, h er parents were busy with their work. She was sitting next to him and writing in her note book. He came closer to her and put his arm around her shoulder. Sami felt suffocated. She wanted to shout and get rid of him so that she never had to see his face again. Her inner voice roared when he leaned forward to kiss her. Again!!! She shouted at him,"You monster! Sit at your own place. I will complain you to my parents." "Do not show your face to me. I will never take tuition with you." Little Sami struggled to find words. The only thing that she could not do was: Slap him! Beat him! Kick him! The silence grew deeper like the ocean. For the first time in her life, Sami felt so light. She took off the weight that she had been carrying for so long, all alone. He stepped back after seeing Sami's brave and bold part. While his ego was hurt, he became little bit angry. He left the room. She was still afraid if he would do something bad. Sami told her parents about the incident. Her father never insisted her to study with him since that day. Sami learned four lessons: 1. Say "NO" when it feels uncomfortable. 2. Leave the situation immediately. Do not suffer if you do not like it. 3. Talk to your parents, teachers, close friends or someone you highly trust. ﻿ 4. IT IS NEVER YOUR FAULT. Even though the person threatens you, do not be afraid. You will always get support. Today is Sami's birthday. "Happy Birthday Sami! May your dreams come true."

title: Let's Hug the Rain
text: Paru and Unni woke up suddenly. " What’s that sound?", they asked each other. "Is it something falling down?" "Is it music? Let’s go and check!" "Oh! It’s the sound of RAIN!" Paru jumped with excitement. "Look, Paru- the courtyard is filled with water!" "Let’s put paper boats!" "Hey! Unni,” Paru pointed. “Look, the puddles are joining hands.” Unni traced the water path with his finger. “This little lake hugs that one… and that one… Now it’s a river escaping our courtyard! Where does it go? All the way to the ocean?” Paru gasped. “Let’s tell our friends that there was a river in our house!” Paru got paper and folded a boat. "I made one! Let me try it!" SPLASH. The boat sank. Paru’s face fell. Unni said, "Let me try. I know how to make a better boat." (Paru watched, sad and quiet.) He put his boat in the water. "Look, Paru- mine will go far!" SPLASH. Unni's boat sank too. "Your boat also drowned!" Paru shouted. "Amma! Amma! Help!" they shouted together. Amma said, "Yes, coming!" She hurried from the kitchen. “Amma, listen!" Paru said. "Amma, listen!" Unni said. Amma smiled. "Be patient. Can one of you tell me what happened?" Paru shared, and Unni added more. Amma giggled. "Both of you..." "Amma, why are you smiling?" they frowned. Amma said, “Rain is many little drops joined together." "Really?" Unni asked, eyes wide. "Yes," Amma nodded. "They fall heavy- that’s why your boats sank! Wait until the rain stops …Then your boats will float." "Amma, is Indra the God behind this rain?" Paru asked. Amma smiled. "Ammumma told me that Indra is the rain god." “Maybe he is... or maybe the clouds are happy today," Amma said. "Amma, how is rain made?" Unni asked. Amma tapped Paru’s bangle. "It’s like this—round and round!" "The sun shines and warms up water from lakes and seas. The water turns to vapour and dances up, up, up!" "The vapour forms cotton candy clouds in the sky!" Paru and Unni imagined themselves floating among the clouds. “Hey! Where are you two?" Amma called. "Ha-ha! We were just floating in the clouds, Amma!" "When clouds become heavy-POP, they burst! Like when Unni blew too much air in his balloon and it popped!", Amma said. "So, clouds cry when they’re full?" Paru asked. Amma smiled. "Maybe... or maybe they fall to kiss the ground and rise again!" "If that's true," said Unni, "can we touch them too? Can we play with the rain?" Amma paused, then nodded. "Okay... you can." Paru and Unni ran outside "Raindrops, we will hug you too!” And when the rain slowed. Paru and Unni’s boats FLOATED- Just like Amma said they would.
author: Anjali A

title: Adventures of Bulbul - Part 2
text: Andril and Hedwig are friends. They were sleeping peacefully at home. Andril woke up and realised something. She got angry and splashed water on hedwig's face. “Why did you do that?” Hedwig shouted. “We said we will go to Mountain Shadow. But you are still sleeping!” Andril shouted back. Hedwig rubbed his eyes. “Oh! Sorry, little one. Let’s go.” Just then, the bell rang. Ding dong! It was Bulbul at the door! Bulbul sat down. He told them about his old adventures. “Can you take us to Mountain Shadow?” asked Hedwig. “Yes,” Bulbul said. “But you must know how the place looks.” So they called Suganya. Suganya smiled and said, “Mountain Shadow is on the banks of a big lake. Behind the lake rise tall greenish mountains, covered in trees. The banks are full of flowers - red, yellow, purple, and pink. The lake shines with water, and when it rains, the whole place sparkles even more.” Andril clapped her little hands with excitement. “Wow! I want to go there!” she said. That night, they curled up under the magic bedsheet, dreaming of Mountain Shadow. But in the morning, they woke up in Kabini Forest! “You tricked us!” Hedwig shouted. Bulbul shook his head. “No! Something went wrong. A feather is missing from the bedsheet” Bulbul explained, “I once gave my peacock bedsheet to Javin. Later, Javin returned it to me. I placed it on top of my magic bedsheet near my pillow. Somehow, in the night, the two bedsheets merged into one. Maybe that is why this happened.” Just then—ping! A message came. It was from the peacock. “Please help me,” the peacock wrote. “I am hurt. A tiger, elephant, leopard, and panther are close by. I cannot escape.” Andril tilted her head. “So that’s why we are here!” she whispered. Hedwig spread his wings. Andril held on tight as Bulbul guided them through the trees. They rushed to the location from where peacock texted them. They reached and saw pugmark of tiger and elephant. But there was no sign of the peacock. Suddenly—ROAR! The sound shook the forest. Andril and Hedwig quickly hopped onto a tall tree branch. They looked down carefully. It wasn’t a tiger at all. It was Gowthy w ith Sahana and Sanjana, and Divi. They were staying at the Serai Resort and stepped out for birdwatching that morning. Sahana had just asked, “How does a tiger look in the wild? How will it sound?” So Gowthy was showing them pictures and playing the sound of a tiger’s roar on his phone. That was the roar Andril and Hedwig had heard! Everyone laughed in relief. Then the groups greeted each other warmly. Andril, Bulbul and Hedwig told that they got lost in Kabini forest and was looking to save peacock. Gowthy said that he knows a friend who can help - Ruddy the mongoose. He is a naturalist and loves to solve mysterious problems. They met Ruddy the mongoose. Ruddy, after listening to the problem, said that we need necessary tools - a compass, GPS, binoculars, notebook, and pen. He also said, “We need to talk to kutti who can connect us to Princess Jasmine. She can help us find peacock” He called Kutti, "Hello Kutti!" "Bonjour," replied Kutti. "I dont want Bun. Listen to me." Sanjana and Sahana laughed and corrected Ruddy, "Bonjour means Hi / Hello in French." "Oh really! Bonjour Kutti," said ruddy with a smile. Then he told the story and asked for him help. Kutti shared Princess Jasmine's location. Immediately, everyone rushed to Princess Jasmine's palace located in the middle of the forest and asked her help. "I understand. Kutti told me everything. I will definitely help you. But lets eat first." Jasmine replied in a sweet voice. On the table there was food - pasta, pizza, curd rice, juice, and milk. After they ate, Princess Jasmine clapped her hands and whoosh! They were inside the jungle. It was magical. Sahana and Sanjana got excited. "There are three obstacles that you need to cross. You will have to solve the puzzles for the last two. And you will find peacock," said Jasmine. "Wow! Puzzle. I will solve it. I will solve it." Sahana and Sanjana shouted in excitement. Then Jasmine pointed to a tall pine tree and asked them to climb. "Thats your first task. Good luck." Jasmine smiled and disappeared. Hedwig flapped his strong wings. Andril tried climbing, but she was too small. Suddenly—whoosh! Her arms turned into wings. Her little feet became claws. Andril had transformed into a tiny bird! Everyone was stunned. “Look! Andril is a bird!” cried Sahana. At first Andril struggled but after a little practise, she dived in the air like an expert. Then she chirped with delight, “I can fly now!” Together, Hedwig and Andril helped the others climb up the tree. After climbing up, they saw a thundering waterfall blocked the path. Mist made it hard to see. One of the rocks glowed and the words started to appear slowly. It was a riddle: “I have no mouth, but I roar. I have no legs, but I run. What am I?” “Water! Water!” shouted Sanjana and Sahana together. The rocks glowed and slowly moved forming a walking path. A safe path appeared. Sahana bravely stepped first, "Follow me!" Everyone held hands and crossed together. Carefully, everyone crossed the waterfalls and found a bridge made of tree roots. It was loosely hanging above a deep river. As they stepped on it, they saw the riddle slowly appeared on the root. “I grow tall, I give you shade. Cut me down, and I am afraid. What am I?” “Tree!” said both girls at once. The bridge became steady. Sahana and Sanjana led everyone across. They met Peacock on the other side of the bridge. Immediately, a feather appeared on bulbul's magic bedsheet. "Look" he said and everyone looked at it with amazement. "Now we can go to Mountain Shadow" Andril shouted enthusiastically. Sahana and Sanjana also wanted to join. Bulbul said let them go and meet their parents. Sahana and Sanjana slept using the magic bedsheet and woke up at the Mountain Shadow. Senthil and Suganya was very happy to meet them. The girls told them the entire story. It was a happy day - meeting new friends and having fun.

title: molly and dolly adventure
text: One day, Molly the cat and Dolly the duck found a mysterious map under a couch cushion. “Treasure!” squeaked Dolly. “ Snacks,” corrected Molly, licking her lips. They followed the map to the backyard, where an X marked the spot… right on top of Mr. Jenkins' tortoise shell. “Excuse us, sir,” said Dolly. Mr. Jenkins blinked once and farted.... The treasure turned out to be a half-eaten sandwich and a glittery sock.... Dolly wore the sock as a hat. Molly ate the sandwich. “Best. Adventure. Ever,” they agreed, and fell asleep on the tortoise. The End. 🐱🦆🐢

title: Kidnapped
text: Hi, My name is Jasmine, this year I am twelve years old! believe it or not, I was kidnapped by my Friend! It all started of one day, on the 5th of September, I was eating my porridge in a bad mood, I hated porridge a lot! The only thing I hated more than my porridge was my sisters, I got Sophie as my little sister, and Mildred as my older sister! I quickly pushed the bowl of porridge away and ran out of the house before anyone could see me. Too bad I could hear footsteps coming, Mildred handed me the bowl of porridge and asked me to try again. I closed my eyes and drank the porridge. After I gave the porridge back to Mildred, I ran of to school as fast as a cheetah. When I arrived, the school gate was not opened yet, I was too early! suddenly, I heard a voice crying, it could ewwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww only mean one thing..."Sophie!" I cried, "you're disturbing my time!" I pushed her away before she could harm me any more." now now." I heard A voice say, I looked up, it was Anna! My best friend! She gave me a bowl of porridge and she told me her mom made it for me. I knew I hated porridge, but this was different" thanks" I said taking it into my hands. suddenly a l loud RING came through the radio"REPORT TO PLAYGROUND NOW!" I put away the porridge, and ran out as quick as the speed of light. Suddenly, a hand gripped tight around my throat, some tape was wraped through my neck, I tried to scream, but it was too late. All I could do was wait and wait for someone to save me. But all I could hear were muffled sounds. If I could scream, I would have told them to stay thanks! away. When I could finally open my eyes, I found out I was in a creepy room. I was desprate to find a way out. I spent my time thinking about a way to escape. Until one morning I woke up hearing strange snores, it was Anna! she gave me some noodles, and we both ate noodles. She told me that she was having a play date with her friend until, she got thrown into a well, but when she found her way out, soldiers took her here. I hugged her as we talked about a plan to escape."those punks don't know we're friends!", I said angrily. Then Anna said,"I've been torcherd by my friend! Then she said the friend was actually Rebecca! "Rebecca!"I gasped, my second best friend! Rebecca! So I sat and waited. I knew Rebecca would come to rescue us one day. When she came, we had already made ourselves at the creepy place. "Anna and Jasmine!"she shouted, I looked at her and ran up to hug her. But she pushed me away, and said,"we have no time to lose!", so we ran away quickly. When we went back home Rebecca locked us into our room, and we screamed for help. we soon were able to find a phone and call the ambulance. When the ambulance arrived, I told them all about Rebecca and her kidnapping skills. We soon had Rebecca to a trial. "what exuse do you have young lady?", said the judge. Rebecca said we were good friends until she wanted to do something more exiting, so she decided to look for a adventure. "HALT!" shouted Anna. "for she may have been a good friend, but a bad student!" Then the judge made a face, "how old are you young lady?" Rebecca shifted a bit, then she said she was 12 years old. then the judge said,"you are too young to be in jail, but it is no exuse to do a crime, so I say you will have terrible reports!" I heard Rebecca sniffing, " but sir, I've always wanted to be a general!" The judge paused and said" for no woman shall be offended, but shall no woman be offensive!" Rebecca was dismissed, but she hated herself for it. When they grew up, Anna said sorry to Rebecca. Even if it was nice, it recalled back everything from her younger ages. So she started Recalling Anna's father's death to Anna. Anna felt more offended than ever, since she was born. Both Anna and Rebecca have hated themselves for who they were. So I told Anna that Rebbeca was being a bully. at first she didn't think so, but at last she admitted that she was not concerned about her fathers death, it was friendship she was worried about. So I reminded her I was a friend of her. When Rebecca said sorry to Anna, she felt dizzy to regret it, so at the end we promised each other that we were forever friends. Anna got used to the pain of her father's death. But it still was a deep memory inside her head. As for me and Rebecca, we swore to always be friends no matter what case. INTRODUCTION THIS STORY ALWAYS GOES ON AND ON INSIDE MY HEAD, IT REMINDS ME THAT WHEN THINGS GET TOUGH, WE CAN ALWAYS RELY ON OUR FRIENDS
author: Lily L

title: The Room That Wasn't There
text: There was never a door on that wall. Mara would’ve noticed — she’d lived in the house for nearly five years. The cottage was small, a rental on the edge of the woods, far enough from town to enjoy silence but close enough for groceries and the occasional pizza. She liked it that way: isolated, quiet, unchanging. But that morning, when she came down the narrow stairs with coffee on her mind, the door was just there. On the north wall of the living room, between the fireplace and the old bookcase. White. Closed. Completely ordinary… except that it hadn’t existed yesterday. Mara stopped halfway down the stairs. She stared. Her first thought: Did someone break in? But what kind of intruder installs a door? She crept down and stood in front of it. Her heart beat faster, more confused than afraid. The door looked aged—faded paint, brass handle oxidized to green in spots—like it had been part of the house for decades. She reached out, pressed her palm to the wood. Cold. She knocked. Hollow. Then came a sound. A soft, unmistakable creak from the other side. Not loud. Just enough to make her step back. Something moved behind it. She didn’t open it. The door didn’t go away. By evening, Mara had searched every photo she had of the room. Not one showed the door. She called the landlord. “That wall is solid brick,” he said. “There’s no door. Never has been.” Mara didn’t sleep that night. The next day, she taped a large wooden dresser in front of the door. The night after, she woke to a dragging noise. A soft scraping. She crept out of bed with her phone light. The dresser was five feet from the wall. No one else was in the house. She moved out a week later. One Year Later She told herself it was fine. A new apartment in the city. Bright walls, loud neighbors, everything the cottage wasn’t. But Mara had changed. She barely slept. Shadows moved where they shouldn’t. Doors she knew she’d locked would be ajar in the morning. Every creak of floorboards, every whisper of wind sent her heart racing. Worse, she couldn’t stop dreaming of the door. It appeared in every nightmare, always just about to open, always with something waiting behind it. The letter arrived in a plain white envelope. No return address. Just her name. Inside was a single piece of paper. YOU LEFT IT OPEN. That night, her apartment smelled like soil. Wet, earthy, decayed. She checked the windows. All locked. The next day, her neighbor’s cat was found dead in the hallway. No marks. Just lying there, eyes wide open. Like it had seen something it couldn’t understand. Two Weeks Later The door was back. Not in the same place — this time, it was in her bedroom wall, beside the closet. Mara screamed. She screamed until her throat hurt, until the neighbors banged on the walls. She packed a bag, called a friend, and stayed at a hotel. But the door followed. Everywhere she went, within a day or two, it would appear. Always closed. Always silent. But never unfamiliar. It had become hers. She stopped running. Mara returned to the cottage. It was still empty. Dusty, but untouched. She moved in with only what she could carry. The door, of course, was already there, waiting for her. She didn’t tape it. Didn’t block it. She placed a chair in front of it and sat. Every day. For hours. Staring. Daring it to open. Weeks passed. The dreams got worse. In them, the door did open. And from the darkness came voices — whispers in languages she didn’t understand. And eyes. Too many eyes. Then, one night, it opened. Mara didn’t remember falling asleep, but when she blinked awake, the door stood ajar. Darkness pooled from it like smoke. Cold air rushed out, smelling of iron and rot. And something was stepping through. Not walking. Crawling. Long, pale limbs. Fingers too many-jointed. A face half-formed, as though sculpted in clay by a trembling hand. Mara couldn’t move. It reached for her with one long arm — then paused. The thing tilted its head, listening. Then it smiled. Its mouth was on the wrong side of its face. “You left it open.” Three Days Later The landlord came to check on her, after several missed rent payments. He found the door. Just one. On the north wall. Locked tight. No one answered his knock. No response. No sounds inside. He called the police. They broke the door down. The cottage was empty. Not just of Mara — completely empty. No furniture. No dishes. No books. Nothing. Even the wallpaper was gone. Like no one had ever lived there. Present Day The cottage is still for rent. The listing is cheap — too cheap — for such a cozy place near the woods. There’s only one oddity: the landlord always includes a strange instruction in the rental agreement, written in fine print. “Do not open the north door.”

title: Layers of Wonders
text: Paru and Unni skipped along the road, one on each side of 1 Appuppan. Slap-slap-slap went their sandals. Unni pointed down. “Appuppan, what is this black thing called?” Appuppan smiled. “That’s called 2 Tar,” “Tar…Tar…Car…VROOOM!” Unni zoomed ahead, arms wide like a bike. Appuppan smiled. “Be careful, little rider!” Paru tugged his hand, “Appuppan, is that this black thing? 1 Grandfather in the Malayalam language used in Kerala, India 2 A common Indian English term for road surface (asphalt or bitumen) "Yes", Appuppan nodded. “It's tiny, tiny rocks packed tight. That’s what makes the road strong.” Unni frowned, “But when I put rocks together, they just go thud…thud…thud!” Appuppan chuckled. “That’s why we add Cement – It’s like the super-glue for stones.” Paru giggled. “Oh! Like the glue we use to stick papers!” Unni sat down to look. “Appuppan…what’s under the stones?” Unni asked. "Soft soil,” Appuppan said with a smile. “When I was little like you, the roads were just soil. We ran and cycled right on it.” Unni’s eyes went wide. “Appuppan, can you ride a cycle?” Appuppan laughed. “Yes, yes! But first, let’s keep walking.” Paru tugged again. “And under the soil?” “Roots and worms,” Appuppan answered. Unni bent down and stared at the ground. "Worms? Real worms?" "Ayyo...ayyo!” He jumped up quickly. "Paru, worms are wiggling under our feet RIGHT NOW!" Paru giggled. "Hello, worms down there!" Appuppan laughed. “Don’t worry, They are very busy. They make the soil soft. Just like you two, always busy! They dig tiny tunnels so air can breathe into the ground. That's how they help plants grow.” Unni leaned closer. "I'm listening... I can't hear them digging. I wish I could see them.” Appuppan smiled. "They work very quietly, Just like you two when you sneak into the kitchen for chocolates." “What’s under the worms, Appuppan? Tell me, tell me!” Appuppan held their hands. “Ah, now we reach tiny streams, hiding deep below the soil, thinner than your fingers, carrying cool water everywhere.” Paru’s eyes lit up. “Oh! Tiny streams under our feet?” “Yes,” Appuppan nodded, “Secret streams that trees love to drink from.” Unni’s eyes lit up. “This is the water 3 Ammumma talks about! The one the plants drink! If we dig in our courtyard, can we find it, Appuppan?” Unni asked. Appuppan smiled. “Maybe roots, maybe worms. But the streams hide deeper— like the earth’s secret treasures.” Unni leaned close. “After that, what comes?” Appuppan chuckled. “After that… we reach home!” “Nooo!” Unni groaned. “Appuppan, please…please…. please tell…what comes after that?” 3 Grandmother in Malayalam language used in Kerala, India Appuppan bent down. “Hmm… what do you think hides under all that, Unni?” Paru said. “Maybe another secret treasure – Like in your painting cupboard!” Appuppan gasped. “Eh! You little mischief-makers. You searched my cupboard?” Both children burst into giggles. “But Appuppan,” Paru said, “Just like your cupboard, the road has secrets too!” Appuppan nodded. “Yes, treasures everywhere… waiting for curious explorers like you.” He pointed at the ground. “Deep under the soil and streams are strong rocks. They hold everything up like the pillars of a castle.” Paru’s mouth opened wide. “Woooow! A castle under our feet!” “Appuppan, more…more…more? “ Unni asked eagerly. Appuppan whispered. “Even deeper is hot, hot rocks so hot it glows like fire! They keep the Earth warm, like the heart that keeps us alive.” Unni and Paru’s eyes sparkled. “Wooow! Hot fire rocks deep down! The Earth is so warm inside!” Unni jumped up and pointed around. “Paru, on top of all this, we run, play, cycle, dig, and walk!” Paru smiled. “I wish we could go and see all the layers!” Worms wriggling. Streams sparkling. Rocks standing tall. Appuppan laughed, messing their hair. “Every step hides a treasure for curious explorers like you. Look closely you will always find something new.” “Tomorrow,” Unni shouted, “we’ll find more treasures!” Paru nodded. “Starting with your cupboard, Appuppan!” Appuppan laughed. “The world is full of treasures, my little explorers… but the best treasure is you two with me.”

title: Journey of  JANES
text: Janes was born in a cramped, dusty neighborhood where the sounds of honking horns and barking dogs were louder than any lullaby. His family didn’t have much — a small apartment, second-hand clothes, and barely enough money for meals. But what they lacked in wealth, they made up for in heart. From the moment he could walk, Janes had a ball at his feet. Old, scuffed, and barely holding together, it was his constant companion. Every alleyway, every cracked pavement, every abandoned field became his stadium. While other kids played for fun, Janes played as if every kick could change his life. School was a struggle. Books were heavy, teachers were strict, and there was always the teasing — “Poor kid, will never be anything.” But Janes didn’t care. His mind was on the ball, on the next goal, on the next dream. At age 12, he joined a small local team. He was smaller than the other kids, weaker too. But his speed, his vision, and his refusal to give up made him stand out. Every missed goal, every defeat, every harsh word from the coach was fuel. He trained in secret, late into the night, often with just a single flickering streetlight as his guide. Not just any goal — it was a goal that made the spectators stop, the rivals stare, and even the skeptical coach nod in approval. In that moment, something inside him shifted. He realized that maybe, just maybe, he could rise above everything that tried to hold him down. But the road ahead was far from easy. Bigger teams, tougher opponents, betrayals, and injuries awaited him. And somewhere along the way, he would find a rival who could push him to his limits — someone who would challenge not just his skill, but his very belief in himself. Janes’ journey had begun. And even though the world saw only a poor boy with a worn-out ball, in his heart, he was already dreaming of stadiums, trophies, and the roar of millions. PART 2 COMING SOON

title: The stone of luck
text: Long ago, in the mountains of Ararat, there was a legend. It said that anyone who carried a stone from these mountains would be lucky and succeed in everything they did. This stone was called the Lucky Stone. The mountain was cone-shaped and always covered with snow. The path was very difficult to climb. But people believed that to get the Lucky Stone, they had to make the journey there. One of these families was Anisa’s family. Anisa’s grandmother asked her, “Go to Mount Ararat and bring back a stone with you!” Anisa listened to her grandmother and set off for Mount Ararat. On the way, she faced many hardships. She didn’t have enough food and often felt very weak, sometimes thinking she might not survive. But each time, she reminded herself, “This journey will bring me luck. After all this hardship, I will reach it safely.” And she continued on her path. It took her a month to reach the volcano where everyone searched for the stone. She picked up a piece of stone that looked the most beautiful to her and said to herself, “This stone will bring me luck from now on.” She put the stone in her bag and began to go down the mountain. The weather became very cold and snowy. The wind blew so hard, it felt like it might carry Anisa away. She told herself, “How can I be lucky? I have the Lucky Stone with me. It will bring me luck.” “I will be protected. I will survive,” Anisa whispered to herself. These words calmed her heart, but the outside world was not so easy. Her hands were frozen, and because she didn’t have enough food, her body grew weak. At any moment, she might faint. Still, she tried to reach a tree at the side of the mountain. Slowly, she dragged herself there. Hours passed. Anisa no longer noticed anything. Night had fallen, and everything was dark… Anisa had fallen down, and snow covered her body. Half asleep and half awake, she realized she could no longer move. She was buried under the heavy snow, weak and cold. She had lost all hope. Still, sometimes she reminded herself, “Grandmother asked me to bring back the Lucky Stone. How can I die here under the snow? By early morning, the sky was growing light. Suddenly, Anisa felt the ground shaking. With fear, she cried out, “Oh no! An avalanche is coming!” In a rush, the snow began to move, and Anisa was carried away with it. Anisa had no strength left. She screamed loudly, calling for help. Her voice echoed through the whole mountain. It seemed this time Anisa might never return home. But still, she did not lose hope. She held the stone and whispered, “You are my luck. You will save me.” At that very moment, she crashed violently into a massive boulder and fell unconscious. For hours, she lay motionless on the cold ground. When everything had finally calmed down, a skier passing by suddenly caught sight of her body. Horrified, he shouted, “Help! Someone has fallen here!” In her delirium, Anisa whispered faintly, “My lucky stone… find my stone… I must deliver it to my grandmother…” The skier helped Anisa calm down, but as she regained a little consciousness, she realized that she had lost her lucky stone. She had dropped it somewhere and it was gone. The skier told her that he was amazed at how she had managed to stay alive. Her body was covered in bruises, her right arm was broken from the collision with the rock, and her head was bleeding heavily. She answered with tears in her eyes, “It was my stone that kept me alive. But now my stone is lost… I will surely die.” The skier tried to calm her down. “Little girl, what are you saying? You are alive because of the courage you carried inside you, not because of a piece of rock!” Years passed after that incident, and Anisa finally understood the lesson her grandmother had wanted her to learn. “In the search for anything, you become that very thing,” she realized. “Seek luck, and you will find luck. Whatever you truly believe in, you will eventually become.”

title: Who's on Divya's Map?
text: It was her first day of vacation. Divya was very excited to see her cousin, Ravi. He was coming from the faraway city of Cuttack to meet Divya. Divya thought of all the fun things they would do together, like playing games, riding cycles, swimming in the pond, plucking mangoes....... Ravi was going to travel to Gajapur for the first time. Divya had given him directions over the phone. "Walk straight, straight, straight. You will see the pond, then take a right...... no, no, take a left, then go straight to the post office, then turn right...." But Ravi was confused. Divya was worried for Ravi. How can Divya help Ravi find her place easily? ﻿ "Idea! I will become a cartographer. I will make a map for Ravi." "The map will help Ravi to find his way." She took a big size of paper, a pencil, some colours and went outside to make the map. First, she drew a symbol of her house. Divya walked straight ahead and saw a shop. It was Binoy Uncle and Sarita Aunty's shop. Sarita Aunty always gave candies to Divya from her shop. "I will draw the shop in the map. I will draw a yellow square to show the shop." Next, Divya crossed the road and reached the ISPAT hospital. "Let's add the hospital to the map." She jumped in excitement as the map was coming along. Divya made a red cross (+) to show the ISPAT hospital. Next, she saw the banyan tree near the hospital. Uncle Ramesh was sitting under the banyan tree. Divya made the symbol of a small green tree on the map. Divya continued on her way. She reached the post office next, where she also met Mohan uncle. Divya drew a red rectangle for the post office. Next, Divya walked southwards. After five minutes, she reached a pond where some women were washing clothes. Divya drew a blue circle to show the pond in the map. Divya finished making the map and excitedly showed the map to her friends. "Gajapur is so big, but we can show its landmarks in a small map like this," said Divya. She was very happy with her map. "But how will Ravi know the exact directions from your map?" asked her friend Kala. Divya looked at the map. She remembered that she did not draw the directions. "I will draw the path", she said. She coloured the path yellow and added red arrows ﻿to show directions. The map looked good now. Divya folded the map, put it in an envelope, stuck some stamps on it and posted it to Ravi in Cuttack. One week later, Ravi reached Divya's house. Ravi had the map of Gajapur in his hand. They were both smiling at each other. Divya can be a cartographer A person who makes maps is called a cartographer. Cartography is a study that combines science, geography, art, and mathematics. Maps help you 1. Find a new place 2. 3. 4. Scale When you draw a map, how do you show that a mountain is very tall, or that a house is half the height of a coconut tree? You use a scale. This is the relationship between the size of something on the map and its actual size.
