title: last over hero
text: Hi all, my name is Rohan and I am from Andhra Pradesh. I always wanted to write a book and I love cricket so I wrote this story about cricket called the "Last Over Hero" The school cricket ground was filled with excitement as Greenfield School played the final match of the tournament. Students, teachers, and parents cheered loudly from the sidelines. The match was very close, and everything depended on the last over. Greenfield needed 8 runs from 6 balls to win. Ravi, a quiet 5th grader, was at the crease. He was nervous because he was not the best batsman on the team. His hands were shaking as he held the bat, and his heart beat fast. The bowler looked confident as he ran in and bowled the first ball. Ravi tried to hit it but missed. Everyone groaned The second ball came, and Ravi managed to hit it softly. They ran one run. The next ball was short, and Ravi remembered his coach’s words: “Believe in yourself.” He hit the ball hard, and it went to the boundary for four runs. The crowd cheered loudly.. Now only three runs were needed from three balls. Ravi felt more confident. On the fourth ball, he hit and ran two runs. Just one run was needed to win The field was silent for the last ball. Ravi took a deep breath as the bowler delivered the ball. Ravi tapped it gently and ran as fast as he could. The fielder threw the ball, but it was too late. Greenfield School won the match! Everyone rushed onto the field. Ravi’s teammates hugged him and lifted him up. The shy boy had become the hero of the day. Ravi smiled proudly. He had learned that courage, practice, and belief can help anyone shine when it matters most. Ravi knew he would never forget that match, because it taught him an important lesson: when the pressure is high, believing in yourself can turn you into a true champion.
author: Rohan lingutla

title: Be Grateful for what you have!
text: One time, Roben, Kaulista, Jordan and Zeli(4 siblings) were very hungry. They asked their mom to cook something, because they were starving. Mom cooked them steak and rice with spinach. The children looked at their plate with disgust. Roben said rudely," MOM! What is this! This food is gross! I want Pizza!" Mom replied,"Guys, we just ordered pizza a while ago!" So the children begin insisting and protesting," Pizza! We want pizza!" The noisy and cheerful voice spread across the room. Mom looked at dad with hope, for him to say something. Dad, however, did not do anything and stayed quiet. When the children were still protesting for pizza, their dad said," Do you guys wanna know a story?" The kids stopped chanting and said," Anything for a story, Dad!" And thus, the story begin. It was a poor and dry village. It had a large amount of monkeys. There were monkeys here as there was a rainforest nearby. Some monkeys had migrated to the village due to intense population in the jungle. This is a story of one such monkey. Once, a monkey was eating a mango. He lived on the branch since he was born. However, the monkey was not satisfied at all and started complaining," Ugh, these mangoes aren't sweet enough! I wish I had sweeter mangoes!" He kept on complaining, even though the mangoes were delicious! Other monkeys, who lived deep in the forest, were happily enjoying the mangoes nature had given to them. They were very sour but the enjoyed. Andtem, one of the monkeys sitting under the tree, pointed out,"Bro, these mangoes are great! How can anyone complain about these mangoes! These are so sweet!" Arnd said," I know right! How are these so sweet!" These monkeys named their clan ' Oyosuva ' There was another group of monkeys who were eating bananas. They were grateful as well. The name of their group was ' Lingakayi ' These happy monkeys were joking around but saw the group of monkeys (who loved the mangoes) coming their way. Tuntun, their leader, pointed towards the group of monkeys. These two groups were best friends. These monkeys were happily jumping as their friends were coming and they hadn't seen them in a long time. However, one of the monkeys(son of Tuntun), went to check if it really was the Oyosuva clan. But, it was the Julez clan. They were the most powerful in the whole desert. They were planning to attack the Lingakayi. The whole Lingakayi clan went to the ponds, because the son of Tuntun told them to go there, because he has a special ability to track enemies. Tuntun had appointed two people from his clan to protect their area. Therefore, Tuntun, his son and the clan people went to the pond. The Julez clan saw them heading to the pond. The Lingakayi had a plan to act normal in front of the Julez. It was Tuntun's son's idea and everybody obeyed him. The Julez started to attack the Lingakayi clan. They fought and fought. However, they came to a conclusion. The leader of the Julez clan said," We are sorry for attacking on you guys. We were jealous of the bananas you had." The Lingakayi responded," So if we give you bananas, you will stop attacking us, right?" Julez said," Yes, indeed we will stop! Get us the bananas NOW!" Tuntun said," Let me get the bananas. I will not scam you guys." "Good", said Julez. Tuntun gets the bananas and gives it to the Julez clan. The monkeys started to share and both clans became friends. Now, what about the first ungrateful monkey? The first monkey observed all of this and said," I will take back what I said about the mangoes! I don't want to go through this chaos, just for sweeter mangoes!" Finally, the monkey went back to his tree and started enjoying the mangoes mother nature gave him. " These mangoes are actually really juicy! Why did I say that these were bad?" "So," said dad, " be grateful for what you have and don't be greedy for more",serving the children, he said. The children were so engrossed in the story, that they forgot about spinach, rice and steak. Their mom was happy as well, because dad taught them a story, a lesson and made them finish their food without them complaining. THINK!! How would the story change if Tuntun didn't bring the bananas to the Julez clan.

title: Jack Learns To Swim
text: One day, Jack the fox found Ella the elephant returning after a bath in the river. Jack asked Ella “Do you know to swim?” Ella answered, “Yes, elephants are natural swimmers”. Jack said “I always wanted to swim and bathe in the river but I am scared of being washed away”. Ella said, “You come with me and I will help you in the river”. Jack followed Ella the next day to the river. Surprisingly, the river was flowing gently that day. Ella got down into the river and asked Jack to follow her. Jack said, “I am afraid of the river, so I can’t”. Ella folded her trunk like as a ring and asked Jack to jump into the ring. Ella lowered her trunk into the water and Jack started swimming. After a while, Ella put Jack on a large, smooth and black stone in the river and started bathing. She scooped water in her trunk and sprayed water all over her body. In the meanwhile, Jack felt that the stone had moved. In panic, he said “Ella, I felt the stone move”. Ella laughed and replied “Jack, you might have slipped on the stone as you are wet”. Jack felt the stone move again and he yelled, “No! The stone is moving”. As Ella got near to the stone, she realized that it was not a stone but Marie, the hippo. So she called out, “Marie, Jack does not know to swim, so be steady”. Marie realized that Jack was slipping into the river and she stood still. After some time, Ella carried Jack safely out of the river. Jack thanked Ella and Marie for making it an enjoyable day in the river.

title: Raju the rising star.
text: Once upon a time, there was a boy named Raju. Raju lived in a small village. The village was far from the city. Raju was a simple and honest boy. He liked to help everyone. He always spoke the truth. People in the village knew him well. Raju dreamed of a better life. Raju came from a very poor family. His house was small and weak. The roof leaked during rain. There was no fan in the house. Raju slept on the floor. He had only a few clothes. Life was very hard for him. Still, Raju never complained. Raju’s father was a farmer. He worked in other people’s fields. He earned very little money. Sometimes he did not get work Many days, Raju ate very little food. Sometimes he was very hungry. He shared food with his parents. He never asked for more. Raju knew his parents were poor. He wanted to help them. He promised to study well. He wanted to change their life. Raju’s mother washed clothes. She worked all day long. They were very tired every day. But they loved Raju a lot. Raju went to a government school. The school was far from his house. He walked every day to school. He had no school bag. His books were old and torn. He had no proper shoes. Still he loved going to school. raju grow up. Some rich children teased Raju. They laughed at his clothes. They made fun of his shoes. Raju felt sad inside. His eyes filled with tears. But he stayed quiet. Raju studied very hard every day. He woke up early in the morning. He helped his parents first. Then he went to school. At night, there was no light. He studied under a streetlight. One evening, Raju saw an old man. The old man fell on the road. People passed by him. No one stopped to help. Raju ran to the old man. He helped him. the old man gave him a hug. He was motiva ted because the old man said that his future is bright. Raju continued his studies happily. He moved to a nearby town. The city life was new for him. He lived in a small rented room. He missed his parents a lot. For going to his college everyday he has to use bus. Raju faced many problems. He felt lonely and scared sometimes. The studies were harder than before. But Raju did not lose hope. He missed his parents a lot. After studies, Raju searched for jobs. He faced many rejections. Some interviews went badly. He felt disappointed. Raju decided to start a small business. He used his small savings. The beginning was very difficult. Slowly, the business started growing. More customers began trusting him. Raju treated everyone with respect. His hard work showed results. After years, Raju became rich. He gave speeches about his life. He earned a lot of money. But money did not change him. He was still kind. Raju returned to his village happily. People were surprised to see him. His parents felt very proud. Their tears were of happiness. He built a strong house for parents. Raju wanted to help others too. He opened a small school. Poor children got free education. He provided books and food. On one night,Raju looked at the sky.He saw a big star. He remembered his long journey. Pain, struggle, and hard work Raju proved hard work always wins.

title: Gauri's colourful day
text: One day Gauri a cow, was passing through a forest when she met a rhino who was grazing in the open ground. Surprised to see such an animal, she asked “Who are you?” The rhino answered “Hello Ms. Cow. I am Riya, a rhinoceros. What are you doing in the jungle?” Gauri said, “I am crossing the jungle to go to my village near the Iravati river. But I lost my way. Can you help me?” Riya replied, “Okay, I know the Iravati river. That’s the place I go to drink water in the summer. Come with me.” And so they started walking to the river. Along the way, Gauri could not hold her curiosity and asked “I saw many animals grazing along the way such as deer, goats and buffalos. How come you have horns above your nose and not above your head?” Riya smiled and replied: “Hmmm. I am a special animal as I can see my own horns unlike others. Rhinos have horns on their face to protect themselves. With my horns, I can dig holes and find tubers and roots to eat.” Amazed by the answer, Gauri said “Wow, you can do so much with your horns!” Riya replied, “Yes, what about you?” Gauri said “Well, I don’t use my horns like you do. But the village folks colour my horns and hang trinkets around them.” Riya was surprised at what the cow said and she wished her horns could be coloured too. Gauri asked, “Where can we find colours in a jungle?” Riya replied, “Oh, don’t worry, we can find some blue berries and raspberries near the banks of the Iravati river and use them for colouring”. Upon reaching the Iravati river, the cow found the berries. She crushed the berries and coloured the rhino's horns. Looking at her brightly coloured horns, Riya exclaimed “Wow, I have never seen my horn look so beautiful. Do you want me to colour your horns too?” To which, Gauri said “Sure, I would love to have my horns coloured too”. Upon colouring Gauri’s horns, Riya said, “Now your horns look beautiful too!” However, Gauri could not find a way to look at her own horns and felt sad. Riya said, “Don’t worry, you can look into the water and see your reflection.” Gauri saw her beautifully coloured horns in the water and called out “Moo Moo” in happiness. Then she thanked Riya for showing the way to her village and for making her horns look beautiful. Thereafter, the two animals said goodbye and went their own way.

title: The Great School Treasure Hunt
text: Mehar, Aadhya, Kartik, and Suman were in Ms. Patel’s classroom. Today, something exciting was about to happen! Ms. Patel smiled. “Yes! Today, you’ll solve clues, work as a team, and find the treasure. But remember, only teamwork will lead you there.” The friends formed a team. Aadhya held the first clue, which said: “Where books live, your next step gives.” They rushed to the library. Behind the big red books, they found the next clue. "Cloud?” Suman asked. “Maybe the playground has a cloud?” At the playground, they found a small, white cloud drawn on the noticeboard. Under it, there was another clue. “Stories come alive… That must be the library again!” Mehar said. Back in the library, they saw a book glowing slightly. When Suman opened it, a secret key fell out. The key had a note: “Unlock the treasure where the music plays.” Inside the music room, they saw a locked box. Aadhya inserted the key, and click! The box opened. Suddenly, they heard a voice behind them. It was their classmates. The friends laughed as they shared the treasure. They realized that solving clues was fun, but helping each other was even better. Ms. Patel came in. “Remember, the real treasure is teamwork and friendship.” The next day, they decided to play a new game—finding the “hidden kindness” in school. Mehar helped a younger student tie his shoelaces. Kartik shared his lunch with someone who forgot theirs. Aadhya made a beautiful friendship bracelet for Suman. Everyone smiled and realized small acts matter. By the end of the week, their whole class was filled with teamwork, smiles, and laughter. The friends remembered the treasure hunt every day and realized that adventure is fun, but friendship lasts forever. Whenever a new challenge came, they knew that by helping each other, nothing was impossible. And so, Mehar, Aadhya, Kartik, and Suman grew closer, learning that teamwork, kindness, and friendship were the real treasures of life.
author: Aadhya Kukkar

title: Jewel-less Crown: Saga of Life
text: This saga in the Indian milieu is about the rise and fall of an ambitious man, the decline and the decay of his conniving wife, the trials and tribulations of their wayward son and the grit and gall of a spirited woman, who romantically enters into his life. Truly, it’s the tale of a lifetime.
author: BS Murthy

title: Glaring Shadow - A stream of consciousness novel
text: In a stream of consciousness mode, this is the self-account of a man that depicts the agony and ecstasy of his life as he makes it big in our materialistic world, losing his soul in the bargain, and regaining it when tragedy strikes him makes one ponder over the meaning of success in life.
author: BS Murthy

title: Of No Avail Wedlock of Deadlock
text: Lured by the pitch - All marriages are made in heaven but some are delayed on earth: We endeavor to hasten them all - Priya goes to Renuka Marriage Bureau. Scanning the prospects, when she spotted Venu, whom she slighted long ago, she rushes to him to bring about a dramatic encounter. What brought about Priya’s change of heart to seek her former suitor and how Venu responds to his old flame’s fresh overtures lend suspense to their romance in this eclectic novella.
author: BS Murthy

title: Bhagvad-Gita Treatise of Self-help
text: Bhagavad-Gita is the most beautiful, perhaps the only true philosophical song existing in any known tongue’ – William von Humboldt. In this the beauty of the Sanskrit slokas is reflected in the rhythmic flow of the English verse of poetic proportions even as the attendant philosophy of the Gita is captured in contemporary idiom for easy comprehension.

title: The Great Vegetable Heist of Sector 4
text: The garden was quiet. Too quiet. Barnaby the rabbit crouched behind a terracotta pot, his nose twitching so fast it looked like a blurry vibration. "Marmalade," he whispered frantically. "This is a terrible idea. My heart is beating like a bongo drum. I think I might faint." Marmalade, the ginger cat, was draped casually over a low stone wall, looking bored. He yawned, showing off a set of sharp white teeth. "Relax, Barnaby. You’re always vibrating. It’s part of your charm." "We are entering Sector 4," Barnaby hissed. "The Human calls it 'The Prize Patch.' There are rumors of a motion-sensor sprinkler. A Sprinkler of Doom, Marmalade!" "I don't care about water," Marmalade lied (he hated water). "I care about the target. The Human planted a row of Crunch-tastic Swiss Chard yesterday. And I, being a generous god of this garden, have decided you should have some." "You just want me to flush out the field mice so you can chase them," Barnaby accused. "A distinct possibility," Marmalade winked. "Now, Operation Fluffy Lightning is a go. Move!" The Infiltration Barnaby took a deep breath, puffed out his chest, and darted forward. He didn't run; he flowed. He zig-zagged between tomato plants, froze like a statue when a leaf fell, and performed a tactical commando crawl under a overgrown zucchini leaf. Marmalade followed, but with less stealth and more swagger. He stepped gingerly over the dirt, looking around as if he owned the real estate. They reached the edge of the Prize Patch. There it was: The Swiss Chard. Its leaves were emerald green with ruby red stalks. It looked delicious. "Go on," urged Marmalade from the safety of a dry rock. "Grab the goods." Barnaby hopped forward. He opened his mouth to take a glorious bite of the forbidden leaf. CLICK. The sound came from a plastic nozzle sticking out of the ground. Barnaby froze. "Marmalade?" "Uh oh," said the cat. WHOOSH-CH-CH-CH-CH! The Sprinkler of Doom exploded into life! A jet of icy cold water blasted across the garden, spinning wildly. "ABORT! ABORT MISSION!" Barnaby screamed. He panicked, slipped in the mud, and accidentally did a backflip. Marmalade, usually the picture of grace, lost all dignity. The water hit him squarely in the face. "THE SKY IS LEAKING!" he yowled, his fur instantly spiking up until he looked like an angry, orange pufferfish. The Great Escape "Run, you fuzzy fool!" shouted Marmalade, scrambling for grip on the wet soil. His paws spun like cartoon wheels before he finally found traction. Barnaby, however, was in the zone. The cold water had activated his 'flight' mode. He grabbed a giant leaf of Swiss Chard in his teeth, ripping it free with a mighty tug. "I have the cargo!" Barnaby muffled through the leaf. The rabbit shot past the cat like a cannonball. Marmalade, his dignity ruined and his tail soaked, galloped after him. The sprinkler hissed and spat behind them, a mechanical dragon guarding its treasure. They scrambled under the fence, dove through the bushes, and didn't stop running until they reached the safety of the old potting shed. The Victory Feast Panting heavily, they collapsed on the dry wooden floor. Marmalade began frantically grooming himself, trying to fix his ruined fur. "That," Marmalade grumbled, shaking a wet paw, "was entirely undignified. I shall never speak of it again." Marmalade paused. He looked at the rabbit, then at the peace offering. He purred, a low, rumbling motor sound. "I suppose I did save your life, didn't I? I am a hero." "Sure," Barnaby chewed. "A wet hero." The two friends sat in the dusty sunbeams of the shed—one wet and grumpy, one full and happy—plotting their next big heist.
author: Abdullah Bin Monash

title: Forest Tails
text: Willa the wolf came with her family to see her grandmom who lived in the forest along the Ganges. Willa was a naughty little wolf, and she also liked to brag about herself. Having spent the afternoon playing with her grandmom, she set out to see the animals in the forest. Willa came across Pete the python, who was coiled and resting on a tree. She started to laugh loudly and said “Look at you! Where is your body? You just have a head and a long tail!” Willa bragged about her beautiful bushy tail. Pete was annoyed at being disturbed. Next, Willa came across Riya the rhino grazing along the river. She exclaimed, “Wow! You have such a huge body!” But then, when she noticed the tail, she started laughing and said, “Look at your tiny tail, and look at my beautiful bushy tail!” Riya wondered, Who is this little brat? Willa came across Helen the horse drinking water from the river. Willa scorned and said, “You have hair on your head and your butt!” Helen was shocked with the little wolf’s comment. Willa walked away with pride. Willa saw Lana the langur feeding on fruits on a tree. She could not control her laughter and said loudly, “Hey, you have a rope instead of a tail!” Lana felt humiliated at the comment. Then she turned around and saw Ella the elephant. Willa said, “You have a strong trunk on one side and a paintbrush on the other side!” Willa burst out laughing and continued to brag about her beautiful bushy tail. This made Lana and Ella angry. Willa left the place and reached a burrow. She saw Rinku the rabbit collecting lettuce. She was surprised and said, “Ah! You too have a bushy tail!” Then, she added, “It’s tiny and not as beautiful as my bushy tail.” Willa proclaimed, “Nobody in this forest has such a beautiful bushy tail.” Rinku wanted to teach this little naughty wolf a lesson. So, he met Kittu the crocodile and told him what had happened. Kittu said, “Don’t worry, I will teach the little wolf a lesson.” Finally, Willa met Kittu and said “Look at you, dragging that heavy tail. Do you know I have a beautiful bushy tail?” Kittu replied, “Oh really! Show me then.” When Willa turned around, Kittu caught hold of her tail. Willa cried for help. Rinku came and said, “You will not have a bushy tail anymore.” Rinku added, “If you stop teasing others, then Kittu will let you free.” Willa begged for forgiveness and was set free. Later, Willa became friends with Rinku and others.

title: Vidhya and the Garden Spirit
text: Vidhya loved her garden more than anything. Every morning, she helped her mother water the plants and whispered hello to the jasmine, the tulsi, and the mango tree. Her mother said gardens listened to people who were kind. That morning, while watering the marigolds, Vidhya noticed something strange. Four tiny fruits glowed softly among the plants—one by the tulsi, one under a pot, one in a puddle, one rolling gently in the breeze. They looked like they belonged to the garden itself, but Vidhya had never seen them before. As she leaned closer to the first fruit, something appeared above it—poof! A spirit no bigger than her thumb. It was emerald green with golden speckles, with hair like tiny leaves and wide, worried eyes. "Squeak! Squeak!" it cried, pointing at the glowing fruits. "What's wrong?" Vidhya asked. The spirit couldn't speak words, but it showed her: it tried to lift the nearest fruit. Its tiny hands passed right through it, like trying to hold sunlight. "Oh," Vidhya said. "You can touch magic things, but not garden things?" The spirit nodded eagerly. The spirit pointed at the sky. The sun was already climbing. It made a gesture like something wilting, drooping. Vidhya understood. "The garden needs them back before it gets too hot?" Already, the tulsi's leaves looked a little less bright than usual. The spirit nodded desperately. "I'll help you," Vidhya said. The first fruit lay openly near the tulsi plant. Vidhya picked it up easily—it felt warm and alive, like captured sunshine. The spirit caught it in mid-air and dropped it carefully into a tiny woven basket. The tulsi's leaves immediately perked up. The second fruit had rolled under a heavy clay pot during last night's wind. Vidhya lay on her stomach and stretched her arm carefully underneath. Her fingers just barely reached it. The third fruit had fallen into a puddle after the morning watering and was trapped between stones. Vidhya moved slowly, slowly, so the water wouldn't push it deeper, and lifted it out dripping. Only one fruit remained. This one was different—it bounced gently wherever the morning breeze blew it, rolling along with the garden's natural rhythms. Vidhya tried to chase it, but it always rolled away just before she could grab it. She stopped and watched. The garden wasn't playing tricks. The fruit was following where the ground sloped, where the breeze flowed, where water had softened the earth. Vidhya knelt where everything seemed to flow together—a small dip near the mango tree—and waited. The breeze shifted. The fruit rolled right to her. As she handed over the last fruit, the garden sighed—actually sighed—as if it had been holding its breath. The plants stood straighter. Colors deepened. Even the earthworms seemed to wiggle more happily. The spirit's glow steadied and brightened. The spirit reached into its now-full basket and pulled out one small seed, glowing softly green. It placed the seed in Vidhya's palm and squeaked something that sounded like "thank you." "What does it do?" Vidhya asked. The spirit just smiled and disappeared—poof!—back into the garden. That evening, Vidhya showed the seed to her mother. Amma held it up to the light. "Some gardens give gifts to people who listen carefully. Plant it tomorrow." Vidhya did. The seed never grew into anything she could see— but from that day on, whenever Vidhya worked in the garden, she noticed things others didn't. When plants needed water. When insects needed help. When the soil was happy. And sometimes, just sometimes, when she whispered hello to the jasmine, she heard the tiniest squeak in reply.

title: The Snowy Olympic Surprise (Winter Olympics 2026)
text: Tina and Milo were sitting near the window, watching the snow fall outside. “Let’s go and play!” Tina suggested with a grin. “Aachoo!” Milo sneezed. “It’s really cold out there.” Tina smiled. “Did you know that people actually play sports on snow and ice?” Milo looked surprised. “Really?” “Yes!” Tina replied. “It is called the Winter Olympics.” Milo said excitedly, “Please tell me more!” Tina explained, “The first Winter Olympics were held in France in 1924. They happen every four years, and athletes from many countries come together to compete. The five rings on the Olympic flag represent the five major continents of the world, all united by sport.” Milo’s eyes grew big, “What games do they play?” Tina replied, “There are several games like ice skating, ice hockey, skiing, snowboarding, curling, biathlon, etc.” Milo,” Wow, it’s really exciting. I want to see it.” Tina, “ Don’t worry this year it is taking place in two cities of Italy, Milan and Cortina d’ Ampezzo, starting from 6 th February 2026 and will continue till 22 nd February.” Milo,” Thanks Tina for sharing such valuable information. Lets tell our friends who we are.” Tina," Yes, Milo". Tina and Milo together, “ We are this year’s Olympics Mascot.” (Mascot-person, animal or object used as a symbol to represent a group)

title: The Lonely Dragon
text: Long ago, deep inside a dark forest, there lived a dragon all alone. The palace was big and beautiful, but it felt very, very quiet. One night, the sky suddenly lit up! For the first time, the dragon flew out of his palace. Animals were laughing and playing together. The dragon tries to hide behind a tree The ball rolled away…right toward the dragon. The ball flattened under the dragon’s foot. The dragon gently offering the ball. The rabbit faints dramatically Everyone screamed. The festival turned into chaos. “My child is still inside!” cried a mother frog. “I will help.” He rescued the little frog. The dragon carried water. Again and again, until the fire went out. The dragon was so tired…he fell asleep. When he woke up, he was not alone. “Thank you for saving us,” said the rabbit. “From now, He’s our friend!” said the raccoon. And from that day on, the dragon was never lonely again.
author: Alya Niswatul Fadilah

title: Mother Works on a Hill
text: My name is Esther. I study in Standard II. My mother’s name is Kumudini Bara. She is a nurse and works in a village on a hill. My mother has told me that nurses like her are called ANM—Auxiliary Nurse Midwife. When I get ready to go to school, I see that my mother is not at home. Why? Because my mother has already left for work. I ask my mother whenever she is around: “Ayo, where do you work? I want to see where you work. Take me to your office.” One December, Mother takes me to work with her. I wear a yellow frock with red flowers and my favourite hoodie. Mother wears her clean, white uniform, a navy blue cardigan and a batik scarf. I carry my favourite backpack with a bottle of water and lots of biscuits and potato chips. Mother carries her huge bag. In it, there is a machine to measure blood pressure. Another machine to measure blood sugar. Another machine to measure haemoglobin. And lots of medicines. And a stethoscope, too. We take a bus, which drops us at a village at the base of a hill. Mother says that the village she works at is on that hill. Someone is waiting for us at the bus stop. Mother tells me that her name is Salgi Purty. I call her Salgi Aunty. She is a Sahiya, the local healthcare worker. Salgi Aunty has come with her nephew whom I call Jado Bhaiya. Salgi Aunty is carrying a blue box that looks like a huge Ludo die. I wonder what it is. We begin climbing the hill. There is no road. Just a track cut by the villagers. Only bicycles and motorcycles can go up the hill. We have neither, so we trudge. “During the rains, this track becomes a river,” says Salgi Aunty. “But your mother still comes, and we climb the hill together, carefully.” The hills are pretty. There are trees like sal, jamun, palash and karanj. There are lovely flowers too, like putus, kudrum and posta. There is a stream where people gather water. We pass villagers carrying big logs of wood on their shoulders and walking down the hill. Finally, we reach the top of the hill, and I can see the village! “Maiya Esther, today is Thursday,” Mother tells me, “On Thursdays, children and pregnant women are given vaccines.” Now I know what that big blue box is that Salgi Aunty is carrying. It is a vaccine carrier! “The older carriers were small and easy to carry up the hill,” Salgi Aunty says. “These big ones are difficult. But what to do?” She laughs. Mother begins vaccinating the children and pregnant women. Some children cry as they are jabbed. But Mother takes a toffee from her bag and gives it to the crying child, who immediately stops crying. I did not know Mother carried toffees in her bag! Mother then checks the blood pressure, blood sugar, and haemoglobin of the pregnant women. She checks the villagers who are ill, and gives them medicines. After some time, I get bored. I join some children who are playing. At the end of the day, Salgi Aunty and Jado Bhaiya accompany us down the hill. Salgi Aunty gifts me a bag full of kudrum, which Mother will cook into a tart chutney. Jado Bhaiya takes the vaccine carrier to th e auto rickshaw that has come to collect it. Salgi Aunty flags down a bus and sees us off. I have finally seen where my mother works. I am happy. I am proud of my mother.
author: Hansda Sowvendra Shekhar

title: Mr. Spectacles and the case of missing spectacles
text: He misplaced his keys in teapots, his shoes in the refrigerator, and once even threw away his lunch box. Losing objects wasn’t a flaw—it was his lifestyle. There was, however, one sacred exception. His spectacles. They were enormous, round, and powerful enough to spot bacteria. With them, Mr. Spectacles could function like a responsible adult. Without them, he mistook umbrellas for friends and apologized to furniture. So, when he woke up one morning and reached for his spectacles— —and found nothing— He gasped, so loudly that a sock fell out of his pillowcase. (He had misplaced it there three weeks earlier). “Well,” he said, “this is alarming.” He searched the bedside table. The drawer. The drawer inside the drawer. Under the bed. Inside the bed. He found a spoon, a whistle, and a sandwich he distinctly remembered losing during winter. But no spectacles! Without them, the house immediately turned hostile. A chair attacked his knee. A wall moved unexpectedly toward his face. He poured orange juice into his cereal, then congratulated himself on his creativity. “I misplace things all the time,” he muttered, walking into a doorframe. “But this feels different.” In the living room, he froze. The door was open. Mr. Spectacle never left doors open. Open doors invited insects, burglars, and—most terrifying of all—tiny yapping dogs, a lifelong fear stemming from a childhood incident involving sharp teeth and public screaming. He squinted closer. The rug was twisted. The sofa cushion was gone. And on the floor were muddy paw prints. Paw prints. Mr. Spectacle swallowed. “This,” he whispered, “is a crime.” Determined to solve the case like his detective father (who never misplaced anything except his sense of humour), Mr. Spectacle grabbed his coat. Unfortunately, he grabbed a curtain instead and wore it proudly around his shoulders for several minutes before noticing. Outside, the neighbourhood was a blur of suspicious shapes. He questioned everyone. “Have you seen my spectacles?” he asked Mrs. BobbleMcBobble. “No, dear.” “Are you absolutely sure?” he asked a hedge. The hedge remained uncooperative. Then came the sound. Yap. Yap. Yap. Mr. Spectacles froze so hard that he briefly became furniture. A tiny dog zoomed past him, dragging something enormous and shiny behind it. “My spectacles!” Mr. Spectacles cried, chasing it—slowly, cautiously, and mostly in the wrong direction. The dog ducked into the park and vanished behind a bush. When Mr. Spectacles approached, trembling, he found the dog happily chewing one lens and staring at the other as if it were a portal to another universe. “Excuse me,” Mr. Spectacles said politely. “Those are my eyes.” The dog wagged its tail, dropped the spectacles, and immediately stole Mr. Spectacles' sock, which he had no memory of wearing. As Mr. Spectacles put his spectacles back on, the world snapped into sharp, glorious focus. He saw the dog clearly now—tiny, muddy, and proudly wearing the missing sofa cushion like armor. He laughed. “Well,” he said, “at least someone knows where my things are.” Traumatized by the experience, Mr. Spectacles returned home and installed three extra locks, two alarms, and one sign on the door that read: NO DOGS. ESPECIALLY SMALL ONES. The very next morning, he opened the drawer. The spectacles were gone. And somewhere nearby, the dog was seeing the world far too clearly—and thoroughly enjoying it.

title: The real face
text: How Yogesh Fought Using Writing One day in school, a problem was happening in the class. Some students were creating trouble even though they were good in studies. Seeing this, the sir asked a question: “If fighting is wrong, then how does a writer fight?” At that moment, a smart student named Yogesh Devan understood the answer. He decided to fight not with hands, but with writing. Yogesh did not create imaginary characters. He took inspiration from bad people in his own class and wrote a story. In the story, he named three bad people Aradhyan, Takshitan, and Shiranyaan. They were intelligent but used their knowledge in the wrong way and caused harm to the world and the universe. Yogesh wrote about their actions to show how wrong thinking can destroy everything. Even though the real people could not be identified, Yogesh published the story to send a message. The sir understood that Yogesh had answered the question. This was how a writer fights—by exposing bad behavior through words, not violence. Note: This story is based on true events. If anyone fights with you, stay calm and show your strength through sports and studies. If nothing is possible, write a story and put your emotions into it—just like intelligent writers in olden days who fought using words.

title: Blurred Mirror
text: It was a rainy morning. I woke up at 6:30 am and listened to the sounnd of rain. I checked mom's phone. There was no message from school. I smiled.. " Maybe today is a holiday." I thought. I went to terrace. The sky was grey and beautiful. The rain made everything fresh and clean. Suddenly, I saw a peacock. Instead of hiding, it danced happily in the rain. Amma, I asked my mother, Why are other birds hiding, But the peacock is dancing? My mother smiles and said, " peacocks love the rain. other birds are careful about their health." Near a tree, I noticed a pigeon's nest. Inside the next were three tiny chicks, covered with leaves. Wow! I whispered. " Hello little ones." Just then, rainwater started flowing fast,. The leaves shook, and the chicks became scared. The tree chicks looked into the mirror. They titled their heads and chirped loudly. They could not see themselves clearly. I felt sad for them. I carefully carried the mirror and wiped it clean. Now the mirror was clear. I placed it safely near the nest and covered it so rain would not blur again. The chicks looked into the mirror once more. This time, They saw their own reflections. They jumped happily. They touched the mirror and chirped with joy. one small chick even tried to fight its own reflection. I laughed softly. The chicks were calm and happy now. That day, I learnt something important. When we see ourselves clearly, We learn to love ourselves. Best practice of self confidence is seeing you in the mirror.
author: Sachin S S

title: The Little Gaur and His Friends
text: Babu was a baby gaur with wobbly legs and a big heart. Every morning, he watched his dad lift huge rocks. Up, up, up into the air! "I want to be strong like you, Dad!" said Babu. Dad touched his nose gently to Babu's head. "Practice every day, little one. That's how you grow strong." Babu found the perfect rock. Smooth and round, just right for a baby gaur. He pushed it with his head to the sunny spot on the hill. "This is my training rock!" Babu said. "I'll practice every single day!" He tried to lift it. Push, push, push! His little legs wobbled. "Almost," Babu huffed. "I'll try again tomorrow!" But then—oh no! The ground was slippery from last night's rain. The rock wiggled. The rock jiggled. Rumble-roll! Tumble-roll! Down the hill it went, bouncing and bumping, faster and faster! SPLASH! It disappeared into the thick bushes below. Babu's ears drooped. His eyes got big and wet. "My rock! Where did it go?" He looked down the hill. So many bushes. So many rocks. Which one was his? Where could it be? Where, oh where? Babu took a deep breath. "I have to find it. I have to be brave." Down the hill he went, step by careful step. His hooves made soft sounds on the wet grass. Squelch, squelch, squelch. He pushed his nose under the first bush. Rustle, rustle! No rock. Just wet leaves and a surprised beetle. "Sorry, beetle!" said Babu. He looked behind a fallen log. The bark felt rough against his nose. No rock. Just some mushrooms growing in a line. Where could it be? Where, oh where? "CROAK! CROAK!" Babu jumped! There on a big wet leaf sat Frodo the frog. "Are you looking for something, little gaur?" Frodo's throat puffed in and out. "My training rock rolled down the hill," said Babu. "Have you seen it?" Frodo's eyes bulged. "Hmm. I saw something roll past. Try looking near the mud puddle!" "Thank you, Frodo!" Babu hurried to the puddle. His reflection looked back at him from the brown water. Splash, splash went his hooves. But that wasn't his rock. Just a puddle with wiggly tadpoles swimming around. "Croak!" said Frodo, hopping closer. "Oops! My mistake. Those are my children, not a rock!" Babu giggled even though he felt frustrated. "That's okay, Frodo. I'll keep looking." Through the bushes, something grey and round caught his eye. "There it is!" Babu ran over fast. His heart jumped with joy. But wait... He touched it with his hoof. Soft. Squishy. Not smooth and hard like his rock. This boulder was covered in thick green moss, all wet and slippery. "Maybe I can climb it to look around," thought Babu. He put one hoof on the mossy rock. Then another hoof. Then— WHOOOOSH! His legs flew out from under him! SPLAT! Babu slid right into the mud! Brown mud splashed on his nose. Brown mud squished between his hooves. Brown mud got on his ears! For a moment, Babu just sat there. Then he started to laugh. "I'm a mud gaur now!" A chattering sound came from above. "Hee-hee-hee!" Babu looked up. Swinging through the trees was Mira the langur, her long tail curling and uncurling. Swing, swing, swing! She landed on a low branch right above him. "What happened to you?" Mira hung upside down, her bright eyes twinkling. "I'm looking for my training rock," said Babu, shaking mud off his ears. "It rolled away and I can't find it anywhere! I've looked and looked!" Mira swung to another branch. "Are you searching, or are you rushing?" Babu stopped. "What do you mean?" "You're running fast, looking quick-quick," said Mira. "But sometimes you need to stop. Think. Use your clever brain!" She pointed with her long fingers. "Where did you see the rock go?" Babu closed his eyes and remembered. "It rolled down... down... down toward the sound of water!" His eyes popped op en. "The stream! I should follow the sound of water!" "Now you're thinking!" Mira swung away through the trees. "I'll look from up high. You look from down low!" Babu walked more slowly now. He listened carefully. Trickle, trickle, trickle. The sound of water! Getting louder! He followed the sound, step by step. Past tall ferns that tickled his sides. Under branches that still dripped from the rain—drip, drop, drip. The air smelled fresh and clean. The moss under his hooves felt cool and soft. And then he saw it—a little stream, sparkling in the sunlight. Babu's heart beat faster. "My rock has to be near here!" He looked left. He looked right. He saw small pebbles. He saw big boulders. He saw smooth river stones. But where was HIS rock? Then, down near the water's edge, between two thick tree roots, he spotted something round and gray. "MY ROCK!" Babu ran down to the stream. Yes! It was definitely his rock, wedged tight between the roots! He pushed with his head. The rock didn't move. He pulled with his mouth. The rock stayed stuck. He dug at the mud with his hooves, but the roots held the rock like fingers gripping tight. Babu sat down. His legs felt tired. His head hurt a little from pushing. "It's too stuck," he said quietly. "I'm not strong enough yet." For a moment, Babu felt like crying. He'd searched so hard. He'd been so brave. But now... Then he remembered something Dad said once: "Even the strongest gaur asks for help sometimes. That's wisdom, not weakness." Babu stood up tall. "I know what to do!" He took a deep breath and called out loud: "MIRA! FRODO! I NEED HELP!" Swing, swing, swing! Mira came flying through the trees and landed beside him. Hop, hop, hop! Frodo jumped from stone to stone across the stream. "You found it!" said Mira. "But it's stuck," said Babu. "I can't get it out by myself. Will you help me?" "Of course!" said Mira. "That's what friends do!" croaked Frodo. Mira examined the rock. "Okay. Babu, you push from the left. I'll pull from the right. Frodo, you watch and tell us if it's moving!" "Ready?" said Babu. "Ready!" said Mira. "Ready-croak!" said Frodo. "Let's count together," said Babu. "One... two... THREE!" PUSH! Babu pressed his head against the rock with all his might. PULL! Mira wrapped her strong arms around it and pulled. "Harder!" croaked Frodo. "I see it wiggling!" "One more time!" said Babu. "One... two... THREE!" PUSH! PULL! WIGGLE! POP! The rock came free! It rolled gently onto the soft mud. "WE DID IT!" Babu jumped up and down. "We did it together!" Mira clapped her hands. Frodo puffed up his throat and croaked the loudest croak ever. "CROOOOOAK!" Babu looked at his rock. His wonderful, smooth, round training rock. Then he looked at his friends. Mira with her clever thinking. Frodo with his encouragement. Something warm grew in Babu's chest. Something bigger than his muscles. "You know what?" said Babu slowly. "I think I did get stronger today." "Did you lift the rock?" asked Frodo. "No," said Babu. "But I didn't give up, even when it was hard. I thought carefully about where to look. And I was brave enough to ask for help." He smiled the biggest smile. "That's being strong too, isn't it?" Mira swung onto his back and gave him a hug. "The strongest, little gaur." Together, the three friends carried the rock back up the hill. Well, mostly Babu carried it in his mouth, while Mira rode on his back giving directions and Frodo hopped alongside singing a croaky song. When they reached the top, Dad was waiting. Babu dropped the rock at his feet. "Dad! I found my rock! And I learned something really important!" Dad lowered his big head and touched noses with Babu. "Tell me, little one." "Being strong isn't just about big muscles," said Babu proudly. "It's about having a brave heart that doesn't give up. It's about thinking carefully with your clever brain. And it's about helping your friends and letting them help you!" Dad's eyes were warm and shiny. "Now you understand what true strength is, Babu. I'm proud of you." Babu's chest puffed up. Not because he was showing off. But because he felt proud of himself too. Every morning after that, Babu practiced with his rock. Push, push, push! Sometimes Mira swung by to practice climbing and jumping. Sometimes Frodo stopped by to practice his croaking. And every time Babu felt frustrated or tired, he remembered: Try again. Think carefully. Ask for help. That's how you grow strong. Not just in your muscles. But in your heart and your head and your friendships too. And Babu? Little Babu with the wobbly legs? He grew stronger every single day. The End!
author: Bhaskar Rana

title: Feelings
text: It was a school holiday for Pranav that day.As soon as he woke up﻿ in the morning,he ran eagerly to his mother who was in the kitchen. "Mom,mom..."there was excitment in his voice."Tell me,darling..."said mom.There was love mixed with surprise in her voice."What is it..., you seemed very enthusiastic so early in the morning?" "Mom,today is my school holiday.. can you make my favorite breakfast?" asked Pranav "Oh! Is this the Case?I will definitely do it. Okay! What will you want to eat?" asked mom "Mom,will you bake dosa? I really want one,"said Pranav. Mom immediately burst into laughter. Smiling,she said, " It's dosa.. if you make it,you'll be fine!" And placed the dosa stone on the stove. Pranav continued his speech.. "Mom,what do you need to make dosa?" Mom said,"If you have a dosa batter,you can make dosa." Pranav question continued.. "What do you need to make dosa batter?" "I want rice and vigna mungo," said mom,pouring the batter into the dosa stone. "How did the rice and vigna mungo become batter?" Pranav asked. " You have to soak both and grind them... let the ground dough ferment for a few hours. Then, the dosa batter will be ready", she explained at length to her fourth grade child. Hearing this, Pranav face showed surprise and happiness. Mom,the next question came from Pranav as he was putting the hot dosas on the plate. " Mom,is it your day off?" Mom was surprised again. "Why are you asking,honey..?"she asked with longing. " I will also bake dosa for you on your day off,mom" Pranav said,hugging mom. Now mom's face was filled with pride. But mom had a slight doubt."Pranav, your favorite food is puri. Why did you ask for dosa instead of that?" she asked,expressing her doubt. To this, Pranav said with a mischievous smile,"I just saw you kneading the dough yesterday, mom..! Let's see!! Mom's eyes also smiled!

title: The hare and the tortoise
text: One day, the hare and the tortoise decided to have a competition. So they asked the lion for advice. So the lion told them both to cross the river. "The tortoise said, 'I will climb on you.'" "No, hare, I will jump on you." They both fell into the river in a fight. Hearing this, the lion laughed. The tortoise and the hare died and the lion ate them.
author: Satvik Ramasubramaniam

title: Supriya and Her 'Crow' Friend!
text: Supriya sat at the big marble counter. Her grandmother was right beside her, rolling tiny white balls. "These are rasgullas!" said Grandma. "Can you help me?" Supriya's little hands pushed and patted. The soft, spongy sweets felt like clouds. One rasgulla. Two rasgullas. Three! "Look, Grandma! Round and round!" Supriya giggled. The kitchen smelled sweet—like warm milk and vanilla. Sunshine poured through the open window. Far away, temple bells went ding-dong, ding-dong. Then—flap-flap-flap! A tiny baby crow flew right through the window! It landed on the counter. Its shiny black feathers sparkled in the sunlight. "Oh!" gasped Supriya. The little crow tilted its head. It hopped closer. Tap, tap, tap with its tiny feet. "Caw?" it chirped softly. "Are you hungry, little crow?" asked Supriya. Grandma smiled. "You can give it a small piece." Supriya picked up a tiny bit of rasgulla. "Here you go!" The crow pecked it gently. "Caw-caw!" "Bounce, bounce, rasgulla round and round!" sang Supriya. The crow flapped its wings. Flap-flap-flap! "Let's play!" said Supriya. She pushed one rasgulla. It wobbled across the counter. The crow tapped it with its foot. The rasgulla wiggled and jiggled. Supriya laughed and laughed. "One rasgulla!" she counted. "Caw!" "Two rasgullas!" "Caw-caw!" Grandma sprinkled colored sugar on top—pink and yellow and green. "Bounce, bounce, rasgulla round and round!" Everything was giggles and colors and sunshine. But then— One big rasgulla started to roll. It rolled toward the edge of the counter. The edge by the window. The edge that was very, very high. "Oh no!" cried Supriya. Her eyes grew wide. The rasgulla kept rolling. Closer. Closer. "Stop!" called Supriya. But it didn't stop. Supriya's heart went thump-thump-thump. Her hands felt shaky. She reached out—but the rasgulla was too far away! "Bounce, bounce—oh no, oh no!" "Help me, crow!" she called. The crow looked at the rolling rasgulla. It looked at Supriya. Then it hopped fast—tap-tap-tap—across the counter! The crow tried to stop the rasgulla with its wing. But the rasgulla was too slippery! It kept rolling. Hey guys! Can we help them? Let's try again! "We have to work together!" said Supriya. She got an idea. "Crow, you push from that side. I'll catch from this side!" Supriya put her hands out. The crow flapped to the other side of the rasgulla. "Ready?" asked Supriya. "One..." "Caw!" "Two..." "Caw-caw!" "Three... PUSH!" Come on guys. Let's push with them! Push, push, push! Supriya's little hands pushed gently. The crow used its wing to nudge. Together, they moved the rasgulla away from the edge. Back to safety. Back to the middle of the counter. "We did it!" cheered Supriya. She let out a big, big breath. Her heart stopped going thump-thump-thump. "Caw-caw-caw!" The crow bounced up and down on its tiny feet. They looked at each other. Then Supriya started giggling and the crow cawing. Supriya carefully picked up the rasgulla. She held it safe and snug. The sunlight made all the colored sprinkles shine like tiny stars. The crow perched happily on the counter, right next to Supriya. Grandma smiled. "You two make a good team." Supriya looked at the crow. The crow looked at Supriya. "We saved it together," whispered Supriya. She gave the crow the gentlest hug. Its soft feathers tickled her cheek. The crow snuggled close and cawed happily. Supriya counted all the safe rasgullas. "One... two... three... four... five! All safe!" "Bounce, bounce, rasgulla round and round! Now safe and sound, with a friend we found!" From that sunny morning on, whenever Supriya made rasgullas with Grandma, a little black crow would flap-flap-flap through the window. Ready to help. Ready to share. Ready to save rasgullas together. Because that's what friends do.
author: Bhaskar Rana

title: All About Snouts and Tails
text: Hammer snout Propeller tail Downward snout Navigator tail Flat snout Rudder tail Detective snout Rattling tail Painted snout Upright tail Maned snout Extra-long tail Three-horned snout Colour-changing tail Air-filter snout Extra-short tail Warming snout Blanket tail Pores along the snouts of great hammerhead sharks detect electrical signals emitted by their prey, stingrays. Their hammer-shaped snouts help pin their prey down! Their asymmetrical tails make them powerful swimmers. Dugongs have snouts that help them chomp on leaves on the seabed. Their tails are split into two equal lobes, or flukes, to help maintain balance when they swim and feed at the same time. More About Snouts and Tails Duck-billed platypuses are the only mammals to have a broad, flat snout. Cells on the bill detect signals from prey underwater. Instead of teeth, their snouts have grinding pads to crush food. They use their flat tails like a rudder to swim. They also store fat in their tails to use it as an energy reserve when food supply is low. Male mandrills have colourful snouts and backs, which help them find mates, communicate and be visible in the dark, dense forest. Their short, stumpy, upright tails help them communicate with other troop members. Nilgiri langurs use their snouts to grasp and pluck leaves and fruits. Their long tails help them to maintain stability and balance as they jump from tree to tree. The three-horned snouts of male Jackson’s chameleons make them appear larger and scarier to predators. Their prehensile tails work like a fifth limb. They wrap the tails around branches for a firmer grip. Their tails can change colours according to the chameleons’ health or habitat! Indian crested porcupines have pointy snouts that are good at detecting smells. When attacked, the porcupines rattle the hollow quills on their short tails as a warning. They can charge backwards and stab their attacker with the quills. The snouts of Saiga antelopes look swollen and hang over their mouths. These snouts have a filter that removes dust particles inhaled during migration across dry and dusty open steppes. Their short tails don’t seem to have any function in their semi-desert environment. When snow leopards breathe in, their extra-wide noses heat up the cold Himalayan air! To stay warm, they wrap their extra-long tails around their body and tuck in their snouts. Their tails also help them keep their balance when climbing the steep terrain.
author: Radha Rangarajan

title: The wealth I have acquired
text: What are you doing?” Vinodini asked him. “Akka! I am doing my homework. Why are you bothering me?” Mukunda asked. “Dad, I have to go out urgently. Come quickly. I have something to tell you,” Vinothini called. Mukundan left the lesson he was writing halfway and got up. The two of them went to their father. My sister called me to tell me something. Now she's bringing me to my father. Is she going to say something about me for not doing my homework? It was the wisdom of always telling the truth to his sister. Mukundan trembled with fear. "What will Dad do? What will he ask?" he was afraid. “Mukunda! Have you finished your homework properly?” asked his father. “I haven’t finished it yet. My sister has already brought it,” said Mukunda. "Dad! Yesterday I asked...?" my sister interrupted. "I remember Vinothini. I'll buy it today without forgetting," said my father. Mukundan wondered what his sister had asked his father. His father looked at his watch. It's time to go to the office. "You two go to school." "It's time for me," said Dad and left. "Sister! What did you ask your father to buy?" Mukundan asked. "I won't tell you that now. I'll tell you when I get home from school," said my sister. Vinodini packed lunch for her younger brother and herself and they both went to school. “Mukunda! Mukunda!” the teacher called him. He stood up, frightened. All the other students looked at him. He hadn't finished his homework yet. His body trembled, afraid of what the teacher was going to ask. “Mukunda! The principal has asked you to come. Go and see him,” the teacher said. Mukunda's fear increased when he heard that the principal had asked him to come. "I didn't do anything wrong. Did someone make a mistake and blame me?" he thought, hesitating. "Mukunda, go quickly. The principal is waiting for you", his teacher insisted. Mukundan walked slowly, hesitantly. The principal came out of his room. “Mukunda, come!” he called. Mukunda hesitantly approached him. He hugged him and patted him on the back. “Do you have a mother? What does your father do for work?” he asked. “I don’t have a mother. My father works in the office,” Mukundan said. “Don’t you have a mother? Is that why you drew the picture of your mother?” asked the headmaster. When he heard the word "mother's picture," Mukundan remembered the picture of his mother at home. In that picture, when he was a two-year-old child, she was holding out both her arms to lift him up as he walked. Mukundan also runs with both hands raised to take refuge in his mother's arms. Mukundan's mother, her face beaming with joy, comes to pick up her son. This memory never left Mukundan's mind. He would look at that picture every day. He would feel like his mother was reaching out and calling him. His father has seen his son looking at his mother's picture many times. When Vinothini teaches Mukundan a lesson, he looks at his mother's picture. So, she hid her mother's picture where he couldn't see it. One day he got a fever. He cried out, "Mom! Mom!" Vinothini showed him the picture of her mother that she had hidden. He didn't look at the picture. Mukundan is good at drawing. There was a drawing competition in his school. Students from many schools participated in the competition. Each student drew a different picture. Mukundano had drawn a picture of his mother at home, to the amazement of the lookers. The judges of the competition gathered to select the paintings drawn by the students. Among the many paintings, Mukundan's painting caught everyone's attention. He won the first prize. The principal had invited him to his room to tell him that and praise him. “Mukunda! The picture of your mother that you drew in the painting competition has won first prize,” said the headmaster. "The first prize for the picture I drew of my mother? Mom... I drew it thinking of you. I don't have the prize for you," he muttered. He returned to class from the principal's office. His classmates congratulated him on winning first prize. “Mukunda! You have brought glory to our school with your painting skills,” said the teacher. That evening, a felicitation meeting was held for Mukundan at school. The principal presented Mukundan with a silver cup and a thousand rupees. Everyone clapped and cheered. Viyothini never thought her younger brother would win first prize in the painting competition. She learned from the gift that he was good at painting. In the evening, his father left the office and left for home. He remembered what Vinothini had said in the morning. He rushed home to buy the paintbrush that Mukundan needed and give it to him. Mukundan was worshipping the gifts he had received near his mother's picture. When his father returned home, he was stunned to see it. “Dad! My brother has won first prize in the painting competition. "The ones next to the picture of mom are the gifts he got," said Vinothini. Father went near Mukundan and handed him the brush in his hand. He placed it in front of his mother's picture. He fell at his father's feet, standing next to him, and bowed. Vinodini shed tears of joy upon seeing this. Father hugged them both and said, “You are the wealth I have received. "There is no greater wealth in this world than you," he said, hugging them.
author: Satvik Ramasubramaniam
illustrator: Adonay Gebru; Asha Susan  Alex; Dr. Sushma  Singh; Ishmeet Kaur; Jemma Jose; Nan Hom Noon; Radhika Tipnis; Rohit Kelkar; ROSH; Sain Thuokna; Sonia Dearling; Trần Lưu  Đăng Nguyên; Yuvaka  Srestha

title: Jim Jam Diaries
text: There was a little girl named, Navyaa. She loved to look at birds! She sometimes dreamt of having pet birds, and from that day on, she started research... Navyaa found out that 'Budgies' were one of the best birds to have as a pet. And then she told her mom and dad about her 'Research' and they did not want pets! That`s when she lost hope:(But then she spoke many times to her parents and her father went to the pet shop! And they saw so many birds together, in a cage, Navyaa and her father saw two beautiful, bright yellow and blue budgies! She told her father that she wanted them and guess what? Her father took them! Navyaa jumped with joy on her face! She immediately clicked a photo of them and sent the photo to her mom. After they reached home, Navyaa`s mom and her brother were surprised! "Mother started shooting a video for my channel, and my brother literally started staring at the birds! What a moment it was! But the birds were scared and sad at the same time, because they were separated from the rest of their friends... Days passed, but the names for the birds were not decided yet... It could feel weird by saying the word 'Birds' again and again but as i said, their names were not decided, i asked my friends, but they told names like cookie-coco, mochi-mocha, and more. But i did not like these kind of names, but one said Jim-Jam and i liked it! I told my family members and that`s how the name, 'Jim Jam' was born. Day by day, Jim Jam got familiar with us. And I don`t know how, but without training, they even started taming on our fingers! We started to give them spinach leaves, carrot leaves and more refreshing leaves with sweet, refreshing water, and they enjoyed it! We even tried to give them fruits and veggies (bird-friendly) but they refused it:(And then, after months passed, something happened that i could not believe! We had to go to Nagpur the other day, but we could not take Jim Jam with us!. I cried a lot because i wanted to take Jim Jam with us but we could not... But then, i agreed, so i released them from their cage into the room so that they could fly a bit, but my father was not aware about it, so when he came in the room, he did not see Jim Jam and turned the fan on. Jim got a cut on her nose, but thank god she was alive. The other day, our neighbors came and took Jim Jam with them... And after some days, they observed that Jam was looking dizzy, but they took it lightly, and even they didn`t know how, Jam lost his life.. They told my brother, and my dad to not tell me about everything that had happened but somehow i came to know... I literally started crying and my heart sank. When we returned to our home, we got another Jam (bird) so that Jim wouldn`t feel alone all her life. But the two did not get along well. After months, another day left me heartbroken. Nobody was at home. Before everyone left, no one paid attention to Jim Jam and that is why no one kept the cage inside the home. When i came back and saw the cage, Jam`s head and his body were literally torn apart by an eagle. And i shouted "Pappaaaaaa!!!!!" My brother cam downstairs and saw what had happened.My brother then cleaned the cage, and then my father said "Enough, now Jim will live with Nilu Pilu (our neighbours birds) from now on." And now I can meet Jim whenever I want!
author: navyaa vd
illustrator: Canato Jimo; Krishnagopal Shreshtha; Lavanya Karthik; Maithili  Joshi; Nivong  Sengsakoun; R. C. Pradeep Kumar; Sarthak Sinha

title: The Woman and Her Ghee
text: Once upon a time, there lived a woman in a small village. She had two sons who worked hard and earned money for the family. They lived a simple but happy life. One day, a terrible fire broke out in the village. It spread very quickly. Sadly, both of her sons died in the fire. The woman was heartbroken and left all alone. After some days, she needed to find a way to earn money. She decided to make and sell ghee. She worked hard every day and took her ghee to the village to sell. But the villagers were very superstitious. They believed that buying ghee from her would bring bad luck because her sons had died. So no one wanted to buy from her. The woman felt very sad and worried. She did not know what to do. One day, a kind old man saw her sitting quietly with her cart of ghee. He felt sorry for her. He said, “Why don’t you go to the next town? There is a busy market there. You may be able to sell your ghee.” The woman thought this was a good idea. She thanked the old man for his advice. The next morning, she packed her ghee carefully onto her cart and traveled to the nearby town, hoping for a better future. Upon reaching the town, she set up her cart in an empty corner of the busy market. This town was much bigger and more populated than her own village. Merchants were selling their goods. Children were playing cricket. Some people were setting up their shops. It was a lively place. After about an hour, just as the old man had said, people began coming to her cart. They tasted sample of her ghee and smiled. “This is very tasty,” they said. “It has a unique aroma and flavor we have never had tasted in any ghee before.” Soon, more people came. By the end of the day, she had sold all her ghee and earned around Rs. 100. That was a lot of money at that time. She was very happy and proud. Her business grew bigger each day. Even people from her own village heard about her ghee. They realized they were wrong to avoid her before. They forgave her and praised her hard work The woman smiled. She had worked hard, stayed brave, and never gave up. She had built a good life for herself. One day, a rich man came to her cart. He said, “I am holding a feast for around 200 people for my daughter's birthday. I want to buy 20 large pots of ghee. Each pot should be enough for 10 people.” The woman shook her head. “I cannot carry so many pots,” she said. The man smiled. “Don’t worry. My workers will come to your home to carry the pots. I will pay you 20 rupees for each pot.” Hearing this, the woman became very happy. She agreed at once. That night, she made 10 pots of ghee. But then she realized she did not have enough milk to make the other 10 pots. But then an idea struck her mind. She quickly took three large pots and went to a shop nearby that sold cooking oil. She bought pots full of vegetable oil and took them back home. The shop owner was suspicious. “Why does she need so much oil?” she wondered. “Ghee is made from milk, not oil. Maybe she is cooking for herself, but this is a lot of oil.” That night, the shop owner quietly went to her house and peeked through the window. SHE WAS SCHOCKED AT WHAT SHE SAW. The woman was carefully adding oil to the ghee she had already made, filling the remaining pots to sell. The oil shop owner had always been a proud customer of the woman. Now she felt ashamed and decided she needed to teach that woman a lesson. At the feast, the cooks used the ghee made by the woman to cook all the food. Some guests enjoyed the dishes, but many found the taste strange. Something about it felt different. Suddenly, the door burst open! The shop owner, who had seen her mixing the oil the night before, ran in and told everyone what the woman had done. The guests were shocked and disgusted. They could not believe that someone would trick them like this. The rich man was very angry. He said, “You cannot trick people like this! Ghee must be pure and made from milk.” The guests and villagers were shocked and disgusted. They decided they would never buy ghee from the woman again. The woman felt sad, but she had no one to blame but herself. Her vile trick had caused her to lose everyone’s trust. From that day on, no one in the town or her village bought ghee from her. She had to find another way to live, and she realized that cleverness without honesty can bring only trouble. Even though she worked hard, she learned the hard way that honesty is more important than getting quick money. ﻿Fact box- Pure, traditional desi ghee is made solely from milk fat (cow or buffalo) and does not contain added vegetable oil. However, adulteration is common in some commercial products, where cheaper vegetable oils, hydrogenated fats, or vanaspati may be added to mimic the texture and increase volume. Pure Ghee: Made by simmering butter to remove water and milk solids, resulting in nearly 100% milk fat. Adulteration: Some market-bought or cheaper "ghee" substitutes may contain added refined oils. ﻿﻿ Vanaspati Ghee: This is a, often misunderstood, product derived from vegetable oils, which is hydrogenated and not pure milk ghee. To ensure purity, it is recommended to buy branded ghee with recognized quality certifications or to make it at home from butter. Refined oils can break down into toxic compounds when heated to high temperatures (like frying). Desi ghee, on the other hand, has a higher smoke point, making it stable and safe even for deep-frying. Perfect for Indian cooking styles like tadka, roasting, or frying. Source: Read Wikipedia to learn more about it!

title: The plate and the clever trick
text: She is five years old. After studying at the Anganwadi for two years, she joined UKG. The school reopened. The school bus came. She went to the new school with her big sister. In just a few days, she became everyone’s favourite. She learned many new games from her new friends. She liked everything – the school, the bus, the class, the teacher, and her friends. They all ate their meals together. In the afternoon, her big sister and friends came to check whether she had eaten her meal, used the washroom, and whether anyone was troubling her. One day, she went to see her sister’s class too. One day, when she opened her bag after returning home, she found that her plate was missing. Instead, there was another plate in the bag, and it was an old one. She could not control her sadness and burst into tears. Her father and mother comforted her. They said that the plate must have been exchanged and that one of her friends might have taken it by mistake. They told her she would get it back when she went to school the next day. Her sister also comforted her. She said that her bag had also been exchanged once before. Later, they had tied a ribbon on it so that it would not get mixed up again. “Like this,” she said. Hearing this, Sami felt relieved. The next day, she reached school earlier than usual. There was her plate, as if it were looking at her and smiling! The moment she saw her plate, she felt happy. She ran and picked it up. Her eyes filled with tears of happiness. That evening, her father came home with a trick. A bottle of nail polish! This time, he had bought the nail polish not to paint nails, but to write on the plate. She and her mother wrote her name on the plate using nail polish. From then on, the plate was never mixed up again. How do you like this trick?
author: Latha Romikuttan

title: The Journey Of A Toy
text: A toy is one of the things that take us back to our childhood, that remind us of the nostalgia, the chaos, and our little mind that were dreamy and lively. but after that, what happened to the nostalgia, the reminder? The journey of a toy is exciting but rather endless. Some people decide to keep their toys as a childhood keepsake, while some pass the legacy. But some, give away their toys to the most needful kids of time. to them, the smile means more than keepsakes, and their laughter matters more than memories. However, some toys travel farther. The people, on several occasions, mail their toys in post as a gesture of kindness and sympathy. Some toys, travel far enough, but finally they make a spark of laughter.

title: Pratheek and the Wobbly Palanquin
text: The streets of Mysuru were wearing their finest clothes. Every doorstep glowed with a golden lamp. Every gate wore a fat garland of orange marigolds. The air was warm with jasmine and sweet with sandalwood, and from somewhere down the road — thump-thump, thump-thump — the Dasara drums had already begun their big, bold song. Pratheek stood on his tiptoes and placed his small clay lamp — painted red and gold, painted by him — on the window ledge. He stepped back. He squinted one eye. He smiled. Perfect. Can you see Pratheek's lamp? What colours is it? Just then, a fat white goat trotted past. It sniffed Pratheek's shoelaces. It sneezed. Then it wandered cheerfully around the corner, completely unbothered by the entire festival. Pratheek giggled. "Silly goat." But then — Jiggle-jiggle. Creak. Jiggle-JIGGLE. Pratheek spun around. At the end of the narrow lane, the great golden palanquin — t he one carrying Goddess Chamundeshwari, gleaming like a small sun — was wobbling. The four bearers were stepping carefully, but the lane had grown thin and twisty. And right in the middle of the path sat a big basket of marigolds, two scattered clay pots, and a tangle of rope — left behind by the morning's decorators. Nobody had cleared the way. Pratheek's tummy dropped. His fingers went cold. His feet felt stuck to the ground. He was so small. The palanquin was so big. He looked at his hands. Then he ran. "AANYA!" he shouted, spotting his friend by the sweet stall. "The palanquin — the path isn't clear — come on!" Aanya didn't ask questions. That was the thing about Aanya — she never wasted time asking questions when there was something to do. She was already running. Pratheek grabbed the two clay pots and pulled them to the side of the lane — grunt, scrape, thud. Aanya grabbed the big basket with both arms — heave, wobble, done. Together they kicked the tangle of rope out of the way. Can you help? Let's push! One — two — three — PUSH! The path was almost clear. And that is exactly when the fat white goat came back. It looked at the basket of marigolds. It looked at Pratheek. It walked straight into the basket — bonk — and sent orange petals flying like a small, fluffy explosion. The palanquin gave one tremendous — WOBBLE. "Oh no," Pratheek whispered. His hands were shaking. His heart was hammering. But he looked at Aanya, and Aanya looked at him, and neither of them moved a single step backwards. Aanya threw both arms around the goat's neck. The goat froze, deeply surprised to be hugged at a festival. A boy watching from the side saw what they were doing and ran forward to help. Then a girl. Then an old grandfather pulled his grandchildren back to make the lane wider. One by one — like lamps lighting other lamps — small hands appeared all down the narrow lane. And then the crowd began to chant. Softly at first. Then louder. Then louder still. "Hold steady, hold tight! Step slowly, step right!" Can you chant with them? Hold steady, hold tight! Step slowly, step right! "Hold steady, hold tight! Step slowly, step right!" The drums kept going — thump-thump, thump-thump. The cymbals rang. The bearers looked at the clear path stretching ahead of them, took one deep breath together, and stepped forward. Step. Step. Step. Slow and careful and steady. Step. Step. Step. And then — they were through. The lane opened wide. The crowd burst into the biggest cheer Pratheek had ever heard. Orange petals swirled up into the golden evening air like tiny dancers. The smell of laddus and jasmine came rushing back all at once, warm and sweet and wonderful. Pratheek's chest felt so full he thought it might overflow. Aanya let go of the goat. The goat shook itself from nose to tail, gave Aanya a deeply offended look, and walked away with its nose pointed at the sky. A festival helper knelt down in front of Pratheek and Aanya, smiling so wide his whole face was in it. "You two," he said, "went first. And look what happened." Pratheek looked down the lane. He saw the boy who had run forward. The girl. The grandfather. The child with the lantern. All those hands. All those people — because two small children had decided not to stand still. He walked back to his window ledge. His little clay lamp — red and gold, painted by him — was right where he had left it. Glowing warm and steady and bright, just like always. Just like him. The drums played. The dancers twirled in colours so bright they hurt your eyes in the best possible way. And somewhere nearby, a fat white goat was eating someone's marigold garland — and absolutely nobody was surprised. Thump-thump. Thump-thump. Dasara glowed on. The End!
author: Bhaskar Rana

title: MILA'S FUN ADVENTURE
text: Once upon a time, there lived an ambitious young girl named Mila. She lived in a small cottage in a faraway town in Egypt. One day, she decided to walk to the magical forest to explore and collect some fruits for her sickly grandmother. While in the magical forest, Milla explored different kinds of trees. Although Mila was worried about her sick grandmother, she enjoyed the magic that surrounded the forest. ''How beautiful it looks!'' Mila exclaimed. Suddenly, she saw an angry wolf. Mila got scared and thought about ways of running away. However, more wolves kept coming, surrounding her. Mila held tightly to her dress, making a silent prayer to the magical forest. Miraculously, different tree leaves rattled, and a hissing sound came from the faraway corner of the most enormous tree of the forest. Scared, Mila bent down and thought about her sickly grandmother. She cried out loud. Fortunately, the goddess of the magical forest scared the wolves away in an angry commanding tone. Later, a magnificent golden horse emerged from the most enormous tree of the forest. The horse asked Mila to make a wish. ''Make a wish, make a wish,'' it said. Quickly, Mila stood up and made a wish. In her calmest voice, she said, ''I wish for my grandmother to heal from all sickness.'' Suddenly, the horse disappeared into thin air, and a small path appeared in the forest, which Mila used to walk back to the house. She found her grandmother well without any pain. Indeed, the magical forest had granted her wish. END Great appreciation goes to all students of 3B class who worked tirelessly with their teacher of English and came up with such an amazing book.
