Found in non stick pans, waterproof clothing and food packaging, they accumulate over time and disrupt immune and hormonal function. Switch to cast iron or stainless steel cookware. U is for UV & Sunscreen Chemical sunscreens are absorbed through skin and some are classified as endocrine disruptors. Children's skin absorbs chemicals more readily than adults. Choose mineral sunscreens with zinc oxide for effective, hormone safe sun protection. V is for VOCs Paints, cleaning products and new furniture release volatile organic compounds that children breathe in at higher concentrations than adults. Choose low VOC products, ventilate rooms thoroughly and allow new furniture to off gas before use. W is for Water Tap water can contain heavy metals, PFAS and microplastics. Children are more vulnerable due to their smaller body size. Invest in a quality filter certified to remove heavy metals and PFAS and serve water in glass. X is for Xenoestrogens Xenoestrogens are found in plastics, pesticides and cosmetics and accumulate in body tissue over time. In children they have been linked to early puberty and hormonal imbalance. Reduce plastic use, choose organic and select natural personal care products. Y is for You You don't need to overhaul everything overnight. Every small swap adds up to a reduced toxic load for your child. Knowledge is not meant to create anxiety, it is meant to create agency. You are already doing the most important thing. You are paying attention. Z is for Zzz During deep sleep children's bodies detoxify, repair cells and release growth hormone. Consistent quality sleep is one of the most protective things a parent can offer. Create a dark, cool, screen free sleep environment and protect those hours fiercely. ﻿ *The “Dirty Dozen” is a list created using U.S. data by the Environmental Working Group, highlighting fruits and vegetables that tend to carry higher pesticide residues—such as strawberries, spinach, apples, grapes, peppers, and tomatoes. While this list is not specific to India, similar types of produce (especially leafy greens and thin-skinned fruits) are often more heavily sprayed worldwide. When possible, choosing organic for these can help reduce exposure.
author: Nidhi Mahule Kandpal

title: The Hardships of a Kid
text: When things go wrong and I just want to cry, I sit and think, then try to smile again, The clouds are big, but they will pass me by, And I won’t feel this way forever, then. I trip and fall and scrape my knees a lot, But I get up and try to run once more, I learn from every little thing I got, And don’t feel quite as scared like before. The hard days help me see I can be strong, Even if I feel a little small, And even when the days feel way too long, I know I still can get back up from all. So I will laugh and keep on going through, ‘Cause hard times help me find the happy too.
author: Vihaan Rajput

title: The Magic Within: How I Found My Voice
text: The year I found my voice began with a new house, a new school… and a girl I had never planned to meet before. My summer vacation began right after I finished Upper Kindergarten (UKG). Just as the holidays started, my parents decided it was time for a new beginning—we were moving to a new home, and along with it, I would be joining a new school. This meant going through an entirely new admission process. Listening to all of this made me even more excited. This wasn’t just an ordinary school—it had a chess room, a drama room, a language room, a pottery room, an art room, and even an AV room. What I didn’t know then was that a whole new adventure was waiting for me! The night before my first day, I was so excited that I could barely sleep. The next morning, I woke up so early that even my parents were still asleep! As I got ready, I told myself that this year would be different. I wanted to be more confident, more brave, and less shy. Whenever I met new people, I used to tremble with fear, and a voice in my head would whisper, “Why am I even here?” But this time, I was determined to change. When it was finally time to board the bus, I wondered if I would make any friends or remain the quiet girl who never spoke. An aunt on the bus made me sit next to another girl. What I didn’t know then was that this one moment would change everything. The girl beside me started talking to me as if we were already best friends, but I couldn’t get a single word out. Still, I felt happy. And when I found out she was in the same class as me, I slowly began to open up. This friend of mine was so different. She waved at everyone she met and could talk with me the whole day. I often wondered how she had so much energy and how she could always find something new to talk about. Didn’t she ever get tired? She would hold my hand, and we would walk together to the canteen and around the school. I admired how she had the courage to go anywhere without hesitation. As the days turned into weeks, and weeks into months, we became known as a pair. Teachers would recognise us together and often wonder how two completely opposite personalities could be such close friends. My teachers were kind and encouraging. We had four main subjects—Science, Maths, Kannada, and English—and each teacher brought so much enthusiasm to their class. I loved learning, but whenever I had to answer a question, I would still tremble. Some teachers even asked why I was shaking just to speak. Deep down, I thought maybe I was just too shy—but I was too shy to even explain that. During a parent-teacher meeting later in the year, my teacher and my parents encouraged me to become more bold and confident. Like always, I agreed—but this time, I meant it with all my heart. I truly wanted to change, not just for others, but for myself. A Moment in Class: One day in class, my teacher asked a simple question. I knew the answer. I really did. My hand slowly started to rise… but halfway up, it stopped. My heart began to race, and my fingers started trembling. I looked around—everyone else seemed so confident. I quietly lowered my hand before anyone could notice. Just then, I felt a small nudge. My friend looked at me and whispered, “You knew the answer, right? Next time, just say it. I’ll be right here.” She gave me a quick smile and raised her own hand without any fear. I didn’t answer—but for the first time, I thought… maybe I could try. As the weeks passed, I slowly began to change. I made a few more friends, and each day at school felt a little easier than the one before. Even though I was still shy, I was no longer as afraid as I used to be. A Small Adventure: One afternoon during break, my friend pulled me towards the canteen. “Come on, let’s go explore!” she said, already dragging me along. “We might get late…” I said nervously. “Then we’ll run!” she laughed. As we walked, she waved at almost everyone we passed, and somehow, they all waved back. I just followed beside her, holding her hand, wondering how she made everything look so easy. We ended up laughing so much while running back to class that we almost forgot why we were scared in the first place. For once, I wasn’t thinking about being shy—I was just… happy. The Turning Point: One day, something unexpected happened. The teacher asked a question again. My heart started beating fast—just like always. I glanced at my friend. She looked at me, as if she already knew what I was thinking, and gave me a small nod. That tiny moment gave me courage. This time… I didn’t lower my hand. It was shaking. My voice was soft. But I answered. The classroom didn’t go silent. No one laughed. The teacher smiled and said, “Good.” When I sat down, my friend leaned over and whispered, “See? I told you.” Just one moment. But that moment felt like everything. Before I knew it, the school year was coming to an end. Soon, it was time for the awards ceremony. These awards were given to recognise how students had improved throughout the year. We all followed our teacher to the corridor where the awards were being announced. I was especially excited about one award— “Star of the Month,” given to an all-rounder. From the moment I heard about it, I had always wanted to win it. The announcements began. There were so many awards—almost 50! I received the “Neatest Handwriting in Kannada” award, and I felt so proud. At the beginning of the year, my handwriting hadn’t been very good, so this showed how much I had improved. My best friend received the “Super Speaker” award, and I was really happy for her. Finally, it was time for the “Star of the Month” award. “The Star of the Month award goes to… Mihika Bhat!” Even though I had struggled to speak, I had still achieved it. I felt so happy. The entire year passed in what felt like a flash. On the last day of school, I packed my bag, said goodbye to my teacher, and held my award proudly. As I made my way home, my thoughts were already drifting to Mangalore—because that was where we were going for our summer vacation. I may have started the year in silence, but I ended it with a voice that was finally my own!
author: Mihika Bhat

title: The Naughty Bear
text: In a colorful forest village lived a little bear named Naughty Bear. He wasn’t mean—just a bit too playful. One sunny morning, all the animals were getting ready for a party. “Don’t touch the cake!” said Bunny. “It’s for everyone.” The cake looked delicious—big, chocolatey, and covered in honey. Naughty Bear licked his lips. “I’ll just take a tiny bite,” he whispered. But one bite became two… Then three… Soon—oops!—half the cake was gone! “Oh no!” Naughty Bear said. “What have I done?” Quickly, Naughty Bear hid behind a bush. “Who ate the cake?” cried Fox. Everyone looked confused. Some animals looked sad. Naughty Bear felt a funny feeling in his tummy. Not hunger… something else. “Maybe this isn’t fun,” he thought. Slowly, he walked out. I’m sorry,” said Naughty Bear. “I ate the cake.” The animals were quiet. Then Bunny sighed. “You should have waited.” Naughty Bear nodded. “I know. I want to fix it.” So he worked hard—mixing honey, berries, and flour. It wasn’t perfect, but it was made with care. At the party, everyone shared the new cake. “This one tastes better,” said Fox. “Why?” asked Naughty Bear. “Because you learn something,” Bunny smiled. Naughty Bear grinned.
author: Afreen Khan
illustrator: Jithin Jacob; Pia Meenakshi; Suvidha  Mistry; Vishnu  M Nair

title: Lobo's Flowery Shigmo Festival
text: Boom! Boom! Boom! Somewhere far away, a dhol was drumming. Lobo's eyes flew open. Shigmo! He jumped out of bed so fast his feet barely touched the floor. He pulled on his yellow shirt — the bright one, his favourite. He grabbed his basket — the big round one with the red handle. Inside: golden marigolds. Piles and piles of them! He skipped out the door. Down the garden path. Past the mango tree. The air smelled sweet — like marigolds and warm earth and something happy that had no name. La-la-la! hummed Lobo. Today he was going to make the most beautiful garland in the whole village. Boom, boom, boom went the faraway dhol. La-la-la went Lobo. Plop! He stopped. One marigold had fallen out of his basket. It lay on the path like a little golden sun. Lobo picked it up. He looked ahead. And then he saw them. Three children sat at the edge of the lane. Their baskets sat beside them — empty. No flowers. No petals. Not even one. Their chins were in their hands. Their eyes were very, very sad. Lobo looked at them. He looked at his basket — full of golden marigolds, all the way to the top. He stood very still for one moment. His heart said something. It said: share. Lobo reached into his basket. He pulled out a big, soft handful of marigolds. He walked over and held them out. "Here," he said. "These are for you." The children looked up slowly. "For us?" said the smallest one. "Yes," said Lobo. "Shigmo is for everyone." The smallest child took the flowers with both hands, very carefully, as if they were made of gold. Because to her, they were. 🌼 What did Lobo do when he saw the sad children? Can you stretch your arms out wide — like Lobo sharing his flowers? "I'll show you how to make a garland," said Lobo. He sat down on the warm earth. The sun pressed softly on the back of his neck. He took a stem. He looped the thread. He pulled it through — gently, gently. "Like this," he said. The children leaned in close. They tried. Plop! A petal fell to the ground. Then another. Plop! Then three at once. Plop, plop, plop! The children burst out laughing. Petals landed on noses. Petals stuck to fingers. One bright pink petal sat right on top of Lobo's head like a tiny hat. "You have a petal crown!" shrieked one of the children. Lobo crossed his eyes trying to look at it. That made everyone laugh even more. More children heard the laughter. They came running down the earthen lane — pat, pat, pat — to see what was happening. When they saw the flowers, they sat down too. Petals passed from hand to hand — pink hibiscus, golden marigold, soft and cool between little fingers. Plop, plop, plop went the petals, all along the lane. 🌸 Plop, plop, plop! Can you tap your knees — plop, plop, plop — every time a petal falls? Yip! A small brown puppy came bounding around the corner. His ears flopped. His tail spun. His little nose went sniff, sniff, sniff. He smelled the flowers. He looked at the petals. He made a decision. Yip, yip, yip! — he leapt right into the middle of everything! Petals flew into the air. Children squealed. The puppy spun in a circle, tail going so fast it was just a blur. When he finally stopped — there was a fat golden marigold sitting perfectly on top of his nose. He looked at it, going cross-eyed. Everyone screamed with laughter. Even the mango trees seemed to shake with it. The puppy sneezed the marigold right off — Plop! — and it landed in Lobo's lap. Lobo held it up. "Thank you, puppy!" he announced very seriously. That made everyone laugh all over again. 🐶 Can you sneeze like the puppy? Ready? One, two, three — ACHOO! Plop! They were deep in their garland-making — fingers busy, cheeks round with smiling — when it happened. Whoooooosh. The wind came rushing through the mango trees all at once, like it had been waiting. The leaves went rustle-rustle-rustle. The petals went — everywhere. The half-made garlands trembled. One blew right out of a child's hand and tumbled away down the path. Everyone froze. The smallest child looked at her empty hands. Her lip began to wobble. Lobo felt his heart sink — just a little. He looked at the petals spinning in the air, the scattered marigolds, the thread gone loose. The puppy whined softly. He pressed his warm, furry side against Lobo's leg. Lobo felt that warmth. And then — he thought. "Wait," said Lobo. He stood up straight. "We can fix it." "How?" said the smallest child, lip still wobbling. "Together," said Lobo. He cupped his hands. He showed them. "Cup your hands — catch the petals!" The children cupped their hands. Petals drifted down like tiny slow snowflakes — pink ones, orange ones — landing softly in warm palms. "Now pass them — quick, quick, quick!" Hand to hand to hand they went — a living chain of petals moving all the way down the lane. The puppy ran alongside them, barking with excitement, his paws going tap-tap-tap on the warm earth. New garlands took shape. Tighter this time. Better this time. Made with more hands than before. The smallest child's lip stopped wobbling. She held up her garland — both arms high. "I made one!" she shouted. "I really made one!" 🌬️ The wind tried to blow the petals away! But did Lobo give up? Shake your head — no, no, no! He never gave up! An old woman leaned out of her doorway. She had been watching. She smiled a slow, wide smile. She went inside. She came back with both arms full — pink hibiscus, fresh from her garden. She set them down gently in front of the children. Then a man came out from the next house. He had a long roll of thread. He didn't say anything. He just sat down and started cutting. Then a grandmother came, carrying something on a banana leaf. Mango slices. Ripe and yellow and dripping sweet. The smell hit Lobo first — warm, golden, thick. Crunch. Oh. It was so good. Sticky juice ran down his chin. He wiped it with the back of his hand and left an orange streak across his cheek. The children ate and strung flowers and laughed all at the same time. More neighbours came. Then more. Then more. No one announced it. No one called out. They simply saw joy — and walked towards it. Garlands went up on every doorway. Petals lined every lane. The narrow earthen paths of the village glowed orange and pink and gold in the morning light. The puppy ran from end to end, trailing a string of marigolds someone had looped around his neck. His tail had not stopped wagging since morning. Boom, boom, boom went the dhol — closer now, warm and deep. Plop, plop, plop, plop, plop! sang the petals, falling everywhere at once. 🏘️ Everyone came! Can you count how many neighbours helped? One — two — three — and MORE! Clap for every single one! The sun moved lower. Its light turned soft and golden, the kind of light that makes everything look like it is glowing from inside. The puppy had found a bed of fallen petals near the stream. He turned three circles, sighed one very long sigh, and curled up small. One ear flopped over his nose. The children carried their garlands home, holding them up high so they wouldn't drag. The village was quiet now — the best kind of quiet. The kind that comes after a lot of joy. Lobo sat under the mango tree. The bark was rough and warm at his back. The grass was cool under his feet. Above him, the mango leaves moved very gently — shh, shh, shh. He looked down the lane. Petals everywhere. Garlands on every door. Flowers floating in the stream like tiny boats. His basket sat beside him. It was empty now. He had given away every single marigold. He picked up the basket. He looked inside it for a long time. Then he smiled, slow and quiet and full. Because his basket was empty. But the whole village was full. He leaned his head back against the mango tree and whispered, very softly, to no one and everyone — "The best Shigmo is when everyone shines together." A warm breeze moved through the lane. The petals on the ground lifted — just a little — and settled again. As if they had heard him. As if they agreed. Plop. The End!
author: Bhaskar Rana

title: The Bright Idea
text: Chapter 1: The Bright Idea Deep in a sunny green forest, there lived a little blue fuzzy creature named Pip. Pip was very small, about the size of a teacup, but he had a very big smile. Pip loved his forest, but today he was bored. He had bounced on all the bouncy mushrooms, and he had counted all the sleeping ladybugs. "I need an adventure," Pip said, tapping his chin with a fluffy finger. He looked around his cozy tree stump home. It was filled with treasures: shiny pebbles, interesting sticks, and a collection of acorn cups. Suddenly, he had an idea! He wanted to make a special home, a place all his own, right in the heart of the great oak tree. Chapter 2: The Treasure Hunt Begins "I need supplies!" Pip declared. He packed his little woven leaf backpack. First, he would need the softest building material, and then he would need help. Pip bounced over to the sunny meadow where the fluffiest dandelions grew. He needed the white, fluffy seeds—they were perfect for a soft bed. He was gathering a large, fluffy handful when a very small, bright green lizard named Barnaby scurried over. "Whatcha doin', Pip?" Barnaby asked, his tail twitching with curiosity. Barnaby was fast and very good at climbing. "I’m building a secret treehouse inside the great oak!" Pip whispered excitedly. "Do you want to help? I need to gather these fluffy seeds." Barnaby’s eyes went wide. "A secret treehouse? I'm the fastest climber in the meadow! I can help you gather all the fluff. Together, they made an excellent team. With Barnaby’s speed and Pip’s fluffy backpack, they soon had enough dandelion seed fluff for ten beds. Chapter 3: The Stick Dilemma Now they had fluff, but they needed strong sticks for walls and a floor. "We need the strongest sticks, but the strongest ones are always too big for me to carry," Pip sighed. They were standing by the stream, looking at a pile of perfect, sturdy twigs that had floated down. "If only we had someone strong," Barnaby said, balancing on a rock. Just then, they heard a slow, deep voice. "Did somebody mention... strong?" It was Gemma, the giant orange land snail. Gemma was very slow, but she was the strongest creature Pip knew. Her shell was shiny and swirled with bright colors. "We need to carry these strong sticks to the great oak tree for our secret treehouse," Pip explained. "But they are too heavy for us." Gemma smiled, which took a long time. "I may be slow," she said, "but I can carry many things. Pile the sticks on my shell! Pip and Barnaby carefully loaded the strongest twigs onto Gemma’s beautiful shell. She smiled again and began her slow, steady journey toward the great oak. "We need the strongest sticks, but the strongest ones are always too big for me to carry," Pip sighed. They were standing by the stream, looking at a pile of perfect, sturdy twigs that had floated down. "If only we had someone strong," Barnaby said, balancing on a rock. Just then, they heard a slow, deep voice. "Did somebody mention... strong?" It was Gemma, the giant orange land snail. Gemma was very slow, but she was the strongest creature Pip knew. Her shell was shiny and swirled with bright colors. "We need to carry these strong sticks to the great oak tree for our secret treehouse," Pip explained. "But they are too heavy for us." Gemma smiled, which took a long time. "I may be slow," she said, "but I can carry many things. Pile the sticks on my shell!" Pip and Barnaby carefully loaded the strongest twigs onto Gemma’s beautiful shell. She smiled again and began her slow, steady journey toward the great oak. Chapter 4: The Construction Crew Finally, they reached the Great Oak. Its roots were like giant, twisting arms, and its trunk was very wide. High above, there was a perfect, cozy hollow. "It's very high," Barnaby said, measuring the distance with his eyes. "And the door is very bare," Gemma noted, arriving slowly with the sticks. "It needs decoration." "If only we could decorate it with light," Pip said, thinking of his shiny pebble collection. "And we need a door!" Just then, they heard a soft buzz-buzz. A fuzzy yellow bumblebee named Boris landed on a mossy root. Boris always carried a little bucket of golden, glowing pollen. "I can help with the light!" Boris buzzed cheerfully. "I can use my glowing pollen to make the doorway shine!" With Barnaby climbing fast, Gemma supplying the strong sticks, and Boris making everything glow, the friends worked together. Pip supervised, making sure the dandelion fluff bed was perfectly soft. Chapter 5: The Sweetest Home As the sun began to set, painting the sky in deep purples and pinks, the secret treehouse was finally finished. It was perfect. The walls were strong, the bed was soft, and Boris’s pollen made the doorway glow with a warm, welcoming light. Pip, Barnaby, Gemma, and Boris all gathered inside. The treehouse was cozy, especially with four friends sharing the space. They sat together, eating sweet forest berries and sipping dewdrop tea. "This is the best secret treehouse ever," Barnaby whispered, his green eyes reflecting the golden glow. "And it's not secret from us," Gemma added slowly. Pip looked at his new friends and smiled the biggest smile he had ever smiled. He realized that the best part of his adventure wasn't the cozy new home; it was the friends who helped him build it. And even though they were all very different, together, they were a perfect team. title: The Crystal Cave Mystery
text: Chapter 1: The Crystal Cave Mystery Luna was a tiny, fuzzy white creature with large, friendly, moon-shaped eyes. She lived high up in the Whispering Mountains, in a little burrow lined with soft moss. Luna was excellent at observing things, and she loved to collect smooth, colorful pebbles. One morning, while digging for a particularly shiny blue stone, Luna’s shovel went clink. She had found the top of a tunnel! It was too dark for her to see inside, but as she peered in, she saw a faint, deep purple glow far in the distance. "Oh my!" Luna whispered, her eyes wide. "A secret cave! But I can’t go down there alone. It's too scary and dark." She needed help to explore this mystery. Chapter 2: The Fast and the Fluffy Luna scrambled away from the cave mouth. She needed someone who was not afraid of high places or tight spaces, someone who could move quickly and maybe bring a bit of light. She thought of Oliver. Oliver was a bright orange squirrel. He wasn't just fast; he was lightning fast. He always carried a bushy tail full of fuzzy dandelion fluff, which he used to make things soft and cozy (or to cushion his many safe tumbles). Luna found Oliver bouncing from branch to branch on the sturdy mountain oaks. "Oliver! I found a secret cave with a mysterious purple glow!" she puffed, trying to keep up. Oliver paused, his tail twitching. "A secret purple cave? I love secrets! And I am the fastest climber around! I can dash in and out before you can say 'acorn'!" He happily agreed to help, stuffing a fresh handful of fuzzy dandelion seeds into his pocket. Chapter 3: The Light and the Slow Now they had speed and fluff, but they still needed real light. "My moon-eyes help me see a little," Luna said, "but we need to glow!" They needed Beatrice. Beatrice was a giant bumblebee, perhaps the largest one in the mountains. She didn't make much honey, but she had something better: she carried a special pouch of glowing, golden pollen. It was so bright it could turn night into day. Luna and Oliver found Beatrice slow-buzzing near the sweet clover meadow. "A secret cave? And you need my glow?" Beatrice buzzed, her voice deep and gentle. She was very slow, but she was the only creature whose light never faded. "Of course, little ones. I can provide the warmth and the light. It just may take me a little time." With Luna’s observations and Oliver’s speed, they made excellent scouts, while Beatrice began her slow, steady flight toward the mountain cave. Chapter 3: The Light and the Slow Now they had speed and fluff, but they still needed real light. "My moon-eyes help me see a little," Luna said, "but we need to glow!" They needed Beatrice. Beatrice was a giant bumblebee, perhaps the largest one in the mountains. She didn't make much honey, but she had something better: she carried a special pouch of glowing, golden pollen. It was so bright it could turn night into day. Luna and Oliver found Beatrice slow-buzzing near the sweet clover meadow. "A secret cave? And you need my glow?" Beatrice buzzed, her voice deep and gentle. She was very slow, but she was the only creature whose light never faded. "Of course, little ones. I can provide the warmth and the light. It just may take me a little time." With Luna’s observations and Oliver’s speed, they made excellent scouts, while Beatrice began her slow, steady flight toward the mountain cave. Chapter 4: The Tunnel Team They were all gathered at the cave entrance. It was very high up, but with Oliver’s help, even Beatrice made the climb. "Okay," Luna whispered, her large eyes fixed on the distant purple glow. "Oliver, you go first and check if the floor is safe. Don't go too far! Beatrice, you stay close to me and use your light." They entered the cave. Oliver darted ahead, testing every stone, while Beatrice pulsed her golden light, making the entire tunnel glow like sunshine. The purple light grew brighter and warmer. Then they saw it. "Look!" Luna exclaimed. The cave floor was covered in smooth, glittering purple crystals! But they were all messy, mixed with grey dust and sharp stones. Chapter 4: The Tunnel Team They were all gathered at the cave entrance. It was very high up, but with Oliver’s help, even Beatrice made the climb. "Okay," Luna whispered, her large eyes fixed on the distant purple glow. "Oliver, you go first and check if the floor is safe. Don't go too far! Beatrice, you stay close to me and use your light." They entered the cave. Oliver darted ahead, testing every stone, while Beatrice pulsed her golden light, making the entire tunnel glow like sunshine. The purple light grew brighter and warmer. Then they saw it. "Look!" Luna exclaimed. The cave floor was covered in smooth, glittering purple crystals! But they were all messy, mixed with grey dust and sharp stones. The friends looked at the messy crystal garden. "We can make it beautiful," Luna said decisively. They got to work. Oliver used his super speed to sweep away all the dust and grey stones. Beatrice flew slowly, using her large, gentle eyes and bright golden light to spot every sharp rock, making sure the floor was safe and soft. Luna carefully picked up the largest, smoothest purple crystals and arranged them into beautiful patterns. Oliver then sprinkled his soft dandelion fluff between the crystals, making the whole floor look and feel like a cozy violet cloud. When they were finished, the Crystal Cave wasn't just glowing purple; it was glowing golden-purple. It was warm, soft, and perfect. They all sat together on the fuzzy fluff, drinking sweet mountain berry nectar and admiring their work. "This is the best secret cave ever," Oliver declared, bouncing on a particularly soft spot. Luna smiled, her moon-eyes bright. She had found a mystery, but together, they had created a magical home. And she knew that the secret to the perfect adventure was making new friends. title: The Windy Meadow Worry
text: Chapter 1: The Windy Meadow Worry The Sky-Blue Meadow was a happy place, filled with whispering grass and flowers that giggled when the wind tickled them. Here lived Barnaby, a tiny, bright green lizard with large, curious eyes. Barnaby loved observing things, especially the sky. One morning, Barnaby was worried. The wind, usually gentle, was huffing and puffing too hard. A large, fluffy white cloud—the one that always gave the meadow its soft, morning shade—had floated too low and got stuck! It was tangled in the branches of the Great Whispering Willow on the hill. "Oh dear," Barnaby squeaked, looking up. The willow tree looked sad, and the cloud looked squished. "If the cloud stays stuck, it might pour rain all day, or worse, lose all its fluff! I need to help it." But Barnaby was small and could not fly. He needed a team. Chapter 2: The Soft and Sticky Solution Barnaby scuttled fast, his tail a little blur, to find someone who wasn't afraid of sticky situations or small spaces. He needed Gemma. Gemma was a giant orange land snail, slow but incredibly strong. Her shell was smooth and painted with swirls that looked like sunset colors. She always had a small collection of shiny pebbles and interesting leaves, which she carried like treasures. Barnaby found Gemma resting near the cool moss stream. "Gemma! The fluffy morning cloud is stuck in the Whispering Willow!" Barnaby puffed. "We need to get it down safely, and I need something soft to cushion it. You know all the softest spots!" Gemma blinked slowly. "A cloud? That is a sticky situation indeed," she said with her deep, calm voice. Gemma thought carefully. "For something so light and fluffy, we need the softest thing. I know where the finest silk spiderweb is, and if you help me carry a few large, sticky dandelion leaves, they can catch anything!" Together, Gemma and Barnaby began their slow but steady journey, collecting sticky dandelion leaves along the way. Chapter 3: The Slow and The Steady They had the sticky leaves and the strength, but they still needed height. The stuck cloud was very high, too high for Barnaby to reach and too high for Gemma to glide. "We need someone very tall, but also very slow," Gemma noted, as they approached the base of the Great Whispering Willow. The tree looked even bigger up close. Just then, they saw a very large shadow. It was Pip. Pip was a giant, fuzzy blue creature. He was very slow, but he was the tallest and strongest friend in the entire meadow. His long, thick blue arms were strong enough to lift rocks, and his fuzzy blue fingers could gently hold a butterfly. Pip always smiled, even if his smiles were very big and took a long time. "Did I hear... sticky situations?" Pip asked slowly, bending down from his incredible height. "Pip! The soft cloud is stuck!" Barnaby explained. "We have these sticky dandelion leaves, but we need you to lift Gemma and Barnaby all the way up to the cloud! Then Gemma can catch it with the leaves." Pip smiled the biggest, slowest smile. "My strong arms love to help," he said. "Climb on my fuzzy shoulders Chapter 4: The Fluffy Fight They were at the top of the willow! Pip was tall, so tall that his fuzzy blue ears were almost touching the stuck cloud. High above, the tangled cloud was trembling in the fierce wind. "Hold tight!" Barnaby squeaked, balancing on Gemma’s swirling shell. Pip lifted them even higher. Gemma got ready. She had arranged the sticky dandelion leaves like a very soft, super-sticky blanket, holding them gently with her strong foot. Barnaby secured the finest spiderweb silk from Gemma’s collection to make sure they had a safety net. Then, Pip used his very large, very slow fingers to gently nudge the squished cloud, untangling it from the stubborn branches. Whoosh! The huffing wind tried to grab the cloud! But Gemma was ready. With perfect, slow timing, she caught the large, fluffy white cloud right in the middle of the sticky dandelion blanket. Chapter 5: The Sweetest Float As the sun began to set, painting the Sky-Blue Meadow with deep purple and warm orange light, the huffing wind became gentle again. It was time for the cloud to float freely. Barnaby, Gemma, and Pip all gathered on the hill near the Whispering Willow. The cloud was now clean and untangled, floating in its sticky dandelion blanket. It looked even softer and happier than before. It wasn’t a sad, squished cloud anymore; it was a special, friend-rescued cloud. "It's time to let it go," Barnaby whispered, his green eyes reflecting the sunset colors. Pip used his massive blue hands to lift the entire sticky dandelion blanket high, high into the soft breeze. Gemma slid slow and smooth, gently pushing the cloud from its cozy sticky bed. The cloud lifted slowly, floating over the meadow and giggling as the soft breeze tickled it. It was the best cloud ever, especially with three friends sharing the sunset. Pip looked at Barnaby and Gemma and smiled the biggest, slowest smile. He realized that the best part of his adventure wasn't the cozy new home; it was the friends who helped him build it. And even though they were all very different, together, they were a perfect team. title: A Doll or Four Books
text: This is a story from the early 1990s. H.N. Singh was thinking of taking his children to a mela in the local bazaar after his daily shift. He worked as a security guard in a tiny coal-mining town called Singrauli in Madhya Pradesh. Once a year, the temple premises in Singrauli would transform into a mela ground. The fair brought great splendour to this otherwise slow and colourless town in Koyalanchal.* Since the town had many open coal mines, there would be loud blasts and earthquake-like tremors every now and then. As a result, the town was not permitted to have big halls or auditoriums. *A region with an abundant supply of koyala or coal. H.N. Singh had come to Singrauli from Bhojpur in Bihar, with his wife Lakhpati Devi and two children, Rekha and Akash. H.N. Singh was an educated man. After completing his matriculation from his village in Bihar, he was recruited as a soldier in the Bangladesh Liberation War, 1971. While he served in the Bihar regiment, he studied further through correspondence (Intermediate, BA and MA ‘previous’). After retiring in 1989, he joined the colliery in Singrauli. He was the first man from his family to ever step into a school. Neither women of his generation nor men of previous generations had ever been to a school. By enrolling Rekha in a school, H.N. Singh nurtured the first lettered woman in his family. Lakhpati Devi had spent most of her life in a village in Bhojpur. She was so used to her life there that life in the colliery made her unhappy. When H.N. Singh returned from his shift, Rekha was busy with her homework. “Chaliye, let us go to the fair today,” he told Rekha. Rekha was a serious child. Was it because of her mother’s sadness? Who knows? Rekha immediately changed into her frock and combed her hair. H.N. Singh washed Akash’s hands and face and got him ready. Singrauli did not have any public transport. The working classes either walked or used their own bicycles. H.N. Singh rode a bicycle to his workplace. He often took his children for bicycle rides—Rekha on the back carrier and Akash in the front basket. But it would be difficult to ride a bicycle with two children and Lakhpati Devi. Thus, they decided to walk to the mela. In this colliery town of independent India, the workers and the officers were assigned separate housing colonies. H.N. Singh lived in the colony meant for workers. It was named ‘lower class housing colony’. “Who named it so?” Rekha often wondered. At the school, the officers’ children called the workers’ children ‘neeche colonywale’. The neeche colony was set up on the edge of the town in a low-lying area. The officers’ colony, or ‘upar colony’, stood on a hilltop. In the early 1990s, Singrauli did not have any private schools. The children of workers and officers studied in the same school: Kendriya Vidyalaya, Singrauli. On their way to school, children from the ‘neeche colony’ saw the world of the ‘upar colony’. They compared life in these colonies and thought of education as a way to overcome the difference. Today, H.N. Singh’s family started their walk to the mela ground from their home in the ‘neeche colony’. On their way, they came across a roundabout or traffic island. It divided the road into two—one leading to the market and the other to the colliery headquarters. There used to be a library in the headquarters for its employees. It did not have any books for children. Singrauli did not have any public library back then. Neither did the bookshops sell anything other than school textbooks. Even the book stalls at Singrauli railway station did not have any books apart from pulp fiction—of which H.N. Singh did not approve. Only a few stationery shops sold copies of Champak, a children’s magazine. Rekha longed to read. She used to devour her Hindi textbooks within a week of getting them. H.N. Singh had started buying Champak for her. She relished the colourful pictures and stories in the magazine. Whenever H.N. Singh planned to go to the market, Rekha insisted on coming along, just to check whether a new edition of Champak was out. Having walked for nearly half an hour, they reached a steep climb. Climbing up the road, Rekha got thirsty. “We are almost there. A few more steps to go,” H.N. Singh told Rekha. “We will have a mosambi juice before entering the fair.” Rekha always wondered why Papa only bought them juice and never allowed them to eat chaat. The juice quenched Rekha’s thirst. Suddenly, she noticed her friend and neighbour Saroj on the mela grounds. Saroj was from Balia in eastern Uttar Pradesh. Rekha’s eyes followed Saroj. As they entered the grounds, stalls selling toys welcomed them. A few steps later, they were in the midst of big and small sweet stalls. There was imarti, jalebi and gud kathi. Another stall was selling tiny toy kitchen sets made of steel! Rekha’s eyes were still following Saroj. She noticed that Saroj was carrying something in her hands from a shop on the other side of the ground. Their eyes met. With great excitement, Saroj showed Rekha her new possession: a beautiful doll! They reached the stall with the dolls. “May I also buy a doll like Saroj’s?” asked Rekha. “We can then play ghar-ghar together.” Rekha looked at her father with eager eyes. “Let us first see what there is at all the stalls. Then buy what you like!” H.N. Singh promised Rekha. For H.N. Singh, Rekha’s words brought to life images from his village. Of his sisters and nieces who remained unlettered, always working in their homes, absorbed in domestic chores and taking care of the young. H.N. Singh took a deep breath and asked Rekha, “We can buy four Champaks for the price of one doll. What would you like? A doll or four books?” Rekha thought for a moment and answered with her usual seriousness, “I want four books.”

title: Vintage Wisdom: Hand-Me-Down Histories
text: The attic of the old farmhouse was a kingdom of dust and shadows, smelling of cedar, aged parchment, and the faint, spicy scent of the pipe tobacco Grandpa had given up years ago. Vikram, who was twelve and possessed a restlessness that usually resulted in torn jeans, pushed aside a stack of newspapers from the 1970s. Behind them, tucked under a heavy woolen blanket, sat the "Vault." It wasn't a modern safe, but a massive, iron-bound trunk made of dark oak, The key felt icy and heavy. When she slid it into the lock, it didn't just turn; it gave a deep, mechanical thunk that vibrated through the floorboards. Together, they heaved the lid open. It was so heavy it felt as though they were lifting the weight of a whole century. Vikram’s eyes went wide. He had expected gold coins or perhaps a stack of secret cash. Instead, they found a mountain of envelopes with foreign stamps, strange wooden carvings that looked like ancient idols, a compass that spun wildly, and a thick, leather-bound journal. reinforced with brass rivets that looked like they had seen the bottom of the ocean. For years, Grandpa had steered them away from it with a playful wag of his finger. "That’s where the boring stuff lives, kids," he’d say. "Tax returns, mismatched socks, and perhaps a very grumpy ghost." But today, on Grandpa’s eightieth birthday, the air felt different. After the cake was eaten and the candles blown out, he had beckoned them into the hallway and pressed a small, tarnished silver key into Heer’s palm. You're both old enough to handle the truth now," he whispered, his voice like rustling leaves. "Go on. Unlock the vault. But remember—once a story is out, it belongs to the world." Heer, who was ten and far more methodical than her brother, knelt before the trunk. day sandstorm in the Sahara and mapped uncharted islands in the South Pacific. Heer found a small velvet box tucked into a side pocket. Inside wasn't a diamond, but a simple, perfectly smooth river stone. Attached was a handwritten note: 'The most valuable thing I ever found. It reminded me to stay grounded so I could eventually fly home to see the faces I hadn't met yet.' "He was talking about us," Heer whispered, her eyes shimmering. "He kept this so he could find his way back to his family." "Look at this!" Heer gasped, pulling out a sepia-toned photograph. It showed a young man with a daring grin, wearing a grease-stained pilot’s jumpsuit and standing next to a biplane that looked like it was held together by sheer willpower. "Vikram, look at the eyes. That’s Grandpa!" Vikram grabbed the journal, its leather cracked and smelling of old rain. He flipped to a page marked with a dried fern. He began to read aloud: 'October 14, 1974: The engine died over the rainforest canopy. The radio is dead. The only way out is to trade my silver wristwatch for a dugout canoe and follow the river south. I hope I remember the way home.' For the next three hours, the dusty attic ceased to exist. Through the items in the vault, the siblings were transported across the globe. They discovered that their quiet, lawn-mowing grandfather—the man who complained about the price of eggs— had once been a freelance cartographer who had survived a three- " The stairs creaked—a rhythmic thump-tap, thump-tap. Grandpa stood in the doorway, leaning mahogany cane, his silhouette framed by the golden afternoon sun. He looked at the mess of maps and medals scattered around his grandchildren. "Find any tax returns?" he asked, his eyes twinkling behind his spectacles. Vikram looked at the journal, then up at the man he thought he knew. "Grandpa, you were... you were like an explorer. Why didn't you tell us?" Grandpa sat down on an old crate, gesturing for them to join him. The stairs creaked—a rhythmic thump-tap, thump-tap. Grandpa stood in the doorway, leaning on his mahogany cane, his silhouette framed by the golden afternoon sun. He looked at the mess of maps and medals scattered around his grandchildren. "Find any tax returns?" he asked, his eyes twinkling behind his spectacles. Vikram looked at the journal, then up at the man he thought he knew. "Grandpa, you were... you were like an explorer. Why didn't you tell us?" Grandpa sat down on an old crate, gesturing for them to join him. "Because a story needs the right audience to stay alive. If I told you when you were six, you’d have thought it was a fairy tale. But now? Now you know that the world is much bigger than this farm." Heer crawled over and placed the river stone back in his hand. "Is there more?" "Because a story needs the right audience to stay alive. If I told you when you were six, you’d have thought it was a fairy tale. But now? Now you know that the world is much bigger than this farm.". "But let’s start with the one the journal missed. Let me tell you about the time I had to outrun a monsoon in a rickshaw with nothing but a map of the stars and a bag of oranges..." As he began to speak, Vikram and Heer realized that the "Vault" wasn't just the trunk. It was the man himself. And for the first time, they weren't just listening to a story—they were becoming the keepers of his legacy.

title: Detective Eve Dallas and The Stolen Legacy (PART 1)
text: Morning light spilled into the Detective Bureau as Eve sifted through an old case file. Her office phone rang again—hers was always the busiest room, the calls never stopping. She answered, and a trembling voice spoke. It was the curator of the city’s famous museum. “Detective… the Valerious Chain, once worn by Queen Malvoria, is gone. And Augustus, our night guard, has vanished too. Please, we need your help.” Eve’s eyes sharpened. “I’m on my way,” she said, rising from her desk. Another mystery had begun. Eve arrived at the museum, her instincts immediately alert. Something felt wrong—the curator, Cyprian Vane, seemed far too calm for a man who had just lost a priceless artifact. His composure was unnatural, almost rehearsed. She opened her notebook, carefully jotting down the names of both the curator and the missing guard, Augustus, along with every detail that struck her as unusual. Then she began her sweep of the museum. Suspicion grew with each step. Using her magnifying glass, she examined corners and displays until a clue revealed itself: a single strand of burnt sienna hair. She sealed it and sent it to the forensic department. Nearby, she discovered the broken siren control system—smashed with a stone. That too was bagged and dispatched for analysis. The museum was quiet, but Eve knew the silence was deceptive. The pieces of the puzzle were already beginning to surface. Eve closed her notebook and turned her sharp gaze on Cyprian Vane. The curator stood stiffly by the shattered siren panel, his hands clasped too tightly, his expression unnervingly calm. “Mr. Vane,” she began, her voice steady but edged with suspicion, “you don’t seem nearly as concerned as one would expect. A priceless artifact is missing, and your guard has vanished. Why is that?” Cyprian’s lips twitched into a faint smile. “Detective, panic never solved anything. I prefer to remain composed.” Eve leaned forward, her eyes narrowing. “Composed, or rehearsed? Tell me—when was the last time you saw Augustus?” The curator hesitated, just long enough to betray unease. “Yesterday evening. He checked in before his shift. After that… nothing.” She scribbled a note, her pen scratching across the page. “And the siren system? Broken with a stone. That doesn’t happen without someone inside knowing where to strike.” Cyprian’s jaw tightened. “Are you suggesting I had something to do with this?” Eve snapped her notebook shut. “I’m suggesting you know more than you’re admitting. And until I have answers, Mr. Vane, you’re as much a suspect as anyone else.” The silence that followed was heavy, the curator’s calm mask beginning to crack. Just as Eve’s questions began to press harder, her phone rang sharply, cutting through the tense silence. She glanced at the screen—it was the Bureau. “Detective,” the voice on the line said, “we need you back at the office. Your payment for the last case is ready for collection.” Eve closed her notebook with a snap. “Mr. Vane, we’ll continue this tomorrow,” she said firmly, her eyes lingering on the curator’s uneasy expression. Without another word, she turned and strode out of the museum. The mystery of the Valerious Chain would have to wait—but she knew the clues she had already gathered were only the beginning. The following morning, Eve gathered all the museum staff in a line. Her eyes scanned each face, searching for cracks in their composure. The morning guard stepped forward. “Detective… the building across from the museum belongs to me. Last night, I saw a dark figure slip out of the museum. I thought it was Augustus—he has that habit of drinking milk tea during his shift.” Eve noted it down quickly. “Who was the first to notice something unusual?” she asked. The janitor, still drowsy, raised her hand. “I opened the museum with my keys. There’s another spare key with the curator. Normally, Augustus greets me every morning, but yesterday he wasn’t there. When I called, no one answered. I assumed he’d gone to the milk tea shop, as usual. So I started cleaning… and that’s when I saw the chain was gone.” Eve’s pen scratched across the page. Another lead. She left the museum and headed straight to the milk tea shop. The shopkeeper shook his head. “Augustus loved his milk tea. He came every night without fail. But yesterday… he didn’t show. I thought maybe he wasn’t feeling well, so I didn’t think much of it.” Eve closed her notebook. Augustus’s absence was no coincidence. The threads of the mystery were tightening, and she knew the next step would bring her closer to the truth. The next day, Eve followed a trail of reports that led her deep into the dense forest behind the curator’s estate. The air was heavy, the silence broken only by the rustle of leaves. There, half-conscious and battered, lay Augustus. His uniform was torn, and a faint burn mark lingered on his neck. Without hesitation, Eve called for an ambulance. Augustus was rushed to the hospital, where Eve stood at his bedside as he slowly regained strength. “Detective…” his voice was weak but urgent. “I didn’t disappear on purpose. That night, I was about to head out for my milk tea when I saw the curator—Cyprian Vane—walking near the museum. I asked him what he was doing there so late.” Augustus swallowed hard, his eyes clouded with fear. “He didn’t answer. Instead, he pulled out a taser. The shock dropped me instantly. When I woke up… I was here, in the forest, abandoned.” Eve’s jaw tightened. The pieces were falling into place. The curator’s calm demeanor, the spare key, the broken siren—all of it pointed toward Cyprian Vane. She closed her notebook with deliberate care. “Rest, Augustus. You’ve given me exactly what I needed. Tomorrow, the curator will have no place left to hide.” The night was heavy with silence when Eve returned to the Bureau, her mind replaying Augustus’s testimony. The forest, the taser, the curator—it all pointed to one man. Cyprian Vane. By dawn, she was back at the museum. Cyprian stood in the grand hall, his calm mask firmly in place. But Eve's eyes were sharper now, armed with evidence. “Mr. Vane,” she said, her voice cutting through the air, “Augustus is alive. He told me everything. You were seen near the museum, and you attacked him. Care to explain why the city’s most prized artifact vanished the same night?” For the first time, Cyprian faltered. His composure cracked, a bead of sweat tracing his temple. “Detective… you don’t understand. The Valerious Chain isn’t just treasure—it’s power. Queen Malvoria’s legacy… it was never meant to be displayed. It was meant to be controlled.” Eve stepped closer, her notebook snapping shut like a verdict. “And you thought you’d be the one to control it.” The curator’s silence was answer enough. Guards moved in, the echo of their boots filling the hall. Cyprian Vane was taken into custody, his calm demeanor finally shattered. Outside, the city stirred awake, unaware of how close its history had come to being stolen forever. Eve watched the sunrise from the museum steps, her thoughts already drifting to the next mystery. For her, the work never ended—but this case would be remembered.
author: Hemashri Saanvi🌸🌸

title: Detective Eve Dallas and the Stolen Legacy (PART 2)
text: Detective Eve had solved the initial puzzle, recovering the stolen Valerious Chain and exposing the curator’s role. Yet, as she sat at her desk, pieces of the mystery still haunted her. Why would the curator steal the chain? Who used the spare key? Who else was there that night? Each of these questions swirled in her mind and refused to settle, making her realize the case wasn't truly over. Then, just as she was fitting those pieces together, her phone ringed with a chilling message: “The legacy isn’t yours to protect. Stop digging, or you’ll end up like Augustus.” In that moment, Eve understood that the curator was only the beginning. There was a deeper conspiracy, and the real mastermind had just revealed themselves. The stolen legacy was far from reclaimed—the real danger was just beginning. After receiving the message Eve starts compiling things together, she starts to wonder: Was the curator acting alone? Or was someone bullying or blackmailing him into stealing the chain in the first place? That question opens up a whole new layer of the mystery and gives Eve a new lead to chase down. The next morning, Detective Eve returned to the museum archives. Though the Valerious Chain had been recovered, her mind was restless. Questions echoed like whispers: Who used the spare key? Who else was there that night? Was the curator acting alone—or was someone bullying or blackmailing him into the theft? She sifted through the curator’s files, searching for signs of pressure—letters, debts, threats. Nothing concrete appeared, but the silence itself felt suspicious. Then, her phone buzzed. A new message lit up the screen: “The legacy isn’t yours to protect. Stop digging, or you’ll end up like Augustus.I am warning you again ” Eve’s pulse quickened. The curator’s betrayal was only the surface. Someone else had orchestrated the theft, someone powerful enough to manipulate him—and bold enough to warn her directly. The stolen legacy was not about greed alone. It was about control, secrets, and a force determined to keep history buried. And Eve knew: the real investigation had just begun. The next day, Eve couldn’t shake the questions that haunted her Something clicked in her mind. She needed answers straight from the source. Eve walked into the jail, the heavy doors clanging shut behind her. Cyprian Vane, the disgraced curator, sat across from her, his calm mask now replaced with weary resignation. “Tell me,” Eve pressed, “how did your museum even get the Valerious Chain?” Cyprian’s eyes flickered, then he sighed. “It wasn’t the museum’s to begin with. It’s… family. A hereditary possession. Passed down through generations in my bloodline. The museum only displayed it because I allowed it.” Eve leaned back, stunned. The chain wasn’t just an artifact—it was a legacy tied to the curator’s family. That meant his theft wasn’t simply greed. It was personal. And suddenly, the anonymous message on her phone made more sense. Someone wanted that legacy erased, someone powerful enough to manipulate the curator and threaten her. The stolen legacy was no longer just about history—it was about family, inheritance, and a secret war that had been brewing for generations. Eve gathered the curator’s cousins in the grand study, each of them eyeing the others warily. At the center of her focus was the police officer among them—her prime suspect. “Let’s make this simple,” Eve said calmly. “One of you took the spare key, and one of you manipulated the curator into stealing the chain. We’re done with secrets.” Under the weight of her interrogation, the police officer cousin finally crumbled. He confessed that he’d taken the key during the birthday gathering, hoping to keep the chain locked away in the family’s private museum. He had pressured the curator out of a misguided sense of family pride. In the end, Eve realized that the stolen legacy was never just about the chain itself. It was about the hidden battles within families, the lengths people go to protect their heritage, and the costs of keeping secrets. As the case closed, the Valerious Chain was returned to the museum for all to see, and Eve walked away with a deeper understanding of the delicate threads that weave history and family together. When Eve left the room, the confession of the police officer cousin felt like a resolution, but not a conclusion. Something still felt off, like a piece of the puzzle was missing or a shadow lingered in the background. Eve thought and thought, her instincts refusing to rest. As she turned each detail over in her mind, she realized that perhaps the legacy of the chain wasn’t just about the family feud or the cousins’ rivalry—there was still a deeper motive, a hidden history that remained out of sight. But for now, the chain was where it belonged, on display for all to see. Eve understood that not every mystery ends with every question answered, and sometimes the unknown is simply part of the story.
author: Hemashri Saanvi🌸🌸

title: The Whispering Banyan
text: In the heart of a small Indian town stood a banyan tree so old that its roots seemed to touch the memories of centuries. People said it whispered secrets when the wind passed through its leaves. Most dismissed it as folklore, but Hemashri, a curious seventh‑class girl, believed there was truth hidden in those whispers. One evening, while sketching the tree’s tangled roots, she noticed strange carvings etched deep into the bark—symbols that looked like codes. Her love for social studies sparked curiosity: were these marks part of history? Soon, the town faced a heated dispute. Developers wanted to cut down the banyan to build a shopping complex. Some villagers agreed, hoping for jobs and progress, while others mourned the idea of losing their heritage. The banyan stood at the center of conflict, silent yet powerful. Hemashri couldn’t ignore the carvings. She spent nights decoding them, using her creativity from painting and discipline from dance to stay patient. Slowly, the message revealed itself: the banyan had once been the gathering place where village elders met to deliver justice. It was not just a tree—it was a living monument of dharma. Armed with this discovery, Hemashri presented her findings to the town council. She spoke with clarity and courage, recalling Krishna’s teachings about duty and righteousness. “This tree is not an obstacle to progress,” she said. “It is the foundation of our identity. We must build around it, not over it.” Her words carried weight. The council agreed to preserve the banyan, designing the new complex so the tree remained at its heart. The town celebrated, realizing that true progress honors the past while embracing the future. As Hemashri stood beneath the banyan’s whispering leaves, she felt a quiet strength. Protecting heritage, serving society, and standing for justice—this was the path she wanted to walk. Her dream of becoming an IAS officer no longer felt distant; it felt like destiny.
author: Hemashri Saanvi🌸🌸
illustrator: Joanna Davala; Manasi Parikh; Ridhi Arora; Svar Shroff; Vusi  Malindi

title: Mumma, tell me a story
text: Come on, Lari! let me tuck you in bed now, Mumma pleaded. No, I want to play some more, Lari said. Let me tuck you in bed, then I will tell you a story, Mumma said. Y A Y! Lari thought, she loved when Mumma told her a story. After she brushed and washed, Lari cuddled up in her blanket, waiting for Mumma to come. Come on Lari, I am here, Mumma called out.
